## Abstract

The invention relates to the technical field of integrated optoelectronics, in particular to a low-loss lithium niobate waveguide and a preparation method thereof. The low-loss lithium niobate waveguide comprises a substrate layer, an oxygen buried layer, a lithium niobate waveguide layer, a coating layer and an upper cladding layer which are sequentially arranged from bottom to top, wherein the coating layer is coated on the lithium niobate waveguide layer, and the upper cladding layer is coated on the coating layer; the refractive index of the cladding layer is equal to that of the lithium niobate waveguide layer; the low-loss lithium niobate waveguide takes an LNOI basic structure formed by a substrate layer, an oxygen-buried layer and a lithium niobate waveguide layer as a platform, and a coating layer is deposited on the lithium niobate waveguide layer, so that LiNbO can be effectively filled and repaired 3 Undulation of waveguide surface and side wall, core layer LiNbO 3 The lattice structure is not damaged, and meanwhile, the refractive index of the coating layer is designed to be equal to that of the lithium niobate waveguide layer and the thickness of the coating layer is controlled, so that most of light can be ensured to be LiNbO 3 The normal propagation in the waveguide significantly reduces the scattering loss due to the roughness of the waveguide surface and sidewalls.

## Description

Low-loss lithium niobate waveguide and preparation method thereof 

Technical Field

The invention relates to the technical field of integrated optoelectronics, in particular to a low-loss lithium niobate waveguide and a preparation method thereof.

 

Lithium niobate LiNbO 3 The optical waveguide medium is a commonly used optical waveguide medium in integrated optics, has a very high electro-optic coefficient, is a very good nonlinear material, can perform frequency conversion with high efficiency, and therefore, a modulator based on the optical waveguide medium is widely applied. In recent years, smart Cut technology has been used as a method for producing high-refractivity single-crystal LiNbO 3 The mainstream scheme of the film utilizes He ion implantation technology and wafer bonding technology to enable the single-crystal LiNbO 3 Thin films and SiO deposited on LN substrates 2 Layer combination to prepare LiNbO sequentially from top to bottom 3 Thin film layer, siO 2 Layer, LNOI base structure of LNOI substrate. At the same time, LNOI has a high refractive index difference that can severely limit the propagation of the beam in the waveguide, and therefore becomes an ideal integrated optical platform with much interest following SOI.

At present, optical devices such as a multimode interference coupler, a Mach-Zehnder modulator, a micro-ring resonator, a Y-type beam splitter and the like are successfully manufactured on an LNOI; with thin film LiNbO 3 The preparation process is mature and complete day by day, and the important application value of manufacturing optical devices on the LNOI is more and more prominent.

The greatest advantage of LNOI is the ability to achieve high index-contrast waveguide structures like SOI by etching, however, the etching process to obtain low-loss LN waveguides has long been a challenge to the scientific community. LN materials are inherently hard and chemically inert, and therefore have significant difficulties with either physical or chemical etching. When RIE is adopted to etch lithium niobate, liF precipitates can be generated in a chemical etching part containing F-based gas, lithium niobate can be redeposited in a physical bombardment part, and the lithium niobate waveguide is rough no matter which deposition is dominant. In addition, pattern transfer from the hard mask may also exacerbate the roughness of the lithium niobate waveguide. One typically optimizes the roughness of the lithium niobate waveguide by adjusting the etching conditions (e.g., pressure, gas flow, etc.) to reduce deposition during etching. However, there is a limit to this single approach and the process window is small. As wafer size increases, uniformity requirements become higher and process window problems become increasingly severe.

 

Disclosure of Invention

The invention provides a low-loss lithium niobate waveguide and a preparation method thereof, which are used for solving the technical problems of the existing lithium niobate waveguide 3 Undulation of waveguide surface and side wall, core layer LiNbO 3 The lattice structure is not damaged, and meanwhile, the refractive index of the coating layer is designed to be equal to that of the lithium niobate waveguide layer and the thickness of the coating layer is controlled, so that most of light can be ensured to be LiNbO 3 Normal propagation in the waveguide, significantly reduces scattering losses due to surface roughness.

According to a first aspect of the present invention, the present invention provides a low-loss lithium niobate waveguide, comprising, sequentially from bottom to top:

a substrate layer;

an oxygen burying layer;

a lithium niobate waveguide layer;

the coating layer is coated on the lithium niobate waveguide layer; the refractive index of the cladding layer is equal to that of the lithium niobate waveguide layer;

and the upper cladding layer is coated on the cladding layer.

Further, the refractive index of the clad is 2.15-2.25.

Further, the thickness of the coating layer is 10nm-100nm; the cladding layer has less than 10% influence on the optical field energy distributed in the lithium niobate waveguide layer.

Further, the cladding layer comprises silicon oxide or silicon oxynitride; and/or the oxygen burying layer is a silicon dioxide layer; and/or the upper cladding is silica or air.

Further, the cladding layer is coated on the upper surface and the side wall of the lithium niobate waveguide layer.

Further, the waveguide of the lithium niobate waveguide layer is a ridge waveguide or a strip waveguide; and/or the waveguide of the lithium niobate waveguide layer is a single-mode waveguide, a multi-mode waveguide or a periodic structure waveguide; and/or the thickness of the lithium niobate waveguide layer is 200nm-700nm.

According to a second aspect of the present invention, the present invention further provides a method for preparing the above-mentioned low-loss lithium niobate waveguide, comprising the following steps:

taking an LNOI material as a starting material; the LNOI material comprises a substrate layer, an oxygen-buried layer and a lithium niobate thin film layer which are sequentially arranged from bottom to top;

depositing a hard mask layer on the lithium niobate thin film layer;

spin-coating photoresist on the surface of the hard mask layer and completing photoetching;

completing hard mask etching by adopting a dry etching process, and then completing the forming etching of the lithium niobate thin film layer to form a lithium niobate waveguide layer;

removing the hard mask layer and the residues;

depositing a coating layer on the surface of the lithium niobate waveguide layer; the refractive index of the cladding layer is equal to that of the lithium niobate waveguide layer;

carrying out thermal annealing treatment on the lithium niobate waveguide layer deposited with the coating layer;

depositing an upper cladding layer on the cladding layer after the annealing is completed.

Further, the deposition mode of the coating layer on the surface of the lithium niobate waveguide layer comprises LPCVD, PECVD, ALD or PVD; and/or the deposition mode for depositing the hard mask layer on the lithium niobate thin film layer comprises LPCVD, PECVD or PVD.

Further, the interface annealing temperature of the thermal annealing treatment is 300-800 ℃.

Further, the hard mask layer is removed by adopting a wet etching process.

The low-loss lithium niobate waveguide provided by the invention is respectively a substrate layer, an oxygen buried layer, a lithium niobate waveguide layer, a coating layer and an upper cladding layer from bottom to top, and the coating layer is deposited on the lithium niobate waveguide layerLayer capable of effectively filling and repairing LiNbO 3 Undulation of waveguide surface and side wall, core layer LiNbO 3 The lattice structure is not damaged, and the refractive index of the coating layer is designed to be equal to that of the lithium niobate waveguide layer, so that most of light can be ensured to be still LiNbO 3 Normal propagation in the waveguide, significantly reduces scattering losses due to surface roughness.

 

Drawings

In order to more clearly illustrate the technical solutions of the present invention or the prior art, the drawings needed for the description of the embodiments or the prior art will be briefly described below, and it is obvious that the drawings in the following description are some embodiments of the present invention, and those skilled in the art can also obtain other drawings according to the drawings without creative efforts.

FIG. 4 is a schematic structural diagram of a lithium niobate thin film layer after a metal mask layer is sputter deposited thereon in an embodiment of the present invention;

FIG. 5 is a schematic diagram of a lithium niobate waveguide structure after completion of photolithography and dry etching in an embodiment of the present invention;

FIG. 6 is a schematic structural diagram of a lithium niobate waveguide after deposition of a SiN cladding layer in an embodiment of the present invention;

FIG. 7 is a diagram showing the simulation result of the optical field mode performed by bringing a low-loss lithium niobate waveguide into COMSOL according to the present invention; fig. 7 (a) shows a simulation result graph of the SiN clad layer 4 at 0nm, fig. 7 (b) shows a simulation result graph of the SiN clad layer 4 at 40nm, fig. 7 (c) shows a simulation result graph of the SiN clad layer 4 at 100nm, and fig. 7 (d) shows a relationship graph of the optical field energy in the lithium niobate waveguide according to the present invention, though the SiN thickness changes.

Detailed Description

In order to make the objects, technical solutions and advantages of the present invention clearer, the technical solutions of the present invention will be clearly and completely described below with reference to the accompanying drawings, and it is obvious that the described embodiments are some, but not all embodiments of the present invention. All other embodiments, which can be derived by a person skilled in the art from the embodiments given herein without making any creative effort, shall fall within the protection scope of the present invention.

According to some embodiments of the present invention, the present invention provides a low-loss lithium niobate waveguide, as shown in fig. 1, whose basic structures are, from bottom to top, a substrate layer 1, a buried oxide layer 2, a lithium niobate waveguide layer 3, a cladding layer 4 and an upper cladding layer 5, respectively. The cladding layer 4 is coated on the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3. The upper cladding layer 5 covers the cladding layer 4. The refractive index of the cladding layer 4 is equal to the refractive index of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3.

In the above embodiments, a low-loss lithium niobate waveguide is, from bottom to top, a substrate layer 1, an oxygen buried layer 2, a lithium niobate waveguide layer 3, a cladding layer 4 and an upper cladding layer 5, where the lithium niobate waveguide deposits the cladding layer 4 on the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3, and can effectively fill and repair LiNbO 3 Undulation of waveguide surface and side wall, core layer LiNbO 3 The lattice structure is not damaged, the refractive index of the coating layer 4 is designed to be equal to that of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3, and the thickness of the coating layer 4 is controlled to ensure that most of light is LiNbO 3 Normally propagated in the waveguide, and the scattering loss caused by the surface and the roughness is obviously reduced.

According to some embodiments of the invention, the substrate layer 1 has a thickness of 400 μm to 600 μm, preferably 500 μm; the thickness of the oxygen burying layer 2 is 2-5 μm.

According to some embodiments of the present invention, the cladding layer 4 has a refractive index of 2.15 to 2.25. In some embodiments, the cladding layer 4 has a refractive index of 2.2.

In the above embodiment, the refractive index of the clad layer 4 is matched with that of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3 by defining the refractive index to be 2.15 to 2.25To ensure that most of the light is still LiNbO 3 Normally propagated in the waveguide, and the scattering loss caused by surface roughness is obviously reduced.

According to some embodiments of the invention, the thickness of the cladding layer 4 is in the range of 10nm to 100nm. The cladding layer 4 has less than 10% effect on the optical field energy distributed in the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3.

In the above embodiment, the thickness of the cladding layer 4 is limited to a reasonable range, so that it is ensured that light is in LiNbO 3 Transmission within the waveguide is substantially unaffected while sidewall scattering losses are significantly reduced. If the thickness of the coating layer 4 is less than 10nm, the reduction of scattering loss is not significant, and if the thickness of the coating layer 4 is more than 100nm, the influence of light on LiNbO is generated 3 Transmission within a waveguide.

According to some embodiments of the present invention, the cladding layer 4 is silicon nitride or silicon oxynitride.

In the above embodiment, the cladding layer 4 is defined as silicon nitride or silicon oxynitride, and the refractive index can be controlled by changing the ratio of silicon elements, so that the refractive index of the cladding layer 4 matches with the refractive index of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3, thereby ensuring that most of light is still LiNbO 3 Normally propagated in the waveguide, and the scattering loss caused by surface roughness is obviously reduced.

According to some embodiments of the invention, the upper cladding 5 is silica or air.

In the above embodiment, the upper cladding 5 is transparent to the optical communication band, no extra optical loss is introduced in the modulator, and the upper cladding 5 is defined as silica or air, which can better achieve the above function.

According to some embodiments of the present invention, the thickness of the upper cladding layer 5 is 1 μm to 5 μm. In some embodiments, the upper cladding layer 5 has a thickness of 3 μm.

According to some embodiments of the invention, the buried oxide layer 2 is a silicon dioxide layer.

In the above embodiment, the buried oxide layer 2 plays a good role in the waveguide transmission process, so that the loss of the waveguide is greatly reduced, and the buried oxide layer 2 is limited to be a silicon dioxide layer, so that the above functions can be better realized.

According to some embodiments of the present invention, the cladding layer 4 is coated on the upper surface and the sidewall of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3.

In the above embodiment, the coating layer 4 is coated on the upper surface and the sidewall of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3, so that LiNbO can be effectively filled and repaired 3 Undulation of waveguide surface and side wall, core layer LiNbO 3 The lattice structure is not damaged, and the scattering loss caused by the roughness of the surface and the side wall of the waveguide can be effectively reduced.

According to some embodiments of the present invention, the waveguide of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3 is a ridge waveguide or a stripe waveguide; and/or the waveguide of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3 is a single-mode waveguide, a multi-mode waveguide or a periodic structure waveguide; and/or the width of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3 is 800nm-1000nm; the thickness of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3 is 200nm-700nm.

In the above embodiment, the width and the thickness of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3 are limited within reasonable ranges, which is beneficial to the transmission of light in the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3.

According to some embodiments of the present invention, the present invention further provides a method for preparing a low-loss lithium niobate waveguide, as shown in fig. 2, which is a schematic flow chart of the method for preparing a low-loss lithium niobate waveguide of the present invention, and the specific preparation method includes the following steps:

taking an LNOI material as a starting material; as shown in fig. 3, the LNOI material comprises a substrate layer 1, a buried oxide layer 2 and a lithium niobate thin film layer 6 which are arranged in sequence from bottom to top;

depositing a hard mask layer on the lithium niobate thin film layer 6;

spin-coating photoresist on the surface of the hard mask layer and completing photoetching;

the dry etching process is adopted to finish the hard mask etching, and then the forming etching of the lithium niobate thin film layer 6 is finished to form a lithium niobate waveguide layer 3;

removing the hard mask layer and the residues;

depositing a coating layer 4 on the surface of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3; the refractive index of the cladding layer 4 is equal to that of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3;

carrying out thermal annealing treatment on the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3 deposited with the coating layer 4;

an upper cladding layer 5 is deposited on the cladding layer 4 after completion of annealing.

In the above embodiment, the preparation method of the low-loss lithium niobate waveguide of the present invention is to use the LNOI material as the initial material, deposit the hard mask layer on the lithium niobate thin film layer 6 of the LNOI material, then spin-coat the photoresist on the surface of the hard mask layer and complete the photolithography, complete the etching of the hard mask layer by the dry etching process, then complete the shaping etching of the lithium niobate thin film layer 6, so as to form the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3; removing the hard mask layer and the residues, and removing impurities generated in the etching process to obtain the surface of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3 which is as smooth as possible; then a coating layer 4 is deposited on the surface of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3, and LiNbO can be effectively filled and repaired 3 Undulation of waveguide surface and side wall, core layer LiNbO 3 The lattice structure is not damaged, and simultaneously, the refractive index of the coating layer 4 is ensured to be equal to that of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3, so that most of light can be ensured to be still LiNbO 3 The scattering loss caused by surface roughness is obviously reduced when the optical waveguide is normally propagated in the waveguide. The lithium niobate waveguide layer 3 deposited with the coating layer 4 is subjected to thermal annealing treatment to eliminate defects and flatten the lithium niobate waveguide layer, and smooth treatment is realized to improve the quality of the film layer. And finally, depositing an upper cladding 5 on the annealed cladding 4 to further improve the surface roughness of the waveguide and reduce scattering loss. The preparation method has simple process, and the etched LiNbO 3 The waveguide is coated with a medium layer with the same refractive index, and the surface roughness of the etched lithium niobate waveguide is repaired by thermal annealing post-treatment, so that the scattering loss of the lithium niobate waveguide caused by the surface roughness can be remarkably reduced, and the low-loss lithium niobate waveguide is realized.

According to some embodiments of the present invention, the cladding layer 4 is deposited on the surface of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3 by LPCVD, PECVD, ALD or PVD.

In the above embodiment, the cladding layer 4 with a required thickness can be deposited on the surface of the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3 by depositing methods such as LPCVD, PECVD, ALD or PVD, so as to ensure that most of the light is LiNbO 3 The scattering loss caused by surface roughness is obviously reduced when the optical waveguide is normally propagated in the waveguide.

According to some embodiments of the present invention, the hard mask layer is deposited on the lithium niobate thin film layer 6 by LPCVD, PECVD or PVD.

In the above embodiment, a hard mask layer with a desired thickness may be deposited on the lithium niobate thin film layer 6 by LPCVD, PECVD, PVD or the like, and the hard mask layer with a desired thickness may be formed as a hard interlayer to transfer a fine pattern of photoresist to a sufficient depth on the lithium niobate thin film layer 6 to prevent pattern collapse.

According to some embodiments of the invention, the thermal annealing process has an interfacial annealing temperature of 300 ℃ to 800 ℃. In some embodiments, the thermal annealing process has an interfacial annealing temperature of 400 ℃ to 800 ℃.

In the embodiment, the interface annealing temperature of the thermal annealing treatment is limited within a reasonable range, so that the aim of effectively improving the quality of the film layer can be fulfilled.

According to some embodiments of the invention, the annealing time of the thermal annealing treatment is 5min to 10min.

In the embodiment, the annealing time of the thermal annealing treatment is limited within a reasonable range, so that the aim of effectively improving the quality of the film layer can be fulfilled.

According to some embodiments of the invention, the annealing is maintained for a certain annealing time and then cooled to room temperature.

According to some embodiments of the present invention, the hard mask layer is removed using a wet etch process.

According to the embodiment, the wet etching process is adopted for removing the hard mask layer, the process is simple, the adaptability is high, the etching rate is high, the surface uniformity is good, and the damage to the substrate is less.

According to some embodiments of the present invention, a method of fabricating a low-loss lithium niobate waveguide comprises the steps of:

step 1, selecting an LNOI material as an initial material, and as shown in fig. 3, obtaining a schematic structural diagram of the initial material LNOI, wherein the LNOI material comprises a substrate layer 1, an oxygen buried layer 2 and a lithium niobate thin film layer 6 which are sequentially arranged from bottom to top, a Cr metal mask layer 7 with a thickness of about 40nm is sputtered on the surface of the lithium niobate thin film layer 6 by a magnetron sputtering (PVD) method, and as shown in fig. 4, a schematic structural diagram of the lithium niobate thin film layer 6 after the Cr metal mask layer 7 is sputtered and deposited on the surface is shown.

Step 2, spin-coating a layer of positive photoresist on the surface of the Cr metal mask layer 7, then baking for 30 minutes at 100 ℃, placing a mask plate with patterns on the photoresist, and then irradiating for 35 seconds by using ultraviolet light; developing and removing the photoresist of the sample in a developing solution, then rinsing the sample in deionized water, and finally baking the sample at 100 ℃ for 15 minutes to transfer the pattern of the photoetching picture to the lower metal mask layer 7.

Step 3, adopting ICP dry etching, taking oxygen and chlorine as gas etching sources to finish etching of the photoresist and the metal mask layer 7, and adopting argon and SF 6 The etching depth of the lithium niobate thin film layer 6 is 300nm as a gas etching source, as shown in fig. 5, the structure of the lithium niobate waveguide after the photoetching and dry etching are completed is schematically shown, the thickness of a slab layer is 300nm, the thickness of a rib layer is 300nm, and the width of a strip waveguide is 900nm in the etched lithium niobate waveguide layer 3.

And 4, removing the Cr metal mask layer 7 by adopting Cr corrosive liquid for corrosion for 10min-30min, and then cleaning the lithium niobate waveguide layer 3 by adopting RCA solution.

And 5, depositing a SiN cladding layer 4 with the thickness of about 50nm on the surface of the etched lithium niobate waveguide layer 3 by adopting an LPCVD (low pressure chemical vapor deposition) mode at the pressure of 100pa and the temperature of 700 ℃, as shown in FIG. 6, and then, depositing the SiN cladding layer 4.

This is a Chinese patent (CN115951449A) titled "Low-loss lithium niobate waveguide and preparation method thereof," filed by Zhongke Xintong Microelectronics Technology Beijing Co., Ltd. on March 13, 2023, and published on April 11, 2023. The patent is currently in pending status and relates to the field of integrated optoelectronics.

**Problem Addressed:** Lithium niobate (LiNbO₃) waveguides suffer from surface and sidewall roughness caused by the material's hardness and chemical inertness during etching. RIE etching produces LiF precipitates and redeposition, creating rough waveguides and high scattering losses. The process window for optimizing roughness is small.

**Invention Structure:** The low-loss lithium niobate waveguide comprises (from bottom to top):
1. A substrate layer (400-600 μm, preferably 500 μm)
2. An oxygen buried layer (2-5 μm, silicon dioxide)
3. A lithium niobate waveguide layer (200-700 nm thick)
4. A coating (cladding) layer deposited on the lithium niobate waveguide layer
5. An upper cladding layer (1-5 μm, silica or air)

**Key Features:**
- The coating layer's refractive index equals that of the lithium niobate waveguide layer (2.15-2.25, preferably 2.2)
- Coating layer thickness: 10-100 nm, with less than 10% influence on optical field energy in the LiNbO₃ waveguide
- Coating material: silicon nitride or silicon oxynitride
- The coating layer fills and repairs surface/sidewall undulations without damaging the LiNbO₃ lattice structure
- Waveguide types: ridge or strip waveguides; single-mode, multi-mode, or periodic structures

**Preparation Method (7 steps):**
1. Use LNOI material (substrate, buried oxide, lithium niobate thin film) as starting material
2. Deposit hard mask layer (via LPCVD, PECVD, or PVD)
3. Spin-coat photoresist and complete photolithography
4. Dry etch hard mask, then etch lithium niobate thin film to form waveguide layer
5. Remove hard mask layer and residues (wet etching)
6. Deposit coating layer on waveguide surface (LPCVD, PECVD, ALD, or PVD)
7. Thermal annealing (300-800°C, 5-10 min), then deposit upper cladding

**Example Embodiment:** Used a Cr metal mask layer (~40nm) sputtered via magnetron PVD, ICP dry etching with O₂/Cl₂ for mask and Ar/SF₆ for LiNbO₃ (300nm etch depth), LPCVD SiN cladding (~50nm) at 700°C/100Pa, annealing at 400-800°C for 8 min, and 3μm SiO₂ upper cladding. COMSOL simulations confirmed that SiN cladding thickness up to 100nm does not significantly affect light transmission in the LiNbO₃ waveguide while substantially reducing sidewall scattering loss.

The patent claims 10 items covering the waveguide structure and its preparation method.
args.key_excerpts: "The low-loss lithium niobate waveguide takes an LNOI basic structure formed by a substrate layer, an oxygen-buried layer and a lithium niobate waveguide layer as a platform, and a coating layer is deposited on the lithium niobate waveguide layer, so that LiNbO₃ undulation of waveguide surface and side wall can be effectively filled and repaired, the core layer LiNbO₃ lattice structure is not damaged, and meanwhile, the refractive index of the coating layer is designed to be equal to that of the lithium niobate waveguide layer and the thickness of the coating layer is controlled, so that most of light can be ensured to be LiNbO₃ normal propagation in the waveguide significantly reduces the scattering loss due to the roughness of the waveguide surface and sidewalls."

99 6.6 Conclusion and outlook . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 102 7 Summary and conclusion 105 Acknowledgment 107 List of publications 109 Bibliography 111 Chapter 1 Introduction and Motivation This thesis treats the fabrication of optical ridge waveguides in lithium niobate (LN, LiNbO3) and potassium titanyl phosphate (KTP, KTiOPO4) by use of a di-amond blade dicing saw and their linear and nonlinear optical characterization.
The used materials, lithium niobate and KTP, are both ferroelectric crystals which have found widespread application due to their favorable nonlinear optic, electro-optic and piezoelectric properties. Lithium niobate is widely used for fabrication of surface acoustic wave devices, such as ﬁlters and transducers, that are needed in all types of radio frequency devices, for instance cellular phones, Wi-Fi ap-pliances and televisions [1, 2]. In the ﬁeld of optics, lithium niobate is used for fabrication of electro-optical modulators for long-haul communication or non-linear optical frequency converters [3–5]. KTP crystals are also used as optical frequency converters and are particularly widespread for frequency doubling of neodymium lasers from 1064 nm wavelength to 532 nm [6, 7]. This technique of obtaining green laser light is for example commonly used in green laser pointers and in laser sources for medical therapy [8]. Further, it is a preferred material for generation of entangled photons at telecommunication wavelength of ∼1550 nm for quantum optics and quantum cryptography because it allows for an especially large phasematching bandwidth [9,10].
Waveguides can be used to guide an optical wave from one optical com-ponent to another and thereby integrate and miniaturize optical systems.
In waveguides optical waves can be kept tightly conﬁned over longer distance with low propagation loss. This is advantageous in optical frequency conversion be-cause the conversion efﬁciency is proportional to intensity (and therefore inverse-proportional to the mode area) and proportional to the squared interaction length.
It is for example also beneﬁcial in optical modulators. Here, the electrodes that surround a waveguide can be placed closer than those of a modulator for a free-beam. Hence, lower voltages are sufﬁcient to achieve a needed ﬁeld strength.
1 2 CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION AND MOTIVATION The most widespread methods for waveguide fabrication in lithium niobate and KTP are titanium diffusion or proton exchange [11, 12], and rubidium ex-change [6,13], respectively. In these methods, a photolithographically structured Ti pattern is in-diffused, or ions are in-diffused through a photolithographically deﬁned mask. The diffused ions have higher polarizability, and hence their con-centration proﬁle goes along with an increase of the refractive index resulting in light guiding. These diffused waveguides conﬁne light in both horizontal and vertical direction.
Also methods exist that result in a planar waveguide formation and need fur-ther processing to enable guiding in lateral direction. Among such planar wave-guides are crystalline thin ﬁlms, which are bonded onto a material of lower re-fractive index [14], epitaxially grown thin ﬁlms [15, 16] or crystalline layers that are separated from bulk by a layer of implanted ions with decreased refractive index [17].
Lateral conﬁnement can be achieved in these planar waveguides by deﬁnition of ridges. Optical modes are then strongly conﬁned in horizon-tal direction due to the refractive index step from material to air. Ridges can be formed by laser ablation [18], wet etching [19], dry etching [20, 21] or mechan-ical grinding [22–24]. Laser ablation results in typical surface roughness of the order of 500 nm (RMS) [18] and this goes along with relatively high attenuation.
Wet etching of crystalline material can result in quite smooth surfaces and low waveguide losses [19], though sharp edges can occur in bends because different faces of crystalline materials are commonly etched at different rates. Dry etching includes methods for material removal by bombardment with charged ions or neutral particles. The character of the etching process can be of physical nature, i. e. sputtering of the surface through impact of swift ions. The process can have a chemical nature, i. e. material removal through a chemical reaction with free radi-cals and formation of a volatile product. Or it can combine physical and chemical etching. When the present work began in 2013 and until we presented our results on cut ridge waveguides, dry etched waveguides in lithium niobate thin ﬁlms of thickness ≲1 µm had rather high losses of 10 −17 dB/cm which were commonly attributed to surface roughness [20,21]. By now optimized dry-etching processes have enabled deﬁnition of ridge waveguides in lithium niobate thin ﬁlms with very low losses of 0.3 −0.4 dB/cm [25,26].
Commonly, wafer saws are used to singulate thousands of electronic semi-conductor chips that are fabricated in parallel on a single wafer [27,28]. In these saws a blade with synthetic diamonds in a polymer or metal matrix cuts wafers that are mounted on a translation stage. Various blades of different width can be 3 acquired that are appropriate for different materials. During dicing it is impor-tant to avoid chipping and microcracks because weakened dies might otherwise break in a following mounting or packaging step. Further, wafer saws are re-quired to precisely cut narrow kerfs along predeﬁned streets. At the same time cutting speed needs to be high and wear low to make the singulation process economic. These requirements, which are fulﬁlled by modern automated wafer saws, make them ideally suited for preparation of low-roughness, low-loss op-tical ridge waveguides in crystalline materials. It shall also be mentioned that wafer saws are standard equipment in semiconductor fabrication plants and well equipped research facilities; and they are hence easily accessible.
Wafer saws were ﬁrst used around 2001 by Kawaguchi et al. from NGK IN-SULATORS and MATSUSHITA ELECTRIC INDUSTRIAL CO. LTD (PANASONIC) for preparation of ridge waveguides [29, 30], and also by Nishida et al. from NTT PHOTONICS LABORATORIES [22,23]. They bonded a lithium niobate wafer to ma-terial of lower refractive index, lapped and polished it down to 3 −10 µm thick-ness, and then deﬁned ridges. Based on these ridge waveguides, frequency con-version modules are available from NTT Electronics1. Kishimoto and Nakamura from OKI ELECTRIC INDUSTRY CO. LTD. [31] and Sun and Xu from MCMAS-TER UNIVERSITY, Canada [32] prepared cut ridge waveguides in planar proton-exchanged lithium niobate. Courjal et al. from FEMTO-ST INSTITUTE in Besancon, France prepared ridge waveguides in lithium niobate of especially large aspect ratio, with 1 µm top width and height of 500 µm [24]. Further they presented a technique to prepare tapers for ridge waveguides by use of a wafer saw to improve in-coupling into narrow ridge waveguides [33]. At HELMUT SCHMIDT UNIVERSITY in Hamburg, Germany optical ridge waveguides have been formed in ion implanted KTP by use of diamond blade dicing saw [34]. In Hamburg as well optical ridge waveguides have been cut in Nd-doped yttrium aluminum gar-net (Nd:YAG) and Nd-doped sapphire, materials that possess high Mohs hard-ness of 8.5 to 9 [35,36].
The ridge geometry allows to strongly conﬁne optical modes because of the large step of refractive index between waveguide material and surrounding air.
Especially when ridge waveguides are formed in a thin-ﬁlm material, that is bonded to a lower-index substrate, strong conﬁnement and good overlap be-tween interacting modes of different wavelengths can be achieved. This allows for high conversion efﬁciency in frequency conversion processes [23, 30, 37]. A drawback of ridge deﬁnition by use of a diamond blade saw is that it only allows 1Model: WH-0780-000-A-B-C, WH-0780-000-F-B-C, WS-0578-000-A-B-C 4 CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION AND MOTIVATION for straight waveguides. It is not possible to cut bends or splitters, which are for example necessary for modulators.
The present work discusses research results on ridge waveguides that are formed in different materials by use of a wafer saw. In chapter 2 theory and fundamentals are reviewed brieﬂy, which are helpful for understanding the fol-lowing chapters on experimental and simulation results (chapters 3-6). These ﬁndings have already been presented on conferences and published in journals [38–43]. It follows a summary and conclusion in chapter 7.
Chapter 3 reviews our results on fabrication of lithium niobate thin ﬁlms via crystal ion slicing, ridge waveguide deﬁnition and characterization.
The crys-tal ion slicing process consists of H+ ion implantation to a depth of ∼1 µm in a LN substrate, bonding this substrate to a material of lower refractive index, and exfoliation of the thin ﬁlm by heat treatment [14,44,45]. A 1 µm thick ﬁlm of monocrystalline lithium niobate on a material of lower refractive index is formed.
Into these thin ﬁlms we cut ridge waveguides. For a 2.1 µm wide and 9 mm long waveguide we measured propagation loss of 1.2 dB/cm (2.8 dB/cm) for TE (TM) polarization at a wavelength of 1550 nm. These values are below losses that other groups achieved at that time for comparable waveguides that they had prepared by dry-etching [20,21]. Research in the material platform of lithium niobate thin ﬁlms, which is also termed lithium-niobate-on-insulator (LNOI), is motivated by the high refractive index step between the core material and the surrounding cladding. This high index step allows for particularly strong mode conﬁnement and hence high efﬁciency in frequency conversion processes [14, 46]. Further, it allows much narrower bending radii of waveguides of about 10 µm instead of 10 mm in conventional waveguides. This allows for a strong reduction of the footprint of optical components and thus enables higher integration density.
A special type of optical ridge waveguide in lithium niobate has been pre-sented by Suntsov et al. [47]. These waveguides are prepared by in-diffusion of titanium (and erbium to provide ampliﬁcation) through the three faces (top and two sides) of a ridge waveguide and proﬁt from a concentration proﬁle that is more homogeneous than those of the waveguides diffused from top only [47,48].
Due to good overlap of modes of different wavelength, these waveguides could also be advantageous for frequency conversion. To enable efﬁcient frequency conversion, lithium niobate needs to be periodically poled. This is achieved by photolithographic patterning of electrodes on the crystal and application of high voltage [49]. In chapter 4 we discuss results on periodic poling of virgin lithium niobate substrates and further demonstrate that it is possible to periodically pole 5 Ti-diffused ridge waveguides. Periodic poling of samples with ridge waveguides is challenging because care needs to be taken during several process steps to not destroy the fragile ridges. Further, the electric ﬁeld is inﬂuenced by the thickness variation due to the ridges and grooves, as well as by the Ti diffusion proﬁle. It is not reasonable to periodically pole lithium niobate wafers ﬁrst and subsequently produce the Ti-diffused ridges because during Ti-diffusion a domain inverted layer is formed [50,51].
Potassium titanyl phosphate possesses favorable nonlinear and electro-optical properties, wide transparency range, high damage threshold and good thermal stability [6]. It is therefore a preferred material for frequency conversion appli-cations and modulators. Further, it has attracted attention because it allows to generate particularly indistinguishable entangled photons at telecommunication wavelength for quantum optics and quantum cryptography [9, 10]. The most common method for waveguide preparation in KTP is Rb-exchange through a photolithographically patterned mask [13]. Since ridge geometry can provide advantages over conventional channel waveguide geometry due to stronger con-ﬁnement, we investigated whether it is possible to combine the methods of Rb-exchange with ridge deﬁnition by use of a wafer saw. In the exchange process, K+ ions are replaced for Rb+ ions and at the surface KTiOPO4 is thus converted to K1−xRbxTiOPO4 with x ≈1. This causes tensions in the surface-near mate-rial and makes the crystal more brittle. Still, we found parameters that allow for deﬁnition of chipping- and fracture-free ridge waveguides with low surface roughness of 1 −2 nm and attenuation of 1.3 −1.6 dB/cm. Results of this research project, that we performed in collaboration with the INTEGRATED QUANTUM OP-TICS workgroup of Prof. Silberhorn from UNIVERSITY OF PADERBORN, are given in chapter 5. The obtained ﬁndings helped to prepare ridge waveguides in peri-odically poled KTP in a following work for second harmonic generation in the ultraviolet [52].
In KTP Rb and Ba ions are only mobile along the crystallographic z axis [6] and we used this characteristic for preparation of a novel type of ridge wave-guide. For fabrication of these waveguides we deﬁned ridges into KTP substrates that have their z axis lying perpendicularly to the waveguide in the substrate’s surface plane. When these samples are immersed into a melt of rubidium and barium nitrate, Rb and Ba ions diffuse through the ridge ﬂanks along the z axis into the waveguide. After annealing homogeneous Rb and Ba concentrations are obtained in the rectangular waveguide cross section, and the refractive index is homogeneously increased in this region. This step-like refractive index proﬁle re-6 CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION AND MOTIVATION sults in an improved overlap of modes of different wavelength and can hence en-able higher conversion efﬁciency in frequency conversion processes. In contrast, in conventional diffusion proﬁles, modes of lower wavelength are pulled closer to the surface while modes of longer wavelength extend further into the depth.
Another advantage of the novel waveguides is that they are resistant against el-evated temperature since the Rb and Ba ions cannot diffuse into depth like in conventional waveguides. This allows to operate the waveguides at higher tem-perature and thereby avoid gray tracking [53]. Experimental results are discussed in detail in chapter 6.
Chapter 2 Fundamental concepts and methods In the following chapter theoretical fundamentals are reviewed which are neces-sary to follow discussions in the subsequent chapters. These fundamentals in-clude theory of guided waves, nonlinear optics and properties of the used crys-talline materials. Further, experimental methods of waveguide fabrication and characterization are discussed. Among the applied fabrication methods are dif-fusion processes, wafer direct bonding, use of a diamond blade dicing saw, and electric ﬁeld poling.

2.2 Diffusion Common methods for waveguide fabrication in lithium niobate are titanium dif-fusion [11] and proton exchange [12]. For Ti diffusion, Ti is deposited onto a lithium niobate substrate, photolithographically patterned and the metal is then diffused at ≳1000 ◦C. Titanium increases the refractive index by about 10−3 to 10−2 [11], and a waveguide is formed. To prepare proton exchanged waveguides, the substrate is masked photolithographically with a metal mask and afterwards immersed into hot benzoic acid near the boiling point of ∼250 ◦C. As proton ex-change increases the extraordinary refractive index of lithium niobate and lowers the ordinary one, it results only in waveguiding for the extraordinary polariza-tion. In KTP, waveguides can be formed through exchange of potassium ions for rubidium or other alkali metal ions, when a masked substrate is immersed into a nitrate melt [6,13].
The driving force of a diffusion ﬂux j is a gradient in concentration c: j = −D ∇c.
(2.11) Here, D is termed diffusion coefﬁcient and it typically increases with increasing temperature. The formula is known as Fick’s ﬁrst law. Mass conservation of the diffusant can be expressed as dc dt + ∇· j = 0 (2.12) 10 CHAPTER 2. FUNDAMENTAL CONCEPTS AND METHODS and from equations (2.11, 2.12) Fick’s second law can be derived: dc dt = D ∇2c.
(2.13) Two cases of one dimensional diffusion in a semi-inﬁnite medium shall be dis-cussed brieﬂy now: (I) Diffusion of a certain amount of diffusive substance on the surface and (II) diffusion from an inﬁnite source at surface. Case (I) corre-sponds to in-diffusion of a titanium layer into lithium niobate, and time t and depth z dependent concentration is given by a Gaussian distribution c(z, t) = M 2 √ πDt exp −z2 4Dt  , (2.14) where constant M = ´ ∞ 0 c dz [56]. For the two previously discussed solutions a constant diffusion coefﬁcient was assumed. However, that is not always the case. For example pro-ton diffusion in lithium niobate is strongly concentration dependent and leads to step-like diffusion proﬁles [12].
2.3 Losses in optical waveguides Propagation losses in optical waveguides occur due to absorption, radiation and scattering. As it is helpful to know about their origin and how to measure them, they shall be discussed in the following.
Absorption Absorption in optical materials occurs due to electronic transitions, lattice vibra-tions, and free-carrier effects [58]. Within the wavelength range of 0.5 −5 µm ab-sorption losses of lithium niobate are negligibly small [58], and the same applies to Ti-diffused waveguides where attenuation of 0.03 dB/cm could be determined 2.3. LOSSES IN OPTICAL WAVEGUIDES 11 at 1.15 µm [59]. KTP is transparent from 0.35 µm to 4.5 µm [58] and losses in Rb exchanged waveguides are < 0.4 dB/cm at 633 nm [13]. Towards the UV, photons whose energy exceeds the band gap, can excite electrons from the valence to the conduction band. The absorption edge is commonly not sharp, but described by a temperature dependent exponential absorption edge - the Urbach tail. At the infrared edge of insulators, absorption is caused by excitation of phonons (lattice vibrations). Since higher harmonics of fundamental resonances can be excited, this absorption edge is not sharp too, but characterized by an exponential law.
Free-carrier absorption occurs typically in metals or in semiconductors, but it can also arise in crystals with larger band gap at elevated temperatures.
KTP, lithium niobate and other nonlinear crystals exhibit transmission loss due to scattering and absorption when they are irradiated with light of shorter wavelength at high intensity. This effect is referred to in lithium niobate as green-induced infrared absorption (GRIIRA) and in KTP as gray tracking (see also sec. 6.4). In KTP electron hole pairs can be generated through nonlinear mech-anisms which are then trapped by vacancies or impurities [53,60,61]. In lithium niobate the effect is assumed to be caused by polarons that form at NbLi anti-site defects, where a Nb ion occupies a Li site. The effect of GRIIRA can be strongly reduced in lithium niobate by doping with Mg, Zn, In, or Hf [62,63] or by heating to ≳160 ◦C [63]; and for KTP gray tracking can be avoided by heating the crystal to temperatures above 170 ◦C [53].

Cut-back method / transmission A very straightforward approach is to endﬁre couple light into a waveguide and detect the transmitted power. The ratio of transmitted Pout to impinging power Pin determines the insertion loss and is commonly given in dB units: αI = 10 dB · log10 (Pout/Pin). That is, the optical properties are independent of light intensity, light rays propagate through each other without interaction and the wavelength remains unchanged when light passes through a medium. In these optically anisotropic materials the refractive index depends on polarization and propagation direction.
The linear optical properties of a material are described in general by three principle refractive indices. When two of these principle refractive indices are equal, such as in lithium niobate, the crystal is called uniaxial. It has one optical axis and if light propagates along it, the refractive index is independent of polar-ization. For all other directions of propagation, one polarization experiences the ordinary, direction-independent refractive index and the other polarization ex-periences the extraordinary, direction-dependent refractive index. Crystals with three different principle refractive indices, such as KTP, are called biaxial because they posses two optical axes.
To enable phasematching in a three-wave mixing process, the polarization of the wave with shortest wavelength is always chosen to have the low refractive index. The polarizations of the two waves of longer wavelength can be chosen to both have high index, and this process is termed type-I phasematching. When the two waves of longer wavelength have different polarizations, the process is called type-II phasematching. The difference between the principle refractive indices ∆n is called birefringence, and generally larger birefringence allows to compensate larger phase-mismatch.

This is a doctoral dissertation by Martin Volk, submitted to the Helmut-Schmidt-Universität / Universität der Bundeswehr Hamburg in 2018 (oral examination held on 08.02.2019, supervised by Univ.-Prof. Dr. Detlef Kip and Univ.-Prof. Dr.-Ing. Christian Schäffer), titled "Optical ridge waveguides in lithium niobate and potassium titanyl phosphate."

The thesis covers the fabrication of optical ridge waveguides in lithium niobate (LN, LiNbO3) and potassium titanyl phosphate (KTP, KTiOPO4) using a diamond blade dicing saw, along with their linear and nonlinear optical characterization. Both materials are ferroelectric crystals with favorable nonlinear optic, electro-optic, and piezoelectric properties. Lithium niobate is used for surface acoustic wave devices and electro-optical modulators, while KTP is used for frequency doubling of neodymium lasers (1064 nm → 532 nm) and generation of entangled photons at ~1550 nm for quantum optics.

Key research findings across chapters:
- Chapter 2 covers theoretical fundamentals: the wave equation and finite element methods, diffusion, waveguide losses (absorption, surface roughness, radiation), loss measurement techniques (cut-back, resonator/Fabry-Perot, scattered light), nonlinear frequency conversion, phasematching (birefringent and quasi-phasematching), properties of LN and KTP, electric field poling, the diamond blade dicing saw, and wafer direct bonding/crystal ion slicing.
- Chapter 3: Ridge waveguides in lithium niobate thin films (LNOI) fabricated via crystal ion slicing (H+ ion implantation to ~1 µm depth, bonding to lower-index substrate, exfoliation by heat treatment). A 2.1 µm wide, 9 mm long waveguide showed propagation loss of 1.2 dB/cm (TE) and 2.8 dB/cm (TM) at 1550 nm — lower than losses achieved by dry-etching at the time (10–17 dB/cm).
- Chapter 4: Electric field poling of lithium niobate, including periodic poling of congruent LN with gel and Cr electrodes, and demonstration that Ti-diffused ridge waveguides can be periodically poled.
- Chapter 5: Ridge waveguides in z-cut KTP, combining Rb-exchange with ridge definition via wafer saw. Chipping- and fracture-free ridges with low surface roughness (1–2 nm) and attenuation of 1.3–1.6 dB/cm were achieved, in collaboration with Prof. Silberhorn's Integrated Quantum Optics group at University of Paderborn.
- Chapter 6: A novel type of side-exchanged ridge waveguide in KTP. Since Rb and Ba ions are only mobile along the crystallographic z axis, ridges defined in KTP with z-axis perpendicular to the waveguide allow Rb/Ba diffusion through the ridge flanks, producing homogeneous step-like refractive index profiles. These waveguides offer improved mode overlap, are resistant to elevated temperatures (helping avoid gray tracking), and enabled subsequent work on SHG in the ultraviolet in periodically poled KTP.

Notable quantitative results and formulas preserved include: Tien's formula for surface roughness scattering loss (showing 0.0016 dB/cm for conventional diffused waveguides vs. 0.62 dB/cm for LNOI at 2 nm roughness and 1.55 µm); bending radius calculations showing Ti-diffused waveguides need ~7.9 mm radius vs. ~7.1 µm for LNOI at 0.1 dB/cm loss; SHG conversion efficiency proportional to intensity and squared interaction length (η = C2L²/A·P1); quasi-phasematching reducing the nonlinear coefficient to dQPM = (2/π)·deff; and d33 coefficient being six times larger (four times for KTP) than other coefficients of the respective materials.
