# Research Article

Fabrication of ridge optical waveguide in thin film lithium niobate by proton exchange and wet etching

Author links open overlay panel Ying Li a b c, Tian Lan a b c, [Dengcai Yang a b c](https://www.sciencedirect.com/author/42361798000/dengcai-yang), [Zhiyong Wang a b c](https://www.sciencedirect.com/author/55851373700/zhiyong-wang)

## Highlights

*   •The etching rate of LN is improved nearly 100 times after introduce proton-exchange process. 
*   •The sidewall surface is covered with beeswax to avoid the damage induced by wet etching process. 
*   •Using PEWE method can fabricate rib waveguides with high optical performance based on the TFLN platform. 
*   •Using the pure benzoic acid PE process in lieu of the lithium benzoic acid process can improve the etch quality of TFLN. 

## Abstract

In this paper, a low-loss ridge [waveguide](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/materials-science/waveguide) based on the [thin film](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/thin-films)[lithium niobate](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/materials-science/lithium-niobate) (TFLN) is successfully fabricated using a proton-exchanged wet etching (PEWE) technique, which can result in a much better vertical sidewall angle and improve the [surface roughness](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/surface-roughness) to reduce the scattering loss. The average etching rate is obviously improved by the structural defects and phase transition induced by our modified PE process, and the finally optimized etching rate is as fast as 13.5 nm/min. The propagation loss of the fabricated straight ridge [waveguide](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/waveguide) is measured to be 4.3 dB/cm by using an 850 nm single mode laser as the [light source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/physics-and-astronomy/light-source). Meanwhile, a Y-branch [waveguide](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/physics-and-astronomy/waveguide) is also measured with a uniform light splitting ratio of nearly 1:1. Furthermore, this work offers the route for the manufacturing of low-cost and high-efficiency [photonic](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/physics-and-astronomy/photonics) integration platform.

## Introduction

Lithium Niobate (LiNbO 3, LN) is well-known as an optically transparent, uniaxial, photoelastic crystal for various applications, such as electro-optic, nonlinear optic, acousto-optic piezoelectric, and ferroelectric. Nowadays, LN thin film can be directly bonded on the surface of silicon dioxide (SiO 2) by ion implantation to form as the thin film lithium niobate (TFLN), which has high refractive index contrast to operate as a waveguide [1,2]. As a result, light can be successfully confined into a much smaller size waveguide using TFLN, producing a dramatic reduction of the device footprint and enhancement of optical effects with respect to implementations in the conventional LN wafer [[3], [4], [5], [6]]. However, the LN material is chemically inert, therefore, it can hardly be etched without any pre-treatments. Besides, mechanical processing for the LN material is also difficult to proceed due to its high hardness and wear resistance. In the last decades, research on manufacturing methods of waveguides based on TFLN platform have intensified and made huge progress. Various techniques to etch LN material have been developed including reactive ion beam etching (RIE) [7,8], inductively coupled plasma RIE (ICP-RIE) [[9], [10], [11]], focused ion beam (FIB) milling [12,13], and wet etching [14], and functional devices have been yielded. Nevertheless, some inevitable problems still exist in these etching methods such as shallow sidewall angle, rough surface and limited etching rate, or combination thereof. Moreover, all of these methods are incompatible with the matured fabrication process in bulk LN platform that based on diffusion technique.

In 1992, Laurell et al. [15] firstly propounded a new wet-etching method by using PE and a mixture of HF/HNO 3 acids for LiNbO 3 to overcome the drawbacks of re-deposition of LiF caused by dry-etching process, and obtained a ridge waveguide with smooth etching surface. Then, Wang et al. [16] proposed a method that used electric-field-assisted PE to suppress the proton diffusion in the lateral directions and solved the etched sidewalls with sloping or curved shapes problems. Subsequently, Ting et al. [17] demonstrated that utilizing the mixed benzoic and adipic acids as the PE source could also get a vertical and smooth LN waveguide. And later in 2008, Lai et al. [18] introduced a novel wet etching method to produce a LN ridge waveguide by using the assistance of gamma-ray irradiation, resulting in an etched depth about 3 times deeper than that of the conventional proton-exchanged wet etching (PEWE) method. However, considering the TFLN as a newly-arisen optical material, the upper thin film LN is bonded on the SiO 2 box layer, such mixture solution, which contains hydrofluoric acid, would also etch the SiO 2 during wet etching process. What's more, the corrosion rate of SiO 2 is much faster than that of LN. Thus, there exists a big challenge to fabricate TFLN ridge waveguide by PEWE. Even though ridge waveguides of 1.0×0.7 μm 2 based on TFLN have been successfully fabricated using PE accelerated chemical etching, of which the sample was first selectively proton exchanged in benzoic acid at 200°C for 0.6–2.4h, and then was soaked in a 1:2 mixture of HF:HNO 3 at room temperature for etching, the propagation loss is still as high as ~6 dB/cm, and etching rate is about 6.7 nm/min [[19], [20], [21]].

In this research, a systematic fabrication process of TFLN ridge waveguides utilizing the PEWE method is investigated comprehensively. And a new PE source and a new protection method of the SiO 2 layer on chip are proposed during the wet etching process, which could result in a TFLN ridge waveguide with much better quality. In comparison, the obtained ridge waveguide exhibits a better sidewall shape and smoother surface than those reports in previous study. Notably, the complexity of the proposed fabrication method is merely increased compared with the conventional method based on the bulk LN platform, showing a high process compatibility.

By exploiting the electric field discontinuity at high-index-low-index interfaces, slot geometries localize optical fields within nanoscale gaps, offering unique advantages over conventional strip and rib waveguides. Over the past two decades, slot waveguides have been demonstrated across diverse material platforms including silicon, polymers, chalcogenide glasses, lithium niobate, III-V semiconductors, and emerging two-dimensional materials. These platforms support a broad range of applications, from nonlinear photonics and electro-optic modulation to biochemical and gas sensing, with recent extensions into mid-infrared spectroscopy, terahertz guiding, quantum photonics, and neuromorphic computing. Despite their promise, slot waveguides face challenges related to fabrication tolerances, propagation losses, and material stability in hybrid designs. This review consolidates their fundamental principles, historical development, material platforms, and key applications, while critically assessing current limitations. Future perspectives highlight heterogeneous integration and application-driven design as pathways for establishing slot waveguides as foundational building blocks of next-generation integrated photonic platforms.

This is a research article published in Optical Materials (Volume 120, October 2021, Article 111433) describing the fabrication of ridge optical waveguides in thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) using a proton-exchanged wet etching (PEWE) technique.

**Authors:** Ying Li, Tian Lan, Dengcai Yang, and Zhiyong Wang.

**Key Findings:**
- The etching rate of lithium niobate (LN) was improved nearly 100 times after introducing the proton-exchange process, with an optimized etching rate of 13.5 nm/min.
- A low-loss ridge waveguide was successfully fabricated on TFLN with a measured propagation loss of 4.3 dB/cm using an 850 nm single-mode laser.
- A Y-branch waveguide was also fabricated with a uniform light-splitting ratio of nearly 1:1.
- The sidewall surface was covered with beeswax to avoid damage induced by the wet etching process.
- Using pure benzoic acid (instead of lithium benzoic acid) for the proton exchange process improved the etch quality of TFLN.
- The technique offers a route for low-cost, high-efficiency photonic integration platforms.

**Methodology Highlights:**
- Lithium niobate is chemically inert and difficult to etch without pre-treatment, which has historically limited TFLN waveguide fabrication.
- Prior methods (RIE, ICP-RIE, FIB milling, and wet etching) suffered from issues such as shallow sidewall angles, rough surfaces, and limited etching rates.
- The proton exchange process (PE) causes H+ ions to diffuse into the LN thin film and substitute Li+ ions, inducing phase transitions and structural defects that improve etching depth and rate.
- The new PE source and a new SiO2 protection method (beeswax covering) during wet etching produced better sidewall shape and smoother surfaces than previous reports.
- Waveguide designs included a cosine-shaped Y-branch (3 μm top width) and a straight waveguide (800 nm width with tapered 3 μm input/output ends for coupling efficiency).
- HRXRD analysis confirmed phase transitions after the PE process, with LN substrate and film peaks detected at ~83.63° and 83.36° respectively, plus a third diffraction peak appearing after PE.

**Historical Context:** The PEWE method builds on work by Laurell et al. (1992) who first proposed wet etching with PE and HF/HNO3 acids, and subsequent improvements by Wang et al., Ting et al. (2008), and Lai et al. Previous TFLN ridge waveguide fabrication achieved only ~6 dB/cm propagation loss and ~6.7 nm/min etching rate; this work significantly improves on both.

**Funding:** Supported by the National Key Research and Development Project of China (Grant No 2020YFB2205700) and the Beijing Postdoctoral Research Foundation (Grant No 2020-Z2-043). Experiments supported by PANWOO Integrated Optoelectronic Inc.

**Article Impact:** Cited by 14 publications as of the page date, including works on slot waveguides, PPLN thin film ridge waveguides, thin-film lithium niobate crystallization methods, and electro-optic modulators.

+ Vol. 35  (3) , e2208113
+ <https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202208113>

##### Abstract

Thin‐film lithium niobate (TFLN) has been widely used in electro‐optic modulators, acoustic‐–optic modulators, electro‐optic frequency combs, and nonlinear wavelength converters owing to the excellent optical properties of lithium niobate. The performance of these devices is highly dependent on the fabrication quality of TFLN. Although state‐of‐the‐art TFLN microrings with an intrinsic quality factor (*Q*‐factor) exceeding 1 × 107 have been realized by inductively coupled plasma–reactive ion etching (ICP‐RIE) and chemical mechanical polishing (CMP), ICP‐RIE has moderate throughput, moderate reproducibility, and high cost in etching TFLN, while CMP features moderate throughput and low cost in etching TFLN. Here, a wet etching method for TFLN, leading to the fabrication of a micro‐racetrack with an intrinsic *Q*‐factor of over 9.27 × 106 is developed. The suitability of this method to fabricate a narrow coupling gap between the bus waveguide and microring enables the coupling conditions of the microring to be customized. This method features a high throughput, a high reproducibility, and a low cost in etching TFLN, showing the potential to boost the mass production of integrated LN photonic devices with high fidelity and affordability dramatically.

Article Open Access Ultra-wideband Waveguide-coupled Photodiodes Heterogeneously Integrated on a Thin-film Lithium Niobate Platform Chao Wei 1, Youren Yu 1, Ziyun Wang 1, Lin Jiang 1, Zhongming Zeng 2, Jia Ye 1, Xihua Zou 1, Wei Pan 1, Xiaojun Xie 1,* and Lianshan Yan 1,* Abstract With the advantages of large electro-optical coefficient, wide transparency window, and strong optical confinement, thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) technique has enabled the development of various high-performance optoelectronics devices, ranging from the ultra-wideband electro-optic modulators to the high-efficient quantum sources. However, the TFLN platform does not natively promise lasers and photodiodes. This study presents an InP/InGaAs modified uni-traveling carrier (MUTC) photodiodes heterogeneously integrated on the TFLN platform with a record-high 3-dB bandwidth of 110 GHz and a responsivity of 0.4 A/W at a 1,550-nm wavelength. It is implemented in a wafer-level TFLN-InP heterogeneous integration platform and is suitable for the large-scale, multi-function, and high-performance TFLN photonic integrated circuits.
Keywords: Photodiodes, Thin-film lithium niobate, Integrated photonics, Ultra-wideband electro-optic modulators Introduction Integrated photonics is a discipline of integrating devices such as waveguides, lasers, photodetectors on a single chip.
Owing to fast and efficient transmission and processing of information, integrated photonics holds a significant potential for applications in communication, computing, and sensing 1. It offers several advantages such as low cost, low power consumption, and scalability 2. Although materials like silicon 3,4, silicon nitride (Si3N4) 5,6, and indium phosphide (InP) 7,8 have been widely used as the photonics integration platform, lithium niobate (LN) has gained considerable attention due to its strong electro-optic coefficient, large nonlinearity, and wide transparency window 9. However, as a photonics integration platform, traditional bulk LN material faces several challenges such as weak mode confinement, large footprint, and reduced nonlinear efficiency 10. To overcome these challenges, thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) technique has emerged as a solution. Owing to the large refractive index difference between LN device layer and SiO2 BOX layer, TFLN technique enables tight mode confinement and high nonlinear efficiency, leading to its wide adoption in optical communications, microwave photonics, THz communications, and quantum photonics 11,12.

Most of these TFLN devices use external lasers and photodetectors since the LN material does not natively provide a light source and photodetection, a challenge faced by the TFLN technique as a potential universal photonics integrated circuits (PICs) platform 12.
The flip-chip bonding technique was recently applied to integrate the InP distributed feedback (DFB) laser die with a pre-fabricated TFLN modulator chip 21. Low-loss and high-power TFLN-InP transmitters were achieved by optimizing the overlap between the respective platform modes. Besides, as an important optoelectronic conversion device, high-performance integrated photodiodes are essential for the TFLN integration platform. Amorphous silicon photodetectors integrated on the TFLN platform was realized within the visible wavelength range 22. It features a bandwidth of 10 MHz and responsivity of 22 to 37 mA/W over the wavelengths ranging from 635 to 850 nm. Further exploration is required for photodiodes operating in the wavelength range of optical communication.
Heterogeneous integration is an effective technique to integrate active components on the chip for indirect-bandgap materials 23. Several heterogeneously integrated photodiodes have been successfully developed on silicon-based platforms 24–27. Recently, heterogeneous integration technique was adopted to achieve broadband photodetection on the TFLN platform 28. A high-performance photodiode with 80-GHz 3-dB bandwidth and 0.6-A/W responsivity at 1,550 nm was demonstrated by using die-bonding technique, with SU-8 as the adhesion layer. Although the broadband photodetection on the TFLN platform had been enabled, an ultra-wideband photodiode with 110-GHz 3-dB bandwidth on the TFLN platform is still highly desired to advance the overall performance of the TFLN PICs, considering that the state-of-the-art TFLN modulator exhibits a 3-dB bandwidth of 110 GHz 29.
Moreover, TFLN technique lacks a wafer-level integration of active components, which is a major challenge to achieve a massive-scale, multi-function, and high-performance TFLN PICs. Therefore, it is of great significance to achieve wafer-level integration of ultra-wideband photodiodes on a thin-film lithium niobate platform.
This study addresses the challenge by wafer-level heterogeneously integrating InP/InGaAs modified uni-traveling carrier (MUTC) photodiode wafer onto the TFLN wafer with pre-defined waveguides and passive components. The MUTC Epi stack featured with p layers down is implemented to simultaneously boost the bandwidth and responsivity. The fabricated waveguide-coupled photodiodes based on the wafer-level TFLN-InP heterogeneous integration technique have a dark current of approximately 1 nA and a responsivity of 0.4 A/W at a wavelength of 1,550 nm. The measured 3-dB bandwidths on 50-Ω load reach up to 110 GHz, which is comparable to that of the state-of-the-art TFLN modulator. The devices are successfully applied in a four-level pulse amplitude modulation (PAM4) data-receiving system, which demonstrates the potential of the photodiodes on the TFLN platform for next-generation high-speed transmission systems. Results Structure and design Table 1 shows the Epi layer structure of the MUTC PDs, which were grown by metal–organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) on a semi-insulating InP substrate.
The n-doped layers were initially grown on the InP substrate to establish a p-down structure after wafer bonding. In this structure, the absorption region had a total thickness of 120 nm, consisting of graded doped absorption layers of 100 nm (5 × 10 17 cm −3 → 5 × 10 18 cm −3) and a depleted absorption layer of 20 nm (1 × 10 16 cm −3). A self-induced electric field in the graded doped absorption layer enhanced the transport of the photo-generated electrons 30.
A 20-nm-thick n-doped cliff layer with 3 × 10 17 cm −3 doping level was incorporated to mitigate the space charge effect 31. A 120-nm-thick drift layer was chosen to balance the junction capacitance and carrier transit time. To enable electron velocity overshoot, the electric field in the drift region was regulated by inserting a p-doped sacrifice layer 32. Heavily doped InGaAs and InGaAsP were used as the n and p contact layers, respectively. In addition, InGaAsP layer acted as an optical coupling layer to achieve an efficient optical coupling between the active layers and lithium niobate waveguide. After optimizing the thickness of the InGaAsP layer, a thin absorption layer could perform an effective light absorption due to the strong optical coupling. Compared to the n-down structure, our structure could achieve a high responsivity since the absorption layers were close to the LN waveguide. The LN waveguide had a total thickness of 600 nm and a slab thickness of 300 nm. The width of the LN waveguide was designed as 1 μm for a low-loss light transmission.
Fig. 1 illustrates the designed fabrication process of the heterogeneously integrated photodiodes on the TFLN wafer, which includes wafer bonding, III-V material etching, and electrode fabrication. Initially, the LN Wei et al. Light: Advanced Manufacturing (2023)4:30 Page 2 of 9 waveguide was obtained by dry etching. The width of the fabricated LN waveguide was approximate 1 μm. The slope of the waveguide sidewall was approximate 63 degrees. Microscope and scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of the LN waveguide can be seen in Fig. 2a, b, respectively. Subsequently, an InP/InGaAs wafer was bonded onto the TFLN wafer with pre-defined waveguides and passive components. A combination of dry and wet etching techniques was utilized to etch III-V material, forming the n- and p- mesa while avoiding undercut and waveguide damage. The etched n mesa and p mesa are shown in Fig. 2c, d. Finally, a metal layer was electroplated as an electrode, as shown in Fig. 2e, f. Further details of the fabrication process can be found in the Materials and Methods section. The heterogeneously integrated MUTC PD were fabricated with the active areas of 2 μm × 6 μm, 2 μm × 8μm, 2 μm × 10 μm, 2 μm × 12 μm and 2 μm × 14 μm. Next, the internal responsivity of the waveguide-coupled PDs was characterized. The fiber-to-waveguide coupling loss and waveguide loss were measured to calculate the internal responsivity of the devices. A lensed fiber with a spot size of 2.5 μm was used to couple the light into and out of the loopback waveguides near the target photodiodes. The coupling and waveguide propagation losses were approximately 7 dB. The photocurrent was measured by coupling light into the photodiode near the loopback waveguide. At the wavelength of 1,550 nm, the internal responsivities of the devices with lengths of 6 – 14 μm were 0.4, 0.48, 0.5, 0.54, and 0.55 A/W, considering the measured coupling and waveguide propagation losses, as shown in Fig. 3b. The measured responsivities of the devices were consistent with the simulated ones. When the PD length increased, the responsivity saturated due to the intrinsic absorption of the metal stack. The absorption of the metal stack can be mitigated by optimizing the thickness of the cladding layer.

To further verify the characteristics of the photodiodes, the devices were applied in the four-level pulse amplitude modulation (PAM4) data-receiving system, as shown in Fig. 8a. PAM4 signals with symbol rates of 10, 20, and 32 Gbaud were sent to the devices for demodulation, respectively. The eye diagrams and waveforms of the signals are presented in Figs. 8c–h. The transmission performance of these signals was evaluated by measuring the bit error rates (BERs). 131,072 data cycles were used as the transmitting signals, and error free transmission at 10, 20, and 32 Gbaud was achieved. In addition, the relationship between the BER and the received optical power of the 32 Gbaud PAM4 signal was studied and is shown in Fig. 8b. When the received optical power exceeded −16 dBm, the BER remained below the 20% soft-decision forward error correction (FEC) limit of 2.4 × 10 −2. Furthermore, when the power exceeded −10 dBm, the BER reached the levels below the 7% hard-decision FEC limit of 3.8 × 10 −3. The fabricated photodiode on the TFLN platform showed the error-free reception of the PAM4 signals, which demonstrates its potential for the next-generation high-speed transmission systems. Discussion This paper presents ultra-wideband waveguide-coupled MUTC photodiodes heterogeneously integrated on the thin-film lithium niobate platform. The bandwidths of the devices with active areas of 2 μm × 6 μm, 2 μm × 8 μm, 2 μm × 10 μm, 2 μm × 12 μm, and 2 μm × 14 μm were 110, 105, 100, 101, and 97 GHz, respectively. The bandwidth of the devices is limited by the transit time of the photo-generated carriers. The carrier transit time can be reduced by optimizing the thickness of the absorption layers and incorporating a diffusion block layer. Another factor limiting the device bandwidth is the large series resistance on p mesa. An InGaAs layer can be added as a p contact to reduce the contact resistance and thus, a larger RC-limited bandwidth. By following these practices, the device has the potential to boost the total bandwidth up to 200 GHz. The measured responsivities of the devices with lengths in the range of 6 – 14 μm were 0.4, 0.48, 0.5, 0.54, and 0.55 A/W. The intrinsic absorption of the metal stack sets the upper limit for the responsivity of the devices. An optimized, thicker cladding layer with a moderate doping level could mitigate the absorption of the metal stack and achieve higher responsivity. The devices were applied to a data transmission system, and the obtained results showed their ability to detect a 32 Gbaud PAM4 signal with high quality. It was demonstrated that the heterogeneously integrated photodiodes on TFLN platform have the potential to be applied in the next-generation high-speed transmission systems. This work paves the way to achieving massive-scale, multi-function, and high-performance TFLN photonic integrated circuits. Moreover, it holds a great promise for ultra-high-speed optical communications, high-performance integrated microwave photonics, and multi-function integrated quantum photonics. Materials and Methods Device fabrication The whole fabrication process of the heterogeneously integrated photodiode started from patterning LN waveguide and passive components by dry etching. A careful wet clean process was followed to ensure the cleanness of the TFLN wafer. Subsequently, a bare InP wafer was bonded onto the pre-patterned TFLN wafer.
After wafer bonding, the InP substrate was mechanically thinned, followed by wet etching to remove the remaining part and expose the heavily doped InGaAs n-contact layer.
N-mesa etch was performed to stop precisely at the InGaAsP p-contact layer by combining dry and selective wet etching. This step defined the size of the active region.
The self-alignment method was applied in the fabrication process to ensure a precise alignment between the active region and the LN waveguide. P-mesa etching was performed using dry etching and selective wet etching to remove the InGaAsP above the LN wafer. To ensure the surface cleanness of the exposed LN wafer region, a wet chemical clean was performed. A 3-μm-thick SU-8 layer was deposited to form the base for the CPW pad. This is an open-access scientific article published in Light: Advanced Manufacturing (2023, Vol. 4, Article 30) by researchers from Southwest Jiaotong University (Chengdu, China) and the University of Science and Technology of China. The paper reports the development of ultra-wideband waveguide-coupled modified uni-traveling carrier (MUTC) photodiodes (PDs) heterogeneously integrated on a thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) platform.

**Key Achievement:** The InP/InGaAs MUTC photodiodes achieve a record-high 3-dB bandwidth of 110 GHz and a responsivity of 0.4 A/W at a 1,550-nm wavelength, implemented via a wafer-level TFLN-InP heterogeneous integration platform.

**Background/Context:** TFLN technology offers large electro-optical coefficient, wide transparency window, and strong optical confinement, enabling devices like ultra-wideband modulators and quantum sources. However, TFLN does not natively provide lasers or photodiodes. Previous attempts included amorphous silicon photodetectors on TFLN (10 MHz bandwidth, 22-37 mA/W responsivity, 635-850 nm range) and a die-bonded photodiode with 80-GHz bandwidth and 0.6-A/W responsivity. This work surpasses these with 110 GHz bandwidth, matching the state-of-the-art TFLN modulator bandwidth.

**Device Design:** The MUTC Epi stack features a p-down structure grown by MOCVD on semi-insulating InP substrate. Key design elements include: 120-nm total absorption region (100 nm graded doped + 20 nm depleted), a 20-nm n-doped cliff layer, a 120-nm drift layer, a p-doped sacrificial layer for electron velocity overshoot, and a 280-nm InGaAsP p-contact layer that also acts as an optical coupling layer. The LN waveguide was 600 nm thick (300 nm slab, ~1 μm width, ~63° sidewall slope). Devices were fabricated with active areas of 2×6, 2×8, 2×10, 2×12, and 2×14 μm².

**Fabrication Process:** (1) Dry etching of LN waveguide and passive components; (2) wafer bonding of InP/InGaAs wafer onto pre-patterned TFLN wafer; (3) InP substrate removal via mechanical thinning and wet etching; (4) N-mesa etch using dry + selective wet etching; (5) P-mesa etch; (6) SU-8 base for CPW pad deposition; (7) metal electrode electroplating and lift-off. Self-alignment was used to ensure precise active region/waveguide alignment.

**Measurement Results:**
- Dark current: approximately 1 nA at −4 V bias
- Internal responsivities at 1,550 nm: 0.4, 0.48, 0.5, 0.54, and 0.55 A/W for lengths 6–14 μm (consistent with simulations)
- 3-dB bandwidths on 50-Ω load: 110, 105, 100, 101, and 97 GHz for active areas of 2×6, 2×8, 2×10, 2×12, and 2×14 μm², respectively
- Transit-time-limited bandwidth estimated at 153 GHz; carrier transit time ~2.9 fs
- Bandwidth limited by carrier transit time for devices below 20 μm²; limited by RC constant above 20 μm²
- Devices exhibit low junction capacitance but relatively large series resistance dominated by p-mesa resistance

**PAM4 System Demonstration:** The photodiodes were successfully applied in a four-level pulse amplitude modulation (PAM4) data-receiving system, achieving error-free transmission at 10, 20, and 32 Gbaud. For 32 Gbaud PAM4, BER remained below the 20% soft-decision FEC limit (2.4×10⁻²) when received optical power exceeded −16 dBm, and below the 7% hard-decision FEC limit (3.8×10⁻³) when power exceeded −10 dBm.

**Discussion/Limitations & Future Work:** Bandwidth is limited by carrier transit time and large series resistance on the p-mesa. Improvements suggested include optimizing absorption layer thickness, adding a diffusion block layer, and adding an InGaAs layer as a p-contact to reduce contact resistance—potentially boosting total bandwidth to 200 GHz. Responsivity is limited by intrinsic absorption of the metal stack; a thicker optimized cladding layer could mitigate this.

**Funding:** National Key Research and Development Program (2022YFB2803800); Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities (2682022CX025).

The work demonstrates the potential of wafer-level heterogeneous integration for massive-scale, multi-function, high-performance TFLN photonic integrated circuits, with applications in ultra-high-speed optical communications, microwave photonics, and quantum photonics.

<webpage_content>
Guided modes of thin-film lithium niobate slabs Manfred Hammer*, Henna Farheen, Jens F¨ orstner Theoretical Electrical Engineering, Paderborn University, Paderborn, Germany Abstract: Dielectric slab waveguides made of thin-film-lithium-niobate (TFLN) media are consid-ered, for operation in the linear regime. We outline and implement a largely analytic procedure for rigorous modal analysis of three-layer slabs with birefringent, anisotropic core. For Z-cut wave-guides, the slab eigenmode problem separates into uncoupled sets of scalar equations for TE and TM modes. Slabs in X-cut configuration support mostly mildly hybrid eigenmodes, with clear pre-dominant TE or TM polarization, and with effective indices that depend on the propagation direction of the modes, relative to the crystal axes. Strong hybridization can be observed for near degenerate modes in singular configurations without vertical symmetry, or in symmetric slabs where two nearly degenerate modes are of the same symmetry class. Dispersion curves for slab thickness and propa-gation angle are discussed, for slabs with oxide and air cover.
Keywords: photonics, integrated optics, thin-film-lithium-niobate, lithium-niobate-on-insulator, X-cut, Z-cut, anisotropic slab waveguide, oblique propagation, eigenmodes, analytic mode solver.
1 Introduction Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) or lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) [1–4] can be counted among the currently most popular technological platforms for integrated photonic circuits. Applications include fields such as photonic quantum systems [5, 6], optical quantum computing [7], or the processing of single photon states [8, 9]. The technology relies on dielectric waveguides with cores made of lithium-niobate (LiNbO3, LN), where the interest in this crystalline medium is motivated by its favorable electrooptic and nonlinear properties [10–12]. Fairly standardized TFLN slabs are available that typically consist of a thin LN slice carried by a silica buffer layer. Channel waveguides are formed by appropriately shaping the LN core. The waveguides provide a comparably large refractive index contrast with correspondingly strong field confinement, and therefore allow for rather compact integrated photonic circuitry.
As it is customary in integrated optics, the design of components relies heavily on numerical simulations, where in many cases the modal properties of the basic slab system forms a convenient starting point. For waveguides made of isotropic media, the theory is covered by standard textbooks [13–15] in the field, and respective slab mode solvers are readily available [16]. The anisotropic, birefringent LN slices embedded in the TFLN slabs, however, are characterized by a tensor relative permittivity. A few related results concern indiffused LN slab waveguides with gradient refractive index profiles [17], analyzed in terms of polynomial power series. Classically, the light propagation through anisotropic slabs has been modelled by certain types of coupled mode theory, based on modal solutions for isotropic waveguides [18]. More recent results tackle the slab mode problem by numerical means, through discretization with finite differences or finite elements [19–21]. At the time of writing, we did not find a reliable, preferably predominantly analytic, theoretical study that covers the guided modes of typical TFLN slabs. This is what we want to provide with this paper. The study led to an online tool [22] that covers most of our present results. Using that solver, the numerical data on TFLN slab modes in Refs. [19–21] can be re-computed in minutes.
Beyond a general interest in the guidance properties of the TFLN slabs, and the benchmarking of alterna-tive simulation techniques, the present results will be relevant for establishing limits in the modal analysis of piecewise slab-like channel waveguides, and in particular for determining the leakage properties of rib or ridge structures [20, 23, 24]. Refs. [19–21] examine slab modes in preparation for the subsequent numerical design of LNOI channels. The latter are often discussed in terms of effective index techniques [25, 26], that reduce scattering or eigenvalue problems into approximate models of a lower spatial dimension. Also here the present solutions for TFLN slab modes should provide a firm basis. Further, with a view to application areas where *Paderborn University, FG Theoretical Electrical Engineering Warburger Straße 100, 33098 Paderborn, Germany Phone: ++49(0)5251/60-3560 Fax: ++49(0)5251/60-3524 E-mail: manfred.hammer@uni-paderborn.de 1 low propagation losses are highly relevant [8,27], one might envision integrated photonic circuits that operate on the basis of “semi-guided waves” [28–31], i.e. that rely entirely on slab modes directly.
To that end, we investigate rigorous, mostly analytic solutions for three layer TFLN slab waveguides in X-cut and Z-cut configurations, for operation in the linear regime. Section 2 clarifies these terms, introduces appro-priate coordinates, and states the optical properties of the media involved, in particular the tensor permittivity of the LN core. Next, in Section 3 we discuss the details of the modal analysis procedure, and comment on its im-plementation. A few general properties of the modes in question can be worked out directly by examination of the previous theory. These are summarized in Section 4. In the last Sections 5, 6 we review our computational results for TFLN slabs in X-cut and Z-cut configurations at a typical telecom wavelength.
The present findings are prospectively relevant also in a context of nonlinear optics, specifically for second harmonic generation (SHG) [32] or parametric down conversion (PDC) [9]. Besides the longer wavelength as-sociated with the pump (SHG) or signal/idler (PDC), a second, shorter signal (SHG) or pump (PDC) wavelength needs to be considered. Therefore, we include results for half of the former target wavelength in Appendix A.
When compared to standard isotropic waveguides, the most notable feature of the TFLN slabs is a coupling between polarizations, driven by the nonzero off-diagonal elements of the permittivity in X-cut configurations at oblique propagation angles. In Appendix B we show that this effect, and also the shifts of effective index levels, can be understood reasonably well in terms of coupled mode theory (CMT, [13, 33–35]). The findings might provide hints on the possibilities and limitations of respective CMT modelling of TFLN channel waveguides.
2 TFLN slab waveguides At present, two distinct types of thin film lithium niobate slabs are discussed for use in integrated photonic circuitry. Their different optical properties originate from the manufacturing process, where the thin films are cut from the birefringent bulk lithium niobate (LN) medium [1] along planes that are either perpendicular to one of the ordinary, optically equivalent X- and Y -axes of the crystal, or perpendicular to its extraordinary Z-axis. Correspondingly, the samples are termed X-cut or Z-cut. Fig. 1 illustrates the embedding of the LN thin films as core layers in photonic slab waveguides, and the respective orientation of the optical axes.
Y X Z z' x, x' y' z y θ (a) Y Z X z' x, x' y' z y θ (b) Figure 1: Oblique guided light propagation in three layer TFLN slab waveguides, X-cut (a) and Z-cut configurations (b), schematically. The (linear) relative permittivity of the lithium niobate films [11] is expressed with respect to this slab system. 3.3 Interface conditions To that end, we now consider the conditions of continuity for the electromagnetic field components at the two interfaces that form the slab waveguide. These are interfaces between nonmagnetic media without free charges, where, for an optical field in modal form (10), the transverse components Ey, Ez, Hy, Hz of the electric and magnetic fields, and the normal components of the dielectric displacement ϵ0(ˆ ϵE)x and the magnetic induction µ0Hx are continuous. Inspection of Eqs. (12) shows that all conditions are satisfied, if the principal functions and their field-coupled partial derivatives, the quantities e, h, ∂xe, 1 ϵz (∂xh −ikδe), (21) are continuous at both interfaces. The last coupled term implements the continuity of Ez. By evaluating and equating the alternatives of the field template (20) on both sides of the two interfaces at x = 0 and x = d, for each of the four quantities (21), one arrives at a linear system of equations M(β) A = 0 (22) with an 8×8-matrix M (expressions for elements not given) that operates on the vector A of amplitudes that have been introduced in Eq. (20).
6 Trivial solutions A = 0 of the homogeneous system (22) are not of interest in the present context. By con-struction, however, the trial value β enters all equations and procedures beyond Eqs. (13) that lead to the field ansatz (20). Based on the local wavenumbers κs,j,c and eigenstates ej, hj, the entire matrix M can be viewed as a function of this quantity. Guided modes are thus determined by identifying values β where the system (22) permits a nonzero solution A, i.e. where M becomes singular. This condition can be viewed as the “transverse resonance condition” for the present anisotropic slab waveguides.
3.4 Solver procedure Roughly, our present solver relies on the following pragmatic procedure. Given a trial value β, eigenvalues of the matrix M(β) are computed numerically. With those, M can be assigned a “singularity level” T(β) in the form of the absolute value of the product of these eigenvalues. This turns out to be a quantity that depends smoothly on β. The transverse resonance condition is satisfied if T(β) = 0; in that case β represents a valid propagation constant. Numerical means are applied to find these roots.
The maximum of the outer refractive indices, and the larger one of the directional refractive indices of the core, establish an interval [max{ns, nc}, max{ne, no}] for potential effective indices N = β/k of guided modes.
Over this interval, we scan T(β) for configurations that bracket a minimum, with a suitably small stepsize in the trial value β. Zeroes in T are identified by means of a standard search algorithm (bisection, golden section search [39]). After convergence, values β are accepted as valid propagation constants, if their minimum levels T(β) fall below a certain threshold.
Once a value for β is accepted, the eigenvector A for the eigenvalue of M(β) with smallest absolute value determines the coefficients Ac e, . . . , As h in Eq. (20). Then the mode profile can be assembled by computing subsequently the local wavenumbers κs,j,c through Eqs. (17) and (19), next the principal functions in the form (20), and finally all electromagnetic profile components (12).
3.4.1 Remarks In principle, fully analytical solutions of the eigenvalue problem (17) for the local coupled solutions in the core layer can be obtained, e.g. with the help of a computer algebra system. These, however, tend to be rather lengthy and convoluted. Further, a few steps ahead, we need to resort to numerical root finding / minimization procedures anyway. We therefore opt for the numerical eigenvalue solver. Alternatively, we use the analytical expressions (not given here) for the eigenvalues κ and solve the associated, then singular, system (17) for q and r numerically by singular value decomposition (SVD, [39]).
Likewise, a procedure for complex numerical singular value decomposition, or its real “equivalent” [39], can also be applied to evaluate the “singularity level” T of the system matrix M in (22). The product of the singular values then defines the level T, the associated column of one of the decomposition matrices establishes the solution for A.
Starting with Eq. (11), it should be possible to establish a “purely real”, and therefore potentially more efficient, alternative formalism, if one introduces principal functions e = √ϵ0Ey and h′ = i√µ0Hy = ih. Eqs. (13) are replaced by real equations that couple e and h′, for which one then looks for real solutions. Correspondingly, the mode profiles in Sections 5 and 6 can be adjusted by a complex amplitude such that all components are either purely real or purely imaginary, at all positions x, as shown in the figures. Such a “real” approach, however, would require to handle the variants of harmonic or exponential behavior of the principal fields in Eq. (20) (core layer) explicitly. We therefore stick with the partly redundant, but more convenient complex expressions as discussed above.
For δ = 0, Eqs. (11) split into two entirely separate sets of equations, one for TE modes, with principal function e, and another set for TM modes, with principal function h. This concerns all Z-cut waveguides, and, according to Eq. (8), also X-cut configurations for propagation angles θ = jπ/2, for integer j. If interest is in those cases only, one can set up a simpler, more efficient, and more robust algorithm by following standard procedures for the modal analysis of slab waveguides made of isotropic media.
The eigenvalue problem for slabs that are, in the present coordinates, mirror symmetric with respect to the plane x = d/2 (“vertically symmetric”) yields eigenfunctions that are of a definite parity with respect to that plane.
7 The slab modes satisfy conditions of either perfect magnetic conductor (PMC) or perfect electric conductor (PEC) type at x = d/2. If one is interested in these symmetric slabs only, the computational domain can be restricted to an interval x ∈[d/2, ∞], requiring normalizable fields that obey PMC or PEC boundary conditions at the core center. Also here one would be led to a simpler, more efficient and more robust solver. This would be the proper way to address symmetric configurations with degenerate eigenmodes, as considered e.g. in Fig. 5(f).
4 Properties of slab modes The propagation angle θ enters the previous theory through the definitions (8) of ϵy, ϵz, and δ only, where all functions involved are π-periodic. Consequently, one obtains identical effective indices and mode profiles for propagation in opposite directions at angles θ and θ ± π. Note, however, that the associated fields differ, if viewed from a perspective of the slab, due to the rotation of the wave coordinates (cf. Fig. 1).
A change of signs θ →−θ in the propagation angle leads to modes with equal effective indices, but with profiles that differ in relative signs of TE and TM related components. This can be realized by inspecting Eqs. (13) and (21): If functions e, h and eigenvalue N for angle θ and related δ are available, a profile e, −h satisfies the equations for −δ, i.e. for negative propagation angle −θ, with the same effective index N. Likewise, a change of propagation angles θ →π −θ yields modes with opposite relative signs of e and h (this latter operation can be seen as a combination θ →−θ →−θ + π). These properties imply that the coupling between e and h vanishes at θ = jπ/2, for all integer j, as observed in one of the remarks in Section 3.4.1.
In slabs of large thickness d, one can expect that the profiles of the modes of lowest orders flatten out, with only small changes of the principal functions along x. In that regime, Eqs. (13) reduce to the approximate equations (k2(ϵy −δ2/ϵz) −β2)e ≈0 and (k2 −β2/ϵx)h ≈0. Consequently, for TE modes with nonzero e, and for TM modes with nonzero h, the effective indices approach the limits N − − − → d→∞ q ϵy −δ2/ϵz (TE), N − − − → d→∞ √ϵx (TM).

4.1 Modal orthogonality and power We assume that a set of guided modes in the form (10) of the same waveguide, and for the same wavelength, are at hand, given in terms of profiles Em, Hm and a real propagation constant βm for a mode with index m.
By construction, these fields are integrable over the cross section axis x. Each mode can be assigned its power Pm = 1 2 Re Z (E∗ m × Hm)z dx = 1 4 Z (E∗ mxHmy −E∗ myHmx + EmxH∗ my −EmyH∗ mx) dx (24) per lateral (y) unit length by integrating the z-component of the time-averaged Poynting vector associated with the field (10). Eq. (24) serves for a normalization of the modes, through scaling of the coefficients A in Eq. (20).
Similar to standard isotropic slab waveguides [13,40], orthogonality properties can be established for the modes of the TFLN slabs. As a starting point, we consider two electromagnetic fields E1, H1 and E2, H2 that solve Eqs. (6) for permittivity functions ˆ ϵ1 and ˆ ϵ2. These fields satisfy the “reciprocity identity” ∇· (E∗ 1 × H2 + E2 × H∗ 1) = iωϵ0E∗ 1 · (ˆ ϵ† 1 −ˆ ϵ2)E2.
(25) Here the symbol † denotes the adjoint. Our TFLN slab modes are supported by the same lossless and reciprocal waveguides, with Hermitian permittivity (7). Hence, if one specializes Eq. (25) to a pair of the former modal 8 fields with indices l and m, the right hand side becomes zero. Further, by evaluating the divergence on the left hand side for the y-independent fields, and integrating over x, where boundary terms vanish with the mode profiles for x →±∞, we arrive at the identity (βl −βm) Z (E∗ lxHmy −E∗ lyHmx + EmxH∗ ly −EmyH∗ lx) dx = 0.

(28) According to Eq. (26), the property holds for each pair l, m of non-degenerate (βl ̸= βm, if l ̸= m) modal solutions. This includes all cases of near degeneracies of modes (“avoided crossings”) observed in Section 5 for X-cut slabs at oblique propagation angles. Eq. (28) is formally identical to respective expressions for common lossless isotropic multilayer slab waveguides [40].
However, as we shall see in Sections 5, 6, in the present framework of combined solutions of Eqs. (13), also instances of strict degeneracies of modes occur, in the form of actual crossings of dispersion curves. On the one hand, that concerns the Z-cut slabs and X-cut configurations with crystal-axis-aligned propagation.
These support strict TE and TM modes with profiles of the form E = (0, Ey, 0), H = (Hx, 0, Hz) (TE) and E = (Ex, 0, Ez), H = (0, Hy, 0) (TM). The product (27) between any TE and TM modes l, m is zero, such that the orthogonality relation (28) holds in the form as given also for potentially degenerate modes of this kind.
On the other hand, we observe strict degeneracies for vertically symmetric X-cut waveguides (cf. the remarks at the end of Section 3.4.1), also at oblique angles, for hybrid modes that are of different symmetry classes.
Each of the terms in a product (27) of those modes combines one field that is even and another that is odd under mirroring at x = d/2, such that the integrals of all terms vanish individually. Hence, also for these modes, orthogonality can be stated in the form of Eq. (28).

Nevertheless we observe that, in most of the many configurations examined in Section 5 and Appendix A, the modes are rather well polarized in either TE (y) or TM direction (x, z). Since the largest part of the respective mode fields is contained in the thick core layers, these limits are deter-mined by the core properties only, i.e. apply to waveguides both with and without cover layers. The convergent behavior leads to configurations where, for large d beyond a certain critical value, the lowest order TM mode is the fundamental field, with the highest effective index. When comparing the data for slabs with air cover in Fig. 4 and with silica cladding in Fig. 5, at a first glance one notices only minor quantitative differences. Effective index levels at the same thickness are slightly shifted. For growing d, higher order modes appear at different thickness values, where, unlike for the slabs with air cover, there is no cutoff thickness for the fundamental modes in the symmetric silica covered slabs.
Major qualitative differences, however, are observed where curves come close, with (nearly) degenerate modes that differ in polarization elsewhere. As an example, parts (f) of both figures show respective zoom-ins of the panels (c) for θ = 45◦, for thickness intervals where the effective index curves for the fundamental TE and TM modes are close. For the non symmetric slabs with air cover in Fig. 4, the curves do not intersect, but “repel” each other. Close to these avoided crossings, the modes are pronouncedly hybrid, as shown by the polarization ratios in the lower part of Fig. 4(f). The gray marker color indicates a similar behavior for other instances of near degeneracy of these or other modes, for all oblique propagation angles θ ̸= 0◦, 90◦.
On the contrary, for the vertically symmetric slabs with SiO2 cladding in Fig. 5, panel (f) reveals that the curves actually intersect. No particular change in polarization ratio happens near the crossing; the modes involved are predominantly TE or TM polarized just as at other thicknesses. Given the theory of Section 3, we state these findings here as observations only, as results of the solver procedures as described.
Some more intuitive explanations can be found along a line of arguments as in Refs. [24,41]. On the one hand, as argued already in Section 3.4.1, in case of the vertically symmetric structures with silica cover, the mode eigenvalue problem for the full slab can be separated into two distinct problems for half the cross section, where one set is governed by PMC boundary conditions at x = d/2, while the other satisfies PEC conditions at that position. According to Fig. 9, the modes involved in the crossing are of different symmetry classes, i.e. would be solutions of distinct problems (for a solver implemented in this way). There is therefore no reason for an interaction of any kind.
On the other hand, as elaborated further in Section B, one can examine the slab system from a viewpoint of coupled mode theory [13,33]. The permittivity tensor (7) is split into a diagonal part ˆ ϵ0 and a perturbation ∆ˆ ϵ that includes only the off-diagonal elements δ. Basis modes of strict TE and TM polarization are computed for the permittivity ˆ ϵ0. The perturbation is expected to drive the interaction between modes 1, 2 through coupling integrals of the form ∼ R (E∗ 1 · ∆ˆ ϵ E2) dx, where the integral extends over the core layer (cf. Eq. (34) in Appendix B). In case of a strict TE mode 1, with zero components Ex, Ez, and and a strict TM mode 2, with vanishing Ey, the integral reduces to the simpler expression ∼ R (δ E∗ 1,y E2,z) dx. For TE and TM modes of the same order, the components involved are of different symmetry with respect to x = d/2 (see e.g. the fields in Fig. 15), while δ is a constant in this context, such that the coupling integral cancels out. The symmetry of the slab system suppresses the hybridization.
Note that here we consider symmetric slabs of moderate thickness (cf. the range for d in Figs. 5 and 12(b)), where, for the material parameters as considered, intersections are observed only for TE- and TM-like modes of the same order, but with different parity. The situation changes at larger thicknesses. As an example, we focus on the N-vs.d-curves for the lowest order TE and first order TM modes in Fig. 5(b). At d = 2 µm, these modes have effective indices of N = 2.1108 (TE0) and N = 2.0593 (TM1), while for growing thickness, according 11 to Eq. (23), the curves approach the levels 2.1369 (TE0) and no = 2.1837 (TM1). An avoided crossing with two strongly hybrid modes appears around d = 2.92 µm (not shown). In that case both modes are of the same symmetry class, such that the former arguments on the suppression of the interaction do not apply.

args.summary:
This paper presents a rigorous, largely analytic procedure for modal analysis of three-layer thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) slab waveguides in X-cut and Z-cut configurations, operating in the linear regime. The research was conducted at Paderborn University (Theoretical Electrical Engineering) by Manfred Hammer, Henna Farheen, and Jens Förstner.

Key points:

**Context:** TFLN/lithium-niobate-on-insulator (LNOI) is among the most popular platforms for integrated photonic circuits, with applications in photonic quantum systems, optical quantum computing, and single photon state processing. The crystalline LN medium offers favorable electrooptic and nonlinear properties.

**Methodology:** The authors developed an analytic mode solver that handles birefringent, anisotropic slab cores. For Z-cut waveguides, the eigenmode problem separates into uncoupled scalar equations for TE and TM modes. X-cut slabs support mostly mildly hybrid eigenmodes with clear predominant TE or TM polarization, and effective indices that depend on propagation direction relative to crystal axes (propagation angle θ). The solver reduces the problem to an 8×8 matrix M(β) whose singularity (transverse resonance condition) determines guided mode propagation constants. Numerical eigenvalue solving and root-finding (bisection, golden section search) are employed.

**Key physical results:**
- Strong hybridization occurs for near-degenerate modes in singular configurations without vertical symmetry, or in symmetric slabs where two nearly degenerate modes are of the same symmetry class.
- For large core thicknesses, effective indices approach limits: TE → √(εy − δ²/εz) and TM → √εx (with values no/ne depending on cut and propagation angle).
- Modes exhibit power orthogonality, formally identical to standard isotropic multilayer slabs.
- The polarization hybridization ratio Π quantifies TE/TM balance (Π=1 pure TE, Π=0 pure TM, Π=1/2 balanced).
- X-cut slabs with air cover show avoided crossings with pronounced hybridization of near-degenerate modes at oblique angles, while vertically symmetric silica-covered slabs show actual curve intersections with no hybridization due to different symmetry classes of the modes involved.
- Z-cut slabs have propagation-angle-independent permittivity; TE and TM modes fully separate with no hybridization even at degeneracies.

**Material parameters:** At λ=1.55 µm, refractive indices are ns=1.4483 (silica buffer), nc=1.0 or ns (cover), no=2.1837, ne=2.1220. At λ=0.775 µm, no=2.2242, ne=2.1565. Results include both air and SiO2 cover configurations.

**Applications:** Findings are relevant for benchmarking alternative simulation techniques, establishing limits in modal analysis of channel waveguides, determining leakage properties of rib/ridge structures, effective index techniques, semi-guided wave operation, and nonlinear optics (SHG, PDC). An online tool was developed covering most results. Coupled mode theory (CMT) interpretations are provided in an appendix.

Slabs in X-cut configuration support mostly mildly hybrid eigenmodes, with clear predominant TE or TM polarization, and with effective indices that depend on the propagation direction of the modes, relative to the crystal axes."

## Laserlab-Europe Talk: Femtosecond laser fabricated glass photonic integrated circuits for stuctured illumination microscopy, 16 September 2026

16 September 2026

**Title: Femtosecond laser fabricated glass photonic integrated circuits for stuctured illumination microscopy**  
**Speaker: Francesca Bragheri ([The Institute for Photonics and Nanotechnologies](https://www.ifn.cnr.it/), National Research Council)**  
**Date: Wednesday, 16 September, 16:00 Central European Summer Time (CEST)**

Structured illumination microscopy (SIM) is a powerful imaging technique that enables resolution enhancement beyond the diffraction limit while preserving low phototoxicity and compatibility with conventional fluorescence microscopy. Traditional SIM implementations, however, typically rely on complex and bulky optical systems, limiting their robustness and widespread adoption.

In this talk, femtosecond laser micromachining (FLM) will be presented as a versatile enabling technology for the fabrication of three-dimensional integrated photonic circuits in glass for structured illumination microscopy. By inducing localized refractive index modifications inside transparent materials, FLM enables the direct writing of buried optical waveguides, directional couplers, and interferometric structures with true three-dimensional design freedom and micrometric precision. When combined with selective chemical etching (FLICE), the same technology also allows the fabrication of reflective micro-optical elements, including flat and curved mirrors, which are subsequently metal-coated to guide the beams and generate structured illumination patterns. Thermal phase shifters integrated onto the chip surface provide fast, dynamic control of the relative phase between the interfering beams without mechanical movement, enabling the pattern translation required for SIM image reconstruction.

Different device architectures will be presented, ranging from compact two-output interferometers to more sophisticated multi-beam photonic circuits capable of generating both two- and three-dimensional interference patterns. The resulting glass chips can be directly interfaced with conventional widefield microscopes, transforming them into compact and reconfigurable SIM platforms. Overall, the presented work highlights the unique capabilities of femtosecond laser micromachining for the rapid prototyping and fabrication of complex three dimensional integrated photonic systems, opening new opportunities for compact, alignment-free, and field deployable super-resolution imaging devices.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694)Abstract

We report on fabrication of high-Q lithium niobate (LN) whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) microresonators suspended on silica pedestals by femtosecond laser direct writing followed by focused ion beam (FIB) milling. The micrometer-scale (diameter ~82 μm) LN resonator possesses a Q factor of ~2.5 × 10 5 around 1550 nm wavelength. The combination of femtosecond laser direct writing with FIB enables high-efficiency, high-precision nanofabrication of high-Q crystalline microresonators.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694)Results and Discussion

### Characterization LN microresonator

The details on the fabrication of LN microresonator can be found in **Methods**. The thicknesses of the LN thin film and silica layer were 700 nm and 2 μm, respectively. Briefly speaking, we first fabricated a cylindrical post with a diameter of ~59 μm and a total height of ~15 μm (corresponding to a cutting depth of 12 μm into the LN substrate beneath the silica), which is shown in [Fig. 2(a)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694#f2), by femtosecond laser micromachining. Since the roughness on the laser ablated sidewall of the cylindrical post is on the order of a few tens of nanometers, which is too poor for high-Q microresonator application, FIB milling was used to smooth the periphery of the cylindrical post. The FIB milling was operated twice, beginning with a coarse milling and followed with a fine one. In the coarse milling, a 30-keV ion beam with a beam current of 4 nA was used to polish the periphery; whereas in the fine milling, the beam current was reduced to 1 nA. The milling was stopped at a depth of 3 μm from the top surface. The total FIB milling process took ~15 min. After the FIB milling, the diameter of the microresonator was reduced to 55 μm. Most importantly, the LN microresonator shows a highly smooth edge, as evidenced in its scanning electron microscope (SEM) image ([Fig. 2(b)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694#f2)). [Figure 2(c)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694#f2) shows another cylindrical post with a smaller diameter of 33 μm after the FIB milling. In principle, microresonators of diameters below 10 μm can be fabricated using our technique. It should be noted that the FIB process frequently induces the creation of lattice defects (i.e., vacancies and atomic nuclei), leading to the formation of amorphous material due to keV ion beam side dose or lateral ion straggle at the periphery of the microresonator. However, such defects are not critical in our experiments, since no free carrier is involved in the nonlinear generation process.

To form the freestanding microresonator (i.e., a thin disk sitting on top of a micro-pedestal), the silica layer sandwiched between the LN thin film and the LN substrate needs to be selectively etched to form the micro-pedestal under the LN microdisk. Therefore, the sample was immersed in a solution of 5% HF diluted with water for 8 min to form the silica pedestal. The upper LN microdisk suspended on the pedestal serves as the high-Q microresonator.

At last, a thermal annealing (500°C for 2 hrs in air) was applied to further smooth the rim of the LN thin disk. It should be mentioned that since the top and bottom surfaces of the LN thin film naturally possess an ultra-high smoothness with a surface roughness as low as 0.35 nm[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694#b17), a high Q factor of the LN microresonator can be ensured after smoothing its rim. As shown by the side view of the freestanding microresonator in the inset in [Fig. 2(d)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694#f2), an air gap between the LN microdisk and LN substrate can clearly be seen.

To measure the Q-factor of the fabricated LN microresonators, an evanescent fiber taper coupling method was employed (for details, see **Methods**). The transmitted spectrum measured from the output end of the fiber taper showed a series of sharp dips at the WGM resonant wavelengths. In these measurements, coarse scans over a wide wavelength span were first performed to decide the WGM resonant wavelengths. As an example, the transmission spectrum obtained with the coarse scan with a step size of 1 nm for the 55 μm LN microresonator without annealing is shown in [Fig. 3(a)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694#f3). After the coarse scan, fine scans with a step size of 0.5 pm around the resonant wavelengths were performed to measure the linewidths of the dips indicated by the Lorentzian fit.

The transmission spectra of the fiber taper coupled to the 55 μm microresonators before and after the annealing are shown in [Figs. 3 (b)–(c)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694#f3). The resonance at 1554.28 nm wavelength showed a loaded Q factor of 5.2 × 10 4 ([Fig. 3(b)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694#f3)) of the microresonator before the annealing. After the annealing, the Q factor of the same microresonator was significantly improved to 1.6 × 10 5 around the resonant wavelength of 1554.90 nm, as evidenced in [Fig. 3(c)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694#f3). Furthermore, the Q factor of the microresonator with a diameter of 82 μm was measured to be 2.5 × 10 5 after the annealing process, as indicated in [Fig. 3(d)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694#f3). The result shows that the Q factor increases with the increasing diameter of the fabricated LN microresonator, as a result of radiation loss at the curved surface which has been well described by A. M. Armani et al[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694#b22).

In conclusion, we demonstrate the fabrication of high-Q on-chip LN microresonators on single crystal LN thin film wafer by femtosecond laser 3D micromachining. The Q factor is measured to be 2.5 × 10 5 around 1550 nm wavelength. Since our technique uses high precision ablation of materials with femtosecond laser pulses, it is intrinsically material insensitive. In fact, in the past few years, we have fabricated high-Q optical microresonators in various materials such as fused silica[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694#b23), an active Nd: glass[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694#b19), and CaF 2 crystal[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694#b20). It should be noticed that although femtosecond laser micromachining allows for efficient and precision ablation of dielectric materials, the surface roughness is typically too high for high-Q microresonator applications. The incorporation of FIB milling provides an ideal solution without spoiling the flexibility in femtosecond laser microfabrication. We envisage that our technique can be extended for fabricating high-Q on-chip microresonators on various types of dielectric materials.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694)Methods

### Fabrication of LN microresonator

A Ti: sapphire femtosecond laser source (Coherent, Inc., center wavelength: ~800 nm, pulse width: ~40 fs, repetition rate: 1 kHz) was used for fabricating LN microresonators. A variable neutral density filter was used to carefully adjust the average power. An objective lens with a numerical aperture (NA) of 0.80 was used to produce the tightly focused spot with a diameter of ~1 μm. The laser beam then focused into the LN thin film sample immersed in water. The sample was mounted on a computer-controlled XYZ translation stage with 1-μm resolution. A charged coupled device (CCD) connecting with the computer was installed above the objective lens to monitor the fabrication process in real time.

A layer-by-layer annular ablation from the top surface to internal substrate with 1 μm interval between the adjacent layers was adopted, so that the ablation always occurred at the interface between the water and the material. In this manner, the ablation debris can be more efficiently removed with the assistance of water. The laser power was chosen to be 0.35 mW for ablation in both the LN thin film and the LN substrate beneath the silica layer, whereas the laser power was raised to 1 mW for ablation in silica layer, because the ablation thresholds of LN crystal and silica glass are different.

### Measurement of Q-factor

The Q factors were measured by the fiber taper coupling method. An external cavity continuous wave tunable laser diode (New Focus, Model: 6528-LN; output power: 0.08 mW; wavelength range: 1510 nm ~ 1620 nm; step resolution: 0.1 pm) was coupled into the fiber taper. The fiber taper with a diameter of ~1 μm was home made by heating and stretching a section of a commercial optical fiber (Corning, SMF-28). A transient optical power detector was used to measure the transmission spectra at the output end of the fiber taper. The detector can record the light signal over a 100 nm-wavelength-span with 0.5 pm wavelength resolution and 0.015 dB power accuracy in less than 1 second. A piezo-stage was used to control the relative position between the microresonator and the fiber taper waist. The critical coupling between the WGMs and the evanescent field of the fiber taper can be achieved by carefully adjusting the gap between the fiber taper and the microresonator. We used two CCD cameras whose optical axes are arranged to be perpendicular and parallel to the equatorial plane of the microresonators to simultaneously acquire both the side-view and top-view images of the microresonators coupled with the fiber taper. In the fine scan for measuring the Q factor, a slow scan speed of 2 nm/s was chosen.

args.summary:
This scientific article, published in Scientific Reports on January 28, 2015 (PMCID: PMC4308694, PMID: 25627294, DOI: 10.1038/srep08072), reports on the fabrication of high-quality (high-Q) lithium niobate (LN) whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) microresonators using a combination of femtosecond laser direct writing and focused ion beam (FIB) milling.

METHODOLOGY:
- LN thin film (700 nm) and silica layer (2 μm) on an LN substrate were used
- A cylindrical post (~59 μm diameter, ~15 μm height) was first created by femtosecond laser micromachining (Ti:sapphire laser, ~800 nm center wavelength, ~40 fs pulse width, 1 kHz repetition rate, 0.35 mW for LN ablation, 1 mW for silica)
- FIB milling was performed twice (coarse milling with 30-keV ion beam at 4 nA, then fine milling at 1 nA) to smooth the periphery, reducing the diameter to 55 μm
- The silica layer was selectively etched using 5% HF solution for 8 minutes to form a freestanding microdisk on a silica pedestal
- Thermal annealing at 500°C for 2 hours in air further smoothed the rim of the LN disk
- Q factors were measured using an evanescent fiber taper coupling method

RESULTS:
- The 82 μm diameter LN resonator achieved a Q factor of ~2.5 × 10⁵ around 1550 nm wavelength
- A 55 μm resonator showed Q factor improvement from 5.2 × 10⁴ (before annealing) to 1.6 × 10⁵ (after annealing)
- Q factor increases with increasing diameter due to reduced radiation loss at the curved surface
- Microresonators below 10 μm diameter can potentially be fabricated using this technique
- The top and bottom surfaces of the LN thin film naturally have ultra-high smoothness with surface roughness as low as 0.35 nm

CONCLUSION:
The technique combines the flexibility and material insensitivity of femtosecond laser micromachining with the precision of FIB milling, enabling high-efficiency, high-precision nanofabrication of high-Q crystalline microresonators. The authors have previously used similar techniques to fabricate microresonators in fused silica, active Nd:glass, and CaF₂ crystals, and envisage extending this approach to various dielectric materials.

The work was supported by the National Basic Research Program of China (No. 2014CB921300), NSFC grants, and Fundamental Research Funds for Central Universities. Authors include Jintian Lin, Yingxin Xu, Zhiwei Fang, Min Wang, Jiangxin Song, Nengwen Wang, Lingling Qiao, Wei Fang, and Ya Cheng.
args.key_excerpts: "The micrometer-scale (diameter ~82 μm) LN resonator possesses a Q factor of ~2.5 × 10⁵ around 1550 nm wavelength. The combination of femtosecond laser direct writing with FIB enables high-efficiency, high-precision nanofabrication of high-Q crystalline microresonators."

# FemtoLAB All-in-one R&D platform for laser micromachining

FemtoLAB is a femtosecond laser micromachining workstation. A perfect choice for scientific laboratories and R&D centers requiring custom solutions for various tasks.

FemtoLAB laser workstation offers combined laser micromachining processes at a submicron resolution and can perform a variety of applications.

#### Key applications:

* Surface and volume micro- and nano- structuring

This webpage is the product page for FemtoLAB, an all-in-one femtosecond laser micromachining workstation manufactured by WOP | Workshop of Photonics (Altechna R&D, UAB), based in Vilnius, Lithuania (Mokslininku st. 6A, LT-08412).

**Product Overview:**
FemtoLAB is a femtosecond laser micromachining workstation designed for scientific laboratories and R&D centers requiring custom solutions. It offers combined laser micromachining processes at submicron resolution (smallest feature size of 200 nm) and supports both planar samples and optical fibers machining.

**Key Applications:**
- Surface and volume micro- and nano-structuring
- Femtosecond laser ablation (FSLA)
- Laser grooving
- Multiphoton polymerization (MPP) / direct laser writing (DLW)
- Laser cutting & drilling

**Main Features:**
- Fabrication of complex objects with submicron resolution
- High-speed and ultra-high precision micromachining
- Efficient beam delivery and power control
- High-end industrial-grade femtosecond laser
- High-performance galvanometer scanners
- Object movement and laser pulse synchronization in time and space
- Unique software interface controlling all hardware units

**Technical Specifications:**
- Recommended materials: All materials (glass, sapphire, silicon, ceramics, metal, plastic, optical fibers)
- Laser: High power ultrashort pulse IR, Green, UV laser
- Optical path selection: Automated
- Sample size: Up to 160 mm x 160 mm
- Smallest feature size: 200 nm
- Positioning: XYZ mechanical axes, accuracy ±0.3 μm with continuous wafer level patterning
- Scanning: Galvo system for all laser wavelengths
- Vision: Real-time camera with feature recognition
- Metrology: Integrated microscope
- Sample handling: Manual with automatic alignment
- Construction: Granite base with passive vibration isolation
- Dimensions: 1500 x 1350 x 1400 mm (L x W x H)
- Weight: 1100 kg
- Power supply: 2x 220 VAC, 16 A
- Supported file formats: STL, DXF, DWG, AMF, PLT, FAB, BMP, GIF, JPG, JPEG, PNG, TXT, RTF, TEX

**Benefits:** All-in-one platform, combined additive and subtractive processes, 200 nm submicron resolution, full installation/training support, 1-year warranty with after-warranty service.

**Customers (worldwide institutions):** ALPhANOV (Bordeaux), University of Applied Sciences Upper Austria, Technische Universität Berlin (#158 QS), Indian Institute of Technology Bombay (#172), Delft University of Technology (#61), Technische Universität Dresden (#200), Guilin University of Electronic Technology, Shanghai Jiao Tong University (#46), University of Southampton (#78), Swinburne University of Technology (#296), Texas A&M University (#164), Tokyo Institute of Technology (#55), Politecnico di Torino (#325), Tsinghua University (#14), University of Science and Technology of China (#94), Xi'an Technological University, Wuhan University (#194), and Institute for Systems and Computer Engineering, Technology and Science (Portugal). Applications across these institutions include 3D direct laser writing/MPP, surface structuring, laser ablation, micro cutting/drilling, photo-induced etching, FBG writing, nanograting writing, SERS sensors, acoustic sensors, MEMS, and quantum computing waveguides.

**Customer Review:** Luigino Criante, Technology Researcher at Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia Genoa, Italy, gave a positive review noting 10 years of experience with the system: "After 10 years of experience, working with your femtosecond system, my honest opinion is more than positive and we are satisfied with the product. Compared to other systems, ours 'full optional facility' allows us to explore valuable processing on many different materials."

**Related Products:** FemtoLAB KIT (for those with existing laser source), FemtoMPP (optimized for multiphoton polymerization), S-Waveplate (polarization converter), and contract manufacturing services.

The page also includes 13 scientific references (SPIE proceedings, Micromachines, Biofabrication, Optics Materials Express, arXiv papers, etc.) documenting applications of the technology, plus company contact details, ISO 9001 certification, and a downloadable FemtoLAB brochure.
