--- SOURCE 2: Long Low-Loss-Litium Niobate on Insulator Waveguides with Sub-Nanometer Surface Roughness ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6265866

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article from the journal Nanomaterials (Basel), published November 6, 2018 (DOI: 10.3390/nano8110910), titled "Long Low-Loss-Lithium Niobate on Insulator Waveguides with Sub-Nanometer Surface Roughness." The paper, authored by researchers from the Shanghai Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics (Chinese Academy of Sciences) and East China Normal University, including corresponding author Ya Cheng, reports a novel technique for fabricating multi-centimeter-long lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) waveguides with record-low propagation loss.

Key results:
- Achieved propagation loss as low as 0.027 dB/cm in LNOI waveguides, an improvement over the previous state-of-the-art of 0.04 dB/cm.
- Surface roughness (Rq) of 0.452 nm measured via atomic force microscope.
- Fabricated a continuous 11-cm-long optical waveguide (femtosecond laser ablation took 90 minutes).
- Demonstrated a whispering-gallery ring resonator (160 μm diameter) with an intrinsic Q factor of 1.14 × 10^7, loaded Q factor of 5.70 × 10^6, and effective refractive index of 1.79.

Methodology: The fabrication technique involves (1) depositing a 600-nm chromium thin film on LNOI by magnetron sputtering, (2) patterning the Cr film into a hard mask using femtosecond laser ablation (~1 μm focused spot via 100× objective lens with NA 0.7), and (3) chemo-mechanical (CM) polishing to transfer the pattern to the LNOI, followed by an additional low-pressure CM polishing step to improve upper-surface smoothness. The approach avoids ion beam etching (FIB or electron beam writing), which inherently leaves residual sidewall roughness that is difficult to remove and has low throughput. The technique is compatible with optical and electron beam lithography and laser direct writing, enabling high-throughput manufacturing of large-scale LNOI photonic integrated circuits (PICs).

Key context: The paper notes that the measured loss is still one order of magnitude away from the theoretical limit (~10^-3 dB/cm) set by absorption in crystalline LN. Limitations are attributed to radiative loss in the ring resonator, surface contamination, absorptive defects from crystal growth, and residual roughness from CM polishing. The authors suggest that optical lithography (achieving sub-micron or 100-nm patterning) could enable narrower single-mode waveguides for devices such as Mach-Zehnder interferometers and polarization convertors, and that coating with fused silica could tune mode fields and reduce scattering loss. The method promotes fabrication efficiency and reduces manufacturing costs for LNOI PICs, applicable to optical communication and computation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In this paper, we develop a technique for realizing multi-centimeter-long lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) waveguides with a propagation loss as low as 0.027 dB/cm."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Low-loss thin-film periodically poled lithium niobate waveguides fabricated by femtosecond laser photolithography ---
URL: https://opg.optica.org/ol/abstract.cfm?uri=ol-50-13-4310

SUMMARY:
<summary>

The research addresses the problem that dry etching of periodically poled lithium niobate on insulator (PPLNOI) ridge waveguides generates rough sidewalls and etching rate variations in oppositely poled ferroelectric domains, leading to high propagation losses (0.25–1 dB/cm) that limit conversion efficiency and scalable photonic integration. - Average surface roughness of only 0.27 nm

- Efficiency improved to 1742% W⁻¹·cm⁻² at optimal temperature of 59°C

The performance is close to the best conversion efficiency reported in nanophotonic PPLNOI waveguides fabricated by expensive electron-beam lithography followed by dry etching. Authors are affiliated with multiple Chinese institutions including the Shanghai Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics (CAS), East China Normal University, ShanghaiTech University, and others. Data underlying the results are not publicly available but may be obtained from the authors upon reasonable request.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Dry etching of PPLNOI waveguides frequently generates rough sidewalls and variations in the etching rates of oppositely poled lithium niobate ferroelectric domains, leading to relatively high propagation losses (0.25–1 dB/cm), which significantly limits net conversion efficiency and hinders scalable photonic integration."

--- SOURCE 5: Lithium niobate ridged waveguides with smooth vertical sidewalls fabricated by an ultra-precision cutting method ---
URL: https://opg.optica.org/oe/viewmedia.cfm?uri=oe-22-22-27733&seq=0

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (published in Optics Express, November 2014, DOI:10.1364/OE.22.027733) demonstrates the application of ultra-precision cutting to fabricate low-loss ridged LiNbO3 (lithium niobate) waveguides for photonic integrated circuits. The work was conducted by researchers at Kyushu University, The University of Tokyo, and NICT in Japan.

**Methodology:** An 80 nm thick Ti film was deposited on the negative Z surface of a polished LiNbO3 wafer via electron-beam evaporation and diffused at ~1030°C for 6 hours in oxygen to ensure vertical optical confinement. The wafer was cut into 2×2 cm chips using a dicing saw. Ridged waveguides were fabricated using a 5-axis ultra-precision cutting machine (FANUC ROBONANO α-0iB) with a single-crystal diamond cutting tool (50 μm width) operating in ductile mode cutting. Two microgrooves (top-width 50 μm, depth 4 μm) were cut with a feeding depth of 50 nm and cutting speed of 1 mm/min, with tool-tip lapping force kept below 10 mN to avoid breaking the crystal or tool.

**Results:**
- Straight ridged waveguides achieved sidewall verticality of ~88° and ultra-smooth sidewalls.
- Bent ridged waveguides (bending radius 300 μm) were also successfully fabricated with no cracks in the waveguide or diamond tool, demonstrating the ability to make photonic integrated circuits such as micro-ring resonators.
- Maximum depth, minimum width, and bending radius of bent structures: 4.5, 5.5, and 300 μm respectively.
- Surface roughness (RMS) of the sidewall: 4.5 nm (Ra: 3.5 nm) over 2.5 × 10 μm area; bottom of microgroove: RMS 1.4 nm (Ra: 1.1 nm).
- Propagation loss measured by the cut-back method at 1550 nm: ~0.1 dB/cm for TE polarization and ~0.6 dB/cm for TM polarization, well below 1 dB/cm.

**Conclusions:** The ultra-precision cutting method produces low-loss ridged waveguides with smooth vertical sidewalls and enables fabrication of bent structures—something impossible with conventional dicing methods. The technique has significant potential for micromachining ferroelectric materials and fabricating highly confined optical waveguides (ridged waveguides and photonic wires), offering an alternative to etching, ion implantation, and laser ablation approaches that suffer from rough surfaces, structural defects, or limited geometry control.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: Advanced Crystallization Methods for Thin-Film Lithium Niobate and Its Device Applications ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11901258

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Materials (Basel) journal on February 21, 2025 (DOI: 10.3390/ma18050951, PMCID: PMC11901258, PMID: 40077179), titled "Advanced Crystallization Methods for Thin-Film Lithium Niobate and Its Device Applications." The authors are Rongbang Yang, Haoming Wei, Gongbin Tang, Bingqiang Cao, and Kunfeng Chen, affiliated with Shandong University, Qufu Normal University, and University of Jinan in China. The academic editor was Federico Bella.

The review focuses on thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN), which has become a research hotspot due to its excellent optical, electrical, and mechanical properties. The paper covers LiNbO₃ material properties, five main TFLN preparation methods, and device applications.

KEY MATERIAL PROPERTIES:
- LiNbO₃ is a trigonal ferroelectric material (3m point group, R3c space group, ilmenite-type ABO₃ structure)
- Spontaneous polarization is approximately 50 μC/cm² along the c-axis
- Curie temperature is about 1210 °C
- Electro-optic coefficient r33 is approximately 30.8 pm/V (prominent linear Pockels effect)
- The EO effect enables nanosecond or even picosecond modulation speeds

PREPARATION METHODS (five main techniques):
1. Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD): Uses organometallic precursors (Li(OtBu) and Nb(OEt)₅, etc.); high deposition rate (~320 nm/h) and large-area uniformity suitable for industrial production; precursors are often highly toxic requiring strict handling; Li/Nb precursor ratio close to stoichiometric yields excellent crystalline quality.
2. Molecular Beam Epitaxy (MBE): Ultra-high-vacuum atomic-level control; typically requires high substrate temperature (~800-1050 °C); lithium volatilization at high temperature is a challenge; oxygen radical-assisted laser MBE (ORA-LMBE) improves crystal quality at lower temperatures; growth of single-phase NbO, NbO₂, LiNbO₂, Li₃NbO₄, LiNbO₃, and LiNb₃O₈ films demonstrated on c-plane sapphire.
3. Pulsed Laser Deposition (PLD): Uses single-crystal LiNbO₃ target with sapphire substrate; uniform deposition on X-cut, Y-cut, and Z-cut substrates (homoepitaxial layers nearly defect-free per TEM); substrate temperature 500-800 °C; suitable for film bulk acoustic resonators (FBARs) for 5G applications; slow growth rate limits large-area production.
4. Magnetron Sputtering: Physical vapor deposition at lower temperatures (380-550 °C); Ar/O₂ mixed gas used; multi-step sputtering process improves film quality; Nb-rich TFLN exhibits third-order nonlinear optical properties with nonlinear refractive index γ ≈ 10⁻¹¹ cm²/W and absorption coefficient β ≈ 10⁻⁷ cm/W; challenges include composition deviation due to different Li/Nb sputtering rates and film uniformity issues.
5. Smartcut Technology: Advanced technique that strips high-quality LiNbO₃ film from a bulk crystal via ion implantation and bonding; produces single-crystal films; widely used in LiNbO₃ devices.

DEVICE APPLICATIONS:
- Sensors
- Memories (ferroelectric)
- Optical waveguides
- Electro-optic modulators (EOMs) with higher modulation bandwidths, lower driving voltages, and lower insertion losses
- Surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices
- Photonic integrated circuits

The review emphasizes that while single-crystal thin-film preparation via Smartcut is relatively mature, the development of epitaxial thin films (via CVD, MBE, PLD, magnetron sputtering) is an important means to reduce costs and improve performance for future photonic integrated circuits. The article was received December 31, 2024, revised February 11, 2025, and accepted February 12, 2025. It is published under a Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) license.
</summary>

SUMMARY:

URL: https://lasers4.eu/event/laserlab-europe-talk-femtosecond-laser-fabricated-glass-photonic-integrated-circuits-for-stuctured-illumination-microscopy-16-september-2026

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page announces a Laserlab-Europe Talk webinar scheduled for Wednesday, 16 September 2026, from 16:00 to 17:00 CEST (held online). The talk is titled "Femtosecond laser fabricated glass photonic integrated circuits for structured illumination microscopy" and will be presented by Francesca Bragheri from The Institute for Photonics and Nanotechnologies (IFN), National Research Council (CNR), Italy.

The presentation focuses on using femtosecond laser micromachining (FLM) as an enabling technology to fabricate three-dimensional integrated photonic circuits in glass for structured illumination microscopy (SIM). SIM is a powerful imaging technique that achieves resolution enhancement beyond the diffraction limit while maintaining low phototoxicity and compatibility with conventional fluorescence microscopy. Traditional SIM implementations rely on complex, bulky optical systems that limit robustness and adoption.

Key technical points covered in the talk include:
- FLM induces localized refractive index modifications inside transparent materials, enabling direct writing of buried optical waveguides, directional couplers, and interferometric structures with true 3D design freedom and micrometric precision.
- When combined with selective chemical etching (FLICE), the technology enables fabrication of reflective micro-optical elements (flat and curved mirrors), which are metal-coated to guide beams and generate structured illumination patterns.
- Thermal phase shifters integrated onto the chip surface provide fast, dynamic control of relative phase between interfering beams without mechanical movement, enabling pattern translation for SIM image reconstruction.
- Device architectures range from compact two-output interferometers to sophisticated multi-beam photonic circuits generating both 2D and 3D interference patterns.
- The resulting glass chips can be directly interfaced with conventional widefield microscopes, transforming them into compact, reconfigurable SIM platforms.

Registration is available via the Laserlab-Europe website. The event is categorized under Webinars on the Lasers4EU platform. Related upcoming events include a "360 Carla Training: Quantum Materials — from ARPES to trARPES" (16 September 2026) and a "Lasers4EU Webinar: The use and impact of artificial intelligence in research and innovation" (24 September 2026).

URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published in Scientific Reports on January 28, 2015 (PMCID: PMC4308694, PMID: 25627294, DOI: 10.1038/srep08072), reports on the fabrication of high-quality (high-Q) lithium niobate (LN) whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) microresonators using a combination of femtosecond laser direct writing and focused ion beam (FIB) milling.

METHODOLOGY:
- LN thin film (700 nm) and silica layer (2 μm) on an LN substrate were used
- A cylindrical post (~59 μm diameter, ~15 μm height) was first created by femtosecond laser micromachining (Ti:sapphire laser, ~800 nm center wavelength, ~40 fs pulse width, 1 kHz repetition rate, 0.35 mW for LN ablation, 1 mW for silica)
- FIB milling was performed twice (coarse milling with 30-keV ion beam at 4 nA, then fine milling at 1 nA) to smooth the periphery, reducing the diameter to 55 μm
- The silica layer was selectively etched using 5% HF solution for 8 minutes to form a freestanding microdisk on a silica pedestal
- Thermal annealing at 500°C for 2 hours in air further smoothed the rim of the LN disk
- Q factors were measured using an evanescent fiber taper coupling method

RESULTS:
- The 82 μm diameter LN resonator achieved a Q factor of ~2.5 × 10⁵ around 1550 nm wavelength
- A 55 μm resonator showed Q factor improvement from 5.2 × 10⁴ (before annealing) to 1.6 × 10⁵ (after annealing)
- Q factor increases with increasing diameter due to reduced radiation loss at the curved surface
- Microresonators below 10 μm diameter can potentially be fabricated using this technique
- The top and bottom surfaces of the LN thin film naturally have ultra-high smoothness with surface roughness as low as 0.35 nm

CONCLUSION:
The technique combines the flexibility and material insensitivity of femtosecond laser micromachining with the precision of FIB milling, enabling high-efficiency, high-precision nanofabrication of high-Q crystalline microresonators. The authors have previously used similar techniques to fabricate microresonators in fused silica, active Nd:glass, and CaF₂ crystals, and envisage extending this approach to various dielectric materials.

The work was supported by the National Basic Research Program of China (No. 2014CB921300), NSFC grants, and Fundamental Research Funds for Central Universities. Authors include Jintian Lin, Yingxin Xu, Zhiwei Fang, Min Wang, Jiangxin Song, Nengwen Wang, Lingling Qiao, Wei Fang, and Ya Cheng.
</summary>

"The micrometer-scale (diameter ~82 μm) LN resonator possesses a Q factor of ~2.5 × 10⁵ around 1550 nm wavelength. The combination of femtosecond laser direct writing with FIB enables high-efficiency, high-precision nanofabrication of high-Q crystalline microresonators."

- Uniform waveguide width design (for comparison) only achieves 3724%W⁻¹ with broadened central peaks and side lobes.

**Advantages of the approach:** (1) Uses standard single-period periodic poling, reducing electrode fabrication complexity; (2) allows placement of multiple waveguides without individual poling designs; (3) uses existing micro-nano fabrication technology; (4) achieves ultrahigh SHG efficiency surpassing other related work.

## Scientific Paper Summary: Watt-level second harmonic generation in periodically poled thin-film lithium tantalate

### Overview
This arXiv preprint (2512.07968) reports the first demonstration of watt-level continuous-wave (CW) second-harmonic generation (SHG) in periodically poled thin-film lithium tantalate (PPLT) photonic integrated waveguides. The work addresses a key limitation of lithium niobate (LiNbO3) — its low optical damage threshold — by leveraging lithium tantalate's (LiTaO3) higher optical damage threshold to achieve high-power operation.

### Key Results
- Demonstrated 7 mm-long PPLT waveguides achieving SH output exceeding 1 W on-chip (specifically 1.065 W), with directly measured off-chip SH power above 0.5 W at 775 nm wavelength
- Pumped with 4.5 W of off-chip pump power at 1550 nm
- The output was limited only by experimental setup constraints (powermeter limit of 0.5 W and EDFA output limit)
- Measured SHG efficiency of 107 %W⁻¹cm⁻² — lower than typical PPLN values but sufficient for watt-level output due to higher damage threshold
- No observable sample damage or performance degradation at watt-level operation

### Significance
- First PPLT photonic integrated circuit demonstration achieving watt-level output
- Power output comparable to state-of-the-art PPLN ridge waveguides but achieved in a shorter (7 mm) waveguide, preserving bandwidth
- Extends the LiTaO3 integrated photonic platform toward on-chip optical parametric oscillators, quadrature-squeezed light sources, visible lasers, and frequency metrology applications

1. **Periodic Poling**: Optimized electrode geometry (elliptical tips, 25 µm-long, 1:15 axis ratio, 40% duty cycle) and high-voltage pulse sequences (20-30 pulses with 0.5 ms rise/flat/fall segments at 1 kV peak) to achieve reproducible domain inversion despite LiTaO3's coercive field being nearly 4× higher than MgO-doped LiNbO3
2. **Fabrication**: Used X-cut LiTaO3 chip (576 nm film, 4.7 µm SiO2 insulation), E-beam lithography, argon ion beam etching, and KOH wet etching for smooth sidewalls
3. **Characterization**: Two-photon SH microscopy for domain inspection, SEM imaging for non-destructive domain visualization, and calibrated high-power measurements with energy conservation fitting to avoid efficiency overestimation

- The reduced SHG efficiency compared to PPLN (which can exceed 2000 %W⁻¹cm⁻²) is attributed to lower effective nonlinearity in thin films, possible thickness non-uniformity, and crystal quality issues
- The authors note that at high pump powers, even low-efficiency waveguides can reach the depletion regime over short lengths, meaning efficiency improvements primarily reduce required pump power
- Future work: MgO-doped or stoichiometric LiTaO3 substrates would lower poling voltages and simplify fabrication

--- SOURCE 1: Broadband Second Harmonic Generation in a z-Cut Lithium Niobate on Insulator Waveguide Based on Type-I Modal Phase Matching ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2304-6732/10/1/80

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a scientific research article published in Photonics (MDPI) in January 2023, titled "Broadband Second Harmonic Generation in a z-Cut Lithium Niobate on Insulator Waveguide Based on Type-I Modal Phase Matching" (DOI: 10.3390/photonics10010080). The authors are Changwen Wang, Haozong Zhong, Minghao Ning, Bin Fang, Lin Li, and Ya Cheng, affiliated with East China Normal University, China Jiliang University, Shanxi University, and the Shanghai Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics (CAS).

The research numerically investigates second harmonic generation (SHG) in a z-cut lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) waveguide using type-I modal phase matching (MPM) between two fundamental modes (TE00 of the fundamental wave and TM00 of the second harmonic wave). Key findings include:
- A mode overlap factor close to unity (ζ = 0.9890) was achieved
- Normalized SHG efficiency up to 72.1% W⁻¹cm⁻² at the telecommunication band (1.55 μm)
- Large spectral tunability of 2.5 nm/K via temperature tuning
- Broad bandwidth of ~50 nm for strip waveguide and ~100 nm for ridge waveguide (5 mm-long devices)
- Effective mode area Aeff = 3.05 μm² for strip waveguide

The design uses a few-micron-thick LNOI waveguide (h = 2 μm, w = 2.71 μm for strip; h1 = 1.35 μm, h2 = 0.3 μm, w = 2 μm, θ = 75° for ridge) fabricated via electron beam lithography and inductively coupled plasma etching. Compared to traditional approaches (birefringent phase matching, quasi-phase matching, and conventional modal phase matching), this method achieves phase matching between two fundamental modes, dramatically improving mode overlap and conversion efficiency. The approach is applicable to other guided structures like micro-rings and micro-disks, offering advantages over nano-LNOI in terms of power handling, coupling efficiency, and simplified fabrication.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We numerically investigate a second harmonic generation (SHG) in a z-cut lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) waveguide based on type-I mode phase matching (MPM) between two fundamental modes. A mode overlap factor that is close to unity is achieved and the normalized SHG efficiency reaches up to 72.1% W−1cm−2 at the telecommunication band, together with a large spectral tunability of 2.5 nm/K."

--- SOURCE 3: Recent progress in thin-film lithium niobate photonic crystal ... ---
URL: https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJ24e9c8231f751afd

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an invited review article published in *Chinese Optics Letters* (Vol. 22, Issue 3, 033602, 2024), titled "Recent progress in thin-film lithium niobate photonic crystal" by Rui Ge, Jiangwei Wu, Xiangmin Liu, Yuping Chen (corresponding author), and Xianfeng Chen from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Ningxia University, Shanghai Research Center for Quantum Sciences, and Shandong Normal University. It was selected as an Editors' Pick.

The review covers the fabrication, characterization, and applications of thin-film lithium niobate photonic crystals (TF-LNPhC), a platform that confines light at sub-wavelength scales for on-chip integration.

**Key fabrication methods discussed:**
- **Focused Ion Beam (FIB):** Most popular technique, uses Ga+ ions at 30 kV with Cr or Au masks. Limited to small areas (<50×50 holes) due to drift and long process times. Can produce 2D and 3D structures. A "redeposition-free FIB" technique (using small probe currents, e.g., 24 pA, and prefabricated air regions) improves hole quality.
- **Electron Beam Lithography (EBL) with Ar+ plasma etching:** Enables wafer-scale patterning using ZEP-520 or HSQ photoresists. Achieves sidewall angles of 60°, 70°, and 85°.
- **Ion Beam Enhanced Etching (IBEE):** Uses ion irradiation-induced defects and HF wet etching; achieves 90° sidewalls and high aspect ratios, though requires the optical axis parallel to the waveguide direction.
- **Reactive ion etching combined with proton exchange:** Achieves 85° sidewall angles.
- **Etchless LNPhC:** The TFLN itself is not etched; instead a mask layer (silica or polymer) is patterned, including designs based on bound states in the continuum (BIC).
- **Laser writing-assisted nanolithography:** Femtosecond laser writing combined with wet etching can produce 100 nm holes with high aspect ratios.

**Characterization methods:** Tapered fiber coupling, end-face coupling, cross-polarized resonant scattering coupling (~20% coupling efficiency), and grating coupling.

**Q-factor results (Table 1):** The highest reported simulated Q-factor is 1.23×10⁸ (mode-gap cavity, 2019, EBL+Ar+ etching) with a corresponding experimental value of 1.41×10⁶ and modal volume of 0.78 (λ/n)³. Experimental Q-factors range from 75 (redeposition-free FIB bulk cavity, 2022) to 1.41×10⁶. Other notable values include 3.51×10⁵ (2019), 4.7×10⁵ (2020), and 12,010 for a BIC etchless cavity (2022). An L4/3 inverse-designed cavity achieved 9.7×10⁶ (simulation, 2020). Most high-Q cavities are mode-gap (heterostructure) designs.

**Applications:**
- **Parametric up-conversion (SHG):** SHG efficiency is quadratically dependent on intra-cavity power (QT^0.5/V)². Reported efficiencies: 6.4×10⁻⁹ (L3 cavity), 0.078% W⁻¹ (mode-gap cavity with Q~10⁶), 2×10⁻⁴ (pulsed excitation). Slow light waveguides also support SHG with an efficiency of 8×10⁻⁵ W⁻¹.
- **Parametric down-conversion:** Theoretical/simulated designs for path-entangled photon pairs and spectrally unentangled biphoton states (for single-photon heralding) using double-slot PhC slow light waveguides, though experiments are lacking.
- **Sensors:** Temperature sensors with sensitivities of 0.359 nm/°C (slow light) and 0.77 nm/°C (Fano resonance); electric field sensors with minimum detectable fields of 50 µV/m (simulation), 23 mV/m, and 25 µV/m (BIC-based); a sucrose sensor with sensitivity of 1016.35 nm/RIU and limit of detection 2.28×10⁻⁴ RIU.
- **Electro-optic modulators:** Small size compared to LN waveguide modulators; a nanobeam-based modulator achieved bit-switching energy of 22 fJ and can be used for high-speed electro-optic switching.

The review emphasizes that fabrication imperfections (conical holes, redeposition, surface roughness) remain challenges, and discusses the photorefractive effect saturation behavior in LNPhC cavities.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Lithium niobate is a material that exhibits outstanding electro-optic, nonlinear optical, acousto-optic, piezoelectric, photorefractive, and pyroelectric properties. A thin-film lithium niobate photonic crystal can confine light in the sub-wavelength scale, which is beneficial to the integration of the lithium niobate on-chip device."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Troubleshooting Electro‑Optic Drift in Lithium Niobate Phase Modulators ---
URL: https://en.liobate.com/Blog/troubleshooting-electro-optic-drift-in-lithium-niobate-phase-modulators

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a technical blog article published by Liobate (a thin-film lithium niobate technology company) on April 16, 2026, titled "Troubleshooting Electro-Optic Drift in Lithium Niobate Phase Modulators." The article addresses the persistent reliability challenge of electro-optic drift in lithium niobate phase modulator systems—where a DC bias voltage causes slowly shifting optical phase over time even with constant drive voltage, degrading control stability in applications such as optical frequency combs, coherent sensing, and quantum photonics.

KEY TECHNICAL CONTENT:

1. Root Causes: Drift originates from mobile charge carriers (ions like H⁺ and Li⁺) migrating under an applied electric field in bulk lithium niobate, which partially screens the field. TFLN (thin-film lithium niobate) devices significantly reduce this effect due to thin-film geometry and high-quality crystalline layers, though drift can still arise from packaging materials (adhesives, solders) or surface contamination.

2. Diagnostic Techniques: Separate thermal effects from true electro-optic drift by using a temperature-controlled chamber (±0.1°C), monitoring with a Mach-Zehnder interferometer or homodyne detector, applying step DC voltage and recording phase change over minutes to hours. Healthy TFLN devices should show <5% of Vπ drift per hour. Additional diagnostics include dry-nitrogen purge at 50°C for 24 hours (for moisture ingress) and reversing bias polarity (symmetric drift = ionic contamination, asymmetric drift = electrode/interface issues).

3. Mitigation Strategies: (a) Use AC-coupled drive with low-frequency dither and feedback control (bias controller); (b) Select TFLN devices with passivation layers (SiO₂ or SiN); (c) Operate at reduced DC field strength with lower Vπ (<2.5 V); (d) Pre-age the modulator at 85°C for 100 hours.

4. Practical Workflow: (1) Verify temperature stability; (2) Measure drift with static DC bias (if >10% Vπ over 10 minutes, inspect hermeticity); (3) Apply bipolar square wave at 1 kHz (if drift reduces, implement active bias feedback); (4) Replace modulator with known-good TFLN device to isolate component issues.

Liobate's TFLN phase modulator specifications highlighted: 25 GHz RF bandwidth, <2.5 V half-wave voltage, <9 dB insertion loss, compact high-integration package. The article claims achievable drift rates below 0.1% Vπ per hour with proper techniques.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Electro-optic drift remains one of the most persistent reliability challenges in lithium niobate phase modulator systems. Over time, a DC bias voltage applied to the modulator produces a slowly shifting optical phase—even when the drive voltage remains constant."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Integrated electro-optics on thin-film lithium niobate ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.06398

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive review paper on integrated electro-optics on thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN), authored by Yaowen Hu, Di Zhu, Marko Loncar, and colleagues from Harvard University, Peking University, National University of Singapore, University of Virginia, and other institutions. The paper presents fundamental principles, device architectures, and state-of-the-art developments in TFLN-based electro-optic technology.

KEY TOPICS AND FINDINGS:

1. **TFLN Platform Advantages**: Lithium niobate has been used in optics for over seven decades, with strong χ(2) nonlinearity (~30 pm/V), high refractive index (~2.2), and wide transparency window (0.4-5.5 µm). Recent commercialization of wafer-scale TFLN-on-insulator and argon-based physical etching enabled nanoscale optical confinement with low optical losses. Key performance metrics include: half-wave voltage (V_π) of ~1V, optical propagation loss of ~1 dB/m, and EO bandwidth of ~100 GHz.

2. **Basic Principles**: The Pockels (EO) effect uses the largest EO tensor element r33 (~31 pm/V) along the crystal z-axis. Two film orientations exist: x-cut and z-cut TFLN. Three fundamental rules govern EO coupling: energy conservation, momentum conservation (relevant above 10 GHz for traveling-wave configurations), and selection rules.

3. **Major Device Classes**: Three classes of TFLN EO devices exist: waveguide-based, single-cavity, and coupled-cavity devices. Waveguide devices include phase modulators and Mach-Zehnder amplitude modulators (MZMs). State-of-the-art TFLN MZMs achieved V_π of ~1V, extinction ratio >20 dB, 3-dB bandwidth >100 GHz. A dual-polarization IQ modulator achieved record 1.96 Tb/s single-wavelength data rate. Visible-wavelength modulators achieved V_π·L as low as 0.17 V·cm at 450 nm with ~35 GHz bandwidth.

4. **Frequency Combs**: Waveguide-based EO combs achieved >40 spectral lines spanning 10 nm with a single phase modulator. Cavity-based EO combs achieved 100-fold improvement in efficiency (30%) and 2.2-fold span improvement (132 nm) using general critical coupling (GCC) in coupled-resonator designs.

5. **Frequency Conversion**: Record-breaking frequency shifting with >99% shift efficiency, 0.45 dB on-chip insertion loss, and 10-30 GHz shift range. Cascaded frequency shifting achieved four-step cascade to 120 GHz using a 30 GHz microwave. Spectral shearing achieved ±641 GHz (±5.2 nm) shifts with Δf/δf > 1, and up to 8-fold pulse bandwidth suppression.

6. **Cryogenic Electro-Optics**: TFLN EO effects persist at cryogenic temperatures, enabling photonic links for superconducting circuits. Cavity EO transduction achieved 1.02% efficiency (15.2% internal). Superconducting (niobium) TFLN MZMs with effective length of 1m achieved V_π as low as 42 mV. RSFQ signal transmission at 4K through optical fibers was demonstrated.

7. **Emerging Applications**: The paper discusses photonic computing/accelerators (heterogeneous laser integration, EO/Kerr combs for massive parallel processing) and quantum photonics (frequency-domain quantum computing, coupled-ring systems for beam splitting, quantum transduction). TFLN enables strong EO coupling (~10 GHz) versus low optical loss rates (~100 MHz), a regime inaccessible to other platforms.

8. **Synthetic Dimensions**: High-dimensional frequency crystals extending to four dimensions were demonstrated on a single EO cavity, with each dimension encompassing over 100 lattice points. A frequency-domain mirror with reflectivity exceeding 0.9999 was proposed and demonstrated.

The review concludes that TFLN electro-optics is transitioning from novel device-level demonstrations to advanced system-level applications, with the platform offering unprecedented reconfigurability, scalability, and performance compared to other photonic platforms.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"TFLN-based modulators feature a very low half-wave voltage V_π (voltage required for a π phase shift of light, ~1V), low optical propagation loss (α~1 dB/m), and high EO bandwidth (BW~100 GHz)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: [PDF] Fabrication of Ridge Waveguides in Lithium Niobate - KTH ---
URL: https://www.kth.se/polopoly_fs/1.422561.1600688634!/Menu/general/column-content/attachment/Ashraf_Mohamedelhassan%20_msc_thesis.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Master of Science thesis by Ashraf Mohamedelhassan (KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden, 2012) on the fabrication of ridge waveguides in Lithium Niobate (LiNbO3). The thesis was supervised by Dr. Katia Gallo and co-supervised by Michele Manzo, within the Laser Physics group at the Applied Physics department, in collaboration with the Albanova Nanofabrication laboratory.

**Main Objective:** To develop a reliable dry-etch (reactive ion etching, RIE) process to fabricate ridge waveguides in LiNbO3 using standard photoresist masks, enabling strong optical confinement for integrated nonlinear optical devices (potentially combined with periodically poled LiNbO3, PPLN).

**Key Methodology:** The work combines:
1. **Proton exchange (PE)** – an ion exchange process substituting lithium ions with protons (H+) from an acidic melt, which (a) increases the extraordinary refractive index by ~0.12 at 633 nm, creating the guiding layer (nPELN~2.3 vs nLN~2.2), and (b) weakens the LiNbO3 surface structure to significantly enhance subsequent etching rates.
2. **Photolithography** – using standard photoresist to pattern the ridge structures.
3. **Reactive ion etching (RIE)** – dry plasma etching to transfer the pattern into the substrate.

**Key Results:**
- Ridge waveguides fabricated on both -Z and +Z faces of undoped and MgO-doped congruent LiNbO3 substrates.
- Etching depths of ~500 nm on undoped and ~300 nm on MgO-doped materials.
- Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) used for ridge profile characterization.
- PELN ridge waveguides achieve a lateral index step of ~1.2 (air-LN index difference) compared to only ~0.12 for embedded PELN channels.
- The ridge geometry allows bi-dimensional light confinement in the transverse plane.

**Background on LiNbO3:** An artificial (not found in nature), negative uniaxial, non-centrosymmetric, ferroelectric crystal with large pyroelectric, piezoelectric, nonlinear and electro-optic coefficients. Grown via the Czochralski technique from Li2CO3 and Nb2O5 (melting point ~1250°C). Congruent composition (48.45% Li) is preferred for its optical quality and uniformity. MgO (5 mol%) doping improves resistance to photorefractive damage. Crystal is trigonal, 3m point group, R3c space group, ferroelectric below Curie temperature (1140°C).

**Key Fabrication Steps (flowchart):** Dicing wafers → Cleaning → Proton exchange (on top and bottom surfaces) → Photoresist coating → Photolithography patterning → Reactive ion etching → Polishing.

**Etching details:** The main challenge is LiNbO3's hardness and chemical inertness, giving low etching rates. The thesis explores parameters including etch selectivity, pressure, RF and ICP powers, etchant gases, and temperature. The PE layer enhances etching rates, allowing ridges several hundred nanometers deep with simple photoresist masks (avoiding the need for chromium masks).

**Waveguide physics:** Includes analysis of total internal reflection conditions, effective index method for ridge waveguides, prism coupling for light injection, and TE/TM mode descriptions. PE waveguides on z-cut substrates guide only extraordinary polarization (TM mode); ridges fabricated along the x-axis as propagation direction.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The main challenge to be faced comes from the fact that LiNbO3 is a hard and relatively inert material, hence relatively difficult to etch. In this master thesis I explored a new technological solution to enhance the etching rate in LiNbO3 which allowed me to develop a dry-etch process to fabricate the ridges with standard photo-resist masks."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Redeposition-free inductively-coupled plasma etching of ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper, published in Nanophotonics (2023 Jan 16;12(8):1601, doi: 10.1515/nanoph-2022-0676), reports on redeposition-free inductively-coupled plasma (ICP) etching of lithium niobate for integrated photonics. The study was conducted at ETH Zurich (Department of Physics, Institute for Quantum Electronics, Optical Nanomaterial Group) by Fabian Kaufmann (corresponding author), Giovanni Finco, Andreas Maeder, and Rachel Grange. Received Oct 31, 2022; accepted Dec 16, 2022. PMCID: PMC11501321, PMID: 39634587.

The paper addresses the challenge of argon (Ar) sputtering of lithium niobate-on-insulator (LNOI) waveguides, which provides the best optical quality but suffers from micro-masking effects caused by material redeposition and close-to-one etch mask selectivity. The authors present a workflow to identify optimal etching parameters independent of the plasma system used, and propose three methods to achieve redeposition-free lithium niobate etching without wet chemistry cleaning.

Key experimental details and findings:

1. Wafer preparation: A full 4-inch LNOI wafer (400 nm x-cut film, 2 μm SiO2 insulation layer from NANOLN) was patterned using 100 kV electron beam lithography (Vistex EBPG 5200+), with HSQ-based flowable oxide (FOX16) as negative resist (~500 nm thick). Samples were diced into 52 10×10 mm2 pieces with 5×5 mm2 effective area each.

2. ICP etching: Performed in a Plasma Pro 100 (Oxford Instruments) ICP system. Only Cl2, SF6, O2, and Ar gases were used, as CHF3 was found to contaminate the chamber and harm reproducibility. Etch depth (200-250 nm) was controlled via interferometric endpointing (Horiba, 670.1 nm).

3. Influence of DC bias: Sweeping DC bias from 100 V to 800 V (Ar flow 10 sccm, pressure 1 mTorr, 20 °C) showed that total redeposition decreased almost fourfold from 100 V to 800 V, trending toward redeposition-free etching above 1 kV (though not readily achievable). Trench depth increased by a factor of five with higher bias. Selectivity remained near one, sidewall angle 60-63° for both +Z and −Z crystal faces. Sample bow changed from concave to flat to convex with increasing bias: 300 V gave 20 nm thickness variation over 8×8 mm2, while 600 V gave below 5 nm. Surface roughness (Sq) was ~0.08 nm for biases above 200 V, four times better than un-etched surface (0.31 nm).

4. Influence of chamber pressure: Sweeping pressure from 1 to 15 mTorr (400 V) and 0.3 to 13 mTorr (600 V) showed redeposition vanishing completely after 7 mTorr, but with significant structural damage. Redeposition-free regime occurred at 5-7 mTorr for 600 V (preferred DC bias) and around 11 mTorr for 400 V. Etch rates dropped to minimum values of 27 nm/min (400 V) and 12 nm/min (600 V) before increasing again at higher pressures. Surface roughness degraded with pressure (Sq of 0.10, 0.12, 0.15 nm for 3, 5, 7 mTorr).

5. Aspect ratio dependent etching (ARDE): Redeposition decreased with decreasing gap size (from 1 μm to 100 nm) due to ions bouncing between sidewalls. Trench merging occurred at gaps up to 400 nm, with loading effects below 400 nm. Dense structures were redeposition-free down to 1 μm gaps at 300 W ICP power, 600 V DC bias, and 11 mTorr.

6. Etch depth and IBE: Redeposition decreased with increasing etch depth (110-260 nm). Ion beam etching (IBE) experiments at incidence angles 0°-35° simulating trapezoidal masks (85°, 70°, 60°, 50°) showed reduced redeposition with increasing angle, confirming that trapezoidal masks help achieve redeposition-free etching.

7. Reproducibility and optical results: Four samples etched with 300 W ICP power, 600 V DC bias, 1 mTorr showed excellent reproducibility with Q-factor variation below 2% and calculated propagation loss of 1.55 dB/cm. Etch rate scaled linearly: 0.09 nm/min per watt of ICP power and 0.10 nm/min per volt of DC bias. Optical measurements used ring/racetrack resonators with 600 nm top width, 80 μm bend radius, operating near 1550 nm; a resonance linewidth of 25 pm was observed.

The three proposed methods for redeposition-free etching are: (1) careful balancing of ICP parameters (especially DC bias and chamber pressure), (2) increasing structure density so ion deflection between neighboring walls aids redeposition removal, and (3) tailoring the etching mask toward a trapezoidal shape.

Conclusions note that redeposition-free etching is achievable but requires a very sensitive, well-maintained system—challenging in research environments with mixed use. Alternative approaches include using dense structures with positive masks, keeping a remaining slab near waveguides, or using trapezoidal masks (e.g., via SiO2 PECVD hard mask deposition, or SiNx/a-Si which can be removed without damaging the thermal oxide layer).

URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0925346715301816

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in the journal Optical Materials (Volume 53, March 2016, Pages 1-5) describing a study on fabricating smooth sidewall thin film lithium niobate (TFLN) waveguides using Argon plasma inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etching (ICP-RIE). The paper was authored by G. Ulliac, V. Calero, A. Ndao, F.I. Baida, and M.-P. Bernal.

Key findings and methodology:
- The researchers fabricated ridge waveguides on 700 nm thickness thin film lithium niobate (TFLN), using argon plasma etching on an ICP-RIE system rather than the more common fluorine-containing gases.
- The fabrication process was optimized in three key steps: mask fabrication, plasma etching parameters, and a final wet chemical cleaning step to remove lithium niobate redeposition on side walls.
- Using argon plasma eliminates the problem of lithium fluoride (LiF) redeposition that occurs with fluorine-based gases (CF4, SF6, CHF3), which causes non-vertical sidewall profiles, increased roughness, and reduced etching rates.
- The etching process used argon-based chemistry at low pressure (2 mTorr) with an S1828 photoresist layer as the etching mask (with a soft post-bake to increase etching selectivity).
- The parametric study was performed on 1.1×1.2 cm² chips of X-cut 500 μm thickness lithium niobate due to the high cost of thin film wafers, before fine-tuning on a 3-inch X-cut 700 nm thickness LN film bonded to an LN substrate via a 2 μm SiO2 layer (provided by NanoLN).
- Results: single mode propagation was achieved with overall optical losses of only 5 dB/cm, which is superior to previously demonstrated argon etching of photonic wires with propagation losses of 7.5 dB/cm and 9.9 dB/cm for both light polarizations.
- Optical characterization was performed at 1550 nm wavelength using a tunable CW laser, polarization controller, and lensed fiber with 1-μm diameter spot and 3 mm working distance.

Background context: The paper discusses how lithium niobate is an excellent material for photonics due to its electro-optical, acousto-optical, and nonlinear properties, and how sub-micrometric LN thin films (now commercially available via crystal ion slicing and wafer bonding) are crucial for competing with silicon photonics. Traditional methods like titanium in-diffusion and proton exchange waveguides offer low losses (0.01 dB/cm) but suffer from large mode sizes, whereas ridge waveguides provide better light confinement. The paper notes that LN is hard and relatively inert, making it difficult to etch. Alternative methods discussed include ion implantation assisted HF wet etching, fluorine-containing gas plasma etching (with LiF redeposition issues), and ion-beam enhanced etching (which showed losses around 61 dB/cm).

The work was supported by the ANR ASTRID project "Esencyal" (ANR-13-ASTR-0019-01). The article has been cited 117 times, with notable citing works including "Integrated lithium niobate electro-optic modulators" (Optica, 2021), "Integrated photonics on thin-film lithium niobate" (Advances in Optics and Photonics, 2021), and "Advances in on-chip photonic devices based on lithium niobate on insulator" (Photonics Research, 2020).
</summary>

The fabrication has been done by developing and optimizing three steps of the technological process, the mask fabrication, the plasma etching, and a final cleaning wet etching step in order to remove the lithium niobate redeposition on the side walls. We have obtained single mode propagation with light overall losses of only 5 dB/cm."

--- SOURCE 10: PE vs RIE vs ICP-RIE: Which Plasma Etching Process Should You Choose? ---
URL: https://ninescrolls.com/insights/understanding-differences-pe-rie-icp-rie-plasma-etching

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive technical guide from NineScrolls (published January 25, 2025, by NineScrolls Engineering) comparing the three dominant plasma etching technologies: Plasma Etching (PE), Reactive Ion Etching (RIE), and Inductively Coupled Plasma RIE (ICP-RIE). Target readers are semiconductor process engineers, equipment engineers, R&D scientists, and technical decision-makers.

**Key Differences Summary:**
- **PE (Plasma Etching/Chemical Dry Etching):** The most basic form, relying on chemical radicals (F*, Cl*, O*) for isotropic etching at 100–300 nm/min. Ion energy <20 eV (below sputtering threshold), operates at 300–1000 mTorr, RF power 100–300 W, plasma density 10^9–10^10 cm^-3. Achieves very high selectivity (>50:1) with minimal surface damage. Used for photoresist stripping, ashing, surface preparation, and isotropic release etching for MEMS.
- **RIE (Reactive Ion Etching):** Uses a capacitively coupled plasma (CCP) reactor where the substrate sits on the powered electrode, creating a DC self-bias (-100 to -500 V) that accelerates ions perpendicular to the surface. Combines chemical reaction with physical ion bombardment (50–500 eV) for anisotropic profiles (80–90° sidewalls). Etch rate 200–500 nm/min, pressure 10–200 mTorr, plasma density 10^10–10^11 cm^-3. Key limitation: plasma density and ion energy are coupled (not independently controllable) in single-RF systems. Used for pattern transfer, dielectric/metal etching, and MEMS fabrication.
- **ICP-RIE:** Solves RIE's coupling limitation with a dual RF system — an ICP coil (300–3000 W) generates high-density plasma (10^11–10^12 cm^-3, 10–100× higher than CCP-RIE) while a separate RF bias (0–600 W) independently controls ion energy (0–300 eV). Etch rate 500–5000+ nm/min, pressure 1–50 mTorr, substrate temperature -20 to 200 °C. Enables the Bosch process (DRIE) for aspect ratios exceeding 50:1.

**Bosch Process (DRIE):** Patented by Robert Bosch GmbH (1994), alternates between SF₆ etch steps (3–10 µm/min isotropic Si etching) and C₄F₈ passivation steps (depositing fluorocarbon polymer), producing near-vertical sidewalls with aspect ratios >50:1, though with characteristic scalloping (50–200 nm roughness per cycle).

**Source Power vs. Ion Density (ICP-RIE):** Plasma density scales approximately linearly with source power (ion flux increases, but ion energy barely changes since it's set by bias). Two non-idealities: E-to-H mode transition (abrupt density jump of 1–2 orders of magnitude near low power threshold) and saturation at high power (due to wall losses and neutral gas depletion). Rule of thumb: use source power for density/etch rate, bias power for anisotropy/selectivity/damage.

**Comparison Matrix (quantitative):**
| Feature | PE | RIE | ICP-RIE |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plasma Density | 10^9–10^10 cm^-3 | 10^10–10^11 cm^-3 | 10^11–10^12 cm^-3 |
| Ion Energy | <20 eV | 50–500 eV | 0–300 eV (independent) |
| Etch Rate (Si) | 100–300 nm/min | 200–500 nm/min | 500–5000+ nm/min |
| Pressure | 300–1000 mTorr | 10–200 mTorr | 1–50 mTorr |
| Profile | Isotropic | Anisotropic (80–90°) | Highly Anisotropic (88–90°) |
| Selectivity | Very High (>50:1) | Moderate (10–30:1) | High (20–100:1, tunable) |
| Max Aspect Ratio | N/A | 5–10:1 | 50:1+ (Bosch) |
| Equipment Cost | $50K–$150K | $100K–$300K | $200K–$600K+ |

**Gas Chemistries:** Silicon (SF₆, CF₄/O₂, Cl₂/HBr); SiO₂ (CHF₃, C₄F₈, CF₄/CHF₃); Si₃N₄ (CHF₃/O₂, CF₄/H₂); Al (Cl₂/BCl₃); GaAs/InP (Cl₂/Ar, SiCl₄); Photoresist/organics (O₂, O₂/Ar).

**Common Etch Defects and Solutions:**
- **Undercut:** lateral etching beneath mask — reduce pressure, add passivation gas, increase RF bias
- **Bowing:** convex sidewall bulging — optimize mask profile, reduce pressure, use pulsed bias
- **ARDE (Aspect Ratio Dependent Etching):** narrow trenches etch slower — increase ICP power, reduce pressure, use time-multiplexed recipes
- **Micro-masking/Grass:** needle-like residues — chamber conditioning, add O₂, optimize Bosch ratio
- **Notching (Footing):** lateral etching at silicon/insulator interface — use pulsed bias, reduce bias near endpoint

**Endpoint Detection Methods:** OES (Optical Emission Spectroscopy — most widely used, non-invasive, requires >1–5% exposed wafer area); Laser Interferometry (for transparent films like SiO₂/Si₃N₄); Mass Spectrometry/RGA (high sensitivity, slower, R&D-oriented).

**Selection Guidelines:**
- **Choose PE** for isotropic etching, maximum selectivity, minimal damage, stripping/descum, constrained budgets
- **Choose RIE** for anisotropic pattern transfer with moderate aspect ratios (<10:1), standard semiconductor processing, cost-effective solutions
- **Choose ICP-RIE** for high-aspect-ratio features (>10:1 to 50:1+), independent etch rate/ion energy control, deep Si etching (DRIE/Bosch), hard-to-etch materials (GaN, SiC, diamond, sapphire), advanced R&D

**Future Trends:** Atomic Layer Etching (ALE), Pulsed Plasma Etching, Machine Learning Process Control, new material challenges (2D materials, high-entropy alloys, ferroelectric HfO₂), and 3D integration (TSV, hybrid bonding, chiplet packaging).

The article also details NineScrolls' RIE Etcher Series and ICP-RIE systems (ICP source up to 3000 W, RF bias up to 600 W, plasma density to 10^12 cm^-3, temperature control -20 to 200 °C, up to 8 gas lines, Bosch process ready, process design kits for Si DRIE, SiO₂, GaN/SiC, III-V, and diamond). Includes 13 academic references (Lieberman & Lichtenberg, Coburn & Winters, Hopwood, Laermer & Schilp Bosch patent, etc.).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"PE relies on chemical radicals for isotropic etching at 100–300 nm/min; RIE adds ion bombardment for anisotropic profiles at 200–500 nm/min; ICP-RIE provides independent control of plasma density (10^11–10^12 cm−3) and ion energy, achieving etch rates above 1 µm/min with excellent profile control."
</key_excerpts>

Monolithic ultra-high-Q lithium niobate microring resonator MIAN ZHANG,1,† CHENG WANG,1,† REBECCA CHENG,1,2 AMIRHASSAN SHAMS-ANSARI,1,3 AND MARKO LONČAR1,* 1John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138, USA 2Department of Physics, Brown University, Providence, Rhode Island 02912, USA 3Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Howard University, Washington, DC 20059, USA *Corresponding author: loncar@seas.harvard.edu Received 9 November 2017; revised 26 November 2017; accepted 27 November 2017 (Doc. ID 313057); published 18 December 2017 We demonstrate an ultralow loss monolithic integrated lithium niobate photonic platform consisting of dry-etched subwavelength waveguides with extracted propagation losses as low as 2.7 dB/m and microring resonators with quality factors up to 107.
© 2017 Optical Society of America under the terms of the OSA Open Access Publishing Agreement OCIS codes: (130.3730) Lithium niobate; (230.5750) Resonators; (130.3990) Micro-optical devices.
https://doi.org/10.1364/OPTICA.4.001536 Lithium niobate (LN) is a material with a wide range of applica-tions in optical and microwave technologies, owing to unique properties that include large second-order nonlinear susceptibility (χ230pm∕V), large piezoelectric response (C33 ∼250 C∕m2), a wide optical transparency window (350 nm to 5 μm), and a high refractive index (∼2.2) [1]. Conventional LN devices, including fiber-optic modulators and periodically poled frequency convert-ers, have been the workhorse of the optoelectronics industry.
Optical waveguides in these components are defined by ion dif-fusion or proton exchange methods, which result in low index contrast and weak optical confinement. An integrated LN plat-form, featuring sub-wavelength scale light confinement and dense integration of optical and electrical components, has the potential to revolutionize optical communication and microwave photonics [1–7].
The major roadblock for the practical application of inte-grated LN photonics is the difficulty of fabricating devices that simultaneously achieve low optical propagation loss and high con-finement. Recently developed thin-film LN-on-insulator technol-ogy makes this possible, and has resulted in the development of two complementary approaches to define nanoscale optical wave-guides: hybrid and monolithic. The hybrid approach integrates an easy-to-etch material (e.g., silicon or silicon nitride) with LN thin films to guide light [2–4] with a relatively low propagation loss (0.3 dB/cm) [4]. However, the resulting optical modes only par-tially reside in the active material region (i.e., LN), reducing the nonlinear interaction efficiency. The monolithic approach relies on direct etching of LN to achieve high optical confinement in the active region, but has suffered from a relatively high propa-gation loss. While freestanding LN microdisk resonators have achieved optical quality factors (Q) of ∼106 [5,6], integrated microring resonators typically feature Q ∼105 with waveguide propagation loss on the order of 3 dB/cm [7]. Since LN is per-ceived as a difficult-to-etch material, it is commonly accepted that low-loss propagation in a monolithic waveguide is not possible, and therefore is not the most promising path forward.
Here we challenge the status quo and show that sub-wavelength scale lithium niobate waveguides can be fabricated with a propa-gation loss as low as 2.7  0.3 dB∕m through an optimized stan-dard etching process. We demonstrate nearly critically coupled ultra-high Q-factor optical cavities with measured QL  5 × 106 corresponding to intrinsic QI ∼107.
We fabricate an integrated waveguide-coupled microring and racetrack resonators with a bending radius r  80 μm, and vari-ous straight arm lengths l and waveguide widths w [Fig. 1(a)].
The optical modes in these resonators have different interaction strength with the etched sidewalls, which allows us to identify the source of the optical losses [Fig. 1(b)]. We fabricate the devices using 600 nm thick X-cut LN thin films on 2 μm of silicon dioxide (SiO2) on silicon substrates (NanoLN). We use standard electron beam lithography to define patterns in hydrogen silses-quioxane (HSQ) resist with multipass exposure. The patterns are subsequently transferred into the LN thin film using a commer-cial inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etching (ICP RIE) tool. We use Ar plasma to physically etch LN where the plasma power and chamber condition are tuned to minimize surface re-deposition of removed LN and other contaminations present in the chamber. We etch a total of hrib  350 nm of LN with a bias power of 112 W, leaving a hslab  250 nm thin LN slab. After cleaning and removal of the resist, the devices are cladded by depositing 1.5 μm of SiO2 using plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD).
The optical Q-factors of these resonators are measured using a tunable telecom external cavity diode laser (Santec TSL-510, Komaki, Japan). To calibrate the Q measurement, we modulate (500 MHz) the laser output using an external electro-optic modu-lator. Figure 2(a) shows a close to critically coupled micro-racetrack resonator with a loaded (intrinsic) Q-factor of 5.0 (10.0  0.7) million at an optical excitation wavelength of 1590 nm.
Memorandum Vol. 4, No. 12 / December 2017 / Optica 1536 2334-2536/17/121536-02 Journal © 2017 Optical Society of America To confirm the Q-factor, we directly ascertain the photon lifetime of the resonator using ring-down measurements [Fig. 2(b)]. The fitted data show a lifetime of 4.2  0.2 ns in good agreement with the spectral measurements.
We show that sidewall scattering is still a significant loss chan-nel in our devices by investigating structures with different wave-guide widths. Figure 2(c) shows the intrinsic Q measured for fabricated ring and racetrack resonators. Increasing the waveguide width from 800 nm to 2.4 μm leads to a Q improvement from ∼1.5 to ∼4 million. This improvement is expected from the re-duced interaction of the light and the etched sidewalls [Fig. 1(b)].
We extract the straight optical waveguide propagation loss by comparing the optical Q-factors of micro-racetrack resonators with different straight section lengths from 0 to 14 mm, with the same waveguide width of 2.4 μm and a bending radius of 80 μm. Indeed, racetrack resonators with longer straight sections exhibit higher optical Q-factors, because light in the straight sec-tion interacts less with the sidewall scattering centers than in the bending region [Fig. 1(b)]. The results are shown in Fig. 2(d), where we extract a straight waveguide loss of 2.7  0.3 dB∕m from the intersection of the fitted line. The extracted bending loss of 9.3  0.9 dB∕m agrees well with the measurements in ring resonators. By comparing the straight section loss of two race-track resonators with different widths (1.2 and 2.4 μm) and using numerical modeling, we estimate an upper bound of 1.5 dB/m for the intrinsic loss of our platform. The possible contributing factors are ion-implantation damage introduced during the LN thin-film production process, top-surface roughness due to LN polishing, and finite PECVD SiO2 cladding absorption.
Importantly, these loss mechanisms could be mitigated by a com-bination of defects annealing and finer top-surface polishing [8].
We expected the loss contributions of the monolithic LN plat-form could be further reduced toward its material intrinsic loss limit of <0.1 dB∕m [1].
In conclusion, we show that the monolithic LN nanophotonic platform is a viable path forward. The ultralow loss, high optical confinement and tight bending radius combined with the ability to integrate microwave electrodes [7] will bring electro-optic [2,7] and nonlinear optical [4] systems into a new design parameter space that has been inaccessible until now. This could enable a wide range of applications, including those in ultralow-loss quan-tum photonics [9], coherent microwave-to-optical conversion [10,11], and active topological photonics [12]. We emphasize that the LN device layer sits atop a standard silicon handle wafer and our platform therefore can also be integrated with many existing photonic technologies. Finally, we hope that our work will stimulate further activities and a renewed interest in mono-lithic LN nanophotonics, which could ultimately lead to the development of dedicated LN nanofabrication foundries and/or the introduction of etched LN into existing silicon photonics processes.

- Increasing waveguide width from 800 nm to 2.4 μm improved Q from ~1.5 to ~4 million (reducing sidewall scattering)

The platform, which sits atop a standard silicon handle wafer, is positioned to enable applications in electro-optic modulation, nonlinear optics, ultralow-loss quantum photonics, coherent microwave-to-optical conversion, and active topological photonics. ## Abstract

The single-mode microring resonators on lithium niobate thin films were designed and simulated using 2.5-D variational finite difference time domain mode simulations from Lumerical mode Solutions. The single-mode conditions and the propagation losses of lithium niobate planar waveguide with different SiO2 cladding layer thicknesses were studied and compared systematically. The optimization of design parameters such as radii of microrings and gap sizes between channel and ring waveguides were determined. The key issues affecting the resonator design such as free spectral range and Quality Factor were discussed. The microring resonators had radius R = 20 μm, and their transmission spectrum had been tuned using the electro-optical effect.

Keywords:

[microring resonator](/search?q=microring+resonator); [integrated photonic](/search?q=integrated+photonic); [varfdtd](/search?q=varfdtd); [electro-optical](/search?q=electro-optical); [LNOI](/search?q=LNOI)

## 1. Introduction

Lithium niobate (LiNO3, LN) is one of the most promising materials because of its excellent electro-optical, piezoelectric, pyroelectric, photo-elastic and non-linear properties [[1](#B1-crystals-08-00342)]. Due to the high electro-optical coefficient (γ33 = 31.2 pm/V) in LN, highly efficient electro-optical modulator in such material is very promising and always an interesting topic in optical interconnect technology [[2](#B2-crystals-08-00342)]. In last ten years, high-refractive-index contrast, which is LN thin film on a low refractive index SiO2 cladding layer or other substrates (lithium niobate on insulator, LNOI) has emerged, as it is compatible with the silicon on insulator (SOI) manufacturing technology [[3](#B3-crystals-08-00342)]. LNOI is an interesting platform for integrated photonics due to the good confinement and strong guiding of light [[4](#B4-crystals-08-00342)].

The microring resonator is one of the important elements in integrated photonic systems. Optical microring resonators are the promising candidates for a variety of applications, including wavelength filtering, multiplexing, switching and modulation [[5](#B5-crystals-08-00342),[6](#B6-crystals-08-00342),[7](#B7-crystals-08-00342)]. The basic structure of the microring resonator consists of a channel and a ring. The microring resonators have been designed on various types of materials such as silicon [[8](#B8-crystals-08-00342)], germanium-doped silica-on-silicon [[9](#B9-crystals-08-00342)], polymers [[10](#B10-crystals-08-00342)], lithium niobate [[11](#B11-crystals-08-00342),[12](#B12-crystals-08-00342),[13](#B13-crystals-08-00342)] and so forth. The utmost waveguide width with the single-mode behavior is the optimum condition, because no higher order modes were excited and the fundamental mode had the highest light confinement [[14](#B14-crystals-08-00342)]. Therefore, the single-mode condition in the waveguide should be fulfilled in order to prevent signal distortion during transmission. Many articles have reported the fabrication of microring resonators in LN on insulator [[11](#B11-crystals-08-00342),[12](#B12-crystals-08-00342),[13](#B13-crystals-08-00342)] and simulation of microring resonators in SOI [[15](#B15-crystals-08-00342),[16](#B16-crystals-08-00342)], but few reports have involved the simulation of single-mode microring resonators in LNOI in the literature so far. Therefore, a search for the simulation and analysis of single-mode microring resonators in LNOI seems to be important. Our work has focused on LNOI-based devices in order to obtain a high Quality Factor (Q-factor) and wide free spectral range (FSR) that are crucial in developing ultra-compact integrations of planar lightwave circuits [[4](#B4-crystals-08-00342),[17](#B17-crystals-08-00342),[18](#B18-crystals-08-00342)].

In this paper, we presented results from finite difference time domain (FDTD) numerical simulations. Key optical design parameters of laterally coupled LNOI-based microring resonators were characterized using 2.5-D variational FDTD (varFDTD). Waveguide simulations based on full-vectorial finite difference method were performed by varying the geometrical parameters of waveguide configurations to investigate the single-mode conditions and the propagation losses of LN planar waveguides at different SiO2 cladding layer thicknesses. In order to obtain an improved wavelength filtering, we performed the optimization for the design parameters which includes ring radii and gap sizes. These parameters affected FSR and Q-factor directly. As a very important element for practical application we described the electro-optical tunable microring resonators on LNOI.

## 2. Device Description

The material of the device studied in this paper was a z-cut LN thin film stuck to SiO2 cladding layer deposited on a LN substrate. The schematic of a microring resonator is shown in [Figure 1](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00342-f001). The modulator consisted of a ring resonator made by the z-cut LN thin film, which was coupled to a channel. If the signal was on-resonance with the ring, then that signal coupled into the cavity from channel. The device parameters such as ring radii and gap sizes between channel and ring resonator were optimized to have the optimum characteristics.

![Crystals 08 00342 g001](/crystals/crystals-08-00342/article_deploy/html/images/crystals-08-00342-g001-550.jpg "Crystals 08 00342 g001")

**Figure 1.**
A schematic of the waveguide-coupled microring resonator on LNOI.

The varFDTD method with perfectly matched layers boundary conditions (PML) in this work could show how to design and simulate a microring resonator using the finite difference eigen (FDE) mode solver to achieve a desired FSR and Q factor for a LNOI based. The varFDTD method was a direct time and space solution for solving Maxwell’s equations in complex geometries. By performing Fourier transforms, such as the Poynting vector, normalized transmission, and far field projections could be obtained. PML boundaries could absorb electromagnetic energy incident upon them, allowing radiation to propagate out of the computational area without interfering with the field inside [[19](#B19-crystals-08-00342)]. The total ring loss was due to the bend loss and other scattering losses at the coupling region. For the high index contrast wave-guides we were considering, at wavelengths around 1.55 μm, the propagation loss and bend loss were small. For this analysis we would neglect all losses, but the different loss contributions could easily be considered in a more detailed analysis [[20](#B20-crystals-08-00342)].

## 3. Results and Discussion

The high refractive index difference between the LN (no = 2.2129 and ne = 2.1395 at λ = 1.55 μm) [[21](#B21-crystals-08-00342)] and the SiO2 (n = 1.46) required the waveguide thickness and the waveguide width to be smaller than a limiting value to achieve single-mode operation. The single mode conditions had been firstly simulated.

We had calculated the modal curves at λ = 1.55 μm for LN ridge waveguides with 0.7 μm width on SiO2 layer. The effective index dependence on the thickness is presented in [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00342-f002). The first order mode of the transverse electric (TE) and transverse magnetic (TM) modes appeared at the LN thicknesses of 0.86 μm and 0.84 μm, respectively. To ensure that only one electric field intensity peak was supported in the vertical direction of the LN thin film, the thickness of LN thin film should be less than this critical value. In the following simulation, the thickness of LN thin film was all selected as 0.5 µm.

![Crystals 08 00342 g002](/crystals/crystals-08-00342/article_deploy/html/images/crystals-08-00342-g002-550.jpg "Crystals 08 00342 g002")

**Figure 2.**
Effective index of the TE (solid lines) and TM (dashed lines) modes in LN waveguides as a function of the film thickness for a waveguide with 0.7 μm width; the modes were calculated at λ = 1.55 μm.

The dependence of the effective index on the waveguide width, assuming a 0.5-μm thick waveguide is shown in [Figure 3](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00342-f003). The curves showed the boundary between the single-mode and multi-mode conditions. For LN ridge waveguides, the single mode conditions of the TE and TM modes were 1.08 μm and 1.04 μm, respectively. In the following simulations, the widths of LN ridges were all selected as 0.7 μm to ensure that only one mode was supported in the LN thin film.

![Crystals 08 00342 g003](/crystals/crystals-08-00342/article_deploy/html/images/crystals-08-00342-g003-550.jpg "Crystals 08 00342 g003")

**Figure 3.**
Effective index of the TE (solid lines) and TM (dashed lines) modes in LN waveguides as a function of the width for a 0.5 μm thick film. The modes were calculated at λ = 1.55 μm.

The SiO2 layer worked as the cladding layer with a thickness of a limiting value, which was sufficiently thick to prevent the field penetration into the bottom layer. The propagation losses of LN planar waveguide with the different SiO2 layer thicknesses are shown in [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00342-f004). The propagation losses descended with increasing SiO2 cladding layer thicknesses. At the same SiO2 layer thickness, the propagation losses of TE modes were less than those of the TM modes. The diffracted field radiated in the transmission of light, some power was lost into the substrate, but the structure of LN-SiO2-Au had a metal bottom reflector, the power transmitted to the substrate was reflected by the Au bottom reflector, which resulted a decrease of the propagation losses [[22](#B22-crystals-08-00342)]. The propagation losses of LN-SiO2-Au were less than those of LN-SiO2-LN at the same SiO2 layer thickness. At a SiO2 layer thickness of 2 μm, the LN planar waveguide losses were all less than 10−3 dB/cm, which is negligible. Therefore, the thicknesses of SiO2 layer were all selected as 2 µm in the following simulation.

![Crystals 08 00342 g004](/crystals/crystals-08-00342/article_deploy/html/images/crystals-08-00342-g004-550.jpg "Crystals 08 00342 g004")

**Figure 4.**
The propagation losses of LN planar waveguide with the different SiO2 layer thicknesses.

A critical dimension in this optical structure was the gap separating the ring from the tangential waveguide. The gap size determined the input and output couple ratios of the microring resonator, which determined the magnitude of the finesse and the at-resonance transmittance in turn. In the case of a microring coupled to channel, the gaps were very small due to the strong optical confinement and the small coupling interaction length [[14](#B14-crystals-08-00342)].

Because the FSR defined as the separation between two adjacent resonant wavelengths, increased and might become even larger than the wavelength range used for wavelength division multiplex (WDM) applications. However, one of the most critical factors limiting the minimum useful ring radius was the bending loss. These could be qualitatively understood by describing the bend as a straight waveguide, while the effective index was decreasing function in the radial direction. This implied that at a certain distance from the waveguide core, the solution of the Maxwell equations became a radiating field; this radiation was a loss source, as in a leaky waveguide [[11](#B11-crystals-08-00342)].

Using varFDTD, we have calculated Q-factor, bending loss and FSR for a single-mode waveguide at different ring radii and gap sizes (channel and ring width w = 0.7 μm, λ = around 1.55 μm). The results are shown in [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00342-f005) and [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00342-f006). According to the [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00342-f005)a, when the radius was smaller than 20 μm, the Q-factor significantly ascended with increased radii, while it was larger than 20 μm, it preserved almost unchangeable values. We also observed that Q-factor ascended with increasing gap sizes and the TE and TM modes showed different results in terms of the achievable Q-factor for this geometry. In the case of gap = 0.29 μm, a Q-factor more than 10,000 was achieved for the TE mode whilst for the TM mode the Q-factor was significantly smaller ~2000. [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00342-f005)b shows Bending loss descended with increasing ring radius, and the bending losses are very low as the radii more than 20 μm. Loss in practical structures would inevitably come up for the following two reasons: on one hand, the scattering by the residual roughness of the etched walls of the photonic wires [[17](#B17-crystals-08-00342)], on the other hand, the modal mismatch at the interface between SiO2 layer and LN thin film [[23](#B23-crystals-08-00342)]. However, the losses of the LN waveguides could be reduced as much as possible by optimizing the fabrication process of waveguides. At 1590 nm wavelength, the propagation losses of sub-wavelength scale LN waveguides could be as low as 2.7 dB/m by Ar+ ion etching [[12](#B12-crystals-08-00342)]. As shown in [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00342-f006), FSR descended with increasing ring radius. Both TE and TM modes achieved the largest FSR for the ring with the smallest radius 3 μm. When the radius was larger than 40 μm and the gap size was 0.1 μm, the FWHM (full-width at half-maximum) of the dip was close to the FSR, the dip became less obvious. Because the effective index of TE mode was larger than that of TM mode, the Q-factor of TE mode was greater than that of TM mode, and FSR of TE mode was less than that of TM mode.

![Crystals 08 00342 g005](/crystals/crystals-08-00342/article_deploy/html/images/crystals-08-00342-g005-550.jpg "Crystals 08 00342 g005")

**Figure 5.**
(**a**) Q-factor of microring resonator as different ring radii for different gap sizes, (**b**) Bending loss variation as bending radius. The modes were calculated at λ = around 1.55 μm.

![Crystals 08 00342 g006](/crystals/crystals-08-00342/article_deploy/html/images/crystals-08-00342-g006-550.jpg "Crystals 08 00342 g006")

**Figure 6.**
FSR of microring resonators as different ring radii. The modes were calculated at λ = around 1.55 μm.

The electro-optical properties of LN microring resonator have been simulated by applying a static electric field to the device electrodes to shift transmission spectrum. In [Figure 7](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00342-f007), a LN microring resonator is embedded in the middle of SiO2 layer, and the electrodes are placed over below and above the SiO2 layer. A tuning range of microring resonators depend on the strength of the electro-optical effect. However, the electric field achieved in the LN film was relatively weak because the upper and lower cladding materials exhibited one order of magnitude smaller dielectric constants. Due to the large difference between the dielectric constant of the LN thin film (εLN = 28.5) and the SiO2 (εSiO2 = 3.9), the field in the LN thin film was considerably far less than in the SiO2 layer. The field in the two layers could be calculated from the applied voltage ΔV using the continuity of the vertical component of the electric displacement field D:

ELN dLN + ESiO2 dSiO2 = ΔV,

D = ε0 εLN ELN = ε0 εSiO2 ESiO2 = const,

dLN and dSiO2 were the thicknesses of LN thin film and SiO2 layer, which have been determined. Therefore, the electric field in the LN thin film layer is given by Equations (1) and (2).

![Crystals 08 00342 g007](/crystals/crystals-08-00342/article_deploy/html/images/crystals-08-00342-g007-550.jpg "Crystals 08 00342 g007")

**Figure 7.**
The LN microring resonator was embedded in the middle SiO2 layer, and the electrodes were placed over below and above the SiO2 layer.

Optical transmission simulations were performed to characterize the electrical tuning of optical resonances. To observe the electro-optic effect, an electric field applied between the top and the bottom electrodes by applying different direct current (DC) voltages was considered uniform. [Figure 8](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00342-f008) shows the simulated TM-mode spectrum as a function of different electric field intensities. The resonance wavelength shifted ascending with increasingly electric field intensity. The resonance shifts were 99 pm, 198 pm, 297 pm, and 395 pm for the chance in different electric field intensities from 0 V/μm to 1 V/μm, 2 V/μm, 3 V/μm, and 4 V/μm, respectively.

![Crystals 08 00342 g008](/crystals/crystals-08-00342/article_deploy/html/images/crystals-08-00342-g008-550.jpg "Crystals 08 00342 g008")

**Figure 8.**
Transmission spectra of wavelength shift due to different electric field intensities in the Z-direction. The calculations referred to the TM mode at the microring radius R = 20 μm.

## 4. Conclusions

In conclusion, a VarFDTD method was used to design and simulate various waveguides and waveguide-coupled single-mode microring resonators in z-cut LNOI. Single mode conditions were obtained. The propagation losses of LN planar waveguides were calculated by full-vectorial finite difference method. The propagation losses of LN planar waveguides decreased with the increase of the SiO2 cladding layer thickness. The thickness of LN Film, width of ridge waveguide and thickness of SiO2 layer were optimized to 0.5 μm, 0.7 μm and 2 μm, respectively. Q-factor ascended with increasing radius and gap sizes, while FSR descended with increasing radius. A microring resonator with Q-factor more than 10,000 and FSR more than 8 nm was achieved in the case of gap = 0.29 μm and radius R = 20 μm. Our simulation showed that the resonance wavelength of the electro-optical microresonators in LNOI shifted ascending with increasingly electric field intensity. This work will continue with fabrication and characterization. For this purpose, the results provided here will be of useful guidance before laboratory works are carried out.
