This arXiv paper reports the first directional atomic layer etching (ALE) process for lithium niobate (LiNbO3, LN), a nonlinear optical material used in integrated photonics for applications such as optical communications and quantum information processing. The process uses sequential exposures of HBr/BCl3/Ar plasma for surface modification followed by Ar plasma for removal, conducted in an Oxford Instruments PlasmaPro 100 Cobra system at 0°C and 200°C.

Key results: At 0°C, the directional ALE process achieved an etch rate of 1.04±0.01 nm/cycle with 84.6% synergy. At 200°C, the etch rate increased to 1.25±0.01 nm/cycle but synergy dropped to 56.8%. The HBr chemistry significantly reduces redeposition of involatile compounds (lithium and magnesium halides) compared to F- and Cl-based plasmas, attributed to the higher vapor pressures of Br-based products. Saturation was observed at 40 seconds of HBr/BCl3/Ar plasma exposure, with a "soft saturation" of the Ar plasma half-step due to a bromine concentration gradient.

Surface analysis: After 50 ALE cycles at 0°C, surface bromine concentration was 0.50±0.04%, decreasing to 0.35±0.06% at 200°C, confirming better removal of etch products at higher temperature. Surface roughness was Rq=0.30±0.04 nm for the polished original, increasing to Rq=0.73±0.06 nm after 20 cycles at 0°C, but remaining smooth at Rq=0.25±0.03 nm after 20 cycles at 200°C (unchanged from control). A 120-cycle test (149 nm etch) at 200°C showed no roughening (Rq=0.28±0.03 nm). In comparison, a Cl2/BCl3 process at the same temperature produced rougher surfaces. On a TFLN chip with waveguides previously fabricated by Ar ion milling, 50 cycles of ALE smoothed the top surface from Rq=2.07±1.16 nm to Rq=0.34±0.07 nm (84% reduction).

Device demonstration: A TFLN grating structure (19 waveguides, 1.2 μm top width, gaps from 1 μm down to 150 nm) was etched entirely by 200 cycles of directional ALE at 200°C (total depth 223 nm, EPC 1.12 nm/cycle). The process exhibited aspect ratio independent etching (ARDE) down to the smallest tested gap of 150 nm, in contrast to ion milling where ARDE manifests at gaps below 300 nm for the same etch depth. Sidewall angle was 68 degrees.

An isotropic ALE process was also reported using H2 plasma followed by HBr/BCl3/Ar plasma at 0°C, achieving 1.43±0.02 nm/cycle with 97.9% synergy and Rq=0.77±0.07 nm surface roughness.

The authors propose combining directional and isotropic ALE processes for complete TFLN device fabrication, which could overcome limitations of physical Ar+ ion milling including sidewall roughness, redeposition, ARDE, and lack of nanometer-level etch depth control. The work was supported by Oxford Instruments and the Broadcom Innovation Fund at Caltech.

Introduction Dry and wet etch processes are important and widely used for the fabrication of electronic and optoelectronic devices. Recently, there has been an increasing interest in many micro and nanoscale short-wave (SW-) and mid-wave (MW) infrared (IR) devices including transistors [1,2], photodiodes [3], light emitting diodes (LEDs) [4] and diode lasers [5] due to a wide range of emerging applications. Development of these devices at this wavelength regime requires the novel (AlGaIn)(AsSb) material system on GaSb substrates. As opposed to III-Vs such as phosphides and arsenides, antimonide materials exhibit a few unusual etching behaviors such as undesired weak etching by commonly used developers with an etch rate of up to 0.6 nm/sec and very fast oxidation rate with atmospheric oxygen. It is also observed that hydrofluoric acid (HF) etches plasma-exposed antimonides unlike other III-Vs. Moreover, GaSb and its alloys show poor selectivites in commonly used wet and dry etchants that are typical in other III-V’s device processing. Due to the strong and fast oxidation, Al-containing materials are not useable as etch-stop layers [6]. Sidewalls can also be seen here after, (c) 50-μm wide stripes covered with resist and Ti//Au metal layer underneath after dry etching in Cl2/N2 plasma and (d) the close-up view of the ridges are shown at the bottom. Fig. 5. (a) Schematic of the test structures for active/passive definition test, (b) simulated and measured (smoothed out) reflectivity data as a function of etch depth are superimposed; (c) system’s original raw data for the detection of endpoint during dry etching using Cl2/N2 plasma; and (d) microscope image of the test structure after the etching, showing active/passive regions. Vol. 9, No. 4 | 1 Apr 2019 | OPTICAL MATERIALS EXPRESS 1791 In order to assess the effect of the developed plasma etch process on our material structure, Fabry Pérot broad-area lasers with a wide ridge using this ICP dry etch were fabricated. I-V characteristics of the device were then measured under both forward and reverse biases. Laser devices exhibit reasonable dark current and threshold current at room temperature, hinting that the plasma etch did not affect the device performance. 3.2 Wet chemical etching A number of etchants along with the etch rates for different materials are listed in Table 2. One of the most-used wet etchants is Solution-1. Using this etchant, GaSb, InAs, and InGaAsSb are etched with a smooth surface and a good reproducibility. For Al-containing layers, this etchant shows fast etching rate when the Al-content is low (Al<30%). For the Solution-2, we found the same etch rates as reported by Dier et al. [10]. Most importantly, selective removal of InAsSb from GaSb can be done by this solution. Table 2. Wet-Etchants for Antimonide Materials Used in This Study HCl-based etchant (Solution-3) could also be used in removing antimonide materials. However, the surface morphology of GaSb and low-Al containing materials usually gets rough with this etchant. Figure 6 presents the microscope image of the Al0.5GaAsSb surface after being etched by this etchant, showing the surface roughness is about 8 nm, as measured by the surface profilometer. However, this etchant is useful because it shows good selectivity between lattice-matched quinternary AlGaInAsSb and AlGaAsSb with 80% Al-compostion. In fact, one could obtain a selectivity higher than 30 between the Al0.85GaAs0.07Sb and Al0.2In0.25GaAs0.23Sb layer with a reproducible etch rate and smooth surface after the etching [17]. The etching rate for the etch stop layer is accurate and reproducible. The HCl etchant shows fast etching rate for Al-rich (Al>50%) layers. This high degree of selectivity confirmed that the Al0.2In0.25GaAs0.23Sb alloy could be suitable for the etch stop layer [17]. Solution-4 can be used to etch antimonides with a moderate etching rate in an unselective way. It could be used for processing interband cascade laser [18] devices where several hundred to over a thousand epilayers of short-period antimonide-based superlattice with different constituents are grown as a part of the device structure. Solution-5 and 6 are not that useful as etchants. However, the device manufactures should be aware of these two etchants as well as their etch rates. # Wet etchants Etching rate (nm/sec) GaSb In0.43GaAsSb Al0.5GaAs0.04Sb InAs0.91Sb Al0.2In0.2GaAs0.19Sb 1 C4H4KNaO6:HCl:H2O2 = 50 : 40 : 3.5 12 6 5 0.4 4 2 C6H8O7:H2O2 = 2 : 1 0.01 0.23 - 1.5 - 3 HCl:H2O2:H2O = 100 : 1 : 100 4.2 - 10 0.8 1 4 H3PO4 : H2O2 : C6H8O7 : H2O = 3 : 5: 55 : 22 2.5-3 (fairly unselective) 5 AZ726 MIF developer 0.17 (GaSb/InAs superlattice) 6 Buffered HF 570 (plasma exposed GaSb, AlGaAsSb and InAs) Vol. 9, No. 4 | 1 Apr 2019 | OPTICAL MATERIALS EXPRESS 1792 Fig. 6. Optical microscope image of the etched surface after wet chemical etching (left) of Al0.5GaAsSb by HCl-based etchant. Roughness measurement of the etched surface is also shown by the profilometer (right). 3.3 GaSb substrate removal The substrate removal procedure is described in detail in ref [19]. This could be done by the SIRTL etchant which is referred to the mixture of HF/CrO3. Transene Inc. stocks two premixes, 1:5 and 1:10 Sirtl: H2O. The former solution shows a very high etch rate of GaSb material, which one could begin with to remove the bulk of the material. Given that, this etchant exhibits very high selectivity between GaSb and InAsSb, 1:100 Sirtl: H2O could be used to stop etching on thin layers of InAsSb. Thus, a smooth, mirror-like light-blue colored thin InAsSb layer can be obtained at the end of the removal process. 4. Conclusion Selective wet and dry etching processes have been explored for the quaternaries lattice-matched to GaSb. Useful wet etchants and dry etching processes are given. In particular, materials and processes relevant to establishing a fabrication procedure for widely-tunable SG-DBR lasers in the SW/MW-IR wavelength regime using antimonide materials system have been defined. By employing an MQW InGaAsSb/AlGaAsSb/GaSb gain material and necessary processing steps, one could develop a PIC technology in the GaSb material system that contains a MQW active region, which is selectively removed either by a wet or dry etch using an etch stop layer or by a time-controlled etch, aided by a laser monitor if done by dry ion-etching. This makes the integration platform the simplest way to combine active and passive components on a chip. In fact, the fabrication of many other optoelectronic devices could benefit from the etching and processing technology outlined in this paper. args.summary:
This paper (published in Optical Materials Express, Vol. 9, No. 4, April 1, 2019, DOI: 10.1364/OME.9.001786) by Shamsul Arafin and colleagues from UCSB, The Ohio State University, and the National Research Council of Canada reports on optimized dry and wet etching processes for antimonide-based photonic integrated circuits (PICs), specifically for the (AlGaIn)(AsSb) material system on GaSb substrates.

**Key Findings:**

**Dry Etching (ICP-RIE):**
- Used Cl2/N2 chemistry (Cl2 with N2 added for sidewall passivation) in an inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etcher (Panasonic E640 system)
- Optimized parameters: RF bias 75 W, ICP 900 W, pressure 0.2 Pa, gas flow 20 sccm Cl2 / 10 sccm N2, etch rate 8.7 nm/sec, selectivity vs SiO2 mask of 8:1
- No argon used in gas chemistry to avoid physical etching damage
- In situ 670-nm-wavelength laser reflectance monitoring enables stop-etching at material interfaces with endpoint depth precision within ±10 nm
- Process produces high aspect ratio structures with smooth sidewalls and vertical profiles
- No crystallographic etching observed for various orientations
- N2 addition reduces surface roughness; Al0.5GaAs0.04Sb quaternary cladding layer was the primary target
- Fabry-Pérot broad-area lasers fabricated with this etch showed reasonable dark current and threshold current at room temperature, confirming minimal plasma damage

**Wet Chemical Etching (Key etchants and rates):**
1. Tartaric acid-based "Rochelle" etch (C4H4KNaO6:HCl:H2O2 = 50:40:3.5): GaSb 12 nm/s, In0.43GaAsSb 6 nm/s, Al0.5GaAs0.04Sb 5 nm/s, InAs0.91Sb 0.4 nm/s, Al0.2In0.2GaAs0.19Sb 4 nm/s
2. Citric acid (C6H8O7:H2O2 = 2:1): GaSb 0.01 nm/s, In0.43GaAsSb 0.23 nm/s, InAs0.91Sb 1.5 nm/s — selectively removes InAsSb from GaSb
3. HCl-based (HCl:H2O2:H2O = 100:1:100): GaSb 4.2 nm/s, Al0.5GaAs0.04Sb 10 nm/s, InAs0.91Sb 0.8 nm/s, Al0.2In0.2GaAs0.19Sb 1 nm/s — shows selectivity >30 between Al0.85GaAs0.07Sb and Al0.2In0.25GaAs0.23Sb layers, making the latter suitable as an etch stop layer; produces rough surfaces on GaSb and low-Al materials (~8 nm roughness)
4. H3PO4:H2O2:C6H8O7:H2O = 3:5:55:22: fairly unselective, 2.5-3 nm/s — useful for interband cascade laser processing
5. AZ726 MIF developer: 0.17 nm/s (GaSb/InAs superlattice) — weak undesired etching noted
6. Buffered HF: 570 nm/s (plasma-exposed GaSb, AlGaAsSb and InAs) — unusually fast etching of plasma-exposed antimonides

**GaSb Substrate Removal:**
- SIRTL etchant (HF/CrO3 premix from Transene Inc.): 1:5 dilution removes bulk GaSb quickly; 1:100 dilution stops on thin InAsSb layers due to very high selectivity, yielding smooth mirror-like light-blue InAsSb surface

**Motivation/Context:**
- Antimonide materials exhibit unusual etching behaviors: weak etching by common developers (up to 0.6 nm/s), fast oxidation with atmospheric oxygen, HF etching of plasma-exposed antimonides, and poor selectivities in conventional etchants
- Al-containing layers cannot serve as etch stop layers due to fast oxidation
- Need for dry etch with optical (laser) etch-stop monitoring because InAsSb etch-stop layers introduce undesirable type-II band alignment in SG-DBR laser structures
- Study supports fabrication of widely-tunable SG-DBR lasers and photonic ICs in the short-wave/mid-wave IR regime
- Etching was optimized using n-type GaSb substrates with MBE-grown epistacks; SiO2 hard masks (100 nm) and photoresist masks used

**Conclusion:**
The developed selective wet and dry etching processes enable fabrication of widely-tunable SG-DBR lasers and monolithic PICs in the GaSb material system, where MQW active regions can be selectively removed via wet/dry etch with etch-stop layer or time-controlled dry etch aided by laser monitoring. This integration platform provides the simplest approach to combining active and passive components on a chip.
args.key_excerpts: "The optimized ICP etch process is capable of producing high aspect ratio structures with smooth sidewalls. In situ reflectance monitoring with a 670-nm-wavelength laser was used to enable stop-etching at a material interface with high accuracy."

## Abstract

Waveguides formed by etching, proton-exchange (PE), and strip-loaded on single-crystal lithium niobate (LN) thin film were designed and simulated by a full-vectorial finite difference method. The single-mode condition, optical power distribution, and bending loss of these kinds of waveguides were studied and compared systematically. For the PE waveguide, the optical power distributed in LN layer had negligible change with the increase of PE thickness. For the strip-loaded waveguide, the relationships between optical power distribution in LN layer and waveguide thickness were different for quasi-TE (q-TE) and quasi-TM (q-TM) modes. The bending loss would decrease with the increase of bending radius. There was a bending loss caused by the electromagnetic field leakage when the neff of q-TM waveguide was smaller than that of nearby TE planar waveguide. LN ridge waveguides possessed a low bending loss even at a relatively small bending radius. This study is helpful for the understanding of waveguide structures as well as for the optimization and the fabrication of high-density integrated optical components.

## 1. Introduction

Lithium niobate (LN) is one of the best known ferroelectric crystals gifted with many advantages—such as excellent electro-optic, nonlinear-optic, acousto-optic, piezoelectric, and pyroelectric properties—which makes it an attractive material for photonic, electronic, and sensor applications [[1](#B1-crystals-08-00191),[2](#B2-crystals-08-00191)]. In recent years, high-refractive-index contrast, single-crystal LN thin film on a low refractive index SiO2 cladding layer (lithium niobate on insulator, LNOI) or other substrates, has been fabricated using ion implantation and wafer bonding technologies [[3](#B3-crystals-08-00191),[4](#B4-crystals-08-00191)]. The high-refractive-index contrast between LN and SiO2, enabling good confinement and strong guiding of light, and a high-density photonic integrated circuit is expected. Various photonic devices based on LN thin films have been reported, such as photonic crystals [[5](#B5-crystals-08-00191),[6](#B6-crystals-08-00191),[7](#B7-crystals-08-00191)], electro-optical modulators [[8](#B8-crystals-08-00191),[9](#B9-crystals-08-00191),[10](#B10-crystals-08-00191),[11](#B11-crystals-08-00191)], wavelength conversion devices [[12](#B12-crystals-08-00191),[13](#B13-crystals-08-00191),[14](#B14-crystals-08-00191),[15](#B15-crystals-08-00191)], and heterogeneous LN photonic devices [[16](#B16-crystals-08-00191),[17](#B17-crystals-08-00191),[18](#B18-crystals-08-00191)].

Waveguides are fundamental elements that can form various devices of an optical integrated circuit. Nano-scale waveguides in LNOI is essential for photonic integrated circuits with low power consumption and high integration density. Many methods have been reported to fabricate waveguides with good performance on LN thin film, including dry etching [[19](#B19-crystals-08-00191),[20](#B20-crystals-08-00191)], proton-exchange (PE) [[21](#B21-crystals-08-00191)], and strip-loaded [[22](#B22-crystals-08-00191)]. The transmission losses of LN ridge waveguides fabricated via dry etching were reported to be 0.027, 0.3, and 0.4 dB/cm, respectively [[19](#B19-crystals-08-00191),[20](#B20-crystals-08-00191),[23](#B23-crystals-08-00191)]. The losses of the PE waveguides were 0.2 and 0.6 dB/cm, respectively [[21](#B21-crystals-08-00191),[24](#B24-crystals-08-00191)]. Various materials were used as loading strip to fabricate strip-loaded waveguides. For example, SiN strip-loaded waveguides presented the transmission losses of 0.3, 1, and 7 dB/cm, respectively [[14](#B14-crystals-08-00191),[25](#B25-crystals-08-00191),[26](#B26-crystals-08-00191)]. The transmission losses of Si strip-loaded waveguides were 0.8, 1.3, and 6 dB/cm, respectively [[18](#B18-crystals-08-00191),[27](#B27-crystals-08-00191),[28](#B28-crystals-08-00191)]. Bent waveguide is a basic building block for many integrated optical devices, such as Y-junctions, optical delay lines, resonators, and interferometers [[29](#B29-crystals-08-00191),[30](#B30-crystals-08-00191),[31](#B31-crystals-08-00191)]. Small bending radius is preferred to reduce the dimensions of the photonic devices. Low bending loss is important to low power consumption devices. In this paper, LN ridge, PE, and strip-loaded waveguides have been analyzed and compared. Waveguide simulations based on full-vectorial finite difference method were performed by varying the geometrical parameters of different waveguide configurations to investigate the single-mode condition, optical power distribution in the straight waveguides, and bending loss of the bent waveguides. The different variation trends in optical power distribution in LN layer between q-TE and q-TM modes were explained. The mechanisms of leakage loss in TM polarization were studied.

## 2. Design of Waveguide Geometry

Three different configurations—including ridge waveguides, PE waveguides, and strip-loaded waveguides on LN thin film—were discussed. [Figure 1](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00191-f001)a shows the schematic and cross-section of an LN ridge bent waveguide. From the bottom to the top, there are the LN substrate, SiO2 cladding layer, and LN ridge. [Figure 1](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00191-f001)b shows the schematic and cross-section of an LN PE bent waveguide. The PE region is embedded in LN thin film. Since the lateral diffusion could be ignored when the exchanged depth was much smaller than the waveguide width and the exchange process results in step-like index profiles, the designed PE region was set as a rectangle. [Figure 1](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00191-f001)c shows the schematic and cross-section of a strip-loaded bent waveguide, which could be regarded as a combination of the LN planar waveguide and a superincumbent strip. The refractive index of the strip material was larger than 1, which could effectively define the waveguide path [[32](#B32-crystals-08-00191)]. Here in, four materials (SiO2, SiN, TiO2, and Si) which were commonly used as loading strip of LN planar waveguide were simulated and discussed.

**Figure 1.**
Schematic and cross-section of the (**a**) LN ridge bent waveguide, (**b**) PE bent waveguide, and (**c**) strip-loaded bent waveguide.

Many numerical methods have been used in the simulation of waveguides [[33](#B33-crystals-08-00191),[34](#B34-crystals-08-00191)]. Among them, the full-vectorial finite difference method is regarded as a simple and effective method to solve the mode profile and bending loss. The mechanism of this method is shown as follows. The finite difference algorithm is used for meshing the waveguide geometry, and has the ability to accommodate arbitrary waveguide structure. Once the structure is meshed, Maxwell’s equations are then formulated into a matrix eigenvalue problem and solved using sparse matrix techniques to obtain the effective index and mode profiles of the waveguide modes. Perfectly matched layer (PML) boundary conditions could absorb electromagnetic energy incident upon them, allowing radiation to propagate out of the computational area without interfering with the field inside. This boundary condition could benefit the bending loss calculation [[35](#B35-crystals-08-00191)]. The telecommunication wavelength of 1.55 µm was used in all the following simulations. The LNOI were all x-cut, and the birefringence of the LN material was considered in the simulations. The ordinary and extraordinary refractive indices of the LN thin film at wavelength 1.55 µm were set to be 2.211 and 2.138, respectively, according to the Sellmeier equation [[36](#B36-crystals-08-00191)]. The ordinary and extraordinary refractive indices of the PE region in LN thin film at wavelength 1.55 µm were 2.161 and 2.218, respectively, which were obtained according to [[21](#B21-crystals-08-00191)]. The refractive indices of SiO2 [[37](#B37-crystals-08-00191)], SiN [[25](#B25-crystals-08-00191)], TiO2 [[38](#B38-crystals-08-00191)], and Si [[22](#B22-crystals-08-00191)] at wavelength 1550 nm were 1.46, 1.9, 2.3, and 3.48, respectively.

## 3. Results and Discussion

In order to discuss how light is confined and guided in different waveguide geometries, the parameters of the waveguides (the thickness T of the LN layer, the thickness D and width W of the PE region and loading strip, and the thickness T and width W of ridge waveguide) were used in the simulation. The single mode condition has been firstly simulated. [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00191-f002) shows the relationship between the LN thin film thickness and the number of mode that could be supported in LN planar waveguide. The first order mode of the TE and TM modes appeared at the LN thickness of 0.6 μm and 0.7 μm, respectively. To ensure that only one electric field intensity peak is supported in the vertical direction of the LN thin film, the thickness of LN should be less than this critical value. In the following simulation, the thickness of LN was all selected as 0.5 μm. [Figure 3](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00191-f003) shows the single-mode condition in the ridge and channel waveguides. The curves show the boundary between the single-mode and multi-mode conditions. The waveguide dimensions beneath the curves fulfilled the single mode condition. For the LN ridge waveguide, the single mode condition of the quasi-TE (q-TE) mode and quasi-TM (q-TM) mode were 1.1 μm and 1.06 μm, respectively (see the green star, the thickness of LN ridge was fixed at 0.5 μm). PE process only increased the extraordinary refractive index of the crystal. Therefore, only q-TE mode was supported in the x-cut PE waveguides. As shown in [Figure 3](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00191-f003)a, as the PE thickness (D) increased, the PE width (W) should decrease in order to fulfill the single-mode condition. For the strip-loaded waveguide, the strip width (W) also decreased with the increase of strip thickness (D) for both q-TE and q-TM modes. The strip width for the single-mode condition would increase for the lower refractive index material at the same strip thickness. In the following simulation, the widths of LN ridge, PE region, and loading strip were all selected as 1 μm to ensure that only one mode was supported in LN thin film.

The optical power in LN layer was defined as the ratio of the optical power in the LN region to the total optical power of all the space. Consequently, the value was between 0 and 1. As shown in [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00191-f004)a, the optical power of the q-TE mode in the LN ridge was 85.6% (see the green star, the thickness and width of LN ridge were fixed at 0.5 μm and 1 μm, respectively). For the PE waveguide, the optical power of the q-TE mode showed a very slight increase with the increase of PE thickness. The reason was that the light confinement by refractive index contrast increased with the increase of the PE thickness as well as the neff of the PE waveguide. For the strip-loaded waveguide, the optical power of the q-TE mode in the LN layer decreased slightly as the strip thickness increased, expect for Si strip, which decreased obviously with the increase of Si thickness. This indicated that the refractive index of strip had some influence on the distribution of the optical power. With the increase of the refractive index of the strip, the optical power confined in LN layer would gradually be attracted into the strip. As shown in [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00191-f004)b, the optical power of the q-TM mode in the LN ridge was 82.5%. For the strip-loaded waveguide, the optical power of the q-TM mode in the LN layer initially increased as the trip thickness increased. The maximum value was obtained at a thickness of approximately 0.12, 0.07, 0.07, and 0.07 μm for the SiO2, SiN, TiO2, and Si strip, respectively. As the strip thickness increased further, the optical power in the LN layer decreased. The reason could be explained as follows. Firstly, the strip thickness is too thin to effectively confine the optical power in LN layer, and a small part of optical power could leak into the SiO2 buffer layer. With the increase of strip thickness, the light confinement by the loading strip increases. The optical power in the LN layer begins decrease when the optical power is gradually attracted into the strip.

![Crystals 08 00191 g004](/crystals/crystals-08-00191/article_deploy/html/images/crystals-08-00191-g004-550.jpg "Crystals 08 00191 g004")

**Figure 4.**

A bent waveguide which possesses both a small bending radius and a low bending loss is preferred. [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00191-f005)a shows the relationship between the bending loss and the bending radius of a LN ridge waveguide. The thickness and width of LN ridge were fixed as 0.5 and 1 μm, respectively. The bending loss decreased sharply with the increase of bending radius. The minimal bending radii having low bending losses (10−5 dB/cm, for example) were 15 and 20 μm for both q-TE and q-TM modes, respectively. In the experiment, a microring resonator with a bending loss of 0.1 dB/cm at a bending radius of 80 μm was realized [[19](#B19-crystals-08-00191)]. The relationship between the bending loss and the bending radius of PE waveguide with different PE depths is shown in [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00191-f005)b. With the increase of bending radius, the bending loss decreased. The thickness of PE region had an obvious influence on bending loss. When D = 0.2 μm, the bending loss was 34 dB/cm at radius of 1 mm, while the bending loss was 10−11 dB/cm when D = 0.5 μm with the same radius. The increase of PE thickness could cause the increase of neff of waveguide, so that the light confinement of the waveguide increased, and the bending loss decreased correspondingly. The Y-junctions based on PE waveguide with 4–8 mm bending radii were designed and fabricated and a stable splitting ratio of 1:1 was obtained [[21](#B21-crystals-08-00191)]. [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00191-f005)c–f shows the relationship between the bending loss and the bending radius as well as strip thickness (D) of the strip-loaded waveguides with four different loading strip materials, respectively. The widths of strips were fixed as 1 μm for all the waveguides. The bending loss decreased with the increase of bending radius for both q-TE and q-TM modes. The refractive index of loading strip had a remarkable influence on bending loss. A higher refractive index would cause a lower bending loss. For q-TE mode, a low bending loss (10−5 dB/cm, for example) could be obtained if the bending radius was large enough. The LN thin film Mach–Zehnder modulator with SiN strip-loaded waveguide has been reported, which demonstrated a Vπ·L of 3 V cm and a 3-dB bandwidth of 8 GHz [[26](#B26-crystals-08-00191)]. While for q-TM mode, there is another loss mechanism. The electric field Ez (coordinate direction is shown in [Figure 1](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00191-f001)) in the q-TM mode would cause leakage loss when the neff of the strip-loaded waveguide was smaller than that of nearby LN planar waveguide in TE polarization [[39](#B39-crystals-08-00191)]. Take the SiN strip-loaded bent waveguide as an example, as shown in [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00191-f005)d, when the thickness of SiN strip was 0.05 μm, the neff of the SiN strip-loaded waveguide (nTM00 = 1.844) was smaller than that of nearby LN planar waveguide (nTE0 = 1.910), and the electric field Ez in the strip-loaded waveguide mode would excite the TE mode in the planar waveguides on both sides of the strip-loaded waveguide, causing waveguide loss. In this case, the minimum loss is 57 dB/cm. [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00191-f006)a,b show the Ez and Ex distributions with a strip thickness of 0.05 μm. [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00191-f006)a shows there was electric field outside the strip-loaded waveguide region, indicating an optical power leakage. When the thickness of SiN strip was 0.3 μm, the neff of the SiN strip-loaded waveguide (nTM00 = 1.922) was larger than that of nearby LN planar waveguide (nTE0 = 1.910), the Ez component could not excite the waveguide mode in the planar waveguides besides the strip-loaded waveguide. The bending loss could be very small (around 10−10 dB/cm at radius of 4 mm). [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_crystals-08-00191-f006)c,d show the Ez and Ex distributions with a strip thickness of 0.3 μm. There was almost no electric field outside the strip-loaded waveguide region, indicating negligible optical power leakage. This kind of leakage loss mechanism caused by TE↔TM mode coupling could be found in straight waveguides [[21](#B21-crystals-08-00191)].

## 4. Conclusions

In conclusion, a full-vectorial finite difference method was used to simulate various waveguides—including ridge waveguide, PE waveguide, and strip-loaded waveguides—in single-crystal LN thin film. Single mode conditions were obtained. The optical power percentage in LN layer was calculated. For q-TE mode, the optical power in the etched LN ridge waveguide was 85.6% when the waveguide width was 1 μm and the LN thickness was 0.5 μm. The optical power in the PE waveguide showed slight increase with the increase of PE thickness, while the optical power decreased with the increase of strip thickness. For q-TM mode, the optical power in the etched LN ridge waveguide was 82.5%. The optical power in the strip-loaded waveguide initially increased as the strip thickness increased. The maximum value was obtained at the thickness of approximately 0.12, 0.07, 0.07, and 0.07 μm for the SiO2, SiN, TiO2, and Si strip, respectively. As the strip thickness increased further, the optical power in the LN layer decreased. The bending loss decreased with the increase of bending radius. For the LN ridge waveguide, the minimal bending radii (with bending loss of 10−5 dB/cm, for example) were 15 and 20 μm for q-TE and q-TM modes, respectively. For the PE waveguide, the bending loss decreased with the increase of PE depths for q-TE mode. For the strip-loaded waveguide, a low bending loss (10−5 dB/cm, for example) could be obtained for q-TE mode if the bending radius was large enough. While for the q-TM mode, there existed an extra loss mechanism. The leakage of Ez component existed in q-TM mode when the neff of waveguide was smaller than that of the nearby planar waveguides in TE polarization. The increase of strip thickness could improve neff of waveguide to be larger than that of nearby planar waveguides, which could avoid the leakage loss. The study is useful for the fabrication of high-density integrated optical components.

args.summary:
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article titled "Analysis of Waveguides on Lithium Niobate Thin Films" published in the journal *Crystals* (Volume 8, Issue 5, article 191) on April 27, 2018, by Yiwen Wang, Zhihua Chen, and Hui Hu from the School of Physics, State Key Laboratory of Crystal Materials, Shandong University, China. The article belongs to the Special Issue "Lithium Niobate: Bulk Crystals, Composites, Thin Films and Nanocrystals."

STUDY OVERVIEW: The authors designed and simulated three types of waveguides on single-crystal lithium niobate (LN) thin films (LNOI) using a full-vectorial finite difference method: (1) ridge waveguides (formed by dry etching), (2) proton-exchange (PE) waveguides, and (3) strip-loaded waveguides (using SiO2, SiN, TiO2, and Si as loading strip materials). They systematically studied the single-mode condition, optical power distribution, and bending loss of each waveguide type.

METHODOLOGY: Simulations were performed at the telecommunication wavelength of 1.55 µm using x-cut LNOI. The ordinary and extraordinary refractive indices of LN were set to 2.211 and 2.138 respectively, according to the Sellmeier equation. The PE region had refractive indices of 2.161 (ordinary) and 2.218 (extraordinary). Refractive indices of SiO2, SiN, TiO2, and Si at 1550 nm were 1.46, 1.9, 2.3, and 3.48 respectively. Perfectly matched layer (PML) boundary conditions were used for bending loss calculations. The LN thin film thickness was set at 0.5 µm, and waveguide widths at 1 µm to ensure single-mode operation.

KEY RESULTS:
- Single-mode condition: First-order TE and TM modes appeared at LN thicknesses of 0.6 µm and 0.7 µm respectively. For ridge waveguides, single-mode conditions were 1.1 µm (q-TE) and 1.06 µm (q-TM). PE waveguides supported only q-TE mode since PE process increases only the extraordinary refractive index.
- Optical power in LN layer: For q-TE ridge waveguide, 85.6% of optical power was in the LN layer (at 1 µm width, 0.5 µm thickness). PE waveguide optical power showed negligible change with increased PE thickness. For strip-loaded waveguides, q-TE optical power decreased slightly with strip thickness (significantly for Si). For q-TM ridge waveguide, 82.5% optical power was in the LN layer. For strip-loaded q-TM, optical power initially increased with strip thickness (maximum at ~0.12 µm for SiO2 and ~0.07 µm for SiN, TiO2, Si), then decreased as light was attracted into the strip.
- Bending loss: Bending loss decreased with increased bending radius for all waveguide types. For ridge waveguides, minimal bending radii achieving 10⁻⁵ dB/cm loss were 15 µm (q-TE) and 20 µm (q-TM). For PE waveguides, bending loss was strongly dependent on PE depth (34 dB/cm at D=0.2 µm vs 10⁻¹¹ dB/cm at D=0.5 µm for radius 1 mm). Higher refractive index strips produced lower bending losses.
- q-TM leakage mechanism: An extra loss mechanism was identified for q-TM modes when the effective index (neff) of the strip-loaded waveguide was smaller than that of the nearby TE planar waveguide (e.g., SiN strip at 0.05 µm thickness with nTM00=1.844 < nTE0=1.910), causing Ez component coupling and optical leakage (minimum loss 57 dB/cm). When strip thickness was increased (0.3 µm, nTM00=1.922 > nTE0=1.910), this leakage was avoided, yielding bending loss around 10⁻¹⁰ dB/cm.

CONCLUSIONS: The study provides useful insights for understanding waveguide structures and optimizing/fabricating high-density integrated optical components on LN thin films. The work was supported by the National Science Foundation of China (grants no. 61575111 and no. 11475105).

## Abstract

In the paper, the most commonly used fabrication techniques of optical waveguides in lithium niobate are reviewed. Diffusion processes such as out-diffusion of lithium oxide from the crystal surface, in-diffusion of metals, ion exchange and proton exchange, and ion implantation are analysed. The characteristics of LiNbO 3 optical waveguides prepared by the different technological procedures, are reported in relation with the fabrication conditions. High quality optical waveguides on lithium niobate can be produced by Ti in-diffusion in a dry O 2 atmosphere at temperatures above 1000°C for long diffusion times (>10h). However, despite the large amount of research done in this field, correlations between optical properties and structural characteristics have not yet been established.

## Key takeaways

![Image 10: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)
AI

1.   Ti in-diffusion in dry O2 at >1000°C for >10h yields high-quality LiNbO3 waveguides.
2.   Various diffusion processes for waveguide fabrication, including out-diffusion and ion exchange, are reviewed.
3.   Optical properties and structural characteristics of waveguides lack established correlations.
4.   The ideal LiNbO3 composition for low-loss waveguides is often not congruent at 48.6 mole% Li2O.
5.   Further research is needed to understand waveguide property relationships and improve fabrication techniques.

We review our recent work on design and fabrication of microstructured waveguides (WG) in birefringent nonlinear crystal, z-cut lithium niobate (LiNbO 3), and describe simulation approaches to both design and optimisation of such structures. We also review our experimental results achieved by using direct fs laser inscription in such hosts using high repetition rate femtosecond oscillator system. Refractive index (RI) contrasts as high as-0.0127 have been demonstrated for individual tracks. High-index contrast waveguides fabricated with precise control and reproducibility are of high interest for nonlinear and/or electro-optical highly efficient and compact devices for quantum and classical optical data processing. Here we present a new process to fabricate planar and channel optical waveguides on lithium niobate substrates that we called High Vacuum Proton Exchange (HiVacPE). The main purpose was to improve the reproducibility and the quality of the produced waveguides by limiting and controlling the water traces in the melt, which is used for the ionic exchange. Moreover, we discovered that, when the acidity of the bath is increased, depending on substrate orientation (Z-cut or X-cut) the waveguides are completely different in term of crystallographic properties, index profiles and nonlinearity. The best-obtained channel waveguides exhibit a refractive index contrast as high as 0.04 without any degradation of the crystal nonlinearity and state of the art propagation losses (0.16dB/cm). We have also demonstrated that the HiVacPE process allows fabricating waveguides on Z-cut substrate with high-index contrast up to 0.11 without degrading the crystal nonlinearity but high strain induced propagation losses. On top of that, we proposed an original and very useful method of analyzing waveguides with complex index profiles. This method can be used for the analysis of any waveguides whose core contains several layers. Index Terms-lithium niobate, nonlinear optics, optical waveguides.

We report the development of a quick process for fabricating lithium niobate ridge waveguides with smooth walls, aspect ratios larger than 500 and side wall verticality of 88°. The method is based on optical grade dicing, and allows the fabrication of ridges with a top width of 1µm and a depth of more than 500µm. Smart-cut ridge waveguides and strongly confined proton exchanged ridge waveguides are demonstrated. We show that the method enables the fabrication of ridge waveguides with propagation losses as low as 0.5dB/cm. A new fabrication process is thus proposed for the fabrication of optical components with enhanced acousto-optic, electro-optic or nonlinear interactions. The high aspect ratios open opportunities toward the development of 3D photonic components in thin films of LiNbO 3 , and toward hybrid integration of LiNbO 3 components.

This demand requires reducing physical component sizes down beyond the diffraction limit of light, while still providing integrated functionalities and tolerable losses. Nanoscale waveguides hold enormous potential for on-chip photonic applications such as intra-chip optical communications, nanolasers, optical modulators, and highly sensitive sensors. Usually, silicon on insulator is chosen as material platform for nanowaveguide-based optical devices [1-4], but this material produces only passive components. However, for many applications, micrometer-sized active devices exhibiting a nonlinear optical behavior are highly suitable [5] since they open up the way to create fully integrated multifunctional optical circuits. Lithium niobate (LN) with its high electro-optic (EO), acousto-optic, and thermo-optic effect is an excellent candidate for these applications. As a result, LN in many cases is the first choice for a variety of highperformance optical devices [6-8]. Most often, waveguides (WGs) fabricated on LN are obtained by annealed proton exchange (APE) or Ti in-diffusion techniques which present extremely low propagation losses at the price of having a spatially broad guided mode. In addition, APE WG propagates several microns underneath the LN surface making this type of geometries not suitable for nano-optical device fabrication [9-12]. Future applications of LN as an integrated optical platform require a technology that can combine ultra-compact and well-performing optical circuits. However, waveguide-based components on these materials are generally bulky for microphotonic standards. As a typical example, LN optical modulators are 4-5 cm long and hundreds of micrometers wide [13]. Also, for nonlinear applications, due to the low intensity of the pump source in the large cross-sectional optical waveguides, the devices must be a few centimeters long in order to achieve efficient Abstract We present here a parametric study of micrometric size waveguides on 700-nm thin-film lithium niobate. Four different configurations in which the guiding takes place in lithium niobate, ridge waveguide, strip-loaded waveguide, slot waveguide and double slot waveguide, are systematically investigated in order to find a good set of optimum guiding parameters for increasing light-matter interaction applications. Our study shows that lithium niobate slot waveguides present high confinement of light in nano-scale guiding cross section and that they are a promising host waveguide for enhanced nonlinear optical applications. However, if one needs a compromise between light confinement and easy fabrication, we believe that strip-loaded lithium niobate waveguides, in which the strip load is fabricated with a dielectric material with an index of refraction smaller than lithium niobate, could be a good choice since in this case, the lithium niobate part does not need to be etched.

What explains the performance improvement in Ti indiffused lithium niobate waveguides?add

The research demonstrates that Ti indiffusion in dry O₂ at temperatures above 1000°C results in significant reductions in optical losses, reaching below 1 dB/cm, and improved resistance to optical damage.

How do out-diffusion processes affect waveguide formation in lithium niobate?add

Out-diffusion of lithium oxide during waveguide fabrication can create unwanted surface guiding layers, negatively impacting performance by altering refractive index profiles in the optical waveguides.

What is the impact of metal in-diffusion on the optical properties of lithium niobate?add

In-diffusion of divalent metals like Mg and Zn typically decreases the extraordinary refractive index (nₑ), while trivalent metals like Ti can enhance both nₑ and n₀, facilitating tighter confinement.

When did notable advances in lithium niobate waveguide fabrication techniques occur?add

Significant advancements in the fabrication of lithium niobate waveguides have been observed since 1974, particularly with the introduction of Ti in-diffusion methods improving optical performance.

How does the crystallographic orientation influence diffusion processes in lithium niobate?add

Diffusion coefficients in lithium niobate exhibit anisotropic behavior, with different diffusion rates reported for y-cut and z-cut samples, affecting optical guiding properties significantly.

Journal of Crystal Growth, 2003

The inherently large chemical stability of crystalline LiNbO 3 has effectively precluded the use of standard photolithographic patterning techniques. We present a two-stage growth method for fabricating patterned crystalline LiNbO 3 structures for photonic applications. The method uses atmospheric chemical vapor deposition (CVD) to produce an amorphous LiNbO 3 film. The film can be patterned using conventional photolithography and rapidly etched (>5 mm/min) with wet or dry chemical techniques. Alternatively, a standard lift-off process, using SiO 2 as a masking material, can be used to produce a desired pattern. When grown on LiNbO 3 substrates, a post-growth anneal converts the amorphous film to single-crystal LiNbO 3 .

Key Information

# Thin-Film Lithium Niobate

A new type of material referred to as "Optical Silicon".

Thin-Film Lithium Niobate, often referring to Lithium Niobate on Insulator (LNOI/TFLN), is a new type of integrated photonic material formed by fabricating lithium niobate crystals into films several hundred nanometers thick and bonding them onto insulating substrates. It is regarded as an important integrated photonic platform. It combines the excellent electro-optic, acousto-optic, and nonlinear optical properties of the bulk material. Simultaneously, its high refractive index contrast enables the realization of submicron-sized optical waveguides, thereby enhancing light-matter interactions. This material serves as a key platform for constructing high-performance, miniaturized photonic integrated circuits. It is widely used in fields such as high-speed electro-optic modulators, nonlinear frequency converters, optical frequency combs, quantum light sources, and highly sensitive sensors. With the maturation of preparation processes such as Smart-cut, thin-film lithium niobate has achieved wafer-level processing, transitioning from the laboratory to industrialization, demonstrating application potential in high-speed Optical Communication , optical computing, and quantum technologies.

Chinese Name

Also Known As
:   Optical Silicon

Physical and Chemical Properties

Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) is a new material known as "Optical Silicon." It combines the advantages of high-performance photonic materials and integrated photonics, establishing itself as a key platform for next-generation integrated photonics.

5

Lithium niobate(LN) crystal itself possesses multiple physical effects, including electro-optic, acousto-optic, nonlinear optical, piezoelectric, ferroelectric, photorefractive, photoelastic, and pyroelectric effects. It also boasts stable mechanical properties and a broad optical transparency window from ultraviolet to mid-infrared (approximately 0.3-5μm or 350-5000nm).

9

Thin-Film Lithium Niobate(LNOI), fabricated using technologies such as ion implantation, cutting, and bonding, not only completely retains the excellent characteristics of the bulk material but also, due to its thin-film form (typical thickness 300-900 nanometers), achieves a large refractive index contrast. This enables the fabrication of submicron-sized optical waveguides, laying the foundation for achieving high-density photonic integration.

9

Its core physical and chemical performance parameters include electro-optic performance (high electro-optic coefficient), a high second-order nonlinear coefficient, and low optical propagation loss. Thin-Film Lithium Niobatefeatures a high electro-optic modulation bandwidth (commercially available bandwidth ≥110GHz, with laboratory demonstrations exceeding 170GHz) and low drive voltage. Furthermore, its Curie temperature is as high as approximately 1100℃, ensuring performance stability in high-temperature environments.

9

In summary, the Thin-Film Lithium Niobateplatform integrates the dual advantages of high-performance photonic materials and integrated photonics. It serves as a material platform for Photonic Integrated Circuits (PICs) used to realize various functionalities such as high-speed electro-optic modulation, nonlinear frequency conversion, Optical Frequency Combs, and high-sensitivity sensing.

1

Fabrication Methods

The fabrication of Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) primarily consists of two aspects: the preparation of the thin-film wafers themselves and the processes for fabricating waveguides and devices on these wafers.

9

The current mainstream commercial fabrication technology is the Smart-cut technique (involving ion implantation and bonding/delamination). This technology enables precise control of thin-film thickness (typically 300-900 nanometers), with wafer sizes reaching up to 8 inches. Other thin-film fabrication methods, such as Pulsed Laser Deposition (PLD), Sol-gel Method , Radio Frequency Magnetron Sputtering, and Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD), may face challenges like resulting polycrystalline film structures and relatively high optical transmission losses.

9

The fabrication of optical waveguides and devices on Thin-Film Lithium Niobate wafers is a crucial process. Dry etching, such as Inductively Coupled Plasma (ICP) Etching, is the mainstream technology for producing low-loss waveguides and is suitable for wafer-level processing. Wafer-level processes based on deep ultraviolet lithography and ICP etching enable high-uniformity fabrication. Wet etching processes (using chemicals like Hydrogen peroxide solution , Ammonia Water ) represent a low-cost, high-efficiency, and highly reproducible alternative, capable of fabricating devices such as micro-ring resonators with high quality factors (e.g., approaching tens of millions).

4

Depending on the structure, Thin-Film Lithium Niobate optical waveguides are mainly categorized into three types: single-layer etched structures, heterogeneous loaded structures (where high-refractive-index materials like Silicon nitride (SiN) or Silicon (Si) are deposited on the lithium niobate thin film), and heterogeneous bonded structures (where the lithium niobate thin film is bonded onto a substrate with pre-fabricated waveguides).

16

Optical Communications and Data Centers

Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) serves as a modulator material for high-speed optical modules (such as 800G, 1.6T, and 3.2T), finding applications in long-haul backbone networks, metropolitan area networks (MANs), Data Center , and data center interconnects. Thin-Film Lithium Niobate possesses a relatively broad bandwidth characteristic, making it suitable for application in the packaging of long-distance/ultra-long-distance products. Due to its features of low power consumption and high bandwidth, Thin-Film Lithium Niobate modulators are considered potentially applicable in 3.2T pluggable solutions. Thin-Film Lithium Niobate is applied in single-wavelength 200G/400G ultra-high-speed modulation, capable of supporting the requirements of 800G, 1.6T, and 3.2T optical modules.

20

Microwave Photonics and Sensing

Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) is used to realize highly sensitive electric field sensors, microwave-optical signal conversion, and ultra-broadband optoelectronic fusion chips. The electric field sensor based on thin-film lithium niobate has achieved a performance capable of real-time measurement of electric field strength and phase, with a detection sensitivity of 5.2 μV/(m·Hz¹ᐟ²). The ultra-broadband thin-film lithium niobate optoelectronic fusion chip has, for the first time, enabled the generation, modulation, transmission, and reception of wireless signals at any frequency point covering an ultra-wide frequency band from 0.5 GHz to 115 GHz.

4

Nonlinear Photonics and Frequency Combs

Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) utilizes its second-order/third-order nonlinear properties for achieving frequency doubling, cascaded harmonic generation, nonlinear frequency conversion, and optical frequency combs. In periodically poled lithium niobate ridge waveguides, experimental demonstrations of frequency doubling and cascaded harmonic generation have been provided. Highly efficient ultraviolet SHG has been realized. The first successful implementation of a high-performance dark-pulse optical frequency comb system based on a Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) micro-resonator has been achieved. Owing to the second-order nonlinearity of the lithium niobate material, an enhancement of the second-order nonlinear response at topological interface states has been experimentally observed.

2

Dynamic Holography and Optical Field Control

Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN), when combined with technologies such as metasurfaces, enables addressable, fast-response dynamic holographic displays and optical field control on the nanosecond timescale. By integrating electro-optic switches constructed from lithium niobate modulators with on-chip metasurface networks, an addressable and fast-response optical field control function has been achieved, demonstrating the rapid switching of eight holographic display images.

3

Other Applications

Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) also finds applications in integrated mode-locked lasers, Laser Radar , and free-space sensing. A mode-locked laser based on a Thin-Film Lithium Niobate photonic chip has been developed. Thin-Film Lithium Niobate is also applied in lidar and free-space sensing.

19

Testing Methods

Characterization of fundamental waveguide performance involves testing transmission loss, etching uniformity, and yield rate using methods such as Microring Resonators. For example, transmission loss can be less than 0.15 dB/cm, etching depth error is controlled within 10%, and the yield rate is greater than 85%. Tests for nonlinear optical efficiency measure the Normalized Conversion Efficiency for frequency conversion and the Visible Light Sensitivity, such as achieving a Normalized Conversion Efficiency of up to 1350% W⁻¹ cm⁻² and a Visible Light Sensitivity of 95 mA/W.

1

Evaluation of sensing performance assesses Detection Sensitivity, Minimum Detectable Field Strength, bandwidth, and dynamic range. For instance, an electric field sensor may have a Detection Sensitivity of 5.2 μV/(m·Hz¹ᐟ²), Minimum Detectable Field Strengths of 8.8 μV/(m·Hz¹ᐟ²) and 29.5 μV/(m·Hz¹ᐟ²), bandwidths of 414 MHz and 101 MHz, and dynamic ranges of 123 dB and 122 dB, respectively.

4

Characterization of Optical Frequency Comb performance includes metrics such as bandwidth, repetition rate, phase noise, and tuning range. Examples include a bandwidth reaching 200 nm, a repetition rate of 25 GHz, a repetition rate tuning range extending up to 292 kHz, and phase noise as low as -143 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz.

26

Device function verification targets specific applications, such as switching speed for dynamic holographic displays, as well as an Entanglement Visibility exceeding 97% and a Photon Pair Generation Rate reaching 2.79 × 10¹¹ Hz/mW for entangled light sources.

3

Distribution Overview

The industry chain for Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) has taken initial shape. Its distribution landscape can be overviewed from aspects such as the industry chain structure, market size, major manufacturers, and regional layout.

23

The Thin-Film Lithium Niobate industry chain can be divided into upstream lithium niobate crystal materials, midstream Thin-Film Lithium Niobate wafer manufacturing, and downstream modulator chips and optical module packaging segments.

23

Driven by the surge in AI computing power and iterations of high-speed optical modules, the Thin-Film Lithium Niobate industry has entered a high-growth cycle. Market research institutions predict the global LNOI market size will be approximately 600 million USD in 2024, potentially exceeding 3 billion USD by 2030. Other analyses indicate that the market space for Thin-Film Lithium Niobate modulators driven by 3.2T optical modules alone could approach 3 billion RMB (approximately 418 million USD) by 2031. The global TFLN modulator market size is projected to reach 8.2 to 11 billion RMB (approximately 1.14 to 1.53 billion USD) in 2026.

21

Regarding upstream materials, domestic manufacturers such as TDG Holding Co.,Ltd. , Nanzhi Xincai Materials, Hengyuan Semiconductor, etc., have achieved mass production of optical-grade lithium niobate crystals. Among them, Tiantong Co., Ltd. successfully fabricated a 12-inch crystal in June 2025.

23

For midstream wafers, Jinan Jingzheng in China is a leading company, realizing full coverage of 4-inch to 8-inch sizes and all categories (acoustic-grade and optical-grade), and taking the lead in mass-producing 8-inch X-axis optical-grade Lithium niobate films; Shanghai Xinguijuhe has also achieved product layouts for 4-inch to 6-inch sizes. The main international wafer supplier includes France's Soitec.

23

In the downstream device and module segment, domestic companies involved in R&D and production include Lightware Technology, Accelink Technologies, and Jiangsu Ni'ao Optoelectronics. International research institutions and enterprises include Yale University and Harvard University in the United States, Japan's NTT, as well as the Netherlands' QuiX Quantum and the United States' HyperLight.

23

Technically, single-channel 400G modulation is seen as a critical node where Thin-Film Lithium Niobate's advantages become prominent. Domestic and international manufacturers have showcased related chip products at exhibitions such as the Optical Fiber Communication Conference (OFC) 2026. In terms of regional layout, China Mainland has established a preliminary industry chain layout covering materials, R&D, and manufacturing.

23

Major Events

In 2026, the industry designated 2026 as the inaugural year for the commercial scaling of Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN), marking the industry's transition into the "second half" of moving from performance breakthroughs to mass production engineering. The industry points out that the industrialization of Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) still faces seven major challenges: size, driving method, functional integration, packaging, reliability, mass production capability, and cost. FiberHome Technologies has integrated miniaturized Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) chips into coherent IC-TROSA modules and has achieved batch shipments. A company in Zhuhai announced the integration of Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) onto silicon photonic chips using heterogeneous integration technology, solving the challenge of high-precision modulation. Reports from multiple institutions indicate that Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) has become a key material supporting the development of ultra-high-speed Optical module such as 1.6T and 3.2T, and the industry chain has entered a period of explosive growth.

11

In 2025, the Peking University research team's achievement, the "Ultra-Broadband Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) Optoelectronic Integration Chip," was selected for the 2025 "Top Ten Semiconductor Research Advances." This chip, for the first time, achieved the generation, modulation, transmission, and reception of wireless signals at any frequency point covering an ultra-wide frequency band from 0.5 GHz to 115 GHz, with a maximum wireless transmission rate of 120 Gbps. A team led by Professor Li Tao and Academician Shi-ning Zhu at Nanjing University made new progress on the Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) platform. Through the deep integration of an electro-optic switch and an on-chip integrated metasurface network, they realized an addressable, fast-responsive optical field modulation function, opening up disruptive technological pathways for Virtual Reality , Optical Communication , and optical computing. A research group led by Yang Qifan and collaborators made progress in Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) optical frequency comb research, achieving for the first time a high-performance dark-pulse optical frequency comb system based on a Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) microresonator.

3

In 2023, a team from the Advanced Science Research Center at the City University of New York and the California Institute of Technology , by combining III-V semiconductors with Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN), developed the world's first modelocked laser based on a Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) photonic chip. Its output pulse energy and peak power were the highest among modelocked lasers on nanophotonic platforms. The research was published as a cover article in Science.

19

On July 1, 2021, Physical Review Letters published the latest findings by Professor Xiao Meng on Weyl point topological physics in LNOI chips, providing new insights for studying linear/nonlinear topological optics on LNOI chips and achieving topologically robust transmission.

30

## Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN) — "Optical Silicon"

This webpage provides a comprehensive overview of Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (LNOI/TFLN), a new type of integrated photonic material created by fabricating lithium niobate crystals into films several hundred nanometers thick and bonding them onto insulating substrates. It is regarded as a key platform for high-performance, miniaturized photonic integrated circuits, widely used in high-speed electro-optic modulators, nonlinear frequency converters, optical frequency combs, quantum light sources, and highly sensitive sensors.

### Physical and Chemical Properties
- Combines excellent electro-optic, acousto-optic, and nonlinear optical properties of bulk lithium niobate with high refractive index contrast from its thin-film form (typical thickness 300-900 nm)
- Optical transparency window: ~0.3-5 μm (350-5000 nm)
- High electro-optic modulation bandwidth: commercially available ≥110 GHz, laboratory demonstrations exceeding 170 GHz; low drive voltage
- Curie temperature ~1100°C for high-temperature stability
- Possesses multiple physical effects: electro-optic, acousto-optic, nonlinear optical, piezoelectric, ferroelectric, photorefractive, photoelastic, and pyroelectric

### Fabrication Methods
- Mainstream commercial technology: **Smart-cut technique** (ion implantation and bonding/delamination), achieving wafer sizes up to 8 inches
- Other methods (PLD, Sol-gel, RF Magnetron Sputtering, CVD) face challenges like polycrystalline film structures and higher optical losses
- Dry etching (ICP Etching) is mainstream for low-loss waveguides with wafer-level processing; wet etching (hydrogen peroxide, ammonia water) offers low-cost alternative capable of fabricating micro-ring resonators with quality factors approaching tens of millions
- Three waveguide categories: single-layer etched, heterogeneous loaded (SiN/Si deposited on LN film), and heterogeneous bonded structures

### Applications
1. **Optical Communications & Data Centers**: Modulator material for 800G, 1.6T, and 3.2T optical modules; applied in single-wavelength 200G/400G ultra-high-speed modulation; suitable for 3.2T pluggable solutions
2. **Microwave Photonics & Sensing**: Electric field sensor with detection sensitivity of 5.2 μV/(m·Hz^½); ultra-broadband optoelectronic fusion chip enabling wireless signal generation/modulation/transmission/reception from 0.5 GHz to 115 GHz
3. **Nonlinear Photonics & Frequency Combs**: Frequency doubling, cascaded harmonic generation, highly efficient UV SHG; first high-performance dark-pulse optical frequency comb based on LNOI micro-resonator
4. **Dynamic Holography & Optical Field Control**: With metasurfaces enables addressable, fast-response (nanosecond timescale) dynamic holographic displays — demonstrated rapid switching of 8 holographic images
5. **Other**: Integrated mode-locked lasers, lidar, and free-space sensing

### Testing Methods & Key Metrics
- Waveguide performance: transmission loss <0.15 dB/cm, etching depth error within 10%, yield >85%
- Nonlinear optical efficiency: Normalized Conversion Efficiency up to 1350% W⁻¹ cm⁻²; Visible Light Sensitivity of 95 mA/W
- Electric field sensor: Minimum Detectable Field Strengths of 8.8 and 29.5 μV/(m·Hz^½), bandwidths of 414 MHz and 101 MHz, dynamic ranges of 123 dB and 122 dB
- Optical frequency comb: bandwidth to 200 nm, repetition rate of 25 GHz, tuning range to 292 kHz, phase noise as low as -143 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz
- Entangled light sources: Entanglement Visibility >97%, Photon Pair Generation Rate 2.79 × 10^11 Hz/mW

### Distribution / Industry Chain
- Chain: upstream LN crystal materials → midstream wafer manufacturing → downstream modulator chips and optical module packaging
- Market: Global LNOI market ~600M USD in 2024, potentially >3B USD by 2030; TFLN modulator market projected 8.2-11B RMB (1.14-1.53B USD) in 2026
- Upstream manufacturers: TDG Holding, Nanzhi Xincai Materials, Hengyuan Semiconductor (China); Tiantong Co. fabricated 12-inch crystal in June 2025
- Midstream: Jinan Jingzheng (China) — full 4-8 inch coverage, leading in 8-inch X-axis optical-grade LN films; Shanghai Xinguijuhe (4-6 inch); France's Soitec internationally
- Downstream: Lightware Technology, Accelink Technologies, Jiangsu Ni'ao Optoelectronics (China); international players include Yale, Harvard, NTT (Japan), QuiX Quantum (Netherlands), HyperLight (US)
- Single-channel 400G modulation is the critical adoption node

### Major Events (Chronological)
- **2021 (July 1)**: Physical Review Letters published Professor Xiao Meng's findings on Weyl point topological physics in LNOI chips
- **2023**: City University of New York & Caltech teams developed the world's first mode-locked laser based on an LNOI photonic chip (published as Science cover article)
- **2025**: Peking University's "Ultra-Broadband TFLN Optoelectronic Integration Chip" (0.5-115 GHz, max 120 Gbps) selected for "Top Ten Semiconductor Research Advances"; Nanjing University team (Li Tao, Shi-ning Zhu) achieved addressable dynamic metasurface optical field control; Yang Qifan group achieved first high-performance dark-pulse optical frequency comb
- **2026**: Designated as inaugural year for commercial scaling of TFLN; industry identified seven major challenges (size, driving method, functional integration, packaging, reliability, mass production capability, cost); FiberHome Technologies integrated miniaturized LNOI chips into coherent IC-TROSA modules with batch shipments; Zhuhai company integrated LNOI onto silicon photonic chips via heterogeneous integration

Etching of Lithium Niobate: From Ridge Waveguides to Photonic Crystal Structures H. Hu, R. Ricken and W. Sohler Angewandte Physik,, Universität Paderborn, 33098 Paderborn, Germany sol_hu@physik.upb.de Abstract. Recent progress of wet etching of Z-cut LN, of inductively coupled plasma (ICP-) etching of X-cut LN, and of ICP-etching of proton-exchanged X-cut LN is reported to fabricate low loss ridge guides, micromechanical, and photonic crystal structures. Introduction The development of lithium niobate (LiNbO3, LN) integrated optical devices requires etching techniques for a reliable fabrication of deep (sub-) micrometer structures. Examples are ridge guides, Bragg gratings, and photonic crystal structures. The existing etching methods can be classified into two categories: wet (chemical) etching and dry (ion) etching. Wet etching is generally performed in a mixture of HF and HNO3, which attacks the –Z-face of the crystal, whereas the +Z-face is hardly affected. Therefore, se-lective chemical etching can either be achieved by depositing a metallic mask of the structure to be fabricated on the –Z-face [1] or by defining the structure first by a cor-responding domain inversion [2]. Wet etching can also be applied to proton-exchanged or ion-implanted LN to form (sub-) micrometer structures in the surface of the crystal [3, 4]. In dry etching, plasma etching, ion beam milling and focussed ion beam etching are generally used [5, 6, 7]. In this contribution we report our recent progress of wet etching of Z-cut LN to fabricate low loss ridge guide and micromechanical structures, of inductively coupled plasma (ICP-) etching of X-cut LN to get ridges and other microstructures, and of ICP-etching of proton-exchanged X-cut LN to develop photonic crystal structures. Wet etching of Z-cut LN: ridge waveguides and micromechanics Wet etching of Z-cut LN with HF/HNO3 proved to be a simple and reliable method to fabricate low loss Ti-doped ridge waveguides with TE propagation losses of 0.3 dB/cm only [4]. To get optical guiding, the ridges were defined in a planar Ti:LiNbO3 waveguide. Cr-stripes have been used as etch masks. Here we report a modified procedure yielding ridge guides of propagation losses nearly one order of magnitude lower (TE). They were fabricated in three steps using undoped (congruent) Z-cut LN as substrate: 1. Ridge fabrication: Using a Cr-mask on the –Z sur-face of the LN substrate 4 to 12 µm wide ridges were fabricated by wet chemical etching in a mixture of 21 ml HF (40% concentration), 14 ml HNO3 (100% concentra-tion) and 5 ml ethanol, following the procedure described in [1]. A ridge of 6.5 µm (10 µm) height (top width) is shown in Fig. 1 (left); it is aligned parallel to the X-axis. 2. Ti-stripe definition: A novel photolithographic process was developed, which allows coating the surface of a ridge selectively. Spin-coating of the sample with photo-resist results in an inhomogeneous thickness distribution with a thinner layer on top of the ridge. This is exploited by the following flood exposure (5 seconds), which leads to full exposure only on top of the ridge. By the subsequent development the photo-resist on Proc. 14th European Conference on Integrated Optics (ECIO`08), Eindhoven, Netherlands, pp. 75-78 (2008) the top of the ridge is totally removed, while a thin layer remains besides the ridge and on the ridge walls. After lift-off a Ti-stripe is precisely defined on top of the ridge only (see Fig. 1-middle). 3. Ti-indiffusion: The Ti-stripe can now be indiffused using conventional parameters (1060 oC @ 8.5 hrs in Ar (7.5 hrs) and O2 (1 hr) atmosphere, respectively). The result is a Ti-doped ridge waveguide as shown in Fig. 1 (right); the edges are rounded and the surface roughness is reduced (see Fig. 1-right). Fig. 1: Wet etched ridge on Z-cut LN, (left), Ti-coated ridge before indiffusion (middle), and after indiffusion (right). The height (top width) of the ridge is 6.5 µm (10 µm), aligned parallel X. Therefore, also the propagation losses of the ridge guides, monomode up to a top width of 9 µm, are significantly lower than previous results [1]. They were measured using the Fabry-Perot resonance method at 1.55 µm wavelength. Both, the TE and TM losses decrease with increasing width. For TE-polarization the loss drops from 0.22 dB/cm at 5 µm width to 0.05 dB/cm at 7 µm width. For TM-polarization the losses are 1.3 and 0.36 dB/cm at 5 µm and 9 µm widths, respectively. They are significantly larger than TE-losses, though the TM mode is smaller than the TE-mode with lower field strength at the ridge walls. An explanation for the strongly polarization-dependent losses might be that due to the growth of Cr2O3 under the mask and due to outdiffusion of Li2O the concentration of Li and O might vary near the surface leading to corresponding fluctuations of the extraordinary index of refraction (the ordinary index would remain nearly unaffected). Such index fluctuation would lead to scattering losses of the TM-mode alone. It was even possible to control the slope of the ridge walls by adjusting the etching temperature. This allows getting even steeper walls and to fabricate micromechanical structures such as the interdigital fingers given as example in Fig. 2. It was etched at a temperature of 8 oC. The lamellas have a width of 2.6 µm with a separation of 2.8 µm. The etching depth is 7.7 µm. Fig. 2: Wet etched interdigital lamellas of 2.6 µm width and of 2.8 µm separation on Z-cut LN. The etching depth is 7.7 µm. ICP-etching of X-cut LN: ridges and microstructures Plasma etching is a very controllable process and has the advantage of being highly anisotropic. Plasmas based on fluorine gases are generally used for plasma etching of LN due to the good volatility of fully fluorinated niobium species at temperatures around 200 °C. However, a problem is the formation and re-deposition of LiF, which has a melting temperature of more than 800 oC. It will be deposited on all surfaces and will lower in this way the etching rate. Therefore, if re-deposition dominates the pro-cess, vertical side walls, which are necessary for the definition of small structures, can hardly be obtained. Our solution for this problem is as follows: at first, the sample with a Cr layer defining the structure to be fabricated is ICP-etched for several minutes in a C4F8/He (1:1) plasma. Then the etching process is stopped and the sample is cleaned in SC-1 solution (70% H2O, 20% H2O2, 10% NH4OH) for 1 minute to remove the deposi-tion, before ICP-etching is continued. These two steps are repeated several times until the desired etching depth is reached. Fig. 3 shows as an example etched ridges in X-cut LN, aligned along the Y-direction; the ridges have a height (width) of 5.8 µm (8 µm). On the right of Fig. 3 more complicated microstructures of the same height are shown demonstrating that even small connections between the squares can be fabricated in a reproducible way with nearly vertical walls. Fig. 3: ICP-etched ridges on X-cut LN of 5.8 µm height and 8 µm width (left and middle). Further microstructures of the same height with nearly vertical side walls (right). ICP-etching of H+-exchanged X-cut LN: photonic crystal structures Another way to reduce the problem of LiF re-deposition is to lower the Li concentra-tion in LN by a proton exchange (PE) process [8]. Thus, the rate of LiF re-deposition will be significantly reduced in comparison to etching of pure LN. As a consequence, the etching rate will be increased and the etch profiles will be improved. We demon-strated the realization of this concept be performing first a PE of congruent X-cut LN to a depth of 1.4 µm. Then the surface of the PE-LN was covered by a 110 nm thick Cr film deposited by sputtering and coated with a 120 nm thick photo-resist layer. Using conventional optical contact lithography, photonic crystal structures were defined in the Fig. 4: Holes of a photonic crystal structure defined in photo resist (left), transferred by wet etching in the Cr film (middle) and by ICP-etching into the LN substrate. photo-resist (Fig. 4, left). The smallest lines have a width of 170 nm. By wet etching these structures were transferred into the Cr film (Fig. 4, middle). Then the sample was ICP-etched for several minutes, and cleaned afterwards in SC-1 solution to remove all depositions. This process was repeated several times until the desired etching depth in the PE-LN was reached (Fig. 4, right). Fig. 5 shows the photonic crystal structure as a whole together with some details in higher magnification. Fig. 5: Photonic crystal structure in PE-LN as a whole (left) and with more details in higher magnification (middle and right). Proton exchange is also used for the fabrication of single polarization waveguides, as it increases only the extraordinary index of refraction. A subsequent reverse proton exchange (RPE) can even increase the Li concentration again to form buried waveguide profiles. Conclusions In conclusion, significant progress has been achieved to improve wet etching of Z-cut LN, ICP-etching of X-cut LN, and ICP-etching of proton-exchanged X-cut LN allowing a reliable fabrication of integrated optical devices with deep (sub-) micrometer structures. As examples ridge guides of very low propagation losses, micromechanical, and photonic crystal structures have been demonstrated. References [1] H. Hu, R. Ricken, W. Sohler, and R. B. Wehrspohn, “Lithium Niobate Ridge Waveguides Fabricated by Wet Etching”, IEEE Photon. Technol. Lett., vol. 19, pp. 417–419, Mar. 2007. [2] I. E. Barry, G. W. Ross, P. G. R. Smith, and R. W. Eason, “Ridge waveguides in lithium niobate fabricated by differential etching following spatially selective domain inversion,” Appl. Phys. Lett., vol. 74, pp. 1487–1488, Mar. 1999. [3] T.-L. Ting, L. -Y. Chen, and W.-S. Wang, “A novel wet-etching method using joint proton source in LiNbO3”, IEEE Photon. Technol. Lett., vol. 18, pp. 568–570, Feb. 2006. [4] D. M. Gill, D. Jacobson, C. S. White, Y. Shi, W. J. Minford, and A. Harris, “Ridged LiNbO3 modulators fabricated by a novel oxygen-ion implant/wet-etch technique”, J. Lightwave Technol. vol. 22, pp. 887–894, Mar. 2004. [5] Masashi Tamura, Shinzo Yoshikado, “Etching characteristics of LiNbO3 crystal by fluorine gas plasma reactive ion etching”, Surface and Coatings Technology, Vol. 169 –170, pp. 203–207, 2003. [6] P. Rabiei and W. H. Steier, “Lithium niobate ridge waveguides and modulators fabricated using smart guide,” Appl. Phys. Lett., vol. 86, Art. No. 161115, 2005. [7] F. Lacour, N. Courjal, M.-P. Bernal, A. Sabac, C. Bainier, M. Spajer, “Nanostructuring lithium niobate substrates by focused ion beam milling”, Optical Materials, Vol. 27, pp. 1421–1425, 2005. [8] H. Hu, A. P. Milenin, R. B. Wehrspohn, H. Herrmann, and W. Sohler, “Plasma etching of proton-exchanged lithium niobate”, J. Vac. Sci. Technol. A, vol. 24, pp. 1012-1015, Jul./Aug., 2006
