This is a conference paper (ECIO'08, Eindhoven, Netherlands, pp. 75-78, 2008) by H. Hu, R. Ricken, and W. Sohler from the Angewandte Physik department at Universität Paderborn, Germany, reporting recent progress in etching techniques for lithium niobate (LiNbO3, LN) to fabricate integrated optical devices with deep sub-micrometer structures. The paper covers three etching approaches:

**1. Wet etching of Z-cut LN (HF/HNO3 mixture):** A modified three-step process to fabricate low-loss Ti-doped ridge waveguides: (1) ridge fabrication using Cr-mask wet etching in a mixture of 21 ml HF (40%), 14 ml HNO3 (100%), and 5 ml ethanol; (2) selective Ti-stripe definition using a novel photolithographic process exploiting inhomogeneous photoresist thickness on ridge tops with flood exposure and lift-off; (3) Ti-indiffusion at 1060°C for 8.5 hrs in Ar/O2 atmospheres. Resulting ridge guides (6.5 µm height, 10 µm top width, monomode up to 9 µm) achieved dramatically improved propagation losses: TE losses dropped from 0.22 dB/cm at 5 µm width to 0.05 dB/cm at 7 µm width; TM losses were 1.3 dB/cm at 5 µm and 0.36 dB/cm at 9 µm. The polarization-dependent losses are attributed to Cr2O3 growth and Li2O outdiffusion causing extraordinary index fluctuations near the surface. Etching temperature can control ridge wall slope, enabling micromechanical structures such as interdigital lamellas (2.6 µm width, 2.8 µm separation, 7.7 µm etching depth at 8°C).

**2. ICP-etching of X-cut LN:** Uses C4F8/He (1:1) plasma with a Cr mask. The key challenge is LiF formation and re-deposition (melting point >800°C), which lowers etch rate and prevents vertical sidewalls. The solution is an iterative process: ICP-etch for several minutes, then clean in SC-1 solution (70% H2O, 20% H2O2, 10% NH4OH) for 1 minute to remove deposition, repeating until desired depth. Demonstrated ridges of 5.8 µm height and 8 µm width with nearly vertical walls, plus more complex microstructures.

**3. ICP-etching of H+-exchanged X-cut LN (photonic crystal structures):** Proton exchange (PE) to 1.4 µm depth reduces Li concentration and thus LiF re-deposition, increasing etch rate and improving profiles. Process: PE of congruent X-cut LN, 110 nm Cr film sputtered, 120 nm photoresist, optical contact lithography (smallest features 170 nm), wet etching to transfer pattern to Cr, then repeated ICP-etching and SC-1 cleaning. This produced photonic crystal structures in PE-LN. Proton exchange also creates single-polarization waveguides (increases only extraordinary index), and reverse proton exchange (RPE) can form buried waveguide profiles.

**Conclusions:** Significant progress in wet etching of Z-cut LN, ICP-etching of X-cut LN, and ICP-etching of proton-exchanged X-cut LN enables reliable fabrication of integrated optical devices with low-loss ridge guides, micromechanical, and photonic crystal structures.

args.summary: This is a Semantic Scholar record for a 2008 conference paper titled "Etching of Lithium Niobate: From Ridge Waveguides to Photonic Crystal Structures" by H. Hui, R. Ricken, and W. Sohler (fields: Physics, Engineering, Materials Science). The paper reports recent progress in three etching approaches for lithium niobate (LN) fabrication: (1) wet etching of Z-cut LN, (2) inductively coupled plasma (ICP) etching of X-cut LN, and (3) ICP-etching of proton-exchanged X-cut LN. These techniques are used to fabricate low-loss ridge waveguides, micromechanical structures, and photonic crystal structures. The paper includes 5 figures and has 30 citing papers and 10 references. Key related works cited include: wet etching of LiNbO3 ridge waveguides using HF/HNO3 with Cr masks (Hu et al., 2007); plasma etching of proton-exchanged lithium niobate (Hu et al., 2006); wet-etching methods using joint proton sources (Ting et al.); focused ion beam milling of lithium niobate (Lacour et al., 2005); and lithium niobate ridge waveguides fabricated by wet etching (Lee & Shin, 1995). Notable citing works span lithium niobate ridge waveguides via ion implantation and ion beam etching (Zhao et al., 2010), reactive ion etching of X-cut LiNbO3 in ICP/TCP systems (Kozlov et al., 2023), advanced etching techniques of LiNbO3 nanodevices (Shen et al., 2023), thin-film lithium niobate photonics (Rao, 2018), and polarization analysis of LNOI devices (Wang et al., 2024).
args.key_excerpts: "Recent progress of wet etching of Z-cut LN, of inductively coupled plasma (ICP-) etching of X-cut LN, and of ICP-etching of proton-exchanged X-cut LN is reported to fabricate low loss ridge guides, micromechanical, and photonic crystal structures."

## Abstract

Single LiNbO3 (LNO) crystals are widely utilized in surface acoustic wave devices, optoelectronic devices, and novel ferroelectric memory devices due to their remarkable electro-optic and piezoelectric properties, and high saturation and remnant polarizations. However, challenges remain regarding their nanofabrication that hinder their applications. The prevailing etching techniques for LNO encompass dry etching, wet etching, and focused-ion-beam etching, each having distinct merits and demerits. Achieving higher etching rates and improved sidewall angles presents a challenge in LNO nanofabrication. Building upon the current etching researches, this study explores various etching methods using instruments capable of generating diverse plasma densities, such as dry etching in reactive ion etching (RIE) and inductively coupled plasma (ICP), proton exchange-enhanced etching, and wet chemical etching following high-temperature reduction treatment, as well as hybrid dry and wet etching. Ultimately, after employing RIE dry etching combined with wet etching, following a high-temperature reduction treatment, an etching rate of 10 nm/min and pretty 90° sidewall angles were achieved. Furthermore, high etching rates of 79 nm/min with steep sidewall angles of 83° were obtained using ICP dry etching. Additionally, using SiO2 masks, a high etching rate of 108 nm/min and an etching selectivity ratio of 0.86:1 were achieved. Distinct etching conditions yielded diverse yet exceptional results, providing multiple processing paths of etching for the versatile application of LNO.

## 1. Introduction

LNO, an artificially grown single crystal, boasts rich and extensive researches in the history. It possesses a unique combination of exceptional properties, including piezoelectricity, the electro-optic effect, acousto-optic effect, nonlinear optical behavior, and optical birefringence [[1](#B1-nanomaterials-13-02789),[2](#B2-nanomaterials-13-02789),[3](#B3-nanomaterials-13-02789),[4](#B4-nanomaterials-13-02789),[5](#B5-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. With its impressively high electro-optic coefficient, high intrinsic bandwidth, elevated refractive index, and wide transparency range in the light frequency, LNO has emerged as a remarkably versatile and captivating photonic material [[6](#B6-nanomaterials-13-02789),[7](#B7-nanomaterials-13-02789),[8](#B8-nanomaterials-13-02789),[9](#B9-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. Moreover, its substantial electromechanical coupling coefficient and low propagation loss have positioned it as a focal point for research in surface acoustic wave devices [[10](#B10-nanomaterials-13-02789),[11](#B11-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. In recent years, the exploration of domain-wall conductivity has triggered a surge in the development of domain wall devices [[12](#B12-nanomaterials-13-02789),[13](#B13-nanomaterials-13-02789),[14](#B14-nanomaterials-13-02789),[15](#B15-nanomaterials-13-02789),[16](#B16-nanomaterials-13-02789),[17](#B17-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. LNO, characterized by its high Curie temperature, large saturation polarization and remanent polarization, has taken center stage in the realm of domain wall memory-device research [[18](#B18-nanomaterials-13-02789),[19](#B19-nanomaterials-13-02789),[20](#B20-nanomaterials-13-02789),[21](#B21-nanomaterials-13-02789),[22](#B22-nanomaterials-13-02789),[23](#B23-nanomaterials-13-02789),[24](#B24-nanomaterials-13-02789),[25](#B25-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. Despite its immense potential, LNO still encounters certain challenges in practical applications. It currently lags behind its integrated photonics counterparts in optoelectronic applications, and the commercialization of domain wall memory chips, centered around LNO, has yet to be realized. The primary impediment lies in the formidable processing difficulties associated with LNO materials [[26](#B26-nanomaterials-13-02789),[27](#B27-nanomaterials-13-02789),[28](#B28-nanomaterials-13-02789),[29](#B29-nanomaterials-13-02789)].

The nanofabrication processes of LNO mainly involve several techniques, such as dry etching, wet etching, and focused-ion-beam etching [[30](#B30-nanomaterials-13-02789),[31](#B31-nanomaterials-13-02789),[32](#B32-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. Dry etching can be further divided into F-based-gas and Cl-based-gas dry etching. With the dry-etching process with F-based gas, LiF by-products are generated. Due to its high melting point, LiF is not easily removed and tends to accumulate on the sidewalls, resulting in a reduced etching sidewall angle. For instance, in 2023, Kozlov et al. used SF6 and Ar in ICP to fabricate LNO optical waveguide devices, but the sidewall angle of the waveguide was only 60–75° [[33](#B33-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. On the other hand, Cl-based gas generates LiCl by-products during the etching of LNO, and as LiCl has a lower melting point, it can be easily removed without accumulating on the sidewalls, ultimately leading to better etching morphology. Additionally, Cl-based gas avoids the consumption of non-metal masks, addressing the compatibility issues between metal masks and traditional semiconductor processes. However, the etching rate of Cl-based gas is not as high as F-based gas, and it demands strict requirements for etching equipment, limiting its use in large-scale production and deep-etching processes. For instance, in 2019, Bahadori et al. utilized a SiO2 mask and a mixture of Ar, Cl2, and BCl3 in ICP to achieve an etching selectivity ratio of 1.45:1, and the sidewall angle reached 83°, presenting a smooth LNO etching surface [[34](#B34-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. Similarly, in 2020, Shen et al. employed a SiO2 mask and a mixture of Ar, Cl2, and BCl3 as the etching gas, obtaining an etching sidewall angle close to 80° [[35](#B35-nanomaterials-13-02789)].

Wet etching includes acid wet etching (HF/HNO3) and alkaline wet etching (H2O2/NH40H/H2O (SC-1) solution, NaOH solution) [[10](#B10-nanomaterials-13-02789),[36](#B36-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. The wet-etching process is isotropic and results in a lower sidewall angle during the etching of LNO. Additionally, several studies have demonstrated that the wet etching of LNO can lead to non-uniform etching morphology due to different etching rates along different crystal orientations. For instance, in 2022, Zhuang et al. used SC-1 solution to etch LNO samples covered with a SiO2 mask, achieving a depth of nearly 300 nm. However, different crystal orientations exhibited significant differences in the etching sidewall angle. The −Z direction showed a favorable angle, reaching approximately 80°, while the +Z and −Y directions exhibited angles of only about 45° [[4](#B4-nanomaterials-13-02789)].

Focused-ion-beam etching encompasses direct-ion-beam cutting and ion-beam bombardment followed by wet etching, and it is characterized by its fast processing speed and excellent etching morphology. It is not affected by the crystal orientation of LNO, making it easy to achieve the desired etching sidewall angle [[37](#B37-nanomaterials-13-02789),[38](#B38-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. However, due to its lower processing precision and significant surface damage to LNO, it is seldom used in the research of nanoscale LNO devices. By using high-energy ion implantation followed by wet chemical etching, the crystal structure of LNO is damaged, rendering the wet etching process non-isotropic. This leads to better results in terms of etching morphology. For instance, in 2013, Nicola et al. used high-energy Cu ion implantation followed by HF acid etching in LNO. The etching rate reached 100 nm/s, resulting in a smooth waveguide with a 90° sidewall angle and a depth of 2.75 μm [[39](#B39-nanomaterials-13-02789)].

In addition, there are combined dry- and wet-etching processes. For instance, the use of F-based gas etching combined with HF acid or SC-1 solution wet chemical etching to remove the etching by-products LiF has also resulted in favorable sidewall morphology [[10](#B10-nanomaterials-13-02789),[40](#B40-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. In 2019, Osipov et al. employed SF6/O2 and SF6/Ar etching gases in ICP. They heated the LNO sample during etching and intermittently used hydrofluoric acid to corrode the LiF etching by-products, significantly increasing the etching rate of LNO and achieving excellent sidewall angles in etch depths at the micrometer-sized scale [[41](#B41-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. Another approach involves covering the LNO surface with metal Ti and performing high-temperature treatment, followed by electrochemical etching and subsequent wet chemical etching. This method has also been shown to be effective in processing LNO. In 2010, Zhang et al. covered the LNO surface with a Ti film and then annealed it in wet O2 at 1050–1100 °C. Afterward, they used a mixture of HF and HNO3 solutions for wet chemical etching. Despite a lower etching rate, they achieved an etch depth of approximately 260 nm [[42](#B42-nanomaterials-13-02789)].

Lastly, a clever process that has been widely studied in recent years is the dry etching/wet etching of proton-exchanged (PE) LNO. PE at temperatures above 180 °C can replace Li ions in the LNO surface with H ions (as shown in below chemical equation) [[43](#B43-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. This process effectively prevents the formation of LiF by-products during subsequent F-based gas etching, ultimately achieving a well-defined sidewall angle of 90°. For instance, in 2012, Deng et al. used PE LNO covered with a Cr mask and etched it using SF6/Ar gases to easily obtain an etching depth of over 3 μm, but the sidewall smoothness was relatively low [[44](#B44-nanomaterials-13-02789)].

LiNbO3 + iH+ ↔ HiLi1−iNbO3 + iLi+

Furthermore, PE LNO, due to its altered crystal structure, is more susceptible to wet chemical etching. This effectively circumvents the issue of different etching rates on different crystal orientations. For example, in 2020, Li et al. used proton-exchanged Z-cut LNO and wet-etched it with HF/HNO3, resulting in a symmetric etching morphology on both sides. The authors also conducted kinetic simulations of the PE reaction in LNO [[36](#B36-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. This clever etching process has received wide applications in LNO optical waveguide devices and surface acoustic wave devices. However, it cannot be applied to LNO domain-wall memory devices because PE damages the crystal structure, severely weakening its ferroelectric properties. This makes it impossible for LNO to undergo domain switching and domain-wall formation under voltage, ultimately leading to the failure of LNO domain-wall memory devices.

Different etching instruments have a significant impact on the etching morphology of LNO [[33](#B33-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. They can be mainly divided into two categories: RIE can only produce low-density plasmas, and ICP can generate high-density plasmas with the option of applying bias voltage. Moreover, the choice of etching masks also greatly affects the etching morphology and applications of LNO. Currently, the mainstream etching masks are made of metallic materials such as Cr, Ni, and Al [[41](#B41-nanomaterials-13-02789),[45](#B45-nanomaterials-13-02789),[46](#B46-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. Non-metallic masks like SiO2 and Si3N4, due to their relatively small etching selectivity with LNO, have received less attention in research. However, they have made a significant progress in studies involving Cl-based gas etching. The development of micro-nanostructures in LNO needs to be integrated with silicon-based integrated circuits. The use of metallic etching masks severely hampers its progress. Therefore, the challenge and focus lie in the use of non-metallic etching masks to achieve superior sidewall morphology in LNO.

In summary, achieving a well-defined etching sidewall angle without compromising the ferroelectric properties of LNO has become a challenging and critical issue, significantly impacting the development of LNO domain-wall memory chips. In response to these problems, this study investigated the effects of different etching machines capable of generating varying plasma densities, different etching masks (metal and non-metal), and various etching gases on LNO etching rates, selectivity, and sidewall morphology. Ultimately, using a metal mask resulted in excellent etching morphology, high selectivity, and favorable sidewall angles. When using a non-metal SiO2 mask, good etching morphology and a high selectivity were achieved. Finally, by combining dry etching, high-temperature metal corrosion, and wet etching, a novel process was developed to obtain a damage-free, perfectly smooth 90° inclined sidewall of LNO. These findings contribute to addressing the challenges associated with LNO domain-wall memory devices and provide potential strategies for improving the etching process to achieve desired sidewall characteristics without compromising the ferroelectric properties of LNO.

## 2. Experimental Methods

After undergoing ultrasonic cleaning using ethanol and acetone, 10 × 12 mm2 X-cut LNO single crystals with the 5 mol.% Mg dopant were used for the preparation of etching masks. The Cr and Ni metal films are commonly used etching masks for LNO. The fabrication processes for these masks are as follows: For the Cr masks, a 130 nm thick poly methyl methacrylate (PMMA) photoresist layer was spin-coated on the LNO surface, and then patterned using electron-beam lithography (EBL JEOL 6300FS, Tokyo, Japan). Cr films 50 nm thick were then grown using thermal resistance evaporator (Nano 36, Kurt J. Lesker, Pittsburgh, PA, USA) and were lift off. For the Ni masks, a 30 nm seed layer of Au was first prepared on the LNO substrate using magnetron sputtering (PVD-75, Kurt J. Lesker, Pittsburgh, PA, USA). Subsequently, a 130 nm PMMA photoresist layer was spin-coated, and then patterned using EBL. Finally, 60 nm thick Ni masks were fabricated using electroplating techniques and were lift off. Subsequently, the Au layer on the surface of LNO was removed using RIE with the etching parameters 40 sccm Ar, 2 Pa, 100 W, and 150 s. To achieve compatibility with conventional semiconductor processes, in addition to the mentioned metal masks, SiO2 masks, which are commonly used in semiconductor processes, were prepared on LNO. Unlike metal masks, the SiO2 masks were fabricated using etching. A 200 nm thick SiO2 layer was prepared using plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD). Then, a 290 nm PMMA photoresist layer was spin-coated, and then patterned using EBL. Finally, the SiO2 etching masks were produced using RIE.

Sample 1 with Cr masks and sample 2 with Ni masks were etched using RIE (SAMCO Corporation, Kyoto, Japan). The process parameters were set as follows: 5 sccm SF6, 45 sccm Ar, 4 Pa, and 150 W.

Sample 3 with Cr masks was placed in molten benzoic acid liquid and subjected to proton exchange at 180 °C for 0.5 h. After removing the benzoic acid with ethanol, the sample underwent the same etching process as sample 1 in RIE.

Sample 4 with 50 nm SiO2 masks was subjected to a 2 h heat treatment at 400 °C in 10% H2 + Ar atmosphere, followed by 10 min wet etching in SC-1 solution at 85 °C.

Sample 5 with Cr masks underwent a 2 h heat treatment at 400 °C in 10% H2 + Ar atmosphere, and then the same etching process as sample 1 in RIE.

Sample 6 and sample 7 with Cr masks underwent the same etching process as sample 1 in RIE, followed by a 2 h annealing process at 400 °C in 10% H2 + Ar atmosphere (sample 7 had a 300 nm Al layer grown using PVD after etching and removed with a mixture of H3PO4:HNO3 (10:1) at 50 °C after annealing). Finally, both samples were subjected to a 10 min wet etching process using SC-1 solution at 85 °C.

Sample 8 with Cr masks and sample 9 with Ni masks were etched in ICP (Northern Microelectronics Corporation, Beijing, China). The process parameters were set as follows: 20 sccm SF6, 160 sccm Ar, 1.3 Pa, 800 W, with a bias power of 250 W.

Sample 10 with SiO2 masks was etched in ICP using the following recipe: 10 sccm SF6, 15 sccm BCl3, 50 sccm Ar, 1.3 Pa, 400 W, with a bias power of 250 W.

## 3. Results and Discussion

SEM cross-sectional images of the Cr, Ni, and SiO2 masks are shown in [Figure 1](#fig_body_display_nanomaterials-13-02789-f001)a–c, respectively. From the images, it can be observed that the evaporated Cr masks exhibit an elliptical shape at the top, the electroplated Ni masks appear to be rectangular, and the etched SiO2 masks have a trapezoidal shape. All three types of masks exhibit uniform and consistent characteristics, making them suitable for use as etching masks for LNO.

![Nanomaterials 13 02789 g001](/nanomaterials/nanomaterials-13-02789/article_deploy/html/images/nanomaterials-13-02789-g001-550.jpg)

**Figure 1.**
SEM images of (**a**) Cr masks, (**b**) Ni masks, (**c**) SiO2 masks.

[Figure 2](#fig_body_display_nanomaterials-13-02789-f002)a is SEM cross-sectional image of sample 1 with Cr masks after 10 min of RIE etching. It can be observed that the Cr mask is nearly completely consumed, and the sidewalls and bottom of the LNO grating are smooth. The etching depth is approximately 102 nm, corresponding to an etching rate of approximately 10 nm/min. The etching selectivity between the LNO and the mask is approximately 3:1. The sidewall inclination angle is approximately 60°. The conventional approach of the direct etching of LNO has been widely employed for fabricating various LNO devices, particularly emerging ferroelectric domain-wall memories. The reduced sidewall inclination has resulted in suboptimal retention performance and imprint effects in LNO memories [[47](#B47-nanomaterials-13-02789),[48](#B48-nanomaterials-13-02789),[49](#B49-nanomaterials-13-02789),[50](#B50-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_nanomaterials-13-02789-f002)b shows the result of 10 min of RIE etching on sample 2 with a Ni mask. Approximately 40 nm of the Ni mask remains, and the depth of the LNO is approximately 110 nm. The etching rate for sample 2 is approximately 11 nm/min, resulting in an etching selectivity between the LNO and the mask of approximately 5.5:1. Compared to sample 1, sample 2 exhibits a significant improvement in the sidewall inclination angle, measuring approximately 72°. This improvement can be attributed to the superior morphology of the electroplated Ni mask compared to the evaporated Cr mask. The Ni mask has a higher hardness, which prevents the collapse of the grating sidewalls during the etching process, thus providing better protection for the LNO sidewalls [[45](#B45-nanomaterials-13-02789),[51](#B51-nanomaterials-13-02789)].

![Nanomaterials 13 02789 g002](/nanomaterials/nanomaterials-13-02789/article_deploy/html/images/nanomaterials-13-02789-g002-550.jpg)

**Figure 2.**
SEM images after RIE dry etching of (**a**) sample 1 with Cr masks and (**b**) sample 2 with Ni masks.

It is evident that both types of masks do not yield sidewalls with angles close to 90°. This is due to the formation of a LiF byproduct during the etching process (As shown in the following chemical equation), which has a high melting point and is not easily vaporized. The LiF byproduct accumulates on the sidewalls of the LNO, forming sidewall protection and impeding further etching, resulting in smaller etching angles [[30](#B30-nanomaterials-13-02789)].

LiNbO3 + F\* → LiF↓ + NbFx↑ + O2↑ + OF2↑

To address the issue of LiF by-product accumulation during the etching process, sample 3 with Cr masks underwent PE and subsequent dry etching in RIE for 10 min. The SEM cross-sectional image of sample 3 is presented in [Figure 3](#fig_body_display_nanomaterials-13-02789-f003)a. It is evident that sample 3 exhibited an etching depth of approximately 130 nm, an etching rate of around 13 nm/min, and an etching angle of about 70°. In comparison to sample 1, which underwent direct dry etching, sample 3 subjected to PE showcased an increased etching rate and a notable enhancement in the inclination angle, albeit with a slightly rougher sidewall surface. Upon close examination, it can be observed that after PE in molten benzoic acid at 180 °C for 0.5 h, a distinct boundary existed between the PE-LNO and the intrinsic LNO, with an exchange depth of approximately 210 nm. The XRD characterization, shown in [Figure 3](#fig_body_display_nanomaterials-13-02789-f003)b, of both non-PE and PE LNO reveals distinct phase transition peaks near the (110) and (220) LNO substrate peaks. This signifies a discrepancy in the lattice spacing between the PE-HiLi1−iNbO3 and the substrate LNO [[36](#B36-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. The observed phase transition is primarily attributed to an increase in lattice constants and lattice distortion of the HiLi1−iNbO3. According to previous studies, this phase is identified as the β1 phase of LNO. With longer PE durations and higher temperatures, deeper exchange layers along with the emergence of new β2 and β3 phases can be generated [[52](#B52-nanomaterials-13-02789),[53](#B53-nanomaterials-13-02789),[54](#B54-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. Additionally, these phase transitions introduce more defects, contributing to the accelerated etching rate and increased sidewall roughness in PE-LNO.

![Nanomaterials 13 02789 g003](/nanomaterials/nanomaterials-13-02789/article_deploy/html/images/nanomaterials-13-02789-g003-550.jpg)

**Figure 3.**
(**a**) SEM image of sample 3 after dry etching in RIE following proton exchange. (**b**) XRD patterns of LNO before and after proton exchange.

Under a high-temperature reducing atmosphere, Li on the surface of LNO will volatilize, and the oxygen vacancy concentration on the surface will also increase [[55](#B55-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. This phenomenon prompts the formation of voids on the LNO surface, rendering its more easy etching in both dry and wet etching processes. This perspective holds promise as a potential avenue for novel approaches in the etching of LNO. The SEM images in [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_nanomaterials-13-02789-f004)a,b depict LNO with SiO2 masks, subjected to treatment in a 10% H2 + Ar atmosphere at 400 °C, followed by wet etching in SC-1 solution at 85 °C for 10 min. As demonstrated in the figures, the etching depth of LNO was approximately 49 nm, and the upper surface of LNO also exhibited lateral erosion in a horizontal direction, resulting in lateral separation from the overlying SiO2 masks. However, distinctive etching rates can be observed for LNO in the +Z and −Z directions, leading to dissimilar sidewall inclinations of 44° and 85°, respectively. Moreover, the lateral erosion distances differed between these directions, with the +Z direction notably smaller than the −Z direction.

![Nanomaterials 13 02789 g004](/nanomaterials/nanomaterials-13-02789/article_deploy/html/images/nanomaterials-13-02789-g004-550.jpg)

**Figure 4.**
SEM images for (**a**) +Z direction and (**b**) −Z direction of sample 4 without the Al thin-film coverage, after annealing in a reducing atmosphere and wet etching with SC-1 solution.

Sample 5 with Cr masks underwent a similar process to sample 4. It was subjected to treatment in high-temperature reducing conditions followed by a 10 min dry-etching step in RIE. The SEM image in [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_nanomaterials-13-02789-f005)a shows the post-etching result. The etched depth of the LNO is approximately 115 nm, corresponding to an etching rate of about 11.5 nm/min, and displaying an etching sidewall angle of around 85°. In comparison with the direct dry etching of sample 1, the high-temperature reduction treatment and etching process applied to sample 5 caused a slight increase in the etching rate but a significant enhancement in the sidewall angle.

![Nanomaterials 13 02789 g005](/nanomaterials/nanomaterials-13-02789/article_deploy/html/images/nanomaterials-13-02789-g005-550.jpg)

**Figure 5.**
(**a**) SEM image of sample 5 without the Al thin-film coverage, after annealing in a reducing atmosphere and dry etching with RIE. (**b**) SEM image of sample 6, after dry etching with RIE and annealing in a reducing atmosphere without the Al thin film coverage, followed by wet etching with SC-1 solution. (**c**) SEM image of sample 7, after dry etching with RIE and annealing in a reducing atmosphere with the Al thin-film coverage, followed by wet etching with SC-1 solution.

On the contrary, sample 6 with Cr masks, was subjected to a reversed procedure. It first underwent a 10 min dry-etching step in RIE, followed by treatment in high-temperature reducing conditions and subsequent 10 min wet etching in SC-1 solution. The SEM image in [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_nanomaterials-13-02789-f005)b reveals a final depth of around 112 nm for the Cr mask-removed LNO. Notably, an inward concavity shape is observed on the sidewall. Interestingly, the LNO grating’s top part in sample 6 did not exhibit lateral etching, while the mid-section of the sidewall showed lateral etching. This phenomenon raises suspicions that the top Cr mask might have diffused into the underlying LNO at elevated temperatures, leading to alloy formation [[56](#B56-nanomaterials-13-02789),[57](#B57-nanomaterials-13-02789),[58](#B58-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. The alloyed LNO layer at the top appeared less susceptible to wet etching than the middle part, resulting in the formation of the inward concavity sidewall. While the inward concavity sidewall is not favorable for LNO device fabrication, it does, however, offer new avenues for the refinement of etching techniques.

Subsequently, sample 7 with Cr masks underwent a process nearly identical to sample 6, except for an additional step involving the deposition of a 300 nm Al layer through PVD after the dry etching of LNO. Prior research has indicated that LNO covered by highly active metal films, when annealed under reducing atmospheres, can lead to a significant reduction of oxygen in the LNO due to the metal’s strong reactivity at elevated temperatures [[55](#B55-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. This ultimately results in the creation of a porous and loosely packed surface on the LNO, rendering it more susceptible to dry and wet etching. As depicted in [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_nanomaterials-13-02789-f005)c, the LNO achieved a final depth of approximately 115 nm, and the sidewall exhibited a pretty 90° angle. In the case of LNO subjected to dry etching, followed by the high-temperature annealing of the deposited Al layer, and then wet etching, the presence of the Cr-LNO alloyed layer on top rendered it less susceptible to wet etching. Consequently, the sidewall, initially at a 60° angle, was enhanced into a 90° angle. This hybrid process ingeniously uses the alloyed LNO layer, resulting in smooth sidewalls with precise 90° angles. Moreover, this process preserves the ferroelectric properties of LNO, making it suitable for large-scale fabrication of LNO domain-wall memory arrays.

The SEM image of sample 8 with Cr masks, after 3 min of ICP etching, is shown in [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_nanomaterials-13-02789-f006)a. The etched depth of the LNO is approximately 112 nm, corresponding to an etching rate of approximately 37 nm/min. The sidewall inclination angle is approximately 71°. However, the grating top width is near to 0, indicating that the Cr mask was no longer effective as a mask. This is due to the tendency of the Cr mask to undergo sidewall indentation during the etching process, resulting in a triangular shape for the overall grating. Due to the higher plasma density generated by the ICP instrument compared to RIE, although it increased the etching rate of LNO and correspondingly improved the etching angle to some extent, it also resulted in significant damage to the Cr mask.

![Nanomaterials 13 02789 g006](/nanomaterials/nanomaterials-13-02789/article_deploy/html/images/nanomaterials-13-02789-g006-550.jpg)

**Figure 6.**
SEM images after ICP dry etching of (**a**) sample 8 with Cr masks, (**b**) sample 9 with Ni masks and (**c**) sample 10 with SiO2 masks.

[Figure 6](#fig_body_display_nanomaterials-13-02789-f006)b displays the result of 5 min of ICP etching on sample 9 with a Ni mask, where the Ni mask and Au seed layer were removed. The depth of the LNO is approximately 394 nm, with an etching rate of approximately 79 nm/min, and the etching inclination angle is approximately 83°. Compared to the Cr mask, due to the greater hardness of Ni, it exhibited better shape retention during ICP etching, consequently resulting in a higher inclination angle of LNO sidewalls. Additionally, the etching rate of LNO in sample 9 was relatively higher compared to that observed with the Cr mask. This is because the F ions participate more in the reaction with Cr than with Ni during the high-density plasma-etching process [[41](#B41-nanomaterials-13-02789),[45](#B45-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. As a result, when using a Cr mask, the consumption of etching gas is higher than when using a Ni mask, leading to a slight difference in the etching rate of LNO.

Finally, to etch LNO gratings to a certain depth using SiO2 masks, the same etching recipe as that used for metal masks cannot be applied. This is because F-based gases etch SiO2 at a significantly higher rate [[29](#B29-nanomaterials-13-02789),[34](#B34-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. Therefore, in the case of sample 10 with SiO2 masks, the proportion of F-based gases in the recipe was reduced while increasing the proportion of Cl-based gases, which exhibited lower etching rates for SiO2. [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_nanomaterials-13-02789-f006)c illustrates the result of 1 min of ICP etching on sample 10. The remaining thickness of SiO2 is approximately 75 nm, while the etched depth of LNO is approximately 108 nm, resulting in an etching rate of 108 nm/min and an etching selectivity of 0.86:1. Like the Cr masks, the SiO2 masks also experienced sidewall indentation during the etching process, leading to a degradation of the etching inclination angle of LNO to approximately 65°. Although the etching inclination angle of LNO was relatively poor compared to previous studies that employed non-metal masks for etching LNO, a significant improvement in etching selectivity was achieved [[35](#B35-nanomaterials-13-02789)]. Further research holds the potential to achieve even better etching profiles, thereby facilitating the effective integration of LNO memories with traditional semiconductor processes in the future.

[Table 1](#table_body_display_nanomaterials-13-02789-t001) compiles the key etching processes for the 10 samples and presents essential parameters including the etching rate, etching selectivity ratio, and sidewall angle. The high-hardness Ni masks demonstrate excellent mask integrity in both RIE and ICP etching processes for LNO. Moreover, they yield superior etching angles and slightly higher etching rates compared to the Cr masks. Employing a post-dry-etching annealing process with Al metal-film coverage at an elevated temperature in a reducing atmosphere enhances the sidewall profile from an initial 60° to a perfect 90°. Finally, when utilizing SiO2 masks and ICP with a recipe comprising Cl-based, F-based, and Ar gases, remarkable etching rates and favorable etching selectivity are achieved. However, the sidewall inclination of 65° still requires improvement.

## 4. Conclusions

In conclusion, this research underscores the significance of understanding and optimizing etching techniques for LNO nanofabrication. The outcomes of this study hold potential for advancing the integration of LNO into various applications, thereby contributing to the advancement of cutting-edge technologies across multiple domains. This study delved into the field of LNO etching techniques, which play a pivotal role in enabling the transformation of its unique properties into functional devices. Building upon existing etching research, this investigation explored diverse etching strategies, capitalizing on instruments capable of generating varied plasma densities. The utilization of RIE dry etching, proton exchange-enhanced etching, wet etching following high-temperature reduction treatment, and hybrid dry and wet etching unveiled new avenues for LNO nanofabrication. The optimized approach, combining RIE dry etching with subsequent wet etching after high-temperature reduction treatment, yielded an impressive etching rate of 10 nm/min and pristine 90° sidewall angles. Furthermore, by embracing ICP dry etching, significantly enhanced etching rates of 79 nm/min alongside steep sidewall angles of 83° were achieved. Additionally, the integration of SiO2 masks facilitated a high etching rate of 108 nm/min, coupled with a respectable etching selectivity ratio of 0.86:1. The diverse range of etching conditions generated exceptional results, paving the way for multiple pathways in harnessing the versatile capabilities of LNO.

This is a scientific research article published in Nanomaterials (2023, 13(20), 2789, DOI: 10.3390/nano13202789) titled "Advanced Etching Techniques of LiNbO3 Nanodevices" by Bowen Shen, Di Hu, Cuihua Dai, Xiaoyang Yu, Xiaojun Tan, Jie Sun, Jun Jiang, and Anquan Jiang from the School of Microelectronics, Fudan University, Shanghai, China. The article is part of the Special Issue "Fabrication of Nanoscale Electronics Devices."

**Background/Purpose:** Lithium niobate (LiNbO3 or LNO) single crystals are widely used in surface acoustic wave devices, optoelectronic devices, and novel ferroelectric memory devices due to their exceptional electro-optic and piezoelectric properties. However, nanofabrication challenges (particularly achieving high etching rates and improved sidewall angles) hinder their applications. This study systematically investigated various etching techniques using instruments capable of generating different plasma densities (RIE and ICP), different etching masks (metal Cr/Ni and non-metal SiO2), and various etching gases.

**Key Methods & Results (10 samples tested):**
1. **RIE dry etching with Cr masks (Sample 1):** ~10 nm/min etching rate, 60° sidewall angle, 3:1 selectivity. LiF byproduct accumulation reduces sidewall angle.
2. **RIE dry etching with Ni masks (Sample 2):** ~11 nm/min, 72° sidewall angle, 5.5:1 selectivity. Ni masks have higher hardness and better shape retention.
3. **Proton exchange (PE) + RIE dry etching (Sample 3):** PE at 180°C in molten benzoic acid for 0.5h; ~13 nm/min, 70° sidewall angle. PE creates β1 phase, preventing LiF formation but increasing surface roughness.
4. **High-temperature reduction + wet etching with SiO2 masks (Sample 4):** Annealed at 400°C in 10% H2+Ar, then wet etched in SC-1 solution at 85°C. Depth ~49 nm, with directional etching differences (44° in +Z, 85° in −Z directions).
5. **Reduction treatment + RIE dry etching (Sample 5):** ~11.5 nm/min, 85° sidewall angle.
6. **RIE dry etching + reduction annealing + wet etching (Sample 6):** ~112 nm depth, inward concavity sidewall due to Cr-LNO alloying at elevated temperatures.
7. **RIE + Al thin-film coverage + reduction annealing + wet etching (Sample 7):** Achieved a pretty 90° sidewall angle and ~115 nm depth using a novel hybrid process with a 300 nm Al layer, preserving ferroelectric properties. This is the optimized approach.
8. **ICP dry etching with Cr masks (Sample 8):** ~37 nm/min, 71° sidewall angle; Cr mask suffered significant damage under high-density plasma.
9. **ICP dry etching with Ni masks (Sample 9):** ~79 nm/min, 83° sidewall angle, ~394 nm depth — high etching rate with steep sidewalls.
10. **ICP dry etching with SiO2 masks (Sample 10):** Using SF6/BCl3/Ar recipe; ~108 nm/min etching rate with 0.86:1 selectivity, but only 65° sidewall angle.

**Key Conclusions:**
- RIE dry etching combined with wet etching after high-temperature reduction treatment (with Al metal-film coverage) achieved 10 nm/min etching rate and pristine 90° sidewall angles while preserving ferroelectric properties — suitable for large-scale LNO domain-wall memory fabrication.
- ICP dry etching achieved 79 nm/min with 83° sidewall angles.
- SiO2 (non-metal) masks enabled 108 nm/min etching rate with 0.86:1 selectivity, important for silicon-based circuit integration, though sidewall angle (65°) still needs improvement.
- Ni masks outperform Cr masks due to higher hardness and better shape retention.
- Proton exchange cannot be applied to domain-wall memory devices as it damages the crystal structure and weakens ferroelectric properties.

**Funding:** Natural Science Foundation of Shanghai (23ZR1403900), National Key Basic Research Program of China (2019YFA0308500, 2022YFA1402904), National Natural Science Foundation of China (62174034).

Additionally, using SiO2 masks, a high etching rate of 108 nm/min and an etching selectivity ratio of 0.86:1 were achieved."

Any further distribution of this work must maintain attribution to the author(s) and the title of the work, journal citation and DOI.
TECHNICAL NOTE Navigating plasma etching of photonic chips in shared cleanrooms: a practical tutorial for researchers Kashif Masud Awan Photonic Inc., Coquitlam, British Columbia, Canada E-mail: kashifmasudawan@gmail.com Keywords: photonic integrated circuits, plasma etching, semiconductor device fabrication Abstract The research and commercialization of integrated photonic devices have seen rapid growth, driven by their broad applicability and importance in both technological innovation and fundamental research. Among the key steps in the fabrication of such devices, plasma etching plays a critical role in fabrication of high optical quality integrated photonic devices. This work presents a practical tutorial for developing a robust plasma etching process from the ground up, specifically within the constraints of a shared academic semiconductor cleanroom—an environment often limited in resources and process isolation. Key topics covered include chamber preparation, selection of etch chemistries and process parameters, mask material considerations, and techniques for characterizing etch quality. Strategies for achieving process repeatability and post-etch enhancements to improve optical performance are also discussed. This tutorial is intended to serve as a starting point for graduate students and researchers working on the fabrication of photonic integrated circuits in academic settings.
1. Introduction Photonic integrated circuits (PICs) have demonstrated increasing potential for the commercialization of photonic technologies. While early efforts in integrated photonics were predominantly based on the indium phosphide (InP) platform for optical communication applications [1], the field has since expanded to encompass a broad range of material platforms, including gallium arsenide (GaAs) [2], silicon (Si) [3], silicon nitride (Si3N4) [4], gallium nitride (GaN) [5], silicon carbide (SiC) [6], and lithium niobate (LiNbO3) [7]. These platforms support a diverse array of applications such as optical communications [8], LIDAR [9], ultra-sensitive sensing [10], biosensing [11], quantum computing [12], gas sensing [13], and display technologies [14].
The majority of photonic integrated devices are fabricated using planar processing techniques derived from the CMOS semiconductor industry [15]. In academic and research settings, proof-of-concept devices are typically fabricated by first finalizing the design and then patterning it onto wafers or chips using optical or electron-beam lithography. The resulting pattern is subsequently transferred into the substrate through dry etching techniques, most commonly inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etching (ICP-RIE).
Academic research in this field often relies on shared semiconductor cleanroom facilities, which are used by a broad user base employing diverse applications and process flow on the same equipment. This environment presents notable challenges in achieving high device quality and ensuring reproducibility of fabrication processes.
This article addresses these challenges and provides a practical tutorial on developing and optimizing plasma etching processes for integrated photonic devices within shared cleanroom environments.
2. Best practices when using shared facilities etch chambers Due to resource limitations, academic cleanrooms often employ a single etch chamber for processing multiple materials using various etch chemistries. This multipurpose use introduces significant challenges © 2025 The Author(s). Published by IOP Publishing Ltd J. Phys. Photonics 7 (2025) 046001 K M Awan related to cross-contamination and process reproducibility. In practice, most academic semiconductor facilities maintain at least two dedicated etch chambers: one for fluorine-based chemistries (commonly used for silicon and related materials), and another for chlorine-based chemistries (used for III–V semiconductors, metals, and sometimes silicon).
Etch processes result in sputtering and redeposition of materials onto the chamber walls, which can later be unintentionally redeposited onto subsequent wafers, posing a risk of contamination—especially when etching dissimilar materials in the same chamber. Furthermore, repeatability is often compromised due to fluctuating chamber conditions caused by varying materials and chemistries. Even within a single chemistry family, such as fluorine-based etching, a wide range of gases may be used—e.g. CF4, C4F8, SF6, CHF3—each with distinct plasma characteristics. Similarly, chlorine-based chambers may use Cl2, BCl3, or HCl, among others. In addition to etch by-products, resist materials (typically polymer-based photoresists or electron-beam resists) can also deposit on chamber surfaces, affecting subsequent etch uniformity and selectivity.
To mitigate these issues, routine oxygen plasma cleaning is employed to remove polymer-based contamination [16]. A standard best practice in shared etch chambers is to begin with a high-power oxygen clean—typically using the tool’s maximum inductively coupled plasma (ICP) and reactive ion etching (RIE) powers and the highest available oxygen flow rates—for 10–15 min. Following this, the chamber is conditioned by running the desired etch chemistry on a dummy wafer for 5–15 min. This step helps stabilize the chamber environment and reduces residual contamination. If end-point spectroscopic in-chamber detection is available, it can be used to observe the species in the chamber during an oxygen plasma clean and during a dummy etch run, to confirm all contaminants have been successfully removed. After cleaning and conditioning, the actual sample can be loaded for etching. The same procedure is repeated when switching to a different etch chemistry. In many facilities, users are required to perform an oxygen clean at the end of each session, ensuring the chamber is in a clean state for the next user. It is also advised to operate the etch chamber near the lowest base pressure as per the tool specifications, this also mitigates contamination, most ICP-RIE tools have a base pressure in the range of 10−6–10−8 Torr.
While this approach is generally effective, some materials—such as metals in silicon etch chambers or lithium-based compounds—are more difficult to remove and can persist within the chamber. For this reason, most silicon etch chambers in academic cleanrooms prohibit the use of exposed metal layers or metal-based masks. Understanding the history of materials and processes used in a shared etch chamber is critical when developing new etch recipes. Tool managers and cleanroom staff must rigorously monitor chamber usage to prevent cross-contamination. In severe cases, only a full wet clean—manual scrubbing of the chamber walls using acetone and/or isopropyl alcohol—can restore chamber integrity. Such contamination events can significantly degrade process repeatability and reliability.
State-of-the-art dry etching tools, such as ICP-RIE systems, are costly and not always available in multiple configurations in academic settings. Some cleanrooms may only have a single etch chamber available, serving diverse research needs across multiple groups. In these cases, a pragmatic approach involves time-sharing the chamber between distinct chemistries. For example, a month could be allocated exclusively to fluorine-based processing, followed by an extensive oxygen plasma clean and chamber conditioning, before switching to chlorine-based processing for the next cycle. Some systems also support replaceable chamber liners, which can help mitigate contamination risks when switching between chemistries.
Although this practice is not ideal, it provides a viable path to support a wide range of etch processes in resource-constrained environments, while minimizing cross-contamination and maintaining process repeatability. Close collaboration between cleanroom staff and end users is essential to prolong tool lifetime and ensure the reliability of etch processes.
3. Preparing etch tests When preparing for etch testing, the first critical consideration is the selection of an appropriate lithography technique, as it directly impacts the resolution, pattern fidelity, and process compatibility of the final device.
Once the lithographic method is chosen, the corresponding resist must be selected to suit both the patterning and etching requirements.
Among the various lithographic techniques available, electron beam lithography (EBL) is particularly well-suited for academic research and prototyping in PICs. EBL enables high-resolution patterning down to tens of nanometers, with sufficient throughput for proof-of-concept device fabrication. Its flexibility and precision have also led to the development of EBL-based rapid prototyping foundries [17]. Consequently, this article focuses on etch test patterns defined using EBL.
2 J. Phys. Photonics 7 (2025) 046001 K M Awan Figure 1. Snap shot from the etch test CAD showing trenches of varying sizes ranging from a width of 2 µms down to 50 nm.
Triangular latticed holes are also visible, useful for testing photonic crystal structures.
EBL resists are broadly classified into two categories: positive-tone and negative-tone. In positive-tone resists, the exposed regions are removed during development, leaving the unexposed areas as the masking layer. Conversely, in negative-tone resists, the exposed regions undergo cross-linking and remain after development, while the unexposed regions are removed. The choice between positive and negative tone resists should be guided by the device layout: if the design requires masking of a large area with only small features cleared (e.g. waveguides or trenches), a positive-tone resist is preferred. If, on the other hand, only a small area needs to be masked and the rest etched, a negative-tone resist may be more appropriate.
For positive-tone EBL applications, common resist choices include ZEP520A and polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA), both of which offer high resolution and compatibility with a variety of etch chemistries. Negative-tone resists such as hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ) and the ma-N 2400 series are widely used for their etch resistance and nanoscale resolution capabilities [18–21].
For the etch test example presented in this study, we utilize a negative-tone electron beam resist, specifically hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ). However, the same patterning strategy can be readily adapted for use with positive-tone resists. When developing etch test patterns, it is advisable to design features that are representative of the most critical elements in the final device layout. This ensures that the etch process is optimized for the specific dimensions, aspect ratios, and feature geometries relevant to the intended application.
For pattern design, we recommend using the industry-standard GDSII format, which is widely supported by fabrication tools and compatible with open-source layout software such as KLayout (freely available at: www.klayout.de/). Figure 1 illustrates a typical etch test pattern for PICs. The design includes variable-width trenches (ranging from 2000 nm to 40 nm in this case) and hole arrays, which can be tailored to match the specific requirements of the final device architecture. These structures are typically fabricated with a minimum length of 4 mm to facilitate cleaving and enable high-resolution cross-sectional imaging using scanning electron microscopy (SEM).
Once the resist and pattern design have been finalized, electron beam dose tests must be performed to optimize feature dimensions. These tests are conducted at a fixed development time to determine the appropriate exposure dose required to achieve the desired critical dimensions (CDs), as defined by the target device specifications.
In previous projects, a practical approach has been to pattern a large-area chip with multiple, identical copies of the etch test structures. The wafer or chip is then cleaved using a diamond scribe to produce smaller individual test chips. This method significantly reduces the time and cost associated with performing separate EBL exposures for each etch test, while maintaining consistency across test samples.
It is essential that the etch test chips be fabricated on the same material platform and film stack as the final device. In many cases, it is also advisable for the test chip to match the size and layout density (i.e., open area) of the intended device. This ensures that the etch behavior observed during testing accurately reflects the conditions encountered in the actual device fabrication. Once the etch test chips are prepared, systematic etch parameter sweep experiments can be conducted to optimize process conditions.
4. Design of experiment (DOE) for etch parameter sweeps Plasma etching operates through three primary mechanisms: sputtering, chemical etching, and ion-enhanced chemical etching. Figure 2 presents a schematic illustration of these mechanisms as they occur in a plasma environment [22, 23].
3 J. Phys. Photonics 7 (2025) 046001 K M Awan Figure 2. Schematic showing etching mechanisms of plasma etching: sputtering, chemical etching and ion-enhanced chemical etching [22].
Sputtering is a purely physical process, in which material is removed from the substrate surface by the kinetic energy of incident ions. These ions, typically accelerated by electric fields within the plasma sheath, bombard the substrate and physically dislodge surface atoms.
Chemical etching resembles wet etching in its fundamental reaction mechanism, but utilizes reactive gaseous species rather than liquid-phase reactants. In this case, neutral radicals generated within the plasma chemically react with the substrate material to form volatile by-products, which are then evacuated from the chamber.
Ion-enhanced chemical etching—also referred to as RIE—combines the benefits of both physical sputtering and chemical reactivity. Ion bombardment serves to disrupt surface bonds and promote adsorption of reactive species, thereby accelerating the chemical reaction rates and improving directionality.
This synergistic mechanism is central to achieving anisotropic etching profiles with high fidelity and selectivity [23].
The relative contributions of physical and chemical mechanisms in a plasma etching process determine which of the aforementioned etching modes—sputtering, chemical etching, or ion-enhanced chemical etching—predominates. Sputtering, being purely physical, is highly anisotropic and enables directional etching; however, it often results in increased surface roughness due to energetic ion bombardment. In contrast, chemical etching is typically isotropic, providing smoother etched surfaces but lacking directional control.
Ion-enhanced chemical etching offers a compromise between these two extremes. It leverages both directional ion bombardment and chemical reactivity, enabling anisotropic etching with comparatively low surface roughness. In most applications, a well-optimized plasma etch recipe is designed to favor ion-enhanced chemical etching, thereby achieving high fidelity pattern transfer with acceptable surface morphology. ICP-RIE is generally preferred over capacitively coupled plasma etching for the rapid prototyping of photonic devices. The primary advantage of ICP-RIE lies in its ability to decouple plasma density from ion energy, which enables superior anisotropy and enhanced profile control during the etching process.
A schematic of an ICP-RIE system is shown in figure 3, reproduced from [22]. The key process parameters that influence etch characteristics—such as etch rate, selectivity, and sidewall profile—include gas composition and flow rates (typically measured in standard cubic centimeters per minute, sccm), chamber pressure, ICP power, bias RIE power, and substrate (platen) temperature. By tuning these variables, the plasma conditions can be precisely controlled to meet specific etching requirements. Substrate temperature is also an important parameter. While most etch chambers operate near room temperature, certain systems are capable of elevated temperature processing up to approximately 200 ◦C, whereas others support cryogenic operation down to liquid nitrogen temperatures.
For most etch processes and CDs, the etch rate is approximately linear with time. However, in the case of high-aspect-ratio structures or very narrow openings, etch rates tend to decrease as the etch progresses. This 4 J. Phys. Photonics 7 (2025) 046001 K M Awan Figure 3. Simplified schematic of an ICP-RIE system. Plasma is generated by ICP RF coil using gases in the etching chemistry.
Generated plasma is then accelerated toward helium cooled substrate by RIE (bias) power supply to begin ion-enhanced plasma etching [22].
Figure 4. Scale bars represent 1 µm [22].
reduction is primarily due to limitations in reactive species transport and by-product removal within deep or confined features.
The substrate etch rate (ersub) is defined as the rate at which the target material is removed over time, typically expressed in units such as nm s−1, µm s−1, or µm min−1 [23]. In cyclic etching processes—such as the Bosch process—the etch rate is instead defined per cycle, representing the material removal per individual etch step. In this work, we focus exclusively on single-step (non-cyclic) etch processes.
An additional critical parameter is the mask etch rate (ermask), which quantifies the rate at which the masking material (in our case, HSQ electron beam resist) is eroded during the etch. The etch selectivity is defined as the ratio of the substrate etch rate to the mask etch rate: s = ersub ermask .
The etch rates of both the mask and the substrate material can be quantified using atomic force microscopy or cross-sectional SEM. Among these, cross-sectional SEM is particularly useful for measuring the sidewall angle of etched features, providing detailed insight into the etch profile. An example of such a measurement is shown in figure 4 [22].
To systematically study the influence of process variables, a DOEs approach can be employed using DOE software. Table 1 presents an example DOE matrix for a parameter sweep in an ICP-RIE process [22]. This structured methodology enables efficient exploration of the process space and identification of optimal etching conditions.
Based on experimental characterization from the same study, the effects of key process parameters—namely chamber pressure, ICP power, and bias RIE power—on etch rate, sidewall angle, and selectivity were investigated and quantified, as reproduced in figures 5–7 [22]. These insights are critical for tailoring plasma etch recipes to specific device requirements and material systems. For this study the gas flow ratios were fixed based on a starting recipe provided by the vendor. In practice literature review can provide useful information on gas chemistry to use and the ratios to employ.
Given the observed trends, it is important to recognize that not all unique combinations in the DOEs matrix need to be experimentally investigated, as such exhaustive testing can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. Instead, focusing on key process parameters—often referred to as ‘knobs’—can offer an efficient route to optimization. of incident ions. This can be achieved by lowering the RIE (bias) power or increasing the chamber pressure, both of which reduce ion bombardment energy and favor chemical over physical etching.
5. Evaluating etch test trials For each etch test, the process begins with a standard chamber cleaning and conditioning step, followed by execution of the etch run. This procedure is repeated identically for each test condition to ensure consistency.
After etching, the resulting structures are analyzed using cross-sectional SEM or focused ion beam cross-sectioning to evaluate key metrics, including etch rate, selectivity, and sidewall angle, as shown in the representative SEM image reproduced from [22].
These measured values are then plotted as functions of the varied etch parameters to identify trends and inform the selection of improved process conditions, as illustrated in figures 5–7 [22, 23]. This demonstrates the progressive refinement of an etch process across a parameter sweep during process engineering [22].
This iterative trial-and-error approach is continued until an etch process meets the target specifications.
Once an acceptable process is identified, it is repeated multiple times to evaluate repeatability and reliability.
If the process consistently meets device tolerances across multiple trials, it can then be adopted for fabrication of the final devices.
In the context of shared cleanroom facilities, it is advisable to revalidate the etch process after the chamber has been used for a different chemistry or material system. This is particularly important in multi-user environments where contamination or drift in chamber conditions may occur. Repeating a standard chamber cleaning (e.g. high-power oxygen plasma) followed by chamber conditioning using the intended etch chemistry on a dummy wafer helps restore baseline conditions. Performing control etches after such resets ensures that the engineered etch process remains robust under varying tool conditions and continues to deliver reliable results over time.
7 J. Phys. Photonics 7 (2025) 046001 K M Awan 6. How to further improve the etch quality Once an optimized and repeatable etch process has been developed and successfully used to fabricate devices, further improvements in optical performance may still be necessary—particularly in applications where line edge roughness (LER) contributes to optical losses. Since plasma etching is a major contributor to LER, several post-processing and optimization strategies can be employed to further enhance device performance: (a) Surface passivation Certain integrated photonic devices, such as lasers, light-emitting diodes, and photovoltaic cells, are highly sensitive to dangling bonds at the etched surfaces. These surface states can act as non-radiative recombination centers, degrading optical performance. Surface passivation techniques aim to neutralize these dangling bonds, thereby stabilizing the etched facets and improving optical quality. For example, sulfur passivation is commonly used for III–V semiconductors to reduce surface recombination [24]. Passivation can be performed using either wet chemical treatments or dry processes in high-vacuum chambers, where passivating agents are introduced in the gas phase.
(b) Wet post processing Plasma etching processes can often result in rough sidewalls, which in turn increase optical scattering and propagation losses in photonic waveguides. A widely used technique to mitigate this issue involves applying a wet etching step after dry etching to smooth the sidewalls. This approach has been demonstrated to significantly reduce sidewall roughness and improve etch profile fidelity, leading to lower propagation losses [5, 24]. Wet post-processing can be adapted for various semiconductor materials by selecting appropriate etchants.
In most cases, it is essential to remove the residual mask after etching. For polymer-based resists such as ZEP520A and PMMA, a combination of oxygen plasma treatment and solvent cleaning is typically employed [25]. In contrast, for HSQ (hydrogen silsesquioxane), dilute HF (hydrofluoric acid) or BOE (buffered oxide etch) is commonly used. In the example presented in this work, a 20 s treatment in 10% HF was sufficient to completely remove the residual HSQ without inducing any undesirable oxidation of the device layers.
(c) Reducing LERs of the lithographic mask If the etch process already yields relatively smooth sidewalls, further improvement can be achieved by minimizing the LERs of the mask itself. In EBL, low-temperature development has been shown to reduce LER by suppressing resist swelling and diffusion during development. Additionally, the choice of resist plays a critical role: for instance, hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ) exhibits inherently lower LER compared to organic resists due to its short-chain, inorganic molecular structure [26]. Employing low-LER resists and optimized development conditions can result in smoother etched features, thereby enhancing the optical quality of the final devices.
7. Conclusion In this article, a concise tutorial was presented outlining key considerations and challenges involved in developing a repeatable and reliable plasma etching process for the fabrication of integrated photonic devices within academic shared semiconductor cleanroom facilities. The discussion began with chamber cleaning and conditioning protocols, followed by the design of representative etch test patterns for evaluating process performance. The operational principles of ICP-RIE systems were introduced, along with the primary process control parameters (‘knobs’) that influence etch characteristics. Methods for measuring critical etch parameters—such as etch rate, selectivity, and sidewall angle—were described in detail. Lastly, advanced post-etch processing techniques were explored to enhance the optical quality and performance of the etched devices, including surface passivation, wet post-processing, and lithographic LER reduction strategies.
It is hoped that this work will serve as a practical entry point for graduate students and researchers embarking on the development of plasma etch processes for PICs, particularly in resource-constrained, multi-user academic fabrication environments.

This is a technical tutorial (published in J. Phys. Photonics 7, 046001, October 2025) by Kashif Masud Awan (Photonic Inc., Coquitlam, British Columbia, Canada) that provides a practical guide for developing robust plasma etching processes for photonic integrated circuits (PICs) within the constraints of shared academic semiconductor cleanrooms.

KEY SECTIONS AND CONTENT:

1. **Context**: PICs have grown rapidly across material platforms including InP, GaAs, silicon, Si3N4, GaN, SiC, and LiNbO3, supporting applications in optical communications, LIDAR, sensing, quantum computing, and displays. Most PICs are fabricated using planar CMOS-derived techniques with ICP-RIE (inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etching) as the dominant dry etching method.

2. **Chamber Best Practices**: Shared academic cleanrooms typically maintain two dedicated etch chambers—one for fluorine-based chemistries (silicon materials) and one for chlorine-based chemistries (III-V semiconductors, metals). Recommended protocol: begin with a high-power oxygen plasma clean (10-15 min at max ICP/RIE powers and highest O2 flow), then condition the chamber with the target etch chemistry on a dummy wafer (5-15 min). Operate near the lowest base pressure (typically 10⁻⁶–10⁻⁸ Torr). Some materials (metals, lithium compounds) are difficult to remove and require prohibitions on metal masks in silicon chambers. In single-chamber facilities, time-sharing between chemistries (e.g., monthly rotations) with extensive oxygen cleans between is recommended. Severe contamination may require manual wet cleaning with acetone/IPA.

3. **Etch Test Preparation**: EBL (electron beam lithography) is preferred for academic PIC prototyping due to high resolution (tens of nm). Positive-tone resists (ZEP520A, PMMA) are used when large areas need masking; negative-tone resists (HSQ, ma-N 2400 series) when small areas need masking. HSQ is used in the example. Test patterns should include variable-width trenches (2000 nm down to 40 nm), hole arrays, and features ≥4 mm in length for cleaving and SEM cross-sectioning. GDSII format with KLayout is recommended. Chips should match the final device's material platform, film stack, size, and layout density.

4. **DOE for Parameter Sweeps**: Plasma etching operates via three mechanisms—sputtering (purely physical, anisotropic, rough surfaces), chemical etching (isotropic, smooth), and ion-enhanced chemical etching/RIE (combines both, preferred for high-fidelity anisotropic pattern transfer). ICP-RIE is preferred over CCP because it decouples plasma density from ion energy. Key process parameters ("knobs"): gas composition/flow rates (sccm), chamber pressure, ICP power, bias RIE power, and substrate temperature (ranging from cryogenic to ~200°C). Etch selectivity is defined as s = substrate etch rate / mask etch rate. The article presents a 40-run DOE matrix for AlGaAs etching with Ar–BCl3 chemistry (Table 1), with results on etch rate, selectivity, and sidewall angle as functions of pressure, ICP power, and RIE power (Figures 5-7). Not all DOE combinations need testing—focusing on key knobs is more efficient. Selectivity can be improved by lowering RIE power or increasing pressure.

5. **Evaluating Etch Trials**: Each test follows chamber cleaning/conditioning, then etching, then cross-sectional SEM or FIB analysis to measure etch rate, selectivity, and sidewall angle. Results are plotted against varied parameters to identify trends. Iterative refinement continues until specifications are met, then processes are repeated multiple times to validate repeatability. Revalidation is advised after the chamber has been used for different chemistries/materials in shared facilities.

6. **Post-Etch Quality Improvements**: (a) Surface passivation—for lasers, LEDs, and photovoltaics sensitive to dangling bonds; e.g., sulfur passivation for III-V semiconductors. (b) Wet post-processing—applying wet etch after dry etch to smooth rough sidewalls and reduce propagation losses. Mask removal: oxygen plasma + solvent for polymer resists (ZEP520A, PMMA); dilute HF or BOE for HSQ (e.g., 20 s in 10% HF worked in this study). (c) Reducing mask LER—low-temperature EBL development suppresses resist swelling; HSQ exhibits inherently lower LER than organic resists due to its inorganic short-chain structure.

7. **Conclusion**: The tutorial provides a starting point for graduate students and researchers developing plasma etch processes for PICs in resource-constrained, multi-user academic fabrication environments, covering chamber protocols, test pattern design, ICP-RIE principles, parameter optimization, etch characterization, and post-etch enhancements.

Following this, the chamber is conditioned by running the desired etch chemistry on a dummy wafer for 5–15 min."

The etching characteristics of congruent LiNbO3 single crystals including doped LiNbO3 and proton-changed LiNbO3 have been studied in reactive ion etching (RIE) and inductively coupled plasma (ICP) etching tools, using different recipes of gas mixtures. The effects of parameters including working pressure, RIE power, and ICP power are investigated and analyzed by measurement of etching depth, selectivity, uniformity, etched surface state, and sidewall profile by means of focused ion beam etching, energy-dispersive x-ray analysis, secondary ion mass spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and surface profilometry. The effects of a sample carrier wafer coating have also been investigated. Optimized processes with high etching rates, good mask selectivity, and a near-vertical profile have been achieved. Ridge waveguides on proton-exchanged LiNbO3 have been fabricated and optically measured.

This is a scientific journal article published in the Journal of Applied Physics (J. Appl. Phys.) on February 1, 2008, authored by Z. Ren, P. J. Heard, J. M. Marshall, P. A. Thomas, and S. Yu. The article, titled "Etching characteristics of LiNbO3 in reactive ion etching and inductively coupled plasma," DOI: https://doi.org/10.1063/1.2838180, investigates the etching characteristics of congruent LiNbO3 single crystals, including doped LiNbO3 and proton-exchanged LiNbO3, using reactive ion etching (RIE) and inductively coupled plasma (ICP) etching tools with different gas mixture recipes.

The study examined the effects of key process parameters including working pressure, RIE power, and ICP power, which were analyzed through measurements of etching depth, selectivity, uniformity, etched surface state, and sidewall profile. Characterization techniques employed included focused ion beam etching, energy-dispersive x-ray analysis, secondary ion mass spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and surface profilometry. The effects of a sample carrier wafer coating were also investigated.

Key results: Optimized processes with high etching rates, good mask selectivity, and near-vertical profiles were achieved. Ridge waveguides on proton-exchanged LiNbO3 were successfully fabricated and optically measured, demonstrating practical application of the optimized etching processes.
