URL: https://lasers4.eu/event/laserlab-europe-talk-femtosecond-laser-fabricated-glass-photonic-integrated-circuits-for-stuctured-illumination-microscopy-16-september-2026

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page announces a Laserlab-Europe Talk webinar scheduled for Wednesday, 16 September 2026, from 16:00 to 17:00 CEST (held online). The talk is titled "Femtosecond laser fabricated glass photonic integrated circuits for structured illumination microscopy" and will be presented by Francesca Bragheri from The Institute for Photonics and Nanotechnologies (IFN), National Research Council (CNR), Italy.

The presentation focuses on using femtosecond laser micromachining (FLM) as an enabling technology to fabricate three-dimensional integrated photonic circuits in glass for structured illumination microscopy (SIM). SIM is a powerful imaging technique that achieves resolution enhancement beyond the diffraction limit while maintaining low phototoxicity and compatibility with conventional fluorescence microscopy. Traditional SIM implementations rely on complex, bulky optical systems that limit robustness and adoption.

Key technical points covered in the talk include:
- FLM induces localized refractive index modifications inside transparent materials, enabling direct writing of buried optical waveguides, directional couplers, and interferometric structures with true 3D design freedom and micrometric precision.
- When combined with selective chemical etching (FLICE), the technology enables fabrication of reflective micro-optical elements (flat and curved mirrors), which are metal-coated to guide beams and generate structured illumination patterns.
- Thermal phase shifters integrated onto the chip surface provide fast, dynamic control of relative phase between interfering beams without mechanical movement, enabling pattern translation for SIM image reconstruction.
- Device architectures range from compact two-output interferometers to sophisticated multi-beam photonic circuits generating both 2D and 3D interference patterns.
- The resulting glass chips can be directly interfaced with conventional widefield microscopes, transforming them into compact, reconfigurable SIM platforms.

Registration is available via the Laserlab-Europe website. The event is categorized under Webinars on the Lasers4EU platform. Related upcoming events include a "360 Carla Training: Quantum Materials — from ARPES to trARPES" (16 September 2026) and a "Lasers4EU Webinar: The use and impact of artificial intelligence in research and innovation" (24 September 2026).

--- SOURCE 2: Fabrication of high-Q lithium niobate microresonators using femtosecond laser micromachining ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published in Scientific Reports on January 28, 2015 (PMCID: PMC4308694, PMID: 25627294, DOI: 10.1038/srep08072), reports on the fabrication of high-quality (high-Q) lithium niobate (LN) whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) microresonators using a combination of femtosecond laser direct writing and focused ion beam (FIB) milling.

METHODOLOGY:
- LN thin film (700 nm) and silica layer (2 μm) on an LN substrate were used
- A cylindrical post (~59 μm diameter, ~15 μm height) was first created by femtosecond laser micromachining (Ti:sapphire laser, ~800 nm center wavelength, ~40 fs pulse width, 1 kHz repetition rate, 0.35 mW for LN ablation, 1 mW for silica)
- FIB milling was performed twice (coarse milling with 30-keV ion beam at 4 nA, then fine milling at 1 nA) to smooth the periphery, reducing the diameter to 55 μm
- The silica layer was selectively etched using 5% HF solution for 8 minutes to form a freestanding microdisk on a silica pedestal
- Thermal annealing at 500°C for 2 hours in air further smoothed the rim of the LN disk
- Q factors were measured using an evanescent fiber taper coupling method

RESULTS:
- The 82 μm diameter LN resonator achieved a Q factor of ~2.5 × 10⁵ around 1550 nm wavelength
- A 55 μm resonator showed Q factor improvement from 5.2 × 10⁴ (before annealing) to 1.6 × 10⁵ (after annealing)
- Q factor increases with increasing diameter due to reduced radiation loss at the curved surface
- Microresonators below 10 μm diameter can potentially be fabricated using this technique
- The top and bottom surfaces of the LN thin film naturally have ultra-high smoothness with surface roughness as low as 0.35 nm

CONCLUSION:
The technique combines the flexibility and material insensitivity of femtosecond laser micromachining with the precision of FIB milling, enabling high-efficiency, high-precision nanofabrication of high-Q crystalline microresonators. The authors have previously used similar techniques to fabricate microresonators in fused silica, active Nd:glass, and CaF₂ crystals, and envisage extending this approach to various dielectric materials.

The work was supported by the National Basic Research Program of China (No. 2014CB921300), NSFC grants, and Fundamental Research Funds for Central Universities. Authors include Jintian Lin, Yingxin Xu, Zhiwei Fang, Min Wang, Jiangxin Song, Nengwen Wang, Lingling Qiao, Wei Fang, and Ya Cheng.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The micrometer-scale (diameter ~82 μm) LN resonator possesses a Q factor of ~2.5 × 10⁵ around 1550 nm wavelength. The combination of femtosecond laser direct writing with FIB enables high-efficiency, high-precision nanofabrication of high-Q crystalline microresonators."

--- SOURCE 6: Efficient Second-Harmonic Generation in Adapted-Width Waveguides Based on Periodically Poled Thin-Film Lithium Niobate ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2072-666X/15/9/1145

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents an open-access research article published in the MDPI journal *Micromachines* (Volume 15, Issue 9, 2024, article 1145, DOI: 10.3390/mi15091145) titled "Efficient Second-Harmonic Generation in Adapted-Width Waveguides Based on Periodically Poled Thin-Film Lithium Niobate." The article was submitted on 13 August 2024, revised 6 September 2024, accepted 11 September 2024, and published 12 September 2024. It belongs to the Special Issue "Photonic and Optoelectronic Devices and Systems, Second Edition."

**Authors:** Junjie He, Lian Liu (equal first authors), Mianjie Lin, Houhong Chen, and Fei Ma (corresponding author, associate professor at the School of Physics, Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou, China). Fei Ma holds a PhD in Quantum Information Physics from the University of Science and Technology of China (2018) and did postdoctoral work at City University of Hong Kong (2019-2020), focusing on efficient optical frequency conversion based on lithium niobate photonic devices.

**Background/Problem:** Periodically poled thin-film lithium niobate (PPTFLN) waveguides are important for quantum information and photonic signal processing. While nanophotonic TFLN waveguides achieve normalized conversion efficiency (NCE) more than 20 times higher than bulk LN waveguides, their power conversion efficiency is limited by inherent nanoscale thickness inhomogeneity of TFLN (for a 600 nm thick LN layer, a deviation of ±15 nm occurs during manufacturing). This thickness inhomogeneity causes phase errors that limit coherent interaction length to only a few millimeters. Prior work by Chen et al. used adapted poling design to achieve ~10^4 %W⁻¹ SHG efficiency, but this requires complex electrode fabrication for many irregular poling periods and only accommodates one waveguide at a time.

**Proposed Solution:** The authors theoretically propose an "adapted waveguide width design" based on dispersion engineering. Instead of adjusting the poling period, they locally adjust the waveguide width at positions of different thicknesses to eliminate phase errors, using standard periodic poling with a single period (Λ = 4.20 μm for etched waveguides).

**Key Results:**
- **Etched waveguide:** Achieves peak SHG power conversion efficiency of 2.1 × 10^4 %W⁻¹ (21,780%W⁻¹ in simulation), comparable to adapted poling design performance. Waveguide length is 21 mm, composed of 420 sections (50 μm each), with width precision at 10 nm scale. Width varies from 1.54 μm to 1.66 μm (320 nm range for 30 nm thickness change). Simulated transmission is 95% for FF wave; actual transmission is higher since adjacent-section width differences are below 20 nm.
- **Loaded (polymer) waveguide:** Using polymer ARP6200 (500 nm thick) on TFLN, achieves power conversion efficiency of 6936%W⁻¹, surpassing reported loaded waveguides based on PPTFLN. Uses poling period Λ = 5.05 μm.
- Uniform waveguide width design (for comparison) only achieves 3724%W⁻¹ with broadened central peaks and side lobes.

**Advantages of the approach:** (1) Uses standard single-period periodic poling, reducing electrode fabrication complexity; (2) allows placement of multiple waveguides without individual poling designs; (3) uses existing micro-nano fabrication technology; (4) achieves ultrahigh SHG efficiency surpassing other related work.

**Methodology:** The design uses TE modes in X-cut TFLN to exploit the largest nonlinear coefficient d₃₃ = 27.4 pm/V. The FF wave is at 1600 nm, SH wave at 800 nm. The poling period equation is Λ = λ_ω/2(n_2ω − n_ω), and power conversion efficiency is η_SHG = η_nor·L². Waveguide structural parameters include etched depth h = 300 nm, sidewall angle θ = 75°, and 2 μm silicon dioxide layer.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In this paper, we theoretically present a novel approach to solve this problem. Based on dispersion engineering, we aim at adjusting the waveguide structure, making local waveguide width adjustment at positions of different thicknesses, thus eliminating the phase errors."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Watt-level second harmonic generation in periodically poled thin-film lithium tantalate ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2512.07968v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Scientific Paper Summary: Watt-level second harmonic generation in periodically poled thin-film lithium tantalate

### Overview
This arXiv preprint (2512.07968) reports the first demonstration of watt-level continuous-wave (CW) second-harmonic generation (SHG) in periodically poled thin-film lithium tantalate (PPLT) photonic integrated waveguides. The work addresses a key limitation of lithium niobate (LiNbO3) — its low optical damage threshold — by leveraging lithium tantalate's (LiTaO3) higher optical damage threshold to achieve high-power operation.

### Key Results
- Demonstrated 7 mm-long PPLT waveguides achieving SH output exceeding 1 W on-chip (specifically 1.065 W), with directly measured off-chip SH power above 0.5 W at 775 nm wavelength
- Pumped with 4.5 W of off-chip pump power at 1550 nm
- The output was limited only by experimental setup constraints (powermeter limit of 0.5 W and EDFA output limit)
- Measured SHG efficiency of 107 %W⁻¹cm⁻² — lower than typical PPLN values but sufficient for watt-level output due to higher damage threshold
- No observable sample damage or performance degradation at watt-level operation

### Significance
- First PPLT photonic integrated circuit demonstration achieving watt-level output
- Power output comparable to state-of-the-art PPLN ridge waveguides but achieved in a shorter (7 mm) waveguide, preserving bandwidth
- Extends the LiTaO3 integrated photonic platform toward on-chip optical parametric oscillators, quadrature-squeezed light sources, visible lasers, and frequency metrology applications

### Methodology Highlights
1. **Periodic Poling**: Optimized electrode geometry (elliptical tips, 25 µm-long, 1:15 axis ratio, 40% duty cycle) and high-voltage pulse sequences (20-30 pulses with 0.5 ms rise/flat/fall segments at 1 kV peak) to achieve reproducible domain inversion despite LiTaO3's coercive field being nearly 4× higher than MgO-doped LiNbO3
2. **Fabrication**: Used X-cut LiTaO3 chip (576 nm film, 4.7 µm SiO2 insulation), E-beam lithography, argon ion beam etching, and KOH wet etching for smooth sidewalls
3. **Characterization**: Two-photon SH microscopy for domain inspection, SEM imaging for non-destructive domain visualization, and calibrated high-power measurements with energy conservation fitting to avoid efficiency overestimation

### Discussion Points
- The reduced SHG efficiency compared to PPLN (which can exceed 2000 %W⁻¹cm⁻²) is attributed to lower effective nonlinearity in thin films, possible thickness non-uniformity, and crystal quality issues
- The authors note that at high pump powers, even low-efficiency waveguides can reach the depletion regime over short lengths, meaning efficiency improvements primarily reduce required pump power
- Future work: MgO-doped or stoichiometric LiTaO3 substrates would lower poling voltages and simplify fabrication

### Funding & Attribution
- Funded by Swiss National Science Foundation (grant 216493, HEROIC), EU Horizon Europe EIC programme (grant 101187515, ELLIPTIC), and Swiss SERI
- Samples fabricated at EPFL Center of MicroNanoTechnology (CMi) and Institute of Physics cleanroom
- Corresponding supervision by T.J. Kippenberg
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Here, we overcome this challenge and demonstrate 7 mm-long periodically poled thin-film lithium tantalate (PPLT) waveguides that achieve high SH output in the CW regime, with generated power exceeding 1 W and off-chip output above 0.5 W at 775 nm under 4.5 W pump power – limited only by our experimental setup."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Broadband Second Harmonic Generation in a z-Cut Lithium Niobate on Insulator Waveguide Based on Type-I Modal Phase Matching ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2304-6732/10/1/80

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a scientific research article published in Photonics (MDPI) in January 2023, titled "Broadband Second Harmonic Generation in a z-Cut Lithium Niobate on Insulator Waveguide Based on Type-I Modal Phase Matching" (DOI: 10.3390/photonics10010080). The authors are Changwen Wang, Haozong Zhong, Minghao Ning, Bin Fang, Lin Li, and Ya Cheng, affiliated with East China Normal University, China Jiliang University, Shanxi University, and the Shanghai Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics (CAS).

The research numerically investigates second harmonic generation (SHG) in a z-cut lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) waveguide using type-I modal phase matching (MPM) between two fundamental modes (TE00 of the fundamental wave and TM00 of the second harmonic wave). Key findings include:
- A mode overlap factor close to unity (ζ = 0.9890) was achieved
- Normalized SHG efficiency up to 72.1% W⁻¹cm⁻² at the telecommunication band (1.55 μm)
- Large spectral tunability of 2.5 nm/K via temperature tuning
- Broad bandwidth of ~50 nm for strip waveguide and ~100 nm for ridge waveguide (5 mm-long devices)
- Effective mode area Aeff = 3.05 μm² for strip waveguide

The design uses a few-micron-thick LNOI waveguide (h = 2 μm, w = 2.71 μm for strip; h1 = 1.35 μm, h2 = 0.3 μm, w = 2 μm, θ = 75° for ridge) fabricated via electron beam lithography and inductively coupled plasma etching. Compared to traditional approaches (birefringent phase matching, quasi-phase matching, and conventional modal phase matching), this method achieves phase matching between two fundamental modes, dramatically improving mode overlap and conversion efficiency. The approach is applicable to other guided structures like micro-rings and micro-disks, offering advantages over nano-LNOI in terms of power handling, coupling efficiency, and simplified fabrication.
</summary>

"We numerically investigate a second harmonic generation (SHG) in a z-cut lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) waveguide based on type-I mode phase matching (MPM) between two fundamental modes. A mode overlap factor that is close to unity is achieved and the normalized SHG efficiency reaches up to 72.1% W−1cm−2 at the telecommunication band, together with a large spectral tunability of 2.5 nm/K."

3. Mitigation Strategies: (a) Use AC-coupled drive with low-frequency dither and feedback control (bias controller); (b) Select TFLN devices with passivation layers (SiO₂ or SiN); (c) Operate at reduced DC field strength with lower Vπ (<2.5 V); (d) Pre-age the modulator at 85°C for 100 hours.

Practical Workflow: (1) Verify temperature stability; (2) Measure drift with static DC bias (if >10% Vπ over 10 minutes, inspect hermeticity); (3) Apply bipolar square wave at 1 kHz (if drift reduces, implement active bias feedback); (4) Replace modulator with known-good TFLN device to isolate component issues.

Key limitation: plasma density and ion energy are coupled (not independently controllable) in single-RF systems. Used for pattern transfer, dielectric/metal etching, and MEMS fabrication.
- **ICP-RIE:** Solves RIE's coupling limitation with a dual RF system — an ICP coil (300–3000 W) generates high-density plasma (10^11–10^12 cm^-3, 10–100× higher than CCP-RIE) while a separate RF bias (0–600 W) independently controls ion energy (0–300 eV). Etch rate 500–5000+ nm/min, pressure 1–50 mTorr, substrate temperature -20 to 200 °C. Enables the Bosch process (DRIE) for aspect ratios exceeding 50:1.

**Bosch Process (DRIE):** Patented by Robert Bosch GmbH (1994), alternates between SF₆ etch steps (3–10 µm/min isotropic Si etching) and C₄F₈ passivation steps (depositing fluorocarbon polymer), producing near-vertical sidewalls with aspect ratios >50:1, though with characteristic scalloping (50–200 nm roughness per cycle).

**Source Power vs. Ion Density (ICP-RIE):** Plasma density scales approximately linearly with source power (ion flux increases, but ion energy barely changes since it's set by bias). Two non-idealities: E-to-H mode transition (abrupt density jump of 1–2 orders of magnitude near low power threshold) and saturation at high power (due to wall losses and neutral gas depletion). Rule of thumb: use source power for density/etch rate, bias power for anisotropy/selectivity/damage.

**Comparison Matrix (quantitative):**
| Feature | PE | RIE | ICP-RIE |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plasma Density | 10^9–10^10 cm^-3 | 10^10–10^11 cm^-3 | 10^11–10^12 cm^-3 |
| Ion Energy | <20 eV | 50–500 eV | 0–300 eV (independent) |
| Etch Rate (Si) | 100–300 nm/min | 200–500 nm/min | 500–5000+ nm/min |
| Pressure | 300–1000 mTorr | 10–200 mTorr | 1–50 mTorr |
| Profile | Isotropic | Anisotropic (80–90°) | Highly Anisotropic (88–90°) |
| Selectivity | Very High (>50:1) | Moderate (10–30:1) | High (20–100:1, tunable) |
| Max Aspect Ratio | N/A | 5–10:1 | 50:1+ (Bosch) |
| Equipment Cost | $50K–$150K | $100K–$300K | $200K–$600K+ |

**Gas Chemistries:** Silicon (SF₆, CF₄/O₂, Cl₂/HBr); SiO₂ (CHF₃, C₄F₈, CF₄/CHF₃); Si₃N₄ (CHF₃/O₂, CF₄/H₂); Al (Cl₂/BCl₃); GaAs/InP (Cl₂/Ar, SiCl₄); Photoresist/organics (O₂, O₂/Ar).

**Common Etch Defects and Solutions:**
- **Undercut:** lateral etching beneath mask — reduce pressure, add passivation gas, increase RF bias
- **Bowing:** convex sidewall bulging — optimize mask profile, reduce pressure, use pulsed bias
- **ARDE (Aspect Ratio Dependent Etching):** narrow trenches etch slower — increase ICP power, reduce pressure, use time-multiplexed recipes
- **Micro-masking/Grass:** needle-like residues — chamber conditioning, add O₂, optimize Bosch ratio
- **Notching (Footing):** lateral etching at silicon/insulator interface — use pulsed bias, reduce bias near endpoint

**Endpoint Detection Methods:** OES (Optical Emission Spectroscopy — most widely used, non-invasive, requires >1–5% exposed wafer area); Laser Interferometry (for transparent films like SiO₂/Si₃N₄); Mass Spectrometry/RGA (high sensitivity, slower, R&D-oriented).

**Selection Guidelines:**
- **Choose PE** for isotropic etching, maximum selectivity, minimal damage, stripping/descum, constrained budgets
- **Choose RIE** for anisotropic pattern transfer with moderate aspect ratios (<10:1), standard semiconductor processing, cost-effective solutions
- **Choose ICP-RIE** for high-aspect-ratio features (>10:1 to 50:1+), independent etch rate/ion energy control, deep Si etching (DRIE/Bosch), hard-to-etch materials (GaN, SiC, diamond, sapphire), advanced R&D

**Future Trends:** Atomic Layer Etching (ALE), Pulsed Plasma Etching, Machine Learning Process Control, new material challenges (2D materials, high-entropy alloys, ferroelectric HfO₂), and 3D integration (TSV, hybrid bonding, chiplet packaging).

The article also details NineScrolls' RIE Etcher Series and ICP-RIE systems (ICP source up to 3000 W, RF bias up to 600 W, plasma density to 10^12 cm^-3, temperature control -20 to 200 °C, up to 8 gas lines, Bosch process ready, process design kits for Si DRIE, SiO₂, GaN/SiC, III-V, and diamond). Includes 13 academic references (Lieberman & Lichtenberg, Coburn & Winters, Hopwood, Laermer & Schilp Bosch patent, etc.).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"PE relies on chemical radicals for isotropic etching at 100–300 nm/min; RIE adds ion bombardment for anisotropic profiles at 200–500 nm/min; ICP-RIE provides independent control of plasma density (10^11–10^12 cm−3) and ion energy, achieving etch rates above 1 µm/min with excellent profile control."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: [PDF] Investigation of focused ion beam induced damage in single crystal ... ---
URL: https://strathprints.strath.ac.uk/53356/1/Tong_Luo_ASS_2015_Investigation_of_focused_ion_beam_induced_damage_in_single.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper investigates focused ion beam (FIB) induced damage in single crystal diamond tools used for ultra-precision machining. The research was conducted by Zhen Tong (Harbin Institute of Technology) and Xichun Luo (University of Strathclyde, UK) and combines transmission electron microscope (TEM) measurements with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.

Methodology:
- A FEI Nova 200 nanolab dual beam FIB system with Ga ion source was used to irradiate a diamond tool's (1 0 0) rake face at three acceleration voltages: 8 kV, 16 kV, and 30 kV
- Ion fluences ranged from 7.54 × 10^20 to 9.71 × 10^20 ions/cm² depending on voltage
- Cross-sectional TEM samples were prepared using standard lift-out technique with Pt protection layers
- EFTEM, CBED (convergent beam electron diffraction), and elemental mapping were used to characterize damage layers
- Large-scale multi-particle collision MD simulations (1,217,161 atoms, using Tersoff-ZBL potentials in LAMMPS) emulated the ion-solid interactions

Key Results:
- FIB-induced damage layer thicknesses on diamond tool surfaces increased from 11.5 nm (8 kV) to 19.4 nm (16 kV) to 27.6 nm (30 kV) — increasing with beam energy
- The damage layers are amorphous carbon (a-C), consisting of a mixture of sp2 and sp3 hybridization, and accommodate significant implanted gallium
- MD simulations showed residual damage layers of 14.5 nm (8 keV) and 19.6 nm (16 keV), closely matching experimental results
- Maximum gallium implantation depths were 10.5 nm (8 keV) and 12.8 nm (16 keV), with gallium concentrated at the a-C/diamond interface (matching dark patches observed in EFTEM images)
- Higher beam voltages produced higher local thermal spikes (1454.6 K peak for 16 keV vs lower for 8 keV) and longer thermal spike lifetimes
- Number of atomic defects accumulates linearly up to an ion fluence of 2.0 × 10^14 ions/cm², then approaches a stable equilibrium value due to competition between damage formation and sputtering
- Residual defects per ion collision: 271 (8 keV) and 416 (16 keV), with recrystallization completing within 0.8 ps
- Higher beam voltages increase the amorphization level (confirmed by CBED showing weaker diamond signals)

Conclusions & Recommendations:
- FIB irradiation creates impulse-dependent damage layers in diamond tools
- The non-diamond phase of the residual damage layer will wear first during nanometric cutting, contributing to tool wear initiation (alongside compressive stress at tool tip sides)
- Low-energy FIB polishing is recommended when shaping diamond tool tips via FIB
- The 27.6 nm maximum damage layer is only ~1 part in 10^4 of a micro cutting tool's functional dimension, so ion-induced damage may be negligible for micro-scale applications but becomes critical for nanoscale multi-tip tools
- The study was funded by EPSRC (EP/K018345/1)
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The results indicate that during the FIB processing cutting tools made of natural single crystal diamond, the energetic Ga+ collision will create an impulse-dependent damage layer at the irradiated surface. For the tested beam voltages in a typical FIB system (from 8 kV to 30 kV), the thicknesses of the damaged layers formed on a diamond tool surface increased from 11.5 nm to 27.6 nm."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Avoiding Common Types of Lamella Defects Caused by the Focused Ion Beam ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_pKw8SMnFiM

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an educational video by Covalent (posted 25 April 2022, 381 views) featuring Ryan Dudschus, Covalent's resident expert on sample preparation for S/TEM analysis. The video summarizes common defects in S/TEM lamella caused by the focused ion beam (FIB) and strategies to avoid them.

Key content covered:

1. **Amorphous Layer Damage (Gallium Ion Damage)**: When using a 30 kV gallium ion beam, the FIB creates an amorphous damaged layer approximately 20 nanometers thick on the lamella surface. This damage causes blurry, low-quality TEM images due to electron scattering from embedded gallium islands and interstitial atoms. Critical insight: for an 80 nm lamella thinned with a 30 kV beam on both sides, up to 60 nm (30 nm per side) can be damaged, leaving only 20 nm of good material to image.

2. **Mitigation Strategy - Lower Beam Energies (Polishing)**: Dropping the FIB energy to 5 kV (polishing) reduces the damaged layer to about 6 nm thick, significantly improving image resolution and allowing atoms to be discerned. Dropping further to 2 kV reduces damage to roughly 3 nm thick. The damaged layer correlates nearly 1:1 with the FIB energy used. Some modern FIBs can operate at a few hundred volts for even better image quality.

3. **Redeposition**: The FIB beam has tails/sides that mill surrounding material in addition to the target window. This milled material can reattach to the lamella face, appearing as bubble-like deposits that cause grayscale and thickness variations in the TEM image, degrading resolution. Avoiding redeposition requires careful attention to milling materials, beam shape, tilt, and box placement—described as taking on the form of an art form.

The video thanks Mark (of Thermo Fisher) for providing the referenced paper by Gertz and Regnold (as transcribed) that demonstrates how gallium islands and interstitial atoms affect TEM imaging.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In 1a you're looking at amorphous layer damage which is this fuzzy layer that's caused by 30 kv gallium ion beam and you can see that this thickness is about 20-ish nanometers thick."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: High-Quality Etching of Lithium Niobate Ridge Waveguides ---
URL: https://www.mi-net.co.uk/application-note/high-quality-etching-of-lithium-niobate-ridge-waveguides

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an application note from Mi-Net Technology (a UK-based supplier of semiconductor materials, testing equipment, and thin-film processing tools) describing an optimized plasma etching process for producing high-quality lithium niobate (LiNbO₃ or LN) ridge waveguides.

**Context:** Lithium niobate is a versatile nonlinear optical crystal valued for its strong electro-optic coefficients, piezoelectric properties, broad transparency range, and wide intrinsic bandwidth. When implemented as lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI), it enables high-index-contrast optical waveguides and densely integrated photonic circuits (PICs), supporting next-generation miniature radio-frequency modulators and advanced photonic devices.

**The Challenge:** LiNbO₃'s hardness makes it difficult to etch. Conventional dry etching can produce rough surfaces and sidewall redeposition, which increase optical losses and degrade device performance.

**The Solution:** The application note demonstrates an optimized etching process using sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆) mixed with argon (Ar) as the plasma gas, performed on a SENTECH Instruments SI500 ICP plasma etcher. Key elements of the process include:
- Use of SF₆/Ar plasma mixtures, which have proven effective for producing smooth ridges
- A chromium (Cr) mask for its resistance to high bias power, preserving the etch profile and ensuring high selectivity
- Relatively high bias power required to physically remove low-volatility reaction by-products such as LiF and NbFₓ (without sufficient energy, micro-masking can cause surface roughness)

**Key Benefits:**
- Smooth LiNbO₃ ridge waveguides with minimal optical loss
- No sidewall redeposition
- High etch selectivity and pattern fidelity using Cr masks
- Compatible with next-generation PICs and compact RF modulators

The note is available as a PDF by request via the site or by emailing sales@mi-net.co.uk. The page also includes related application notes on viscoelastic analysis of rubber with nanoindentation DMA (March 10, 2026), in situ wear measurement at high temperature (January 29, 2026), and mechanical & tribological properties of carbon fibre composite (July 23, 2025).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆), used alone or mixed with argon (Ar), is a common plasma etching gas for LiNbO₃. SF₆/Ar mixtures have proven effective for producing smooth ridges. However, due to the low volatility of reaction by-products such as LiF and NbFₓ, relatively high bias power is required to physically remove these residues. Without sufficient energy, micro-masking can occur, resulting in surface roughness."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Optimization of waveguide fabrication processes in lithium ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11194688

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific paper published in PMC (PubMed Central) under the NIST Author Manuscripts collection, titled "Optimization of waveguide fabrication processes in lithium-niobate-on-insulator platform" by CH S S Pavan Kumar, Nikolai N Klimov, and Paulina S Kuo (NIST).

**Purpose/Context:** The paper addresses the fabrication challenges of lithium-niobate-on-insulator (LNOI) waveguides (WGs), which are critical for integrated photonic devices in applications such as spectroscopy, remote sensing, and quantum communications. Lithium niobate (LN) is hard, dense, and chemically inert, making etching difficult, with issues including anisotropic etch behavior and material redeposition during reactive-ion plasma etching.

**Key Methodology (Section II - Fabrication):**
- 4-inch LNOI wafer (700 nm x-cut film, 2 μm SiO2 insulation, 525 μm Si substrate from NANOLN) diced into 10×10 mm² chips
- Cleaned with piranha solution (H2SO4:H2O2 = 3:1) then standard RCA process
- Three mask types tested: soft e-beam resist mask, metallic Cr mask (50 nm, e-beam deposition), and dielectric SiO2 hard mask (500 nm PECVD + 10 nm Cr)
- Etch structures: 800 nm wide, 300 μm long WGs defined with ZEP520A positive-tone e-beam resist
- LN etching performed in Oxford PlasmaLab 100 ICP RIE tool with Ar gas; ICP power 1500 W, pressure 5 mTorr, Ar flow 20 sccm, temperature 5°C
- Etch performed in 1-minute segments with 5-minute cooldown periods to prevent thermal damage
- Redeposition removal via RCA-1a solution (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O = 2:2:1) heated to 85°C

**Key Results (Section III):**

*RF Power Optimization (III.A):* RF power varied from 50 W to 500 W; etch rate ranged from 50 nm/min (50 W) to 107 nm/min (500 W). At low RF power (~50 W), sidewalls fully enveloped by redeposit; at 300 W, redeposit completely eliminated from sidewalls. However, above 300 W, line-edge roughness transferred to the WG causing striations, and WG damage (trenches/pits) occurred. Optimal RF power range determined as 100-200 W.

*Redeposit Cleaning (III.B):* RCA-1a solution superior to Piranha and RCA-1b. Optimized cleaning: 15 minutes each at 0° and 90° boat orientations (30 min total). Prolonged cleaning (beyond 30 min) caused chipping and peeling of WGs. Cleaning for 24 hours changed WG geometry (sidewall angles became asymmetric, film thickness reduced from 700 nm to ~630 nm). Properly cleaned samples had equal sidewall angles of ~70°.

*Soft vs. Hard Mask (III.C):* Soft (resist) mask produced striated sidewall defects that persisted regardless of RF power tuning; Cr hard mask produced markedly improved sidewall profiles.

*Hard Mask Comparison (III.D):* Cr hard mask produced granular features on sidewalls (due to Cr polycrystalline grain size of ~55 nm), while SiO2 mask produced striations and "trenching" at the base of sidewalls (attributed to charge buildup on insulating materials deflecting ions). Cr hard mask was selected for final fabrication.

*Optical Characterization (III.E):* Rib LNOI WGs fabricated with Cr mask using optimized parameters (Table II: RF 150 W, ICP 1500 W, 5 mTorr, 20 sccm Ar, 5°C, 30 min cleaning). WG dimensions: top width 600 nm, sidewall angle 70°, rib height 350 nm over 350 nm slab, single-mode at 1550 nm. Eight identical 4.5 mm straight WGs measured with lensed fibers (2.5 μm mode field diameter), no anti-reflection coatings. Transmission ranged from 0.075 (-11.2 dB) to 0.107 (-9.7 dB); average transmission 8.9 ± 1.3%, corresponding to -10.5 ± 0.6 dB total insertion loss (propagation + coupling). Upper-bound propagation loss estimated at ~2 dB/cm (assuming 4.8 dB/facet coupling loss). These values are comparable to literature.

**Key Conclusions:** A comprehensive, reproducible fabrication recipe for low-loss LNOI WGs was developed at the NIST NanoFab (a shared-use facility where the ICP RIE tool is also used for other materials including Al, Cr, Cr2O3, Mo, Ta, and Ti). The approach emphasizes RF power optimization to control sidewall redeposition, hard mask selection (Cr preferred over SiO2 and soft masks), and optimized wet cleaning protocol. The findings provide an accessible resource for advancing LNOI technology.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Using the recipe established, we realized optical WGs with total (propagation and coupling) loss value of -10.5 dB, comparable to established values found in the literature."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Analysis of Waveguides on Lithium Niobate Thin Films ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/8/5/191

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article titled "Analysis of Waveguides on Lithium Niobate Thin Films" published in the journal *Crystals* (2018, Volume 8, Issue 5, Article 191, DOI: 10.3390/cryst8050191) by Yiwen Wang, Zhihua Chen, and Hui Hu from the School of Physics, State Key Laboratory of Crystal Materials, Shandong University, Jinan, China. The paper was received 5 April 2018, revised 24 April 2018, accepted 24 April 2018, and published 27 April 2018.

**Purpose:** The study analyzes and compares three types of waveguides fabricated on single-crystal lithium niobate (LN) thin films — ridge waveguides (dry-etched), proton-exchange (PE) waveguides, and strip-loaded waveguides — using a full-vectorial finite difference method. The research focuses on single-mode conditions, optical power distribution, and bending loss at the telecommunication wavelength of 1.55 µm.

**Key Methodology:**
- Simulations used full-vectorial finite difference method with PML boundary conditions.
- LNOI films were x-cut with birefringence considered (ordinary n=2.211, extraordinary n=2.138 at 1550 nm).
- PE region refractive indices were 2.161 (ordinary) and 2.218 (extraordinary).
- Loading strip materials simulated: SiO2 (n=1.46), SiN (n=1.9), TiO2 (n=2.3), and Si (n=3.48).
- LN thickness was set at 0.5 µm; waveguide widths were 1 µm for single-mode operation.

**Key Results:**
1. **Single-mode conditions:** First-order TE and TM modes appeared at LN thicknesses of 0.6 µm and 0.7 µm, respectively. For ridge waveguides, single-mode limits were 1.1 µm (q-TE) and 1.06 µm (q-TM). PE waveguides only supported q-TE mode (since PE increases only extraordinary refractive index). For both PE and strip-loaded waveguides, width must decrease as thickness increases to maintain single-mode operation.

2. **Optical power distribution:** In the LN ridge waveguide, optical power in the LN layer was 85.6% for q-TE and 82.5% for q-TM. PE waveguides showed negligible power change with increasing PE thickness. For strip-loaded waveguides, q-TE power decreased slightly with strip thickness (notably for Si), while q-TM power initially increased then decreased, with maximum values at strip thicknesses of ~0.12 µm (SiO2), 0.07 µm (SiN), 0.07 µm (TiO2), and 0.07 µm (Si).

3. **Bending loss:** Bending loss decreased with increasing bending radius. LN ridge waveguides achieved low bending loss (10⁻⁵ dB/cm) at minimal radii of 15 µm (q-TE) and 20 µm (q-TM). PE waveguides showed bending loss decreasing with PE depth (34 dB/cm at D=0.2 µm vs. 10⁻¹¹ dB/cm at D=0.5 µm, both at 1 mm radius). For q-TM strip-loaded waveguides, an additional leakage loss mechanism exists: when the waveguide neff is smaller than that of nearby TE planar waveguides, the Ez field component excites the TE mode in adjacent planar waveguides, causing loss (minimum 57 dB/cm for 0.05 µm SiN strip). This leakage can be avoided by increasing strip thickness so neff exceeds that of nearby planar waveguides.

**Conclusions:** The study provides guidance for designing and fabricating high-density integrated optical components on LN thin films, including understanding mode confinement, power distribution trends, and minimizing bending/leakage losses. Work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (grants 61575111 and 11475105). Authors declared no conflict of interest.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Waveguides formed by etching, proton-exchange (PE), and strip-loaded on single-crystal lithium niobate (LN) thin film were designed and simulated by a full-vectorial finite difference method."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: Plasma Etching Lithium Niobate on an Optoelectronic Chip ---
URL: https://spectrum.ieee.org/lithium-niobate-a-new-and-viable-platform-for-optoelectronics

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IEEE Spectrum news article (published 16 January 2018, updated same day) by Alexander Hellemans reports on a breakthrough by Harvard University researchers in plasma etching lithium niobate (LiNbO3) for optoelectronic chips. Lithium niobate is a hard, chemically inert crystalline material with exceptional optical properties used in electro-optics, acousto-optics, and nonlinear optics, found in devices like cellphones, optical modulators, and frequency converters. Unlike silicon, lithium niobate is not amenable to chemical etching, and previous techniques (ion diffusion, proton exchange) produced too-low optical-index contrast for effective waveguides. Hybrid silicon-lithium niobate approaches were also impractical due to insufficient light coupling. The Harvard team, led by Marko Lončar, applied plasma reactive ion etching—bombarding the chip surface with argon ions to remove material exposed by an electron-beam lithography mask—to create micro-ring and micro-racetrack resonators (~1 micrometer wide, 80 µm curvature radius). Results showed optical power losses of only 50% over 1 meter, compared to 99% loss in previous lithium niobate devices, due to improved optical confinement. Independent expert Marco Bazzan (University of Padova) called the result remarkable, noting it could elevate lithium niobate resonators above standard silicon photonics and holds importance for integrated quantum photonics. Lončar's team plans next to integrate niobate into silicon photonic processing, though this is challenging as niobium is not favored in the silicon industry; the team may need dedicated fabrication facilities or to couple separately-made niobium and silicon chips. Bazzan noted the thin-film substrates are commercially available, meaning the technological steps are ready for standardization.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Over the years, we have dealt with many materials that have nice properties but that are difficult to work with," says Marko Lončar, who led the research. "Diamond is actually easier to etch than niobate, but it doesn't exist as thin films."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: Photorefraction Management in Lithium Niobate Waveguides: High-Temperature vs. Cryogenic Solutions ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2601.15817v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (arXiv preprint) investigates photorefraction management in lithium niobate (LiNbO3, LN) waveguides, comparing high-temperature and cryogenic operation strategies. Photorefraction—an optically induced change in refractive index and absorption caused by trapped charge carriers forming internal electric fields—limits nonlinear optical processes such as sum-frequency generation (SFG), second-harmonic generation (SHG), and spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) in LN-based devices.

METHODOLOGY: The study uses titanium in-diffused periodically-poled lithium niobate (Ti:PPLN) waveguides on congruent, z-cut LN substrates. Two experimental configurations were employed: (1) a high-temperature sample (320-470 K) using a 7 µm wide waveguide with 4.35 µm poling period for type-II SFG between a TM-polarized ~860 nm field (150 fs pulses from a Ti:Sapphire laser) and TE-polarized 1550 nm field, producing ~560 nm output; and (2) a cryogenic sample at ~7 K using a 5 µm wide waveguide with 9.90 µm poling period for type-0 SFG between 1570 nm and 960 nm pumps (both CW), producing ~595 nm output. The cryogenic setup used an Attocube attoDRY800 cryostat with controlled cooldown rate ≤1 K/min.

KEY FINDINGS:
- At high temperatures (above ~380 K), increasing the pump power causes a shift of the phase-matched SFG to shorter wavelengths (blue shift), but this is significantly suppressed at elevated temperatures due to increased carrier mobility and reduced polaron lifetime. Below 380 K, hysteresis in the phase-matching spectrum was observed, with no recovery within 4.5 minutes at 320 K.
- At cryogenic temperatures (7 K), photorefractive damage becomes much more severe due to "frozen in" charge carriers with very low mobility. Pyroelectric effects from cooldown also contribute to internal electric fields, particularly affecting TM-polarized beams.
- A critical photorefraction threshold was identified at cryogenic temperatures: approximately 18 mW pump power at ~960 nm with ~14 µW generated SFG power around 595 nm. Exceeding this causes serious device performance impairment.
- The proposed mitigation approach adapts the "optical cleaning" method (from Kösters et al. and Kirsch et al.) by coupling an auxiliary 532 nm green laser (1 mW) into the waveguide alongside the pump light. This green illumination successfully mobilizes trapped charge carriers even at 7 K, restoring the phase-matching spectrum toward an ideal sinc² shape and increasing generated power from 0.25 µW to 1.87 µW after 12 minutes of exposure.
- However, recovery is only partial. A persistent blue shift was observed throughout measurements (peak wavelength shifted from 964.16 nm to 963.48 nm), indicating that photorefractive damage is not fully reversible at cryogenic temperatures with the current green laser approach.

CONCLUSIONS: High-temperature operation is effective for suppressing photorefraction but incompatible with cryogenic applications. The green-laser-based optical cleaning method offers an alternative route for photorefraction management compatible with cryogenic operation and energy-constrained environments like space applications. Future work could optimize the auxiliary laser parameters (wavelength, pulsing, power, duration), study cryogenic material parameters and bi-polaron energy levels, and explore external electric fields or conductive coatings for improved charge carrier relaxation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The origins of photorefraction in LN are complex and involve various mechanisms, including one- and two-photon absorption on energy levels of intrinsic (e.g. Nb antisites and Li vacancies) and extrinsic (e.g. iron impurities) defects. The process is then followed by the ferroelectric photovoltaic effect, and the formation of stable charge distributions in the form of (bound) polarons."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Wideband thin-film lithium niobate modulator with low half-wave-voltage length product ---
URL: https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJ9d03e04e9a0ee503

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a peer-reviewed research article from Chinese Optics Letters (Vol. 19, Issue 6, page 060016, 2021) titled "Wideband thin-film lithium niobate modulator with low half-wave-voltage length product" by Xuecheng Liu, Bing Xiong (corresponding author), and colleagues from Tsinghua University's Beijing National Research Center for Information Science and Technology (BNRist). 6. The 738 cm^-1 mode in virgin samples is attributed to ilmenite-like stacking defects in nonstoichiometric LiNbO3.
7. 2D Raman imaging of patterned (masked) irradiation samples shows high uniformity of damage (standard deviation ~0.010 for 875 cm^-1 mode, ~0.015 for 631 cm^-1 mode) and a transition region at mask boundaries due to imperfect mask adhesion and edge scattering (~4% radius increase).
8. Edge scans reveal longer "tails" of damage toward the surface than predicted by SRIM (~3 μm effective width vs. ~1 μm calculated), a phenomenon also observed in diamond; the origin is unclear but may involve irradiation-induced strain.
9. Beveled geometry enabled detection of buried meandering line defects (spacing ~5 μm) that are otherwise invisible to optical microscopy; these defects produce strong Raman signals that can obscure the broad straggle-region signal.

**Conclusions:** Confocal micro-Raman spectroscopy provides a laboratory-based, ambient-pressure alternative to accelerator-based techniques (RBS, NRA, PIXE) for characterizing ion-irradiation damage in complex oxides, with ~1 μm lateral resolution, depth resolution limited by ~2 μm Rayleigh length, and the ability to map composition, crystallinity, strain, and defect distributions.
</summary>

## Abstract

This chapter provides a contemporary overview of the main properties of bulk lithium niobate (LiNbO3), highlighting the advantages of thin LiNbO3 films and their various applications in integrated electronics and optoelectronics. The chapter discusses different deposition techniques, each with its specific advantages and disadvantages. The structural and electrical properties of thin LiNbO3 films are significantly affected by the deposition regimes. Charge transport in LiNbO3-based heterostructures is influenced by both contact and bulk electron phenomena. Additionally, this chapter addresses the major application-focused challenges in the synthesis of thin LiNbO3 films.

This chapter provides a contemporary overview of the main properties of bulk lithium niobate (LN, LiNbO3), highlighting the advantages of thin LN films and their various applications in integrated electronics and optoelectronics. The chapter discusses different deposition techniques, each with its specific advantages and disadvantages. The structural and electrical properties of thin LN films are significantly affected by the deposition regime used. Charge transport in LN-based heterostructures is influenced by both contact and bulk electron phenomena. In addition, this chapter addresses the major application-focused challenges in the synthesis of thin LN films.

## 1.1. The structure and main properties of bulk lithium niobate

In 1965, bulk lithium niobate was grown by the Czochralski method for the first time [[1](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib1)], and Abrahams investigated its structure in a series of works [[2](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib2), [3](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib3)]. LN belongs to an R3c space group, and its oxygen atoms are arranged in nearly hexagonal close-packed planar sheets, as shown in figure [1.1](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1fig1). The unit cell is either rhombohedral (trigonal, *a* = 5.4944 Å, *α* = 55°52′) or hexagonal (*a**H* = 5.1483 Å, *c**H* = 13.8631 Å, *c*/*a* = 2.693) with six formula units per unit cell. The stacking sequence of cations in these octahedral sites is Nb, Li, vacancy, Nb, Li, vacancy, and so on [[3](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib3)]. The octahedral interstices formed in this structure are one-third filled by lithium atoms, one-third filled by niobium atoms, and one-third vacant.

Thus, bulk crystals with a stoichiometric composition (*R* = Li/Nb = 1) have a nearly ideal structure. In both lithium niobate crystals and congruent crystals (*R* = 0.946), a cation sublattice is considerably disordered. As demonstrated, excess niobium ions replace lithium ions at the lithium positions; the resulting fairly loose cation sublattice allows various ions to be introduced into it [[4](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib4)].

The distance from the Li+ ion to the nearest oxygen plane is 0.37 Å. Its lattice asymmetry makes lithium niobate a polar material, and oxygen atoms reside in the oxygen triangles shown in figure [1.1](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1fig1). To reverse the polarization, the Li+ ion must be replaced on the other side of the nearest oxygen triangle, whereas the Nb5+ ion moves only within the oxygen cages. Two stable positions (before and after reversal) determine two possible spontaneous polarization directions.

In stoichiometric crystals, defects are affected by the cation sublattice ordering, and they play a crucial role in the formation of the material’s optical characteristics. Even insignificant changes in the Li/Nb ratio or the presence of impurities—for example, the replacement of Li and Nb ions and the occupation of vacant octahedral voids—lead to local changes in the cation order along the polar axis. Impurity concentrations in the order of hundredths of a percent can greatly influence the dielectric and optical properties of these crystals, leading to negative effects such as laser damage.

The observed inhomogeneity in the cation sublattice of lithium niobate changes the translational invariance of a structure and does not disrupt the unit cell symmetry. The uniform composition along the growth axis does not mean that the crystal corresponds to the congruent melting conditions. The degree of crystallinity can be greatly improved if the growth process is performed under an electric field or through thermal annealing near the melting point accompanied by a weak electric field. Single crystals of lithium niobate grown under congruent melting conditions have a disordered cation sublattice. They are very sensitive to laser damage, limiting their application in optical devices. There is no principal difference between congruent and stoichiometric crystals from the physical and chemical points of view—they differ only in the degree of defectiveness.

At the Curie temperature of 1210 °C [[5](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib5)], LN manifests a phase transition from the ferroelectric to a paraelectric state, corresponding to the ![$R\bar{3}$](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=) space group. The density of LN single crystals depends on the Li content, and it equals 4.648 g cm−3 for congruent LN [[4](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib4)].

![$R\bar{3}$](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=)

As shown in figure [1.2](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1fig2) and demonstrated in [[6](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib6)], LN is a material with a variable composition, demonstrating a wide range of solid solutions. Specifically, there are areas in the phase diagram consisting of both LN oxide and either Li3NbO4 or LiNb3O8 that are centrosymmetric (non-ferroelectric) phases. Therefore, LN single crystals must be grown with extra care and at low temperatures because a slight deviation results in the formation of Li3NbO4 or LiNb3O8 oxides, provoking degradation of ferroelectric properties.

With the aim, for example, of observing better grain boundary or forming the required topology for thin film devices, chemical etching sometimes attracts interest. Although lithium niobate is relatively inert at room temperature, it has been reported that LN single crystals can be etched by boiling (110 °C) in an HF:HNO3 (1:2) mixture [[7](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib7)]. Nevertheless, the etching of thin LN films by this method leads to their exfoliation from the substrate after a few minutes. Reactive ion etching (RIE) (‘dry’) using various reactive gas recipes is among the most popular methods in contemporary thin film technologies. Regarding lithium niobate, there are a wide range of etching approaches that utilize a variety of fluorine-based and chlorine-based plasmas, such as CF4, CCl2F2, and CHF3 [[8](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib8)]. For instance, using a CF4/Ar/H2 reactive gas environment, it was revealed [[9](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib9)] that the etch rate and degree of surface crystallinity depend on the etching duration and H2 flow rate. Other authors have reported that depending on the compound ratio in their Ar/C3H8 reactive gas mixture, various degrees of etching anisotropy are attainable [[10](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib10)].

It is generally accepted that the coefficient of thermal expansion is a critical parameter for understanding lattice distortion. Due to symmetry, there are two linear coefficients of thermal expansion for lithium niobate (longitudinal and transverse) with magnitudes of *α*11 = 15.0 × 10−6 and *α*33 = *α*11 = 7.5 × 10−6, respectively.

The design of memory units requires controllable and tuned dielectric permittivity. According to axial symmetry, the dielectric permittivity tensor for lithium niobate has only two independent elements, whereas the low-frequency dielectric permittivity of bulk LN is *ε*11 = 30, *ε*33 = 80 [[7](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib7)].

Both optical properties and electro-optic effects are the most attractive features of lithium niobate. Bulk lithium niobate is an optically transparent material in the wavelength range from 0.35 to 5 μm where lattice absorption is observed. Even though the optical properties of lithium niobate are well established, the optical bandgap reported in the research literature varies significantly. For example, theoretical and experimental works have shown that the optical bandgap ranges between 3.57 eV [[11](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib11)] and 4.7 eV [[12](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib12)]. Some authors argue that this phenomenon occurs due to the presence of defects in LN, generating localized states (even the band tails) and influencing absorption in single crystals. Lithium niobate manifests birefringence, exhibiting principal ordinary and extraordinary refractive indexes of *n**o* = 2.289 and *n**e* = 2.201, respectively (*λ* = 633 nm). The refractive indexes depend on the Li/Nb ratio and vary significantly depending on the composition [[13](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib13)].

The results reported for the electrical properties of lithium niobate in the research literature are controversial; they are affected by the structure and composition of the studied material. Thus, this issue will be discussed in the following chapters.

## 1.2. Applications of thin LiNbO3 films

The idea of ferroelectric–semiconductor integration was realized in the 1960s. Since then, a wide range of multifunctional devices utilizing the unique properties of ferroelectrics (nonvolatile memory, electro-optic modulation, ferroelectric sensitivity) has been created. In this section, we briefly review some of the most popular devices.

### 1.2.1. Waveguide-based optical devices

Lithium niobate shows promise as a key component of electro-optic devices, particularly high-speed (>20 GHz) modulators. In contrast to bulk material, thin LN films provide higher intensity per unit power in waveguides and hence stronger nonlinear optical effects and shorter interaction lengths. The ability to fabricate such films on various substrates extends the spectrum of their possible applications.

One of the key issues associated with the application of thin LN films in waveguides is an understanding of the mechanisms that allow us to exclude or minimize optical losses (absorption, leakage, bulk scattering, surface scattering, and scattering triggered by grain boundaries) and to satisfy the requirements of the film grain boundary structure.

Optical leakage takes place, for instance, when a thin film waveguide is fabricated on a substrate with a high refractive index (for example, Si with *n* = 3.8 for *λ* = 633 nm), and an optical mode then inevitably ‘leaks’ into the substrate. The degree of leakage depends on the film thickness. To achieve the maximum allowed leakage of 1 dB cm−1, LN films must have a thickness of about 400 nm [[14](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib14)].

Bulk scattering is an essential process for optical mode coupling in a waveguide when the optical mode interacts with the radiative one. The change in the refractive index inevitably leads to scattering in the waveguide. This can be caused by any inhomogeneity in the waveguide material, for example, the presence of amorphous inclusions, parasitic phases (LiNb3O8, Li3NbO4), or grain disorder in a polycrystalline film. Even in epitaxial films, significant bulk scattering can be observed due to the presence of subgrains and mechanical stress. The surface scattering and scattering at the grain boundaries depend greatly on surface roughness and can overwhelm the bulk scattering. Roughness of the order of 1 nm is critical, posing a complex technological problem that requires a solution in the growth stage of LN film production. It has been shown that regardless of the fabrication method of thin ferroelectric films on sapphire substrates, there is a stable correlation between film thickness and surface roughness, which is 1% of the thickness [[15](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib15)]. The authors explained that this tendency was due to the effect of grain boundary groove formation caused by competition between the surface energy of grain boundaries and the energy of the free surface in the process of island coalescence. Total energy minimization originates from groove formation.

As a result, the main way to decrease the optical losses is to fabricate high-quality, two-axis textured or epitaxial LN films, which is a challenging problem.

### 1.2.2. Surface acoustic wave devices

Surface acoustic waves (SAWs) transfer the major part of their energy in the surface layer of a material, i.e. within a thickness of about one or two acoustic wavelengths. This allows them to interact with matter on such surfaces. Moreover, SAWs can have an electric field associated with them if they are generated in a piezoelectric material. This interaction leads to changes in the wave characteristics (amplitude, phase, speed, etc.) that underlie the operation of chemical sensors. Here, we do not discuss the operational principle of such sensors (it has been described in detail in some comprehensive reviews, for example, [[16](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib16)]); instead, we focus only on requirements relevant to the fabrication of these materials.

Materials for SAW devices should primarily possess the following properties: the piezoelectric effect, a high Curie temperature, significant resistivity, and high piezoresponse. Lithium niobate has all the listed properties, so it is ranked as the most popular piezoelectric material, surpassing competitors such as Pb(ZrTi)O3, BaTiO3, and Bi4Ti3O12. Specifically, lithium niobate is characterized by extremely high values for both its Curie temperature and its piezoelectric constant, making it a unique material for high-temperature acoustic sensors.

It has been emphasized [[17](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib17)–[19](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib19)] that the parameters of SAW filters are affected to a great extent by the structure and surface morphology of LN. It was demonstrated [[18](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib18)] that SAW filters had poor characteristics due to the high surface roughness and porosity of LN films. The authors of [[19](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib19)] associated the presence of preferable orientation and low surface roughness with the basic film characteristics for SAW filters, which depend on the fabrication technique. Emphasizing the challenge of forming c-oriented LN films using the chemical vapor deposition (CVD) process, the authors of [[20](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib20)] demonstrated that their fabricated SAW device operated at a frequency of 6.3 GHz, which corresponds to an SAW velocity of the order of 12 500 m s−1, i.e. a value that exceeds the analogous characteristic for bulk LN.

The authors of [[21](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib21)] investigated the fabrication of an SAW filter based on LN films deposited on diamond substrates by the radio-frequency magnetron sputtering (RFMS) method. They reported a strong dependence of the structure on the fabrication regime, and the optimal parameters (substrate temperature, RF magnetron power, reactive gas composition) were given. Single-phase films with low surface roughness (∼10 nm) allowed SAW filters to operate at a frequency of 2 GHz and an SAW speed of 8200 m s−1.

### 1.2.3. Memory units and neuromorphic systems

Thin LN films can be the basis for the creation of various types of RAM[1](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1fn1)
, such as FRAM (FeRAM)[2](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1fn2)
and RRAM (ReRAM)[3](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1fn3)
.

A wide range of works has focused on the study of the possible application of thin LN films in FRAM units (for example [[22](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib22)–[24](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib24)]). In doing so, the following issues arise:

Provided these issues are solved, thin LN films can replace traditional ferroelectric materials (PbZrxTi1−xO3, BaTiO3, and SrBi2Ta2O9) as a functional element of contemporary FRAM units. The use of metal, LN, and Si in metal–oxide–semiconductor (MOS)-like heterostructures potentially allows the introduction of FRAM units, which adds two masking steps to the process of fabricating regular complementary MOS (CMOS) structures. Such an approach makes it possible to integrate FRAM into microcontrollers. Simplifying the technological stages required for the creation of FRAM units would allow FRAM to compete with the currently dominant flash memory due to its significant advantages [[25](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib25)].

The possibility of utilizing LN films in RRAM units and neuromorphic systems was demonstrated in [[26](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib26)–[29](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib29)]. The main aim of this research was the development of a fundamental model describing the behavior of memristors. For example, [[30](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib30), [31](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib31)] reported the memristive effect in TiO2 films, where the change of resistance was associated with the motion of oxygen vacancies activated by electrical current (the electroforming effect). In [[32](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib32)], the memristive effect was revealed in VO2 films, which was caused by the insulator–metal transition in these structures.

The memristive effect in LN-based heterostructures is explained in [[26](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib26)–[29](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib29)] by the motion of oxygen vacancies. However, the resulting theoretical predictions do not correlate with experimental data (see [[27](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib27)]). Moreover, some evidence pointing to the role of Li ions in the process of memristive switching was presented in [[28](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib28)].

Currently, LN seems to be an alternative material for RRAM, although solutions based on this material are more technologically complex, making it hard for them to compete with RRAM technology based on amorphous SiO2. Nevertheless, LN is more promising in the context of neuromorphic systems [[26](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib26), [28](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib28)].

As a result of the creation of RAM units based on FRAM and RRAM, it will be possible to produce more reliable, high-speed, durable, and protected storage memory compared to flash memory units or HDDs.[4](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1fn4)
At the same time, neuromorphic systems can become the basis for creating self-learning artificial intelligence.

The potential application of LN films has been greatly expanded due to the discovery of their ferromagnetic property. The authors of [[33](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib33), [34](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib34)] proposed the doping of films by Co ion implantation such that the Co ions replaced the Nb ions in lithium niobate. This mechanism is supported by the fact that oxygen vacancies are responsible for the ferromagnetic properties of LN nanoparticles [[35](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib35), [36](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib36)]. As stated in [[35](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib35)], the mechanical–chemical synthesis of LN with subsequent annealing leads to the formation of a high concentration of oxygen vacancies and allows for the fabrication of samples manifesting ferromagnetic properties.

Although the practical application of the multiferroic properties of lithium niobate is at the development stage, active and promising work on LN film synthesis is a precursor to the integration of LN films into optoelectronic devices.

## 1.3. Fabrication methods of thin LiNbO3 films

When selecting an appropriate synthesis method for thin LN films, it is crucial to consider the method’s ability to preserve the elemental composition and structure of the bulk material, as well as its reproducibility. Various fabrication techniques have been proposed to meet these requirements, including the sol–gel method, pulsed laser deposition (PLD), discrete thermal evaporation in vacuum, RFMS, CVD, liquid-phase epitaxy (LPE), ion-beam sputtering (IBS), and the Pechini method [[37](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib37)].

### 1.3.1. Liquid-phase epitaxy

In 1975, the possibility of synthesizing LN films by LPE on the surface of single-crystal LiTaO3 was demonstrated [[38](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib38), [39](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib39)]. Although the LPE method is now rarely used for fabricating LN films, some researchers have reported the successful fabrication of optical waveguides on single crystals of LN [[40](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib40), [41](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib41)]. It has been noted that doping the films with Zn atoms increases surface roughness as the dopant concentration rises. Under these conditions, a low degree of optical loss was achieved (0.154 ± 0.002 dB mm−1 at *λ* = 1 μm), and the surface roughness was minimized to 0.2–0.3 nm. During the process of pseudomorphic epitaxial growth, an intermediate Zn:LN layer forms, in which the Zn content varies according to the substrate temperature. In addition, the refractive index difference at the film–substrate interface depends on the Zn concentration in the LN film [[40](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib40)].

### 1.3.2. Chemical vapor deposition

In the CVD process, the reactive gas mixture used in the reaction chamber significantly impacts the synthesis of LN films. At low reactive gas pressures (approximately 266.6 Pa), polycrystalline films comprising two phases, namely LN and LiNb3O8, are formed on sapphire substrates. When the reactive gas pressure is increased to around 2666 Pa, single-phase LN films with a ![$\langle 0001\rangle $](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=) texture are produced [[42](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib42)]. In addition, the mechanical stress in the films decreases from 1.3 to 0.9 GPa as the pressure increases from 666.5 Pa to 101.3 kPa.

![$\langle 0001\rangle $](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=)

### 1.3.3. Sol–gel process

The first instance of the successful fabrication of complex oxides was demonstrated in [[43](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib43)]. Since the 1980s, the sol–gel method has been extensively employed for depositing LN films [[44](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib44)]. This method facilitates film formation at significantly lower temperatures compared to alternative techniques due to the high reactivity of the gel. However, it is noteworthy that the sol–gel method is both time- and resource-intensive, as it necessitates the use of expensive precursors for gel fabrication. In addition, the synthesized LN films often contain additional non-ferroelectric phases, such as LiNb3O8 and Nb2O5.

The emergence of the LiNb3O8 phase can be attributed to the phase reaction between LN and the inherent oxide present on a Si substrate [[45](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib45)]. The quantity of the LiNb3O8 phase present in synthesized films is influenced by the annealing temperature.

The surface roughness varies depending on deposition conditions and the molar concentration of compounds in the solution. Notably, as the concentration increases from 0.25 to 1 mol l−1, surface roughness ranges from 10.6 to 16 nm [[46](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib46)].

### 1.3.4. Pulsed laser deposition

The initial demonstration of the feasibility of depositing ferroelectric films using the PLD method was first illustrated in [[47](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib47)]. In the 1990s, this method became widely adopted for synthesizing LN films [[48](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib48)–[50](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib50)].

The PLD method operates on the principle of ablating a target using short pulses (20–30 s) of focused laser radiation. The substrate holder is positioned in an atmosphere with high oxygen pressure, which is necessary for oxide formation. Film parameters are contingent upon numerous factors, including the distribution of compounds during ablation, the reactive gas pressure, the substrate–target distance, and the energy and frequency of laser radiation.

LN films fabricated via the PLD technique exhibit nonuniform composition and structure. Initial studies [[48](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib48), [49](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib49)] disclosed the formation of a Li-deficient phase, LiNb3O8. To circumvent this issue, the use of Li-rich targets was suggested [[48](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib48)]. In addition, there is evidence linking the appearance of the LiNb3O8 phase to the relative positioning of the substrate and target, as well as the presence of oxygen in the reaction chamber [[51](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib51)].

Research findings [[52](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib52)–[54](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib54)] have demonstrated that the elemental composition, structure, and surface morphology are correlated with the target structure and PLD parameters. Uniform single-phase, crack-free LN films with grain sizes ranging from 50 to 200 nm were deposited onto sapphire substrates and SiO2/Si heterostructures at a substrate temperature (*T*sub) of 700 °C [[52](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib52)]. Interestingly, films deposited onto sapphire exhibited greater transparency compared to those on SiO2/Si heterostructures.

In [[53](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib53)], a nonlinear relationship between average roughness and partial oxygen pressure for LN films deposited onto diamond/Si heterostructures (*T*sub = 650 °C) was unveiled. This relationship was elucidated in terms of the competition between two processes: scattering by atoms in a reactive environment (at high pressure) and re-sputtering of the growth front (at low pressure). Moreover, the successful synthesis of highly oriented LN films with ![$\langle 0001\rangle $](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=) texture onto SiO2/Si substrates at *T*sub = 650 °C has been reported [[54](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib54)]. It was noted that the degree of preferred orientation produced during film formation was contingent upon substrate temperature, as an increase in *T*sub resulted in a decrease in the orientation degree, ultimately leading to the formation of films with arbitrary grain orientation at 750 °C. Notably, single-phase c-oriented LN films were exclusively formed at an oxygen pressure of 40 Pa in the reaction chamber, whereas further increases in oxygen pressure suppressed the formation of the LiNb3O8 phase.

![$\langle 0001\rangle $](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=)

Minimal roughness (4.3 nm) was achieved at a substrate temperature of 600 °C; however, at *T*sub = 500 °C, roughness increased to 5.1 nm, and at *T*sub = 700 °C, it further rose to 5.8 nm. The minimum optical losses corresponded to minimal roughness. The authors attributed this roughness–*T*sub dependency to an alteration in the mobility of adatoms.

### 1.3.5. Radio-frequency magnetron sputtering

The first sputtering triode setup to produce LN films utilized a powdered LN target [[55](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib55)]. Subsequently, the synthesis of LN films progressed through radio-frequency diode sputtering (RF sputtering) [[56](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib56)–[59](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib59)], which was associated with a low deposition rate and compositional irregularities in the deposited films.

The advent of magnetron sputtering and RFMS supplanted RF sputtering entirely, offering several advantages:

The initial exploration of the synthesis of LN films through the RFMS method commenced in the latter half of the 1980s [[60](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1bib60)]. Nevertheless, ongoing research is still elucidating the influence of technological parameters and plasma effects (specifically, the ion-assist effect) on the structural characteristics of deposited LN films.

Table [1.1](#bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1t1) delineates the advantages and drawbacks associated with each of the aforementioned methods.
