The stability of the material is mainly determined by the [microparticle](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/materials-science/microparticle "Learn more about microparticle from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") arrangement and lattice type, and the differences in particle arrangement in different directions lead to different etching rates. Depending on different etching rates in different crystal directions, the etching process exhibits isotropic and [anisotropic](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/anisotropic "Learn more about anisotropic from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") characteristics. The isotropic etching rate is the same in all directions during the etching process and is independent of the crystal axis and crystal direction [75,76], as shown in Fig. 3(b). However, the etching rate of [anisotropic etching](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/materials-science/anisotropic-etching "Learn more about anisotropic etching from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") is often related to the crystal axis and crystal orientation, and there will be crystal planes and dislocations after etching[77], as shown in Fig. 3(c). The anisotropy of wet etching can also be used to achieve controlled preparation of microstructures. For example, in silica, anisotropy etching can be used to alter the aspect ratio of modification defined by focal spot demensions[78]. Various structures can be fabricated through wet etching after mask lithography. However, the [directionality](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/directionality "Learn more about directionality from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") of wet etching depends heavily on the properties of the material; thus, the designability and complexity of the structures can be limited.

Femtosecond laser processing has a high degree of freedom and can realize the fabrication of arbitrary 3D structures inside and on the surfaces of materials. Directional etching of materials can be realized via controlled phase transformation of materials using femtosecond laser. Fig. 3(d) indicates the capability of femtosecond laser with wet etching processing. Using the femtosecond laser direct writing-assisted wet etching technique, various 3D [microfluidic channels](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/microfluidic-channel "Learn more about microfluidic channels from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") with [high aspect ratios](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/high-aspect-ratio "Learn more about high aspect ratios from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") have been fabricated on [glass substrates](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/glass-substrate "Learn more about glass substrates from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")[79–81]. This technology has broad application prospects in the field of 3D microfluidic network integration. Owing to the high [selectivity](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/physics-and-astronomy/selectivity "Learn more about selectivity from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") of wet etching, it can be used to fabricate high-aspect ratio structures, as shown in Fig. 3(e) [82]. Using an etch selectivity of up to 10 4 for sapphire in a [hydrofluoric acid solution](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/hydrofluoric-acid-solution "Learn more about hydrofluoric acid solution from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), researchers achieved highly selective etching of sapphire via a femtosecond laser-induced phase transition and fabricated millimeter-long [nanopores](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/nanopore "Learn more about nanopores from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")[61].

Normally, after laser modification of hard materials such as quartz and silicon, the chemical potential and microstructure of the material are changed, which results in a different etching rate of the material during chemical etching compared with the areas that have not been laser-modified. According to this principle, many researchers have fabricated complex 3D structures with good surface quality inside or on the surface of materials with high efficiency. This technology is known as femtosecond laser with chemical wet etching processing. It can significantly increase the processing efficiency and improve the surface quality of the structures.

#### 2.3 Dry etching

Dry etching is indispensable for pattern transfer in the semiconductor process, and it uses physical and chemical reactions between the etching gas and the material to remove material [83–85]. There are several types: [ion beam](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/physics-and-astronomy/ion-beams "Learn more about ion beam from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") etching (IBE), reactive-ion etching (RIE), and [inductively coupled plasma](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/inductively-coupled-plasma "Learn more about inductively coupled plasma from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (ICP) etching (Table 2). These three methods are used in various fields owing to their different etching principles, etching directions, and selection ratios. Next, we discuss the differences among the methods.

Table 2. Dry etching systems.

| Technology | Acting particle | Reaction principle | Etching direction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **IBE** | Plasma | Physical process | Vertical etching |
| **RIE** | Plasma | Physical and chemical processes | Horizontal and vertical etching |
| **ICP** | Plasma | Physical and chemical processes | Horizontal and vertical etching |

[IBE](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/physics-and-astronomy/ion-beams "Learn more about IBE from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") is performed via physical [bombardment](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/bombardment "Learn more about bombardment from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") only [86–89]. The commonly used etching source gas is argon, and the material is etched vertically. Its advantage is that it can etch any material with a high etching precision. It can etch several [atomic layers](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/atomic-layer "Learn more about atomic layers from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") through control of the etching energy and etching time. Its disadvantages are that the etching rate is low and that it is difficult to realize the etching preparation of deep structures. In RIE and [ICP etching](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/materials-science/plasma-etching "Learn more about ICP etching from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), there are two simultaneous processes: physical sputtering and ion reaction. Therefore, in addition to vertical etching, some ionic chemical reactions allow horizontal etching of the material. RIE does not allow controlled adjustment of the rate ratio of physical sputter etching to ion chemical etching [90–93]. As the most widely used etching technology in industry, [ICP](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/inductively-coupled-plasma "Learn more about ICP from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") can effectively increase the etching rate without severe physical bombardment [94–96]. Moreover, it can increase the RF power of the lower electrode, improve the ratio of physical bombardment etching to chemical etching, and increase the flexibility of the preparation structures. Thus, it can achieve deep etching of structures.

Different gases play different roles in the etching process. Table 3 presents the dry etching processes for several commonly used materials [97,98]. For example, argon plays the role of physical etching in the etching process. Additionally, it can be introduced to fulfill the function of [partial pressure](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/partial-pressure "Learn more about partial pressure from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") of various gases. Fluorine-based gases (SF 6, CF 4, CHF 3, etc.) are commonly used in silicon-based materials. After the reaction, the fluoride formed in silicon is released in gaseous form. Oxygen is often used in the etching of polymers owing to the presence of carbon in the molecules. Oxygen is used to convert it into gaseous CO x.

Table 3. Dry etching processes of various materials.

| **Material** | **Etching system** | **Reaction gases** | **Ref.** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Sapphire** | ICP | Cl 2, BCl 3 | 129 |
| **Silicon** | ICP | SF 6 | 55 |
| **SiO****x** | RIE | Ar, O 2, CF 4 | 83 |
| **Black silicon** | ICP | SF 6, O 2 | 97 |
| **ZnO** | RIE | Ar, O 2 | 136 |
| **Diamond** | ICP-RIE | Ar, Cl 2, O 2 | 84 |
| **LiNbO****3** | ICP | Ar, SF 6, CHF 3, O 2 | 98 |
| **SiC** | IBE | Ar | 44 |

This is a ScienceDirect topic page on "Femtosecond Laser" in the Engineering subject area, aggregating chapters and review articles related to femtosecond laser technology. The page compiles several key publications on the topic:

1. **Medical nanorobots (2020)**: A chapter discussing femtosecond laser neurosurgery. Femtosecond lasers emit ultrashort optical pulses measured in femtoseconds (1 fs = 10⁻¹⁵ seconds). They are widely used in molecular structure manipulation, ophthalmic surgery for vision correction, and "nanoscissors" applications—using low-energy near-infrared laser pulses to cut cell organelles without harming surrounding tissue. These lasers can perform precise operations on nerve cells by heating targeted areas and cutting through them.

2. **Femtosecond laser machining for optical fiber microstructures (2022, Optics & Laser Technology)**: A review by Mao-qing Chen et al. covering the use of femtosecond lasers to fabricate true three-dimensional structures due to small heat-affected areas, high processing accuracy, and efficiency. The technology is used to fabricate Fabry-Perot interferometers (FPI), Mach-Zehnder interferometers (MZI), fiber Bragg gratings (FBG), and combined FPI-FBG and MZI-FBG structures. The review compares manufacturing processes, repeatability, size, sensitivity, stability, and cross-sensitivity with traditional sensors.

3. **Femtosecond vs. nanosecond lasers on bulk metallic glasses (2023, Optics & Laser Technology)**: A review by Weilin Zhang et al. explaining that femtosecond lasers (pulse width below femtosecond, also called ultrafast lasers) offer ultra-short pulse width, high laser energy density, and small heat-affected zones, making them advantageous for fine processing. Nanosecond lasers belong to the short pulse laser category with longer pulse widths but still fast energy transmission. The article discusses how femtosecond lasers have broken through bottlenecks in high-precision micromachining of hard materials, including surface micromachining and 3D internal structuring. Nonlinear absorption occurs only at the focus, resulting in highly localized material ablation. The review also compares laser processing with traditional methods (electroplating, sandblasting, shot blasting) which suffer from low efficiency, complex processes, and material damage. Micro-nano processing of metallic glasses can create porous structures, microgrooves, microconvexities, and corrugations, with applications including enhanced hydrophobicity and antibacterial surfaces.

4. **Femtosecond laser processed superhydrophobic surfaces (2024, Journal of Manufacturing Processes)**: A review by Yu Guo and Haibin Zhao covering femtosecond laser as a precise, controllable, environmentally friendly solution for manufacturing superhydrophobic surfaces with micro and nanostructures. Applications include self-cleaning, anti-icing, drag reduction, droplet manipulation, water/fog harvesting, corrosion resistance, wear resistance, oil-water separation, and antibacterial functionality. The review covers LIPSS (laser-induced periodic surface structures), microgroove hierarchical structures, microcolumn/microcone structures, and micro pits/holes structures.

5. **Biological sensors based on long period fiber grating (2023, Optics & Laser Technology)**: Discusses femtosecond laser pulse technology. In 1999, Y. Kondo et al. first fabricated LPFG using infrared femtosecond laser pulses. The method uses high-intensity pulses with ultra-short pulse width and ultra-high peak power, producing nonlinear effects of multiphoton absorption and avalanche ionization on transparent materials. Advantages include precise spatial localization, injury thresholds, and extremely low thermal effects. Two main methods exist: direct inscription and amplitude mask method, with direct inscription being most widely adopted. Limitations include additional insertion loss from Mie scattering and the high cost of femtosecond laser equipment.

6. **Femtosecond laser with etching technology for micro-optical components (2023, Optics & Laser Technology)**: A detailed review by Jia-Xin Zheng et al. covering femtosecond laser modification principles, including single-photon vs. multiphoton absorption mechanisms. Multiphoton absorption enables 3D microfabrication within transparent materials even when photon energy is below the bandgap. The article covers laser ablation (when energy significantly exceeds damage threshold) versus laser modification (near damage threshold, causing phase changes). Wet etching methods are detailed for various materials (sapphire, silicon, SiC, silica, LiNbO₃, GaN, etc.) with specific etching solutions and temperatures. Dry etching techniques covered include ion beam etching (IBE), reactive-ion etching (RIE), and inductively coupled plasma (ICP) etching, with details on reaction gases for different materials (SF₆, CF₄, CHF₃ for silicon-based materials; Cl₂/BCl₃ for sapphire; Ar for SiC, etc.). The combination of femtosecond laser modification with etching enables fabrication of smooth 3D micro/nanostructures, high-aspect-ratio structures, and microfluidic channels with applications in micro-optical component fabrication.

Because of their ultrashort and ultralong pulses, ease in usage, and precision, femtosecond lasers are widely used in molecular structure manipulation and localization."

## Abstract

Timely repair of fused silica damage ensures the stable operation of high-power laser systems. In the traditional repair process, the material nearby the damaged area is gradually ablated with CO 2 or femtosecond laser. Subsequently, homogenization and residual stress removal are required because of the microcracks and thermal accumulation generated with the ablation. As a result, the repair efficiency is greatly restricted. In this paper, a new method using in-volume, selective femtosecond laser-induced etching to repair the damage of fused silica is proposed. The region irradiated by femtosecond laser becomes more susceptible to the etching solution due to its constitutive characteristics having undergone chemical restructuring. In this way, material nearby the damaged area transparent to the laser radiation is modified locally inside the volume. A femtosecond laser is used to scan the damaged area with a 3D hollow trajectory. The applicable modification of fused silica occurs when the single pulse energy is approximately 2 μJ to 5 μJ, the repetition frequency is approximately 200 kHz to 500 kHz, and the scanning speed is approximately 10 mm/s. Then, the etching solution reacts quickly along the 3D profile of the modified path, and the damaged area is removed as a whole piece. This method can greatly reduce the workload of repair, and the etching process of fused silica is carried out synchronously. So, the etching efficiency is not affected by the number of damage points. In addition, the weak reaction between the etching solution and the substrate could homogenize the interface. It provides an efficient way to repair the surface damage of fused silica.

## 1. Introduction

Fused silica is an important component of large high-power laser devices and electro-optic information systems [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B1-crystals-13-00309),[2](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B2-crystals-13-00309)]. Surface damage frequently occurs in the process of high-throughput operation. The damage point will expand dramatically if it is not repaired in time, which will degrade the property of the fused silica and even damage other components [[3](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B3-crystals-13-00309),[4](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B4-crystals-13-00309)]. The optical element can be repaired by removing the damaged point and the surrounding material. This will ensure the economical and stable operation of the device. Traditional damage repair methods mainly include CO 2 laser ablation and femtosecond excision. The material around the damage point is vaporized using the focal point of the CO 2 laser [[5](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B5-crystals-13-00309),[6](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B6-crystals-13-00309),[7](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B7-crystals-13-00309),[8](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B8-crystals-13-00309)] or femtosecond laser [[9](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B9-crystals-13-00309),[10](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B10-crystals-13-00309)]. The scanning track of the focus point has to fill up the area gradually and completely. Thus, processing efficiency and heat accumulation become thorny issues. Fused silicon possesses high transmittance, and it is a kind of friable material. Microcracks and residual stresses are found on the acting surface after the ablation process. A smoothing operation is required with CO 2 laser. That is, parameters need to be reset, or the light source needs to be replaced using traditional damage repair methods. For the most part, the number of damage points is large. The efficiency will be greatly affected, so it is urgent to develop a new and efficient repair method.

Selective femtosecond laser-induced etching has been widely adopted in the three-dimensional processing of various materials, especially for brittle materials such as fused silica [[11](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B11-crystals-13-00309),[12](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B12-crystals-13-00309),[13](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B13-crystals-13-00309),[14](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B14-crystals-13-00309),[15](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B15-crystals-13-00309),[16](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B16-crystals-13-00309),[17](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B17-crystals-13-00309)]. Femtosecond laser modification by irradiation is the first step in this method. In this case, the irradiation energy is below the ablation threshold. The properties of irradiated materials have changed. Compared with the unirradiated area, the modified materials can be more easily etched using an acid or alkali solution, so that the modified material is removed with an etching solution while the substrate material is maintained. It means that we can realize the processing of three-dimensional topography by controlling the laser scanning trajectory. The laser energy used for material modification is relatively smaller than ablation, which partially avoids microcracks in the processing of brittle materials. Researchers have applied this method to the fabrication of micropores, microfluidics, microchannels, etc. [[18](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B18-crystals-13-00309),[19](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B19-crystals-13-00309),[20](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B20-crystals-13-00309),[21](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B21-crystals-13-00309)]. The etch selectivity ratio of the modified area to the non-modified area can be as high as 1000:1 [[12](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B12-crystals-13-00309)]. It should be noted that the etching solution will cause a certain weak etching in the material substrate, which just homogenizes the laser irradiation interface. The effect of the interface smoothing plays a positive role in improving the processing quality of selective femtosecond laser-induced etching. Therefore, it is suitable for arbitrary 3D microfabrication processing of brittle materials.

In this paper, we have proposed a new method for the repair of fused silica damage, which has several advantages in comparison with traditional methods. The influence of femtosecond laser parameters, displacement system parameters, and the etching solution ratio was studied to obtain the optimized repair quality and efficiency. Femtosecond laser scanning is used to modify the three-dimensional contour of the area around the damaged points, and then an etching solution is used to remove the modified materials in the damaged point area. In the traditional repair process, the material nearby the damaged area is ablated with CO 2 laser bit by bit. We redesigned the removal path based on the selective femtosecond laser-induced etching technology, which would improve the repair efficiency. The damage point is located on the surface of the element. In the process of femtosecond laser modification, only the side and bottom surfaces around the damage point need to be covered by the focus scanning track. The modified area forms a box covering the damage point area as a whole. Multiple damage points can be treated synchronously during the etching process. The increase in the number of damage points will not affect work efficiency. When the number of damage points is large, the efficiency advantage is more obvious than that of traditional methods. Another advantage is that the particular weak etching reaction on the substrate material, which synchronously completes the interface smoothing, omits the secondary treatment process used in the traditional method. We also present results of the effect of laser processing parameters such as single pulse energy, repetition frequency, and scan speed on etching depth and surface morphology. Therefore, based on the characteristics of the femtosecond laser of low energy and high power, the rapid scanning modification brings a new and efficient method for repairing the surface damage points of fused silica components.

## 2. Materials and Methods

### 2.1. Experimental Samples

As the typical transparent medium material, quartz glass has been widely used as substrate material for optical elements. In general, glass whose main component is SiO 2 could be collectively called quartz glass, mainly including fused quartz and doped quartz glass. For fused quartz, the melting temperature is about 1700 °C. This experiment used Corning 7980 fused silica material, and its basic performance parameters are shown in [Table 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#table_body_display_crystals-13-00309-t001).

**Table 1.** The main properties of the fused quartz glass used in the experiment. 

![Image 17](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#table_body_display_crystals-13-00309-t001)

### 2.2. Principle

Fused silica is a kind of transparent dielectric material with very stable chemical properties, which generally did not react with an acidic or alkaline solution. However, after being irradiated by femtosecond laser, the properties of fused silica changed. The immediate expression was that it easily reacted with hydrofluoric acid or potassium hydroxide. Whether the material was ablated or modified was determined by the flux of femtosecond laser irradiation. For material removal, the minimum flux value that is sufficient to overcome the sum of the binding energy and ionization-potential energy of ions in the lattice is considered the threshold flux [[22](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B22-crystals-13-00309)]. The ablation threshold of the laser on the material is such that, under a certain laser flux, the lattice of the material is unstable and the structure is destroyed [[23](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B23-crystals-13-00309)]. The ablation threshold of femtosecond laser is proportional to the square root of the pulse width in the long pulse range [[24](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B24-crystals-13-00309),[25](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B25-crystals-13-00309)]. The fused silica is ablated when the irradiation energy is greater than the ablation threshold. There will be microcracks left on the interface due to its frangibility. However, the femtosecond laser flux used for material modification is relatively small and has little impact on the surrounding area. It is suitable for the high-precision processing of hard and brittle materials because of its relatively mild processing.

Matsuo et al., found that the stable fused silica will change into an amorphous form after irradiating by laser. The chemical bond angle (144°) of Si-O-Si decreases due to the change of material state and density. The valence state of oxygen ions in them changes, which increases its chemical reactivity with acid. Therefore, the selectivity of chemical etching appears between the modified and unmodified materials [[26](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B26-crystals-13-00309),[27](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B27-crystals-13-00309)]. The main chemical reactions between the hydrofluoric acid etching solution and the fused silica are:

$$
\equiv Si - O - Si \equiv + H^{+} F \rightarrow \equiv Si - OH + \equiv SiF \rightarrow SiF_{4} \uparrow + H_{2} O
$$

(1) 

Hydrofluoric acid is widely used in various research areas and industries [[28](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B28-crystals-13-00309),[29](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B29-crystals-13-00309)]. However, the safety and environmental protection of hydrofluoric acid is demanding because of its volatile and highly toxic properties. In recent years, it has been found that a potassium hydroxide solution can also be used for the optional etching after modification. In addition, the etching selectivity of potassium hydroxide is higher than that of hydrofluoric acid, so it is a better etching solution. Photoluminescence and confocal Raman spectra of the modified fused silica were studied. Kiyama et al. found that the formation of a silicon-rich structure SiOx (x > 2) is the main reason that potassium hydroxide has better etching efficiency than that of hydrofluoric acid [[30](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B30-crystals-13-00309),[31](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#B31-crystals-13-00309)]. This structure more easily reacts with potassium hydroxide. The chemical reactions involved were:

$$
\equiv Si - O - Si \equiv + OH^{-} \rightarrow \equiv Si - OH + \equiv SiO^{-} \rightarrow SiO_{3} + H_{2} O
$$

(2) 

### 2.3. Methods

The damage points on the surface of fused silica were repaired using the selective femtosecond laser-induced etching. There were two steps to complete the repair process. The first step was to modify the materials around the damage point. The femtosecond laser is focused on the interior of the transparent substrate. The material at the focal position was modified. We designed the scanning path of femtosecond laser to improve the overall efficiency. As the focus shifted, the modified area gradually expanded into a hollow three-dimensional geometry in which the central position was the damage point. In this way, it would reduce the amount of scanning compared to the point-by-point ablation of traditional methods. The size of the geometry was determined according to the size of the damage point. The next step was etching to remove the materials around the damage point. All of the fused silica was immersed in the etching solution. Because the modified material had a faster reaction rate than the unmodified material, the etching solution would permeate along the modified trajectory and eventually surround the damage point. The damage point was broken off from the fused silica as a whole. When there were a lot of damage points, the modification process was completed successively. However, the etching process was simultaneous no matter how many damage points there were. That is, this method had more advantages when there were many damage points.

The schematic diagram of the whole repair process is shown in [Figure 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f001). The wavelength of the femtosecond laser is 1030 nm, the pulse width of 290 fs, and the repetition frequency range of 50 kHz to 500 kHz. The fused silica sample is polished on four sides, which is convenient for observing the modification and etching effect from the side. The geometric dimensions are 4 mm × 6 mm × 50 mm. The femtosecond laser was focused into the sample using a microscope objective. The samples were placed on a high-precision XY plane displacement table, and the microscope objective for focusing moved along the Z-axis. Thus, the three-dimensional scanning of femtosecond laser inside the sample was realized using the plane motion of the sample and the vertical motion of femtosecond laser. In this way, the material around the damage point of the sample could be modified by irradiation. After the modification, the sample was immersed in a potassium hydroxide solution to etch the modified materials. Finally, the samples were washed with alcohol and ultrapure water.

![Image 18: Crystals 13 00309 g001](https://www.mdpi.com/crystals/crystals-13-00309/article_deploy/html/images/crystals-13-00309-g001-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f001)

**Figure 1.** Schematic diagram of the repair process with a femtosecond laser. (**a**) The three-dimensional scanning path of modification; (**b**) etching and cleaning. 

The influence of the femtosecond laser parameters, displacement system parameters, and etching solution ratio was studied. In the course of the experiment, the comparison of samples morphology was taken using an optical microscope (5X, 50X) and a laser confocal microscope. The optical microscope observes the surface morphology. The laser confocal microscope can conduct nondestructive scanning imaging of three-dimensional structures, which is more conducive to observing the etching depth, material morphology changes, and so on. The potassium hydroxide solution with a mass fraction of 58% was used for etching, and the commonly used hydrofluoric acid solution with a mass fraction of 5% was used as the control group. The samples were ultrasonically cleaned with alcohol, acetone, and ultrapure water after etching. The etching rate of the substrate was obtained by comparing the weight of the unmodified fused silica sample before and after etching. It was found that the etching rate in the hydrofluoric acid solution and the potassium hydroxide solution was about 2 μm/h and 1 μm/h, respectively. This is less than one-thousandth of the thickness of the substrate material, so it can be ignored.

## 3. Results and Discussion

### 3.1. The Femtosecond Laser Modification Repair of Damage Point

The damage points of the fused silica had been modified and etched as shown in [Figure 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f002). The morphology of a typical damage point is shown in the insets of [Figure 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f002)a. The top view shows that its horizontal dimension is about 1.5 mm, and the side view shows that its depth is about hundreds of microns. It is an irregular pit with some cracks around it. These damage points on the optical components were irreversible. At present, the general method is to remove the materials around it to prevent it from expanding rapidly. We proposed repairing the damage points using selective femtosecond laser-induced etching. The rest of [Figure 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f001)a shows the modified fused silica, which is the first step of the repair process. Here, we show two typical examples. It can be found that each damage point is surrounded by a hollow geometry, which is translucent. These were formed by the scanning track of the femtosecond laser focus in modification. The middle cylinder has a circle radius of 1 mm and a height of 500 μm. The right rectangle has a side length of 2 mm and a height of 500 μm. This means that different modification trajectories can be preset according to the size and shape of the damage point. [Figure 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f002)b shows the fused silica that had been etched. It could be found that the damage point had been successfully removed from the substrate.

![Image 19: Crystals 13 00309 g002](https://www.mdpi.com/crystals/crystals-13-00309/article_deploy/html/images/crystals-13-00309-g002-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f002)

**Figure 2.** (**a**) Microphotograph of the damage point after modification; (**b**) photograph of fused silica after repair. 

### 3.2. Femtosecond Laser Parameters

In this experiment, the wavelength of the femtosecond laser is 1030 nm, the energy variation range of a single pulse is 1 μJ to 10 μJ, and the repetition frequency range is 50 kHz to 500 kHz. We scan the line on the surface of fused silica at a constant speed (10 mm/s). The line is 2 mm long and about 10 μm wide. The fused silica after scanning at varied levels of single pulse energy and repeat frequencies of the femtosecond laser are shown in [Figure 3](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f003). The scanning lines of various parameters were obviously different. It is found that when the single pulse energy was low (<2 μJ) or the repetition frequency was small (<100 kHz), there was a slight trace of modification on the sample, as shown in the microscope picture of [Figure 3](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f003)b. On the contrary, when the laser single pulse energy is too high (>10 μJ), the fused silica was ablated with violent splashing, as shown in [Figure 3](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f003)c. These results show that for the given scanning speed, the modification of fused silica is possible only for the single pulse energy and repeat frequency within a certain range; furthermore, the highest laser flux for modification corresponds to the optimum processing speed. [Figure 3](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f003)d shows the microscope photos of the uniform modification effect when the single pulse energy is approximately 5 μJ and the repetition frequency is 200 kHz. It can be clearly seen that the modified part shows brighter colors than the surrounding area, and it is a continuous scanning line with uniform line width. There were a few splashing attachments on both sides. After many experiments, it is confirmed that the modification of fused silica occurs when the laser parameters are in an appropriate range. The single pulse energy is approximately 2 μJ to 5 μJ, and the repetition frequency is approximately 200 kHz to 500 kHz.

![Image 20: Crystals 13 00309 g003](https://www.mdpi.com/crystals/crystals-13-00309/article_deploy/html/images/crystals-13-00309-g003-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f003)

**Figure 3.** Images of various modification effects with different single pulse energy and repetition frequency of femtosecond laser parameters: (**a**) Macroscopic picture; (**b**) 1 μJ/100 kHz; (**c**) 10 μJ/500 kHz; (**d**) 5 μJ/200 kHz. 

### 3.3. Scanning Speed in Modification

The scanning speed is adjusted by the three-dimensional motion platform. Laser scanning speed was a key factor in judging the efficiency of the sample modification. In order to study the effect of the laser scanning speed on the modification effect of fused silica, the modified lines were set at different scanning speeds when the laser single pulse energy was 5 μJ and the repetition rate is 200 kHz. The effect of scanning speed on sample modification efficiency was obtained by observing and comparing the modification effect of samples obtained using different parameter combinations. [Figure 4](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f004) shows the modified morphology obtained using different parameter combinations. As shown in [Figure 4](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f004), when the scanning speed is less than 10 mm/s, the surface roughness and the edge collapse around the scanning line will increase as the scanning speed decreases. This is because when the scribing speed is low, the energy per unit area irradiated by the laser pulse on the surface of the material is high, which easily causes ablation and melting, the heat affected area is large, and there are many splashes, as shown in [Figure 4](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f004)a. When the scanning speed is 10 mm/s, the section roughness and the edge collapse of the glass reach the minimum, as shown in [Figure 3](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f003)c. When the speed is greater than 10 mm/s, the energy radiated by the laser pulse on the unit area of the material surface is low, resulting in the discontinuity of the scanning line area, as shown in [Figure 4](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f004)b.

![Image 21: Crystals 13 00309 g004](https://www.mdpi.com/crystals/crystals-13-00309/article_deploy/html/images/crystals-13-00309-g004-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309#fig_body_display_crystals-13-00309-f004)

This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the journal *Crystals* (MDPI) in 2023, titled "Repair of Fused Silica Damage Using Selective Femtosecond Laser-Induced Etching." The paper was authored by Zhenhua Fang, Jing Chen, Xiaolong Jiang, Chuanchao Zhang, Lijuan Zhang, Jingxuan Wang, Xiaoyu Luan, Haijun Wang, Qiankun Wu, and Wei Liao, from the Laser Fusion Research Center, China Academy of Engineering Physics, Mianyang, China. The article has DOI 10.3390/cryst13020309, was submitted on 28 January 2023, revised 3 February 2023, accepted 9 February 2023, and published 13 February 2023. It received 4224 article views and 5 citations, and belongs to the Topics section on Laser-Induced Damage Properties of Optical Materials.

**Purpose/Problem:** Fused silica is a critical component of high-power laser systems, and surface damage points frequently occur during high-throughput operation. If not repaired in time, damage expands dramatically. Traditional repair methods (CO2 laser ablation or femtosecond excision) ablate material point-by-point, generating microcracks, thermal accumulation, and residual stresses that require secondary smoothing operations, severely limiting efficiency—especially when many damage points are present.

**Proposed Method:** The authors propose a new approach using in-volume, selective femtosecond laser-induced etching. In this method, the laser irradiates material at energies below the ablation threshold, causing chemical restructuring (the Si-O-Si bond angle of 144° decreases, and the material becomes amorphous and more reactive to etchants). A femtosecond laser scans a 3D hollow trajectory around the damage point (e.g., a cylinder with 1 mm radius and 500 μm height, or a 2 mm-side rectangle with 500 μm height), then the entire sample is immersed in an etching solution. The modified material reacts faster than the unmodified substrate, so the etching solution permeates along the modified trajectory and removes the damaged area as a whole piece. Multiple damage points can be etched synchronously, so etching efficiency is not affected by the number of damage points.

**Key Experimental Parameters and Results:**
- Laser: 1030 nm wavelength, 290 fs pulse width, repetition frequency 50–500 kHz, single pulse energy 1–10 μJ.
- Optimal modification parameters: single pulse energy ~2–5 μJ, repetition frequency ~200–500 kHz, scanning speed ~10 mm/s.
- Sample: Corning 7980 fused silica, dimensions 4 mm × 6 mm × 50 mm, polished on four sides.
- Etching solutions: potassium hydroxide (KOH) at 58% mass fraction was the primary etchant; 5% hydrofluoric acid (HF) was used as a control.
- Substrate etching rates were ~1 μm/h (KOH) and ~2 μm/h (HF), less than one-thousandth of substrate thickness (negligible).
- Etch selectivity ratio between modified and unmodified areas can be as high as 1000:1.
- KOH has higher etching selectivity than HF; the formation of a silicon-rich structure SiOx (x>2) is the reason for KOH's better etching efficiency.
- Scanning speeds below 10 mm/s caused increased surface roughness, edge collapse, and splashing due to excessive energy per unit area; speeds above 10 mm/s caused discontinuous scanning lines.
- The weak reaction between the etching solution and the substrate homogenizes the interface, eliminating the need for secondary smoothing treatments used in traditional methods.

**Chemical Reactions:** The paper provides the reactions of fused silica with HF (producing SiF4 and H2O) and with KOH (producing SiO3 and H2O).

**Advantages over traditional methods:** (1) Greatly reduced repair workload since the material is removed as a whole piece rather than point-by-point ablation; (2) synchronous etching of multiple damage points; (3) interface homogenization during etching eliminates secondary processing; (4) lower laser energy reduces microcrack formation in brittle materials.
args.key_excerpts: "In this paper, a new method using in-volume, selective femtosecond laser-induced etching to repair the damage of fused silica is proposed. The region irradiated by femtosecond laser becomes more susceptible to the etching solution due to its constitutive characteristics having undergone chemical restructuring."

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Reduced material loss caused by Electron Beam Lithography in thin-film lithium niobate through post-process annealing ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0925346724002325

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research article published in Optical Materials (Volume 149, March 2024, Article 115049) titled "Reduced material loss caused by Electron Beam Lithography in thin-film lithium niobate through post-process annealing." The paper investigates how high-energy electron beams used in Electron Beam Lithography (EBL) introduce material damage and increase optical loss in thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN), and demonstrates that post-process annealing can effectively repair this damage.

Key findings:
- The authors compared EBL and Deep Ultraviolet Lithography (DUV) techniques to systematically analyze loss sources in TFLN fabrication.
- High-energy electron beams (above 100 keV) used in EBL penetrate the TFLN surface and accumulate within the LN, causing damage through radiolysis, knock-on displacement, and electrostatic charging, leading to increased material absorption loss.
- A new slow-heating post-process annealing method was designed to repair fabrication damage, reducing waveguide loss by approximately 50% and increasing the intrinsic Q-factor of micro-ring resonators by around 100%.
- They achieved an intrinsic Q-factor (Q_int) as high as 3.93 × 10^6 in X-cut TFLN micro-ring resonators, corresponding to waveguide loss of approximately 0.1 dB/cm.

Methodology:
- Used a 600 nm thick X-cut TFLN single-crystal film prepared via the Smart Cut method from NanoLN, with a 4.7 μm thick SiO2 bonding layer and 500 μm thick Si substrate.
- Fabricated a series of all-pass micro-ring resonators with bending radius of r=300 μm, waveguide widths from 1.1 μm to 2.0 μm, and coupling gaps from 0.4 μm to 0.65 μm.

Background context: TFLN is valued for its low optical loss, remarkable optical nonlinearity, and electro-optic properties. --- SOURCE 11: Directional atomic layer etching of lithium niobate using Br-based plasma ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2511.01825v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research paper (arXiv preprint) reporting the first directional atomic layer etching (ALE) process for lithium niobate (LiNbO3, LN) using Br-based plasma chemistry, specifically HBr/BCl3/Ar plasma for surface modification followed by Ar plasma for removal.

**Key findings:**
- A directional ALE process for LN was developed using sequential exposures of HBr/BCl3/Ar plasma (40s, 300W ICP, 5W RIE, 30V DC bias) followed by Ar plasma (60s, 300W ICP, 6W RIE, 45V DC bias) at 10 mTorr chamber pressure.
- At 0°C: etch per cycle (EPC) of 1.04±0.01 nm/cycle with 84.6% synergy; half-cycle EPCs were 0.02 nm/cycle (HBr/BCl3/Ar) and 0.14 nm/cycle (Ar).
- At 200°C: EPC increased to 1.25 nm/cycle but synergy dropped to 30% (due to increased spontaneous etching and ion energy distribution); surface remained atomically smooth (Rq=0.25±0.03 nm after 20 cycles, unchanged from control).
- HBr chemistry reduces redeposition compared to F- and Cl-based plasmas due to higher vapor pressures of Br-based etch products. A Cl2/BCl3 comparison process produced rougher surfaces at the same temperature.
- An isotropic HBr-based ALE process was also developed (H2 plasma + HBr/BCl3/Ar plasma) yielding 1.43 nm/cycle with 97.9% synergy at 0°C and smoother surfaces (Rq=0.77 nm) than previously reported Cl2/BCl3 chemistry.
- XPS analysis showed surface bromine concentration of 0.50±0.04% after 50 cycles at 0°C, decreasing to 0.35±0.06% at 200°C, confirming better removal of Br etch products at higher temperature.
- A TFLN grating structure (total etch depth 223 nm, 200 cycles) etched entirely by ALE at 200°C showed NO aspect ratio dependent etching (ARDE) down to the smallest tested gap of 150 nm, in contrast to ion milling where ARDE manifests at gaps below 300 nm for similar depths.
- 50 cycles of ALE on a TFLN waveguide chip reduced surface roughness from Rq=2.07 nm to Rq=0.34 nm (84% reduction), with minimal lateral etching (waveguide top width maintained).
- At 200°C, 120 cycles (149 nm etch) produced no surface roughening (Rq=0.28 nm).

**Materials and methods:** Bulk 3-inch 5% MgO-doped LN wafers (G & H Photonics), diced to 7x7 mm substrates; patterned with AZ5214E photoresist (0°C) or HSQ via e-beam lithography (200°C); etched in Oxford Instruments PlasmaPro 100 Cobra system; characterized by AFM and XPS.

**Significance:** This is the first reported directional ALE process for lithium niobate and the first to use Br-based chemistry. The combined directional and isotropic ALE processes could enable complete TFLN device fabrication flow, overcoming limitations of physical Ar+ ion milling including sidewall roughness, redeposition, ARDE, and lack of nanometer-level etch depth control. Potential applications include coupler gratings, periodically-poled LN devices, and low-loss waveguides for integrated photonics.

**Funding/acknowledgements:** Supported by Oxford Instruments and the Broadcom Innovation Fund at Caltech; work carried out in part at JPL/Caltech under NASA contract; facilities at Kavli Nanoscience Institute and Beckman Institute at Caltech.
</summary>

"Here, we report a directional ALE process for LN consisting of sequential exposures of HBr/BCl3/Ar plasma for surface modification and Ar plasma for removal. The HBr chemistry is found to decrease redeposition compared to F- and Cl-based plasmas, which we attribute to the higher vapor pressures of Br-based products."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research paper (published June 9, 2006, in J. Vac. Sci. Technol. A) investigating plasma etching of proton-exchanged lithium niobate (PE-LN). The paper is authored by H. Hu, A. P. Milenin, R. B. Wehrspohn, H. Hermann, and W. Sohler from the University of Paderborn (Germany) and the Max Planck Institute of Microstructure Physics (Halle, Germany).

CONTEXT AND PROBLEM: Lithium niobate (LiNbO3, LN) is important for integrated optics due to its electro-optical, acousto-optical, and nonlinear optical properties. Plasma etching of LN with fluorine gases is limited by redeposition of LiF (melting point >800°C), which causes low etch rates and nonvertical walls. Proton exchange (PE) replaces Li ions with protons (up to 85% substitution), greatly reducing LiF formation and improving etchability.

METHODOLOGY: Z-cut LN samples were proton-exchanged in pure benzoic acid at 240°C for 5 hours (PE depth 2.8 µm). A 120–400 nm Cr layer served as the etch mask. Etching was performed using either a parallel-plate RIE (Tepla 100-E) or an inductively coupled plasma ICP-RIE (Oxford Plasmalab System 100 with ICP 380 source). Five experimental conditions were tested with various gases (CF4, SF6, CHF3/Ar), chamber pressures, powers, and cooling conditions.

KEY RESULTS (from Table I):
1. CF4 at 500 mTorr: PE-LN etch rate 480 nm/h (selectivity vs Cr = 3.43:1); pure LN rate was 157 nm/h; surface cracks observed.
2. SF6 at 500 mTorr: PE-LN etch rate 1.53 µm/h (selectivity vs Cr = 46:1); pure LN could not be etched at all; highly isotropic etching with significant underetching (3.5–4.0 µm/h lateral rates) and strongly nonvertical side walls.
3. SF6 ICP-RIE at 6 mTorr, 1500 W, 153 V dc bias, He-cooled: PE-LN rate 2.74 µm/h (selectivity 30:1).
4. CHF3/Ar ICP-RIE at 6 mTorr, 1500 W, 122 V dc bias, He-cooled: PE-LN rate 2.88 µm/h (selectivity 48:1).
5. CHF3/Ar ICP-RIE at 6 mTorr, 1500 W, 130 V dc bias, NO cooling: PE-LN rate 5.76 µm/h (selectivity 32:1). This condition yielded nearly vertical etched walls (82° angle) with negligible underetching.

TEMPERATURE EFFECT: Etching rate nearly doubled (2.88 to 5.76 µm/h) without He-backside cooling due to the volatility of NbF5 (boiling point ~234°C), confirming substrate temperature dependence.

APPLICATIONS: Using recipe 5, photonic crystal waveguide structures were successfully fabricated with pore diameter of 340 nm, interpore distance of 500 nm, and etch depth of about 1.5 µm.

CONCLUSION: The best result was achieved with CHF3/Ar gas at 6 mTorr chamber pressure and 130 V dc bias (ICP-RIE, no cooling), yielding ~5.7 µm/h etch rate, 32:1 selectivity to Cr mask, negligible underetching, and nearly vertical walls — dramatically improved over literature values of ~0.6 µm/h for PE-LN. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a ScienceDirect research article (published in Thin Solid Films, Volume 768, Article 139719, dated 1 March 2023, DOI: 10.1016/j.tsf.2023.139719) authored by Eric Lang, Thomas Beechem, Anthony McDonald, Tom Friedmann, Roy H. Olsson III, Jeffrey O. Stevens, Blythe G. Clark, and Khalid Hattar.

The study systematically examines defect structures formed in lithium niobate (LiNbO3, LNO) as a function of ion irradiation and post-irradiation annealing. The research is motivated by the need to improve crystal ion slicing—a process where ion irradiation creates a buried defective sacrificial layer in bulk single-crystal LNO that can be fractured or etched to produce thin films for RF and photonic applications, as sputter-deposited films are lower quality than bulk crystals.

METHODOLOGY: The researchers used 128° Y-cut LiNbO3 wafers (100 mm diameter, 350 µm thick, from Roditi International) diced into ~1 cm² coupons. They systematically varied:
- Ion species: H, He, and N
- Irradiation energy: 150 keV to 2 MeV
- Implantation fluence: 1×10^12 to 1×10^18 ions/cm²
- Post-irradiation heat treatment: 250 to 750°C

Irradiation was performed using a 350 kV HVEE implanter or a 3 MV NEC single-ended Pelletron accelerator. Resulting defect structures were analyzed via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and Raman spectroscopy. SRIM (Stopping and Range of Ions in Matter) calculations were used to model ion rest locations and matrix damage distributions.

KEY RESULTS:
- Defect formation suitable for fracture-based processes (ion slicing) can be achieved with He ion implantation using a fluence of 1×10^18 ions/cm² followed by heat treatment at 250 or 500°C.
- N ion implantation causes significantly more displacement damage than other species.
- Other irradiation and annealing recipes mimicking material fabrication conditions show defect evolution in LNO dependent on irradiation conditions.
- He implantation can cause amorphization through formation of He "bubbles" that coalesce under annealing (drawing on prior work showing similar behavior in gadolinium zirconate, where bubbles formed and grew into chains when annealed to ~350°C).

BACKGROUND CONTEXT: Ion implantation is commonly used in LNO device fabrication for optical property engineering (waveguides, modulators, second harmonic generators, SAW devices). Prior work has used He, N, O, B, and H ions with annealing to sculpt LNO optical properties. Crystal ion slicing in LNO has been hampered by challenges in repeatability and scalability, motivating this systematic study.

The article concludes that a buried damage layer suitable for fracture-based processing may be possible with He implantation at 1×10^18 ions/cm² and annealing at 250 or 500°C. The paper has 5 citations and 5 Mendeley readers, and cites 40 references.

One notable citing article (Huang R. et al., Vacuum, 2024) builds on this work by studying He ion-implanted LNO thin film exfoliation and transferring LiNbO3 films to amorphous SiO2 via Ar plasma-activated bonding, successfully fabricating LNOI substrates and etching Y-shaped branching waveguides.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IEEE Spectrum news article (published 16 January 2018, updated same day) by Alexander Hellemans reports on a breakthrough by Harvard University researchers in plasma etching lithium niobate (LiNbO3) for optoelectronic chips. Lithium niobate is a hard, chemically inert crystalline material with exceptional optical properties used in electro-optics, acousto-optics, and nonlinear optics, found in devices like cellphones, optical modulators, and frequency converters. Unlike silicon, lithium niobate is not amenable to chemical etching, and previous techniques (ion diffusion, proton exchange) produced too-low optical-index contrast for effective waveguides. Hybrid silicon-lithium niobate approaches were also impractical due to insufficient light coupling. The Harvard team, led by Marko Lončar, applied plasma reactive ion etching—bombarding the chip surface with argon ions to remove material exposed by an electron-beam lithography mask—to create micro-ring and micro-racetrack resonators (~1 micrometer wide, 80 µm curvature radius). Results showed optical power losses of only 50% over 1 meter, compared to 99% loss in previous lithium niobate devices, due to improved optical confinement. Independent expert Marco Bazzan (University of Padova) called the result remarkable, noting it could elevate lithium niobate resonators above standard silicon photonics and holds importance for integrated quantum photonics. Lončar's team plans next to integrate niobate into silicon photonic processing, though this is challenging as niobium is not favored in the silicon industry; the team may need dedicated fabrication facilities or to couple separately-made niobium and silicon chips. Bazzan noted the thin-film substrates are commercially available, meaning the technological steps are ready for standardization.
</summary>

"Over the years, we have dealt with many materials that have nice properties but that are difficult to work with," says Marko Lončar, who led the research. "Diamond is actually easier to etch than niobate, but it doesn't exist as thin films."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Advanced Etching Techniques of LiNbO3 Nanodevices ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific research article published in Nanomaterials (Basel) journal on October 18, 2023 (DOI: 10.3390/nano13202789), titled "Advanced Etching Techniques of LiNbO3 Nanodevices" by Bowen Shen, Di Hu, Cuihua Dai, Xiaoyang Yu, Xiaojun Tan, Jie Sun, Jun Jiang, and Anquan Jiang from the School of Microelectronics at Fudan University, Shanghai, China.

**Context:** Lithium niobate (LNO) is a versatile single crystal used in surface acoustic wave devices, optoelectronic devices, and ferroelectric/domain-wall memory devices due to its electro-optic and piezoelectric properties. However, its nanofabrication remains challenging, particularly achieving high etching rates and good sidewall angles without compromising ferroelectric properties.

**Background on etching techniques:** The prevailing etching techniques include dry etching (F-based and Cl-based gas), wet etching (acid HF/HNO3 and alkaline SC-1/NaOH), focused-ion-beam etching, and hybrid approaches. F-based gas creates LiF by-products that accumulate on sidewalls and reduce sidewall angles (e.g., Kozlov 2023 achieved only 60-75° angles). Cl-based gas creates easily-removed LiCl by-products but has lower etching rates. Proton-exchanged (PE) LNO prevents LiF formation and enables 90° sidewall angles, but damages ferroelectric properties, making it unsuitable for domain-wall memory devices.

**Methodology:** Ten LNO samples (X-cut, 5 mol.% Mg-doped) were prepared with different mask types (Cr, Ni, and SiO2) and etched using different instruments (RIE vs. ICP) and processes. Masks were fabricated using electron-beam lithography, thermal evaporation, electroplating, and PECVD. Samples underwent various combinations of dry etching, proton exchange (180°C molten benzoic acid), high-temperature reduction treatment (400°C in 10% H2 + Ar), wet etching in SC-1 solution, and annealing with Al film coverage.

**Key results (10 samples):**
- Sample 1 (Cr mask, RIE dry etch): 10 nm/min etching rate, ~60° sidewall angle, 3:1 selectivity
- Sample 2 (Ni mask, RIE dry etch): 11 nm/min, ~72° sidewall angle, 5.5:1 selectivity
- Sample 3 (Cr mask, proton exchange + RIE): 13 nm/min, ~70° angle, exchange depth ~210 nm, β1 phase detected by XRD
- Sample 4 (SiO2 mask, high-temp reduction + SC-1 wet etch): ~49 nm depth, asymmetric sidewalls (44° in +Z, 85° in −Z directions)
- Sample 5 (Cr mask, high-temp reduction + RIE): 11.5 nm/min, ~85° sidewall angle
- Sample 6 (Cr mask, RIE + high-temp reduction + wet etch): ~112 nm depth, inward concavity sidewall due to Cr-LNO alloying
- Sample 7 (Cr mask, RIE + Al layer + annealing + wet etch): ~115 nm depth, perfect 90° sidewall angle—the optimized hybrid process that preserves ferroelectric properties
- Sample 8 (Cr mask, ICP): 37 nm/min, ~71° angle, but Cr mask severely consumed
- Sample 9 (Ni mask, ICP): 79 nm/min, ~83° sidewall angle (best ICP result)
- Sample 10 (SiO2 mask, ICP with SF6/BCl3/Ar): 108 nm/min etching rate, 0.86:1 selectivity, ~65° sidewall angle

**Conclusions:** The optimized RIE dry etching combined with wet etching after high-temperature reduction treatment achieved 10 nm/min etching rate with pristine 90° sidewall angles. ICP dry etching with Ni masks achieved 79 nm/min with 83° angles. SiO2 masks enabled 108 nm/min rate with 0.86:1 selectivity, advancing semiconductor-process compatibility. Ni masks outperformed Cr masks in both RIE and ICP due to higher hardness. The hybrid process (dry etching + Al film annealing + wet etching) produced damage-free, perfectly smooth 90° sidewalls while preserving LNO ferroelectric properties, making it suitable for large-scale domain-wall memory array fabrication.

**Funding:** Supported by the Natural Science Foundation of Shanghai (23ZR1403900), the National Key Basic Research Program of China (2019YFA0308500 and 2022YFA1402904), and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (62174034).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Ultimately, after employing RIE dry etching combined with wet etching, following a high-temperature reduction treatment, an etching rate of 10 nm/min and pretty 90° sidewall angles were achieved. Furthermore, high etching rates of 79 nm/min with steep sidewall angles of 83° were obtained using ICP dry etching. Additionally, using SiO2 masks, a high etching rate of 108 nm/min and an etching selectivity ratio of 0.86:1 were achieved."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Isotropic atomic layer etching of MgO-doped lithium niobate using sequential exposures of H2 and SF6/Ar plasmas ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2310.10592v3

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (arXiv preprint 2310.10592) reports the first atomic layer etching (ALE) process developed for lithium niobate (LiNbO3, LN), a ferroelectric crystal critical for integrated photonics due to its large second-order optical nonlinearity and periodic poling capability. The process is isotropic ALE for xx-cut MgO-doped lithium niobate using sequential exposures of H2 and SF6/Ar plasmas.

Key findings:
- Etch rate of 1.59±0.02 nm/cycle with a synergy of 96.9% for the nominal H2 + SF6/Ar recipe
- Both half-steps exhibited saturation (self-limiting behavior), though the SF6/Ar step showed soft saturation attributed to diffusion-limited fluorination and a hydrogen concentration gradient
- Alternate recipes using O2/SF6 or Cl2/BCl3 plasma exposures yielded EPCs of 2.24±0.02 and 1.65±0.03 nm/cycle with synergies of 99.5% and 91.5%, respectively
- The process reduced sidewall surface roughness of TFLN (thin-film lithium niobate) waveguides etched by physical Ar+ milling by 30% (from Rq=0.82±0.25 nm to 0.55±0.13 nm after 50 cycles) without additional wet processing
- The lateral etch rate of ~1 nm/cycle per side versus 1.59 nm/cycle vertical rate confirms the largely isotropic nature of the process
- XPS analysis revealed formation and redeposition of LiF and MgF2 (low-volatility compounds) on the surface after ALE, and increased surface Mg concentration suggesting MgF2 formation

Methodology details: Samples were 3-inch 5% mol MgO-doped LN wafers (G & H Photonics) diced to 7mm×7mm, etched in an Oxford Instruments PlasmaPro 100 Cobra system. The nominal recipe used 40-second H2 plasma (300W ICP, 52.5W RIE, 209V DC bias) followed by 40-second SF6/Ar plasma (300W ICP, 3.5W RIE, 50V DC bias, 17 sccm SF6, 35 sccm Ar), with 5-second Ar purges between steps, 10 mTorr chamber pressure, and substrate cooled to 0°C. Etch depths were measured via AFM on photolithographically defined step patterns.

Application: The ALE process could serve as a post-processing treatment to smooth sidewall roughness and corrugations in periodically-poled TFLN devices, thereby increasing photonic performance. This addresses a key limitation where propagation losses from surface roughness and corrugations currently restrict on-chip TFLN device performance to at least an order of magnitude below intrinsic limits.

Funding: Supported by Oxford Instruments and NSF Award #2234390, with work carried out at JPL/Caltech and Kavli Nanoscience Institute. A US provisional patent was submitted on this technology by I.I.C., J.S., R.S., A.M., F.G., and A.J.M.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We report an isotropic ALE process for xx-cut MgO-doped LN using sequential exposures of H2 and SF6/Ar plasmas. We observe an etch rate of 1.59±0.02 nm/cycle with a synergy of 96.9%."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: TMAH vs. KOH Silicon Etch | Rogue Valley Microdevices ---
URL: https://roguevalleymicrodevices.com/tmah-vs-koh-silicon-etch

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Rogue Valley Microdevices (a pure play MEMS foundry) provides a comprehensive technical guide comparing TMAH (tetramethylammonium hydroxide) and KOH (potassium hydroxide) anisotropic wet silicon etchants for MEMS fabrication.

**Core Similarity:** Both etchants are hot alkaline solutions that anisotropically etch silicon along crystal planes, producing the same fundamental geometry: 54.74° sidewalls along (111) planes on (100) silicon, creating V-grooves, pyramidal pits, trapezoidal cavities, and thin membranes. The crystal structure, not the etchant, determines the shape.

**Key Differences:**
- **Chemistry/CMOS compatibility:** KOH contains potassium (alkali metal ions) that can contaminate gate oxides and degrade MOS devices—NOT CMOS compatible. TMAH is organic and metal ion free—CMOS compatible and safe for wafers with active devices.
- **Etch rate & anisotropy:** KOH provides the highest silicon etch rate and highest anisotropy (run at ~20-45% concentration, 70-80°C). TMAH etches more slowly with slightly lower anisotropy (run at ~20-25%, 80-90°C).
- **Mask selectivity:** KOH etches silicon dioxide relatively fast, so silicon nitride (LPCVD) is the preferred mask. TMAH has very high oxide selectivity, allowing a silicon dioxide mask without added nitride steps.
- **Aluminum compatibility:** KOH attacks exposed aluminum quickly. TMAH can be buffered (with dissolved silicon and additives) to protect exposed aluminum and other metals, making it suitable for post-CMOS micromachining.
- **Surface finish:** KOH produces the smoothest surfaces; TMAH can roughen with hillocks unless optimized.
- **Cost:** KOH is lower cost and simpler; TMAH is more expensive but offers CMOS and metal compatibility.

**Etch Stops:** Both use heavily boron doped layers, buried oxide of SOI wafers, or electrochemical etch stops to define precise membrane thicknesses. Photoresist cannot survive either hot alkaline bath—hard masks (silicon nitride or silicon dioxide) are required.

**Selection Guidance:**
- Choose TMAH when: wafer carries CMOS devices or must avoid metal ion contamination; exposed aluminum/metal present during etch; silicon dioxide mask preferred.
- Choose KOH when: fastest etch rate, smoothest surfaces, and lowest cost are priorities, with no CMOS devices or exposed metals present.

**Rogue Valley Microdevices capabilities:** Offers both KOH and TMAH anisotropic wet silicon etching on 100mm, 150mm, and 200mm substrates in a class 100 cleanroom, with LPCVD silicon nitride and thermal oxide masks, front-to-back alignment, and combination with dry etch/DRIE for vertical sidewalls.

**Typical Applications:** TMAH for post-CMOS micromachining, membranes/cavities near metal layers, pressure sensors and microfluidic structures requiring CMOS compatibility, contamination-sensitive flows. KOH for bulk micromachining, V-grooves for optical fiber alignment, pressure sensor membranes, through-wafer holes, pyramidal texturing, and fast economical deep etching.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"KOH is an alkali metal hydroxide that carries potassium, while TMAH is a purely organic quaternary ammonium hydroxide that contains no metal ions. That single distinction drives the most important practical difference between them, which is compatibility with CMOS devices."

## Patent WO2009008958A2 - Method of Post Etch Polymer Residue Removal

### Patent Overview
This is a WIPO (PCT) patent application filed by Lam Research Corp, titled "Method of post etch polymer residue removal." The patent's legal status is listed as "Ceased." The inventors are Seokmin Yun, Mark Wilcoxson, Ji Zhu, Kevin Chuang, Hsiao Wei Chang, and David Lou. It has a French language version and a related publication WO2009008958A3. Application number: PCT/US2008/007759.

### Technical Field and Problem
The invention relates to semiconductor substrate processing, specifically an improved technique for removing post-etch polymer residues from substrate surfaces through optimization of dry and wet processes. The context is the deep sub-micron regime where IC chips contain tens of millions of devices. The industry has transitioned to copper interconnects and low-k dielectric materials (instead of aluminum and silicon dioxide) to reduce electrical resistance and parasitic capacitance.

### Background
- Copper interconnects are fabricated using the dual damascene process, the most popular dielectric etch approach.
- Damascene process: metal conductor pattern embedded in dielectric material, metal deposited to fill trenches, excess metal removed via chemical-mechanical polishing.
- The damascene etch process uses mixtures of fluorocarbon, hydrofluorocarbon, oxygen, and nitrogen gases, which leave polymer residues on dielectric sidewalls and bottoms.
- Two etching schemes: photoresist (PR) mask scheme and hard mask scheme.
- In the PR mask scheme, stripping chemicals can damage the low-k dielectric film layer.
- In the hard mask scheme, PR stripping is avoided but the hard mask must be carefully removed.
- Conventional wet chemical cleaning is adept at removing metallic residues (like copper oxides) but struggles with carbon-containing organic residues in narrow vias/trenches, and prolonged exposure damages dielectric structures.

### Invention Summary
The invention provides a combined dry flash process followed by wet cleaning:
1. **Dry flash chemistry** is identified and applied in a short flash process (approximately 5-7 seconds) to selectively remove post-etch polymer residue while minimizing damage to the low-k dielectric film layer.
2. **Wet cleaning chemistry** is then applied to substantially remove the remaining polymer residue.

### Key Technical Details
- **Low-k dielectric film layer**: Formed via spin coating, dip coating, or CVD; materials include SiCOH and porous SiCOH; doped with carbon and sub-micron pores to lower dielectric constant.
- **Dry flash chemistry**: Includes low-pressure gases such as carbon-dioxide, oxygen, ammonia, nitrogen, hydrogen, methane, carbon monoxide, argon, or combinations. Exposure is isotropic (uniform in all directions). Uses oxidation or reduction processes to release polymer residue.
- **Dry flash parameters** (promising results): Pressure 5-40 mTorr (avg ~20 mTorr), flow rate 50-1000 sccm (avg ~400 sccm), power 50-1000W (avg ~500W), exposure time 3-20 seconds (avg 5-10 seconds).
- **Wet cleaning chemistry**: Simple chemistries such as hydrogen fluoride and ammonium fluoride; applied via proximity head (as liquid meniscus), brush box, wet tank dip, or spray nozzle.
- **Meniscus**: A volume of liquid chemistry contained by surface tension between a proximity head's opposing surface and the substrate surface; controllable and moveable.
- The flash process is kept short because prolonged exposure damages dielectric walls—carbon atoms in the low-k dielectric react with free radicals in the plasma.

### System Embodiments
- **Figure 2A**: Three-chamber system — first housing chamber (plasma etching reactor with RF source, TCP or capacitive coupled plasma, shower head for etchant), second housing chamber (flash chemistry applicator/shower head for dry flash), third housing chamber (wet cleaning applicator/proximity head with meniscus delivery).
- **Figure 2B**: Alternative single-chamber configuration where one shower head supplies both etchant and dry flash chemistry, followed by a second chamber for wet cleaning. This reduces cycle time and prevents ambient air contamination from chamber-to-chamber transfer.
- A computing system communicatively connects to controls to adjust parameters (pressure, flow rate, power, exposure time) of the etchant, dry flash, and wet cleaning chemistries, and controls RF generators and vacuum port outlets.

### Process Method (Figure 3)
1. Receive substrate after post-etch operation (operation 310).
2. Analyze polymer residue characteristics and identify dry flash chemistry (operation 315).
3. Apply dry flash chemistry using a short flash process (operation 320).
4. Analyze polymer residue and dry flash chemistry characteristics; identify wet cleaning chemistry (operation 325).
5. Apply wet cleaning chemistry in controlled manner (operation 330).
6. Form additional layers/features to define integrated circuit chips (operation 335).

### Advantages
- Enables use of less complex, less expensive wet cleaning chemistry.
- Greatly reduces wet cleaning application time since substantial residue is removed by the flash process.
- Less damage to low-k dielectric film layer and higher throughput.
- Reduced cleaning cost and effective polymer-free substrate production.

### Classifications
Primary classification areas: H10P70/00 (Cleaning of wafers, substrates or parts of devices), H10P70/20 (Cleaning during device manufacture), H10P70/23 and H10P70/234 (Cleaning during processing of insulating materials, particularly formation of vias or contact holes), and H10P72/00 series (Handling or holding of wafers/substrates during manufacture, including wet etching apparatus). --- SOURCE 1: Thin-Film Lithium Niobate Modulation Technology_Baiduwiki ---
URL: https://baike.baidu.com/en/item/Thin-Film%20Lithium%20Niobate%20Modulation%20Technology/4652042

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Thin-Film Lithium Niobate (TFLN) Modulation Technology is an optical modulation technology based on Lithium Niobate (LiNbO₃) material, used for ultra-high-speed optical modules (800G, 1.6T, and higher). It leverages the linear electro-optic effect (Pockels Effect) and thin-film fabrication processes (ion slicing, wafer bonding) to create sub-micron waveguides on substrates like silicon, sapphire, or silicon dioxide, forming "Lithium Niobate-on-Insulator" structures.

KEY SPECIFICATIONS:
- Ultra-high electro-optic bandwidth: commercial ≥110 GHz, laboratory demonstrations exceeding 170 GHz
- Drive voltage reduced to 1-2V (vs. much higher for bulk devices)
- Power consumption as low as several tens of femtojoules per bit
- Maximum wafer size currently 150mm (6-inch), with 200mm (8-inch) wafers under development
- Compatible with silicon photonics platforms and standard CMOS/semiconductor manufacturing processes

DEVELOPMENT HISTORY:
- Lithium niobate used in electro-optic modulators since the 1960s
- Traditional bulk modulators were limited by large size (mm-to-cm scale), high drive voltages, and poor silicon compatibility
- Maturation of thin-film technology resolved these integration challenges
- 2019: Guangku Technology acquired Lumentum's lithium niobate high-speed modulator product line
- 2023: Feisiling Microelectronics launched a Coherent IC-TROSA integrating a miniaturized thin-film lithium niobate chip at ECOC
- 2026 is regarded by the industry as the inaugural year for large-scale commercial adoption

APPLICATION AREAS:
1. Optical communications: core chip for 800G/1.6T/3.2T optical modules, coherent communications, PAM4 schemes, data center interconnects, long-haul backbone networks (driven by AI computing power growth)
2. Passive optical networks (PON): supports multiple standards on single platform, low insertion loss, operates in outdoor wide-temperature environments without active cooling
3. Quantum information processing: ultra-low loss waveguides maintain qubit coherence, χ(2) nonlinearity supports on-chip photon pair generation, can integrate photon sources/routers/detectors on one substrate
4. Lidar and free-space sensing: eye-safe ~1.55 µm band transparency, extends into mid-infrared
5. Microwave photonics and aerospace: radiation resistance, suitable for satellite payloads, phased array antennas, RF-over-fiber links
6. Sensing and spectroscopy: broad optical window enables compact spectrometers, portable/battery-powered applications in industrial IoT and medical diagnostics

RESEARCH PROGRESS:
- Heterogeneous integration (e.g., "universal ion knife" lift-off transfer of TFLN onto silicon nitride wafers) has produced hybrid-waveguide modulators with >110 GHz bandwidth and 260 Gbit/s PAM-4 transmission
- Novel electrode designs (e.g., periodically capacitive-loaded traveling-wave electrodes with 12-micron SiO₂ buffer layer) achieve 1.76V half-wave voltage in 7mm devices with only 1.3dB electro-optic response drop within 67 GHz
- Integration with AI chips (CMOS-compatible) is being explored with NVIDIA, Google, and Xizhi Technology completing verification; TFLN modulators can form "AI-LNOI" intelligent modulators for optoelectronic co-computing
- Industry (Feisiling) is advancing miniaturized folded electrode designs integrated into Coherent IC-TROSA for mass production; wafer size transitioning from 150mm to 200mm

CHALLENGES:
- Relatively large device size
- Immature differential drive schemes
- High packaging and heterogeneous integration complexity
- Insufficient long-term reliability verification
- Production yield and cost control during 6-inch to 8-inch wafer transition
- Only a few companies worldwide have mastered mass-production technology

The technology is transitioning from a "performance benchmark" to an "engineering necessity" driven by AI computing power demands for higher-speed, lower-power optical interconnects.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Thin-Film Lithium Niobate is currently one of the platforms capable of simultaneously providing >100 GHz electro-optic bandwidth, V-level drive voltage, and athermal operation. Its commercial bandwidth is generally ≥110 GHz, with laboratory demonstrations exceeding 170 GHz."
</key_excerpts>
