URL: https://strathprints.strath.ac.uk/53356/1/Tong_Luo_ASS_2015_Investigation_of_focused_ion_beam_induced_damage_in_single.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper investigates focused ion beam (FIB) induced damage in single crystal diamond tools used for ultra-precision machining. The research was conducted by Zhen Tong (Harbin Institute of Technology) and Xichun Luo (University of Strathclyde, UK) and combines transmission electron microscope (TEM) measurements with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.

Methodology:
- A FEI Nova 200 nanolab dual beam FIB system with Ga ion source was used to irradiate a diamond tool's (1 0 0) rake face at three acceleration voltages: 8 kV, 16 kV, and 30 kV
- Ion fluences ranged from 7.54 × 10^20 to 9.71 × 10^20 ions/cm² depending on voltage
- Cross-sectional TEM samples were prepared using standard lift-out technique with Pt protection layers
- EFTEM, CBED (convergent beam electron diffraction), and elemental mapping were used to characterize damage layers
- Large-scale multi-particle collision MD simulations (1,217,161 atoms, using Tersoff-ZBL potentials in LAMMPS) emulated the ion-solid interactions

Key Results:
- FIB-induced damage layer thicknesses on diamond tool surfaces increased from 11.5 nm (8 kV) to 19.4 nm (16 kV) to 27.6 nm (30 kV) — increasing with beam energy
- The damage layers are amorphous carbon (a-C), consisting of a mixture of sp2 and sp3 hybridization, and accommodate significant implanted gallium
- MD simulations showed residual damage layers of 14.5 nm (8 keV) and 19.6 nm (16 keV), closely matching experimental results
- Maximum gallium implantation depths were 10.5 nm (8 keV) and 12.8 nm (16 keV), with gallium concentrated at the a-C/diamond interface (matching dark patches observed in EFTEM images)
- Higher beam voltages produced higher local thermal spikes (1454.6 K peak for 16 keV vs lower for 8 keV) and longer thermal spike lifetimes
- Number of atomic defects accumulates linearly up to an ion fluence of 2.0 × 10^14 ions/cm², then approaches a stable equilibrium value due to competition between damage formation and sputtering
- Residual defects per ion collision: 271 (8 keV) and 416 (16 keV), with recrystallization completing within 0.8 ps
- Higher beam voltages increase the amorphization level (confirmed by CBED showing weaker diamond signals)

Conclusions & Recommendations:
- FIB irradiation creates impulse-dependent damage layers in diamond tools
- The non-diamond phase of the residual damage layer will wear first during nanometric cutting, contributing to tool wear initiation (alongside compressive stress at tool tip sides)
- Low-energy FIB polishing is recommended when shaping diamond tool tips via FIB
- The 27.6 nm maximum damage layer is only ~1 part in 10^4 of a micro cutting tool's functional dimension, so ion-induced damage may be negligible for micro-scale applications but becomes critical for nanoscale multi-tip tools
- The study was funded by EPSRC (EP/K018345/1)
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The results indicate that during the FIB processing cutting tools made of natural single crystal diamond, the energetic Ga+ collision will create an impulse-dependent damage layer at the irradiated surface. For the tested beam voltages in a typical FIB system (from 8 kV to 30 kV), the thicknesses of the damaged layers formed on a diamond tool surface increased from 11.5 nm to 27.6 nm."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Avoiding Common Types of Lamella Defects Caused by the Focused Ion Beam ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_pKw8SMnFiM

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an educational video by Covalent (posted 25 April 2022, 381 views) featuring Ryan Dudschus, Covalent's resident expert on sample preparation for S/TEM analysis. The video summarizes common defects in S/TEM lamella caused by the focused ion beam (FIB) and strategies to avoid them.

Key content covered:

1. **Amorphous Layer Damage (Gallium Ion Damage)**: When using a 30 kV gallium ion beam, the FIB creates an amorphous damaged layer approximately 20 nanometers thick on the lamella surface. This damage causes blurry, low-quality TEM images due to electron scattering from embedded gallium islands and interstitial atoms. Critical insight: for an 80 nm lamella thinned with a 30 kV beam on both sides, up to 60 nm (30 nm per side) can be damaged, leaving only 20 nm of good material to image.

2. **Mitigation Strategy - Lower Beam Energies (Polishing)**: Dropping the FIB energy to 5 kV (polishing) reduces the damaged layer to about 6 nm thick, significantly improving image resolution and allowing atoms to be discerned. Dropping further to 2 kV reduces damage to roughly 3 nm thick. The damaged layer correlates nearly 1:1 with the FIB energy used. Some modern FIBs can operate at a few hundred volts for even better image quality.

3. **Redeposition**: The FIB beam has tails/sides that mill surrounding material in addition to the target window. This milled material can reattach to the lamella face, appearing as bubble-like deposits that cause grayscale and thickness variations in the TEM image, degrading resolution. Avoiding redeposition requires careful attention to milling materials, beam shape, tilt, and box placement—described as taking on the form of an art form.

The video thanks Mark (of Thermo Fisher) for providing the referenced paper by Gertz and Regnold (as transcribed) that demonstrates how gallium islands and interstitial atoms affect TEM imaging.
</summary>

"In 1a you're looking at amorphous layer damage which is this fuzzy layer that's caused by 30 kv gallium ion beam and you can see that this thickness is about 20-ish nanometers thick."

- Redeposition removal via RCA-1a solution (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O = 2:2:1) heated to 85°C

**Key Results (Section III):**

*RF Power Optimization (III.A):* RF power varied from 50 W to 500 W; etch rate ranged from 50 nm/min (50 W) to 107 nm/min (500 W). At low RF power (~50 W), sidewalls fully enveloped by redeposit; at 300 W, redeposit completely eliminated from sidewalls. However, above 300 W, line-edge roughness transferred to the WG causing striations, and WG damage (trenches/pits) occurred. Optimal RF power range determined as 100-200 W.

*Redeposit Cleaning (III.B):* RCA-1a solution superior to Piranha and RCA-1b. Optimized cleaning: 15 minutes each at 0° and 90° boat orientations (30 min total). Prolonged cleaning (beyond 30 min) caused chipping and peeling of WGs. Cleaning for 24 hours changed WG geometry (sidewall angles became asymmetric, film thickness reduced from 700 nm to ~630 nm). Properly cleaned samples had equal sidewall angles of ~70°.

*Soft vs. Hard Mask (III.C):* Soft (resist) mask produced striated sidewall defects that persisted regardless of RF power tuning; Cr hard mask produced markedly improved sidewall profiles.

*Hard Mask Comparison (III.D):* Cr hard mask produced granular features on sidewalls (due to Cr polycrystalline grain size of ~55 nm), while SiO2 mask produced striations and "trenching" at the base of sidewalls (attributed to charge buildup on insulating materials deflecting ions). Cr hard mask was selected for final fabrication.

*Optical Characterization (III.E):* Rib LNOI WGs fabricated with Cr mask using optimized parameters (Table II: RF 150 W, ICP 1500 W, 5 mTorr, 20 sccm Ar, 5°C, 30 min cleaning). WG dimensions: top width 600 nm, sidewall angle 70°, rib height 350 nm over 350 nm slab, single-mode at 1550 nm. Eight identical 4.5 mm straight WGs measured with lensed fibers (2.5 μm mode field diameter), no anti-reflection coatings. Transmission ranged from 0.075 (-11.2 dB) to 0.107 (-9.7 dB); average transmission 8.9 ± 1.3%, corresponding to -10.5 ± 0.6 dB total insertion loss (propagation + coupling). Upper-bound propagation loss estimated at ~2 dB/cm (assuming 4.8 dB/facet coupling loss). These values are comparable to literature.

**Key Conclusions:** A comprehensive, reproducible fabrication recipe for low-loss LNOI WGs was developed at the NIST NanoFab (a shared-use facility where the ICP RIE tool is also used for other materials including Al, Cr, Cr2O3, Mo, Ta, and Ti). The approach emphasizes RF power optimization to control sidewall redeposition, hard mask selection (Cr preferred over SiO2 and soft masks), and optimized wet cleaning protocol. The findings provide an accessible resource for advancing LNOI technology.
</summary>

"Using the recipe established, we realized optical WGs with total (propagation and coupling) loss value of -10.5 dB, comparable to established values found in the literature."

--- SOURCE 8: Analysis of Waveguides on Lithium Niobate Thin Films ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/8/5/191

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article titled "Analysis of Waveguides on Lithium Niobate Thin Films" published in the journal *Crystals* (2018, Volume 8, Issue 5, Article 191, DOI: 10.3390/cryst8050191) by Yiwen Wang, Zhihua Chen, and Hui Hu from the School of Physics, State Key Laboratory of Crystal Materials, Shandong University, Jinan, China. The paper was received 5 April 2018, revised 24 April 2018, accepted 24 April 2018, and published 27 April 2018.

**Purpose:** The study analyzes and compares three types of waveguides fabricated on single-crystal lithium niobate (LN) thin films — ridge waveguides (dry-etched), proton-exchange (PE) waveguides, and strip-loaded waveguides — using a full-vectorial finite difference method. The research focuses on single-mode conditions, optical power distribution, and bending loss at the telecommunication wavelength of 1.55 µm.

**Key Methodology:**
- Simulations used full-vectorial finite difference method with PML boundary conditions.
- LNOI films were x-cut with birefringence considered (ordinary n=2.211, extraordinary n=2.138 at 1550 nm).
- PE region refractive indices were 2.161 (ordinary) and 2.218 (extraordinary).
- Loading strip materials simulated: SiO2 (n=1.46), SiN (n=1.9), TiO2 (n=2.3), and Si (n=3.48).
- LN thickness was set at 0.5 µm; waveguide widths were 1 µm for single-mode operation.

**Key Results:**
1. **Single-mode conditions:** First-order TE and TM modes appeared at LN thicknesses of 0.6 µm and 0.7 µm, respectively. For ridge waveguides, single-mode limits were 1.1 µm (q-TE) and 1.06 µm (q-TM). PE waveguides only supported q-TE mode (since PE increases only extraordinary refractive index). For both PE and strip-loaded waveguides, width must decrease as thickness increases to maintain single-mode operation.

2. **Optical power distribution:** In the LN ridge waveguide, optical power in the LN layer was 85.6% for q-TE and 82.5% for q-TM. PE waveguides showed negligible power change with increasing PE thickness. For strip-loaded waveguides, q-TE power decreased slightly with strip thickness (notably for Si), while q-TM power initially increased then decreased, with maximum values at strip thicknesses of ~0.12 µm (SiO2), 0.07 µm (SiN), 0.07 µm (TiO2), and 0.07 µm (Si).

3. **Bending loss:** Bending loss decreased with increasing bending radius. LN ridge waveguides achieved low bending loss (10⁻⁵ dB/cm) at minimal radii of 15 µm (q-TE) and 20 µm (q-TM). PE waveguides showed bending loss decreasing with PE depth (34 dB/cm at D=0.2 µm vs. 10⁻¹¹ dB/cm at D=0.5 µm, both at 1 mm radius). For q-TM strip-loaded waveguides, an additional leakage loss mechanism exists: when the waveguide neff is smaller than that of nearby TE planar waveguides, the Ez field component excites the TE mode in adjacent planar waveguides, causing loss (minimum 57 dB/cm for 0.05 µm SiN strip). This leakage can be avoided by increasing strip thickness so neff exceeds that of nearby planar waveguides.

**Conclusions:** The study provides guidance for designing and fabricating high-density integrated optical components on LN thin films, including understanding mode confinement, power distribution trends, and minimizing bending/leakage losses. Work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (grants 61575111 and 11475105). Authors declared no conflict of interest.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Waveguides formed by etching, proton-exchange (PE), and strip-loaded on single-crystal lithium niobate (LN) thin film were designed and simulated by a full-vectorial finite difference method."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: Plasma Etching Lithium Niobate on an Optoelectronic Chip ---
URL: https://spectrum.ieee.org/lithium-niobate-a-new-and-viable-platform-for-optoelectronics

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IEEE Spectrum news article (published 16 January 2018, updated same day) by Alexander Hellemans reports on a breakthrough by Harvard University researchers in plasma etching lithium niobate (LiNbO3) for optoelectronic chips. Lithium niobate is a hard, chemically inert crystalline material with exceptional optical properties used in electro-optics, acousto-optics, and nonlinear optics, found in devices like cellphones, optical modulators, and frequency converters. Unlike silicon, lithium niobate is not amenable to chemical etching, and previous techniques (ion diffusion, proton exchange) produced too-low optical-index contrast for effective waveguides. Hybrid silicon-lithium niobate approaches were also impractical due to insufficient light coupling. The Harvard team, led by Marko Lončar, applied plasma reactive ion etching—bombarding the chip surface with argon ions to remove material exposed by an electron-beam lithography mask—to create micro-ring and micro-racetrack resonators (~1 micrometer wide, 80 µm curvature radius). Results showed optical power losses of only 50% over 1 meter, compared to 99% loss in previous lithium niobate devices, due to improved optical confinement. Independent expert Marco Bazzan (University of Padova) called the result remarkable, noting it could elevate lithium niobate resonators above standard silicon photonics and holds importance for integrated quantum photonics. Lončar's team plans next to integrate niobate into silicon photonic processing, though this is challenging as niobium is not favored in the silicon industry; the team may need dedicated fabrication facilities or to couple separately-made niobium and silicon chips. Bazzan noted the thin-film substrates are commercially available, meaning the technological steps are ready for standardization.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Over the years, we have dealt with many materials that have nice properties but that are difficult to work with," says Marko Lončar, who led the research. "Diamond is actually easier to etch than niobate, but it doesn't exist as thin films."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: Photorefraction Management in Lithium Niobate Waveguides: High-Temperature vs. Cryogenic Solutions ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2601.15817v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (arXiv preprint) investigates photorefraction management in lithium niobate (LiNbO3, LN) waveguides, comparing high-temperature and cryogenic operation strategies. Photorefraction—an optically induced change in refractive index and absorption caused by trapped charge carriers forming internal electric fields—limits nonlinear optical processes such as sum-frequency generation (SFG), second-harmonic generation (SHG), and spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) in LN-based devices.

METHODOLOGY: The study uses titanium in-diffused periodically-poled lithium niobate (Ti:PPLN) waveguides on congruent, z-cut LN substrates. Two experimental configurations were employed: (1) a high-temperature sample (320-470 K) using a 7 µm wide waveguide with 4.35 µm poling period for type-II SFG between a TM-polarized ~860 nm field (150 fs pulses from a Ti:Sapphire laser) and TE-polarized 1550 nm field, producing ~560 nm output; and (2) a cryogenic sample at ~7 K using a 5 µm wide waveguide with 9.90 µm poling period for type-0 SFG between 1570 nm and 960 nm pumps (both CW), producing ~595 nm output. The cryogenic setup used an Attocube attoDRY800 cryostat with controlled cooldown rate ≤1 K/min.

KEY FINDINGS:
- At high temperatures (above ~380 K), increasing the pump power causes a shift of the phase-matched SFG to shorter wavelengths (blue shift), but this is significantly suppressed at elevated temperatures due to increased carrier mobility and reduced polaron lifetime. Below 380 K, hysteresis in the phase-matching spectrum was observed, with no recovery within 4.5 minutes at 320 K.
- At cryogenic temperatures (7 K), photorefractive damage becomes much more severe due to "frozen in" charge carriers with very low mobility. Pyroelectric effects from cooldown also contribute to internal electric fields, particularly affecting TM-polarized beams.
- A critical photorefraction threshold was identified at cryogenic temperatures: approximately 18 mW pump power at ~960 nm with ~14 µW generated SFG power around 595 nm. Exceeding this causes serious device performance impairment.
- The proposed mitigation approach adapts the "optical cleaning" method (from Kösters et al. and Kirsch et al.) by coupling an auxiliary 532 nm green laser (1 mW) into the waveguide alongside the pump light. This green illumination successfully mobilizes trapped charge carriers even at 7 K, restoring the phase-matching spectrum toward an ideal sinc² shape and increasing generated power from 0.25 µW to 1.87 µW after 12 minutes of exposure.
- However, recovery is only partial. A persistent blue shift was observed throughout measurements (peak wavelength shifted from 964.16 nm to 963.48 nm), indicating that photorefractive damage is not fully reversible at cryogenic temperatures with the current green laser approach.

CONCLUSIONS: High-temperature operation is effective for suppressing photorefraction but incompatible with cryogenic applications. The green-laser-based optical cleaning method offers an alternative route for photorefraction management compatible with cryogenic operation and energy-constrained environments like space applications. Future work could optimize the auxiliary laser parameters (wavelength, pulsing, power, duration), study cryogenic material parameters and bi-polaron energy levels, and explore external electric fields or conductive coatings for improved charge carrier relaxation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The origins of photorefraction in LN are complex and involve various mechanisms, including one- and two-photon absorption on energy levels of intrinsic (e.g. Nb antisites and Li vacancies) and extrinsic (e.g. iron impurities) defects. The process is then followed by the ferroelectric photovoltaic effect, and the formation of stable charge distributions in the form of (bound) polarons."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Wideband thin-film lithium niobate modulator with low half-wave-voltage length product ---
URL: https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJ9d03e04e9a0ee503

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a peer-reviewed research article from Chinese Optics Letters (Vol. 19, Issue 6, page 060016, 2021) titled "Wideband thin-film lithium niobate modulator with low half-wave-voltage length product" by Xuecheng Liu, Bing Xiong (corresponding author), and colleagues from Tsinghua University's Beijing National Research Center for Information Science and Technology (BNRist). The article is part of a Special Issue on Lithium Niobate Based Photonic Devices and was received May 8, 2021, accepted May 14, 2021, and published online June 10, 2021 (DOI: 10.3788/COL202119.060016).

The paper proposes and demonstrates a novel thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) electro-optic modulator that achieves both wide modulation bandwidth and low half-wave-voltage length product simultaneously. Key innovations include: (1) an LN-silica hybrid waveguide that allows an electrode gap as narrow as 3 µm while maintaining low optical loss (a 100-nm-thick silica buffer layer reduces optical loss by more than two orders of magnitude, enabling loss below 0.1 dB/cm), (2) capacitively loaded traveling-wave electrodes (CL-TWEs) with periodically loaded T-rails to reduce microwave loss while maintaining narrow electrode gaps, and (3) a quartz substrate with low dielectric constant (instead of silicon) to achieve velocity matching and reduce microwave loss.

Key experimental results: The fabricated modulator with a 5-mm-long modulation region exhibits a half-wave voltage of only 3.4 V, a half-wave-voltage length product (VπL) of 1.7 V·cm, an extinction ratio beyond 17 dB, and a merely less than 2 dB roll-off in electro-optic response up to 67 GHz (only 1.3 dB roll-off at 67 GHz). Extended measurements with a 110 GHz VNA verified a 6 dB electrical bandwidth over 110 GHz, with a predicted 3 dB modulation bandwidth over 110 GHz. Total insertion loss was 17 dB for the 5-mm modulator, primarily from coupling losses. The RF electric field enhancement in the LN ridge waveguide exceeded 40% due to the 3-µm-spaced electrodes.

Fabrication details: The modulator was fabricated on TFLN-on-quartz wafer from NanoLN (600-nm-thick X-cut TFLN, 2-µm SiO2 bonding layer, 500-µm quartz substrate). The waveguide was patterned by EBL with HSQ and transferred by argon-based RIE, partially etched 300 nm, and covered with 100-nm SiO2 by PECVD. CL-TWEs were fabricated using a two-step process (PMMA lift-off for T-rails via EBL, then contact UV lithography for main electrodes, thickened to 1.4 µm by electroplating). Signal electrode width was 50 µm, unloaded electrode spacing 15 µm, T-rail period 50 µm with 90% duty cycle, and 3-µm T-rail gap.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A novel thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) electro-optic modulator is proposed and demonstrated. LiNbO3-silica hybrid waveguide is adopted to maintain low optical loss for an electrode spacing as narrow as 3 µm, resulting in a low half-wave-voltage length product of only 1.7 V·cm."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Deep silicon etching and heterogeneous integration for low-loss, low half-wave-voltage, and linear-drive thin-film lithium niobate modulators ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0030399225020729

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a full-length research article published in Optics & Laser Technology (Volume 194, February 2026, Article 114481) by Elsevier, authored by Guanbao Zhao, Jiao Zhang, Min Zhu, Luohan Peng, Jingwei Li, and Jinbiao Xiao. The paper is titled "Deep silicon etching and heterogeneous integration for low-loss, low half-wave-voltage, and linear-drive thin-film lithium niobate modulators."

The research addresses critical bottlenecks in traditional thin-film lithium niobate modulators (TFLNMs), silicon photonics (SiP), and indium phosphide (InP)-based modulators, including high coupling loss, excessive half-wave voltage-length product (VπL), high power consumption, and complex packaging. The authors propose a closed-loop design paradigm integrating three synergistic innovations:

1. **Deep silicon etching**: Thins the Si substrate to below 10 μm, achieving 26% less absorption loss. Monolithic etching creates tri-layer couplers with 10 μm mode field diameter and 0.4 dB/facet loss — 88% lower than traditional TFLNMs.

2. **Air-gap isolation**: A 1.5 μm air gap between Au electrodes and TFLN waveguides suppresses charge accumulation, reducing VπL to 1.52 V·cm — 40% lower than silicon photonics and 50% lower than indium phosphide.

3. **Heterogeneous low-voltage linear-drive architecture**: Uses 1.8 V voltage and 3 W power consumption to replace power-hungry DSP, enabling 200 Gbps PAM4 with 2.36 dB TDECQ at 67 GHz, stable over 2 km for 500 hours.

The design is fabricated on an x-cut TFLN platform with a 600 nm LN layer, 4.7 μm SiO2 layer, and 500 μm Si substrate, optimized via a five-layer SSC (Si3N4-three-layer TFLN-SiO2). The paper's introduction highlights that SiP modulators are limited to 60 GHz bandwidth and 500 m transmission distance, while InP modulators extend to 2 km but suffer from >10 W power consumption, high costs, and poor signal integrity (TDECQ>3 dB). The research was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (62375050) and Jiangsu Key Research and Development Program (BE2023001-2). The authors declare no competing interests. The article has 38 references and a Mendeley reader count of 1.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Traditional thin-film lithium niobate modulators (TFLNMs), along with silicon photonics (SiP) and indium phosphide (InP) based modulators, face critical bottlenecks such as high coupling loss, excessive half-wave voltage-length product (VπL), high power consumption and complex packaging, which severely limit transmission performance."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Buried-electrode Hybrid Bonded Thin-film Lithium Niobate ... ---
URL: https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/2311749

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific paper describing hybrid bonded silicon nitride thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) Mach-Zehnder modulators (MZMs) operating at 1310 nm (O-band), developed by researchers at UC San Diego and Sandia National Laboratories. The modulators use metal coplanar waveguide (CPW) electrodes that are either buried in the silicon-on-insulator (SOI) chip (buried-electrode, BE, design using a Ti/TiN/Al composite metal layer) or placed on top of the TFLN layer (top-electrode, TE, design using gold). The hybrid approach bonds an unetched 200 nm thick 5 mol-% MgO-codoped TFLN layer above an amorphous SiN waveguide (900 nm wide, 180 nm thick) with a ~40 nm oxide layer between them, providing a CMOS-compatible path to incorporate non-CMOS-compatible LN into silicon photonics foundry processes.

Key results: Both device types achieved a 3-dB electro-optic bandwidth greater than 110 GHz and voltage-driven optical extinction ratios greater than 28 dB. Half-wave voltage-length products (VπL) were 2.8 V·cm for the 0.51 cm long buried-electrode device and 2.5 V·cm for the 0.4 cm long top-electrode device (Vπ of 5.6 V and 6.4 V, respectively). The BE design required standard CPW electrodes achieving near-perfect RF-optical index matching (nRF ≈ ng ≈ 2.095), while the TE design required an inductively-loaded slow-wave electrode (SWE) structure to correct a 10% index mismatch. When normalized by electrode gap (G), the VπL/G values were 0.48 V·cm/µm (BE) and 0.46 V·cm/µm (TE), with the small deviation attributed to the 220 nm vertical separation between the buried electrode and TFLN film reducing RF-optical mode overlap.

Additional details: End-to-end optical insertion loss was ~16 dB for both designs, with optical propagation loss of 0.34 dB/cm in the feeder waveguide and 2.7 dB/facet coupling loss; most loss is attributed to optical mode transition at the bonded TFLN edge. The BE device's active electrode length (0.51 cm) is longer than the TE device (0.4 cm) because the buried metal must extend beyond the TFLN perimeter for RF probe landing, while gold must stay within the bonded region. The work was supported by the U.S. Department of Defense (Grant HR001120S0008) and the Office of Naval Research (Grant N00014-21-1-2805). The conclusion emphasizes that hybrid bonded TFLN modulators can be incorporated with CMOS-compatible silicon photonics processes, and both TE and BE designs can be integrated on the same chip, offering a simpler back-end process for BE at the cost of additional front-end steps.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Hybrid bonded silicon nitride thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) Mach-Zehnder modulators (MZMs) at 1310 nm were designed with metal coplanar waveguide electrodes buried in the silicon-on-insulator (SOI) chip. The MZM devices showed greatly improved performance compared to earlier devices of a similar design... Both devices achieve a 3-dB electro-optic bandwidth greater than 110 GHz and voltage-driven optical extinction ratios greater than 28 dB. Half-wave voltage-length products (VπL) of 2.8 and 2.5 V·cm were measured for the 0.5 and 0.4 cm long buried metal and top gold electrode MZMs, respectively."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: High-Performance Mach–Zehnder Modulator Based on Thin-Film Lithium Niobate with Low Voltage-Length Product ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10018726

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific research paper published in ACS Omega (March 2, 2023) by researchers from Beijing University of Technology (Beijing Engineering Research Center of Laser Technology, Key Laboratory of Trans-scale Laser Manufacturing Technology, and Institute of Advanced Technology on Semiconductor Optics & Electronics). The paper, titled "High-Performance Mach–Zehnder Modulator Based on Thin-Film Lithium Niobate with Low Voltage-Length Product," reports the design, fabrication, and characterization of electro-optic modulators (EOMs) based on the thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) photonic integration platform.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Two on-chip EOMs were demonstrated operating at commercially available wavelengths of 850 nm and 1550 nm.
- The 1550 nm modulator achieved a voltage-length product (Vπ·L) of 1.29 V·cm with a 3-dB electro-optic (E-O) bandwidth beyond 40 GHz (limited by test conditions, not the device itself).
- The 850 nm modulator achieved the lowest reported Vπ·L of 0.78 V·cm — the first time a modulator at 850 nm exhibited such a low half-wave voltage-length product — with a measured 3-dB E-O bandwidth of ~20 GHz (limited by the photodetector bandwidth; the 6.34-dB electrical loss measurement showed the true bandwidth is far beyond 40 GHz).

DESIGN DETAILS:
- Modulators use Mach–Zehnder-interferometer (MZI) configuration with coplanar waveguide (CPW) gold electrodes in a push–pull configuration.
- Cosine-shaped Y-branch waveguides with a 2° intersection angle split and combine light.
- TFLN (X-cut LN thin film, 400 nm thick) bonded on a 4.7-μm-thick buried SiO2 layer on a 500-μm-thick Si substrate (purchased from NanoLN).
- A SiO2 cladding layer is deposited on top to improve electric field distribution, achieve velocity matching, and prevent excessive optical loss.
- Light propagates along the y-axis in quasi-TE mode to utilize the largest electro-optic coefficient γ33, with the strongest electric field along the z-axis.
- Waveguides are partially etched by 180 nm with top width of 1.1 μm (1550 nm) and 410 nm (850 nm).
- The RF peak electric field was increased by 57% compared to conventional structures, greatly reducing Vπ·L.
- Simulated results: characteristic impedance Z0 = 49 Ω, microwave index nRF = 2.24, theoretical E-O response beyond 70 GHz, RF return loss below −17 dB.

FABRICATION PROCESS:
- Cr hard mask (400 nm) deposited via RF magnetron sputtering; waveguide pattern defined by electron-beam lithography (EBL); etching via ICP-RIE with SF6/Ar gas mixture; SiO2 cladding (500 nm) deposited via PECVD; electrodes formed via electroplating (rather than liftoff) using Ti/Au seed layer deposited by electron beam evaporation.
- Waveguide sidewall angle ~73°, etched depth 180 nm, RMS surface roughness 0.74 nm (measured by AFM).
- Modulator size: approximately 5.5 mm × 400 μm.

PERFORMANCE MEASUREMENTS:
- 1550 nm modulator: insertion loss of −15 dB (without specially designed butt coupler), extinction ratio of 19 dB, measured non-push–pull Vπ of 8.6 V (4.3 V in push–pull configuration with 3 mm modulation arm).
- 850 nm modulator: electrode gap of 5.5 μm, single electrode width ~16 μm.
- The theoretical Vπ·L limitation ranges between 0.66 and 13 V·cm depending on effective refractive index, electrode gap, and field overlap parameters.

APPLICATIONS: The modulators are suited for data center internal interconnects, optical interconnections, quantum communication, 5G, satellite data links, and quantum information processing. The study aids understanding of EOM structures on the TFLN platform for high-performance, multifunctional device fabrication.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We proposed on-chip EOMs operating at two commercially available wavelengths of 850 and 1550 nm and successfully demonstrated rather low voltage-length products (Vπ·L) of 0.78 V·cm and 1.29 V·cm, respectively." — Abstract
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: High-Modulation-Efficiency Lithium Niobate Electro-Optic Modulator Based on Sunken Dual-Layer Electrode ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2304-6732/12/11/1129

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in Photonics (MDPI) in 2025 (Volume 12, Issue 11, article 1129, DOI: 10.3390/photonics12111129), titled "High-Modulation-Efficiency Lithium Niobate Electro-Optic Modulator Based on Sunken Dual-Layer Electrode." The paper is an open-access communication article.

**Authors and Affiliations:** The authors are Yicheng Huang, Qing Liao, Yihui Yin, Zanhui Chen, Fabi Zhang, Tangyou Sun, Haiou Li, and Meihua Shou. They are affiliated with the Guangxi Key Laboratory of Precision Navigation Technology and Application, Guilin University of Electronic Technology (Guilin, China) and the 34th Research Institute of China Electronics Technology Group Corporation. The work was funded by several grants including the National Natural Science Foundation of China (52363022) and Guangxi funding programs.

**Objective/Problem:** Electro-optic modulators with high bandwidth, high modulation efficiency, and low loss are critical for AI, analog communications, and satellite data links. The central challenge is that modulation efficiency and optical loss are interrelated—reducing electrode spacing improves efficiency but increases metal absorption loss.

**Proposed Design:** The researchers propose a sunken dual-layer electrode structure combining sunken electrodes with dual-layer capacitance-loaded electrodes on thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN). Based on electromagnetic theory, the electric field is strongest at the center between electrodes; sinking the electrodes allows the ridge waveguide to be positioned precisely at this maximum-field location, enhancing electric field-waveguide interaction. A Mach-Zehnder push-pull structure with multimode interferometers (MMIs) is employed.

**Key Results (from finite element analysis simulations):**
- High bandwidth exceeding 60 GHz (electro-optic response −1.4 dB at 60 GHz; reflection coefficient below −10 dB from 1–60 GHz)
- Low optical loss of 0.14 dB/cm
- Low half-wave voltage-length product (VπL) of 1.52 V·cm
- Characteristic impedance of approximately 53 Ω (well-matched to standard 50 Ω system)
- Optimized parameters: upper electrode spacing 2.9 μm, lower electrode spacing 4.5 μm, t1 = 5 μm, t2 = 2 μm, modulator length 0.5 cm, signal electrode width 50 μm

**Key Design Features:** Only the central modulating section of TFLN is retained while other parts are etched away, reducing unnecessary optical loss. The dual-layer electrode consists of a top T-shaped electrode and bottom traveling-wave electrode. The sunken design achieves lower VπL while maintaining low optical loss compared to both conventional single-layer and non-sunken dual-layer configurations.

**Conclusion:** The sunken dual-layer electrode structure successfully addresses the trade-off between modulation efficiency and optical loss, offering a promising approach for high-speed, energy-efficient integrated photonic devices. Future work will focus on experimental fabrication and characterization to validate the simulation results.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"An electro-optic modulator with a high bandwidth (>60 GHz), low optical loss (0.14 dB/cm), and low half-wave voltage–length product (1.52 V·cm) has been realized using finite element analysis software."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Fabrication Techniques for Lithium Niobate on Insulator Photonic ... ---
URL: https://www.latitudeds.com/post/fabrication-techniques-for-lithium-niobate-on-insulator-photonic-structures

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article (published October 16, 2024, by Latitude Design Systems) provides an overview of key fabrication techniques for lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) photonic structures, a promising platform for integrated photonics due to its electro-optic, nonlinear optical, and piezoelectric properties.

**LNOI Wafer Fabrication:** Uses crystal ion slicing, involving (1) He+ ion implantation into an LN wafer, (2) bonding to a substrate with silica buffer layer, (3) thermal treatment to exfoliate a thin LN film, and (4) thinning/polishing. This produces sub-micrometer films with surface roughness below 0.5 nm in both Z-cut and X-cut orientations.

**Fabrication Techniques Covered:**

1. **Ion Milling** — Bombards sample with Ar+ ions to physically etch material. Early attempts produced ~4 dB/cm waveguide losses due to sidewall roughness from redeposition, mask erosion, and low etch selectivity. Optimized processes have improved results dramatically.

2. **Focused Ion Beam (FIB) Milling** — Uses tightly focused Ga+ beam for maskless, direct-write patterning with <10 nm resolution and arbitrary 3D shapes. A two-step process (coarse milling at high current, then fine polishing at low current) enabled microdisk resonators with Q factors >10^6. Limitations: low throughput, redeposition, Ga+ contamination.

3. **EBL + Ion Milling** — Combines electron beam lithography for hard mask patterning (e.g., chromium) with optimized Ar+ ion milling. Key factors include hard masks resistant to milling, optimized ion energy/current, and multi-step etching. Achieved waveguide losses as low as 0.027 dB/cm and Q factors >10^7.

4. **Chemomechanical Polishing (CMP)** — The PLACE (photolithography-assisted chemomechanical etching) technique combines mechanical abrasion with chemical etching. Process: deposit hard mask, pattern mask (e.g., laser ablation), CMP to remove exposed LN, remove mask and undercut. Produces ultra-smooth surfaces (<0.5 nm RMS), controllable sidewall angles, and is compatible with standard photolithography. Achieved record-low 0.027 dB/cm propagation losses and Q factors up to 4.7x10^7.

5. **Mechanical Dicing/Cutting** — Uses precision dicing saws or ultraprecision ductile-mode cutting with single-crystal diamond tools. Produces extremely smooth sidewalls (losses as low as 1.2 dB/cm) but lacks resolution and geometric flexibility.

**Conclusions:** PLACE currently offers the best combination of quality and scalability for large-scale production. FIB or EBL approaches are preferred for prototyping or specialized nanostructures. Future development areas include reducing losses in thin (<200 nm) waveguides, improving mode profile/dispersion control, increasing throughput and yield, developing 3D structures, and integrating electrodes. Reference: Y. Cheng, "Lithium Niobate Nanophotonics," Jenny Stanford Publishing, 2021.
</summary>

PLACE has achieved record-low propagation losses of 0.027 dB/cm in LNOI waveguides and Q factors up to 4.7x10^7 in microdisk resonators., This approach has achieved waveguide losses as low as 0.027 dB/cm and resonator Q factors >10^7., For large-scale production of integrated photonic circuits, PLACE currently offers the best combination of quality and scalability. For prototyping or specialized nanostructures, FIB or EBL-based approaches may be preferred., This technique can produce LNOI wafers with sub-micrometer thick LN films and surface roughness below 0.5 nm., The development of high-quality commercial LNOI wafers has been crucial for advancing LNOI photonics.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research paper published in Optical Materials Express (February 1, 2013, Vol. 3, No. 2) by researchers from Columbia University (Hsu-Cheng Huang, Jerry I. Dadap, Ophir Gaathon, Irving P. Herman, Richard M. Osgood, Jr.) and SUNY at Albany (Sasha Bakhru, Hassaram Bakhru). **Methodology:** Congruent Z-cut LiNbO3 wafers were irradiated with He+ ions along the Z-axis at energies of 1.2-3.8 MeV with doses ranging from 10^12 to 5×10^16 cm^-2. Samples were tilted 7° to prevent channeling, water-cooled, and raster-scanned for uniform dose. A 532 nm diode laser (2.7 mW) with a 100× objective (NA=0.85) and confocal pinhole produced a ~1 μm spot. Three optical configurations were used: (a) depth scan from the top surface, (b) edge scan across a crystal facet, and (c) bevel scan using a 5°-off-angle polished edge to expand the ~0.5-1 μm stopping region spatially by ~11.5× for higher resolution probing.

**Key Results:**
1. In the ion stopping region, irradiation causes substantial intensity loss and line broadening of allowed Raman modes, plus new features at 600-770 cm^-1, including a shoulder near the forbidden A1(TO4) 631 cm^-1 mode and a new peak at ~766 cm^-1.
2. The 631 cm^-1 mode intensity profiles vs. depth match SRIM Monte Carlo simulations for ion stopping ranges (1.2 MeV: 2.81 μm, 3.0 MeV: 7.65 μm, 3.8 MeV: 10.47 μm), confirming the technique's depth-profiling capability.
3. The E(TO1) 152 cm^-1 mode (sensitive to Li content) shows a decrease in Li concentration in the stopping region after irradiation.
4. A threshold dose of >10^16 cm^-2 is required to observe the irradiation-induced Raman features, attributed to nonlinear defect clustering (TRIM simulation: ~0.25 dpa at 10^16 cm^-2 dose).
5. Annealing (250-600°C, 30 min) partially restores crystallinity. Arrhenius analysis gives activation energies of Ea = 0.32 ± 0.07 eV (631 cm^-1 mode) and Ea = 0.30 ± 0.05 eV (766 cm^-1 mode), similar to XRD measurements (Ea = 0.32 ± 0.03 eV), suggesting these features relate to irradiation-induced lattice swelling.
6. The 738 cm^-1 mode in virgin samples is attributed to ilmenite-like stacking defects in nonstoichiometric LiNbO3.
7. 2D Raman imaging of patterned (masked) irradiation samples shows high uniformity of damage (standard deviation ~0.010 for 875 cm^-1 mode, ~0.015 for 631 cm^-1 mode) and a transition region at mask boundaries due to imperfect mask adhesion and edge scattering (~4% radius increase).
8. Edge scans reveal longer "tails" of damage toward the surface than predicted by SRIM (~3 μm effective width vs. ~1 μm calculated), a phenomenon also observed in diamond; the origin is unclear but may involve irradiation-induced strain.
9. Beveled geometry enabled detection of buried meandering line defects (spacing ~5 μm) that are otherwise invisible to optical microscopy; these defects produce strong Raman signals that can obscure the broad straggle-region signal.

**Conclusions:** Confocal micro-Raman spectroscopy provides a laboratory-based, ambient-pressure alternative to accelerator-based techniques (RBS, NRA, PIXE) for characterizing ion-irradiation damage in complex oxides, with ~1 μm lateral resolution, depth resolution limited by ~2 μm Rayleigh length, and the ability to map composition, crystallinity, strain, and defect distributions.

--- SOURCE 1: Reactive Ion Etching of X-Cut LiNbO 3 in an ICP/TCP System for ... - MDPI ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/13/4/2097

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed open-access research article published in Applied Sciences (MDPI) in 2023 (Volume 13, Issue 4, Article 2097, DOI: 10.3390/app13042097) titled "Reactive Ion Etching of X-Cut LiNbO3 in an ICP/TCP System for the Fabrication of an Optical Ridge Waveguide." The article belongs to the Special Issue "Advances and Application of Lithium Niobate."

**Purpose:** The study aimed to develop plasma etching technology for producing ridge waveguides with minimal sidewall roughness and near-waveguide surface defects on lithium niobate (LiNbO3) substrates for miniature photonic integrated circuits (PICs). The research specifically focused on reactive ion etching (RIE) of unmodified (non-proton-exchanged) X-cut LiNbO3 using a chromium hard mask in an SF6/Ar gas mixture with an ICP/TCP plasma source.

**Key Authors & Affiliations:** Andrei Kozlov, Dmitrii Moskalev, Uliana Salgaeva (Perm State University), Anna Bulatova (Perm National Research Polytechnic University), Victor Krishtop (both Perm institutions), Anatolii Volyntsev (Perm State University), and Alexander Syuy (Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology, Far Eastern Federal University — corresponding author).

**Background Context:** LiNbO3-on-insulator (LNOI) substrates are promising for high-frequency (up to 1 THz) miniature PICs. Two European LNOI-based platforms (LOLIPOP and ELENA) were launched in 2022. LNOI enables high-contrast optical waveguides with small curvature radii (100 μm or less) and high integration density (50–100 basic elements per cm²). Dry etching of LiNbO3 is challenging due to formation of non-volatile LiF during fluorine-containing plasma treatment, which reduces etching rate, aspect ratio, and increases surface roughness.

**Methodology:**
- Numerical simulation using finite-difference frequency domain (FDFD) method determined optimal waveguide dimensions: width 1.4 μm, etching depth 0.3 μm, supporting single-mode propagation at 1.5–1.6 μm wavelengths, with critical bend radius of 50 μm and losses <0.001 dB/90°. Simulation used NanoLN wafer configuration (SiO2 layer 4.7 μm, LiNbO3 layer 0.6 μm).
- Samples: bulk X-cut LiNbO3 (CQT, China) used as substrate (due to LNOI expense), with future transfer to LNOI planned.
- Sample preparation: Piranha solution cleaning, 80 nm chromium hard mask via DC magnetron sputtering (500 W, Ar flow 0.7 L/h, 200°C), annealing at 300°C for 1 hour in dry N2, 500 nm negative resist (AZnLOF 2020) with contact lithography, chromium wet etching in cerium ammonium nitrate (CAN) solution, resist removal in dimethyl sulfoxide.
- RIE performed in SF6/Ar mixture using ICP-RIE system Ethna-100; parameters ranged: ICP power 300–600 W, TCP power 50–200 W, pressure 0.007–0.8 mbar, etching time 8 min.
- Chromium hard mask line edge roughness (LER) measured at 20–30 nm.

**Results:**
- Two iterations of recipe development; recipe #13 provided best first-iteration profile; recipes #14–17 improved structure anisotropy.
- Etching depths: 0.23–0.60 μm; mask selectivity: 1:4 to 1:8; best slope angle: 70–75°.
- Recipe #13 (0.03 mbar pressure): slope angle ~62°, smooth near-waveguide surface, microtrenches formed along waveguide base, mask selectivity 1:5.3, bias voltage 186 V.
- Recipe #14 (0.007 mbar pressure): slope angle ~75°, dramatically increased surface roughness in near-waveguide region, no microtrenches, mask selectivity improved to 1:8, bias voltage 141 V, brown film-like layer on surface (EDX: O:F:Nb = 18.56:36.56:44.88 wt%), suggesting LiFx compound formation.
- Microtrench formation attributed to ion trajectory deflection toward sidewalls by accumulated electrons — characteristic of RIE with significant physical plasma component at low pressure (<0.1 mbar) and high bias.

**Proposed Model:** The authors extended Gulyaev et al.'s topochemical model of LiNbO3 plasma-chemical etching to include ion bombardment effects (RIE). They propose that the bias voltage difference between recipes #13 (186 V) and #14 (141 V) caused a transition from RIE to radical chemical etching. Based on Hoekstra et al.'s ion energy distribution data, estimated Ar+ ion average energies were ~90 eV (recipe #13), ~40 eV (transition region), and ~30 eV (recipe #14). At ~90 eV, ion energies were sufficient to create vacancies in the LiF layer, enhancing diffusion of reaction products and surface sputtering (producing smooth surfaces). Below a transition point (30–90 eV range), chemical etching dominates, leaving LiF and causing rough surfaces. A non-monotonic bias voltage vs. pressure relationship was found, with an inflection point at 0.05–0.03 mbar and bias voltage dropping below 0.03 mbar.

**Conclusions:** RIE parameters were identified for producing ridge waveguides on initial LiNbO3 with smooth sidewalls, slope angles of 62°–75°, and minimal near-waveguide defects. Only slope angle and LER were quantitatively described; near-waveguide region quality was qualitative. Future work includes transferring the technology to LNOI and performing optical characterization. The authors acknowledge the current slope angles limit PIC applications but believe the qualitative etching kinetics model will enable achieving near-90° slopes and low-loss waveguides.

**Funding:** Supported by the Competence Center in Photonics of the National Technology Initiative (contract No. 70-2021-00309); SEM analysis supported by Far Eastern Federal University ("PRIORITY-2030" program).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In this study, the technology for producing ridge waveguides with a minimal roughness of the sidewalls and material surface in a near-waveguide region was developed with the purpose of fabricating miniature photonic integrated circuits on a LiNbO3 substrate."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Fabrication of lithium niobate metasurfaces via a combination of ... ---
URL: https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJ8c8a1b62c7c6c8d2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article titled "Fabrication of lithium niobate metasurfaces via a combination of FIB and ICP-RIE," published in Chinese Optics Letters (Vol. 20, Issue 11, page 113602, 2022). The article was authored by Chunyan Jin, Wei Wu, Lei Cao, Bofeng Gao, Jiaxin Chen, Wei Cai, Mengxin Ren, and Jingjun Xu, affiliated with Nankai University (Key Laboratory of Weak-Light Nonlinear Photonics, Ministry of Education), the Science and Technology on Electro-Optical Information Security Control Laboratory in Tianjin, and the Collaborative Innovation Center of Extreme Optics at Shanxi University. The DOI is 10.3788/COL202220.113602.

KEY FINDINGS AND METHODOLOGY:
The paper reports a fabrication technique for lithium niobate (LN) nano-grating metasurfaces that combines focused ion beam (FIB) milling with inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etching (ICP-RIE). This combined approach overcomes limitations of two existing methods: (1) FIB-only milling, which produces round-topped nanostructures with crystal lattice damage requiring hydrofluoric acid treatment that causes lateral etching of the SiO2 bonding layer; and (2) electron beam lithography (EBL) combined with plasma etching, which faces challenges due to LN's chemical inertness and low mask selectivity, requiring complex multilayer masking schemes.

FABRICATION PROCESS STEPS:
1. LNOI wafer (from NANOLN Co., Ltd.) with quartz substrate and 230-nm-thick LN film was cleaned with acetone and isopropanol in an ultrasonic bath.
2. A 40-nm-thick Cr layer was deposited by electron beam evaporation as a conducting layer for FIB.
3. Both Cr and LN layers were milled into nano-grating arrays using Ga+ ion beam at 80 pA current and 30 kV acceleration voltage.
4. The patterned Cr served as a hard mask for ICP-RIE using SF6 gas mixed with Ar gas.
5. Sample was wet treated with SC-1 solution (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O = 1:1:5) for 5 min at 80°C to remove lithium fluoride (LiF) byproduct.
6. Residual Cr was removed by chemical wet etching with standard Cr etchant for 20 min at room temperature.

RESULTS:
- Fabricated ridges have trapezoidal cross-sections with sidewall angles larger than 80° (specifically ~82° for a grating with period Pd = 400 nm, top width 211 nm, bottom width 275 nm, duty cycle 62.5%).
- The metasurface array footprint was 20 μm × 20 μm.
- Sharp quasi-bound states in the continuum (QBIC) were observed under oblique incidence, with transmission spectra matching numerical simulations (performed using COMSOL Multiphysics finite element method).
- At normal incidence, a symmetry-protected BIC (SP-BIC) mode exists with nearly vanishing linewidth around 700 nm, becoming observable QBIC modes with finite spectral widths at oblique incidence angles (5°, 10°, 15°, 20°).
- QBIC resonances shift to longer wavelengths with increasing incident angle, with Q-factors decreasing as angles increase due to electromagnetic mode leakage.
- Near-field electric field (Ey) distributions confirmed anti-symmetric mode profiles at normal incidence with minimal radiation loss.

APPLICATIONS: The technique enables fabrication of high-Q LN metasurfaces with sharp resonances for optical communications, on-chip photonics, laser physics, sensing, optical steering, and nonlinear optics.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Steep sidewalls with angles larger than 80° are achieved. Sharp quasi-bound states in the continuum are observed from our metasurfaces. The measured transmission spectra show good agreement with the numerical simulations, confirming the high quality of the fabricated metasurfaces."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Amorphous Layer Formed during EM Sample Preparation using FIB ---
URL: https://www.globalsino.com/EM/page4493.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a chapter from "Practical Electron Microscopy and Database," an online book (Second Edition, 2006) by Dr. Yougui Liao, focused on the amorphous layer formed during EM (electron microscopy) sample preparation using FIB (focused ion beam) milling.

KEY CONTENT:
- FIB preparation is critical for dopant analysis at nanometer scale but induces surface damage, including amorphization of crystalline surfaces.
- Two mechanisms cause amorphization: (i) sufficient atom displacement within the collision cascade leading to loss of long-range order when point defect density reaches a critical value at the surface, and (ii) local melting and quenching of solid in the sample.
- Amorphous layer thickness is theoretically consistent with ion beam penetration calculated by Monte Carlo simulations. The amorphization layer on the top of specimens is thicker than on the side-walls.
- Even with double cross-section TEM methods, measurements of FIB-amorphized layers may have ±10% inaccuracy due to diffraction contrast interference from amorphous layers.

KEY DATA POINTS:
- Table 4493 compares damaged layer thicknesses: 30 kV FIB ≈ 23 nm, 5 kV FIB ≈ 6.5 nm, 1 kV Argon ≈ 1.6 nm.
- A 2 kV Si amorphous layer remains 3 nm thick even at this very low beam energy.
- If both surfaces are FIB-prepared, total amorphous layer thickness doubles.
- Amorphous thickness is independent of beam current over the 100-500 pA range.
- High-energy beams (e.g., 30 kV) create near-surface defect layers extending more than 100 nm deep, which can trap dopants in semiconducting regions.
- A 30 kV Ga ion beam creates ~23 nm amorphized layer per side on Si, making a specimen entirely amorphous at ~46 nm thickness.
- Argon milling can be used to remove FIB-induced damage.
- Gao et al. applied wedge FIB milling combined with double cross-section technique to study Si crystal-amorphization, showing a fully amorphized Si portion of 355 nm.

REFERENCES: The page cites 7 references, including works by Montoya et al. (2007), Twitchett et al. (2002), Cooper et al. (2006, 2008), Kato et al. (1999), Gao et al. (2006, ISTFA proceedings), and Kempshall et al. (2002).

The paper addresses the challenge of argon (Ar) sputtering of lithium niobate-on-insulator (LNOI) waveguides, which provides the best optical quality but suffers from micro-masking effects caused by material redeposition and close-to-one etch mask selectivity. The authors present a workflow to identify optimal etching parameters independent of the plasma system used, and propose three methods to achieve redeposition-free lithium niobate etching without wet chemistry cleaning.

Key experimental details and findings:

1. Wafer preparation: A full 4-inch LNOI wafer (400 nm x-cut film, 2 μm SiO2 insulation layer from NANOLN) was patterned using 100 kV electron beam lithography (Vistex EBPG 5200+), with HSQ-based flowable oxide (FOX16) as negative resist (~500 nm thick). Samples were diced into 52 10×10 mm2 pieces with 5×5 mm2 effective area each.

2. ICP etching: Performed in a Plasma Pro 100 (Oxford Instruments) ICP system. Only Cl2, SF6, O2, and Ar gases were used, as CHF3 was found to contaminate the chamber and harm reproducibility. Etch depth (200-250 nm) was controlled via interferometric endpointing (Horiba, 670.1 nm).

3. Influence of DC bias: Sweeping DC bias from 100 V to 800 V (Ar flow 10 sccm, pressure 1 mTorr, 20 °C) showed that total redeposition decreased almost fourfold from 100 V to 800 V, trending toward redeposition-free etching above 1 kV (though not readily achievable). Trench depth increased by a factor of five with higher bias. Selectivity remained near one, sidewall angle 60-63° for both +Z and −Z crystal faces. Sample bow changed from concave to flat to convex with increasing bias: 300 V gave 20 nm thickness variation over 8×8 mm2, while 600 V gave below 5 nm. Surface roughness (Sq) was ~0.08 nm for biases above 200 V, four times better than un-etched surface (0.31 nm).

4. Influence of chamber pressure: Sweeping pressure from 1 to 15 mTorr (400 V) and 0.3 to 13 mTorr (600 V) showed redeposition vanishing completely after 7 mTorr, but with significant structural damage. Redeposition-free regime occurred at 5-7 mTorr for 600 V (preferred DC bias) and around 11 mTorr for 400 V. Etch rates dropped to minimum values of 27 nm/min (400 V) and 12 nm/min (600 V) before increasing again at higher pressures. Surface roughness degraded with pressure (Sq of 0.10, 0.12, 0.15 nm for 3, 5, 7 mTorr).

5. Aspect ratio dependent etching (ARDE): Redeposition decreased with decreasing gap size (from 1 μm to 100 nm) due to ions bouncing between sidewalls. Trench merging occurred at gaps up to 400 nm, with loading effects below 400 nm. Dense structures were redeposition-free down to 1 μm gaps at 300 W ICP power, 600 V DC bias, and 11 mTorr.

6. Etch depth and IBE: Redeposition decreased with increasing etch depth (110-260 nm). Ion beam etching (IBE) experiments at incidence angles 0°-35° simulating trapezoidal masks (85°, 70°, 60°, 50°) showed reduced redeposition with increasing angle, confirming that trapezoidal masks help achieve redeposition-free etching.

URL: https://iopscience.iop.org/book/mono/978-0-7503-6305-1/chapter/bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the first chapter of an IOP Publishing book titled "Lithium niobate thin films: potential applications, synthesis methods, structure, and properties" by Maxim Sumets, published in October 2024 (DOI: https://doi.org/10.1088/978-0-7503-6305-1ch1). The author is affiliated with the Department of Science, Grayson College, Denison, TX, USA.

**Structure and properties of bulk lithium niobate (LiNbO3/LN):**
- First grown by Czochralski method in 1965; Abrahams investigated its structure.
- Belongs to R3c space group; unit cell is rhombohedral (a = 5.4944 Å, α = 55°52′) or hexagonal (aH = 5.1483 Å, cH = 13.8631 Å, c/a = 2.693) with six formula units per cell.
- Cation stacking: Nb, Li, vacancy pattern; octahedral interstices one-third filled by Li, one-third by Nb, one-third vacant.
- Stoichiometric (R = Li/Nb = 1) vs. congruent (R = 0.946) crystals differ only in defectiveness.
- Curie temperature: 1210 °C (ferroelectric to paraelectric transition).
- Density of congruent LN: 4.648 g cm⁻³.
- Thermal expansion coefficients: α11 = 15.0 × 10⁻⁶ and α33 = 7.5 × 10⁻⁶.
- Low-frequency dielectric permittivity: ε11 = 30, ε33 = 80.
- Optically transparent from 0.35 to 5 μm; optical bandgap reported between 3.57 eV and 4.7 eV.
- Refractive indexes: no = 2.289, ne = 2.201 (λ = 633 nm), dependent on Li/Nb ratio.
- Etching: can be etched by boiling (110 °C) in HF:HNO3 (1:2) mixture; RIE using fluorine/chlorine-based plasmas (CF4, CCl2F2, CHF3).

**Applications of thin LN films:**
1. **Waveguide-based optical devices:** LN is promising for high-speed (>20 GHz) modulators; thin films provide higher intensity per unit power. Films must be ~400 nm thick to achieve ≤1 dB cm⁻¹ leakage on high-refractive-index substrates. Roughness of ~1 nm is critical; roughness correlates at ~1% of film thickness.
2. **Surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices:** LN is the most popular piezoelectric material (surpassing PZT, BaTiO3, Bi4Ti3O12) due to high Curie temperature and piezoelectric constant. SAW filters depend on film structure and surface morphology. Reported SAW devices operating at 6.3 GHz (velocity ~12,500 m/s) and 2 GHz (velocity 8,200 m/s).
3. **Memory units and neuromorphic systems:** LN films can be used in FRAM (FeRAM) and RRAM (ReRAM). Memristive effect in LN explained by oxygen vacancy motion and possibly Li ion migration. LN is more promising for neuromorphic systems than for competing RRAM based on SiO2. Co-ion doping can induce ferromagnetic properties.

**Fabrication methods:**
- **Liquid-phase epitaxy (LPE):** First demonstrated 1975 on LiTaO3; achieves low optical loss (0.154 ± 0.002 dB mm⁻¹ at λ = 1 μm) and minimal roughness (0.2–0.3 nm with Zn doping).
- **Chemical vapor deposition (CVD):** Low reactive gas pressure (~266.6 Pa) yields polycrystalline two-phase films (LN + LiNb3O8); higher pressure (~2666 Pa) yields single-phase c-oriented films. Mechanical stress decreases from 1.3 to 0.9 GPa as pressure increases from 666.5 Pa to 101.3 kPa.
- **Sol–gel process:** Used since 1980s; allows lower deposition temperatures but is time/resource intensive; often produces non-ferroelectric phases (LiNb3O8, Nb2O5). Surface roughness 10.6–16 nm depending on concentration (0.25–1 mol l⁻¹).
- **Pulsed laser deposition (PLD):** Widely adopted in the 1990s. Li-deficient LiNb3O8 phase is a common issue; Li-rich targets recommended. Films with grain sizes 50–200 nm deposited at Tsub = 700 °C on sapphire. Minimal roughness (4.3 nm) at Tsub = 600 °C. Single-phase c-oriented films formed only at oxygen pressure of 40 Pa.
- **Radio-frequency magnetron sputtering (RFMS):** First explored in the late 1980s; replaced RF diode sputtering. Considered one of the most effective deposition methods for LN films.

**RFMS fundamentals:**
- Sputtering = expulsion of atoms from a target bombarded by energetic plasma ions; Argon is the reaction gas; operates at 13.5 MHz.
- Ring planar magnetron design: water-cooled disc target (cathode), magnet block with central and peripheral magnets, grounded anode. The magnetic field creates a "magnetic trap effect," reducing radial electron diffusion and increasing sputtering intensity at erosion zones.
- Plasma potential tracks the RF signal frequency; ions follow the time-averaged cathode voltage.
- "Plasma effect" regime occurs when substrate is aligned above the target erosion zone.
- Three epitaxial growth models: Volmer–Weber (island), Frank–van der Merwe (layer), and Stranski–Krastanov (layer then island). The Volmer–Weber mechanism prevails for LN film synthesis by sputtering.
- Target composition critically affects film crystallinity; sintered targets (Li2CO3 + Nb2O5 at 1200 °C) may retain Li2CO3, creating Li-poor layers and point defects. Adding ~5% Li2O to targets is recommended to ensure stoichiometric films.

The chapter includes Table 1.1 comparing advantages/disadvantages of PLD, sol–gel, CVD, LPE, and RFMS methods.
</summary>

Crystalline LiNbO3 is very chemically inert and difficult to etch (e.g., a 50% aqueous HF solution has negligible effect on single crystal LiNbO3, and RIE using CCl2F2:Ar:O2 gives only ~3 μm/h etch rates, comparable to mask materials, making high-resolution geometries infeasible).

1. **Thin film deposition and patterning:** The invention allows deposition of amorphous lithium niobate films (via chemical vapor deposition, typically at pressures between 0.1 mm Hg and atmospheric pressure, and temperatures at or below ~600°C), which can be easily etched with conventional wet or dry etchants (e.g., a 4% aqueous HF solution etches at >5 μm/min; a 25% HF solution etches at ~5 μm/min). After etching features such as trenches, the film is annealed at 900°C-1100°C for 0.5-6 hours to crystallize it (in a lithium-rich environment, e.g., powdered LiNbO3). This two-step process enables growth rates of ~2 μm/h (vs. <0.1 μm/h for crystalline growth at >900°C). The inert crystalline substrate naturally stops the etch process, defining feature depth by film thickness.
2. **Trench-based traveling wave modulator (TWM) design:** The patent describes using trenches (or slots) in lithium niobate layers to optimize traveling wave electro-optical modulators. Trenches (typically 2-10 μm wide, at least 5 μm deep, positioned at least 2 μm from electrodes) concentrate the electric field from electrodes, improving microwave/optical field overlap (from about 0.7 to about 1.2, a ~50% improvement) and reducing required drive voltage. The trenches also help match microwave and optical velocities and provide degrees of freedom (width, depth, position) to optimize all four key physical parameters: C0, Cm (capacitances), Γ (field overlap), and drive voltage. Trenches can be filled with low-dielectric-constant materials like SiO2 or photoresist. This enables operation at 40 Gb/s bit rates with the ~±4.5V swing limit of gallium arsenide drive electronics.
3. **Lift-off processing:** A photolithographically patterned SiO2 mask can be overgrown with polycrystalline lithium niobate, then etched away in aqueous HF, producing patterned single-crystal LiNbO3 ridges (demonstrated with 1 μm thick by 40 μm wide features). This works because amorphous deposition occurs at much lower temperatures than epitaxial growth, avoiding mask-oxide reactions.

--- SOURCE 1: Ultra-low loss ridge waveguides on lithium niobate via argon ion milling and gas clustered ion beam smoothening ---
URL: https://opg.optica.org/oe/abstract.cfm?uri=oe-26-4-4421

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Optics Express (Vol. 26, Issue 4, pp. 4421-4430, 2018) by Shawn Yohanes Siew, Eric Jun Hao Cheung, Haidong Liang, Andrew Bettiol, Noriaki Toyoda, Bandar Alshehri, Elhadj Dogheche, and Aaron J. Danner (corresponding author, NUS). DOI: 10.1364/OE.26.004421. The paper is Open Access.

**Topic/Purpose:** The article presents a two-step fabrication method for creating ultra-low loss ridge waveguides on thin-film single crystal lithium niobate (lithium-niobate-on-insulator, LNOI) using argon ion milling followed by gas clustered ion beam (GCIB) smoothening to reduce sidewall roughness, which is the primary source of propagation loss in etched lithium niobate waveguides.

**Background:** Lithium niobate has strong electro-optic (χ²) nonlinear effects useful for modulators, sensors, and SAW devices, but conventional Ti-indiffusion or proton-exchange waveguides require very large turning radii due to weak lateral index confinement. LNOI provides strong vertical confinement but dry etching typically creates rough sidewalls. Prior reported losses include: 17 dB/cm (Guarino et al.), 5 dB/cm (Rabiei et al.), 0.5 dB/cm (Courjal et al., Ti-indiffused ridge), and ~0.086 dB/cm for industrial Ti-diffused waveguides.

**Methodology:**
- Z-cut LNOI wafer (crystal ion slicing + wafer bonding), height h=700 nm, waveguide widths w varied from 1-7 µm.

- Inner ring waveguide loss has a greater impact on transmission spectrum than outer ring loss.
- Critical coupling conditions (Equation 11) were derived to compensate for waveguide losses.
- Fabrication precision in coupling regions is essential to maintain high Q-factor.

The high-Q double ring structure has potential applications in communications and as a promising candidate for chemical and biomedical sensing applications. Key innovations include: (1) an LN-silica hybrid waveguide that allows an electrode gap as narrow as 3 µm while maintaining low optical loss (a 100-nm-thick silica buffer layer reduces optical loss by more than two orders of magnitude, enabling loss below 0.1 dB/cm), (2) capacitively loaded traveling-wave electrodes (CL-TWEs) with periodically loaded T-rails to reduce microwave loss while maintaining narrow electrode gaps, and (3) a quartz substrate with low dielectric constant (instead of silicon) to achieve velocity matching and reduce microwave loss.

Key experimental results: The fabricated modulator with a 5-mm-long modulation region exhibits a half-wave voltage of only 3.4 V, a half-wave-voltage length product (VπL) of 1.7 V·cm, an extinction ratio beyond 17 dB, and a merely less than 2 dB roll-off in electro-optic response up to 67 GHz (only 1.3 dB roll-off at 67 GHz). Extended measurements with a 110 GHz VNA verified a 6 dB electrical bandwidth over 110 GHz, with a predicted 3 dB modulation bandwidth over 110 GHz. Total insertion loss was 17 dB for the 5-mm modulator, primarily from coupling losses. The RF electric field enhancement in the LN ridge waveguide exceeded 40% due to the 3-µm-spaced electrodes.

Fabrication details: The modulator was fabricated on TFLN-on-quartz wafer from NanoLN (600-nm-thick X-cut TFLN, 2-µm SiO2 bonding layer, 500-µm quartz substrate). The waveguide was patterned by EBL with HSQ and transferred by argon-based RIE, partially etched 300 nm, and covered with 100-nm SiO2 by PECVD. CL-TWEs were fabricated using a two-step process (PMMA lift-off for T-rails via EBL, then contact UV lithography for main electrodes, thickened to 1.4 µm by electroplating). Signal electrode width was 50 µm, unloaded electrode spacing 15 µm, T-rail period 50 µm with 90% duty cycle, and 3-µm T-rail gap.
</summary>

"A novel thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) electro-optic modulator is proposed and demonstrated. LiNbO3-silica hybrid waveguide is adopted to maintain low optical loss for an electrode spacing as narrow as 3 µm, resulting in a low half-wave-voltage length product of only 1.7 V·cm."

--- SOURCE 2: High-Speed Electro-Optic Modulators Based on Thin-Film Lithium Niobate ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2079-4991/14/10/867

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article from the MDPI journal *Nanomaterials* (Volume 14, Issue 10, article 867) titled "High-Speed Electro-Optic Modulators Based on Thin-Film Lithium Niobate," published on 16 May 2024 (DOI: 10.3390/nano14100867). The article belongs to the Special Issue "Nano-Optics and Nano-Optoelectronics: Challenges and Future Trends—2nd Edition: Semiconductor Nanophotonics." The authors are Songyan Hou, Hao Hu, Zhihong Liu, Weichuan Xing, Jincheng Zhang, and Yue Hao, affiliated with Xidian University (Guangzhou Institute of Technology and State Key Laboratory of Wide Bandgap Semiconductor Devices) and Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics.

The review covers the foundational principles and technical innovations of electro-optic modulators (EOMs) based on thin-film lithium niobate (LN). Key sections include:

1. **Introduction**: EOMs are critical for optical communication, microwave photonics, computing, frequency metrology, and quantum photonics. The Pockels effect is highlighted as particularly advantageous for ultrafast, pure refractive-index modulation without dissipation loss. Thin-film monolithic LN combines low-loss photonic integration with the robust Pockels effect.

2. **Photonic properties of thin-film LN**: LN has a wide transparency window (350 nm to 5 µm), a refractive index of ~2.2 at 1550 nm, a high Curie temperature (~1210 °C), a large second-order nonlinear coefficient (d33 = 27 pm/V), and a remarkable Pockels coefficient (r33 = 31 pm/V). Thin-film LN provides significantly improved light confinement, integrability, and compactness compared to bulk LN. LNOI wafers are fabricated using "Smart-Cut" technology (similar to SOI wafer production), involving He+ or H+ ion implantation, wafer bonding, thermal annealing, and chemical mechanical polishing (CMP).

3. **Etching of LN waveguides**: Three methods are discussed: (a) CMP polishing, which yields optical loss of 0.027 dB/cm but has shallow sidewalls; (b) wet etching (using H2O2, NH4OH, H2O), which is cost-effective and reproducible, achieving quality factors up to 10^7 and 110 GHz EO bandwidth, but is limited by anisotropic etching rates; (c) dry etching (Ar+ plasma-based physical etching to avoid non-volatile LiF redeposition), which allows well-controlled etch depths and symmetric cross-sections but faces challenges with sidewall roughness (40°–80° angles) and low selectivity. Low-loss LN waveguides of 0.1 dB/cm have been demonstrated.

4. **Non-resonant electro-optic modulators based on thin-film LN**: The section reviews various modulator designs, including phase modulators, Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI) modulators, and heterogeneous/hybrid integrated devices. Key demonstrations include: (a) heterogeneously integrated Si3N4/LN modulators achieving 6.8 V half-wave voltage and 4 V·cm efficiency (2013, S. Fathpour's group); (b) optimized traveling-wave electrodes achieving 3.9 V half-wave voltage and 33 GHz bandwidth with 1.2 dB/cm loss (2016); (c) a 110 GHz operating bandwidth via reverse ridge design (with 7 dB/cm loss); (d) hybrid silicon/LN waveguides from Sun Yat-sen University (2020, Xinlun Cai's team) achieving >70 GHz modulation and 2.2 V·cm efficiency with <2.5 dB insertion loss and up to 112 Gbit/s amplitude modulation; (e) a SiO2-LNOI hybrid waveguide from Tsinghua University (2021, Yi Luo and Bing Xiong's group) with 3.4 V half-wave voltage and 67 GHz bandwidth; (f) a silicon nitride waveguide on LNOI from Lanzhou University (2021, Yonghui Tian's team) achieving 30 GHz bandwidth, 2.24 V·cm efficiency, ~20 dB extinction ratio, and 80 Gb/s switching.

5. **Resonant electro-optic modulators**: These include Bragg grating modulators on x-cut LNOI (achieving Vπ·L = 0.67 V·cm with a compact 0.3 mm × 1.2 mm footprint) and photonic crystal (PhC) modulators (achieving 17.5 GHz bandwidth with a tiny 0.58 μm³ volume).

The review concludes by outlining pathways for further enhancing LN modulators and anticipates larger-scale LN electro-optic circuits beyond singular components, highlighting the transformative potential of thin-film LN technology in electro-optic modulation and integrated photonics. The article received an altmetric score of 4 and has a PubMed ID of 38786823. Academic editor for this article was Borja Sepulveda.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Thin-film monolithic LN has emerged as a promising platform, as this platform combines low-loss, high-quality photonic integration with the robust Pockels effect, enabling superior modulation performance."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper reports the first integrated ultraviolet (UV) electro-optic modulator on a thin-film lithium tantalate (TFLT) platform, operating at 375 nm. The device addresses a long-standing challenge in UV photonics: the lack of a scalable integrated solution combining low insertion loss, extreme compactness, and high modulation efficiency, which previously required bulky bulk crystals.

Key results: The modulator achieves a record-low VπL of 85 mV·cm at 375 nm (and 0.12 V·cm at 448 nm), representing the highest modulation efficiencies achieved in the UV-visible spectrum to date. The device features a compact footprint of 1.16 mm with a 200 μm modulation length and a 1.5 μm electrode gap. The single-mode LT waveguide at 375 nm exhibits a propagation loss of 7.2 dB/cm (with 0.2 nm RMS surface roughness).

Methodology: The modulator uses a Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI) architecture with a push-pull configuration driven by a ground-signal-ground (GSG) lumped electrode. Devices were patterned on a commercial 300 nm-thick x-cut LT-on-insulator platform with a 100 nm etch depth, fabricated via electron beam lithography and wet chemical etching (citric acid/KOH/H2O2 mixture). The platform demonstrates a two-order-of-magnitude improvement in bandwidth/VπL over bulk lithium niobate modulators and a four-order-of-magnitude improvement over traditional BBO/KDP bulk modulators.

Applications: The work enables scalable UV photonic circuits for trapped-ion quantum computing, portable atomic clocks, UV spectroscopy, and high-bandwidth solar-blind (non-line-of-sight) communications. "Here, we report the first integrated UV electro-optic modulator on a thin-film lithium tantalate (TFLT) platform. By employing a compact lumped-electrode design, we achieve a record-low VπL of 85 mV·cm at 375 nm, providing an up to four orders of magnitude improvement in terms of bandwidth/VπL over bulk technologies."

URL: https://optics.ansys.com/hc/en-us/articles/19435937674387-Thin-Film-Lithium-Niobate-Electro-Optic-Phase-Modulator

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Ansys Optics Help Center article presents a simulation example of a thin-film Lithium Niobate (LN) electro-optic phase modulator, based on work by Mercante et al. The model uses a two-stage simulation approach within Ansys's Finite Element IDE: (1) an electrical simulation using the CHARGE solver to calculate RF-induced capacitive electric fields in the LN rib waveguide, leveraging the anisotropic DC dielectric permittivity feature added in the 2023 R1.2 release, and (2) an optical simulation using the FEEM solver to calculate the optical modes of the perturbed LN waveguide at a wavelength of 1.55 µm.

Key results include a constant VπL value of 3.18 V-cm obtained from the simulation, compared to the 3.8 V-cm DC half-wave voltage reported in the cited literature [1]. The loss equation used is Loss = -0.20*log10(e^(-2πκ/λ)), where κ is the imaginary part of the effective index. Losses are almost constant across voltages and are primarily attributed to the Au electrodes, with electrode separation being the key optimization factor.

Important model settings include: a 2D y-normal simulation region with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions at external boundaries; a z-span of 9 µm for CHARGE (based on convergence testing); x-cut LN with extraordinary permittivity of 27.9 along the x-axis and ordinary permittivity of 44.3 along y and z axes; LN as a semiconductor-type material (to enable Poisson equation solution); an x-span of 28 µm and z-span of 9 µm for FEEM (with PML boundary conditions); 4 edges per wavelength with polynomial order of 2 for meshing; and "Lock Mesh" enabled to minimize numerical noise in VπL calculations.

The Pockels effect index perturbation is calculated using a diagonal approximation: n_x = n_e - (n_e³/2)r33·E_x, n_y = n_o - (n_o³/2)r13·E_x, n_z = n_o - (n_o³/2)r13·E_x, with extraordinary refractive index 2.14 and ordinary refractive index 2.21 at 1550 nm. The full tensor calculation in the Appendix confirms the diagonal approximation introduces negligible error (maximum 4.6e-11% along x-direction and 1.55e-06% along y/z directions at waveguide center). Mode tracking uses a TE polarization fraction threshold of 95% due to mode hybridization challenges from Au electrodes and x-cut LN's susceptibility to mode hybridization.

The article also discusses design trade-offs (electrode proximity enables better RF modulation but increases optical loss), extensions using HFSS for RF/travelling wave analysis, and INTERCONNECT for circuit-level OOK validation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We obtain a constant VπL value of 3.18 V-cm. In comparison, the cited literature [1] reported a DC half-wave voltage of 3.8 V per cm. This difference can be due to incomplete material properties reported in the literature, process-specific material properties of LN, and experimental non-idealities."
</key_excerpts>
