--- SOURCE 8: When Does Femtosecond Laser Ablation Outperform Nanosecond Processing?-JPT Laser ---
URL: https://en.jptoe.com/about/newsroom/technical-information/nanosecond-vs-femtosecond-laser-ablation

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a technical article from JPT (JPT Opto-Electronics) published on July 24, 2026, discussing when femtosecond laser ablation outperforms nanosecond processing in industrial material processing.

**Key topic:** The article compares nanosecond vs. femtosecond laser ablation, explaining how pulse duration affects energy delivery into materials and the resulting processing quality.

**Nanosecond limitations:** Nanosecond pulses produce stronger thermal effects because longer pulse durations give heat more time to diffuse into surrounding material. This causes heat-affected zones (which may change local material properties), recast layers (requiring cleaning or secondary finishing), burrs and edge rounding (reducing fit accuracy), microcracks (affecting brittle materials), and thermal deformation (reducing assembly consistency). Thin, brittle, reflective, coated, or dimensionally strict parts are hardest to control with nanosecond ablation.

**Femtosecond advantages:** Femtosecond lasers deliver energy before heat has time to spread significantly—often described as "cold" processing (relative term; it means reduced thermal diffusion, not zero heat). A published comparison found nanosecond pulses induced a heat-affected zone of about 40 μm, while femtosecond processing produced no observable heat-affected zone within the study's observation limit. This enables smaller features, sharper boundaries, and more consistent microstructures, reducing secondary finishing and inspection failures.

**Key application areas:** Consumer electronics (thin, coated, compact parts; less thermal distortion), semiconductor and display production (micro-scale features; cleaner boundaries), EV precision parts (assembly consistency; lower deformation risk), and lithium battery manufacturing (surface/edge quality; more controlled processing window).

**Comparison methodology:** Manufacturers should compare both processes using: same material batch, same feature size target, same inspection method, same acceptable defect limits, and same downstream cleaning/assembly checks—keeping decisions based on real process evidence rather than laser category names.

**JPT product featured:** The Jetlit 20 Femtosecond Laser, available in IR and SH configurations. Key specifications include: 400 fs pulse width (SH model), 3–20 W output range, beam quality M² < 1.2, maximum pulse energy above 90 µJ, passive air-cooling architecture, and IP51-rated enclosure for cleanroom and industrial environments. Applications include micromachining, battery manufacturing, semiconductor production, and display manufacturing.

**Conclusion:** The shift to femtosecond lasers should be approached as a process upgrade, not a simple equipment replacement. Teams should evaluate wavelength, pulse width, beam quality, cooling design, and integration format against their specific material and production cell needs.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: Repair of Fused Silica Damage Using Selective Femtosecond Laser-Induced Etching ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the journal *Crystals* (MDPI) in 2023, titled "Repair of Fused Silica Damage Using Selective Femtosecond Laser-Induced Etching." The paper was authored by Zhenhua Fang, Jing Chen, Xiaolong Jiang, Chuanchao Zhang, Lijuan Zhang, Jingxuan Wang, Xiaoyu Luan, Haijun Wang, Qiankun Wu, and Wei Liao, from the Laser Fusion Research Center, China Academy of Engineering Physics, Mianyang, China. The article has DOI 10.3390/cryst13020309, was submitted on 28 January 2023, revised 3 February 2023, accepted 9 February 2023, and published 13 February 2023. It received 4224 article views and 5 citations, and belongs to the Topics section on Laser-Induced Damage Properties of Optical Materials.

**Purpose/Problem:** Fused silica is a critical component of high-power laser systems, and surface damage points frequently occur during high-throughput operation. If not repaired in time, damage expands dramatically. Traditional repair methods (CO2 laser ablation or femtosecond excision) ablate material point-by-point, generating microcracks, thermal accumulation, and residual stresses that require secondary smoothing operations, severely limiting efficiency—especially when many damage points are present.

**Proposed Method:** The authors propose a new approach using in-volume, selective femtosecond laser-induced etching. In this method, the laser irradiates material at energies below the ablation threshold, causing chemical restructuring (the Si-O-Si bond angle of 144° decreases, and the material becomes amorphous and more reactive to etchants). A femtosecond laser scans a 3D hollow trajectory around the damage point (e.g., a cylinder with 1 mm radius and 500 μm height, or a 2 mm-side rectangle with 500 μm height), then the entire sample is immersed in an etching solution. The modified material reacts faster than the unmodified substrate, so the etching solution permeates along the modified trajectory and removes the damaged area as a whole piece. Multiple damage points can be etched synchronously, so etching efficiency is not affected by the number of damage points.

**Key Experimental Parameters and Results:**
- Laser: 1030 nm wavelength, 290 fs pulse width, repetition frequency 50–500 kHz, single pulse energy 1–10 μJ.
- Optimal modification parameters: single pulse energy ~2–5 μJ, repetition frequency ~200–500 kHz, scanning speed ~10 mm/s.
- Sample: Corning 7980 fused silica, dimensions 4 mm × 6 mm × 50 mm, polished on four sides.
- Etching solutions: potassium hydroxide (KOH) at 58% mass fraction was the primary etchant; 5% hydrofluoric acid (HF) was used as a control.
- Substrate etching rates were ~1 μm/h (KOH) and ~2 μm/h (HF), less than one-thousandth of substrate thickness (negligible).
- Etch selectivity ratio between modified and unmodified areas can be as high as 1000:1.
- KOH has higher etching selectivity than HF; the formation of a silicon-rich structure SiOx (x>2) is the reason for KOH's better etching efficiency.
- Scanning speeds below 10 mm/s caused increased surface roughness, edge collapse, and splashing due to excessive energy per unit area; speeds above 10 mm/s caused discontinuous scanning lines.
- The weak reaction between the etching solution and the substrate homogenizes the interface, eliminating the need for secondary smoothing treatments used in traditional methods.

**Chemical Reactions:** The paper provides the reactions of fused silica with HF (producing SiF4 and H2O) and with KOH (producing SiO3 and H2O).

**Advantages over traditional methods:** (1) Greatly reduced repair workload since the material is removed as a whole piece rather than point-by-point ablation; (2) synchronous etching of multiple damage points; (3) interface homogenization during etching eliminates secondary processing; (4) lower laser energy reduces microcrack formation in brittle materials.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In this paper, a new method using in-volume, selective femtosecond laser-induced etching to repair the damage of fused silica is proposed. The region irradiated by femtosecond laser becomes more susceptible to the etching solution due to its constitutive characteristics having undergone chemical restructuring."
</key_excerpts>

# Lithium Niobate Etching Alternatives and Device-Level Performance Demonstrations: Research Findings

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

1. "lithium niobate alternative etching ion beam etching argon ion milling damage surface roughness comparison ICP-RIE"
2. "thin film lithium niobate micro-ring resonator intrinsic Q factor etching process propagation loss dB/cm"

16. "lithium niobate femtosecond laser ablation surface damage thermal stress cracks comparison dry etch"

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### (a) Physical and Ion-Based Etching Methods (IBE, Ion Milling, FIB, RIBE) and Known Damage Profiles in Lithium Niobate

**Ion Beam Etching (IBE) / Ion Milling for Lithium Niobate**

- AARD Technology (a supplier of ion beam equipment) states that materials like lithium niobate (LN, LiNbO₃) are difficult to etch with common ICP-RIE technologies, so they offer ion beam etching (IBE) as a solution for both R&D and manufacturing. Their stated capabilities for LN waveguides include: physical etching of all materials, optional F- and Cl-based reactive gases for tuning etch selectivities, vertical or slanted smooth sidewalls, excellent uniformity (<1%), in-situ sidewall redeposition/fencing removal, SIMS or OES end point detection, tiltable and rotatable substrate, He backside contact cooling with water (plus chiller option for lower temperatures), and capability for reactive ion beam etching (RIBE) by adding F- and Cl-gases to the Ar mixture. Their SCIA Mill equipment is offered for this application. The page notes that waveguides for PIC applications require vertical, smooth sidewalls for proper optoelectronic properties. [1] (aardtechnology.com/photonics-ion-beam-solutions)

- A NineScrolls engineering comparison guide provides general characteristics of ion beam milling (IBE): it is purely physical sputtering (typically Ar⁺, 300–1000 eV), works on any material, but has low rates (10–100 nm/min), poor selectivity (~1:1 to 3:1), and redeposition risk. Ion beam milling is highly anisotropic (collimated beam, tunable 0°–70°+ via a tiltable stage), often delivering higher anisotropy than RIE since it has no isotropic chemical component. RIBE (Reactive Ion Beam Etching) bridges the gap, combining RIE's chemical selectivity with IBE's directional beam control for damage-sensitive materials; RIBE etch rates are 100–500 nm/min, aspect ratios ≤5:1, and selectivity is moderate-tunable. Surface damage from ion milling can be mitigated by reducing beam energy to 300–500 eV and post-etch annealing; an example given: reducing GaN HEMT beam energy from 800 to 400 eV recovered channel mobility to >95% of pristine value. Redeposition in ion milling can be reduced by rotating the sample stage and using 30°–60° oblique incidence; 45° Ar⁺ with rotation reduced MRAM MTJ short-circuit defects by ~80%. [2] (ninescrolls.com/insights/reactive-ion-etching-vs-ion-milling)

- The ETH Zurich group (Kaufmann et al., Nanophotonics 2023) reported on redeposition-free ICP etching of lithium niobate and explicitly discussed ion beam etching (IBE) experiments at incidence angles 0°–35° simulating trapezoidal masks (85°, 70°, 60°, 50°), showing reduced redeposition with increasing angle, confirming that trapezoidal masks help achieve redeposition-free etching. [3] (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321)

**Argon Ion Milling + Gas Cluster Ion Beam (GCIB) Smoothening**

- Siew et al. (Optics Express, 26(4):4421-4430, 19 February 2018, DOI: 10.1364/OE.26.004421, PMID: 29475292) titled "Ultra-low loss ridge waveguides on lithium niobate via argon ion milling and gas clustered ion beam smoothening" fabricated significantly smoother ridge waveguides using argon ion milling followed by gas clustered ion beam (GCIB) smoothening, achieving propagation losses as low as 0.3 dB/cm at 1.55 µm. The paper notes that "sidewalls of etched waveguides are typically rough in most etching procedures, exacerbating propagation losses." Authors: Shawn Yohanes Siew, Eric Jun Hao Cheung, Haidong Liang, Andrew Bettiol, Noriaki Toyoda, Bandar Alshehri, Elhadj Dogheche, Aaron J Danner. [4] (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29475292)

**Focused Ion Beam (FIB) Milling Damage Profiles**

- FIB milling is known to produce lattice damage. A paper on "Damage in III-V Compounds during Focused Ion Beam Milling" (PubMed PMID: 17481325) reports that "The damage on the side walls of the milled trenches is in the form of amorphous layers associated with direct amorphization from the gallium beam." [5] (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17481325; researchgate.net/publication/6349892)

- A paper "Raman characterization of focused ion beam fabricated lithium niobate film" (Journal of Applied Physics, 135(3), 033101) states: "It has been widely reported that the presence of lattice defects caused by FIB milling can significantly degrade the optical performance of" lithium niobate. [6] (pubs.aip.org/aip/jap/article/135/3/033101/3000637)

- Jin et al. (Chinese Optics Letters, Vol. 20, Issue 11, page 113602, 2022, DOI: 10.3788/COL202220.113602) "Fabrication of lithium niobate metasurfaces via a combination of FIB and ICP-RIE" describe that FIB-only milling of LN "produces round-topped nanostructures with crystal lattice damage requiring hydrofluoric acid treatment that causes lateral etching of the SiO2 bonding layer." Their combined process used Ga+ ion beam at 80 pA current and 30 kV acceleration voltage to mill both Cr (40 nm conducting layer) and LN layers, then ICP-RIE with SF6/Ar using the patterned Cr as hard mask, followed by SC-1 solution (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O = 1:1:5) for 5 min at 80°C to remove lithium fluoride (LiF) byproduct, and Cr removal with standard Cr etchant. Results: ridges with trapezoidal cross-sections, sidewall angles larger than 80° (specifically ~82° for a grating with period Pd = 400 nm, top width 211 nm, bottom width 275 nm, duty cycle 62.5%), metasurface array footprint 20 µm × 20 µm. Sharp quasi-bound states in the continuum (QBIC) were observed matching COMSOL simulations. [7] (researching.cn/articles/OJ8c8a1b62c7c6c8d2)

- General FIB damage layer thickness data from the "Practical Electron Microscopy and Database" (Globalsino): 30 kV FIB ≈ 23 nm damaged layer thickness, 5 kV FIB ≈ 6.5 nm, 1 kV Argon ≈ 1.6 nm. A 2 kV Si amorphous layer remains 3 nm thick even at very low beam energy. Amorphous thickness is independent of beam current over the 100–500 pA range. High-energy beams (e.g., 30 kV) create near-surface defect layers extending more than 100 nm deep. Two mechanisms cause amorphization: (i) sufficient atom displacement within the collision cascade leading to loss of long-range order when point defect density reaches a critical value at the surface, and (ii) local melting and quenching of solid in the sample. The amorphization layer on the top of specimens is thicker than on the side-walls. Argon milling can be used to remove FIB-induced damage. [8] (globalsino.com/EM/page4493.html)

- A Covalent educational video (YouTube, 25 April 2022) on FIB lamella defects notes: a 30 kV gallium ion beam creates an amorphous damaged layer approximately 20 nanometers thick; dropping FIB energy to 5 kV (polishing) reduces the damaged layer to about 6 nm thick; dropping to 2 kV reduces damage to roughly 3 nm thick. "The damaged layer correlates nearly 1:1 with the FIB energy used." Redeposition also occurs due to beam tails/sides milling surrounding material. [9] (youtube.com/watch?v=_pKw8SMnFiM)

- Tong and Luo (Strathclyde, "Investigation of focused ion beam induced damage in single crystal diamond tools," published in Applied Surface Science 2015) showed FIB-induced damage layer thicknesses increased from 11.5 nm (8 kV) to 19.4 nm (16 kV) to 27.6 nm (30 kV), increasing with beam energy; damage layers are amorphous carbon accommodating significant implanted gallium; maximum gallium implantation depths were 10.5 nm (8 keV) and 12.8 nm (16 keV). (This is for diamond, provided as general FIB damage scaling reference.) [10] (strathprints.strath.ac.uk/53356/1/Tong_Luo_ASS_2015)

**Reactive Ion Beam Etching (RIBE)**
- As noted above, AARD Technology offers reactive ion beam etching by adding F- and Cl-gases to the Ar mixture, and NineScrolls describes RIBE as combining RIE's chemical selectivity with IBE's directional beam control for damage-sensitive materials (etch rates 100–500 nm/min, aspect ratio ≤5:1, moderate-tunable selectivity). [1][2]

---

### (b) Systematic Comparative Studies of Different Etch Techniques on Lithium Niobate

**RIE of X-cut LiNbO₃ in ICP/TCP System (Applied Sciences 2023)**

- Kozlov, Moskalev, Salgaeva, Bulatova, Krishtop, Volyntsev, and Syuy (Applied Sciences (MDPI), 2023, Volume 13, Issue 4, Article 2097, DOI: 10.3390/app13042097) studied RIE of unmodified (non-proton-exchanged) X-cut LiNbO3 using a chromium hard mask in an SF6/Ar gas mixture with an ICP/TCP plasma source, aiming to produce ridge waveguides with minimal sidewall roughness. Key findings:
  - Dry etching of LiNbO3 is challenging due to formation of non-volatile LiF during fluorine-containing plasma treatment, which reduces etching rate, aspect ratio, and increases surface roughness.
  - Recipe #13 (0.03 mbar pressure): slope angle ~62°, smooth near-waveguide surface, microtrenches formed along waveguide base, mask selectivity 1:5.3, bias voltage 186 V.
  - Recipe #14 (0.007 mbar pressure): slope angle ~75°, dramatically increased surface roughness in near-waveguide region, no microtrenches, mask selectivity improved to 1:8, bias voltage 141 V, brown film-like layer on surface (EDX: O:F:Nb = 18.56:36.56:44.88 wt%), suggesting LiFx compound formation.
  - Etching depths: 0.23–0.60 µm; mask selectivity: 1:4 to 1:8; best slope angle: 70–75°. Chromium hard mask line edge roughness (LER) measured at 20–30 nm.
  - Proposed model: bias voltage difference between recipes #13 (186 V) and #14 (141 V) caused a transition from RIE to radical chemical etching. Estimated Ar+ ion average energies were ~90 eV (recipe #13), ~40 eV (transition region), and ~30 eV (recipe #14). At ~90 eV, ion energies were sufficient to create vacancies in the LiF layer, enhancing diffusion of reaction products and surface sputtering (producing smooth surfaces). Below a transition point (30–90 eV range), chemical etching dominates, leaving LiF and causing rough surfaces.
  - Microtrench formation attributed to ion trajectory deflection toward sidewalls by accumulated electrons — characteristic of RIE with significant physical plasma component at low pressure (<0.1 mbar) and high bias.
  - The authors acknowledge the current slope angles limit PIC applications. [11] (mdpi.com/2076-3417/13/4/2097)

**NIST Optimization of LNOI Waveguide Fabrication (PMC 2024)**

- Kumar, Klimov, and Kuo (NIST, "Optimization of waveguide fabrication processes in lithium-niobate-on-insulator platform," PMC PMID: 11194688) systematically compared fabrication parameters on 700 nm x-cut LNOI (2 µm SiO2, 525 µm Si substrate from NANOLN):
  - Three mask types tested: soft e-beam resist mask, metallic Cr mask (50 nm, e-beam deposition), and dielectric SiO2 hard mask (500 nm PECVD + 10 nm Cr).
  - LN etching performed in Oxford PlasmaLab 100 ICP RIE tool with Ar gas; ICP power 1500 W, pressure 5 mTorr, Ar flow 20 sccm, temperature 5°C.
  - RF power varied from 50 W to 500 W; etch rate ranged from 50 nm/min (50 W) to 107 nm/min (500 W). At low RF power (~50 W), sidewalls fully enveloped by redeposit; at 300 W, redeposit completely eliminated from sidewalls. However, above 300 W, line-edge roughness transferred to the WG causing striations, and WG damage (trenches/pits) occurred. Optimal RF power range determined as 100-200 W.
  - Redeposit cleaning: RCA-1a solution (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O = 2:2:1) heated to 85°C was superior to Piranha and RCA-1b. Optimized cleaning: 15 minutes each at 0° and 90° boat orientations (30 min total). Prolonged cleaning (beyond 30 min) caused chipping and peeling of WGs. Cleaning for 24 hours changed WG geometry (sidewall angles became asymmetric, film thickness reduced from 700 nm to ~630 nm). Properly cleaned samples had equal sidewall angles of ~70°.
  - Soft (resist) mask produced striated sidewall defects that persisted regardless of RF power tuning; Cr hard mask produced markedly improved sidewall profiles. Cr hard mask produced granular features on sidewalls (due to Cr polycrystalline grain size of ~55 nm), while SiO2 mask produced striations and "trenching" at the base of sidewalls (attributed to charge buildup on insulating materials deflecting ions). Cr hard mask was selected for final fabrication.
  - Final devices: WG dimensions top width 600 nm, sidewall angle 70°, rib height 350 nm over 350 nm slab, single-mode at 1550 nm. Eight identical 4.5 mm straight WGs measured with lensed fibers: transmission ranged from 0.075 (-11.2 dB) to 0.107 (-9.7 dB); average transmission 8.9 ± 1.3%, corresponding to -10.5 ± 0.6 dB total insertion loss. Upper-bound propagation loss estimated at ~2 dB/cm (assuming 4.8 dB/facet coupling loss). [12] (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11194688)

**ETH Zurich Redeposition-Free ICP Etching Study (Nanophotonics 2023)**

- Kaufmann, Finco, Maeder, and Grange (ETH Zurich, Nanophotonics 2023 Jan 16;12(8):1601, doi: 10.1515/nanoph-2022-0676, PMCID: PMC11501321) present a systematic workflow for redeposition-free ICP etching of LNOI (400 nm x-cut film, 2 µm SiO2 on 4-inch wafer from NANOLN; HSQ/FOX16 resist; Plasma Pro 100 ICP system using only Cl2, SF6, O2, and Ar):
  - DC bias sweep from 100 V to 800 V (Ar flow 10 sccm, pressure 1 mTorr, 20 °C): total redeposition decreased almost fourfold from 100 V to 800 V, trending toward redeposition-free etching above 1 kV. Trench depth increased by a factor of five with higher bias. Selectivity remained near one, sidewall angle 60-63° for both +Z and −Z crystal faces. Surface roughness (Sq) was ~0.08 nm for biases above 200 V, four times better than un-etched surface (0.31 nm). Sample bow changed from concave to flat to convex with increasing bias: 300 V gave 20 nm thickness variation over 8×8 mm2, while 600 V gave below 5 nm.
  - Pressure sweep from 1 to 15 mTorr (400 V) and 0.3 to 13 mTorr (600 V): redeposition vanished completely after 7 mTorr, but with significant structural damage. Redeposition-free regime occurred at 5-7 mTorr for 600 V and around 11 mTorr for 400 V. Etch rates dropped to minimum values of 27 nm/min (400 V) and 12 nm/min (600 V) before increasing again at higher pressures. Surface roughness degraded with pressure (Sq of 0.10, 0.12, 0.15 nm for 3, 5, 7 mTorr).
  - Aspect ratio dependent etching (ARDE): redeposition decreased with decreasing gap size (from 1 µm to 100 nm). Trench merging occurred at gaps up to 400 nm. Dense structures were redeposition-free down to 1 µm gaps at 300 W ICP power, 600 V DC bias, and 11 mTorr.
  - Redeposition decreased with increasing etch depth (110-260 nm).
  - Four samples etched with 300 W ICP power, 600 V DC bias, 1 mTorr showed reproducibility with Q-factor variation below 2% and calculated propagation loss of 1.55 dB/cm. Etch rate scaled linearly: 0.09 nm/min per watt of ICP power and 0.10 nm/min per volt of DC bias. Ring/racetrack resonators with 600 nm top width, 80 µm bend radius near 1550 nm showed a resonance linewidth of 25 pm.
  - Three proposed methods for redeposition-free etching: (1) careful balancing of ICP parameters (especially DC bias and chamber pressure), (2) increasing structure density so ion deflection between neighboring walls aids redeposition removal, and (3) tailoring the etching mask toward a trapezoidal shape. [3]

**Mi-Net Technology Application Note (ICP-RIE with SF6/Ar)**

- Mi-Net Technology describes an optimized SF6/Ar ICP plasma etching process (SENTECH SI500) for LN ridge waveguides: SF6/Ar mixtures have proven effective for producing smooth ridges; a Cr mask is used for its resistance to high bias power; "relatively high bias power is required to physically remove low-volatility reaction by-products such as LiF and NbFx (without sufficient energy, micro-masking can cause surface roughness)." Benefits claimed: smooth LiNbO3 ridge waveguides with minimal optical loss, no sidewall redeposition, high etch selectivity and pattern fidelity using Cr masks. [13] (mi-net.co.uk/application-note/high-quality-etching-of-lithium-niobate-ridge-waveguides)

- Similarly, SENTECH Instruments' optoelectronics page lists an application note "ICP Etching of Lithium Niobate (LiNbO₃)" using the SI 500 ICP-RIE with SF₆/Ar gas mixture and a Chromium mask to achieve smooth ridge waveguide etching without sidewall re-deposition. [14] (sentech.com/application/optoelectronics)

**Ion Beam Trimming**

- AARD Technology's ion beam trimming uses physical sputter etching for uniformity improvement: for SiNx films, thickness uniformity improved from 3.0% down to 0.2%, thickness range reduced from 14 nm to 1 nm, roughness improved from 0.41 to 0.22 (Rq), with processing time under 5 minutes per 200 mm wafer. [1]

**Femtosecond Laser Ablation Comparison (damage perspective)**

- A JPT technical article notes that nanosecond pulses produce stronger thermal effects (heat-affected zones, recast layers, burrs, microcracks, thermal deformation) while femtosecond lasers deliver energy before heat spreads ("cold" processing). A published comparison found nanosecond pulses induced a heat-affected zone of about 40 µm, while femtosecond processing produced no observable heat-affected zone within the study's observation limit. [15] (en.jptoe.com/about/newsroom/technical-information/nanosecond-vs-femtosecond-laser-ablation)

- A ScienceDirect topic overview of femtosecond lasers notes: femtosecond laser micromachining offers small heat-affected areas, high processing accuracy, and efficiency; nonlinear absorption occurs only at the focus, resulting in highly localized material ablation. A 2023 review (Jia-Xin Zheng et al., Optics & Laser Technology) on "Femtosecond laser with etching technology for micro-optical components" covers laser ablation (when energy significantly exceeds damage threshold) versus laser modification (near damage threshold, causing phase changes), and wet etching of materials including LiNbO₃, plus dry etching techniques (IBE, RIE, ICP) with reaction gases (SF₆, CF₄, CHF₃ for silicon-based materials; Cl₂/BCl₃ for sapphire; Ar for SiC). [16] (sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/femtosecond-laser)

- Chandra and Marla (JLMN-Journal of Laser Micro/Nanoengineering, Vol. 20, No. 1, 2025, DOI: 10.2961/jlmn.2025.01.2006) studied femtosecond laser micromachining (FLM) of glass in different ambient media. Key findings: FLM in KOH solution exhibited the best surface quality compared to HF, DI water, and ethyl alcohol; minimum surface roughness (Sa) of microchannels in KOH was 1.125 µm at 15 µJ (fluence 1.2 J/cm²) with a hatch distance of 5 µm; microcracks were observed in HF, DI water, and ethyl alcohol media — most prominent in ethyl alcohol; KOH produced defect-free microchannels with no haze band, no microcracks, and more uniform/straight profiles. (Note: this is glass, not LN, but is a comparative laser-vs-etchant study.) [17] (jlps.gr.jp/jlmn/uploads/24-043.pdf)

- Fang et al. (Crystals 13(2):309, 2023, DOI: 10.3390/cryst13020309), "Repair of Fused Silica Damage Using Selective Femtosecond Laser-Induced Etching," describe femtosecond laser-induced etching below the ablation threshold causing chemical restructuring (Si-O-Si bond angle of 144° decreases; material becomes amorphous and more reactive to etchants). Etch selectivity ratio between modified and unmodified areas can be as high as 1000:1; KOH has higher etching selectivity than HF; substrate etching rates were ~1 µm/h (KOH) and ~2 µm/h (HF). (Fused silica, not LN, but the femtosecond laser modification + selective etching mechanism is analogous.) [18] (mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309)

**Waveguide type comparison (simulation)**

- Wang, Chen, and Hu (Crystals, 2018, 8(5), 191, DOI: 10.3390/cryst8050191), "Analysis of Waveguides on Lithium Niobate Thin Films," compared ridge waveguides (dry-etched), proton-exchange (PE) waveguides, and strip-loaded waveguides using full-vectorial finite difference method at 1.55 µm (x-cut LNOI, ordinary n=2.211, extraordinary n=2.138). Ridge waveguides: optical power in LN layer 85.6% (q-TE) and 82.5% (q-TM); low bending loss (10⁻⁵ dB/cm) at minimal radii of 15 µm (q-TE) and 20 µm (q-TM). PE waveguides showed bending loss decreasing with PE depth (34 dB/cm at D=0.2 µm vs. 10⁻¹¹ dB/cm at D=0.5 µm, both at 1 mm radius). [19] (mdpi.com/2073-4352/8/5/191)

---

### (c) Femtosecond Laser Ablation and Laser-Assisted Etching (Including Photonic Crystal and Waveguide Fabrication)

**Femtosecond Laser Micromachining of LN Microresonators (Scientific Reports 2015)**

- Lin, Xu, Fang, Wang, Song, Wang, Qiao, Fang, and Cheng (Scientific Reports, 28 January 2015, DOI: 10.1038/srep08072, PMID: 25627294, PMCID: PMC4308694) fabricated high-Q LN whispering-gallery-mode microresonators using femtosecond laser direct writing combined with FIB milling:
  - LN thin film (700 nm) and silica layer (2 µm) on LN substrate; cylindrical post (~59 µm diameter, ~15 µm height) created by femtosecond laser micromachining (Ti:sapphire laser, ~800 nm center wavelength, ~40 fs pulse width, 1 kHz repetition rate, 0.35 mW for LN ablation, 1 mW for silica); FIB milling twice (coarse 30-keV at 4 nA, fine at 1 nA) reduced diameter to 55 µm; silica selectively etched with 5% HF for 8 minutes; thermal annealing at 500°C for 2 hours in air further smoothed the rim.
  - Results: 82 µm diameter LN resonator achieved Q factor of ~2.5 × 10⁵ around 1550 nm; a 55 µm resonator showed Q improvement from 5.2 × 10⁴ (before annealing) to 1.6 × 10⁵ (after annealing) — demonstrating annealing-induced performance recovery after laser/FIB processing. Top and bottom surfaces of LN thin film have surface roughness as low as 0.35 nm.
  - The technique "combines the flexibility and material insensitivity of femtosecond laser micromachining with the precision of FIB milling." [20] (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4308694)

**Depressed Cladding Waveguides (Optical Materials Express 2013)**

- He et al. (Optical Materials Express, 3(9):1378, 2013, cited by 64) report "the fabrication and characterization of femtosecond laser micromachined depressed cladding waveguides in lithium niobate crystal." [21] (opg.optica.org/fulltext.cfm?uri=ome-3-9-1378)

**Femtosecond Laser Fabrication of Waveguide Structures (APL Photonics)**

- A review in APL Photonics (pubs.aip.org/aip/app/article/10/8/081201/3360218, "The femtosecond laser fabrication of waveguide structures in...") describes femtosecond laser direct writing with pulse energy of 2 µJ focused inside a lithium niobate crystal to fabricate waveguides. [22] (pubs.aip.org/aip/app/article/10/8/081201/3360218)

**Femtosecond Laser Processing of Lithium Niobate — Defects and Crack-Free Processing**

- A paper in Journal of Applied Physics 129, 063102 (2021) titled "Crack-free femtosecond laser processing of lithium niobate" demonstrates "a novel method to improve the processing precision of lithium niobate (LiNbO₃)" — noting that conventional femtosecond processing produces "a considerable amount of structural defects." [23] (pubs.aip.org/aip/jap/article/129/6/063102/287542)

**Femtosecond Laser + Etching (FLICE) for 3D Photonic Circuits**

- A Laserlab-Europe/Lasers4EU webinar announcement (16 September 2026) by Francesca Bragheri (IFN-CNR, Italy) describes femtosecond laser micromachining (FLM) of glass: FLM induces localized refractive index modifications inside transparent materials, enabling direct writing of buried optical waveguides, directional couplers, and interferometric structures with true 3D design freedom; when combined with selective chemical etching (FLICE), the technology enables fabrication of reflective micro-optical elements (flat and curved mirrors), metal-coated to guide beams. [24] (lasers4.eu/event/laserlab-europe-talk-femtosecond-laser-fabricated-glass-photonic-integrated-circuits-for-stuctured-illumination-microscopy-16-september-2026)

**FemtoLAB Workstation Capabilities**

- WOP | Workshop of Photonics' FemtoLAB femtosecond laser micromachining workstation supports femtosecond laser ablation (FSLA), laser grooving, multiphoton polymerization (MPP)/direct laser writing (DLW), laser cutting & drilling, with smallest feature size of 200 nm, XYZ positioning accuracy ±0.3 µm, and sample sizes up to 160 mm × 160 mm. Applications across customer institutions include 3D direct laser writing, surface structuring, laser ablation, photo-induced etching, and quantum computing waveguides. [25] (wophotonics.com/products/femtolab)

---

### (d) Device-Level Demonstrations in TFLN/LNOI and Bulk LN with Explicit Optical Performance After Etching

**Micro-ring Resonators — Intrinsic Q-Factors and Propagation Losses**

- **Q = 10⁷ / 2.7 dB/m (arXiv 1712.04479):** "Monolithic Ultrahigh-Q Lithium Niobate Microring Resonator" shows "microring resonators with a quality factor of 10⁷ and waveguides with propagation loss as low as 2.7 dB/m." [26] (arxiv.org/html/1712.04479v1)

- **Q = 4.04 × 10⁷ / 0.0091 dB/cm (Optics Express 2023):** Li et al., "Ultra-high Q lithium niobate microring monolithically..." (Optics Express 31(19):31556, 2023, cited by 26): "the intrinsic Q factor was determined as high as 4.04 × 10⁷, corresponding to a propagation loss of 0.0091 dB cm⁻¹, which is approximately 3 times lower" than prior work. [27] (opg.optica.org/abstract.cfm?uri=oe-31-19-31556)

- **Record Q = 29.32 million / 1.3 dB/m (Photonics Research 2024):** Harvard University (Lončar group, with Peking University and DRS Daylight Solutions), "Twenty-nine million intrinsic Q-factor monolithic microresonators on thin-film lithium niobate," Photonics Research, Vol. 12, No. 8, August 2024, DOI: 10.1364/PRJ.521172. Key details:
  - Fabrication: 600 nm-thick TFLN wafers with 4.7 µm buried silicon dioxide; EBL (700 nm HSQ resist, 1600 µC/cm² dose, multipass writing); ICP-RIE (~325 nm etch depth, ~0.6 nm/s etch rate) using argon gas; optimized dry etch split into two runs; devices undergo chemical cleaning (hot KOH, hot SC1, diluted HF, piranha) and annealing at 520°C in oxygen.
  - Device design: racetrack geometry with wide waveguide widths (3–5 µm) to reduce overlap between light and sidewall roughness, bending radius 200 µm.
  - Record: intrinsic Q of 29.32 million with loaded Q of 19.56 million, achieved with 4.5 µm width, 10 mm length, 0.6 µm coupling gap racetrack. Intrinsic and loaded linewidths were 6.4 MHz and 9.6 MHz, respectively. Corresponding ultra-low propagation loss of 1.3 dB/m.
  - Statistics: for 3 µm width devices, Q increased with length from 1 mm (avg 8.35 million) to 10 mm (avg 13.40 million); for 10 mm length, Q increased with width from 3 µm (avg 9.46 million) to 5 µm (avg 24.45 million). Reproducibility confirmed across two chips.
  - This is a significant advance over the previous dry-etched TFLN resonator record of 12 million Q, and brings TFLN within one order of magnitude of its theoretical material limit of 163 million Q.

**Vapor Transport Equilibration (VTE) for Stoichiometry Restoration**

- Stanford work (Journal of Applied Physics, 2007; "Optical properties and ferroelectric engineering of vapor-transport-equilibrated...") describes VTE conversion of congruent lithium tantalate to near-stoichiometric: heated at 1360°C then 1100°C with two-phase LiTaO3/Li3TaO4 powder as Li2O source; coercive fields as low as 60 V/mm achieved (~50 ppm lithium deficiency, 350 times closer to stoichiometry than congruent); VTE process is surface-reaction-rate or effusion limited; saturated space-charge field reduced 100-fold in VLT vs. CLT (10±8 V/cm vs. 1270±300 V/cm); photorefraction-limited useful length ~17 cm for VLT vs. 0.13 cm for CLT; 532 nm absorption reduced to 0.04–0.12 %/cm vs. 0.28–0.4 %/cm; damage thresholds: congruent LN 2.3 J/cm², CLT 7.3 J/cm², VLT 7.3 J/cm² (12 ns pulses at 1064 nm); an uncoated 4 cm long, 8 µm period VLT device generated 10.5 W internal cw 532 nm SHG from 29 W internal 1064 nm pump with low-power normalized efficiency 0.4 %/(W cm). (This is for lithium tantalate, but demonstrates the VTE principle for stoichiometry restoration and property recovery.) [42] (web.stanford.edu/~rlbyer/PDF_AllPubs/2007/425.pdf)

- Zhang, Wang, Hua, and Pun (Journal of the American Ceramic Society, 2012, volume 95, pages 2798-2800, DOI: 10.1111/J.1551-2916.2012.05381.X) studied Li-rich VTE temperature dependence of surface composition of initially congruent LiNbO3: the VTE-induced surface Li2O-content increase follows the traditional Arrhenius law with a surface Li2O-content alteration constant of (614 ± 136)/(91 ± 10) mol% and an activation energy of (0.76 ± 0.05)/(0.53 ± 0.03) eV for X/Z-cut crystals (1-mm-thick plates). - The Wisconsin Alumni Research Foundation patent WO2002075444A1 (inventors Mccaughan, Kuech, Saulys, Joshkin, Chowdhury, Staus) describes depositing amorphous lithium niobate films (CVD at pressures 0.1 mm Hg to atmospheric, temperatures at or below ~600°C), etching them easily with conventional wet/dry etchants (4% aqueous HF etches at >5 µm/min; 25% HF at ~5 µm/min), then annealing at 900°C–1100°C for 0.5–6 hours to crystallize the film "in a lithium-rich environment, e.g., powdered LiNbO3." ### Additional Context: LNOI Platform, Material Properties, and Fabrication Background

- **LNOI basics (Applied Sciences 2023):** LNOI enables high-contrast optical waveguides with small curvature radii (100 µm or less) and high integration density (50–100 basic elements per cm²). Two European LNOI-based platforms (LOLIPOP and ELENA) were launched in 2022. [11]

- **LN material properties (IOP book chapter by Maxim Sumets, 2024, DOI: 10.1088/978-0-7503-6305-1ch1):** LN belongs to R3c space group; rhombohedral unit cell (a = 5.4944 Å, α = 55°52′) or hexagonal (aH = 5.1483 Å, cH = 13.8631 Å, c/a = 2.693); stoichiometric (R = Li/Nb = 1) vs. congruent (R = 0.946); Curie temperature 1210 °C; density of congruent LN 4.648 g cm⁻³; optically transparent from 0.35 to 5 µm; optical bandgap 3.57–4.7 eV; refractive indices no = 2.289, ne = 2.201 at 633 nm; can be etched by boiling (110 °C) in HF:HNO3 (1:2); RIE using fluorine/chlorine-based plasmas (CF4, CCl2F2, CHF3). For waveguides, films must be ~400 nm thick to achieve ≤1 dB cm⁻¹ leakage on high-refractive-index substrates; roughness of ~1 nm is critical, correlating at ~1% of film thickness. [46] (iopscience.iop.org/book/mono/978-0-7503-6305-1/chapter/bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1)

- **LNOI wafer fabrication (Nanomaterials 2024 review):** LNOI wafers are fabricated using "Smart-Cut" technology (similar to SOI), involving He+ or H+ ion implantation, wafer bonding, thermal annealing, and chemical mechanical polishing (CMP). [32]

- **IEEE Spectrum context (2018):** Lithium niobate is hard, chemically inert, and not amenable to chemical etching; previous techniques (ion diffusion, proton exchange) produced too-low optical-index contrast; hybrid silicon-LN approaches were impractical due to insufficient light coupling; thin-film substrates are commercially available, "meaning the technological steps are ready for standardization." [30]

- **Dry etching chemistry context (Mi-Net, Applied Sciences, COL metasurface paper):** SF6/Ar and fluorine-based chemistries produce non-volatile LiF and NbFx byproducts that require physical sputtering (high bias) to remove; SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O) wet treatment removes LiF byproduct; Ar-only physical etching (e.g., argon-based RIE, argon ion milling) avoids LiF formation and is widely used for lowest optical loss. [13][11][7]

Abstract

High-_Q_ lithium niobate (LN) optical micro-resonators are an excellent platform for future applications in optical communications, nonlinear optics, and quantum optics. To date, high-_Q_ factors are typically achieved in LN using either dielectric masks or femtosecond laser ablation, while the more standard and commonly available lift-off metallic masks are often believed to lead to rough sidewalls and lowered _Q_ factors. Here, we show that LN microring resonators with strong light confinement and intrinsic _Q_ factors over 1 million can be fabricated using optimized lift-off metallic masks and dry etching processes, corresponding to a waveguide propagation loss of ～$～ 0.3 dB / cm$. The entire process is fully compatible with wafer-scale production and could be transferred to other photonic materials.

Keywords

[lithium niobate](javascript:void(0);)[optical resonators](javascript:void(0);)[microstructure fabrication](javascript:void(0);)

1. Introduction

Lithium niobate ($LiNbO_{3}$, LN) is an excellent photonic material for integrated optics, owing to its unique linear and nonlinear optical properties, including high refractive index, large second-order nonlinear susceptibility ($\chi^{\left(\right. 2 \left.\right)} = 27 \textrm{ } pm / V$), and wide optical transparency window (400 nm to 5 µm)[1,2]. In traditional bulk LN devices, optical waveguides are mainly defined by titanium (Ti)-diffusion or proton-exchange methods with low refractive index contrasts. Recent years have witnessed the rapid development of LN-on-insulator (LNOI) technology, where a sub-micron thick LN thin film is bonded on top of a silica ($SiO_{2}$) substrate, leading to an index contrast of $sim 0.7$, much better optical confinement, and substantially improved device performances[3–22]. In particular, the achievement of high-$Q$ optical micro-resonators in the LNOI platform, including microring resonators[9], microdisk resonators[10,11], and photonic crystal cavities[12], has allowed a variety of nonlinear optical and electro-optic devices with unprecedented functionalities and performances, such as ultra-efficient nonlinear wavelength convertors[13,14], broadband electro-optic/Kerr frequency comb sources[15–17], quantum microwave-to-photon convertors[18,19], efficient acousto-optic modulators[20,21], as well as unidirectional frequency shifters[22].

To date, the majority of high-$Q$ ($> 10^{6}$) LNOI micro-resonators have been realized by dry etching using dielectric etching masks such as Si[23], $SiO_{2}$[24], or hard electron-beam resists like hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ)[9] and ZEP[17]. Although these mask materials typically yield low selectivity of $< 1 : 1$ in the argon ion ($Ar^{+}$)-based dry etching process, they have successfully been used to produce smooth waveguide sidewalls and resonators with $Q$ factors as high as $10^{7}$[9]. An alternative approach is based on chromium (Cr) masks fabricated by femtosecond laser machining, followed by a chemical–mechanical polishing (CMP) process to form smooth wedge-like structures in the LN thin film[25], which has led to $Q$ factors close to the material absorption limit of LN ($sim 10^{8}$)[26]. These methods, however, often involve special processes or chemicals (e.g.,HSQ) that are not readily available in every lab. The low etching selectivity and small wedge angle could also pose challenges in creating deep sub-wavelength photonic structures. In contrast, the more standard and commonly available metallic masks, typically prepared using lithography and lift-off processes, have not been widely used for low-loss LN integrated photonics. It is commonly perceived that lift-off metallic masks inevitably lead to rough sidewalls and large scattering losses.

The origins for exacerbated roughness in lift-off metallic masks are mainly two-fold. First, an unoptimized lithography process could cause mask fencing or even bridging at the lift-off edges, if the resist is not carefully tailored to have the desired undercut profile[27]. Second, metallic materials deposited by sputtering or evaporation naturally form grains on the scale of tens of nanometers, ultimately limiting the edge smoothness of these metallic masks. As a result, LNOI micro-resonators fabricated using lift-off metallic masks and dry etching typically exhibit $Q$ factors in the $10^{5}$ range[28–30]. While excessive post-etching surface polishing has been shown to further improve the $Q$ factors by an order of magnitude[29], the demonstration has been limited to donut-like structures with widths of µ$sim 8 \textrm{ } µm$, which are not compatible for applications that require tight optical confinement and/or dispersion engineering.

Sign up for **_Chinese Optics Letters_** TOC. Get the latest issue of _Chinese Optics Letters_ delivered right to you！[Sign up now](https://www.researching.cn/EN/Login?goToURL=/EN/EmailAlert)

In this article, we show that, contrary to common beliefs, standard lift-off metallic masks can well produce LNOI micro-resonators with $Q$ factors over 1 million. By carefully engineering the lift-off resist profile and dry etching process, we demonstrate microring resonators with a measured loaded (intrinsic) $Q$ factor of $sim 5.5 \times 10^{5}$ ($1.1 \times 10^{6}$), corresponding to a waveguide propagation loss of $sim 0.3 \textrm{ } dB / cm$.

2. Methods

The waveguide-coupled microring resonators are fabricated from a commercially available $x$-cut LNOI wafer (NANOLN). The wafer stack consists of a 600 nm LN thin film, a 4.7 µm buried $SiO_{2}$ layer, and a 500 µm silicon substrate, as shown in Fig.[1(a)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g001). Electron-beam lithography (EBL) is first used to pattern the bus waveguides and microrings in poly-methyl methacrylate (PMMA) resist, as illustrated in Fig.[1(b)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g001). The resist patterns are then transferred to a 180 nm nichrome (NiCr) mask layer through thermal evaporation [Fig.[1(c)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g001)] and a standard lift-off process in acetone [Fig.[1(d)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g001)]. The mask patterns are subsequently transferred to the LN layer by an optimized $Ar^{+}$-based reactive ion etching (RIE) process, as shown in Fig.[1(e)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g001). The $Ar^{+}$ ions physically bombard the exposed LN film with a radio-frequency power of $sim 250 \textrm{ } W$ and a bias voltage of $sim 530 \textrm{ } V$, resulting in an etching selectivity of approximately 2:1. The etching selectivity is significantly higher than that of common dielectric masks and could be beneficial in creating deep sub-wavelength structures. After the residual NiCr mask is removed in Cr etchant [Fig.[1(f)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g001)], an optional CMP process could be applied on the sample surface to further reduce the surface roughness[29]. Here, we only apply a soft $4 \times 10^{4} \textrm{ } min \cdot Pa$ polishing step, which does not significantly change the device $Q$ factors ($< 20 \%$) according to Ref.[[29](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#r29)] and our own experiences. Instead, we focus on the investigation and optimization of the lift-off mask quality for better device performance in this paper. Finally, the chip facets are cleaved for end-fire coupling.

Figure[1(g)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g001) shows the scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of a fabricated microring resonator with a radius of 200 µm and a coupling waveguide. The rib-like waveguides feature a rib height of 240 nm, an unetched slab thickness of 340 nm, and a sidewall angle of $sim 45 \circ$ [Fig.[1(g)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g001)]. The top widths of the bus waveguides and the rings are 1.8 µm and 2.4 µm, respectively. These micron-scale waveguides provide strong optical confinement and possibilities for dispersion engineering in the telecommunication bands. Figure[1(h)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g001) shows the simulated electric field ($E_{z}$) distributions of the fundamental transverse-electric (TE) modes for both the bus waveguide (top) and the ring waveguide (bottom). For the ring waveguide simulation, the bending radius of 200 µm has been taken into account, resulting in the slightly asymmetric mode distribution.

3. Results and Discussions

By performing step-by-step SEM examinations of the device cross-section profiles (Fig.[2](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g002)), we show that the roughness in the lift-off metallic masks mainly originates from non-ideal resist profiles and can be largely eliminated by optimizing the lithography and lift-off processes. The left column of Fig.[2](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g002) shows the PMMA and NiCr profiles during a typical, unoptimized lift-off mask preparation process. The cross-section SEM images are taken by cleaving the chip in the direction perpendicular to the waveguides after each step. The SEM images show different structures, since they are taken from different areas of the chip due to uncertainties in hand cleavage positions. Nevertheless, the images shown in each column are from the same chip and still provide important insights for optimizing the lift-off processes step by step. We find that although the PMMA profile right after EBL looks almost perfectly vertical [Fig.[2(a)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g002)], it often experiences substantial deformation during the thermal evaporation process, which in turn leads to an overcut resist profile [Fig.[2(c)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g002)]. As a result, NiCr is deposited not only at the bottom surface, but also on the resist sidewalls, which ultimately translates into fencing features on the final lift-off masks [Fig.[2(e)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g002), showing top-down view]. Such features are typically hundreds of nanometers in size and will be directly transferred into the sidewall roughness of the final LN devices.

![Image 4: (a) Experimental setup for LN microring resonator characterization. FPC, fiber polarization controller; DUT, device under test; PD, photodetector. Measured optical transmission spectra for typical microring resonators using (b) unoptimized and (c) optimized fabrication processes. (d) and (e) Zoom-in views of (b) and (c) showing critically coupled resonances. Blue dots show the measured data, and red curves correspond to the Lorentzian fits, indicating intrinsic Q factors of 1.4 × 105 and 1.1 × 106 for unoptimized and optimized metallic masks, respectively.](https://www.researching.cn/Images/icon/loading.gif)

The left column [(a), (c), and (e)] shows a typical unoptimized lift-off process with overcut resist profiles and mask fencing features, whereas the right column [(b), (d), and (f)] corresponds to the optimized process with smooth mask profiles. Measured optical transmission spectra for typical microring resonators using (b)unoptimized and (c)optimized fabrication processes. *   [Download full size](javascript:void();)
*   [View all figures](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7/figureandtable)

We show that the rough features on the NiCr masks can be significantly reduced by optimizing each fabrication step in the lift-off process, as shown in the right column of Fig.[2](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g002). First, we create an undercut PMMA resist profile by fine tuning the PMMA film thickness, EBL exposure energy, and development time [Fig.[2(b)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g002)]. For the micron-scale waveguides shown in this paper, we use a 1.3 µm thick PMMA layer (950 A11), with an EBL dose of µ$1000 \textrm{ } µC / cm^{2}$ and 20 s development time in a methyl isobutyl ketone/isopropyl alcohol (MIBK/IPA) 1:3 solution. We then optimize the NiCr mask material quality (i.e.,grain size) by evaporation at relatively low rates (1–2 Å/s, 1 Å = 0.1 nm) and low pressure. We also limit the time for each continuous evaporation step to <15 min to minimize thermal deformation of PMMA. As a result, the desired undercut resist profile is well maintained after metal deposition, as shown in Fig.[2(d)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g002). The final lift-off NiCr mask shows smooth sidewalls without fencing features [Fig.[2(f)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g002)], which lays the foundation for our high-$Q$ micro-resonators. The slightly slanted NiCr sidewalls in Fig.[2(f)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g002) are likely results of non-vertical thermal evaporation with respect to the substrate. In our experience, these slanted masks do not significantly affect the final device sidewall roughness, but could be a reason for the smaller etched LN sidewall angle ($sim 45 \circ$) compared with those commonly achieved using HSQ masks ($sim 70 \circ$)[15]. Using these optimized NiCr masks for the subsequent dry etching step, we achieve LN photonic devices with relatively smooth etched sidewalls, as shown in Fig.[1(g)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g001). The zoom-in view of these etched structures still reveals observable roughness, which is likely induced by the remaining metal grain boundaries. The surface roughness of these devices could be further reduced by applying a longer post-etching CMP process, which has been thoroughly studied in Ref.[[29](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#r29)] and is beyond the focus of this paper.

We characterize the $Q$ factors of the fabricated LNOI microring resonators using an end-fire coupling system shown in Fig.[3(a)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g003). Continuous-wave (CW) light from a tunable telecom laser (Santec TSL-550) is coupled into the input facet of the bus waveguide using a lensed fiber. The output signal is collected by a second lensed fiber and monitored using a photodetector (PD). Figures[3(b)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g003)–[3(e)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g003) show the measured optical transmission spectra of LNOI microring resonators fabricated using unoptimized (left column) and optimized (right column) lift-off metallic masks. The two microrings have different radii of 100 µm and 200 µm resulting in free spectral ranges (FSRs) of 1.7 nm [Fig.[3(b)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g003)] and 0.85 nm [Fig.[3(c)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g003)], respectively, which do not affect our discussions on $Q$ factors in these roughness-limited resonators. Figures[3(d)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g003)–[3(e)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g003) show the zoom-in views of critically coupled resonance dips for the two processes, along with their Lorentzian fits (red curve). For the unoptimized process [Fig.[3(d)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g003)], the fitted curve reveals a resonance linewidth of 22.1 pm, corresponding to a relatively low loaded (intrinsic) $Q$ factor of $7.0 \times 10^{4}$ ($1.4 \times 10^{5}$). In contrast, using our optimized NiCr mask and dry etching process, we achieve microring resonators with a measured intrinsic $Q$ factor over 1 million. As shown in Fig.[3(e)](https://www.researching.cn/articles/OJfb2865c4f2f6baa7#g003), we measure a critically coupled resonance linewidth of 2.86 pm at 1573.5 nm, which corresponds to a loaded $Q$ factor of $5.5 \times 10^{5}$ and an intrinsic $Q$ factor of $1.1 \times 10^{6}$, almost an order of magnitude higher than that achieved using the unoptimized process. From the measured $Q$ factors, we can also estimate the waveguide propagation losses to be $sim 0.3 \textrm{ } dB / cm$. These million-level $Q$ factors, although not as high as some recent LNOI demonstrations[9,10], could already serve the purpose for a majority of LNOI applications and are achieved using standard lift-off metallic masks and wafer-compatible processes. The wavelength-scale photonic structures are ideally suited for dispersion engineering in nonlinear optics and electrode patterning in electro-optic applications. The $Q$ factors can be further improved by applying a longer CMP process[29], as well as cladding the devices in $SiO_{2}$ to reduce the index contrast across the etched surface.

4. Conclusions

In conclusion, we have demonstrated LN microring resonators with intrinsic $Q$ factors over 1 million using standard lift-off metallic masks and dry etching. We show that commonly observed non-ideal features in lift-off masks can be largely eliminated by optimizing the lithography, evaporation, and lift-off processes, leading to smooth etched surfaces and $Q$ factors comparable with other popular LNOI fabrication techniques. Compared with masks based on dielectrics or hard electron-beam resists, these more standard and commonly available metallic masks exhibit substantially higher etching selectivity ($sim 2 : 1$) and could provide opportunities in creating deep sub-wavelength LNOI photonic structures such as metasurfaces or inverse-designed devices. The entire process is fully compatible with wafer-scale production and could also be transferred to other difficult-to-process photonic materials like $TiO_{2}$ and SiC.

args.summary:
This is a scientific article from Chinese Optics Letters (Vol. 19, Issue 6, 060010, 2021) titled "High-Q lithium niobate microring resonators using lift-off metallic masks [Invited]." The paper, authored by Ke Zhang, Zhaoxi Chen, Hanke Feng, Wing-Han Wong, Edwin Yue-Bun Pun, and Cheng Wang (corresponding author) from the Department of Electrical Engineering and State Key Laboratory of Terahertz and Millimeter Waves at City University of Hong Kong, demonstrates that high-Q lithium niobate (LN) microring resonators with intrinsic quality factors exceeding 1 million can be fabricated using standard lift-off metallic masks and dry etching processes.

Key findings and methodology:
- The work challenges the common belief that lift-off metallic masks inevitably produce rough sidewalls and lowered Q factors in LN-on-insulator (LNOI) devices.
- The fabrication process used a 600 nm x-cut LNOI wafer (NANOLN) with a 4.7 µm buried SiO2 layer and 500 µm silicon substrate. Electron-beam lithography (EBL) patterned PMMA resist, which was transferred to a 180 nm nichrome (NiCr) mask layer via thermal evaporation and lift-off. An optimized Ar+ based reactive ion etching (RIE) process with ~250 W RF power and ~530 V bias achieved an etching selectivity of ~2:1 (significantly higher than dielectric masks).
- Optimization steps included: creating an undercut PMMA resist profile (1.3 µm thick PMMA 950 A11, EBL dose of 1000 µC/cm², 20 s development in MIBK/IPA 1:3), evaporating NiCr at low rates (1-2 Å/s) and low pressure, and limiting continuous evaporation steps to <15 minutes to minimize PMMA thermal deformation.
- The microring resonators featured a radius of 200 µm, rib height of 240 nm, unetched slab thickness of 340 nm, sidewall angle of ~45°, with bus waveguide and ring widths of 1.8 µm and 2.4 µm respectively.
- Results: Unoptimized masks produced devices with a loaded (intrinsic) Q factor of 7.0 × 10⁴ (1.4 × 10⁵), while optimized masks achieved a loaded Q of 5.5 × 10⁵ and intrinsic Q of 1.1 × 10⁶ (measured at 1573.5 nm with a 2.86 pm resonance linewidth), corresponding to a waveguide propagation loss of ~0.3 dB/cm.
- The process is fully compatible with wafer-scale production and could be transferred to other difficult-to-process photonic materials like TiO2 and SiC.

The article was received March 7, 2021, accepted April 7, 2021, and published online June 10, 2021. It is part of a Special Issue on Lithium Niobate Based Photonic Devices, with DOI: 10.3788/COL202119.060010.
args.key_excerpts: "Here, we show that LN microring resonators with strong light confinement and intrinsic Q factors over 1 million can be fabricated using optimized lift-off metallic masks and dry etching processes, corresponding to a waveguide propagation loss of ~ 0.3 dB / cm."

# Monolithic Ultrahigh-Q Lithium Niobate Microring Resonator

###### Abstract

We demonstrate an ultralow loss monolithic integrated lithium niobate photonic platform consisting of dry-etched subwavelength waveguides. We show microring resonators with a quality factor of 107 and waveguides with propagation loss as low as 2.7 dB/m.

August 11, 2026

Lithium niobate (LN) is a material with wide range of applications in optical and microwave technologies, owing to its unique properties that include large second order nonlinear susceptibility (χ(2)\chi^{(2)}= 30 pm/V), large piezoelectric response (C33∼C\_{33}\sim 250 C/m2), wide optical transparency window (350 nm −- 5 μ\mum) and high refractive index (∼\sim 2.2) [Maleki and Matsko 2008](#bib.bib1). Conventional LN components, including fiber-optic modulators and periodically poled frequency converters have been the workhorse of the optoelectronic industry. The performances of these components have the potential to be dramatically improved as optical waveguides in bulk LN crystals are defined by ion-diffusion or proton-exchange methods which result in low index contrast and weak optical confinement. Integrated LN platform, featuring sub-wavelength scale light confinement and dense integration of optical and electrical components, has the potential to revolutionize optical communication and microwave photonics [Maleki and Matsko 2008](#bib.bib1); [Chen et al. 2014](#bib.bib2); [Rao et al. 2015](#bib.bib3); [Chang et al. 2016](#bib.bib4); [Luo et al. 2017](#bib.bib5); [Wang et al. 2015](#bib.bib6); [Wang et al. 2017](#bib.bib7).

The major road-block for practical applications of integrated LN photonics is the difficulty of fabricating devices that simultaneously achieve low optical propagation loss and high confinement. Recently developed thin-film LN-on-insulator technology makes this possible, and has resulted in the development of two complementary approaches to define nanoscale optical waveguides: hybrid and monolithic. The hybrid approach integrates an easy-to-etch material (e.g. silicon or silicon nitride) with LN thin films to guide light [Chen et al. 2014](#bib.bib2); [Rao et al. 2015](#bib.bib3); [Chang et al. 2016](#bib.bib4) with a relatively low propagation loss (0.3 dB/cm) [Chang et al. 2016](#bib.bib4). However, the resulting optical modes only partially reside in the active material region (i.e. LN), reducing the nonlinear interaction efficiency. The monolithic approach relies on direct etching of LN to achieve high optical confinement in the active region, but has suffered from a relatively high propagation loss. While freestanding LN microdisk resonators have achieved optical quality factors (QQ) of ∼106\sim 10^{6} [Luo et al. 2017](#bib.bib5); [Wang et al. 2015](#bib.bib6), integrated microring resonators typically feature Q∼105Q\sim 10^{5} with waveguide propagation loss on the order of 3 dB/cm [Wang et al. 2017](#bib.bib7). Since LN is perceived as a difficult-to-etch material, it is commonly accepted that low-loss propagation in a monolithic waveguide is not possible, and that therefore it is not the most promising path forward.

![Refer to caption](1712.04479v1/Figures1.png)
![Refer to caption](1712.04479v1/Figures2.png)

Here we challenge the *status quo* and show that sub-wavelength scale lithium niobate waveguides can be fabricated with a propagation loss as low as 2.7 ±\pm 0.3 dB/m through an optimized etching process. We also demonstrate ultra-high QQ factor optical cavities with intrinsic Q=107Q=10^{7}.

We fabricate waveguide coupled microring and racetrack resonators with a bending radius rr = 80 μ​m\mu m, and various straight arm lengths ll and waveguide widths ww (Fig. [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Monolithic Ultrahigh-Q Lithium Niobate Microring Resonator")). The optical modes in these resonators have different interaction strength with the etched sidewalls which allows us to identify the source of the optical losses (Fig. [2](#S0.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Monolithic Ultrahigh-Q Lithium Niobate Microring Resonator")). We fabricate the devices using a 600 nm thick X-cut LN thin film on 2 μ\mum of silicon dioxide (SiO2) on a silicon substrate (NanoLN). We use standard electron beam lithography to define patterns in hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ) resist with multi-pass exposure. The patterns are subsequently transferred into the LN thin film using a commercial inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etching (ICP RIE) tool. We use Ar+ plasma to physically etch LN where the plasma power and chamber condition are tuned to minimize surface redeposition of removed LN and other contaminations present in the chamber. We etch a total of hribh\_{\textrm{rib}} = 350 nm of LN with a bias power of 112 W leaving a hslabh\_{\textrm{slab}} = 250 nm thin LN slab. After cleaning and removal of the resist, the devices are cladded by depositing 1.5 μ\mum of SiO2 using plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD).

The optical QQ factors of these resonators are measured using a tunable telecom external cavity diode laser (Santec TSL-510). To calibrate the QQ measurement, we also modulate (500 MHz) the laser output using an external electro-optic modulator. Fig. [3](#S0.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Monolithic Ultrahigh-Q Lithium Niobate Microring Resonator")a shows a critically-coupled micro-racetrack resonator with a loaded (intrinsic) QQ factor of 5.0 (10.0±0.7\pm 0.7) million at an optical excitation wavelength of 1590 nm. To confirm the QQ factor, we directly measure the photon lifetime of the resonator using ring-down measurement (Fig. [3](#S0.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Monolithic Ultrahigh-Q Lithium Niobate Microring Resonator")b). The fitted data show a lifetime of 4.2±\pm0.2 ns in good agreement with the spectral measurements.
We show that sidewall scattering is still a significant loss channel in our devices by investigating structures with different waveguide widths. Fig [3](#S0.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Monolithic Ultrahigh-Q Lithium Niobate Microring Resonator")c shows the intrinsic QQ measured for fabricated ring and racetrack resonators. Increasing waveguide width from 800 nm to 2.4 μ\mum leads to a QQ improvement from ∼1.5\sim 1.5 to ∼4\sim 4 million. This improvement is expected from the reduced interaction of the light and the etched sidewalls (Fig. [2](#S0.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Monolithic Ultrahigh-Q Lithium Niobate Microring Resonator")).

We extract the straight optical waveguide propagation loss by comparing the optical QQ factors of micro-racetrack resonators with different straight section lengths from 0 to 14 mm, with the same waveguide width of 2.4 μ\mum and bending radius of 80 μ\mum. Indeed, racetrack resonators with longer straight sections exhibit higher optical QQ factors as light in the straight section interact less with the sidewall scattering centers than in the bending region (Fig [2](#S0.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Monolithic Ultrahigh-Q Lithium Niobate Microring Resonator")). The results are shown in Fig. [3](#S0.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Monolithic Ultrahigh-Q Lithium Niobate Microring Resonator")d, where we extract a straight waveguide loss of 2.7±\pm0.3 dB/m from the intersection of the fitted line. The extracted bending loss of 9.3±\pm0.9 dB/m agrees well with the measurements in ring resonators. By comparing the straight section loss of two race-track resonators with different widths (1.2 and 2.4 μ\mum) and using numerical modeling, we estimate an upper bound of 1.5 dB/m for the intrinsic loss of our platform. The possible contributing factors are ion-implantation damage introduced during the LN thin-film production process, top-surface roughness due to LN polishing, and finite PECVD SiO2 cladding absorption. Importantly, these loss mechanisms could be mitigated by a combination of defects annealing and finer top-surface polishing [Ji et al. 2017](#bib.bib8). We expected that the these loss contributions of the monolithic LN platform could be further reduced towards its material intrinsic loss limit of << 0.1 dB/m [Maleki and Matsko 2008](#bib.bib1).

In conclusion, we show that the monolithic LN nanophotonic platform is a viable path forward. The ultralow loss, high optical confinement and tight bending radius combined with the ability to integrate microwave electrodes [Wang et al. 2017](#bib.bib7) will bring electro-optic [Wang et al. 2017](#bib.bib7); [Chen et al. 2014](#bib.bib2) nonlinear optical [Chang et al. 2016](#bib.bib4) systems into a new design parameter space that has been inaccessible so far. This could enable a wide range of applications including those in ultralow loss quantum photonics [O’Brien 2007](#bib.bib9) ,coherent microwave to optical conversion [Javerzac-Galy et al. 2016](#bib.bib10); [Soltani et al. 2017](#bib.bib11) and active topological photonics [Lin et al. 2016](#bib.bib12). We emphasize that the LN device layer sits atop a standard silicon handle wafer and therefore our platform can also be integrated with many existing photonic technologies. Finally, we hope that our work will stimulate further activities and a renewed interest of the monolithic LN nanophotonic approach, that could ultimately result in the development of dedicated LN nanofabrication foundries and/or introduction of etched LN into existing silicon photonics processes.

The authors thank National Science Foundation ECCS-1609549, DMR-1231319) and REU program; Harvard University Office of Technology Development Physical Sciences and Engineering Accelerator; ARL Center for Distributed Quantum Information W911NF1520067. Device fabrication was performed at the center for nanoscale systems (CNS) at Harvard University.

args.summary:
This is a scientific paper (arXiv, dated August 11, 2026) titled "Monolithic Ultrahigh-Q Lithium Niobate Microring Resonator," which demonstrates a breakthrough in integrated lithium niobate (LN) photonics. The authors challenge the prevailing assumption that low-loss propagation in monolithic LN waveguides is impossible, showing that sub-wavelength scale lithium niobate waveguides can be fabricated with a propagation loss as low as 2.7 ± 0.3 dB/m through an optimized dry-etching process, along with ultra-high Q-factor optical cavities with intrinsic Q = 10^7 (10 million).

Key methodology: The team used a 600 nm thick X-cut LN thin film on 2 μm of SiO2 on a silicon substrate, with standard electron beam lithography and inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etching (ICP RIE) using Ar+ plasma. They etched 350 nm of LN leaving a 250 nm slab, and cladded devices with 1.5 μm of PECVD SiO2. They fabricated waveguide-coupled microring and racetrack resonators with a bending radius of 80 μm.

Key results: A critically-coupled micro-racetrack resonator achieved a loaded (intrinsic) Q factor of 5.0 (10.0 ± 0.7) million at 1590 nm, confirmed via photon lifetime ring-down measurement (4.2 ± 0.2 ns). Increasing waveguide width from 800 nm to 2.4 μm improved Q from ~1.5 to ~4 million (reduced sidewall interaction). Straight waveguide loss was extracted at 2.7 ± 0.3 dB/m, with bending loss of 9.3 ± 0.9 dB/m. The intrinsic loss upper bound was estimated at 1.5 dB/m, attributed to ion-implantation damage, top-surface roughness, and PECVD cladding absorption—all potentially mitigated by annealing and polishing. The authors expect losses could approach the material intrinsic limit of <0.1 dB/m.

The paper concludes that the monolithic LN nanophotonic platform is viable, offering ultralow loss, high optical confinement, and tight bending radius, enabling applications in ultralow-loss quantum photonics, coherent microwave-to-optical conversion, and active topological photonics. The platform sits on a standard silicon handle wafer, allowing integration with existing photonic technologies. Funding came from the NSF (ECCS-1609549, DMR-1231319), Harvard University OTD, and ARL Center for Distributed Quantum Information (W911NF1520067). Fabrication was performed at the Center for Nanoscale Systems at Harvard University.

### Thin film lithium niobate nonlinear photonics

### Position Description

Download and read [the full position description](https://aufrande.eu/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/AUFRANDE_DC15_call3.pdf) before applying

### Proposed Projects

Option 1

**Efficient nonlinear broadband supercontinuum light sources in strip-loaded LNOI**

Despite the high application potential of nonlinear optics for all-optical information processing, no nonlinear material candidate has emerged as a clear choice to complement silicon photonics so far. On the one hand, wide band gap semiconductors have been investigated, but their integration onto silicon photonics is not straightforward. Glass materials have also been explored, but their relatively weak nonlinearity precludes the realization of compact devices. Lithium niobate (LiNBO3) possesses both a second-order (c(2)) and third-order (c(3)) nonlinearity, which proves useful for both electro-optical modulation and also all-optical signal processing devices. Recently, thin-film lithium niobate on insulator wafers have become commercially available and emerged as a highly promising platform for integrated nonlinear optics. Most importantly, this platform supports tightly confining waveguide geometries, a boost for nonlinearities, while additionally opening opportunities for dispersion engineering, which is key to device efficiency and broadband processes, such as supercontinuum. In this context, RMIT has developed a complementary route towards high performance thin-film lithium niobate based devices that exploits strip loading of another thin film, silicon nitride (Si3N4) for instance, which is patterned instead of the lithium niobate so as to support low loss guided modes. This approach elegantly alleviates the need for lithium niobate patterning, while still offering relatively tightly confining geometries (Aeff ~2µm2) and the possibility to engineer the dispersion which is key for broadband supercontinuum.

The aim of this project will be to push this approach for broadband supercontinuum generation that can reach out to the mid-IR band (5um), where many molecules of importance for the defense and environment have strong absorption fingerprint. Part of the strategy will involve quasi phase matching with periodic poling of lithium niobate to increase the efficiency of difference frequency generation processes pumped at telecom wavelengths. This will be also used as a means to increase cascaded c(2) processes and further promote spectral broadening of the pump.

Option 2

**Efficient nonlinear integrated microcombs in thin film LNOI**

Despite the high application potential of nonlinear optics for all-optical information processing, no nonlinear material candidate has emerged as a clear choice to complement silicon photonics so far. On the one hand, wide band gap semiconductors have been investigated, but their integration onto silicon photonics is not straightforward. Glass materials have also been explored, but their relatively weak nonlinearity precludes the realization of compact devices. Lithium niobate (LiNBO3) possesses both a second-order (c(2)) and third-order (c(3)) nonlinearity, which proves useful for both electro-optical modulation and also all-optical signal processing devices. Recently, thin-film lithium niobate on insulator wafers have become commercially available and emerged as a highly promising platform for integrated nonlinear optics. Most importantly, this platform supports tightly confining waveguide geometries, a boost for nonlinearities, while additionally opening opportunities for dispersion engineering, which is key to device efficiency and broadband processes, such as optical frequency combs. The combination of both c(2)and c(3) responses can, in contrast with silicon where only c(3) does exist, provide new ways of electrically tuning all-optical nonlinear functions. Furthermore, the birefringence of lithium niobate and ferroelectric domain inversion capabilities provide opportunities for phase matching and quasi phase matching, which is critical for frequency conversion processes, such as four-wave mixing or high-order harmonic generation.

The specific objectives of this PhD study will be (1) to exploit strip-loaded lithium niobate on insulator resonators to design and realize highly efficient c(3) nonlinear devices with anomalous dispersion for comb generation, (2) to experimentally demonstrate the integration of electro-optical modulators with c(3) ring resonators on a single chip, where the modulation frequency of the modulator can be tuned to match the free spectral range of the ring resonator, which will enable the efficient generation of optical frequency combs, (3) explore the alternative path offered by c(2) nonlinear optics via quasi-phase matching in lithium niobate for the generation of optical frequency combs and (4) use the c(2) response of lithium niobate to realize tunable nonlinear functions.

Option 3

**Ultra-high Q factor lithium niobate resonators for mid-IR Kerr combs**

Despite the high application potential of nonlinear optics for all-optical information processing, no nonlinear material candidate has emerged as a clear choice to complement silicon photonics so far. On the one hand, wide band gap semiconductors have been investigated, but their integration onto silicon photonics is not straightforward. Glass materials have also been explored, but their relatively weak nonlinearity precludes the realization of compact devices. Lithium niobate (LiNBO3) possesses both a second-order (c(2)) and third-order (c(3)) nonlinearity, which proves useful for both electro-optical modulation and also all-optical signal processing devices [1]. Recently, thin-film lithium niobate on insulator wafers [2] have become commercially available and emerged as a highly promising platform for integrated nonlinear optics [3]. Most importantly, this platform supports tightly confining waveguide geometries, a boost for nonlinearities, while additionally opening opportunities for dispersion engineering, which is key to device efficiency and broadband processes, such as optical frequency combs [4,5]. In this context, RMIT has developed a complementary route towards high performance thin-film lithium niobate based devices that exploits strip loading of another thin film, silicon nitride (Si3N4) for instance, which is patterned instead of the lithium niobate so as to support low loss guided modes. This approach elegantly alleviates the need for lithium niobate patterning, while still offering relatively tightly confining geometries (Aeff ~2µm2) and the possibility to engineer the dispersion which is key for the generation of frequency combs.

While much has been done with the lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) platform in the telecom band, this material is transparent up to the mid-IR and could support low loss modes up to about 5um, reaching out the spectral window where many biomolecules of importance for defence and environmental applications have strong molecular fingerprints. The aim of this PhD will be to design and fabricate high quality factor microresonators (microrings, microdisks or photonic crystal cavities) that can support low loss confined modes at these long wavelengths. These will be specifically engineered, using for instance photonic molecules consisting of coupled cavities, and adequate coupling strategies (e.g. using pulley waveguides) will be deployed to sustain optical Kerr microcombs in the mid-IR.
