This webpage describes PhD position DC-15 in the field of Optical Physics / Photonics under the AUFRANDE (Australia-France) network, hosted jointly by École Centrale de Lyon (EC Lyon) in Ecully, France, and RMIT University in Melbourne, Australia. The position is co-supervised by Dr. Christian Grillet, Prof. Christelle Monat, Dist. Prof. Arnan Mitchell, Andy Boes, Thach Nguyen, and Guanghui Ren. The PhD focuses on thin-film lithium niobate (LiNBO3) nonlinear photonics, leveraging the material's dual second-order (χ(2)) and third-order (χ(3)) nonlinearities for all-optical signal processing and frequency comb generation. Three research project options are offered:

Option 1: Efficient nonlinear broadband supercontinuum light sources in strip-loaded LNOI — targeting mid-IR supercontinuum generation up to ~5µm (molecular fingerprint region for defense/environmental applications), using silicon nitride strip-loading on lithium niobate (Aeff ~2µm²) and quasi-phase matching via periodic poling for cascaded χ(2) processes.

Option 2: Efficient nonlinear integrated microcombs in thin film LNOI — focusing on strip-loaded LNOI resonators with anomalous dispersion for comb generation, integrating electro-optical modulators with χ(3) ring resonators on a single chip, and exploring χ(2) quasi-phase matching for optical frequency combs.

Option 3: Ultra-high Q factor lithium niobate resonators for mid-IR Kerr combs — designing and fabricating high-Q microresonators (microrings, microdisks, photonic crystal cavities) supporting low-loss mid-IR modes up to ~5µm, using photonic molecules (coupled cavities) and pulley waveguide coupling to sustain optical Kerr microcombs in the mid-IR.

Key advantages of the LNOI platform highlighted include commercial availability, tight mode confinement for enhanced nonlinearities, dispersion engineering capabilities, transparency up to the mid-IR, and the coexistence of both χ(2) and χ(3) nonlinearities (unlike silicon which only has χ(3)). Applicants must download and read the full position description PDF before applying.

## **What is a Quartz Resonator?**

Often referred to as “Xtal” in circuit diagrams these electronic components work on the principle of converting the mechanical resonance of a vibrating crystal of piezoelectric material into an electrical signal with a fixed frequency. They are widely used for a number of applications from simple clock oscillators, to sophisticated filters.

Quartz crystals exhibit a remarkable number of physical properties which make them particularly well suited to use in crystal resonator technology. Their material properties are extremely stable with temperature and other environmental conditions and highly repeatable from one crystal to the next. Their acoustic loss or internal friction is also very low. These characteristics combine to give quartz crystal resonators a Q factor which is orders of magnitude better than the best LC circuits.

When a dc voltage is applied across the faces of a quartz crystal it causes it to resonate at its natural operating frequency. This is typically at least a third of the fundamental mode frequency and can be as high as several MHz. A resonator may be designed to operate at a single operating frequency or at multiple frequencies at varying resonant modes referred to as overtones.

The resonator’s mode of operation depends on the crystal geometry and cut. For a frequency above 1 MHz most crystals are designed to operate in either the thickness shear or face shear modes. The choice of cut is important for a number of reasons including frequency stability, phase noise and cost.

It has been thoroughly characterized in optical measurements by Stanton, P.L., Graham, R.A., and Morris, R.W., and is useful for a wide variety of nonlinear applications. Its refractive properties make it ideal for various spectroscopic applications, including nonlinear optical polarization and photoelasticity.

The high degree of transparency and the low power consumption make Black Lithium Niobate an attractive material for many applications in electronics and photonics. Its outstanding electro-optic and electro-mechanical coupling properties have made it a useful material in various fields, from medical devices to consumer electronics. The chemical structure of LiNbO3 is similar to that of lithium iodide, and it has asymmetric charge centers.

The two most common materials used to make Black Lithium Niobate are [Lithium Tantalate (LiAtO3) crystal substrate](https://www.universitywafer.com/lithium-tantalate-litao3.html "liato3 wafers") and rustless steel containers. Lithium columbate crystal substrate is a 400mm square piece of lithium in a rustless steel container. Generally, the amount of Zn in the mixture is less than 35% of the total mass ratio in a mixed system. There is also an organic silica gel in the mixture.

The improved phonon to photon conversion makes it an excellent choice for quantum physics research using surface acoustic waves. ### **Device fabrication**

The acoustic nano-filter consisted of two parts: a standing-surface-acoustic-wave (SSAW) chip and a microfluidic channel. The SSAW chip was fabricated on a piezoelectric substrate. **A LiNbO3 wafer with XY 128° cut was purchased (University Wafer)**. Interdigitated transducer (IDT) electrodes were patterned *via* conventional optical lithography, and metal layers (Ti, 50 Å; Au, 800 Å) were deposited. The patterned wafer was then cut into a desired size (21 mm × 21 mm) with a dicing saw. The microfluidic structure was fabricated in polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS; Dow Corning) *via* soft-lithography technique. The channel mold was formed on a Si wafer, using an epoxy-based photoresists (SU-8 2050, Microchem). The cross-section of the channel was 60 µm × 80 µm (width × height). Both the SSAW chip and the microfluidic block were treated with oxygen plasma, aligned and irreversibly bonded. We used ethanol as a temporary lubricant during the alignment. To strengthen the bonding, the assembly was cured on a hotplate (80 °C) for overnight.

## **What is Thin Film Lithium Niobate?**

Thin Film Lithium Niobatate (LiNbO 3) is a material that is used for various nonlinear optical devices. The material ![thin film lithium niobate graph](https://www.universitywafer.com/img/thin-film-lithium-niobate.jpg "learn about thin film lithium niobate")is known to have an excellent crystal-lattice arrangement. Its refractive index is restored to that of the bulk material after annealing.

## **Thin-film lithium niobate (LiNbO 3)**

Lithium niobate is a semiconductor that has a variety of applications in electronics and photonics. This material's nonlinear optical properties are particularly attractive. It also has exceptional environmental stability, making it a useful material for applications in the fields of photonics and holographic recording. Its strong piezoelectric and pyroelectric figures of merit also make it an excellent material for optical modulators and delay lines.

Lithium niobate can be integrated into a conventional MOS structure to produce light-powered devices. These devices use ferroelectric switching, which involves the reorganization of the charge in the channel of the transistor, and bulk photovoltaic effect, which involves a shift in the threshold of the transistor in relation to the intensity of light. Lithium niobate thin-film transistors have been fabricated using a molybdenum liftoff process.

Because of its low density, LiNbO3 is a great candidate for high-density optical elements. Its high refractive index makes it ideal for high-density storage devices. It also has unique piezoelectric and optical properties that make it an ideal material for optoelectronic devices and SHG lasers.

Another promising application of lithium niobate is the development of photonic devices incorporating a topological waveguide. Topological properties are essential for photonic devices, and can be realized using photonic crystals and coupled resonators. In addition to implementing topological photonic effects, LNOI has also been used to demonstrate the development of nanophotonic LN waveguides.

A lead-free LiNbO3 converter can generate a voltage higher than the threshold of conventional semiconductor diodes. The high Curie temperature of LiNbO3 opens the door for high-temperature applications. Additionally, macroscale LiNbO3 energy harvesters have recently been investigated and may be used for powering macroscale devices.

[Thin-film LN on sapphire is an excellent candidate for high-power-handling delay lines.](https://www.universitywafer.com/sapphire-wafers-al2o3.html "ln film on sapphire") Its z-cut structure enables the deposition of metal electrodes between the waveguide and the substrate. This enables the use of the largest electro-optic coefficient of LN, as well as the effect of light polarization along the z-axis.

Lithium niobate has been the subject of considerable research due to its unique properties. It is an ideal candidate for nanophotonic devices due to its low loss and high confinement properties. Furthermore, it has the potential to be used in a wide range of applications, including photonic communication and quantum technologies.

## **Modulators**

Thin-film Lithium Niobate modulators have potential applications in DoD and telecom applications. The material's low electrical permittivity makes it ideal for microwave applications. Furthermore, the material's geometry can make it possible to design low-drive voltage modulators. According to simulation results, the switching voltage of a modulator made from Lithium Niobate can be less than 1 Volt.

Lithium Niobate modulators play an important role in modern network connectivity. This type of modulator offers many advantages, including improved wavelength and increased data security. It also features excellent electrical coefficient properties and minimal wavelength loss. In addition, it is widely used in industrial automation and telecommunications systems.

Lithium Niobate modulators are compact and high-performance devices. This is because Lithium Niobate has strong optical confinement. The modulation bandwidth determines the data rate, power consumption, and size of the optical transmitter. Using new technology to enhance these parameters is the key to the development of better modulators. Moreover, the technology can be directly driven by complementary metal oxide semiconductor circuits. This technology eliminates the need for expensive driver amplifiers.

In the fabrication of LNOI modulators, the initial LNOI wafer is patterned, then the passive components are defined. After defining the passive components, the LN hole etching and SiO2 over-cladding are performed. Once the silicon substrate is patterned, a CLTW electrode is patterned on top.

Electro-optic properties of TFLN modulators have been successfully demonstrated at high frequencies. However, the measured electro-optic response differs from the theoretically predicted curve. Because the device width is so small, integration with other optical devices is a challenge. However, these measurements demonstrate the potential of TFLN modulators.

The proposed modulators feature an ultra-low optical insertion loss of 0.2 dB and a large static extinction ratio of 20 dB. Furthermore, they can modulate 112 Gbit/s, and have a dynamic extinction ratio of 9.7 dB.

The proposed work will result in low drive voltage optical modulators for defense and industrial applications. As the demand for fiberoptic capacity continues to increase, it is crucial to optimize the performance of modulators.

## **Nonlinear Optical Devices**

Thin Film Lithium Niobatate (TFLN) is an optical material with exceptional nonlinear optical properties. The material exhibits a second-harmonic generation and is patterned using a 2D periodic array that supports symmetry-protected BICs. The material can be used in frequency-conversion and nonlinear beam shaping applications.

Lithium niobate devices have gained wide application in nonlinear optics and optical communication. The most fundamental building block of an LN-based nonlinear device is the ultra-low-loss, highly confined LN nanophotonic waveguide. The optical transparency of LN allows the material to be used in high-bandwidth communications.

Using a pulsed laser deposition technique, researchers were able to grow a thin film of LiNbO3 and then study its structural, morphological, and emission properties. They also investigated the nonlinear properties of LiNbO3 thin films and found that they had a third-order nonlinearity. Further research is needed to understand the mechanism of LiNbO3 third-order nonlinearity.

The ultra-short domain periods of TFLN have been shown to improve the efficiency of nonlinear devices. This is particularly important for single-photon generation. The period of a TFLN waveguide is about two nanometers. In contrast, conventional LN modulators require a drive voltage of around three to five volts.

The nonlinearity of this material can be exploited in nonlinear integrated photonics. Optical nonlinearity can be exploited in an integrated photonic device by using a gradient metasurface. Using a gradient metasurface, the LN waveguide can be patterned with a gradient of amorphous silicon nanoantennas.

The X-cut LNOI platform is a nonlinear optical device. The device has a low-voltage tunability and a quality factor of 11.500. In addition, it can achieve resonance tuning of 12.5 pm V-1 using the TM mode, which uses the largest electro-optic coefficient in LN. Further, the LN film is machined to achieve higher confinement and electro-optic properties.

The direct bonding of LN onto the predefined waveguide results in a significant loss of mode transition. In order to minimize the loss, the [LN film is terraced and bonded to an SOI substrate](https://www.universitywafer.com/silicon-on-insulator-soi.html "ln film deposited on soi"). The resulting structure is more robust and has a lower transition loss.

  

## **What is Black Lithium Niobate?**

Black lithium niobate is a type of crystalline material that is known for its unique optical and electrical properties. It is made by heating lithium niobate, a common optical crystal, in the presence of oxygen, which causes it to turn black. Black lithium niobate is often used in the production of nonlinear optical devices, such as frequency converters, waveplates, and electro-optic modulators. It is also used in piezoelectric devices, such as microphones and ultrasonic transducers, due to its ability to convert mechanical energy into electrical energy.

This webpage from UniversityWafer, Inc. provides comprehensive information about Lithium Niobate (LiNbO3) wafers and substrates available for research applications in both SAW (Surface Acoustic Wave) and Optical grades. The page serves as both a product catalog and an educational resource, covering material properties, specifications, and various research applications.

Key material properties: LiNbO3 is a high-performance crystalline material known for its strong electro-optic, piezoelectric, and nonlinear optical properties. It has a Curie temperature of 1142±2.0℃, a refractive index of approximately 2.2 (No=2.2878/Ne=2.2033 at 632nm wavelength), and is used in waveguides, optical modulators, SAW devices, and integrated photonic circuits. The material is piezoelectric (converting mechanical stress to electrical charge and vice versa) and exhibits nonlinear optical behavior.

Product specifications include:
- SAW Grade wafers: 3"/4"/6" diameters (8" under R/D), thickness 0.18-0.5mm, various cutting angles (X/Y/Z/Y36/Y41/Y64/Y128), TTV <3µm, polished side Ra <0.5nm, single or double side polished
- Optical Grade wafers: 2"/3"/4" diameters, thickness 0.18-0.5mm, optional doping with Fe/Zn/MgO, scratch/dig rating 20/10
- LNOI (Lithium Niobate on Insulator): 300-900nm X-cut LN or Y42-cut LT thin film on SiO2/silicon substrates, available in 300nm/400nm/500nm/600nm LN film thicknesses with 2μm or 4.7μm thermal SiO2 layers on 0.5mm high-resistivity (>10000Ω-cm) silicon substrates

Applications covered include: optical waveguides, biosensors, SAW generation, smartphone RF filters, quantum acoustics, optical modulators, nonlinear frequency conversion, Q-switching devices, gyroscopes, MEMS devices, photonic crystals, electric field sensing, and integrated photonics. Recent research includes acoustic purification of extracellular microvesicles using XY 128° cut LiNbO3 wafers, thin-film lithium niobate modulators (achieving <1V switching voltage, 112 Gbit/s modulation, 0.2dB insertion loss, 20dB static extinction ratio), and quantum acoustics applications.

Numerous example quote requests from researchers are documented, including: 1-inch Z-cut optical grade wafers for QCLAM spectrometers, 128°-X wafers for SAW applications, 64 Y-X cut wafers for biosensor fabrication, 6" wafers for smartphone RF filters, X-LN thin film on SiO2/Si for condensed matter physics research, and customized disks. The page also explains cut orientations (X, Y, Z cuts), SSP vs DSP (single vs double side polished) differences, and includes FAQs about full X-cut wafer availability and LN deposition on high-resistivity silicon.

A large inventory list of in-stock wafers is provided, covering various combinations of cut orientation (X, Y, Z, 128° Y-X, 36° Y-X), diameters (2", 3", 4", 6"), thicknesses (0.1-1.0mm), surface finishes (SSP/DSP), and grades (SAW/optical). The page also discusses black lithium niobate, thin-film lithium niobate technology, modulators, nonlinear optical devices, and the advantages of LiNbO3 for high-power SHG lasers and optoelectronic applications.

The etching characteristics of congruent  single crystals including doped  and proton-changed  have been studied in reactive ion etching (RIE) and inductively coupled plasma (ICP) etching tools, using different recipes of gas mixtures. The effects of parameters including working pressure, RIE power, and ICP power are investigated and analyzed by measurement of etching depth, selectivity, uniformity, etched surface state, and sidewall profile by means of focused ion beam etching, energy-dispersive x-ray analysis, secondary ion mass spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and surface profilometry. The effects of a sample carrier wafer coating have also been investigated. Optimized processes with high etching rates, good mask selectivity, and a near-vertical profile have been achieved. Ridge waveguides on proton-exchanged  have been fabricated and optically measured.

This webpage is an AIP Publishing article page for a research paper titled "Etching characteristics of LiNbO3 in reactive ion etching and inductively coupled plasma," published in the Journal of Applied Physics (J. Appl. Phys.) on February 1, 2008 (Vol. 103, Issue 3, Article 034109; DOI: 10.1063/1.2838180). The article was received on July 30, 2007, and accepted on November 30, 2007.

AUTHORS: Z. Ren and S. Yu (Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, University of Bristol, UK), P. J. Heard (Interface Analysis Centre, University of Bristol, UK), J. M. Marshall and P. A. Thomas (Department of Physics, University of Warwick, UK).

ABSTRACT/CONTENT: The study examined the etching characteristics of congruent LiNbO3 single crystals, including doped LiNbO3 and proton-exchanged LiNbO3, using reactive ion etching (RIE) and inductively coupled plasma (ICP) etching tools with different gas mixture recipes. The researchers investigated the effects of process parameters including working pressure, RIE power, and ICP power. Results were analyzed by measuring etching depth, selectivity, uniformity, etched surface state, and sidewall profile using focused ion beam (FIB) etching, energy-dispersive x-ray analysis (EDX), secondary ion mass spectroscopy (SIMS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and surface profilometry. The effects of a sample carrier wafer coating were also investigated. The study achieved optimized processes with high etching rates, good mask selectivity, and near-vertical profiles. Ridge waveguides on proton-exchanged LiNbO3 were fabricated and optically measured.

The dependence of the etch rate for LiNb03 on ion beam energy, beam current density and gas flow rate during reactive ion beam etching (RIBE) with CF 4 and CHF 3 gases have been examined. The influence of the gas flow rate and the pressure in the target chamber on the etched surface topography have also been investigated. The reason for the surface roughening is discussed. The change of the relative dark conductivity of LiNbO 3 surface etched by different ions is given. Experimental results show that RIBE can be successfully applied to etching of the surface acoustic wave devices.

The paper reports fabrication of ridge waveguides on X-cut proton exchange (PE)-LiNbO3 using inductively coupled plasma (ICP) etching techniques. Key findings include: (1) Investigation of various etching masks and fluorine gases; (2) Smooth etched surfaces achieved using Cr as a mask combined with SF6/Ar etching gases; (3) A high etch rate of 97.5 nm/min achieved using CHF3/Ar gases; and (4) Successful fabrication of ridge waveguides with approximately 600nm depth, smooth surfaces, and nearly vertical sidewalls. The paper cites prior work on wet etching of LiNbO3 ridge waveguides (Hu et al., 2007), ridge structure etching via plasma dry etching (Park et al., 2006), and electro-optically tunable microring resonators (Guarino et al., 2007). The effect of substrate temperature on the plasma-chemical etching rate of lithium niobate (LiNbO3) single-crystals in an inductively coupled plasma (ICP) is studied in this paper. we found that the etching rate is a complex function of a substrate temperature with an interval where increases in the temperature lead to a significant growth of the etching rate. comparing the results of LiNbO3 etching in two different gas mixtures (SF6/O2 and SF6/Ar) showed that the etching process in SF6/O2 mixtures provides a higher productivity and a qualitatively better surface roughness. the maximum etching rate achieved during this research was more than 800 nm min−1. 1. Introduction Lithium Niobate (LiNbO3) single-crystals are widely applied as a material used in a variety of optoelectronic devices. In recent years LiNbO3 has become a base for different classes of functional and digital integrated optical circuits (IOCs) such as switching matrixes, spectrum analyzers, ultra-high frequency (UHF) phase and amplitude modulators and different physical value sensors [1]. The application of LiNbO3 as the main material in modern nonlinear optics, electro-optics and acousto-electronics is due to its relatively high values of electrical-, acoustic- and nonlinear-optical coefﬁcients [2–4]. Plasma processing of LiNbO3 in different gas composition discharges is a widely used. The ability to form different LiNbO3 structures with a given qualitative and uniform proﬁle is necessary for various applications, including their use as ridge waveguides [5]. For example, deep (dozens of μm) etching processes are used in the production of LiNbO3-based MEMS devices.
Many works [4, 6, 7] in recent years have been devoted to the etching of the LiNbO3 in CHF3, C4F8, CF4, BCl3 and their mixtures using Ar/N2/O2 plasmas. The LiNbO3 etching process in halogen-containing gas discharges has a relatively low etching rate. The etching rate is usually between 50 and 150 nm min−1 when the power of the inductivity-coupled plasma (ICP) power source is below 1000 W, [2, 3, 8, 9] but it can be increased to 350 nm min−1 by raising the applied power up to 2000 W [10, 11]. It should be noted that the applied power (WRF) is not the only technological parameter that affects the ‘dry’ plasma etching process. Thus, achieving a high etching rate is possible when all the technological process parameters, such as the gas mixture composition (deﬁned by the types of gases and their ﬂow), pressure in the process chamber (P), the bias voltage (Ub) applied to the high frequency (HF) electrode with the sample holder, etc, are optimally combined. The majority of LiNbO3 plasma etching studies concentrate on these four main parameters, their optimization and their inﬂuence on the etching process; however, the temperature of the LiNbO3 substrate has not previously been considered.
Meanwhile, it is well-known that temperature can have a signiﬁcant effect on the chemical reaction rate.
Therefore, the aim of this work was to examine the inﬂuence of the LiNbO3 substrate temperature on the etching rate in SF6 ICP plasma.
RECEIVED 19 November 2018 REVISED 18 December 2018 ACCEPTED FOR PUBLICATION 21 December 2018 PUBLISHED 11 January 2019 © 2019 IOP Publishing Ltd 2. Experimental For this research, the original substrate holder with built-in heater was designed (ﬁgure 1). The design process was mostly focused on the uniformity of the temperature distribution on the outer surface. This decision was connected to the fact that crystalline LiNbO3 is highly sensitive to temperature changes. The uneven heating of a lithium niobate substrate can result in its mechanical destruction. A thermocouple was connected to the central part of the inner space of the holder to control the temperature inside the table. Calibration dependence curves between the temperature of the holder surface and the temperature inside the holder were created. The substrate holder surface temperature was measured with pyrometer Raytek ST20 inserted through the process chamber window.
Z-cut, single-crystal, LiNbO3 substrates with a 76.2 mm diameter and 370 μm thickness produced by MTI Corporation were used as experimental samples. Two types of masks were used: Cr-Cu-Ni and Cr-Cu-Cr 7 μm thick ﬁlms with 3×10 mm windows and 10 μm thick ﬁlms with 0.16×6 mm windows respectively. The experiments were performed in SF6/O2 and SF6/Ar plasmas on an original, specially-designed plasma etching machine with an ICP source. A detailed description of the installation can be found in [12]. The values of the ICP power (WRF), SF6 ﬂow (QSF6), O2 ﬂow (QO2), bias voltage (Ub), and pressure (P) were ﬁxed as 700 W at 6.78 MHz, 10.15 sccm, 3.0 sccm, −50 V and 0.75 Pa, respectively. The etching time was 10 min and the substrate temperature range was 373–598 K.
LiNbO3 single-crystal wafers were tightly ﬁxed to the substrate holder surface. Afterwards, the processing chamber was evacuated to the required pressure. Then, the substrate was slowly heated to the required temperature and cleaned from contaminants in an Ar plasma for 10 min (QAr=21,75 sccm, P=0.7 Pa, WRF=750 W, Ub=25 V). Immediately after these preparation procedures, the etching process was started using the mentioned technological parameter values. The etching rate (Vetch) was derived from the electron microscopy data (Zeiss Supra 55VP Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscope) using the ratio between the depth of the etching proﬁle and the etching process time.
Figure 1. Layout view of the sample holder with heater.
2 Mater. Res. Express 6 (2019) 046306 A A Osipov et al 3. Results and discussion The obtained etching rate dependence on the substrate temperature is presented in ﬁgure 2. The determined dependence has a complex nature with a relatively broad temperature interval. In this region, the variation of the temperature signiﬁcantly affects the etching rate. Nominally, the curve can be separated into three regions according to its behavior. In the ﬁrst region (373–423 K), temperature increments provide only small Vetch increases (only 31 nm min−1 growth) relative to the etching process at room temperature. In the second region (423–523 K), temperature increments of the substrate gives a large increase of the Vetch. Here, the Vetch grows nearly linearly and reaches 711 nm min−1 at 523 K. At even higher substrate temperatures (third region 523–598 K), the rate increment as a function of temperature sharply decreases and provides only 101 nm min−1 growth. As a result, our experiments reached a maximum Vetch at 598 K of 812 nm min−1, which is double the rates obtained in other studies [10, 11] that were performed with higher source powers but without the additional substrate heating.
In the ﬁrst region, there is clearly no thermal activation of the reaction between the chemically active particles (CAP) of the plasma and the LiNbO3. Here, the etching rate is limited by the CAP delivery conditions as well as the desorption and disposal of the volatile reaction products from the reaction zone. In contrast, the second region corresponds to a thermally activated etching process. In this temperature interval, reactions between the plasma CAP and the LiNbO3 surface are thermally enhanced and generate the volatile reaction products, which can be easily removed. We assume that in even higher temperatures, the formation of a non-volatile LiF [11] compound occurs and redeposits on the etching surface to block the CAP delivery. As result, this compound does not give further rate increments, even when the temperature of the substrate continues to rise.
Thus, the third region shows a limited Vetch due to the LiF non-volatile, particle formation.
Microphotographs of the tested samples are presented in ﬁgure 3, which shows the results of the LiNbO3 etching in two different gas mixtures of SF6/O2 and SF6/Ar. Both processes were performed with the mentioned technological conditions and the same temperature of 598 K. Moreover, QAr=QO2=3 sccm. The calculation of the etching rate results shows that the replacement of the oxygen with argon in the initial gas mixture adversely affects the etching rate (only 337 nm min−1 with argon, which is less than half that when processing with the SF6/O2 mixture at 812 nm min−1). In addition, the root mean square roughness is four times greater after etching in the SF6/Ar gas mixture (Rms(SF6/Ar)=119.37 nm and Rms(SF6/O2)=30.52 nm). Our results show that the etching of heated substrate in SF6/O2 mixtures provides a better efﬁciency and better surface quality compared to etching in SF6/Ar mixtures.
To understand the perspective of the presented plasma etching technique for deep opening formations (dozens of microns), an experiment was performed where the etching time was 270 min. To decrease the previously described non-volatile LiF inﬂuence, hydroﬂuoric acid was used for 30 s after every 90 min in the experiment. The values of the technological parameters were nearly the same as in the experiment with a maximum etching rate value (WRF=700 W, P=0.75 Pa, Q SF6=10.15 sccm, and QO2=3 sccm) except for the temperature and bias voltage (T=523 K and Ub=−80 V). That was done to improve the vertical directionality of the etching process. As can be seen from ﬁgure 4, the angle of the side wall after the process was 78 degrees. This occurred because the incoming ions did not have enough energy to continue the vertical, anisotropic etching process during the extended time processing. Thus, the chemical part of the etching process became stronger, which increased the isotropic etching. After 270 min of processing, the etching depth was 113.7 μm (ﬁgure 4), which corresponds to a 421 nm min−1 etching rate, and the etching selectivity ratio of the LiNbO3 substrate to the Cr-Cu-Cr mask was more than approximately 77. The maximum achieved etching rate was more than 800 nm min−1 to an etching depth of 8 μm and a substrate temperature of 598 K with an applied ICP power of less than 1000 W. It was established that etching in a SF6/O2 gas mixture achieves higher etching rates with a lower roughness of the etching surface (Rms=30.52 nm and Vetch=812 nm min−1) than etching in the SF6/Ar gas mixture (Rms=119.37 nm and Vetch=337 nm min−1). args.summary:
This scientific paper (Materials Research Express, 2019, Vol. 6, Article 046306) investigates the effect of substrate temperature on the plasma-chemical etching rate of lithium niobate (LiNbO3) single-crystals in an inductively coupled plasma (ICP) system. The research was conducted by Artem A Osipov, Sergey E Alexandrov, and Gleb A Iankevich from Peter the Great St.-Petersburg Polytechnic University (Russia) and Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (Germany).

METHODOLOGY: A custom substrate holder with a built-in heater was designed to ensure uniform temperature distribution, as crystalline LiNbO3 is highly sensitive to temperature changes and uneven heating can cause mechanical destruction. Experiments used Z-cut single-crystal LiNbO3 substrates (76.2 mm diameter, 370 μm thickness) from MTI Corporation, with Cr-Cu-Ni and Cr-Cu-Cr masks. Etching was performed in SF6/O2 and SF6/Ar plasmas with fixed parameters: ICP power of 700 W at 6.78 MHz, SF6 flow of 10.15 sccm, O2 flow of 3.0 sccm, bias voltage of −50 V, and pressure of 0.75 Pa. Substrate temperatures ranged from 373–598 K, with 10-minute etching times.

KEY RESULTS: The etching rate showed a complex, three-region dependence on substrate temperature:
1. First region (373–423 K): Small increases in etching rate (only 31 nm/min growth).
2. Second region (423–523 K): Large, nearly linear growth in etching rate, reaching 711 nm/min at 523 K, attributed to thermally activated etching reactions.
3. Third region (523–598 K): Sharp decrease in rate increment due to formation of non-volatile LiF compounds that block chemically active particle delivery.

The maximum etching rate achieved was 812 nm/min at 598 K (more than 800 nm/min), which is double the rates from prior studies that used higher source powers but no additional substrate heating. Notably, this was achieved with an ICP power below 1000 W.

GAS MIXTURE COMPARISON: Etching in SF6/O2 mixtures was significantly more effective than SF6/Ar mixtures at 598 K: 812 nm/min versus 337 nm/min etching rates, and surface roughness of Rms = 30.52 nm versus 119.37 nm respectively. The SF6/O2 mixture provided a four times lower root mean square roughness.

DEEP ETCHING EXPERIMENT: A 270-minute deep etching experiment produced a 113.7 μm deep etch profile (etching rate of 421 nm/min) at T = 523 K and Ub = −80 V, with hydrofluoric acid treatments (30 s) applied after every 90 minutes to remove non-volatile LiF. The sidewall angle was 78 degrees due to increased isotropic chemical etching, and the selectivity ratio to the Cr-Cu-Cr mask exceeded 77. This substantially exceeds the typical 15 μm etching depths reported in prior LiNbO3 dry etching research.

CONCLUSIONS: Thermal enhancement of the substrate is an effective method to increase LiNbO3 etching rates. SF6/O2 gas mixtures outperform SF6/Ar in both etching rate and surface quality. The decrease in etching rate during deep etching is attributed to non-volatile LiF particle formation, and the isotropic profile results from an increased chemical etching component during extended processing.

## Abstract:

This work is an extensive study of the plasma chemical etching (PCE) process of single-crystalline lithium niobate (LiNbO3) in the SF6/O2 based inductively coupled plasma (ICP). The influence of the main technological parameters of the LiNbO3 PCE process, including the distance between the sample and the lower edge of the discharge chamber, as well as the temperature of the substrate holder on the etching process rate, has been studied. It was shown that changing the temperature of the substrate holder in the range from 100 to 200°C leads to a gradual rise of the etching rate from 127 to 282 nm/min. A further increase in the temperature to 250°C results in a sharp increase in the etching rate to 711 nm/min. The maximum achieved etching rate in experimental series which were aimed at determining the dependence of the LiNbO3 etching rate on the temperature of the substrate holder was 812 nm/min at a substrate holder temperature of 325°C. With the help of X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) technique was found and shown that during the etching process in fluorinated plasma the nonvolatile LiF compound is formed on the surface of the treated LiNbO3. On the basis of the obtained results, the optimal process of deep ( >80 μ m ) LiNbO3 PCE was developed, with an etched wall inclination angle of ≈110°, with selectivity ratio to Cr mask of ≈ 20, and an etching rate of about 300 nm/min. ### I. Introduction

Monocrystalline lithium niobate (LiNbO 3) is the basis material for the production of different devices of the optical industry, including the microwave photonic branch, which is in the focus of research activities at the moment [1]–[3]. In recent years, a whole class of functional and digital photonic integrated circuit (PIC), such as switching matrices, optical spectrum analyzers, microwave phase and amplitude modulators, holographic memory elements, biomedical devices, as well as sensors of physical quantities have been implemented based on LiNbO 3 crystals [4]–[8]. The reason why LiNbO 3 became a core material of modern nonlinear optics, electro optics and acoustoelectronics is because of its high values of electro-, acousto- and nonlinear optical coefficients [9]–[13]. Besides, the devices made on the basis of LiNbO 3 have found wide application in automobile and oil industries, and also in aircraft engine production [14]. The crucial technological operation at production of such devices is the creation of structures of different patterns (holes, grooves, etc.) in/on the LiNbO 3 substrates. Such problems can be solved by plasma “dry” and liquid etching techniques. The main disadvantages of liquid etching are: low etching rates, isotropic nature of etching and low automation of the etching process [15]–[17]. The above-mentioned disadvantages do not allow the formation of deep vertical structures in lithium niobate. An interesting technique of deep structures formation in LiNbO 3 was proposed by the authors [18]. For creation of deep vertical structures, they used a diamond disk which leaded to high values of the anisotropy. However, it has a number of drawbacks such as: low productivity, limitation on the creation of different shapes and sizes structures due to the original shape of the diamond disk, as well as the introduction of contaminants (abrasive) on the samples surfaces. Plasma etching has a number of benefits such as: possibility of the process automation, and the ability to form highly oriented structures in LiNbO 3. Many works have been devoted to LiNbO 3 etching processes in SF 6, CHF 3, C 4 F 8, CF 4, BCl 3 based plasma and their mixtures with Ar/N 2/O 2/H 2 [6], [19]–[22]. In the vast majority of studies aimed at the different structures creation on the surface of LiNbO 3 substrates at the power of the RF inductively coupled plasma source up to 1000 W the etching rates are in the range from 50 to 150 nm/min [8], [12], [13], [23]. Further increase of etching rate up to 350 nm/min was achieved due to increase of RF power supplied to plasma discharge up to 2000 W [24], [25]. Typical depths of etching areas achieved by ICP etching of LiNbO 3 are lying in the range from 500 nm to [11], [24]–[31]. Thus, the achievement of the high etching rates values is important and is possible only with the right choice of a combination of a specific process parameter, such as the gas mixture composition, which is defined both by the type of gases used and by gases flow rates (Q x, - name of the gas) of individual gas component, pressure (P) in the reaction chamber, substrate holder HF electrode bias voltage (), etc. However, the main problem in the formation of deep structures (more than ) is the generation of a non-volatile LiF compound on the etching surface, which slows down the plasma chemical etching (PCE) process, and with increasing process time can lead to a complete stop of the etching process [24]. Thus, the question of achieving deep structures (more than ) in LiNbO 3 is very relevant, but poorly studied.

This is an IEEE Xplore journal article page for a study titled "Deep Etching of LiNbO3 Using Inductively Coupled Plasma in SF6-Based Gas Mixture," published in the Journal of Microelectromechanical Systems (Volume 30, Issue 1, February 2021, pages 90-95). The article was published on December 3, 2020, with DOI 10.1109/JMEMS.2020.3039350.

The study investigates the plasma chemical etching (PCE) process of single-crystalline lithium niobate (LiNbO3) in an SF6/O2-based inductively coupled plasma (ICP). Key findings include:
- Increasing substrate holder temperature from 100°C to 200°C gradually raises the etching rate from 127 to 282 nm/min
- A further increase to 250°C results in a sharp jump in etching rate to 711 nm/min
- The maximum etching rate achieved was 812 nm/min at a substrate holder temperature of 325°C
- X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) revealed that a nonvolatile LiF compound forms on the treated LiNbO3 surface during etching in fluorinated plasma
- An optimal deep etching process (>80 μm) was developed with an etched wall inclination angle of ≈110°, a selectivity ratio to Cr mask of ≈20, and an etching rate of about 300 nm/min

The introduction discusses LiNbO3's importance as a base material for optical devices including photonic integrated circuits (PICs), switching matrices, optical spectrum analyzers, microwave modulators, and sensors, due to its high electro-, acousto-, and nonlinear optical coefficients. The paper notes that typical ICP etching rates for LiNbO3 range from 50-150 nm/min at RF power up to 1000 W, with rates up to 350 nm/min achievable at 2000 W RF power. The main challenge in forming deep structures is the generation of non-volatile LiF compound on the etching surface, which slows or can completely stop the etching process.

Authors: Artem A. Osipov, Armenak A. Osipov, Gleb A. Iankevich, Anastasiya B. Speshilova, Alexander Shakhmin, and Vladimir I. Berezenko. The article has 11 citations and 1782 full-text views. The content is only partially accessible without purchase/subscription.

# Long low-loss-litium niobate on insulator waveguides with sub-nanometer surface roughness

Research output: Contribution to journal › Article › peer-review

## Abstract

In this paper, we develop a technique for realizing multi-centimeter-long lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) waveguides with a propagation loss as low as 0.027 dB/cm. Our technique relies on patterning a chromium thin film coated on the top surface of LNOI into a hard mask with a femtosecond laser followed by chemo-mechanical polishing for structuring the LNOI into the waveguides. The surface roughness on the waveguides was determined with an atomic force microscope to be 0.452 nm. The approach is compatible with other surface patterning technologies, such as optical and electron beam lithographies or laser direct writing, enabling high-throughput manufacturing of large-scale LNOI-based photonic integrated circuits.

The paper, authored by Rongbo Wu, Min Wang, Jian Xu, Jia Qi, Wei Chu, Zhiwei Fang, Jianhao Zhang, Junxia Zhou, Lingling Qiao, Zhifang Chai, Jintian Lin, and Ya Cheng, presents a technique for fabricating multi-centimeter-long lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) waveguides with ultra-low propagation loss of 0.027 dB/cm. The method involves patterning a chromium thin film on the LNOI surface into a hard mask using a femtosecond laser, followed by chemo-mechanical polishing to structure the waveguides. Surface roughness was measured via atomic force microscopy at 0.452 nm. The approach is noted as compatible with other surface patterning technologies (optical lithography, electron beam lithography, and laser direct writing), enabling high-throughput manufacturing of large-scale LNOI-based photonic integrated circuits. Key keywords include chemo-mechanical polishing, lithium niobate, optical lithography, photonic integrated circuit, propagation loss, and waveguide. The DOI is 10.3390/nano8110910 and the publication is open access under MDPI licensing.

PFEIFFER,2 NICOLAS VOLET,1 MICHAEL ZERVAS,2,3 JON D. PETERS,1 COSTANZA L. MANGANELLI,1,4 ERIC J. STANTON,1 YIFEI LI,1,5 TOBIAS J. KIPPENBERG,2 AND JOHN E. ID 282456); published 13 February 2017 An ideal photonic integrated circuit for nonlinear photonic applications requires high optical nonlinearities and low loss. This work demonstrates a heterogeneous platform by bonding lithium niobate (LN) thin films onto a silicon nitride (Si3N4) waveguide layer on silicon. It not only pro-vides large second- and third-order nonlinear coefficients, but also shows low propagation loss in both the Si3N4 and the LN-Si3N4 waveguides. The tapers enable low-loss-mode transitions between these two waveguides.
This platform is essential for various on-chip applications, e.g., modulators, frequency conversions, and quantum communications.
© 2017 Optical Society of America OCIS codes: (190.4390) Nonlinear optics, integrated optics; (130.3730) Lithium niobate; (040.6040) Silicon.
https://doi.org/10.1364/OL.42.000803 For decades, lithium niobate (LN) has become the most com-monly used nonlinear material in photonics [1], since it has a large electro-optic effect (r33 > 30 pm∕V), a high second-order nonlinear coefficient (27 pm/V), and a broad transparency window (0.35–4.5 μm) [2]. It is widely used for electro-optic modulators [3,4], three-wave-mixing wavelength converters [5,6], and optomechanical cavities [7]. Recently, there has been great interest in integrating LN devices in photonic integrated circuits (PICs) [8–10]. Compared to bulk LN devices, integrated ones have much smaller scale. This not only shrinks the footprint of the optical system but also enhances the nonlinear effects due to the higher photon density [10], potentially reducing the power budget for modulation and wavelength conversion.
Among integrated-photonics areas, silicon (Si) photonics has the highest potential for mass-market applications in indus-try [11]. However, one limitation for it is that, even though Si, Si3N4, and SiO2 have been widely applied based on their third-order optical nonlinearities (Kerr effect, χ3), usually they do not have any second-order nonlinearities (χ2) or electro-optic effect, due to their centrosymmetric crystal structures or amorphous nature. As a result, it is challenging to achieve many important functions, e.g., electro-optic modulation and three-wave mixing on the Si platform. To introduce a signifi-cant second-order nonlinearity, there have been many attempts to integrate nonlinear materials onto Si, especially LN [8,12].
One commonly used technique is to bond thin film LN fab-ricated by an ion slice method [13] onto a Si-on-insulator (SOI) wafer, where Si ridges are used for guiding the mode in the LN-Si waveguide. However, this approach suffers from several shortcomings. First, the losses of these heterogeneous wave-guides are higher (>2.5 dB∕cm) [12,14] than conventional bulk LN waveguides (<1 dB∕cm) [15]. Second, Si is absorp-tive at wavelengths shorter than 1.1 μm, a characteristic that is, however, of great importance for many applications [16,17].
Finally, the refractive index of Si (∼3.48) is much higher than that of LN (∼2.14 for extraordinary polarization at C band).
This dramatically decreases the confinement factor in the LN core, and this decrease is detrimental for nonlinear interactions.
Even though this can be reduced if narrow and thin Si ridges are used [12], it adds difficulties in fabrication. Other materials such as Ta2O5 have also been used to form the heterogeneous waveguide with LN [9]. However, reported loss values for these waveguides are still relatively high. More importantly, tapers for mode conversion between different material cores have not been demonstrated due to their index-matching problem.
Compared to Si, Si3N4 has lower material loss and a broader transparency window (0.4–6.7 μm) [18], and, most impor-tantly, does not suffer from two-photon absorption. Si3N4 waveguides are popular for nonlinear photonics, such as Kerr frequency comb and soliton generation [19]. Recently, a novel photonic Damascene process has been developed for fabricating high-confinement Si3N4 waveguides with high Letter Vol. 42, No. 4 / February 15 2017 / Optics Letters 803 0146-9592/17/040803-04 Journal © 2017 Optical Society of America yield, mitigating common fabrication challenges [20]. The efficient stress control of this method can provide thick Si3N4 waveguides free of cracks, an essential prerequisite to achieve index matching with a bonded LN layer in a hetero-geneous waveguide. Moreover, the planar top surface of this process facilitates integration of LN film by wafer bonding.
Owing to the fully cladded nature, the Si3N4 waveguide fab-ricated using the Damascene process shows low propagation loss (0.11 dB/cm), a benefit for χ3 interactions, according to our previous results [21]. In this work, Si3N4 is used as the rib of the heterogeneous waveguide formed with LN film.
Because the refractive index of Si3N4 (1.98) is slightly smaller than that of LN, the mode of the hybrid waveguide can be highly confined in the LN core (see Fig. 1). Owing to the low-loss nature of the Si3N4 ridge and the low field intensity at the boundaries and sidewalls, such a LN-Si3N4 waveguide can achieve low propagation loss [9,12]. An alternative approach for LN-SiN low-loss waveguides is to deposit SiN on a LN film as shown in our previous work [10]. However, the Damascene process provides a high-quality stoichiometric Si3N4 layer, which can also be thicker for improved index matching for low-loss mode transitions between the Si3N4 and LN-Si3N4 waveguides. This platform provides strong χ2 and χ3 coef-ficients (γ ∼1.4 W−1 km−1 for this work), high confinement factors, low propagation, and coupling losses for waveguides.
The heterogeneous platform presented here consists of two types of waveguides, both illustrated in Fig. 1. The fully cladded Si3N4 waveguide for χ3 nonlinear interaction is 850 nm high and ∼2 μm wide to achieve anomalous group velocity dispersion at C band. Another type is the LN-Si3N4 waveguide for χ2 applications, consisting of a 300-nm-thick LN layer separated from a Si3N4 core by a 150-nm-thin SiO2 spacer. Such geometry matches the indices of these two layers.
The schematic cross-section of the LN-Si3N4 waveguide is shown in Fig. 1. Because the Si3N4 waveguide and the LN layer have nearly the same index, confinement factors in these two cores are sensitive to Si3N4 ridge width, shown in the top right inset of Fig. 1. The ridge width is designed to be 0.8 μm, corresponding to a confinement factor of ∼0.6 in LN core.
A mode converter is designed to enable low-loss mode tran-sition between the two types of waveguides, and a schematic is shown in the center of Fig. 1. The Si3N4 input waveguide is 2 μm wide with 3-μm SiO2 top cladding (A), and input light then passes through an abrupt change of the upper cladding to 150 nm (B). After entering the bonded area with a LN film top, the width of the Si3N4 ridge decreases linearly from 2.0 μm (C) to 0.8 μm (E), adiabatically transitioning the majority of the mode upward into the LN layer. The evolution of simulated mode distributions (performed with FIMMWAVE [22]) for different waveguide geometries is shown in Fig. 1, at 1540 nm wavelength. According to simulations, the loss per LN facet (from A to E) is 0.9 dB, due to the abrupt index change be-tween the Si3N4 and heterogeneous waveguides (B to C). Here a 150-nm-thick SiO2 spacer is introduced to reduce this index change. Further increasing the spacer thickness to 300 nm is expected to reduce the loss to 0.4 dB per facet, but this will also increase the optical mode size. This tradeoff can be ad-justed depending on the application.
The device fabrication process is schematized in Fig. 2. The photonic Damascene process [20] is used to fabricate the Si3N4 waveguide devices on a 100-mm substrate and provide local openings with planar surface for LN bonding. At first, an 850-nm-thick layer of nearly stoichiometric Si3N4 is deposited by low-pressure chemical vapor deposition on a prestructured substrate. The substrate includes not only the waveguide pat-tern but also a dense stress-release pattern, to avoid the forma-tion of cracks during the Si3N4 deposition that cause high scattering loss. Chemical-mechanical polishing is used to re-move excess Si3N4 after deposition, creating a planar top sur-face across the wafer. A 3-μm-thick SiO2 layer is then deposited on Si3N4 as the top cladding. A scanning electron micrograph (SEM) of the cross-section of this Si3N4 waveguide is shown in Fig. 3(a). To reduce the surface roughness in preparation for Fig. 1.

The top and bottom areas show sche-matics of the waveguide cross-sections and simulated profiles of the fundamental TE modes at 1540 nm. Inset is the simulated confine-ment factor in the LN layer for LN-Si3N4 hybrid waveguides calcu-lated as a function of the Si3N4 rib width.
Fig. 2.

804 Vol. 42, No. 4 / February 15 2017 / Optics Letters Letter bonding, the deposited SiO2 cladding layer is repolished.
Figure 3(b) shows the roughness measurement of the as-deposited low temperature SiO2 film as well as after the repolishing step. The bonding area is then opened by dry etch, leaving a thin SiO2 layer as spacer. Additionally, vertical chan-nels are patterned in these areas to release the gas during bond-ing. After that, a chip (purchased from NANOLN) consisting of a 300-nm-thick x-cut LN film on a 2-μm-thick buried SiO2 on a Si substrate is bonded onto the opened area after surface plasma activation. The bonded sample is then annealed to en-hance the bonding strength. The integrated chip is shown in Fig. 3(c). Finally, mechanical polishing, dry etch, and buffered hydrofluoric acid have been used to remove the Si substrate and buried oxide (BOX) layer, leaving only the LN film on chip in the open area, as shown in Fig. 3(d).
For characterizing the devices, a tunable single-frequency CW laser (Keysight 81642A) with spectral range of 1.51–1.64 μm and linewidth ∼0.1 MHz is used as the light source. Collimated light passes through a polarizer (Thorlabs PCB-2.5-1550) aligned to efficiently excite the TE-polarized mode of the wave-guide. A focusing lens (Thorlabs C230TM-C) is used for the input coupling, and a lensed fiber couples the light out of the device. An optical power sensor (Keysight 81634B) is used to monitor the transmitted power.
The testing structure used here is a 1-cm-long hetero-geneous waveguide, with two tapers connecting to the Si3N4 waveguides. TE polarized light is coupled in and out through the Si3N4 waveguides. Compared to the reference Si3N4 wave-guide with the same length, the insertion loss (fiber to fiber) of the heterogeneous waveguide is ∼2 dB larger around C band, shown in Fig. 4. There are small ripples for the heterogeneous waveguide spectrum, possibly due to the taper reflections.
Here, the insertion loss for the reference and the test struc-tures are denoted αref and αtest, respectively, and their propa-gation loss is denoted by αSiN and αheter, respectively. The following equations define the total insertion loss: αref  αSiN  αc; (1) αtest  αheter  2αAB  2αBC  αc; (2) where αAB and αBC are the losses at the A–B and B–C boun-daries in Fig. 1, and αc is the coupling loss in and out of the chip.
The propagation loss for the heterogeneous waveguide is obtained by subtracting Eq. (2) from Eq. (1), as follows: αheter  αSiN −2αAB −2αBC −αref −αtest: (3) The value of αref −αtest is obtained from the testing results of Fig. 4 and αSiN by the prementioned measurements of resonators (0.11 dB∕cm  1 cm), assuming that αAB  αBC ≅0.9 dB as supported by simulations. The calculated propagation loss for the heterogeneous waveguide is 0.2  0.4 dB∕cm. Consider-ing that the coupling loss varies among waveguides, this method may have an extra uncertainty. Here the Fabry–Perot-based method is also used, and a loss of 0.3  0.6 dB∕cm is ex-tracted, resulting in good agreement. Such a low propagation loss is comparable to the loss of a bulk LN waveguide [15].
Considering that the waveguide area is more than 1 order of magnitude smaller than that of bulk waveguides, these wave-guides can improve the efficiency for nonlinear applications by the same proportion without sacrificing additional propaga-tion loss.
In conclusion, a heterogeneous platform on Si is demon-strated with large χ2 and χ3 coefficients by bonding a LN film onto thick Si3N4. With careful design of the waveguide geometry and by using advanced fabrication techniques, high confinements and low propagation losses have been achieved both for Si3N4 and LN-Si3N4 waveguides, with low-mode-transition loss from using a taper. Therefore, this platform is promising for the wide range of chip-level nonlinear applica-tions on Si.

args.summary:
This scientific paper (Optics Letters, Vol. 42, No. 4, February 15, 2017) demonstrates a heterogeneous integration platform combining lithium niobate (LN) thin films with silicon nitride (Si3N4) waveguides on silicon for wafer-scale photonic integrated circuits. The work, authored by Lin Chang and colleagues from UC Santa Barbara, EPFL, and other institutions, addresses the challenge that while silicon photonics offers strong third-order nonlinearities (Kerr effect), it lacks second-order nonlinearities and electro-optic effects due to centrosymmetric crystal structures. By bonding 300-nm-thick x-cut LN films onto thick Si3N4 waveguides fabricated using a photonic Damascene process, the platform achieves both large χ(2) and χ(3) nonlinear coefficients.

Key design elements include a fully cladded Si3N4 waveguide (850 nm high, ~2 μm wide) for χ(3) interactions with anomalous group velocity dispersion at C band, and a LN-Si3N4 hybrid waveguide (300-nm LN separated from a Si3N4 core by a 150-nm SiO2 spacer) for χ(2) applications, with a designed confinement factor of ~0.6 in the LN core. A tapered mode converter enables low-loss mode transitions between the two waveguide types, with simulated loss of 0.9 dB per LN facet (reducible to 0.4 dB with a 300-nm spacer). Fabrication uses the photonic Damascene process (LPCVD Si3N4, chemical-mechanical polishing, plasma-activated wafer bonding) followed by removal of the Si substrate and buried oxide layer.

Measured results show a propagation loss of 0.2 ± 0.4 dB/cm (or 0.3 ± 0.6 dB/cm by Fabry-Perot method) for the heterogeneous waveguide, comparable to bulk LN waveguides (<1 dB/cm), while the Si3N4 waveguide itself exhibits only 0.11 dB/cm loss. The insertion loss of the 1-cm heterogeneous test structure is ~2 dB larger than the reference Si3N4 waveguide around C band. The nonlinear coefficient γ is ~1.4 W⁻¹km⁻¹. The platform is positioned as essential for on-chip applications including modulators, frequency conversions, and quantum communications.

This webpage presents a scientific paper titled "Fabrication of Low Loss Lithium Niobate Rib Waveguides Through Photoresist Reflow" by Karan Prabhakar and Ronald M. Reano, published in IEEE Photonics Journal on 1 December 2022 (DOI: 10.1109/JPHOT.2022.3222184, Corpus ID: 253570660, IEEE article number 9950703). The paper covers research in Engineering, Physics, and Materials Science.

METHODOLOGY: The authors demonstrate lithography and argon plasma etching of lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) rib waveguides using reflowed photoresist etch masks and 405 nm photolithography. Key technique involves melting the photoresist at temperatures greatly exceeding its glass transition temperature while minimizing feature distortion through photoresist adhesion control. This approach reduces sidewall surface roughness and allows the photoresist to serve as both the pattern mask and the hard etch mask, resulting in waveguides with sub-... (sub-nanometer sidewall surface quality, as indicated by the truncated abstract).

SUPPORTING CONTENT: The paper includes 7 figures and lists 6 citations, 48 references, and 2 authors (Prabhakar and Reano).

CITING PAPERS (2022-2025): The work has been cited by subsequent research including: "Mitigating waveguide loss in Ge–Sb–Se chalcogenide glass photonics" (2024, Journal of Physics D); "Recent development in integrated Lithium niobate photonics" (2024, Advances in Physics: X); "Twenty-nine million Intrinsic Q-factor Monolithic Microresonators on Thin Film Lithium Niobate" (2024, Photonics Research); "Recent Progresses on Hybrid Lithium Niobate External Cavity Semiconductor Lasers" (2024, Materials); "Thin-film lithium niobate quantum photonics: review and perspectives" (2025, Advanced Photonics); and "Quantum Microwave Photonics" (2022, Journal of Lightwave Technology).

KEY REFERENCES (2018-2021): The paper builds on prior work including low-loss deep-etch AlGaAs waveguides using nitrogen plasma-assisted photoresist reflow (2014), photolithography-assisted chemo-mechanical etching (PLACE) for LNOI waveguides (2020), LNOI waveguides with sub-nanometer surface roughness achieving 0.027 dB/cm propagation loss (2018), monolithic electro-optic modulators on LNOI (2021), wet-etched lithium niobate ridge waveguides (2007), and sidewall polishing techniques for scattering-loss reduction (2018).

This is a Semantic Scholar academic paper page for the conference paper "Loss characterization of waveguides in lithium niobate on insulator" (DOI: 10.1109/OMN.2016.7565837, Corpus ID: 35999854), published on 1 July 2016 in the International Conference on Optical MEMS and Nanophotonics (OMN). 

The paper is authored by Shawn Yohanes Siew, Eric Jun Hao Cheung, Mankei Tsang, and Aaron J. Danner, spanning pages 1-2. It falls under the fields of Engineering, Materials Science, and Physics.

The abstract describes how single crystal lithium niobate is commonly used in optical electronic applications due to its variety of optical effects, but is a difficult material to pattern with etching typically inducing rough sidewalls. Because of these limitations, commercial devices typically use diffusion-type processes that only create small index increases, resulting in large footprints and high costs. Lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) is presented as a technology created to circumvent these issues (abstract text is truncated on the page).

- 1 citation (a 2017 paper by Zhihua Chen et al. titled "Grating coupler on single-crystal lithium niobate thin film")
- 6 references cited
- 4 figures extracted from the paper (figures 2, 3, 4, and I)
- Available via IEEE Xplore and doi.org links

args.summary:
This is a Semantic Scholar record for the peer-reviewed article "Redeposition-free inductively-coupled plasma etching of lithium niobate for integrated photonics" by Fabian Kaufmann, Giovanni Finco, Andreas Maeder, and Rachel Grange. The paper was published in Nanophotonics (volume 12, pages 1601-1611) on January 16, 2023, and has the DOI 10.1515/nanoph-2022-0676 (Corpus ID 255775848).

The abstract states that lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) is being established as a versatile platform for a new generation of photonic integrated devices. Significant progress has been made in recent years to move fabrication from a research platform toward wafer-scale fabrication in commercial foundries, with optical losses reaching remarkably low values approaching material limits. In this context, argon etching of lithium niobate waveguides in an inductively coupled plasma (ICP) system has been shown to provide the best optical quality devices for integrated photonics.

The record lists 8 figures associated with the paper and indicates it has 52 citations and 22 references. Notable citing works include a 2023 conference paper on redeposition-free ICP etching of thin-film LNOI by the same authors, a 2024 AIP Advances paper on optimizing waveguide fabrication in LNOI (by Kumar, Klimov, and Kuo), a 2024 Optical Materials Express paper on wafer-scale fabrication of low-loss LNOI waveguides (by Younesi, Kasebier, Pertsch), and a 2025 Advances in Materials paper on scalable lithium niobate nanoimprinting for nonlinear metalenses (by Talts, Weigand, Occhiodori, and Grange).

Key references include foundational work on argon plasma ICP-RIE etching for smooth sidewall LNOI waveguides (Ulliac et al., 2016), ultra-smooth LiNbO3 micro/nano structures (Ulliac et al., 2010), a comparative study of dry-etching nanophotonic devices on LNOI (Shen, Wang, Ou, 2021), single-photon detection and cryogenic reconfigurability in LNOI nanophotonic circuits (Lomonte et al., 2021), perovskite oxide etching with argon ICP (Chen et al., 2021), ion-cut LNOI technology reviews (Jia, Wang, Chen, 2021), electro-optically tunable microring resonators in lithium niobate (Guarino et al., 2007), integrated lithium niobate photonics (Qi and Li, 2020), asymmetry ridge structure fabrication and RIE of LiNbO3 (Yang et al., 2005), and reduced material loss in thin-film lithium niobate waveguides (Shams-Ansari, Huang, Lončar, 2022).

# Angle-optimized ion-beam etching for high-verticality and low-loss lithium niobate microresonators

* HZHaoxuan Zhang

* 17 February 2026

+ journal article

+ Vol. 34  (4) , 6870-6879
+ <https://doi.org/10.1364/oe.581687>

##### Abstract

Lithium niobate-on-insulator (LNOI) has emerged as a compelling platform for integrated nonlinear photonics and electro-optics. While notable advances have been made in developing low-loss LNOI waveguides and resonators, their sidewall verticality typically remains below 70°. Here, we present an angle-optimized ion-beam etching (IBE) process with a soft positive-tone resist as the mask. By investigating the correlation between IBE incidence angles (0 ∘ –30 ∘ ) and critical device characteristics, we achieved trench-free LNOI waveguides with sidewall verticality approaching 80° while preserving low propagation loss. This approach enables the fabrication of compact spiral microresonators with intrinsic quality factors up to 5.1 × 10 6 , corresponding to a propagation loss of 0.08 dB/cm. We further validated the device performance by demonstrating pulse-driven Kerr soliton microcombs with repetition rates near 24 GHz. These results establish angled, resist-masked IBE as a simplified fabrication process for realizing high-verticality, low-loss LNOI photonic circuits.

## Abstract

一种铌酸锂晶体高效超光滑化学机械抛光方法，属于非线性光学晶体超精密加工技术领域。其特征是样品为铌酸锂晶片，采用固结磨料研磨、保持环硬抛光垫抛光、保持环软抛光垫化学机械抛光相结合的加工方法，硬抛光垫为合成革或聚氨酯抛光垫，软抛光垫为无纺布或绒毛抛光垫。化学机械抛光液的pH值为10.2-10.6，含有氧化铈、氧化硅、氢氧化钾、氢氧化钠、氢氧化钡、高锰酸钾、双氧水、柠檬酸、醋酸、草酸中的四种。固结磨料研磨时间为15-25min，硬抛光垫抛光时间为50-70min，化学机械抛光时间为3-6min。化学机械抛光的材料去除率为420-460nm/min，抛光后铌酸锂的平面度为3.8-5.5μm，表面粗糙度Ra为0.35-0.5nm，PV值为3.8-6nm。本发明的效果和益处是实现了非线性光学晶体高效超光滑抛光方法。A lithium niobate crystal high-efficiency ultra-smooth chemical-mechanical polishing method belongs to the technical field of nonlinear optical crystal ultra-precision processing. It is characterized in that the sample is a lithium niobate wafer, which is processed by a combination of fixed abrasive grinding, hard polishing pad polishing with a retaining ring, and chemical-mechanical polishing with a soft polishing pad retaining ring. The hard polishing pad is synthetic leather or polyurethane polishing pad, and the soft polishing pad is soft. The pads are non-woven or napped polishing pads. The chemical mechanical polishing liquid has a pH value of 10.2-10.6 and contains four kinds of cerium oxide, silicon oxide, potassium hydroxide, sodium hydroxide, barium hydroxide, potassium permanganate, hydrogen peroxide, citric acid, acetic acid and oxalic acid. The grinding time of fixed abrasive is 15-25min, the polishing time of hard polishing pad is 50-70min, and the chemical mechanical polishing time is 3-6min. The material removal rate of chemical mechanical polishing is 420-460nm/min, the flatness of lithium niobate after polishing is 3.8-5.5μm, the surface roughness Ra is 0.35-0.5nm, and the PV value is 3.8-6nm. The effect and benefit of the invention is to realize the high-efficiency ultra-smooth polishing method of the nonlinear optical crystal.

背景技术Background technique

铌酸锂晶体由于具有优异的铁电、压电、电光、非线性光学、声表面波等性能，广泛应用于光波导基片、光通讯调制器、光隔离器等光电领域，并在光子海量存储器，光学集成等领域具有广阔的应用前景，在非线性光学领域占有垄断地位，享有光学硅的美誉。铌酸锂晶体在具有优异光电性能的同时，也具有独特的力学性能。Bulletin of Materials Science,2000,23(2),147-150文献报道铌酸锂的硬度为6.3GPa，这个硬度值处于软脆晶体碲镉汞(0.5GPa)和硬脆晶体硅(12-14GPa)的中间过渡地带。铌酸锂晶体的晶胞为正交晶系，但是c轴的长度是a轴的2.7倍，两轴的热膨胀系数却相差8倍，使得铌酸锂晶体对温度非常敏感，具有强烈的温度和力学各向异性。Due to its excellent ferroelectric, piezoelectric, electro-optical, nonlinear optics, surface acoustic wave and other properties, lithium niobate crystals are widely used in optoelectronic fields such as optical waveguide substrates, optical communication modulators, and optical isolators. Memory, optical integration and other fields have broad application prospects, occupy a monopoly position in the field of nonlinear optics, and enjoy the reputation of optical silicon. Lithium niobate crystals not only have excellent photoelectric properties, but also have unique mechanical properties. Bulletin of Materials Science, 2000, 23(2), 147-150 reports that the hardness of lithium niobate is 6.3GPa, which is between soft and brittle crystal mercury cadmium telluride (0.5GPa) and hard and brittle crystal silicon (12-14GPa). intermediate transition zone. The unit cell of the lithium niobate crystal is an orthorhombic crystal system, but the length of the c-axis is 2.7 times that of the a-axis, and the thermal expansion coefficients of the two axes differ by 8 times, which makes the lithium niobate crystal very sensitive to temperature and has a strong temperature and Mechanical anisotropy.

传统的铌酸锂晶体的加工方法为游离磨料研磨、抛光以及化学机械抛光方法，由于铌酸锂本身独特的力学特性，使得铌酸锂晶体具有非常低的损伤阈值，较高的韧性和脆性，在加工中极易出现游离磨料嵌入、划痕、崩边、破碎、断裂等加工缺陷。传统的化学机械抛光方法加工效率低，加工精度差，加工成本高，难以满足非线性光学高性能器件对铌酸锂晶片超精密加工的要求。The traditional processing methods of lithium niobate crystals are free abrasive grinding, polishing and chemical mechanical polishing. Due to the unique mechanical properties of lithium niobate itself, lithium niobate crystals have a very low damage threshold, high toughness and brittleness. Processing defects such as free abrasive embedding, scratches, chipping, chipping, and fractures are prone to occur during processing. The traditional chemical mechanical polishing method has low processing efficiency, poor processing accuracy and high processing cost, and it is difficult to meet the requirements of ultra-precision processing of lithium niobate wafers for nonlinear optical high-performance devices.

样品为X-cut，Y-cut和Z-cut铌酸锂晶片。这三种晶片是铌酸锂晶片的典型代表，应用非常广泛。X-cut，Y-cut和Z-cut的Miller指数为(110),(100),和(001)，对应的Miller–Bravais指数分别为(11-20),(10-10)和(0001)。因此选择这三种常用的铌酸锂晶片作为样品。The samples are X-cut, Y-cut and Z-cut lithium niobate wafers. These three wafers are typical representatives of lithium niobate wafers and are widely used. The Miller indices of X-cut, Y-cut and Z-cut are (110), (100), and (001), and the corresponding Miller–Bravais indices are (11-20), (10-10) and (0001) respectively ). Therefore, these three commonly used lithium niobate wafers were selected as samples.

采用固结磨料研磨、保持环硬抛光垫抛光、保持环软抛光垫化学机械抛光相结合的加工方法。为了有效消除游离磨料嵌入的问题，在初始阶段去除从铌酸锂单晶锭切割时留下的较厚的损伤层时，采用固结磨料研磨的方法，能够有效去除较厚的损伤层，同时避免较大的游离磨料嵌入铌酸锂单晶表面。由于传统游离磨料研磨、抛光的方法，加工后的铌酸锂晶片的平面度较差，为了降低工件的平面度值，采用保持环的方法进行抛光和化学机械抛光。保持环硬抛光垫抛光的方法，是为了控制面形精度，主要采用机械去除的方法去除固结磨料研磨阶段剩下的表面损伤层，同时进行面形精度的控制，因此采用硬抛光垫。在化学机械抛光阶段，化学作用和机械去除的作用要达到平衡才能获得高效超光滑的抛光表面，由于化学的作用生成较软的氧化膜，因此采用较软的抛光垫在去除较软的氧化膜的同时，不会在表面留下划伤，因此在化学机械抛光阶段选择软抛光垫。The combination of fixed abrasive grinding, hard polishing pad polishing with retaining ring and chemical mechanical polishing with soft polishing pad retaining ring is adopted. In order to effectively eliminate the problem of free abrasive embedding, when removing the thicker damage layer left when cutting from the lithium niobate single crystal ingot at the initial stage, the method of grinding with fixed abrasives can effectively remove the thicker damage layer, and at the same time Avoid larger free abrasives embedded in the lithium niobate single crystal surface. Due to the traditional free abrasive grinding and polishing method, the flatness of the processed lithium niobate wafer is poor. In order to reduce the flatness value of the workpiece, the method of retaining ring is used for polishing and chemical mechanical polishing. The method of maintaining ring hard polishing pad polishing is to control the surface shape accuracy. The method of mechanical removal is mainly used to remove the surface damage layer remaining in the fixed abrasive grinding stage, and at the same time to control the surface shape accuracy, so a hard polishing pad is used. In the chemical mechanical polishing stage, chemical action and mechanical removal must be balanced to obtain an efficient and ultra-smooth polished surface. Due to chemical action, a softer oxide film is formed, so a softer polishing pad is used to remove the softer oxide film. At the same time, it will not leave scratches on the surface, so choose a soft polishing pad in the chemical mechanical polishing stage.

固结磨料研磨采用防水砂纸为研磨工具，硬抛光垫为合成革或聚氨酯抛光垫，软抛光垫为无纺布或绒毛抛光垫。开率经济和成分因素，固结磨粒研磨采用防水砂轮，种类可以采用氧化硅、氧化铝防水砂纸，硬抛光垫选择常用的合成革或者聚氨酯抛光垫，软抛光垫也是采用应用非常广泛的无纺布或者绒毛抛光垫。Fixed abrasive grinding uses waterproof sandpaper as the grinding tool, hard polishing pads are synthetic leather or polyurethane polishing pads, and soft polishing pads are non-woven or fluffy polishing pads. Open rate economy and composition factors, fixed abrasive grinding adopts waterproof grinding wheel, the type can use silicon oxide, aluminum oxide waterproof sandpaper, hard polishing pad chooses commonly used synthetic leather or polyurethane polishing pad, soft polishing pad is also widely used without A woven or napped polishing pad.

化学机械抛光液的pH值为10.2-10.6，含有氧化铈、氧化硅、氢氧化钾、氢氧化钠、氢氧化钡、高锰酸钾、双氧水、柠檬酸、醋酸、草酸中的四种。考虑化学作用和软抛光垫的机械去除作用的平衡，化学机械抛光液的pH值在10.2-10.6这个区间可以很好地实现高去除率，同时获得超光滑的铌酸锂表面。选择氧化铈、氧化硅、氢氧化钾、氢氧化钠、氢氧化钡、高锰酸钾、双氧水、柠檬酸、醋酸、草酸中的四种，是由于综合考虑常用的氧化剂如双氧水和高锰酸钾。考虑纳米颗粒的去除作用，选择常用的硅溶胶和氧化铈作为配方。pH值调节剂选择常用的强碱，如氢氧化钾、氢氧化钠、氢氧化钡。螯合剂选择弱酸，如柠檬酸、醋酸和草酸，对环境的危害很小。含有其中的四种是综合纳米颗粒的去除作用，氧化剂、螯合剂以及pH调节剂在化学机械抛光中的作用而定的。首先，在氧化剂的作用下，铌酸锂晶体形成较软的氧化膜，以及形成金属铌和金属理离子，在螯合剂的作用下，锂离子和铌离子形成盐类，随着抛光液而排出，从而可以产生更多的铌离子和锂离子，使得化学机械抛光反应正常进行。在软抛光垫以及纳米颗粒的综合作用下，较软的氧化膜被去除，从而露出新鲜的铌酸锂表面，使得氧化过程继续，逐渐去除上一道工序留下的损伤层，从而形成超光滑的铌酸锂表面。The chemical mechanical polishing liquid has a pH value of 10.2-10.6 and contains four kinds of cerium oxide, silicon oxide, potassium hydroxide, sodium hydroxide, barium hydroxide, potassium permanganate, hydrogen peroxide, citric acid, acetic acid and oxalic acid. Considering the balance between the chemical action and the mechanical removal action of the soft polishing pad, the pH value of the chemical mechanical polishing solution in the range of 10.2-10.6 can achieve a high removal rate and obtain an ultra-smooth lithium niobate surface. Four of cerium oxide, silicon oxide, potassium hydroxide, sodium hydroxide, barium hydroxide, potassium permanganate, hydrogen peroxide, citric acid, acetic acid, and oxalic acid are selected because of comprehensive consideration of commonly used oxidants such as hydrogen peroxide and permanganate potassium. Considering the removal effect of nanoparticles, commonly used silica sol and cerium oxide were selected as the formula. The pH regulator is selected from commonly used strong bases, such as potassium hydroxide, sodium hydroxide, and barium hydroxide. Chelating agents choose weak acids, such as citric acid, acetic acid and oxalic acid, which have little harm to the environment. The inclusion of four of them depends on the comprehensive removal of nanoparticles, the role of oxidants, chelating agents and pH regulators in chemical mechanical polishing. First, under the action of oxidant, lithium niobate crystal forms a soft oxide film, and metal niobium and metal ions are formed. Under the action of chelating agent, lithium ions and niobium ions form salts, which are discharged with the polishing solution , so that more niobium ions and lithium ions can be produced, so that the chemical mechanical polishing reaction can proceed normally. Under the combined action of the soft polishing pad and nanoparticles, the softer oxide film is removed, exposing the fresh lithium niobate surface, allowing the oxidation process to continue, and gradually removing the damaged layer left by the previous process, thus forming an ultra-smooth Lithium niobate surface.

抛光盘和抛光头的转速为30-60rpm，抛光头压力为40-60kPa。这个转速以及压力充分考虑了铌酸锂晶体的独特的力学特性，具有较低的损伤阈值，以及较高的脆性和韧性，在低压力以及低速下更不容易发生崩边和断裂的加工缺陷，同时在化学机械抛光阶段，更好地利用化学反应的作用，生成较软的氧化膜，用软抛光垫的机械作用去除，从而形成超光滑表面。The rotating speed of the polishing disk and the polishing head is 30-60rpm, and the pressure of the polishing head is 40-60kPa. 样品为Y-cut铌酸锂晶片，直径为50mm，厚度为1mm。将铌酸锂晶片用石蜡粘接于铝合金的配重块上，配重块的直径为150mm。采用#1200碳化硅防水砂纸作为固结磨料磨具，固定于铸铁研磨盘上。在YJ-Y305型旋转摆动台式精密研磨抛光机上进行固结磨料研磨实验。抛光盘和抛光头的转速均为50rpm，压力为40kPa，研磨时间为20min。The sample is a Y-cut lithium niobate wafer with a diameter of 50mm and a thickness of 1mm. The lithium niobate wafer was bonded to an aluminum alloy counterweight with paraffin wax, and the diameter of the counterweight was 150 mm. Use #1200 silicon carbide waterproof sandpaper as the fixed abrasive abrasive, fixed on the cast iron grinding disc. The fixed abrasive grinding experiment was carried out on the YJ-Y305 rotary swing table precision grinding and polishing machine. The rotational speed of the polishing disc and the polishing head is 50 rpm, the pressure is 40 kPa, and the grinding time is 20 min.

固结磨料研磨结束后，在YJ-Y380型高精度旋转平移立式研磨抛光机上进行保持环合成革抛光垫机械抛光实验。采用W3.5的金刚石研磨膏配制抛光液。甘油、去离子水、研磨膏的体积比为6:6:1配成抛光液。保持环材料为铝合金，与配重块间隙配合。抛光过程中抛光头和抛光盘的转速均为30rpm，压力为40kPa，机械抛光时间为1h。机械抛光后采用FlatMaster220型平面度测量仪测试的平面度值为4077.952nm，采用美国ZYGO公司的New view5022型3D表面轮廓仪测试范围为50μm×70μm，表面粗糙度Ra为3.582nm，PV值为38.008nm。After the fixed abrasive grinding is finished, the mechanical polishing experiment of the holding ring synthetic leather polishing pad is carried out on the YJ-Y380 high-precision rotary translation vertical grinding and polishing machine. The polishing liquid was prepared with W3.5 diamond grinding paste. The volume ratio of glycerin, deionized water, and abrasive paste is 6:6:1 to make a polishing liquid. The material of the retaining ring is aluminum alloy, which is matched with the balance weight. Select silica sol with an average particle size of 20nm, hydrogen peroxide with a volume percentage of 30%, silica sol and deionized water at a volume percentage of 1:1.2:8:56 to prepare a chemical mechanical polishing solution, and use potassium hydroxide Adjust the pH value of the polishing solution to 10.5 to complete the preparation of chemical mechanical polishing solution.
