This is a review article published in Light: Advanced Manufacturing (2025)6:55 by Xia Jingjing, Jinlong Zhang, Zhanshan Wang, and colleagues from the MOE Key Laboratory of Advanced Micro-Structured Materials and Institute of Precision Optical Engineering, Tongji University, Shanghai, China. The paper reviews research progress and prospects of high-power laser coating technology.

**Purpose/Scope:** The review focuses on laser coatings used for manipulating optical fields, their principal limitations, and laser-induced damage in high-power applications. It covers concepts, principles, and progress in exploring optical performance, distinctive functions of optical coatings, and optimizing laser resistance through structural optimization, material engineering, and defect elimination.

**Key Topics Covered:**

1. **Optical Manipulation via Multilayers:** Multilayers are alternating thin films with different refractive indices exploiting interference effects. Key applications include AR and HR coatings, filters, beam splitters, polarisers, and dispersive components. The admittance matrix method is used for calculating reflectance/transmittance.

2. **Microstructures:** Four types are categorized: effective medium nanostructures (porous/textured surfaces controlling effective refractive index, achieving reflectivity below 3% and even below 0.5% across 350–2000 nm), gratings (used in chirped-pulse amplification systems), metamaterials (3D with arbitrary permittivities/permeabilities, but limited at optical frequencies), and metasurfaces (2D subwavelength antennas enabling complete control over scalar and vectorial optical fields).

3. **Laser-Induced Damage Mechanisms:** 
   - Damage depends on laser parameters (wavelength, pulse width, frequency, energy) and film properties
   - Short-pulse lasers (fs to sub-ps) cause "cold" field-induced damage via nonlinear absorption (multiphoton absorption, avalanche and tunnel ionisation)
   - Long-pulse lasers (ps to ns) involve defect-induced linear heat absorption, melting, vaporization, plasma formation, and mechanical damage
   - Three principal damage precursors: intrinsic electric field enhancement, visible defects, and non-visible defects
   - Nodule defects (from particulates/seeds) significantly enhance electric field and cause mechanical damage; nodules of 4 μm or larger can easily cause mechanical film damage
   - Non-visible defects form nano-absorption centres that trigger plasma formation and thermal explosions; even gold particles of 1.9 nm diameter embedded at 60 nm depth reduced the damage threshold by one-third
   - Damage growth follows linear patterns with laser shot number, affected by nodule defects and intensity modulation asymmetry

4. **Progress in High-Power Laser Coatings:**
   - **Thin Film Filters:** Notch filters, bandpass filters, edge filters using multilayer designs; narrowband filters using guided mode resonance (GMR) and surface plasmon resonance (SPR); Fano resonance using dielectric materials for narrowband filtering
   - **Polarisation Selection:** Thin-film polarisers (long-wave pass and F-P bandpass designs); broadband polarisers achieved s-polarised transmittance >98% and p-polarised transmittance <1% at 1064 nm with 50 nm bandwidth (twice traditional performance); HfO2/SiO2 Brewster's polarisers with theoretical extinction ratio >30 dB; grating-based polarisers achieving extinction ratios exceeding 100 dB
   - **Dispersion Control:** Dispersive mirrors with chirped coating layers for CPA systems; dispersion up to 10^5 fs²; multiband design approaches for optimized dispersion control; pulse compression gratings (PCGs) including metal gratings, multilayer dielectric gratings (MDGs), and metal MDGs; all-dielectric gratings (introduced by Perry et al., 1995) achieve >97.5% diffraction efficiency; metal MDGs enable pulse bandwidths of 100-200 nm
   - **Metasurfaces:** Enable beam shaping, planarization, miniaturisation, and integration; "Death Star" cavity design for shaping laser pulses into concentric rings achieving excitation efficiency of 10^4 GPa/J

**Future Directions:** Improving design flexibility, fabrication feasibility, advanced detection techniques for high-resolution defect characterisation, and minimising optical loss to meet evolving demands of modern high-power laser systems.

--- SOURCE 1: Plasma etching of proton-exchanged lithium niobate ---
URL: https://www.academia.edu/66909010/Plasma_etching_of_proton_exchanged_lithium_niobate

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an Academia.edu page for the 2006 scientific paper "Plasma etching of proton-exchanged lithium niobate" by Alexey Milenin (DOI: 10.1116/1.2207150). The paper addresses a key challenge in lithium niobate (LiNbO3) fabrication: plasma etching with fluorine gases is limited by the redeposition of LiF, which results in low etch rates and non-vertically etched walls. The study demonstrates that etching proton-exchanged lithium niobate (PE-LN) prevents LiF deposition to a large extent because proton exchange greatly reduces the lithium concentration in the material.

Key findings from the abstract and AI-generated takeaways include:
- Plasma etching of PE-LN yields an etching rate of approximately 5.7 µm/h.
- CHF3/Ar gas at 6 mTorr chamber pressure and 130 V dc bias produced negligible underetching and nearly vertically etched walls (82° wall angle).
- Proton exchange allows up to 85% substitution of Li ions, resulting in an etching rate ratio of approximately 3 between PE-LN and pure LN.
- Etching selectivity of PE-LN to the chromium mask was 32:1 under optimal conditions (approximately 46:1 with SF6).
- SF6 achieved an etching rate of approximately 1.5 µm/h for PE-LN, significantly higher than for pure lithium niobate.
- First photonic crystal waveguide structures were successfully fabricated with an etching depth of 1.5 µm (interpore distance 500 nm, using CHF3/Ar at 1500 W ICP power, 130 V dc bias, 6 mTorr).

The paper includes 7 figures comparing etching results using SF6 vs. CHF3/Ar, showing that SF6 produces underetching (3.5 and 4.0 µm/h rates on each side of stripes) and asymmetric etching, while CHF3/Ar produces nearly vertical walls. SEM analysis revealed cracks on CF4-etched PE-LN and smooth surfaces on SF6-etched PE-LN. The paper lists 10 references and includes related papers on lithium niobate patterning, dry etching with nickel masks, fluorine gas plasma RIE, and ion implantation modification of LN etching properties.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Plasma etching of lithium niobate with fluorine gases is limited by the redeposition LiF. This results in a low etch rate and nonvertically etched walls. Etching of proton-exchanged lithium niobate can prevent the LiF deposition to a large extent because of the greatly reduced lithium concentration in lithium niobate."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: High-Quality Etching of Lithium Niobate Ridge Waveguides | Mi-Net Technology ---
URL: https://www.mi-net.co.uk/application-note/high-quality-etching-of-lithium-niobate-ridge-waveguides

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an application note from Mi-Net Technology (a UK-based supplier of semiconductor materials, testing equipment, and thin-film processing tools) describing an optimized plasma etching process for producing high-quality lithium niobate (LiNbO₃ or LN) ridge waveguides.

**Context:** Lithium niobate is a versatile nonlinear optical crystal valued for its strong electro-optic coefficients, piezoelectric properties, broad transparency range, and wide intrinsic bandwidth. When implemented as lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI), it enables high-index-contrast optical waveguides and densely integrated photonic circuits (PICs), supporting next-generation miniature radio-frequency modulators and advanced photonic devices.

**The Challenge:** LiNbO₃'s hardness makes it difficult to etch. Conventional dry etching can produce rough surfaces and sidewall redeposition, which increase optical losses and degrade device performance.

**The Solution:** The application note demonstrates an optimized etching process using sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆) mixed with argon (Ar) as the plasma gas, performed on a SENTECH Instruments SI500 ICP plasma etcher. Key elements of the process include:
- Use of SF₆/Ar plasma mixtures, which have proven effective for producing smooth ridges
- A chromium (Cr) mask for its resistance to high bias power, preserving the etch profile and ensuring high selectivity
- Relatively high bias power required to physically remove low-volatility reaction by-products such as LiF and NbFₓ (without sufficient energy, micro-masking can cause surface roughness)

**Key Benefits:**
- Smooth LiNbO₃ ridge waveguides with minimal optical loss
- No sidewall redeposition
- High etch selectivity and pattern fidelity using Cr masks
- Compatible with next-generation PICs and compact RF modulators

The note is available as a PDF by request via the site or by emailing sales@mi-net.co.uk. The page also includes related application notes on viscoelastic analysis of rubber with nanoindentation DMA (March 10, 2026), in situ wear measurement at high temperature (January 29, 2026), and mechanical & tribological properties of carbon fibre composite (July 23, 2025).
</summary>

"Sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆), used alone or mixed with argon (Ar), is a common plasma etching gas for LiNbO₃. SF₆/Ar mixtures have proven effective for producing smooth ridges. However, due to the low volatility of reaction by-products such as LiF and NbFₓ, relatively high bias power is required to physically remove these residues. Without sufficient energy, micro-masking can occur, resulting in surface roughness."

--- SOURCE 3: Redeposition-free inductively-coupled plasma etching of lithium niobate for integrated photonics ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper, published in Nanophotonics (2023 Jan 16;12(8):1601, doi: 10.1515/nanoph-2022-0676), reports on redeposition-free inductively-coupled plasma (ICP) etching of lithium niobate for integrated photonics. The study was conducted at ETH Zurich (Department of Physics, Institute for Quantum Electronics, Optical Nanomaterial Group) by Fabian Kaufmann (corresponding author), Giovanni Finco, Andreas Maeder, and Rachel Grange. Received Oct 31, 2022; accepted Dec 16, 2022. PMCID: PMC11501321, PMID: 39634587.

The paper addresses the challenge of argon (Ar) sputtering of lithium niobate-on-insulator (LNOI) waveguides, which provides the best optical quality but suffers from micro-masking effects caused by material redeposition and close-to-one etch mask selectivity. The authors present a workflow to identify optimal etching parameters independent of the plasma system used, and propose three methods to achieve redeposition-free lithium niobate etching without wet chemistry cleaning.

Key experimental details and findings:

1. Wafer preparation: A full 4-inch LNOI wafer (400 nm x-cut film, 2 μm SiO2 insulation layer from NANOLN) was patterned using 100 kV electron beam lithography (Vistex EBPG 5200+), with HSQ-based flowable oxide (FOX16) as negative resist (~500 nm thick). Samples were diced into 52 10×10 mm2 pieces with 5×5 mm2 effective area each.

2. ICP etching: Performed in a Plasma Pro 100 (Oxford Instruments) ICP system. Only Cl2, SF6, O2, and Ar gases were used, as CHF3 was found to contaminate the chamber and harm reproducibility. Etch depth (200-250 nm) was controlled via interferometric endpointing (Horiba, 670.1 nm).

3. Influence of DC bias: Sweeping DC bias from 100 V to 800 V (Ar flow 10 sccm, pressure 1 mTorr, 20 °C) showed that total redeposition decreased almost fourfold from 100 V to 800 V, trending toward redeposition-free etching above 1 kV (though not readily achievable). Trench depth increased by a factor of five with higher bias. Selectivity remained near one, sidewall angle 60-63° for both +Z and −Z crystal faces. Sample bow changed from concave to flat to convex with increasing bias: 300 V gave 20 nm thickness variation over 8×8 mm2, while 600 V gave below 5 nm. Surface roughness (Sq) was ~0.08 nm for biases above 200 V, four times better than un-etched surface (0.31 nm).

4. Influence of chamber pressure: Sweeping pressure from 1 to 15 mTorr (400 V) and 0.3 to 13 mTorr (600 V) showed redeposition vanishing completely after 7 mTorr, but with significant structural damage. Redeposition-free regime occurred at 5-7 mTorr for 600 V (preferred DC bias) and around 11 mTorr for 400 V. Etch rates dropped to minimum values of 27 nm/min (400 V) and 12 nm/min (600 V) before increasing again at higher pressures. Surface roughness degraded with pressure (Sq of 0.10, 0.12, 0.15 nm for 3, 5, 7 mTorr).

5. Aspect ratio dependent etching (ARDE): Redeposition decreased with decreasing gap size (from 1 μm to 100 nm) due to ions bouncing between sidewalls. Trench merging occurred at gaps up to 400 nm, with loading effects below 400 nm. Dense structures were redeposition-free down to 1 μm gaps at 300 W ICP power, 600 V DC bias, and 11 mTorr.

6. Etch depth and IBE: Redeposition decreased with increasing etch depth (110-260 nm). Ion beam etching (IBE) experiments at incidence angles 0°-35° simulating trapezoidal masks (85°, 70°, 60°, 50°) showed reduced redeposition with increasing angle, confirming that trapezoidal masks help achieve redeposition-free etching.

7. Reproducibility and optical results: Four samples etched with 300 W ICP power, 600 V DC bias, 1 mTorr showed excellent reproducibility with Q-factor variation below 2% and calculated propagation loss of 1.55 dB/cm. Etch rate scaled linearly: 0.09 nm/min per watt of ICP power and 0.10 nm/min per volt of DC bias. Optical measurements used ring/racetrack resonators with 600 nm top width, 80 μm bend radius, operating near 1550 nm; a resonance linewidth of 25 pm was observed.

The three proposed methods for redeposition-free etching are: (1) careful balancing of ICP parameters (especially DC bias and chamber pressure), (2) increasing structure density so ion deflection between neighboring walls aids redeposition removal, and (3) tailoring the etching mask toward a trapezoidal shape.

Conclusions note that redeposition-free etching is achievable but requires a very sensitive, well-maintained system—challenging in research environments with mixed use. Alternative approaches include using dense structures with positive masks, keeping a remaining slab near waveguides, or using trapezoidal masks (e.g., via SiO2 PECVD hard mask deposition, or SiNx/a-Si which can be removed without damaging the thermal oxide layer).

Funding: European Research Council grant 714837 (Chi2-nano-oxides), Horizon 2020 ELENA project (101016138), European Space Agency (4000136423/21/NL/GLC/my), and Swiss National Science Foundation grant 194693 (LINIOS, Bridge-Discovery).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We present a workflow to identify the parameter set offering the best etching results independent of the plasma system being used. We show how to reach the redeposition-free regime and propose three methods to achieve redeposition-free lithium niobate etching with good quality sidewalls without need of wet chemistry for cleaning."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Argon plasma inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etching study for smooth sidewall thin film lithium niobate waveguide application ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0925346715301816

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in the journal Optical Materials (Volume 53, March 2016, Pages 1-5) describing a study on fabricating smooth sidewall thin film lithium niobate (TFLN) waveguides using Argon plasma inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etching (ICP-RIE). The paper was authored by G. Ulliac, V. Calero, A. Ndao, F.I. Baida, and M.-P. Bernal.

Key findings and methodology:
- The researchers fabricated ridge waveguides on 700 nm thickness thin film lithium niobate (TFLN), using argon plasma etching on an ICP-RIE system rather than the more common fluorine-containing gases.
- The fabrication process was optimized in three key steps: mask fabrication, plasma etching parameters, and a final wet chemical cleaning step to remove lithium niobate redeposition on side walls.
- Using argon plasma eliminates the problem of lithium fluoride (LiF) redeposition that occurs with fluorine-based gases (CF4, SF6, CHF3), which causes non-vertical sidewall profiles, increased roughness, and reduced etching rates.
- The etching process used argon-based chemistry at low pressure (2 mTorr) with an S1828 photoresist layer as the etching mask (with a soft post-bake to increase etching selectivity).
- The parametric study was performed on 1.1×1.2 cm² chips of X-cut 500 μm thickness lithium niobate due to the high cost of thin film wafers, before fine-tuning on a 3-inch X-cut 700 nm thickness LN film bonded to an LN substrate via a 2 μm SiO2 layer (provided by NanoLN).
- Results: single mode propagation was achieved with overall optical losses of only 5 dB/cm, which is superior to previously demonstrated argon etching of photonic wires with propagation losses of 7.5 dB/cm and 9.9 dB/cm for both light polarizations.
- Optical characterization was performed at 1550 nm wavelength using a tunable CW laser, polarization controller, and lensed fiber with 1-μm diameter spot and 3 mm working distance.

Background context: The paper discusses how lithium niobate is an excellent material for photonics due to its electro-optical, acousto-optical, and nonlinear properties, and how sub-micrometric LN thin films (now commercially available via crystal ion slicing and wafer bonding) are crucial for competing with silicon photonics. Traditional methods like titanium in-diffusion and proton exchange waveguides offer low losses (0.01 dB/cm) but suffer from large mode sizes, whereas ridge waveguides provide better light confinement. The paper notes that LN is hard and relatively inert, making it difficult to etch. Alternative methods discussed include ion implantation assisted HF wet etching, fluorine-containing gas plasma etching (with LiF redeposition issues), and ion-beam enhanced etching (which showed losses around 61 dB/cm).

The work was supported by the ANR ASTRID project "Esencyal" (ANR-13-ASTR-0019-01). The article has been cited 117 times, with notable citing works including "Integrated lithium niobate electro-optic modulators" (Optica, 2021), "Integrated photonics on thin-film lithium niobate" (Advances in Optics and Photonics, 2021), and "Advances in on-chip photonic devices based on lithium niobate on insulator" (Photonics Research, 2020).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In this letter, we show smooth ridge waveguides fabricated on 700 nm thickness thin film lithium niobate (TFLN). The fabrication has been done by developing and optimizing three steps of the technological process, the mask fabrication, the plasma etching, and a final cleaning wet etching step in order to remove the lithium niobate redeposition on the side walls. We have obtained single mode propagation with light overall losses of only 5 dB/cm."

--- SOURCE 5: Plasma Etching Lithium Niobate on an Optoelectronic Chip - IEEE Spectrum ---
URL: https://spectrum.ieee.org/lithium-niobate-a-new-and-viable-platform-for-optoelectronics

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IEEE Spectrum news article (published January 16, 2018, by Alexander Hellemans) reports on a breakthrough in plasma etching lithium niobate (LiNbO3) for optoelectronic chips. Lithium niobate is a hard, chemically inert crystalline material with exceptional optical properties used in cellphones, optical modulators, and frequency converters, but it has been notoriously difficult to etch chemically (unlike silicon). Previous waveguide fabrication methods (ion diffusion, proton exchange) failed because they produced low optical-index contrast. Hybrid silicon-lithium niobate approaches were also unsuccessful due to poor light coupling between materials.

Researchers at Harvard University, led by Marko Lončar of the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (SEAS), applied plasma reactive ion etching—a technique they had used with other difficult materials like diamond. Their process involved: (1) etching waveguide patterns with electron-beam lithography on a photoresist layer, (2) transferring the mask onto the niobate film, and (3) using argon ion plasma to remove exposed material and form waveguides. They created a micro-ring and micro-racetrack resonators about 1 micrometer wide with an 80 µm curvature radius.

Results showed optical power losses of only 50% over a 1-meter distance, versus 99% loss in previous lithium niobate devices—a dramatic improvement attributed to better optical confinement. Marco Bazzan, a materials scientist at the University of Padova, called the result remarkable, noting it could place lithium niobate resonators on par with or above standard silicon photonic devices, especially for integrated quantum photonics. Lončar's team next plans to integrate niobate into silicon photonic processing, though this faces challenges since niobium is not favored in the silicon industry. Bazzan was optimistic because the thin-film substrates are commercially produced, suggesting the technology is ready for standardization.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Over the years, we have dealt with many materials that have nice properties but that are difficult to work with," says Marko Lončar, who led the research. "Diamond is actually easier to etch than niobate, but it doesn't exist as thin films."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Roughness-Limited Performance in Ultra-Low-Loss Lithium Niobate Cavities ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2505.01913v2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research article published in the journal Optica on "Roughness-Limited Performance in Ultra-Low-Loss Lithium Niobate Cavities." The study presents a systematic investigation of scattering losses due to roughness in thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) racetrack cavities, isolating contributions from sidewall and interface roughness.

Key findings:
- Quality factors up to 27×10^6 were demonstrated in wide waveguides (2.2λ ≈ 3.5 μm width) where interface roughness dominates, and up to 1.2×10^7 in narrower waveguides (0.8λ ≈ 1.2 μm) where sidewall roughness is the primary limitation.
- The intrinsic absorption of TFLN is ~0.2 dB/m, corresponding to an absorption-limited quality factor of ~160×10^6.
- The modeling framework uses 3D wave simulations (Tidy3D FDTD solver) informed by AFM-measured roughness and is material-independent and broadly applicable across integrated photonic platforms.

Methodology highlights:
- Sidewall scattering modeled via the Born approximation with equivalent currents, deriving a scattering coefficient αs that integrates the far-field radiation pattern of a line source weighted by the roughness power spectral density.
- Top/bottom interface roughness modeled using a 2D random function approach with power spectral density analysis.
- AFM measurements in tapping mode (Asylum Research AFM, Bruker TESPA-V2-SS tip) characterized roughness. The Z+ surface showed significantly higher roughness (σ = 1.4-2.45 nm) than the Z- surface (σ = 0.4-0.5 nm), with correlation lengths of 40-65 nm.
- Top interface roughness measured ~180-220 pm RMS with ~80-100 nm correlation length.
- Devices fabricated on both X-cut (Ar-trimmed, removing 200 nm) and Y-cut (CMP-polished) LNOI wafers to isolate interface contributions.

Key results:
- Sidewall roughness scales as σ² and dominates losses in narrow waveguides.
- CMP-polished surfaces achieved higher quality factors in larger devices.
- The constant contribution from interfaces and absorption (1/C) estimated at 42-64×10^6.
- Total simulated quality factors for 3.5 μm waveguides predicted at (29-37)×10^6, consistent with measurements.
- PPLN poling experiments showed narrow devices (1.2 μm) experience >30% degradation, while wider devices (2.5 μm) showed <7% degradation due to crystal-axis-dependent etch roughness.

The authors conclude that their quantitative framework helps identify which fabrication processes to focus on for achieving the material limits of TFLN in real devices. Supported by NTT Research, DARPA INSPIRED program, and NSF; fabrication at Stanford Nano Shared Facilities.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Master of Science thesis by Ashraf Mohamedelhassan, completed at the Royal Institute of Technology (KTH) in Stockholm, Sweden in 2012, under the supervision of Dr. Katia Gallo in the Laser Physics group at the Applied Physics department. The thesis focuses on developing a reliable technological process to fabricate ridge waveguides in Lithium Niobate (LiNbO3) using reactive ion etching (RIE).

**Key Goals and Approach:**
The main objective was to fabricate high-confinement ridge waveguides in LiNbO3 using simple, cheap microfabrication techniques. The key innovation was using proton exchange (PE) to weaken the LiNbO3 surface structure, thereby enhancing the dry etching rate, which allowed the use of standard photoresist masks instead of more expensive Chromium masks. The PE process also increased the refractive index (~0.12 at 633 nm along the extraordinary axis) to create the waveguide core, with the ridge geometry providing a high index step (Δn ~1.2 between LiNbO3 and air) for strong light confinement.

**Fabrication Process:**
The fabrication involved several steps: dicing LiNbO3 wafers, cleaning, proton exchange (PE) on both sides of samples, photolithography to pattern photoresist, and reactive ion etching to transfer the pattern. Ridge waveguides were fabricated on both –Z and +Z faces of undoped and MgO-doped congruent LiNbO3 substrates, achieving etching depths of approximately 500 nm on undoped and 300 nm on MgO-doped materials.

**Materials Background:**
- LiNbO3 is an artificial, negative uniaxial, non-centrosymmetric, ferroelectric crystal with large pyroelectric, piezoelectric, nonlinear and electro-optic coefficients
- Grown via the Czochralski technique from Li2CO3 and Nb2O5 powders
- Congruent composition (Li ratio 48.45%) is preferred for optical quality and uniformity
- MgO doping (5 mol%) improves resistance to photorefractive damage
- Transmission range from 350 nm to ~5 μm in the mid-infrared

**Waveguide Physics:**
The thesis covers waveguide theory including total internal reflection principles, critical angle conditions, effective index theory for ridge waveguides, prism coupling methods, and TE/TM mode descriptions. PELN ridge waveguides guide only extraordinary polarization (TM mode in z-cut substrates). The effective index method is used to calculate guided modes by decomposing the ridge waveguide into three asymmetric planar waveguides.

**Etching Challenges and Solutions:**
LiNbO3 is hard and relatively inert, making it difficult to etch. The thesis discusses etching mechanisms including sputtering, chemical etching, and ion-assisted etching, and optimizes RIE parameters such as pressure, RF/ICP powers, etch selectivity, etching rate, etchants gases, and temperature effects. Proton exchange significantly enhances the dry etching rate, enabling ridge fabrication with standard photoresist masks.

**Characterization:**
Ridge profiles were characterized using Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) techniques at the Albanova Nanofabrication laboratory.

**Potential Applications:**
The developed waveguides could be further optimized in combination with periodically poled LiNbO3 (PPLN) structures for integrated nonlinear optical devices such as parametric oscillators, parametric amplifiers, and second harmonic generators.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The main challenge to be faced comes from the fact that LiNbO3 is a hard and relatively inert material, hence relatively difficult to etch. In this master thesis I explored a new technological solution to enhance the etching rate in LiNbO3 which allowed me to develop a dry-etch process to fabricate the ridges with standard photo-resist masks."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] arXiv:2310.10592v3 [cond-mat.mes-hall] 5 Oct 2024 ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.10592

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research paper (arXiv preprint) reporting the first atomic layer etching (ALE) process for lithium niobate (LiNbO3, LN), a ferroelectric crystal used in integrated photonics. The research was conducted by a team from Caltech (Division of Engineering and Applied Science and Department of Electrical Engineering), Oxford Instruments Plasma Technology (UK), and JPL, dated October 8, 2024.

**Background and Motivation:** LN is important for integrated photonics due to its large second-order optical nonlinearity and periodic poling capability via external electric fields. Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) devices are currently limited by propagation losses from surface roughness and corrugations. No ALE process had previously been reported for LN.

**Key Process Results:**
- An isotropic ALE process for x-cut MgO-doped LN using sequential exposures of H2 and SF6/Ar plasmas
- Etch rate of 1.59 ± 0.02 nm/cycle with a synergy of 96.9%
- Both half-steps exhibit saturation (self-limiting behavior); the SF6/Ar step shows soft saturation attributed to a hydrogen concentration gradient into the LN film
- The H2 plasma half-step alone produced a thickness increase (attributed to amorphization volume expansion); the SF6/Ar step alone gave 0.06 nm/cycle

**Alternate Recipes:**
- SF6/O2 plasma replacement: EPC of 2.24 ± 0.02 nm/cycle, synergy of 99.5%
- Cl2/BCl3 plasma replacement: EPC of 1.65 ± 0.03 nm/cycle, synergy of 91.5%
- SF6/Ar recipe at saturation produced the smoothest surface (Rq = 0.57 ± 0.18 nm after 20 cycles)

**Surface Smoothing:** The ALE process reduced sidewall surface roughness of TFLN waveguides etched by physical Ar+ milling by 30% (from Rq = 0.82 ± 0.25 nm to 0.55 ± 0.13 nm) after 50 cycles, without additional wet processing. The lateral etch rate was 1 nm/cycle per side, confirming the largely isotropic nature. PSD decreased over all measured spatial frequencies.

**Experimental Details:** Process uses 40-second H2 plasma exposure (300 W ICP, 52.5 W RIE, 209 V DC bias, 50 sccm H2) followed by 40-second SF6/Ar exposure (300 W ICP, 3.5 W RIE, 50 V DC bias, 17 sccm SF6, 35 sccm Ar), with 5-second Ar purges between steps. Chamber pressure 10 mTorr, substrate cooled to 0°C. Performed in an Oxford Instruments PlasmaPro 100 Cobra system capable of processing 150 mm substrates.

**XPS Analysis:** After ALE, increased F, Li, and Mg fractions were observed, with evidence of LiF and MgF2 formation and redeposition (peak shifts of 0.3 eV for Nb4s and Li1s, 0.6 eV for Mg2p). Surface lithium content increased after H2 plasma exposure, differing from prior high-power/high-temperature proton-exchange studies.

**Conclusions and Future Directions:** The ALE process could serve as a post-processing treatment after Ar+ milling to smooth sidewall roughness and corrugations in periodically-poled TFLN devices. Future work includes investigating etch selectivity mechanisms, reducing redeposited Li/Mg compounds (possibly via post-ALE wet clean or in-situ gas-based removal), exploring Br-based chemistries for more volatile products, and developing directional (anisotropic) ALE for pattern transfer with ~1 nm precision. The work was supported by Oxford Instruments and NSF (Award #2234390), with a US provisional patent filed by the authors.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Here, we report an isotropic ALE process for x-cut MgO-doped LN using sequential exposures of H2 and SF6/Ar plasmas. We observe an etch rate of 1.59 ± 0.02 nm/cycle with a synergy of 96.9%."
</key_excerpts>

<summary>

**Context:** Lithium niobate (LNO) is a versatile single crystal used in surface acoustic wave devices, optoelectronic devices, and ferroelectric/domain-wall memory devices due to its electro-optic and piezoelectric properties. However, its nanofabrication remains challenging, particularly achieving high etching rates and good sidewall angles without compromising ferroelectric properties.

**Background on etching techniques:** The prevailing etching techniques include dry etching (F-based and Cl-based gas), wet etching (acid HF/HNO3 and alkaline SC-1/NaOH), focused-ion-beam etching, and hybrid approaches. F-based gas creates LiF by-products that accumulate on sidewalls and reduce sidewall angles (e.g., Kozlov 2023 achieved only 60-75° angles). Cl-based gas creates easily-removed LiCl by-products but has lower etching rates. Proton-exchanged (PE) LNO prevents LiF formation and enables 90° sidewall angles, but damages ferroelectric properties, making it unsuitable for domain-wall memory devices.

Masks were fabricated using electron-beam lithography, thermal evaporation, electroplating, and PECVD. Samples underwent various combinations of dry etching, proton exchange (180°C molten benzoic acid), high-temperature reduction treatment (400°C in 10% H2 + Ar), wet etching in SC-1 solution, and annealing with Al film coverage.

**Key results (10 samples):**
- Sample 1 (Cr mask, RIE dry etch): 10 nm/min etching rate, ~60° sidewall angle, 3:1 selectivity
- Sample 2 (Ni mask, RIE dry etch): 11 nm/min, ~72° sidewall angle, 5.5:1 selectivity
- Sample 3 (Cr mask, proton exchange + RIE): 13 nm/min, ~70° angle, exchange depth ~210 nm, β1 phase detected by XRD
- Sample 4 (SiO2 mask, high-temp reduction + SC-1 wet etch): ~49 nm depth, asymmetric sidewalls (44° in +Z, 85° in −Z directions)
- Sample 5 (Cr mask, high-temp reduction + RIE): 11.5 nm/min, ~85° sidewall angle
- Sample 6 (Cr mask, RIE + high-temp reduction + wet etch): ~112 nm depth, inward concavity sidewall due to Cr-LNO alloying
- Sample 7 (Cr mask, RIE + Al layer + annealing + wet etch): ~115 nm depth, perfect 90° sidewall angle—the optimized hybrid process that preserves ferroelectric properties
- Sample 8 (Cr mask, ICP): 37 nm/min, ~71° angle, but Cr mask severely consumed
- Sample 9 (Ni mask, ICP): 79 nm/min, ~83° sidewall angle (best ICP result)
- Sample 10 (SiO2 mask, ICP with SF6/BCl3/Ar): 108 nm/min etching rate, 0.86:1 selectivity, ~65° sidewall angle

**Conclusions:** The optimized RIE dry etching combined with wet etching after high-temperature reduction treatment achieved 10 nm/min etching rate with pristine 90° sidewall angles. ICP dry etching with Ni masks achieved 79 nm/min with 83° angles. SiO2 masks enabled 108 nm/min rate with 0.86:1 selectivity, advancing semiconductor-process compatibility. Ni masks outperformed Cr masks in both RIE and ICP due to higher hardness. The hybrid process (dry etching + Al film annealing + wet etching) produced damage-free, perfectly smooth 90° sidewalls while preserving LNO ferroelectric properties, making it suitable for large-scale domain-wall memory array fabrication.

URL: https://engineering.purdue.edu/oxidemems/conferences/ultrasonics2007/DATA/P4L-4.PDF

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (2007 IEEE Ultrasonics Symposium) by Andrew B. Randles, Shuji Tanaka, and Masayoshi Esashi from Tohoku University presents experimental data on the etch rate of lithium niobate (LiNbO3) as a function of crystal orientation.

METHODOLOGY: 30 mm diameter LiNbO3 spheres (polished from a 76.4 mm diameter ingot) were etched in hydrofluoric acid (HF) and a 1:2 mixture of HF and nitric acid (HF:HNO3). Etch conditions varied (HF at 80°C for 2-3 hours; HF:HNO3 at 80°C for 1-2 hours and 90°C for 1 hour). A CNC coordinate measuring machine (Mitsutoyo Legex 707) measured each sphere every 2°, generating over 9,000 data points per etch condition. The process followed the method developed by Sato et al., with a full sphere (measurable from 0° to 150°) used instead of a hemisphere because LiNbO3 lacks the etch symmetry of silicon.

KEY RESULTS:
- The maximum etch rate occurred on the -Z face, i.e., the (0001) plane
- Etching exhibited three-fold symmetry about the Z axis
- Crystal planes in the (2203) family showed the lowest etch rate in the -Z hemisphere; this plane is close to (1102), which is parallel to layers of Nb, Li, and O atoms
- The etch rate was more uniform for HF-etched spheres than for HF:HNO3-etched spheres
- The etch rate on the +Z face is less than 0.1% of the etch rate on the -Z face (corrected from an initial 25% reading due to sphere center finding inaccuracies)

SIMULATION: The sphere etch data was divided into three symmetry zones, averaged, and used with the Wulff-Jaccodine method to predict etched wafer shapes for various crystal cuts (including Z cut, 128°Y cut, and 163°Y cut). The Wulff-Jaccodine method uses two parts: (1) minimization of free surface energy to predict final exposed planes, and (2) a geometric rule defining final etched structure shapes. The predicted etched shapes showed good agreement with experimental etched wafers, with angle differences of less than 4.3° attributable to crystal axis alignment and measurement errors.

APPLICATION CONTEXT: LiNbO3 is a ferroelectric material used in optics and SAW devices, but its use in MEMS is limited because bulk micromachining etch characteristics are not well understood. This full etch rate map enables simulation and design of complex MEMS structures combining SAW and bulk micromachining technologies.

DATA AVAILABILITY: The etch rate data is available at www.mems.mech.tohoku.ac.jp/esashilab/lnetchrate/etchrate.html. The work was supported by SCOPE from the Ministry of General Affairs, Japan (No. 062302002).

SUMMARY:

1. **Ion Milling** — Bombards sample with Ar+ ions to physically etch material. Early attempts produced ~4 dB/cm waveguide losses due to sidewall roughness from redeposition, mask erosion, and low etch selectivity. Optimized processes have improved results dramatically.

2. **Focused Ion Beam (FIB) Milling** — Uses tightly focused Ga+ beam for maskless, direct-write patterning with <10 nm resolution and arbitrary 3D shapes. A two-step process (coarse milling at high current, then fine polishing at low current) enabled microdisk resonators with Q factors >10^6. 3. **EBL + Ion Milling** — Combines electron beam lithography for hard mask patterning (e.g., chromium) with optimized Ar+ ion milling. Key factors include hard masks resistant to milling, optimized ion energy/current, and multi-step etching. Achieved waveguide losses as low as 0.027 dB/cm and Q factors >10^7.

4. **Chemomechanical Polishing (CMP)** — The PLACE (photolithography-assisted chemomechanical etching) technique combines mechanical abrasion with chemical etching. Process: deposit hard mask, pattern mask (e.g., laser ablation), CMP to remove exposed LN, remove mask and undercut. Produces ultra-smooth surfaces (<0.5 nm RMS), controllable sidewall angles, and is compatible with standard photolithography. URL: https://spectrum.ieee.org/lithium-niobate-a-new-and-viable-platform-for-optoelectronics

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IEEE Spectrum news article (published 16 January 2018, updated same day) by Alexander Hellemans reports on a breakthrough by Harvard University researchers in plasma etching lithium niobate (LiNbO3) for optoelectronic chips. Lithium niobate is a hard, chemically inert crystalline material with exceptional optical properties used in electro-optics, acousto-optics, and nonlinear optics, found in devices like cellphones, optical modulators, and frequency converters. Unlike silicon, lithium niobate is not amenable to chemical etching, and previous techniques (ion diffusion, proton exchange) produced too-low optical-index contrast for effective waveguides. Hybrid silicon-lithium niobate approaches were also impractical due to insufficient light coupling. The Harvard team, led by Marko Lončar, applied plasma reactive ion etching—bombarding the chip surface with argon ions to remove material exposed by an electron-beam lithography mask—to create micro-ring and micro-racetrack resonators (~1 micrometer wide, 80 µm curvature radius). Results showed optical power losses of only 50% over 1 meter, compared to 99% loss in previous lithium niobate devices, due to improved optical confinement. Independent expert Marco Bazzan (University of Padova) called the result remarkable, noting it could elevate lithium niobate resonators above standard silicon photonics and holds importance for integrated quantum photonics. Lončar's team plans next to integrate niobate into silicon photonic processing, though this is challenging as niobium is not favored in the silicon industry; the team may need dedicated fabrication facilities or to couple separately-made niobium and silicon chips. Bazzan noted the thin-film substrates are commercially available, meaning the technological steps are ready for standardization.
</summary>

"Over the years, we have dealt with many materials that have nice properties but that are difficult to work with," says Marko Lončar, who led the research. "Diamond is actually easier to etch than niobate, but it doesn't exist as thin films."

--- SOURCE 16: Redeposition-free inductively-coupled plasma etching of ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper, published in Nanophotonics (2023 Jan 16;12(8):1601, doi: 10.1515/nanoph-2022-0676), reports on redeposition-free inductively-coupled plasma (ICP) etching of lithium niobate for integrated photonics. The study was conducted at ETH Zurich (Department of Physics, Institute for Quantum Electronics, Optical Nanomaterial Group) by Fabian Kaufmann (corresponding author), Giovanni Finco, Andreas Maeder, and Rachel Grange. Received Oct 31, 2022; accepted Dec 16, 2022. PMCID: PMC11501321, PMID: 39634587.

The paper addresses the challenge of argon (Ar) sputtering of lithium niobate-on-insulator (LNOI) waveguides, which provides the best optical quality but suffers from micro-masking effects caused by material redeposition and close-to-one etch mask selectivity. The authors present a workflow to identify optimal etching parameters independent of the plasma system used, and propose three methods to achieve redeposition-free lithium niobate etching without wet chemistry cleaning.

Key experimental details and findings:

1. Wafer preparation: A full 4-inch LNOI wafer (400 nm x-cut film, 2 μm SiO2 insulation layer from NANOLN) was patterned using 100 kV electron beam lithography (Vistex EBPG 5200+), with HSQ-based flowable oxide (FOX16) as negative resist (~500 nm thick). Samples were diced into 52 10×10 mm2 pieces with 5×5 mm2 effective area each.

2. ICP etching: Performed in a Plasma Pro 100 (Oxford Instruments) ICP system. Only Cl2, SF6, O2, and Ar gases were used, as CHF3 was found to contaminate the chamber and harm reproducibility. Etch depth (200-250 nm) was controlled via interferometric endpointing (Horiba, 670.1 nm).

3. Influence of DC bias: Sweeping DC bias from 100 V to 800 V (Ar flow 10 sccm, pressure 1 mTorr, 20 °C) showed that total redeposition decreased almost fourfold from 100 V to 800 V, trending toward redeposition-free etching above 1 kV (though not readily achievable). Trench depth increased by a factor of five with higher bias. Selectivity remained near one, sidewall angle 60-63° for both +Z and −Z crystal faces. Sample bow changed from concave to flat to convex with increasing bias: 300 V gave 20 nm thickness variation over 8×8 mm2, while 600 V gave below 5 nm. Surface roughness (Sq) was ~0.08 nm for biases above 200 V, four times better than un-etched surface (0.31 nm).

4. Influence of chamber pressure: Sweeping pressure from 1 to 15 mTorr (400 V) and 0.3 to 13 mTorr (600 V) showed redeposition vanishing completely after 7 mTorr, but with significant structural damage. Redeposition-free regime occurred at 5-7 mTorr for 600 V (preferred DC bias) and around 11 mTorr for 400 V. Etch rates dropped to minimum values of 27 nm/min (400 V) and 12 nm/min (600 V) before increasing again at higher pressures. Surface roughness degraded with pressure (Sq of 0.10, 0.12, 0.15 nm for 3, 5, 7 mTorr).

5. Aspect ratio dependent etching (ARDE): Redeposition decreased with decreasing gap size (from 1 μm to 100 nm) due to ions bouncing between sidewalls. Trench merging occurred at gaps up to 400 nm, with loading effects below 400 nm. Dense structures were redeposition-free down to 1 μm gaps at 300 W ICP power, 600 V DC bias, and 11 mTorr.

6. Etch depth and IBE: Redeposition decreased with increasing etch depth (110-260 nm). Ion beam etching (IBE) experiments at incidence angles 0°-35° simulating trapezoidal masks (85°, 70°, 60°, 50°) showed reduced redeposition with increasing angle, confirming that trapezoidal masks help achieve redeposition-free etching.

7. Reproducibility and optical results: Four samples etched with 300 W ICP power, 600 V DC bias, 1 mTorr showed excellent reproducibility with Q-factor variation below 2% and calculated propagation loss of 1.55 dB/cm. Etch rate scaled linearly: 0.09 nm/min per watt of ICP power and 0.10 nm/min per volt of DC bias. Optical measurements used ring/racetrack resonators with 600 nm top width, 80 μm bend radius, operating near 1550 nm; a resonance linewidth of 25 pm was observed.

The three proposed methods for redeposition-free etching are: (1) careful balancing of ICP parameters (especially DC bias and chamber pressure), (2) increasing structure density so ion deflection between neighboring walls aids redeposition removal, and (3) tailoring the etching mask toward a trapezoidal shape.

Conclusions note that redeposition-free etching is achievable but requires a very sensitive, well-maintained system—challenging in research environments with mixed use. Alternative approaches include using dense structures with positive masks, keeping a remaining slab near waveguides, or using trapezoidal masks (e.g., via SiO2 PECVD hard mask deposition, or SiNx/a-Si which can be removed without damaging the thermal oxide layer).

Funding: European Research Council grant 714837 (Chi2-nano-oxides), Horizon 2020 ELENA project (101016138), European Space Agency (4000136423/21/NL/GLC/my), and Swiss National Science Foundation grant 194693 (LINIOS, Bridge-Discovery).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We present a workflow to identify the parameter set offering the best etching results independent of the plasma system being used. We show how to reach the redeposition-free regime and propose three methods to achieve redeposition-free lithium niobate etching with good quality sidewalls without need of wet chemistry for cleaning."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://physik.uni-paderborn.de/fileadmin-nw/physik/Alumni/Sohler/2008/ecio08_hu.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a conference paper (ECIO'08, Eindhoven, Netherlands, pp. 75-78, 2008) by H. Hu, R. Ricken, and W. Sohler from the Angewandte Physik department at Universität Paderborn, Germany, reporting recent progress in etching techniques for lithium niobate (LiNbO3, LN) to fabricate integrated optical devices with deep sub-micrometer structures. The paper covers three etching approaches:

**1. Wet etching of Z-cut LN (HF/HNO3 mixture):** A modified three-step process to fabricate low-loss Ti-doped ridge waveguides: (1) ridge fabrication using Cr-mask wet etching in a mixture of 21 ml HF (40%), 14 ml HNO3 (100%), and 5 ml ethanol; (2) selective Ti-stripe definition using a novel photolithographic process exploiting inhomogeneous photoresist thickness on ridge tops with flood exposure and lift-off; (3) Ti-indiffusion at 1060°C for 8.5 hrs in Ar/O2 atmospheres. Resulting ridge guides (6.5 µm height, 10 µm top width, monomode up to 9 µm) achieved dramatically improved propagation losses: TE losses dropped from 0.22 dB/cm at 5 µm width to 0.05 dB/cm at 7 µm width; TM losses were 1.3 dB/cm at 5 µm and 0.36 dB/cm at 9 µm. The polarization-dependent losses are attributed to Cr2O3 growth and Li2O outdiffusion causing extraordinary index fluctuations near the surface. Etching temperature can control ridge wall slope, enabling micromechanical structures such as interdigital lamellas (2.6 µm width, 2.8 µm separation, 7.7 µm etching depth at 8°C).

**2. ICP-etching of X-cut LN:** Uses C4F8/He (1:1) plasma with a Cr mask. The key challenge is LiF formation and re-deposition (melting point >800°C), which lowers etch rate and prevents vertical sidewalls. The solution is an iterative process: ICP-etch for several minutes, then clean in SC-1 solution (70% H2O, 20% H2O2, 10% NH4OH) for 1 minute to remove deposition, repeating until desired depth. Demonstrated ridges of 5.8 µm height and 8 µm width with nearly vertical walls, plus more complex microstructures.

**3. ICP-etching of H+-exchanged X-cut LN (photonic crystal structures):** Proton exchange (PE) to 1.4 µm depth reduces Li concentration and thus LiF re-deposition, increasing etch rate and improving profiles. Process: PE of congruent X-cut LN, 110 nm Cr film sputtered, 120 nm photoresist, optical contact lithography (smallest features 170 nm), wet etching to transfer pattern to Cr, then repeated ICP-etching and SC-1 cleaning. This produced photonic crystal structures in PE-LN. Proton exchange also creates single-polarization waveguides (increases only extraordinary index), and reverse proton exchange (RPE) can form buried waveguide profiles.

**Conclusions:** Significant progress in wet etching of Z-cut LN, ICP-etching of X-cut LN, and ICP-etching of proton-exchanged X-cut LN enables reliable fabrication of integrated optical devices with low-loss ridge guides, micromechanical, and photonic crystal structures.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an application note from Mi-Net Technology (a UK-based supplier of semiconductor materials, testing equipment, and thin-film processing tools) describing an optimized plasma etching process for producing high-quality lithium niobate (LiNbO₃ or LN) ridge waveguides.

**Context:** Lithium niobate is a versatile nonlinear optical crystal valued for its strong electro-optic coefficients, piezoelectric properties, broad transparency range, and wide intrinsic bandwidth. When implemented as lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI), it enables high-index-contrast optical waveguides and densely integrated photonic circuits (PICs), supporting next-generation miniature radio-frequency modulators and advanced photonic devices.

**The Challenge:** LiNbO₃'s hardness makes it difficult to etch. Conventional dry etching can produce rough surfaces and sidewall redeposition, which increase optical losses and degrade device performance.

**The Solution:** The application note demonstrates an optimized etching process using sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆) mixed with argon (Ar) as the plasma gas, performed on a SENTECH Instruments SI500 ICP plasma etcher. Key elements of the process include:
- Use of SF₆/Ar plasma mixtures, which have proven effective for producing smooth ridges
- A chromium (Cr) mask for its resistance to high bias power, preserving the etch profile and ensuring high selectivity
- Relatively high bias power required to physically remove low-volatility reaction by-products such as LiF and NbFₓ (without sufficient energy, micro-masking can cause surface roughness)

**Key Benefits:**
- Smooth LiNbO₃ ridge waveguides with minimal optical loss
- No sidewall redeposition
- High etch selectivity and pattern fidelity using Cr masks
- Compatible with next-generation PICs and compact RF modulators

The note is available as a PDF by request via the site or by emailing sales@mi-net.co.uk. The page also includes related application notes on viscoelastic analysis of rubber with nanoindentation DMA (March 10, 2026), in situ wear measurement at high temperature (January 29, 2026), and mechanical & tribological properties of carbon fibre composite (July 23, 2025).
</summary>

"Sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆), used alone or mixed with argon (Ar), is a common plasma etching gas for LiNbO₃. SF₆/Ar mixtures have proven effective for producing smooth ridges. However, due to the low volatility of reaction by-products such as LiF and NbFₓ, relatively high bias power is required to physically remove these residues. Without sufficient energy, micro-masking can occur, resulting in surface roughness."

--- SOURCE 4: [PDF] Fabrication of Ridge Waveguides in Lithium Niobate - KTH ---
URL: https://www.kth.se/polopoly_fs/1.422561.1600688634!/Menu/general/column-content/attachment/Ashraf_Mohamedelhassan%20_msc_thesis.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Master of Science thesis by Ashraf Mohamedelhassan (KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden, 2012) on the fabrication of ridge waveguides in Lithium Niobate (LiNbO3). The thesis was supervised by Dr. Katia Gallo and co-supervised by Michele Manzo, within the Laser Physics group at the Applied Physics department, in collaboration with the Albanova Nanofabrication laboratory.

**Main Objective:** To develop a reliable dry-etch (reactive ion etching, RIE) process to fabricate ridge waveguides in LiNbO3 using standard photoresist masks, enabling strong optical confinement for integrated nonlinear optical devices (potentially combined with periodically poled LiNbO3, PPLN).

**Key Methodology:** The work combines:
1. **Proton exchange (PE)** – an ion exchange process substituting lithium ions with protons (H+) from an acidic melt, which (a) increases the extraordinary refractive index by ~0.12 at 633 nm, creating the guiding layer (nPELN~2.3 vs nLN~2.2), and (b) weakens the LiNbO3 surface structure to significantly enhance subsequent etching rates.
2. **Photolithography** – using standard photoresist to pattern the ridge structures.
3. **Reactive ion etching (RIE)** – dry plasma etching to transfer the pattern into the substrate.

**Key Results:**
- Ridge waveguides fabricated on both -Z and +Z faces of undoped and MgO-doped congruent LiNbO3 substrates.
- Etching depths of ~500 nm on undoped and ~300 nm on MgO-doped materials.
- Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) used for ridge profile characterization.
- PELN ridge waveguides achieve a lateral index step of ~1.2 (air-LN index difference) compared to only ~0.12 for embedded PELN channels.
- The ridge geometry allows bi-dimensional light confinement in the transverse plane.

**Background on LiNbO3:** An artificial (not found in nature), negative uniaxial, non-centrosymmetric, ferroelectric crystal with large pyroelectric, piezoelectric, nonlinear and electro-optic coefficients. Grown via the Czochralski technique from Li2CO3 and Nb2O5 (melting point ~1250°C). Congruent composition (48.45% Li) is preferred for its optical quality and uniformity. MgO (5 mol%) doping improves resistance to photorefractive damage. Crystal is trigonal, 3m point group, R3c space group, ferroelectric below Curie temperature (1140°C).

**Key Fabrication Steps (flowchart):** Dicing wafers → Cleaning → Proton exchange (on top and bottom surfaces) → Photoresist coating → Photolithography patterning → Reactive ion etching → Polishing.

**Etching details:** The main challenge is LiNbO3's hardness and chemical inertness, giving low etching rates. The thesis explores parameters including etch selectivity, pressure, RF and ICP powers, etchant gases, and temperature. The PE layer enhances etching rates, allowing ridges several hundred nanometers deep with simple photoresist masks (avoiding the need for chromium masks).

**Waveguide physics:** Includes analysis of total internal reflection conditions, effective index method for ridge waveguides, prism coupling for light injection, and TE/TM mode descriptions. PE waveguides on z-cut substrates guide only extraordinary polarization (TM mode); ridges fabricated along the x-axis as propagation direction.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The main challenge to be faced comes from the fact that LiNbO3 is a hard and relatively inert material, hence relatively difficult to etch. In this master thesis I explored a new technological solution to enhance the etching rate in LiNbO3 which allowed me to develop a dry-etch process to fabricate the ridges with standard photo-resist masks."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific research article published in Nanomaterials (Basel) journal on October 18, 2023 (DOI: 10.3390/nano13202789), titled "Advanced Etching Techniques of LiNbO3 Nanodevices" by Bowen Shen, Di Hu, Cuihua Dai, Xiaoyang Yu, Xiaojun Tan, Jie Sun, Jun Jiang, and Anquan Jiang from the School of Microelectronics at Fudan University, Shanghai, China.

**Context:** Lithium niobate (LNO) is a versatile single crystal used in surface acoustic wave devices, optoelectronic devices, and ferroelectric/domain-wall memory devices due to its electro-optic and piezoelectric properties. However, its nanofabrication remains challenging, particularly achieving high etching rates and good sidewall angles without compromising ferroelectric properties.

**Background on etching techniques:** The prevailing etching techniques include dry etching (F-based and Cl-based gas), wet etching (acid HF/HNO3 and alkaline SC-1/NaOH), focused-ion-beam etching, and hybrid approaches. F-based gas creates LiF by-products that accumulate on sidewalls and reduce sidewall angles (e.g., Kozlov 2023 achieved only 60-75° angles). Cl-based gas creates easily-removed LiCl by-products but has lower etching rates. Proton-exchanged (PE) LNO prevents LiF formation and enables 90° sidewall angles, but damages ferroelectric properties, making it unsuitable for domain-wall memory devices.

**Methodology:** Ten LNO samples (X-cut, 5 mol.% Mg-doped) were prepared with different mask types (Cr, Ni, and SiO2) and etched using different instruments (RIE vs. ICP) and processes. Masks were fabricated using electron-beam lithography, thermal evaporation, electroplating, and PECVD. Samples underwent various combinations of dry etching, proton exchange (180°C molten benzoic acid), high-temperature reduction treatment (400°C in 10% H2 + Ar), wet etching in SC-1 solution, and annealing with Al film coverage.

**Key results (10 samples):**
- Sample 1 (Cr mask, RIE dry etch): 10 nm/min etching rate, ~60° sidewall angle, 3:1 selectivity
- Sample 2 (Ni mask, RIE dry etch): 11 nm/min, ~72° sidewall angle, 5.5:1 selectivity
- Sample 3 (Cr mask, proton exchange + RIE): 13 nm/min, ~70° angle, exchange depth ~210 nm, β1 phase detected by XRD
- Sample 4 (SiO2 mask, high-temp reduction + SC-1 wet etch): ~49 nm depth, asymmetric sidewalls (44° in +Z, 85° in −Z directions)
- Sample 5 (Cr mask, high-temp reduction + RIE): 11.5 nm/min, ~85° sidewall angle
- Sample 6 (Cr mask, RIE + high-temp reduction + wet etch): ~112 nm depth, inward concavity sidewall due to Cr-LNO alloying
- Sample 7 (Cr mask, RIE + Al layer + annealing + wet etch): ~115 nm depth, perfect 90° sidewall angle—the optimized hybrid process that preserves ferroelectric properties
- Sample 8 (Cr mask, ICP): 37 nm/min, ~71° angle, but Cr mask severely consumed
- Sample 9 (Ni mask, ICP): 79 nm/min, ~83° sidewall angle (best ICP result)
- Sample 10 (SiO2 mask, ICP with SF6/BCl3/Ar): 108 nm/min etching rate, 0.86:1 selectivity, ~65° sidewall angle

**Conclusions:** The optimized RIE dry etching combined with wet etching after high-temperature reduction treatment achieved 10 nm/min etching rate with pristine 90° sidewall angles. ICP dry etching with Ni masks achieved 79 nm/min with 83° angles. SiO2 masks enabled 108 nm/min rate with 0.86:1 selectivity, advancing semiconductor-process compatibility. Ni masks outperformed Cr masks in both RIE and ICP due to higher hardness. The hybrid process (dry etching + Al film annealing + wet etching) produced damage-free, perfectly smooth 90° sidewalls while preserving LNO ferroelectric properties, making it suitable for large-scale domain-wall memory array fabrication.

**Funding:** Supported by the Natural Science Foundation of Shanghai (23ZR1403900), the National Key Basic Research Program of China (2019YFA0308500 and 2022YFA1402904), and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (62174034).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: [PDF] arXiv:2310.10592v3 [cond-mat.mes-hall] 5 Oct 2024 ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.10592

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research paper (arXiv preprint) reporting the first atomic layer etching (ALE) process for lithium niobate (LiNbO3, LN), a ferroelectric crystal used in integrated photonics. The research was conducted by a team from Caltech (Division of Engineering and Applied Science and Department of Electrical Engineering), Oxford Instruments Plasma Technology (UK), and JPL, dated October 8, 2024.

**Background and Motivation:** LN is important for integrated photonics due to its large second-order optical nonlinearity and periodic poling capability via external electric fields. Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) devices are currently limited by propagation losses from surface roughness and corrugations. No ALE process had previously been reported for LN.

**Key Process Results:**
- An isotropic ALE process for x-cut MgO-doped LN using sequential exposures of H2 and SF6/Ar plasmas
- Etch rate of 1.59 ± 0.02 nm/cycle with a synergy of 96.9%
- Both half-steps exhibit saturation (self-limiting behavior); the SF6/Ar step shows soft saturation attributed to a hydrogen concentration gradient into the LN film
- The H2 plasma half-step alone produced a thickness increase (attributed to amorphization volume expansion); the SF6/Ar step alone gave 0.06 nm/cycle

**Alternate Recipes:**
- SF6/O2 plasma replacement: EPC of 2.24 ± 0.02 nm/cycle, synergy of 99.5%
- Cl2/BCl3 plasma replacement: EPC of 1.65 ± 0.03 nm/cycle, synergy of 91.5%
- SF6/Ar recipe at saturation produced the smoothest surface (Rq = 0.57 ± 0.18 nm after 20 cycles)

URL: https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/2515-7647/ae0ee5/pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a technical tutorial (published in J. Phys. Photonics 7, 046001, October 2025) by Kashif Masud Awan (Photonic Inc., Coquitlam, British Columbia, Canada) that provides a practical guide for developing robust plasma etching processes for photonic integrated circuits (PICs) within the constraints of shared academic semiconductor cleanrooms.

KEY SECTIONS AND CONTENT:

1. **Context**: PICs have grown rapidly across material platforms including InP, GaAs, silicon, Si3N4, GaN, SiC, and LiNbO3, supporting applications in optical communications, LIDAR, sensing, quantum computing, and displays. Most PICs are fabricated using planar CMOS-derived techniques with ICP-RIE (inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etching) as the dominant dry etching method.

2. **Chamber Best Practices**: Shared academic cleanrooms typically maintain two dedicated etch chambers—one for fluorine-based chemistries (silicon materials) and one for chlorine-based chemistries (III-V semiconductors, metals). Recommended protocol: begin with a high-power oxygen plasma clean (10-15 min at max ICP/RIE powers and highest O2 flow), then condition the chamber with the target etch chemistry on a dummy wafer (5-15 min). Operate near the lowest base pressure (typically 10⁻⁶–10⁻⁸ Torr). Some materials (metals, lithium compounds) are difficult to remove and require prohibitions on metal masks in silicon chambers. In single-chamber facilities, time-sharing between chemistries (e.g., monthly rotations) with extensive oxygen cleans between is recommended. Severe contamination may require manual wet cleaning with acetone/IPA.

3. **Etch Test Preparation**: EBL (electron beam lithography) is preferred for academic PIC prototyping due to high resolution (tens of nm). Positive-tone resists (ZEP520A, PMMA) are used when large areas need masking; negative-tone resists (HSQ, ma-N 2400 series) when small areas need masking. HSQ is used in the example. Test patterns should include variable-width trenches (2000 nm down to 40 nm), hole arrays, and features ≥4 mm in length for cleaving and SEM cross-sectioning. GDSII format with KLayout is recommended. Chips should match the final device's material platform, film stack, size, and layout density.

4. **DOE for Parameter Sweeps**: Plasma etching operates via three mechanisms—sputtering (purely physical, anisotropic, rough surfaces), chemical etching (isotropic, smooth), and ion-enhanced chemical etching/RIE (combines both, preferred for high-fidelity anisotropic pattern transfer). ICP-RIE is preferred over CCP because it decouples plasma density from ion energy. Key process parameters ("knobs"): gas composition/flow rates (sccm), chamber pressure, ICP power, bias RIE power, and substrate temperature (ranging from cryogenic to ~200°C). Etch selectivity is defined as s = substrate etch rate / mask etch rate. The article presents a 40-run DOE matrix for AlGaAs etching with Ar–BCl3 chemistry (Table 1), with results on etch rate, selectivity, and sidewall angle as functions of pressure, ICP power, and RIE power (Figures 5-7). Not all DOE combinations need testing—focusing on key knobs is more efficient. Selectivity can be improved by lowering RIE power or increasing pressure.

5. **Evaluating Etch Trials**: Each test follows chamber cleaning/conditioning, then etching, then cross-sectional SEM or FIB analysis to measure etch rate, selectivity, and sidewall angle. Results are plotted against varied parameters to identify trends. Iterative refinement continues until specifications are met, then processes are repeated multiple times to validate repeatability. Revalidation is advised after the chamber has been used for different chemistries/materials in shared facilities.

6. **Post-Etch Quality Improvements**: (a) Surface passivation—for lasers, LEDs, and photovoltaics sensitive to dangling bonds; e.g., sulfur passivation for III-V semiconductors. (b) Wet post-processing—applying wet etch after dry etch to smooth rough sidewalls and reduce propagation losses. Mask removal: oxygen plasma + solvent for polymer resists (ZEP520A, PMMA); dilute HF or BOE for HSQ (e.g., 20 s in 10% HF worked in this study). (c) Reducing mask LER—low-temperature EBL development suppresses resist swelling; HSQ exhibits inherently lower LER than organic resists due to its inorganic short-chain structure.

7. **Conclusion**: The tutorial provides a starting point for graduate students and researchers developing plasma etch processes for PICs in resource-constrained, multi-user academic fabrication environments, covering chamber protocols, test pattern design, ICP-RIE principles, parameter optimization, etch characterization, and post-etch enhancements.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A standard best practice in shared etch chambers is to begin with a high-power oxygen clean—typically using the tool's maximum inductively coupled plasma (ICP) and reactive ion etching (RIE) powers and the highest available oxygen flow rates—for 10–15 min. Following this, the chamber is conditioned by running the desired etch chemistry on a dummy wafer for 5–15 min."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Fabrication Techniques for Lithium Niobate on Insulator Photonic ... ---
URL: https://www.latitudeds.com/post/fabrication-techniques-for-lithium-niobate-on-insulator-photonic-structures

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article (published October 16, 2024, by Latitude Design Systems) provides an overview of key fabrication techniques for lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) photonic structures, a promising platform for integrated photonics due to its electro-optic, nonlinear optical, and piezoelectric properties.

**LNOI Wafer Fabrication:** Uses crystal ion slicing, involving (1) He+ ion implantation into an LN wafer, (2) bonding to a substrate with silica buffer layer, (3) thermal treatment to exfoliate a thin LN film, and (4) thinning/polishing. This produces sub-micrometer films with surface roughness below 0.5 nm in both Z-cut and X-cut orientations.

**Fabrication Techniques Covered:**

1. **Ion Milling** — Bombards sample with Ar+ ions to physically etch material. Early attempts produced ~4 dB/cm waveguide losses due to sidewall roughness from redeposition, mask erosion, and low etch selectivity. Optimized processes have improved results dramatically.

2. **Focused Ion Beam (FIB) Milling** — Uses tightly focused Ga+ beam for maskless, direct-write patterning with <10 nm resolution and arbitrary 3D shapes. A two-step process (coarse milling at high current, then fine polishing at low current) enabled microdisk resonators with Q factors >10^6. Limitations: low throughput, redeposition, Ga+ contamination.

3. **EBL + Ion Milling** — Combines electron beam lithography for hard mask patterning (e.g., chromium) with optimized Ar+ ion milling. Key factors include hard masks resistant to milling, optimized ion energy/current, and multi-step etching. Achieved waveguide losses as low as 0.027 dB/cm and Q factors >10^7.

4. **Chemomechanical Polishing (CMP)** — The PLACE (photolithography-assisted chemomechanical etching) technique combines mechanical abrasion with chemical etching. Process: deposit hard mask, pattern mask (e.g., laser ablation), CMP to remove exposed LN, remove mask and undercut. Produces ultra-smooth surfaces (<0.5 nm RMS), controllable sidewall angles, and is compatible with standard photolithography. Achieved record-low 0.027 dB/cm propagation losses and Q factors up to 4.7x10^7.

5. **Mechanical Dicing/Cutting** — Uses precision dicing saws or ultraprecision ductile-mode cutting with single-crystal diamond tools. Produces extremely smooth sidewalls (losses as low as 1.2 dB/cm) but lacks resolution and geometric flexibility.

**Conclusions:** PLACE currently offers the best combination of quality and scalability for large-scale production. FIB or EBL approaches are preferred for prototyping or specialized nanostructures. Future development areas include reducing losses in thin (<200 nm) waveguides, improving mode profile/dispersion control, increasing throughput and yield, developing 3D structures, and integrating electrodes. Reference: Y. Cheng, "Lithium Niobate Nanophotonics," Jenny Stanford Publishing, 2021.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
PLACE has achieved record-low propagation losses of 0.027 dB/cm in LNOI waveguides and Q factors up to 4.7x10^7 in microdisk resonators., This approach has achieved waveguide losses as low as 0.027 dB/cm and resonator Q factors >10^7., For large-scale production of integrated photonic circuits, PLACE currently offers the best combination of quality and scalability. For prototyping or specialized nanostructures, FIB or EBL-based approaches may be preferred., This technique can produce LNOI wafers with sub-micrometer thick LN films and surface roughness below 0.5 nm., The development of high-quality commercial LNOI wafers has been crucial for advancing LNOI photonics.
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6265866

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article from the journal Nanomaterials (Basel), published November 6, 2018 (DOI: 10.3390/nano8110910), titled "Long Low-Loss-Lithium Niobate on Insulator Waveguides with Sub-Nanometer Surface Roughness." The paper, authored by researchers from the Shanghai Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics (Chinese Academy of Sciences) and East China Normal University, including corresponding author Ya Cheng, reports a novel technique for fabricating multi-centimeter-long lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) waveguides with record-low propagation loss.

Key results:
- Achieved propagation loss as low as 0.027 dB/cm in LNOI waveguides, an improvement over the previous state-of-the-art of 0.04 dB/cm.
- Surface roughness (Rq) of 0.452 nm measured via atomic force microscope.
- Fabricated a continuous 11-cm-long optical waveguide (femtosecond laser ablation took 90 minutes).
- Demonstrated a whispering-gallery ring resonator (160 μm diameter) with an intrinsic Q factor of 1.14 × 10^7, loaded Q factor of 5.70 × 10^6, and effective refractive index of 1.79.

Methodology: The fabrication technique involves (1) depositing a 600-nm chromium thin film on LNOI by magnetron sputtering, (2) patterning the Cr film into a hard mask using femtosecond laser ablation (~1 μm focused spot via 100× objective lens with NA 0.7), and (3) chemo-mechanical (CM) polishing to transfer the pattern to the LNOI, followed by an additional low-pressure CM polishing step to improve upper-surface smoothness. The approach avoids ion beam etching (FIB or electron beam writing), which inherently leaves residual sidewall roughness that is difficult to remove and has low throughput. The technique is compatible with optical and electron beam lithography and laser direct writing, enabling high-throughput manufacturing of large-scale LNOI photonic integrated circuits (PICs).

Key context: The paper notes that the measured loss is still one order of magnitude away from the theoretical limit (~10^-3 dB/cm) set by absorption in crystalline LN. Limitations are attributed to radiative loss in the ring resonator, surface contamination, absorptive defects from crystal growth, and residual roughness from CM polishing. The authors suggest that optical lithography (achieving sub-micron or 100-nm patterning) could enable narrower single-mode waveguides for devices such as Mach-Zehnder interferometers and polarization convertors, and that coating with fused silica could tune mode fields and reduce scattering loss. The method promotes fabrication efficiency and reduces manufacturing costs for LNOI PICs, applicable to optical communication and computation.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: [PDF] Ultra-low loss ridge waveguides on lithium niobate via argon ion ... - HAL ---
URL: https://hal.science/hal-03183505v1/file/oe-26-4-4421.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (published in Optics Express, Vol. 26, No. 4, February 19, 2018) presents a fabrication method for ultra-low loss ridge waveguides on lithium niobate-on-insulator (LNOI) using a two-step process: argon ion milling followed by gas clustered ion beam (GCIB) smoothening.

**Background & Motivation:**
- Lithium niobate has strong electro-optic effects (Pockels effect, sum frequency generation, optical rectification, spontaneous parametric down-conversion) and surface acoustic wave properties, making it valuable for integrated optics.
- Conventional Ti-diffusion or proton exchange methods create only weak index confinement, requiring large turning radii and millimeter-scale devices.
- Thin film single-crystal LNOI provides strong vertical index confinement (similar to SOI approach), but etched sidewalls from dry etching are typically rough, exacerbating propagation losses.
- Prior reported losses: 17 dB/cm (Guarino et al.), 5 dB/cm (Rabiei et al.), 0.5 dB/cm for Ti-indiffused ridge waveguides (Courjal et al.), compared to 0.086 dB/cm for industrial Ti-diffused waveguides.

**Methodology:**
- Z-cut LNOI wafer (700 nm thick lithium niobate) fabricated via crystal ion slicing and wafer bonding; waveguide widths varied from 1 μm to 7 μm.
- Refractive indices measured via prism coupling: n_o = 2.204 ± 0.004 and n_e = 2.155 ± 0.013 at 1539 nm.
- Fabrication steps: (1) dicing LNOI into 1.2 cm x 1 cm pieces, (2) 100 nm Cr deposition as hard mask, (3) 300 nm ma-N 2403 negative resist patterned via e-beam lithography with fixed beam moving stage technique, (4) Cr removal and argon ion milling of 700 nm lithium niobate, (5) resist/Cr removal, (6) end facet dicing and polishing with Ar focused ion beam, (7) characterization followed by GCIB smoothening.
- Argon ion milling: initial high-power milling at 7° off normal (17 nm/min, ~40 min for 680 nm), followed by low-power 3-min step at 60° off normal for intermediate smoothing. Inductively coupled plasma with fluorine was avoided because it reacted with sidewalls and redeposited lithium fluoride.
- GCIB: argon ion clusters (many nm in diameter) accelerated to bombard sidewalls, with monomer ions filtered out via analyzing magnet; samples mounted at an angle.

**Results:**
- SEM images showed clear sidewall smoothening after GCIB; AFM measured RMS roughness of ~8.3 nm (Rq) and 6.9 nm (Ra) on 800x800 nm scan region.
- Propagation losses measured using Fabry-Perot resonance method (1 pm resolution over 1.2 cm waveguide, 45 pm resonance spacing): best results were 0.268 dB/cm (TE, 7 μm waveguide) and 0.33 dB/cm (TE, 5 μm waveguide).
- TM losses were higher, especially at smaller widths, due to weaker confinement (birefringence ~0.08) and greater susceptibility to roughness.
- Results compared favorably to literature: etched rib waveguide (17.4 dB/cm, [5]), optical dicing (1.2 dB/cm TE, [22]), wet etched ridge (7 dB/cm TE, [20]), RIE + wet etching (55 dB/cm, [21]).
- Authors claim the lowest reported etched ridge waveguide losses: 0.33 dB/cm for a 5 μm waveguide with 700 nm deep etching.

**Conclusions:**
- The method yields notably improved propagation losses without significant additional fabrication steps and could be extended to other material systems.
- While under 1 dB/cm loss was achieved, there is room for improvement compared to commercial Ti-diffused waveguides (~0.086 dB/cm).
- Submicron waveguide dimensions cause low input coupling efficiency and higher total insertion loss.
- Authors believe LNOI is very promising for future integrated optics despite remaining engineering challenges.

**Funding:** Singapore National Research Foundation (NRF-CRP15-2015-01) and PHC Merlion program (3.03.15).
</summary>

"We have fabricated and characterized ultra-low loss waveguides with this technique, with propagation losses as low as 0.3 dB/cm at 1.55 μm."
</key_excerpts>
