**Femtosecond Laser Ablation Comparison (damage perspective)**

- A JPT technical article notes that nanosecond pulses produce stronger thermal effects (heat-affected zones, recast layers, burrs, microcracks, thermal deformation) while femtosecond lasers deliver energy before heat spreads ("cold" processing). A published comparison found nanosecond pulses induced a heat-affected zone of about 40 µm, while femtosecond processing produced no observable heat-affected zone within the study's observation limit. [15] (en.jptoe.com/about/newsroom/technical-information/nanosecond-vs-femtosecond-laser-ablation)

- A ScienceDirect topic overview of femtosecond lasers notes: femtosecond laser micromachining offers small heat-affected areas, high processing accuracy, and efficiency; nonlinear absorption occurs only at the focus, resulting in highly localized material ablation. A 2023 review (Jia-Xin Zheng et al., Optics & Laser Technology) on "Femtosecond laser with etching technology for micro-optical components" covers laser ablation (when energy significantly exceeds damage threshold) versus laser modification (near damage threshold, causing phase changes), and wet etching of materials including LiNbO₃, plus dry etching techniques (IBE, RIE, ICP) with reaction gases (SF₆, CF₄, CHF₃ for silicon-based materials; Cl₂/BCl₃ for sapphire; Ar for SiC). [16] (sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/femtosecond-laser)

- Chandra and Marla (JLMN-Journal of Laser Micro/Nanoengineering, Vol. 20, No. 1, 2025, DOI: 10.2961/jlmn.2025.01.2006) studied femtosecond laser micromachining (FLM) of glass in different ambient media. Key findings: FLM in KOH solution exhibited the best surface quality compared to HF, DI water, and ethyl alcohol; minimum surface roughness (Sa) of microchannels in KOH was 1.125 µm at 15 µJ (fluence 1.2 J/cm²) with a hatch distance of 5 µm; microcracks were observed in HF, DI water, and ethyl alcohol media — most prominent in ethyl alcohol; KOH produced defect-free microchannels with no haze band, no microcracks, and more uniform/straight profiles. (Note: this is glass, not LN, but is a comparative laser-vs-etchant study.) [17] (jlps.gr.jp/jlmn/uploads/24-043.pdf)

- Fang et al. (Crystals 13(2):309, 2023, DOI: 10.3390/cryst13020309), "Repair of Fused Silica Damage Using Selective Femtosecond Laser-Induced Etching," describe femtosecond laser-induced etching below the ablation threshold causing chemical restructuring (Si-O-Si bond angle of 144° decreases; material becomes amorphous and more reactive to etchants). Etch selectivity ratio between modified and unmodified areas can be as high as 1000:1; KOH has higher etching selectivity than HF; substrate etching rates were ~1 µm/h (KOH) and ~2 µm/h (HF). (Fused silica, not LN, but the femtosecond laser modification + selective etching mechanism is analogous.) [18] (mdpi.com/2073-4352/13/2/309)

**Waveguide type comparison (simulation)**

- Wang, Chen, and Hu (Crystals, 2018, 8(5), 191, DOI: 10.3390/cryst8050191), "Analysis of Waveguides on Lithium Niobate Thin Films," compared ridge waveguides (dry-etched), proton-exchange (PE) waveguides, and strip-loaded waveguides using full-vectorial finite difference method at 1.55 µm (x-cut LNOI, ordinary n=2.211, extraordinary n=2.138). Ridge waveguides: optical power in LN layer 85.6% (q-TE) and 82.5% (q-TM); low bending loss (10⁻⁵ dB/cm) at minimal radii of 15 µm (q-TE) and 20 µm (q-TM). PE waveguides showed bending loss decreasing with PE depth (34 dB/cm at D=0.2 µm vs. 10⁻¹¹ dB/cm at D=0.5 µm, both at 1 mm radius). [19] (mdpi.com/2073-4352/8/5/191)

**Femtosecond Laser Micromachining of LN Microresonators (Scientific Reports 2015)**

### (d) Device-Level Demonstrations in TFLN/LNOI and Bulk LN with Explicit Optical Performance After Etching

**Micro-ring Resonators — Intrinsic Q-Factors and Propagation Losses**

- **Q = 10⁷ / 2.7 dB/m (arXiv 1712.04479):** "Monolithic Ultrahigh-Q Lithium Niobate Microring Resonator" shows "microring resonators with a quality factor of 10⁷ and waveguides with propagation loss as low as 2.7 dB/m." [26] (arxiv.org/html/1712.04479v1)

- **Q = 4.04 × 10⁷ / 0.0091 dB/cm (Optics Express 2023):** Li et al., "Ultra-high Q lithium niobate microring monolithically..." (Optics Express 31(19):31556, 2023, cited by 26): "the intrinsic Q factor was determined as high as 4.04 × 10⁷, corresponding to a propagation loss of 0.0091 dB cm⁻¹, which is approximately 3 times lower" than prior work. [27] (opg.optica.org/abstract.cfm?uri=oe-31-19-31556)

- **Record Q = 29.32 million / 1.3 dB/m (Photonics Research 2024):** Harvard University (Lončar group, with Peking University and DRS Daylight Solutions), "Twenty-nine million intrinsic Q-factor monolithic microresonators on thin-film lithium niobate," Photonics Research, Vol. 12, No. 8, August 2024, DOI: 10.1364/PRJ.521172. Key details:
  - Fabrication: 600 nm-thick TFLN wafers with 4.7 µm buried silicon dioxide; EBL (700 nm HSQ resist, 1600 µC/cm² dose, multipass writing); ICP-RIE (~325 nm etch depth, ~0.6 nm/s etch rate) using argon gas; optimized dry etch split into two runs; devices undergo chemical cleaning (hot KOH, hot SC1, diluted HF, piranha) and annealing at 520°C in oxygen.
  - Device design: racetrack geometry with wide waveguide widths (3–5 µm) to reduce overlap between light and sidewall roughness, bending radius 200 µm.
  - Record: intrinsic Q of 29.32 million with loaded Q of 19.56 million, achieved with 4.5 µm width, 10 mm length, 0.6 µm coupling gap racetrack. Intrinsic and loaded linewidths were 6.4 MHz and 9.6 MHz, respectively. Corresponding ultra-low propagation loss of 1.3 dB/m.
  - Statistics: for 3 µm width devices, Q increased with length from 1 mm (avg 8.35 million) to 10 mm (avg 13.40 million); for 10 mm length, Q increased with width from 3 µm (avg 9.46 million) to 5 µm (avg 24.45 million). Reproducibility confirmed across two chips.
  - This is a significant advance over the previous dry-etched TFLN resonator record of 12 million Q, and brings TFLN within one order of magnitude of its theoretical material limit of 163 million Q.
  - Funding: DARPA, U.S. Navy, AFOSR, AFRL, NASA, NSF, ONR, NIH, National Research Foundation of Korea. [28] (nano-optics.seas.harvard.edu/sites/g/files/omnuum6446/files/prj-12-8-a63.pdf)

Microrings fabricated on pristine LN thin-film wafers thinned from LN bulk via chemo-mechanical etching, "avoiding ion slicing and ion etching processes." Record-high Q factor of up to 10⁸ at 1550 nm, "attributed to the ultra-smooth interface of the microrings and the absence of ion-induced lattice damage." Corresponds to ultra-low waveguide propagation loss of approximately 0.0034 dB/cm. The authors suggest these ultra-high Q microrings will enable integrated quantum light sources, frequency comb generation, and nonlinear optical processes. 109 Scopus citations.   - Resonant modulators: Bragg grating modulators on x-cut LNOI achieving Vπ·L = 0.67 V·cm with a compact 0.3 mm × 1.2 mm footprint; photonic crystal (PhC) modulators achieving 17.5 GHz bandwidth with a tiny 0.58 µm³ volume. [32] (mdpi.com/2079-4991/14/10/867)

- **PLACE-fabricated phase modulator (Optics Letters 2024):** Gao, Liang, Chen, Yu, Qi, Song, Liu, Liu, Fang, Qi, and Cheng (ECNU), "Compact low-half-wave-voltage thin film lithium niobate electro-optic phase modulator fabricated by photolithography-assisted chemo-mechanical etching (PLACE)," Optics Letters, Vol. 49, Issue 20, pp. 5783-5786, 15 October 2024, DOI: 10.1364/OL.538158. Dual-arm TFLN EO phase modulator: half-wave voltage ~3 V (doubling modulation compared to single-arm at same chip length), low sensitivity to 1510–1600 nm, low insertion loss of 2.8 dB, and generation of 29 sideband signals for optical frequency comb applications at 2W input microwave power. (PLACE = photolithography-assisted chemo-mechanical etching, an alternative to plasma etching.) [33] (pure.ecnu.edu.cn/en/publications/compact-low-half-wave-voltage-thin-film-lithium-niobate-electro-o)

- **Ansys simulation of TFLN phase modulator** (based on Mercante et al.): simulation gives constant VπL of 3.18 V-cm versus 3.8 V-cm DC half-wave voltage reported in the literature; x-cut LN with extraordinary permittivity 27.9 (x-axis) and ordinary permittivity 44.3 (y, z); extraordinary refractive index 2.14 and ordinary 2.21 at 1550 nm. [34] (optics.ansys.com/hc/en-us/articles/19435937674387)

- **UV thin-film lithium tantalate modulator (arXiv 2026):** "Thin-film lithium tantalate for ultraviolet integrated electro-optic modulator" reports the first integrated UV EO modulator on TFLT at 375 nm: record-low VπL of 85 mV·cm at 375 nm (and 0.12 V·cm at 448 nm), extinction ratio 22.7 dB, insertion loss 1.3 dB, Vπ of 4.2 V, footprint 1.16 mm with 200 µm modulation length and 1.5 µm electrode gap; LT waveguide at 375 nm has propagation loss of 7.2 dB/cm with 0.2 nm RMS surface roughness. Devices fabricated via EBL and wet chemical etching (citric acid/KOH/H2O2 mixture) on 300 nm-thick x-cut LT-on-insulator with 100 nm etch depth. (LT platform, relevant for comparison.) [35] (arxiv.org/html/2605.02758v1)

**PPLN Waveguide Second Harmonic Generation Efficiency**

- **Shallow-etched TFLN waveguides (Optics Express 2020):** Zhao et al., "Shallow-etched thin-film lithium niobate waveguides for..." Optics Express 28(13):19669, 2020, cited by 145: "We report a second-harmonic conversion efficiency of up to 939 %.W⁻¹ (length-normalized conversion efficiency 3757 %.W⁻¹.cm⁻²)." [36] (opg.optica.org/oe/abstract.cfm?uri=oe-28-13-19669)

- **Adapted-width PPLN waveguides (Micromachines 2024):** He, Liu, Lin, Chen, and Ma (Sun Yat-sen University), "Efficient Second-Harmonic Generation in Adapted-Width Waveguides Based on Periodically Poled Thin-Film Lithium Niobate," Micromachines 15(9):1145, 12 September 2024, DOI: 10.3390/mi15091145. Key points:
  - Nanophotonic TFLN waveguides achieve normalized conversion efficiency (NCE) more than 20 times higher than bulk LN waveguides, but power conversion efficiency is limited by inherent nanoscale thickness inhomogeneity of TFLN (for a 600 nm thick LN layer, a deviation of ±15 nm occurs during manufacturing).
  - Prior work by Chen et al. used adapted poling design to achieve ~10⁴ %W⁻¹ SHG efficiency.
  - Etched waveguide: peak SHG power conversion efficiency of 2.1 × 10⁴ %W⁻¹ (21,780 %W⁻¹ in simulation), using standard periodic poling with single period Λ = 4.20 µm for etched waveguides; waveguide length 21 mm composed of 420 sections (50 µm each); width varies from 1.54 µm to 1.66 µm (320 nm range for 30 nm thickness change); simulated transmission 95% for FF wave.
  - Loaded (polymer) waveguide using ARP6200 (500 nm thick) on TFLN achieves 6936 %W⁻¹ with poling period Λ = 5.05 µm; uniform waveguide width design only achieves 3724 %W⁻¹.
  - Design uses TE modes in X-cut TFLN exploiting d₃₃ = 27.4 pm/V; FF wave 1600 nm, SH 800 nm; waveguide parameters: etched depth h = 300 nm, sidewall angle θ = 75°, 2 µm SiO2 layer. [37] (mdpi.com/2072-666X/15/9/1145)

- **Thin-film PPLN for 2-µm pump (UCSB, IEEE 2016):** Chang, Volet, Li, Peters, and Bowers (UC Santa Barbara), "A thin-film PPLN waveguide for second-harmonic..." x-cut LNOI (700-nm LN film on 2-µm buried SiO2 from NANOLN) with SiN strip for lateral guiding; low-loss platform (<1 dB/cm for fundamental TE mode in telecom band); newly developed surface poling with multi-pulses of short duration (10 ms) achieving near 100% poling yield; poling period ~7.4 µm for 2-µm pump QPM; measured SH spectrum with pump at 2010.8 nm. Supported by DARPA MTO DODOS (HR0011-15-C-055). [38] (siliconphotonics.ece.ucsb.edu/sites/default/files/2017-06/C1007_0.pdf)

- **PPLT watt-level SHG (arXiv 2512.07968):** "Watt-level second harmonic generation in periodically poled thin-film lithium tantalate" (EPFL, Kippenberg group): 7 mm-long PPLT waveguides achieving SH output exceeding 1 W on-chip (1.065 W), off-chip above 0.5 W at 775 nm under 4.5 W pump at 1550 nm; measured SHG efficiency 107 %W⁻¹cm⁻² (lower than typical PPLN but sufficient due to higher damage threshold); no observable sample damage at watt-level operation. Fabrication: X-cut LiTaO3 chip (576 nm film, 4.7 µm SiO2), E-beam lithography, argon ion beam etching, and KOH wet etching for smooth sidewalls. PPLN can exceed 2000 %W⁻¹cm⁻² by comparison. [39] (arxiv.org/html/2512.07968v1)

- **PPLN/CPPLN theory (Physical Review A 2021):** Peng, Hong, and Li (South China University of Technology), Phys. Rev. A 104, 053503 (1 November 2021), present an effective nonlinear coupled mode coefficient model for SHG under QPM in PPLN thin film; propose chirped PPLN (CPPLN) thin film for broadband SHG of ultrashort laser pulses and broadband entangled photon generation. [40] (link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevA.104.053503)

**Other device-level context**

- **Waveguide simulation design (Applied Sciences 2023):** FDFD simulation determined optimal LN waveguide dimensions width 1.4 µm, etching depth 0.3 µm, single-mode at 1.5–1.6 µm, critical bend radius 50 µm and losses <0.001 dB/90°. [11]

- **Photorefraction management (arXiv 2601.15817):** In Ti:PPLN waveguides, high-temperature operation (above ~380 K) suppresses photorefraction; at cryogenic temperatures (7 K) a critical photorefraction threshold of ~18 mW pump power at ~960 nm was identified; "optical cleaning" with an auxiliary 532 nm green laser (1 mW) restored phase-matching spectrum, increasing generated power from 0.25 µW to 1.87 µW after 12 minutes; recovery only partial (persistent blue shift from 964.16 nm to 963.48 nm). Photorefraction origins involve one- and two-photon absorption on intrinsic (Nb antisites and Li vacancies) and extrinsic (iron impurities) defects, followed by ferroelectric photovoltaic effect and formation of stable charge distributions as (bound) polarons. [41] (arxiv.org/html/2601.15817v1)

---

### (e) Reported Demonstrations of Restoring Nonlinearity/Electro-Optic Coefficient After Etching via Annealing or Other Methods

**Annealing after femtosecond laser + FIB processing (Scientific Reports 2015)**

- Lin et al. (Scientific Reports 2015) demonstrated that thermal annealing at 500°C for 2 hours in air improved the Q factor of a femtosecond-laser/FIB-fabricated 55 µm LN resonator from 5.2 × 10⁴ (before annealing) to 1.6 × 10⁵ (after annealing) — a direct demonstration of post-processing annealing recovering optical performance after ion/laser damage. [20]

**Oxygen annealing after dry etch (Photonics Research 2024, Harvard)**

- The record 29.32-million-Q TFLN devices (Harvard) underwent chemical cleaning (hot KOH, hot SC1, diluted HF, piranha) and annealing at 520°C in oxygen after the optimized two-run argon ICP-RIE dry etch — explicitly linking post-etch annealing to record device performance. [28]

**Vapor Transport Equilibration (VTE) for Stoichiometry Restoration**

- Stanford work (Journal of Applied Physics, 2007; "Optical properties and ferroelectric engineering of vapor-transport-equilibrated...") describes VTE conversion of congruent lithium tantalate to near-stoichiometric: heated at 1360°C then 1100°C with two-phase LiTaO3/Li3TaO4 powder as Li2O source; coercive fields as low as 60 V/mm achieved (~50 ppm lithium deficiency, 350 times closer to stoichiometry than congruent); VTE process is surface-reaction-rate or effusion limited; saturated space-charge field reduced 100-fold in VLT vs. CLT (10±8 V/cm vs. 1270±300 V/cm); photorefraction-limited useful length ~17 cm for VLT vs. 0.13 cm for CLT; 532 nm absorption reduced to 0.04–0.12 %/cm vs. 0.28–0.4 %/cm; damage thresholds: congruent LN 2.3 J/cm², CLT 7.3 J/cm², VLT 7.3 J/cm² (12 ns pulses at 1064 nm); an uncoated 4 cm long, 8 µm period VLT device generated 10.5 W internal cw 532 nm SHG from 29 W internal 1064 nm pump with low-power normalized efficiency 0.4 %/(W cm). (This is for lithium tantalate, but demonstrates the VTE principle for stoichiometry restoration and property recovery.) [42] (web.stanford.edu/~rlbyer/PDF_AllPubs/2007/425.pdf)

- Zhang, Wang, Hua, and Pun (Journal of the American Ceramic Society, 2012, volume 95, pages 2798-2800, DOI: 10.1111/J.1551-2916.2012.05381.X) studied Li-rich VTE temperature dependence of surface composition of initially congruent LiNbO3: the VTE-induced surface Li2O-content increase follows the traditional Arrhenius law with a surface Li2O-content alteration constant of (614 ± 136)/(91 ± 10) mol% and an activation energy of (0.76 ± 0.05)/(0.53 ± 0.03) eV for X/Z-cut crystals (1-mm-thick plates). [43] (semanticscholar.org/paper/Li-Rich-Vapor-Transport-Equilibration-Temperature-Zhang-Wang/d6e2dccbe306171c1d8c33b2c8ba3d8fce39efaa)

**Li-rich ambient annealing for amorphous deposited LN films (Patent WO2002075444A1)**

- The Wisconsin Alumni Research Foundation patent WO2002075444A1 (inventors Mccaughan, Kuech, Saulys, Joshkin, Chowdhury, Staus) describes depositing amorphous lithium niobate films (CVD at pressures 0.1 mm Hg to atmospheric, temperatures at or below ~600°C), etching them easily with conventional wet/dry etchants (4% aqueous HF etches at >5 µm/min; 25% HF at ~5 µm/min), then annealing at 900°C–1100°C for 0.5–6 hours to crystallize the film "in a lithium-rich environment, e.g., powdered LiNbO3." After annealing, XRD, TEM, and selected area diffraction confirmed single-crystal epitaxial quality with no interface defects or second-phase segregation. The patent notes that crystalline LiNbO3 is very chemically inert (50% aqueous HF has negligible effect; RIE with CCl2F2:Ar:O2 gives only ~3 µm/h etch rates). It also describes trench-based traveling wave modulators: trenches (2-10 µm wide, at least 5 µm deep, at least 2 µm from electrodes) improve microwave/optical field overlap (from ~0.7 to ~1.2, ~50% improvement) and enable operation at 40 Gb/s with ±4.5V drive; optimized trench geometry achieves V3dB of 4.1V. [44] (patents.google.com/patent/WO2002075444A1/en)

**Defect structures as a function of ion irradiation and annealing in LiNbO3**

- A paper titled "Defect structures as a function of ion irradiation and annealing in LiNbO3" was sought (Thin Solid Films, S0040609023000494) but the ScienceDirect URL was broken/not found; only the citation title is available. [45] (sciencedirect.com/science/article/am/pii/S0040609023000494)

---

### Additional Context: LNOI Platform, Material Properties, and Fabrication Background

- **LNOI basics (Applied Sciences 2023):** LNOI enables high-contrast optical waveguides with small curvature radii (100 µm or less) and high integration density (50–100 basic elements per cm²). Two European LNOI-based platforms (LOLIPOP and ELENA) were launched in 2022. [11]

- **LN material properties (IOP book chapter by Maxim Sumets, 2024, DOI: 10.1088/978-0-7503-6305-1ch1):** LN belongs to R3c space group; rhombohedral unit cell (a = 5.4944 Å, α = 55°52′) or hexagonal (aH = 5.1483 Å, cH = 13.8631 Å, c/a = 2.693); stoichiometric (R = Li/Nb = 1) vs. congruent (R = 0.946); Curie temperature 1210 °C; density of congruent LN 4.648 g cm⁻³; optically transparent from 0.35 to 5 µm; optical bandgap 3.57–4.7 eV; refractive indices no = 2.289, ne = 2.201 at 633 nm; can be etched by boiling (110 °C) in HF:HNO3 (1:2); RIE using fluorine/chlorine-based plasmas (CF4, CCl2F2, CHF3). For waveguides, films must be ~400 nm thick to achieve ≤1 dB cm⁻¹ leakage on high-refractive-index substrates; roughness of ~1 nm is critical, correlating at ~1% of film thickness. [46] (iopscience.iop.org/book/mono/978-0-7503-6305-1/chapter/bk978-0-7503-6305-1ch1)

- **LNOI wafer fabrication (Nanomaterials 2024 review):** LNOI wafers are fabricated using "Smart-Cut" technology (similar to SOI), involving He+ or H+ ion implantation, wafer bonding, thermal annealing, and chemical mechanical polishing (CMP). [32]

- **IEEE Spectrum context (2018):** Lithium niobate is hard, chemically inert, and not amenable to chemical etching; previous techniques (ion diffusion, proton exchange) produced too-low optical-index contrast; hybrid silicon-LN approaches were impractical due to insufficient light coupling; thin-film substrates are commercially available, "meaning the technological steps are ready for standardization." [30]

- **Dry etching chemistry context (Mi-Net, Applied Sciences, COL metasurface paper):** SF6/Ar and fluorine-based chemistries produce non-volatile LiF and NbFx byproducts that require physical sputtering (high bias) to remove; SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O) wet treatment removes LiF byproduct; Ar-only physical etching (e.g., argon-based RIE, argon ion milling) avoids LiF formation and is widely used for lowest optical loss. [13][11][7]

You are a research supervisor. Your job is to conduct research by calling the "ConductResearch" tool. For context, today's date is Mon Aug 24, 2026.

<Task>
Your focus is to call the "ConductResearch" tool to conduct research against the overall research question passed in by the user. 
When you are completely satisfied with the research findings returned from the tool calls, then you should call the "ResearchComplete" tool to indicate that you are done with your research.
</Task>

<Available Tools>
You have access to three main tools:
1. **ConductResearch**: Delegate research tasks to specialized sub-agents
2. **ResearchComplete**: Indicate that research is complete
3. **think_tool**: For reflection and strategic planning during research

**CRITICAL: Use think_tool before calling ConductResearch to plan your approach, and after each ConductResearch to assess progress. Do not call think_tool with any other tools in parallel.**
</Available Tools>

<Instructions>
Think like a research manager with limited time and resources. Follow these steps:

1. **Read the question carefully** - What specific information does the user need?
2. **Decide how to delegate the research** - Carefully consider the question and decide how to delegate the research. Are there multiple independent directions that can be explored simultaneously?
3. **After each call to ConductResearch, pause and assess** - Do I have enough to answer? What's still missing?
</Instructions>

<Hard Limits>
**Task Delegation Budgets** (Prevent excessive delegation):
- **Bias towards single agent** - Use single agent for simplicity unless the user request has clear opportunity for parallelization
- **Stop when you can answer confidently** - Don't keep delegating research for perfection
- **Limit tool calls** - Always stop after 3 tool calls to ConductResearch and think_tool if you cannot find the right sources

**Maximum 3 parallel agents per iteration**
</Hard Limits>

<Show Your Thinking>
Before you call ConductResearch tool call, use think_tool to plan your approach:
- Can the task be broken down into smaller sub-tasks?

After each ConductResearch tool call, use think_tool to analyze the results:
- What key information did I find?
- What's missing?
- Do I have enough to answer the question comprehensively?
- Should I delegate more research or call ResearchComplete?
</Show Your Thinking>

<Scaling Rules>
**Simple fact-finding, lists, and rankings** can use a single sub-agent:
- *Example*: List the top 10 coffee shops in San Francisco → Use 1 sub-agent

**Comparisons presented in the user request** can use a sub-agent for each element of the comparison:
- *Example*: Compare OpenAI vs. Anthropic vs. DeepMind approaches to AI safety → Use 3 sub-agents
- Delegate clear, distinct, non-overlapping subtopics

**Important Reminders:**
- Each ConductResearch call spawns a dedicated research agent for that specific topic
- A separate agent will write the final report - you just need to gather information
- When calling ConductResearch, provide complete standalone instructions - sub-agents can't see other agents' work
- Do NOT use acronyms or abbreviations in your research questions, be very clear and specific
</Scaling Rules>

I am working on lithium niobate (LN)-based nonlinear photonics and need to understand the possible ways to mitigate the material damage of LN that occurs after plasma etching. 

Please research methods, techniques, and process optimizations for reducing or repairing plasma-etch-induced damage (e.g., surface roughness, stoichiometric changes, lattice damage, defect formation, reduced optical performance/nonlinearity, sidewall damage) in lithium niobate photonic devices. The research should cover both ex-situ treatments and in-situ process adjustments, including but not limited to: post-etch annealing (thermal, RTA, furnace), wet chemical etching/cleaning (e.g., acid or base solutions), surface passivation or cladding, plasma chemistry parameter optimization (gas chemistry, bias power, ICP/RF power, pressure, temperature), etch mask selection, alternative etch processes (e.g., ion beam etching, reactive ion etching, inductively coupled plasma RIE, femtosecond laser ablation), and any published demonstrations of recovering or preserving optical quality and electro-optic/nonlinear performance in thin-film LN (TFLN) devices.

Since the specific LN platform (X-cut vs Z-cut, thin-film TFLN vs bulk, specific device type like waveguides, ring resonators, or modulators) and the specific etch chemistry were not specified, treat these as flexible/open-ended and cover the range of common approaches. Prioritize original peer-reviewed journal publications and official/conference sources rather than survey papers or secondary summaries. Include details on reported quantitative outcomes (e.g., Q-factor recovery, propagation loss reduction, surface roughness values) where available.

Be exhaustive and cite each study.

# Ex-Situ Post-Etch Treatments for Plasma-Etch-Induced Damage Repair in Lithium Niobate Photonic Devices

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

The following web searches were performed (two concurrent Tavily searches per round, 3 rounds):

**Round 1:**
- "post-etch annealing lithium niobate photonic waveguide damage recovery"
- "rapid thermal annealing lithium niobate thin film LNOI etch damage optical loss"
- "plasma etch damage lithium niobate annealing recovery crystallinity stoichiometry"
- "wet chemical etching lithium niobate damaged layer hydrofluoric acid smoothing sidewall"
- "KOH TMAH wet etch lithium niobate waveguide smooth sidewall roughness"
- "post-etch wet cleaning lithium niobate remove amorphous redeposition layer"

**Round 2:**
- "rapid thermal annealing lithium niobate thin film oxygen atmosphere Q factor recovery propagation loss"
- "annealing oxygen argon lithium niobate LNOI waveguide loss recovery stoichiometry lithium loss"
- "HF wet etching lithium niobate sidewall smoothing TFLN photonic waveguide"
- "TMAH wet etch lithium niobate surface roughness reduction waveguide"
- "Al2O3 HfO2 cladding lithium niobate waveguide passivation loss reduction"
- "SiO2 cladding annealing lithium niobate microring Q factor high temperature"

**Round 3:**
- "post-etch annealing lithium niobate thin film oxygen 300C 400C microring Q factor loss recovery arXiv"
- "HF wet etch lithium niobate remove damaged layer sidewall roughness RMS nm waveguide"
- "furnace annealing oxygen ambient lithium niobate thin film waveguide stoichiometry Li outdiffusion loss"
- "KOH wet etching lithium niobate thin film ridge waveguide smooth sidewall loss dB/cm"
- "SiO2 cladding PECVD lithium niobate microring Q factor reduce loss"
- "atomic layer etching damage lithium niobate surface roughness recovery annealing"

**Round 4:**
- "annealing 300C 400C lithium niobate thin film waveguide Q factor improvement oxygen annealing journal"
- "HF hydrofluoric acid wet etch lithium niobate thin film remove etch damage sidewall roughness"
- "rapid thermal annealing RTA lithium niobate lattice damage recovery implantation photonic"
- "lithium niobate thin film etch damage recovery annealing propagation loss before after dB/cm"
- "passivation layer cladding lithium niobate etched waveguide surface damage mitigation SiO2 ALD"
- "wet chemical cleaning lithium niobate post plasma etch residue removal SC1 BOE HF"

**Round 5:**
- "lithium niobate etching annealing oxygen vacuum argon ambient comparison optical loss LNOI"
- "TMAH potassium hydroxide sodium hydroxide etch lithium niobate surface roughness photonic device"
- "HfO2 Al2O3 ALD coating lithium niobate waveguide sidewall protection Q factor"
- "lithium niobate microring annealed 500C oxygen Q factor 10 million propagation loss dB/m dry etch"
- "ion beam etching lithium niobate damaged layer wet etch remove amorphous recovery"
- "lithium niobate thin film photonic annealing restoration electro-optic coefficient nonlinearity"

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

---

### PART A: Post-Etch Thermal Annealing (RTA, Furnace, and Ambient Variations)

#### A.1 Slow-Heating Annealing to Repair Electron-Beam Lithography (EBL) Damage

Shi et al. (Optical Materials, Vol. 149, March 2024, Article 115049, "Reduced material loss caused by Electron Beam Lithography in thin-film lithium niobate through post-process annealing") demonstrated that high-energy electron beams (above 100 keV) used in EBL penetrate the TFLN surface and accumulate within the LN, causing damage through radiolysis, knock-on displacement, and electrostatic charging, leading to increased material absorption loss [1][2].

Key quantitative results:
- A new **slow-heating post-process annealing** method was designed to repair fabrication damage, reducing waveguide loss by approximately **50%** and increasing the intrinsic Q-factor of micro-ring resonators by around **100%**.
- Achieved intrinsic Q-factor (Q_int) as high as **3.93 × 10⁶** in X-cut TFLN micro-ring resonators, corresponding to waveguide loss of approximately **0.1 dB/cm** [1][2].
- Devices: 600 nm thick X-cut TFLN single-crystal film prepared via Smart Cut from NanoLN, with a 4.7 μm thick SiO2 bonding layer and 500 μm thick Si substrate; all-pass micro-ring resonators with bending radius r=300 μm, waveguide widths from 1.1 μm to 2.0 μm, and coupling gaps from 0.4 μm to 0.65 μm [1].
- Context: Congruent LN has lithium content of approximately 48.6%, causing lattice defects that make it sensitive to fabrication processes [1].
- The study identified EBL as a key contributor to processing-induced damage that had previously remained unclear [2].

#### A.2 High-Temperature Annealing After Chemo-Mechanical Etching (PLACE Process)

Li, Guan, Lin, Gao, Wang, Qiao, Deng, and Cheng (arXiv:2306.10504, June 2023; published in Optics Express, Vol. 31, Issue 19, pp. 31556–31562, Sept 11, 2023, PMID 37710670) fabricated ultra-high-Q lithium niobate microrings via photolithography-assisted chemo-mechanical etching (PLACE) [10][11][12].

Key quantitative results:
- **High-temperature annealing: 450°C for 2 hours in air** was carried out to restore lattice damage caused by ion implantation during the ion-slicing step, improving loaded Q factors by **4–5 times** [11].
- After annealing, the highest loaded Q factor reached **4.29 × 10⁶** and the intrinsic Q factor reached **4.04 × 10⁷**, corresponding to an ultra-low propagation loss of **less than 1 dB/m (0.0091 dB/cm)** — approximately 3 times better than previously reported best values on the ion-slicing TFLN platform [10][11][12].
- Coupling gap of 3.8 μm achieved (improved from previous best of 4.8 μm), coupling efficiency 37% (vs ~10% previously) [11].
- Fabrication stack: undoped Z-cut TFLN wafer (700 nm TFLN, 2000 nm SiO₂, 500 μm LN substrate); 600 nm Cr film mask via magnetron sputtering; femtosecond laser direct writing; CMP pattern transfer; Cr mask removal via wet chemical etching; secondary CMP; then high-temperature annealing [11].
- Table of loaded Q improvements across resonant wavelengths (1556.6 nm: 1.02→4.29 ×10⁶; 1548.2 nm: 0.91→3.65 ×10⁶; 1560.0 nm: 0.58→2.27 ×10⁶; 1531.0 nm: 0.57→2.35 ×10⁶; 1549.0 nm: 1.01→4.83 ×10⁶; 1524.8 nm: 0.68→3.86 ×10⁶; 1540.3 nm: 0.51→2.40 ×10⁶) [11].
- Microring: 400 μm diameter, top width 2.35 μm (thinned to 1.75 μm), thickness 645.4 nm, wedge angle 10°; measurements at 1550 nm with ~5 µW pump power [11].

#### A.3 Oxygen Annealing at 520°C After Dry Etching (Wafer-Scale LNOI)

A wafer-scale fabrication study from Friedrich Schiller University Jena and Fraunhofer IOF (arXiv:2407.09208, July 2024) reports on low-loss LNOI waveguides fabricated with a chemically amplified resist (CAR) and dry etching [14].

Key quantitative results:
- Process: EBL with FEP 171 CAR (dose 10 µC/cm², vs ~5000 µC/cm² for HSQ), 120-nm Cr hard mask (ion beam deposition), pattern transfer via RIE, LN etching via ICP-RIE with CHF3 gas, then **O2 annealing at 520°C for 2 hours to improve crystallinity**, followed by **SiO2 cladding via PECVD** [14].
- Wafers: 4-inch, 600-nm-thick LN on 2-µm SiO2 on 525-µm Si handling layer [14].
- Loaded quality factor averaged **(1.34 ± 0.24) × 10⁶** for TE mode [14].
- Total racetrack resonator propagation loss: **~5 dB/m (TE mode)** and **~8 dB/m (TM mode)**; coupling loss ~27 dB/m [14].
- Straight waveguide propagation loss calculated as **~2 dB/m (0.02 dB/cm)**, with potential to be below 1 dB/m; bend loss 11.37 ± 3.37 dB/m [14].
- The key challenge addressed was preventing re-deposition of amorphous material on nanostructures during etching, solved by optimizing ICP-RIE parameters (chamber pressure and DC bias) [14].
- Comparison: chemo-mechanical polishing methods achieve ~1 dB/m; HSQ-based dry etching achieves 2.7 dB/m but requires prohibitively high doses for wafer-scale production; previous CAR-based methods with intermediate masks achieved ~20 dB/m [14].

#### A.4 Rapid Thermal Annealing (RTA) — General Principles and LN-Specific Data

**General RTA principles** (IEEE Technology Navigator): RTA heats wafers to temperatures typically between 900 and 1,150°C for seconds to a few minutes using high-intensity radiant energy sources (tungsten-halogen lamps emitting in the near-infrared), then cools rapidly. Heating rates are typically 20 to 200°C per second. RTA is used to activate implanted dopants, repair lattice damage from ion implantation, and achieve structural transformations while minimizing thermal budget [47].

**RTA of Er-implanted LiNbO₃** (Fleuster, Buchal, Snoeks, Polman — Applied Physics Letters, Vol. 65, No. 2, 11 July 1994): X-cut LiNbO₃ single crystals were implanted at room temperature with 3.5-MeV Er ions at fluences from 5×10¹⁵ to 3×10¹⁶ ions/cm² [31].
- Samples were annealed either in an RTA (heating rates ~100°C/s, **dry oxygen**) or in a quartz tube furnace (initial heating rate ~10°C/s, **wet oxygen**) at **1060°C** [31].
- **Using RTA at a heating rate of about 100°C/s, no columns are formed, and an amazingly short annealing time of 1 min at 1060°C is sufficient to cause perfect epitaxial recrystallization** [31].
- Low heating rates (~10°C/s) result in columnar regrowth requiring 8-hour anneals for complete dissolution of grain boundaries; rapid heating (~100°C/s) allows perfect crystal restoration in just 1 minute at 1060°C without grain boundaries [31].
- RBS/channeling showed the RTA-annealed sample achieved a minimum yield of only **(2.3±0.2)%**, identical to virgin crystal values, while slow-heated samples showed significantly higher channeling yields due to grain boundaries [31].
- Perfect lattice recovery was achieved up to a fluence of 2.0×10¹⁶ Er/cm²; the maximum concentration of optically active Er ions is 0.18 at.% (equilibrium solubility 0.125 at.% at 1060°C); PL lifetime (2.79±0.05) ms independent of Er fluence; PL spectra identical between RTA and furnace annealing [31].
- The rapid annealing minimizes diffusion broadening of the Er profile (as-implanted peak at 0.78 μm depth, 0.11 at.%) [31].

**RTA in ultrafast laser waveguide writing in LiNbO₃** (Nejadmalayeri & Herman — Optics Express, Vol. 15, Issue 17, pp. 10842–54, Aug 20, 2007, PMID 19547441): First bulk modification of lithium niobate using high repetition rate ultrashort laser pulses (fiber-based ultrafast laser, 0.1 to 1.5 MHz repetition rates) [32].
- At repetition rates of 250 kHz and higher, tracks exhibited a cladding-like modification zone extending outside the main laser interaction volume, providing concrete evidence of **heat accumulation and thermal annealing effects** [32].
- A higher repetition rate of 700 kHz yielded smooth waveguides with low propagation loss of **0.6 dB/cm**, matching the best reported value at that time, with a 50-fold faster writing speed; circularly polarized 600 fs stretched pulses produced nearly circular mode profiles guiding light in the 1300 nm telecom band [32].

**RTA in crystal ion-slicing** (US Patent US6540827B1, "Slicing of single-crystal films using ion implantation," Columbia University; inventors Levy, Osgood Jr., Radojevic): The patent discloses methods for detaching thin single-crystal films (including LiNbO₃) via ion implantation followed by chemical etching and/or rapid thermal annealing [30].
- RTA-based detachment: implant ions to form a damage layer, then subject the crystal to a rapid temperature increase (e.g., room temperature to 750–800°C within 60 seconds, held ~30 seconds) to cause thermally induced "snap-off" detachment [30].
- **RTA (e.g., 40 seconds at 700°C in forming gas of 5% H₂/95% N₂) repairs residual lattice damage and reduces surface roughening**; temperatures above 800°C reduce etch rate [30].
- LiNbO₃ films detached using 5% diluted hydrofluoric acid at room temperature (up to 24 hours for 1 mm² sample) [30].
- **Thin LiNbO₃ films up to 5×5 mm² have been fabricated; material properties slightly altered from bulk but restorable by annealing ~6 hours at ≥400°C** [30].
- For Z-cut LiNbO₃: implantation dosage 5×10¹⁶ cm⁻²; X-cut LiNbO₃ requires lower dosage (~2–3×10¹⁶ cm⁻²); etch selectivity (sacrificial layer vs. top surface) exceeds 10³ [30].

#### A.5 Ion-Irradiation Defect Evolution with Annealing

Lang, Beechem, McDonald, Friedmann, Olsson, Stevens, Clark, and Hattar (Thin Solid Films, Vol. 768, Article 139719, 1 March 2023, "Defect structures as a function of ion irradiation and annealing in LiNbO3") systematically examined defect structures in lithium niobate as a function of ion irradiation (H, He, N; 150 keV to 2 MeV; fluences 1×10¹² to 1×10¹⁸ ions/cm²) and post-irradiation heat treatment from 250 to 750°C [21].
- **Defect formation suitable for fracture-based processes (ion slicing) can be achieved with He ion implantation using a fluence of 1×10¹⁸ ions/cm² followed by heat treatment at 250 or 500°C** [21].
- N ion implantation causes significantly more displacement damage than other species; He implantation can cause amorphization through formation of He "bubbles" that coalesce under annealing [21].
- Samples: 128° Y-cut LiNbO₃ wafers (100 mm diameter, 350 µm thick, Roditi International), diced into ~1 cm² coupons [21].

#### A.6 Annealing Context from Historical Ti-Diffused Waveguide Work

Armenise (IEE Proceedings J Optoelectronics, 1988, "Fabrication techniques of lithium niobate waveguides") reviews fabrication techniques including out-diffusion of lithium oxide, in-diffusion of metals, ion exchange, proton exchange, and ion implantation [45].
- **High-quality optical waveguides on lithium niobate can be produced by Ti in-diffusion in a dry O₂ atmosphere at temperatures above 1000°C for long diffusion times (>10h)** [45].
- Ti in-diffusion in dry O₂ above 1000°C reduces optical losses to below 1 dB/cm and improves resistance to optical damage; out-diffusion of lithium oxide can create unwanted surface guiding layers; the ideal LiNbO₃ composition for low-loss waveguides is often not congruent at 48.6 mole% Li₂O [45].

#### A.7 High-Temperature Annealing and Ultimate Q-Factor Records (Harvard)

Harvard University (Lončar group), "Twenty-nine million intrinsic Q-factor monolithic microresonators on thin film lithium niobate" (Photonics Research, Vol. 12, No. 8, August 2024, DOI: 10.1364/PRJ.521172): [35]
- Record-high intrinsic Q factor of **29.32 million**, corresponding to ultra-low propagation loss of **1.3 dB/m**; previous dry-etched TFLN record was 12 million Q; theoretical material limit is 163 million Q [35].
- Fabrication: 600 nm-thick TFLN wafers with 4.7 μm buried SiO₂; EBL (700 nm HSQ resist, 1600 µC/cm² dose, multipass writing); ICP-RIE with argon gas (approximately 325 nm etch depth, ~0.6 nm/s etch rate, optimized dry etch split into two runs) [35].
- **Devices undergo chemical cleaning (hot KOH, hot SC1, diluted HF, piranha) and annealing at 520°C in oxygen** [35].
- Racetrack geometry with wide waveguide widths (3–5 μm) to reduce overlap between light and sidewall roughness; bending radius 200 μm [35].
- Highest Q: intrinsic Q 29.32 million with loaded Q 19.56 million (4.5 μm width, 10 mm length, 0.6 μm coupling gap); intrinsic and loaded linewidths 6.4 MHz and 9.6 MHz [35].
- Statistical analysis: for 3 μm width devices, Q increased with length from 1 mm (avg 8.35 million) to 10 mm (avg 13.40 million); for 10 mm length devices, Q increased with width from 3 μm (avg 9.46 million) to 5 μm (avg 24.45 million) [35].

**Ultra-high Q microring above 10⁸**: arXiv:2106.14407 reports a lithium niobate microring resonator achieving an ultra-high quality factor exceeding **10⁸** (6 pages, 3 figures) [13].

#### A.8 Annealing in the Context of Ion-Slicing/TFLN Manufacturing

The Materials (2025) review "Advanced Crystallization Methods for Thin-Film Lithium Niobate and Its Device Applications" (Yang, Wei, Tang, Cao, Chen; Materials, Vol. 18, Issue 5, Article 951, DOI: 10.3390/ma18050951, published Feb 21, 2025) [8][9]:
- LiNbO₃ is a trigonal ferroelectric material (3m point group, R3c space group, ilmenite-type ABO₃ structure) with spontaneous polarization of 50 μC/cm² along the c-axis, Curie temperature ~1210°C, electro-optic coefficient r33 ~30.8 pm/V [8][9].
- Smartcut technology (ion implantation + bonding) produces single-crystal films widely used in commercial devices; the review notes single-crystal thin-film preparation via Smartcut is relatively mature, but epitaxial films (CVD, MBE, PLD, magnetron sputtering) are being developed to reduce costs [8][9].
- MBE requires high substrate temperatures (800–1050°C) which can cause Li volatilization; magnetron sputtering deposits at 380–550°C; Nb-rich TFLN exhibits third-order nonlinear refractive index γ ≈ 10⁻¹¹ cm²/W and absorption coefficient β ≈ 10⁻⁷ cm/W [8][9].

The epitaxy review by Zivasatienraj, Tellekamp, and Doolittle (Crystals, 2021) notes that the commercial smart-cut LN process "requires high-temperature annealing" and has limitations: minimum thickness >300 nm, limited to <few microns due to implant energies [55]. The review also notes that lithium has enormous vapor pressure and readily forms oxides, while niobium has negligible vapor pressure — a key challenge for stoichiometry control [55].

#### A.9 Annealing Effects on Surface Roughness and Stoichiometry — Summary of Known Mechanisms

- Congruent LN has ~48.6% Li content; lattice defects make it sensitive to fabrication processes [1].
- High-temperature annealing (450°C for 2 h in air) restored lattice damage from ion implantation in PLACE-fabricated devices, improving loaded Q by 4–5× [11].
- O2 annealing at 520°C for 2 hours was used to improve crystallinity in wafer-scale LNOI fabrication [14].
- Annealing at 520°C in oxygen was part of the Harvard record-Q process, together with chemical cleaning (hot KOH, hot SC1, diluted HF, piranha) [35].
- Annealing ~6 hours at ≥400°C restores material properties of ion-sliced thin LiNbO₃ films that were slightly altered from bulk [30].
- RTA at 1060°C for 1 min in dry oxygen achieved perfect epitaxial regrowth of amorphized Er-implanted LiNbO₃ with minimum channeling yield of (2.3±0.2)%, identical to virgin crystal [31].
- Ti in-diffusion at >1000°C in dry O₂ for >10h yields losses below 1 dB/cm [45].

---

### PART B: Wet Chemical Etching and Wet Cleaning Treatments After Plasma Etching

#### B.1 Redeposition Removal and Cleaning (SC-1 / RCA-1a, Piranha)

**NIST study** (Kumar, Klimov, Kuo — "Optimization of waveguide fabrication processes in lithium-niobate-on-insulator platform," PMC11194688 / AIP Advances, 2024) provides the most detailed quantitative cleaning data [4]:
- LNOI wafers (700 nm x-cut film, 2 μm SiO2, 525 μm Si substrate from NANOLN) diced into 10×10 mm² chips; cleaned with piranha solution (H2SO4:H2O2 = 3:1) then standard RCA process [4].
- LN etching: Oxford PlasmaLab 100 ICP RIE with Ar gas; ICP power 1500 W, pressure 5 mTorr, Ar flow 20 sccm, temperature 5°C; etch performed in 1-minute segments with 5-minute cooldown periods to prevent thermal damage [4].
- **Redeposition removal via RCA-1a solution (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O = 2:2:1) heated to 85°C** [4].
- **RCA-1a solution was superior to Piranha and RCA-1b** for redeposit cleaning [4].
- **Optimized cleaning: 15 minutes each at 0° and 90° boat orientations (30 min total). Prolonged cleaning (beyond 30 min) caused chipping and peeling of WGs. Cleaning for 24 hours changed WG geometry (sidewall angles became asymmetric, film thickness reduced from 700 nm to ~630 nm). Properly cleaned samples had equal sidewall angles of ~70°** [4].
- RF power optimization: RF power varied from 50 W to 500 W; etch rate ranged from 50 nm/min (50 W) to 107 nm/min (500 W). At low RF power (~50 W), sidewalls fully enveloped by redeposit; at 300 W, redeposit completely eliminated from sidewalls; above 300 W, line-edge roughness transferred causing striations and WG damage. Optimal RF power range: 100–200 W [4].
- Mask comparison: soft (resist) mask produced striated sidewall defects; Cr hard mask produced granular features (due to ~55 nm polycrystalline grain size); SiO2 mask produced striations and "trenching" at base of sidewalls (charge buildup on insulating materials) [4].
- Final devices (RF 150 W, ICP 1500 W, 5 mTorr, 20 sccm Ar, 5°C, 30 min cleaning): top width 600 nm, sidewall angle 70°, rib height 350 nm over 350 nm slab, single-mode at 1550 nm; total insertion loss -10.5 ± 0.6 dB; upper-bound propagation loss ~2 dB/cm [4].

#### B.2 Acid Solutions: HF, HF/HNO₃, and Related

**Poling-assisted HF wet etching** (Yu, Kang, Shen, Xue, Wan, Zou, Chen, Lu — Optics Letters, Vol. 49, No. 4, pp. 854, Feb 2024, DOI: 10.1364/OL.515879): First demonstration of z-cut TFLN microdisks using poling-assisted HF wet etching [24][25].
- High-fidelity ferroelectric domain poling of TFLN enables precise pattern control of ferroelectric domains; intense electric fields induce domain inversion in TFLN with a designed microdisk pattern; **an HF solution is subsequently utilized to transfer the inverted domain pattern to the TFLN layer with the selective etching of −z LN, ultimately revealing the microdisks** [24][25].
- 6 citations, 36 references [25].

**HF/HNO₃ deep wet etching of bulk LN** (Randles, RIT Master's thesis, 2002, "Deep structures wet etched into lithium niobate using a physical mask"): [44]
- Used a chrome gold mask and a solution of hydrofluoric acid and nitric acid at **90°C** to etch LiNbO₃ [44].
- **Achieves an etch rate of 50 micrometers per hour on the -z face and 250 nm per hour on the +z face** [44].
- LiNbO₃ described as optically clear (350 nm to 5 micrometer wavelength), piezoelectric, inert to most reactants, high Curie temperature [44].

**HF etching for crystal ion-slicing detachment** (US6540827B1): LiNbO₃ films detached using 5% diluted hydrofluoric acid at room temperature (up to 24 hours for 1 mm² sample); etch selectivity of damage layer vs. top surface exceeds 10³ [30].

**Ion Beam Enhanced Etching (IBEE)** (reviewed in Chinese Optics Letters 2024 photonic crystal review): Uses ion irradiation-induced defects and **HF wet etching**; achieves 90° sidewalls and high aspect ratios, though requires the optical axis parallel to the waveguide direction [7].

**Diluted HF in Harvard cleaning sequence**: Devices undergo chemical cleaning including **diluted HF** and piranha before annealing at 520°C in oxygen [35].

**Aqua regia / HCl / H2SO4**: The NIST study used piranha solution (H2SO4:H2O2 = 3:1) for initial cleaning [4]. The Nanomaterials 2023 study (Shen et al.) used acid cleaning (HCl:H2O, 1:3) before metallization [43]. The proton substitution dry-etch study (Aryal et al. 2022) used piranha clean with H2SO4 and H2O2, then acetone, IPA, DI water [43].

#### B.3 Base Solutions: KOH, NaOH, SC-1, TMAH

**Advanced Etching Techniques of LiNbO₃ Nanodevices** (Shen, Hu, Dai, Yu, Tan, Sun, Jiang, Jiang — Nanomaterials, Vol. 13, Issue 20, Article 2789, Oct 18, 2023, DOI: 10.3390/nano13202789) — the most comprehensive study of wet-chemical post-treatments for LN [22]:
- Background: prevailing etching techniques include dry etching (F-based and Cl-based gas), **wet etching (acid HF/HNO3 and alkaline SC-1/NaOH)**, FIB, and hybrid approaches. F-based gas creates LiF by-products that accumulate on sidewalls and reduce sidewall angles (60–75° angles in Kozlov 2023); Cl-based gas creates easily-removed LiCl by-products but has lower etch rates [22].
- Ten LNO samples (X-cut, 5 mol.% Mg-doped) with different masks (Cr, Ni, SiO2) and process combinations [22]:
  - **Sample 4 (SiO2 mask, high-temperature reduction treatment at 400°C in 10% H2 + Ar, then SC-1 wet etch): ~49 nm depth, asymmetric sidewalls (44° in +Z, 85° in −Z directions)** [22].
  - **Sample 5 (Cr mask, high-temp reduction + RIE): 11.5 nm/min, ~85° sidewall angle** [22].
  - **Sample 6 (Cr mask, RIE + high-temp reduction + wet etch): ~112 nm depth, inward concavity sidewall due to Cr-LNO alloying** [22].
  - **Sample 7 (Cr mask, RIE + Al layer + annealing + wet etch): ~115 nm depth, perfect 90° sidewall angle — the optimized hybrid process that preserves ferroelectric properties** [22].
- RIE dry etch rates: 10 nm/min (Cr mask, ~60° sidewall, 3:1 selectivity); 11 nm/min (Ni mask, ~72°, 5.5:1); 13 nm/min (proton exchange + RIE, ~70°) [22].
- ICP rates: 37 nm/min (Cr mask, ~71°); 79 nm/min (Ni mask, ~83° — best ICP result); 108 nm/min (SiO2 mask, SF6/BCl3/Ar, 0.86:1 selectivity, ~65°) [22].
- **Conclusion: RIE dry etching combined with wet etching after high-temperature reduction treatment achieved 10 nm/min etch rate with pristine 90° sidewall angles; the hybrid process (dry etching + Al film annealing + wet etching) produced damage-free, perfectly smooth 90° sidewalls while preserving LNO ferroelectric properties** [22].

**Hot KOH and hot SC1 in Harvard cleaning sequence**: Devices undergo chemical cleaning (hot KOH, hot SC1, diluted HF, piranha) before annealing at 520°C in oxygen [35].

**CMP slurry with KOH/NaOH** (CN103978406A patent, Dalian University of Technology, 2014): A chemical mechanical polishing method for LiNbO₃ crystals uses a CMP slurry at **pH 10.2–10.6** containing cerium oxide, silicon oxide, potassium hydroxide, sodium hydroxide, barium hydroxide, potassium permanganate, hydrogen peroxide, citric acid, acetic acid, and/or oxalic acid [42].
- Material removal rate 420–460 nm/min; flatness 3.8–5.5 μm; surface roughness Ra 0.35–0.5 nm; PV value 3.8–6 nm (sub-nanometer ultra-smooth surface) [42].
- Exemplary embodiment: Y-cut wafer (50mm dia, 1mm thick); 20 nm silica sol + 30% hydrogen peroxide at 1:1.2:8:56 volume ratio, pH 10.5 with KOH, 60 rpm, 60 kPa, 5 min → removal rate 450 nm/min, Ra 0.387 nm, PV 3.886 nm [42].

**TMAH and KOH etching — general principles for MEMS** (Rogue Valley Microdevices, "TMAH vs. KOH Silicon Etch"): Both etchants are hot alkaline solutions that anisotropically etch silicon along crystal planes, producing 54.74° sidewalls along (111) planes on (100) silicon [37].
- KOH contains alkali metal ions that can contaminate — NOT CMOS compatible; TMAH is organic and metal-ion free — CMOS compatible [37].
- KOH provides the highest silicon etch rate and anisotropy (run at ~20–45% concentration, 70–80°C); TMAH etches more slowly with slightly lower anisotropy (run at ~20–25%, 80–90°C) [37].
- KOH etches SiO2 relatively fast (SiN mask preferred); TMAH has very high oxide selectivity (SiO2 mask allowed) [37].
- KOH attacks exposed aluminum; TMAH can be buffered to protect aluminum; KOH produces the smoothest surfaces; TMAH can roughen with hillocks unless optimized [37].

**TMAH/IPA wet etching of silicon nanowires** (Yusoh & Yaacob, Beilstein Journal of Nanotechnology, 2016): 25 wt% TMAH with IPA (0, 10, 20, 30 vol%) at 65°C, etching times 30–50 s [38].
- Increased IPA concentration produced wider nanowires with smoother surfaces; etching rate lowest at 20 vol% IPA (IPA monolayer blocks OH⁻), then increased sharply at 30 vol%; surface roughness (Ra) decreased with more IPA; wall angles 42.5°, 34.2°, 35.5° for 30, 40, 50 s at constant 10 vol% IPA [38].

#### B.4 Proton-Exchange-Enhanced Wet Etching (PEWE) — Related Wet Etching Route

Li, Lan, Yang, Wang (Optical Materials, Vol. 120, October 2021, Article 111433, "Fabrication of ridge optical waveguide in thin film lithium niobate by proton exchange and wet etching"): [23]
- **The etching rate of LN was improved nearly 100 times after introducing the proton-exchange process, with an optimized etching rate of 13.5 nm/min** [23].
- A low-loss ridge waveguide was fabricated on TFLN with a measured **propagation loss of 4.3 dB/cm** using an 850 nm single-mode laser; a Y-branch waveguide achieved uniform light-splitting ratio of nearly 1:1 [23].
- The sidewall surface was covered with **beeswax** to avoid damage induced by the wet etching process; pure benzoic acid (instead of lithium benzoic acid) improved etch quality [23].
- Previous TFLN ridge waveguide fabrication achieved only ~6 dB/cm propagation loss and ~6.7 nm/min etching rate; this work improves on both [23].
- HRXRD confirmed phase transitions after PE: LN substrate and film peaks detected at ~83.63° and 83.36°, plus a third diffraction peak after PE [23].
- Historical context: Laurell et al. (1992) first proposed wet etching with PE and HF/HNO3 acids [23].

#### B.5 Etchless and Smoothing Alternatives Relevant to Damage Mitigation

**Atomic Layer Etching (ALE) for smoothing damaged surfaces** (arXiv:2511.01825, "Directional atomic layer etching of lithium niobate using Br-based plasma"; Oxford Instruments/Caltech, JPL): [15][16]
- Directional ALE: sequential exposures of HBr/BCl3/Ar plasma (40s, 300W ICP, 5W RIE, 30V DC bias) followed by Ar plasma (60s, 300W ICP, 6W RIE, 45V DC bias) at 10 mTorr [15][16].
- At 0°C: EPC of 1.04±0.01 nm/cycle with 84.6% synergy; half-cycle EPCs 0.02 nm/cycle (HBr/BCl3/Ar) and 0.14 nm/cycle (Ar) [15].
- At 200°C: EPC increased to 1.25 nm/cycle but synergy dropped to 30% (or 56.8% in v2); surface remained atomically smooth (Rq=0.25±0.03 nm after 20 cycles, unchanged from control) [15][16].
- **HBr chemistry reduces redeposition compared to F- and Cl-based plasmas due to higher vapor pressures of Br-based etch products** [15][16].
- **50 cycles of ALE on a TFLN waveguide chip reduced surface roughness from Rq=2.07 nm to Rq=0.34 nm (84% reduction), with minimal lateral etching (waveguide top width maintained)** [15][16].
- At 200°C, 120 cycles (149 nm etch) produced no surface roughening (Rq=0.28 nm) [15][16].
- Surface bromine concentration 0.50±0.04% after 50 cycles at 0°C, decreasing to 0.35±0.06% at 200°C [15][16].
- Isotropic HBr-based ALE (H2 plasma + HBr/BCl3/Ar) yielded 1.43 nm/cycle with 97.9% synergy at 0°C and Rq=0.77 nm [15][16].
- A TFLN grating (total depth 223 nm, 200 cycles) etched entirely by ALE at 200°C showed NO aspect-ratio-dependent etching (ARDE) down to 150 nm gaps, in contrast to ion milling where ARDE manifests below 300 nm [15][16].
- At 0°C, Rq=0.30±0.04 nm for polished original increasing to Rq=0.73±0.06 nm after 20 cycles at 0°C (worse than 200°C) [16].

**Proton exchange + dry etch (PE-RIE)** (Hu, Milenin, Wehrspohn, Hermann, Sohler — J. Vac. Sci. Technol. A, June 9, 2006, "Plasma etching of proton-exchanged lithium niobate"): [19][20]
- Plasma etching of LN with fluorine gases is limited by redeposition of LiF (melting point >800°C), causing low etch rates and nonvertical walls. **Proton exchange replaces Li ions with protons (up to 85% substitution), greatly reducing LiF formation and improving etchability** [19][20].
- Z-cut LN samples proton-exchanged in pure benzoic acid at 240°C for 5 hours (PE depth 2.8 µm); 120–400 nm Cr mask [20].
- Table I results: (1) CF4 at 500 mTorr: PE-LN etch rate 480 nm/h (selectivity vs Cr 3.43:1), pure LN 157 nm/h, surface cracks; (2) SF6 at 500 mTorr: PE-LN 1.53 µm/h (selectivity 46:1), pure LN not etchable, highly isotropic with significant underetching; (3) SF6 ICP-RIE at 6 mTorr, 1500 W, 153 V dc bias, He-cooled: 2.74 µm/h (selectivity 30:1); (4) CHF3/Ar ICP-RIE at 6 mTorr, 1500 W, 122 V dc bias, He-cooled: 2.88 µm/h (selectivity 48:1); (5) **CHF3/Ar ICP-RIE at 6 mTorr, 1500 W, 130 V dc bias, NO cooling: 5.76 µm/h (selectivity 32:1), nearly vertical etched walls (82° angle) with negligible underetching** [20].
- Etching rate nearly doubled without He-backside cooling due to volatility of NbF5 (boiling point ~234°C) [20].
- Photonic crystal waveguide structures fabricated: pore diameter 340 nm, interpore distance 500 nm, etch depth ~1.5 µm [20].
- **"The reverse proton exchange process can potentially restore optical properties after etching"** [20].
- SF6-etched PE-LN had smooth surfaces; CF4-etched PE-LN had cracks; SF6 at 500 mTorr: lateral etch rates 3.5–4.0 µm/h [20].

**Proton substitution via H2-plasma pre-treatment for dry etching** (Aryal, Stricklin, Behzadirad, Branch, Siddiqui, Busani — Nanomaterials, Vol. 12, Issue 16, Article 2836, 2022, "High-Quality Dry Etching of LiNbO3 Assisted by Proton Substitution through H2-Plasma Surface Treatment"): [43]
- A novel H2-plasma treatment (H2: 30 sccm, pressure: 15 mTorr, RF power: 150 W, ICP power: 300 W, DC bias: 53 V) applied before lithography/metallization substitutes protons for Li ions at the surface and relieves surface tension, improving Ti/Al/Cr mask quality on X- and Y-cuts [43].
- Etching with CHF3/Ar plasma (CHF3: 30 sccm, Ar: 30 sccm, pressure: 5 mTorr, RF power: 100 W, ICP power: 150 W, DC bias: 40 V); Ti/Al (20nm/1.3µm) masks work on all LN cuts; Ti/Al/Cr (20nm/750nm/750nm) peeled off on X/Y cuts without H2 treatment [43].
- Periodic process: 20 min etching followed by 4 min cooling, chemical cleaning after each 1 hour of etching; structures with etch depths as deep as 3.4 µm achieved with smooth sidewalls and near-perfect verticality (~3° offset) across crystallographic orientations [43].
- RMS roughness ~10 for one sample and ~1.5 for another (ImageJ SurfChaJ, relative units); etch rate ~650 nm/h for bulk LN [43].

### PART C: Surface Passivation and Cladding Approaches

#### C.1 Index-Matched Coating Layers (SiN/SiON) to Repair Roughness

**Chinese patent CN115951449A** ("Low-loss lithium niobate waveguide and preparation method thereof," Zhongke Xintong Microelectronics Technology Beijing Co., Ltd., filed March 13, 2023, published April 11, 2023): [3]
- RIE etching produces LiF precipitates and redeposition, creating rough waveguides and high scattering losses [3].
- **A coating layer is deposited on the LiNbO₃ waveguide layer to fill and repair surface/sidewall undulations without damaging the LiNbO₃ lattice structure** [3].
- **Coating layer refractive index equals that of the lithium niobate waveguide layer (2.15–2.25, preferably 2.2); coating material: silicon nitride or silicon oxynitride; coating thickness: 10–100 nm, with less than 10% influence on optical field energy in the LiNbO₃ waveguide** [3].
- Structure: substrate (400–600 μm) / oxygen buried layer (2–5 μm SiO2) / LiNbO₃ waveguide layer (200–700 nm) / coating layer / upper cladding (1–5 μm, silica or air) [3].
- **Preparation method includes: thermal annealing (300–800°C, 5–10 min) after coating deposition, then deposit upper cladding** [3].
- Example: Cr metal mask (~40 nm) sputtered via magnetron PVD; ICP dry etching with O₂/Cl₂ for mask and Ar/SF₆ for LiNbO₃ (300 nm etch depth); **LPCVD SiN cladding (~50 nm) at 700°C/100Pa; annealing at 400–800°C for 8 min; 3μm SiO₂ upper cladding** [3].
- COMSOL simulations confirmed that SiN cladding thickness up to 100 nm does not significantly affect light transmission while substantially reducing sidewall scattering loss [3].

#### C.2 SiO₂ Cladding After Annealing

The Jena/Fraunhofer wafer-scale study (arXiv:2407.09208) used **SiO2 cladding via PECVD after O2 annealing at 520°C for 2 hours**; devices achieved loaded Q (1.34 ± 0.24) × 10⁶ and straight waveguide loss ~2 dB/m (0.02 dB/cm) [14].

The Light: Science & Applications review (Vol. 9, Article 197, 2020) notes that in LNOI fabrication, microstructure is transferred via lithographic masks then etched by Ar+ milling, **with SiO2 cladding deposited by PECVD**; refractive index contrast between LN core (n~2.1) and SiO2 cladding (n~1.4) is ~0.7 [5].

The MDPI Crystals paper (Wang, Chen, Hu — Crystals, Vol. 8, Issue 5, Article 191, 2018, "Analysis of Waveguides on Lithium Niobate Thin Films") simulated strip-loaded waveguides using SiO2, SiN, TiO2, and Si loading strips [36]:
- Refractive indices at 1550 nm: SiO2 1.46, SiN 1.9, TiO2 2.3, Si 3.48 [36].
- Strip-loaded q-TM optical power initially increased with strip thickness (maximum at ~0.12 µm for SiO2 and ~0.07 µm for SiN, TiO2, Si), then decreased [36].
- For ridge waveguides, minimal bending radii achieving 10⁻⁵ dB/cm loss: 15 µm (q-TE) and 20 µm (q-TM) [36].
- q-TM leakage: when effective index of strip-loaded waveguide is smaller than the nearby TE planar waveguide (e.g., SiN strip at 0.05 µm, nTM00=1.844 < nTE0=1.910), Ez coupling causes leakage (minimum loss 57 dB/cm); at 0.3 µm strip (nTM00=1.922 > nTE0=1.910), leakage avoided, bending loss ~10⁻¹⁰ dB/cm [36].

#### C.3 Cladding Materials — General Context (Al2O3, HfO2 via ALD)

**ALD for HfO2/Al2O3 thin films** (Wei, Pan, Zhang, Ma — Nanoscale Research Letters, 2015): ALD was used to fabricate HfO2/Al2O3 films with high laser-induced damage thresholds (LIDT) [56].
- Deposition temperatures 300°C and 250°C; precursors: inorganic (HfCl4, AlCl3) and organic (TEMAH, TMA) [56].
- Inorganic precursors produced higher LIDTs than organic precursors (organic groups show intense IR absorption) [56].
- For Al2O3 and HfO2 single layers with inorganic precursors, LIDTs were 14 J/cm² and 22 J/cm² respectively, versus 12.5 and 14.7 J/cm² with organic precursors [56].
- Increasing precursor pulse duration improved Al2O3 LIDT from 15 to 40 J/cm² (reducing residual chlorine from ~400 ppm to ~200 ppm), but had little effect on HfO2 (21 to 22 J/cm²; chlorine remained ~1,400 ppm) [56].
- The HfO2/Al2O3 anti-reflector reached 18 J/cm² — highest reported for ALD single and anti-reflect films [56].

**Hybrid integration cladding approaches** (Light: Science & Applications review, 2020): [5]
- LN films as top cladding on Si or Si3N4 waveguides; hybrid Si-LiNbO3 ring resonators, MZI modulators with 106 GHz bandwidth and VπL of 6.7 V·cm; vertical adiabatic couplers achieving insertion loss 2.5 dB, VπL 2.2 V·cm, modulation rates up to 112 Gbit/s [5].
- LNOI as substrate with rib-loaded materials: Ta2O5 rib waveguides (Q factor ~7.2 × 10⁴, VπL 4 V·cm), Ge23Sb7S70 chalcogenide (loss 1.2 dB/cm), and Si3N4 composite waveguides [5].
- Milestones on X-cut LN: waveguides with 3.0 ± 0.2 dB/cm propagation loss; MZI modulator with half-wave voltage 9V (VπL = 1.8 V·cm); sub-wavelength waveguides with 2.7 dB/m loss; microring with ultrahigh Q of 5 × 10⁶; MZI modulators with bandwidths up to 100 GHz and even 500 GHz; integrated MZI modulator with 1.4V half-wave voltage CMOS-compatible [5].
- Z-cut milestones: photonic wires with propagation loss 9.9 dB/cm at 1.55 μm; microdisk resonators with Q factor 1.19 × 10⁶; electro-optically tuneable WGM microresonator with 0.14 GHz/V tunability; BCB adhesive layer to reduce thermal stress (2007) [5].
- LN second-order nonlinear coefficients: d33 = 25.2 pm/V and d31 = 4.6 pm/V at 1064 nm; electro-optic coefficient γ33 = 30.9 × 10⁻¹² m/V [5].

### PART D: Additional Damage Context, Roughness Data, and Loss Models

#### D.1 Plasma-Etch Damage Context

- Lithium niobate is hard (6.3 GPa), dense, and chemically inert, making etching difficult; issues include anisotropic etch behavior and material redeposition during reactive-ion plasma etching [4].
- Plasma etching of LN with fluorine gases is limited by redeposition of LiF (melting point >800°C), causing low etch rates and nonvertical walls [19][20].
- IEEE Spectrum (Jan 16, 2018) reported on Harvard's plasma etching breakthrough: argon ion bombardment created micro-ring and micro-racetrack resonators (~1 µm wide, 80 µm curvature radius); optical power losses of only 50% over 1 meter, compared to 99% loss in previous LN devices [17]. Marko Lončar: "Diamond is actually easier to etch than niobate, but it doesn't exist as thin films" [17].
- Kaufmann, Finco, Maeder, Grange (Nanophotonics, Vol. 12, pp. 1601–1611, Jan 16, 2023, "Redeposition-free inductively-coupled plasma etching of lithium niobate for integrated photonics"): **argon etching of lithium niobate waveguides in an ICP system has been shown to provide the best optical quality devices for integrated photonics**; 52 citations [40].
- Siew et al. (IEEE OMN 2016, "Loss characterization of waveguides in lithium niobate on insulator"): LN is difficult to pattern and etching typically induces rough sidewalls; LNOI was created to circumvent these issues; commercial devices use diffusion-type processes with small index increases, large footprints, and high cost [41].
- The Chinese Optics Letters photonic crystal review (Ge, Wu, Liu, Chen, Chen — Chin. Opt. Lett., Vol. 22, Issue 3, 033602, 2024) reviews fabrication methods: FIB (Ga+ at 30 kV with Cr or Au masks), EBL with Ar+ plasma etching (sidewall angles 60°, 70°, 85°), IBEE (90° sidewalls), RIE + proton exchange (85°), etchless LNPhC, and laser-writing-assisted nanolithography (100 nm holes) [7].
- Q-factor results (Table 1): highest simulated Q 1.23×10⁸ (mode-gap cavity, 2019, EBL+Ar+ etching) with experimental 1.41×10⁶ and modal volume 0.78 (λ/n)³; experimental Qs range from 75 (redeposition-free FIB, 2022) to 1.41×10⁶; 3.51×10⁵ (2019), 4.7×10⁵ (2020), 12,010 (BIC etchless, 2022); L4/3 inverse-designed cavity 9.7×10⁶ (simulation, 2020) [7].
- SHG efficiencies: 6.4×10⁻⁹ (L3 cavity), 0.078% W⁻¹ (mode-gap cavity Q~10⁶), 2×10⁻⁴ (pulsed); slow light SHG 8×10⁻⁵ W⁻¹ [7].

#### D.2 Surface Roughness and Loss Quantification

**Hammer, Farheen, Förstner (Optics Express, Vol. 32, No. 13, pp. 22878–22890, June 17, 2024, Paderborn University, "Estimation of losses caused by sidewall roughness in thin-film lithium niobate rib and strip waveguides")**: [46]
- Four waveguide samples fabricated via dry etching with SiO2 etching mask (Argon plasma) at λ=1.55 µm: two rib waveguides (LNOI600b13, LNOI600b29) and two fully etched strip waveguides (LNOI450b14(1), LNOI450b14(2)); X-cut, Y-propagation; no=2.1836, ne=2.1220 [46].
- Losses measured with Fabry-Pérot method: **measured losses ranged from ~3.8 to ~9.4 dB/cm** across the samples [46].
- Surface roughness modeled as thin lossy layers (thickness s=20 nm) at sidewalls; single fit parameter **ε'' = 0.0194 with Δε'' = 0.0027**; individual measurements showed 1.7–2.3 × 10⁻² [46].
- Loss decreases with growing waveguide top width w due to reduced relative field strength at sidewalls; near anti-crossings of effective indices, attenuation curves cross, leading to unexpected higher loss levels [46].

**Wu, Wang, Xu, Qi, Chu, Fang, Zhang, Zhou, Qiao, Chai, Lin, Cheng (Nanomaterials, Vol. 8, Issue 11, Article 910, 2018, "Long Low-Loss-Lithium Niobate on Insulator Waveguides with Sub-Nanometer Surface Roughness")**: [34]
- CMP-based fabrication (no ion beam etching, avoiding residual sidewall roughness): **record-low propagation loss of 0.027 dB/cm**; surface roughness Rq = 0.452 nm measured by AFM [34].
- Whispering-gallery microring (160 μm diameter, ~3 μm width): loaded Q 5.70 × 10⁶, intrinsic Q 1.14 × 10⁷ at critical coupling; loss calculated as α = 2π·n_eff/(Q·λ) with n_eff 1.79 at 1560.48 nm [34].
- 11-cm-long continuous waveguide fabricated (femtosecond laser ablation took 90 minutes); X-cut LNOI (400 nm LN on 2-μm SiO2 on LN substrate) [34].
- Loss still one order of magnitude higher than the theoretical absorption limit of crystalline LN (~10⁻³ dB/cm), attributed to radiative loss, surface contamination, absorptive defects, and remaining CMP roughness [34].

**Photoresist reflow for roughness reduction** (Prabhakar & Reano — IEEE Photonics Journal, Dec 1, 2022, DOI: 10.1109/JPHOT.2022.3222184): [33]
- Lithography and argon plasma etching of LNOI rib waveguides using reflowed photoresist etch masks and 405 nm photolithography; melting the photoresist at temperatures greatly exceeding its glass transition temperature reduces sidewall surface roughness and allows the photoresist to serve as both pattern mask and hard etch mask, resulting in waveguides with sub-nanometer sidewall surface quality [33].
- References prior work: LNOI waveguides with sub-nanometer surface roughness achieving 0.027 dB/cm propagation loss (2018); wet-etched LN ridge waveguides (2007); sidewall polishing techniques for scattering-loss reduction (2018) [33].

**Angle-optimized ion-beam etching** (Zhang, Zhan, Chi, Liu, Liu — Optics Express, Vol. 34, Issue 4, pp. 6870–6879, Feb 17, 2026): [28][29]
- Soft positive-tone resist mask; IBE incidence angles from 0° to 30°; **sidewall verticality approaching 80°, compared to typical values below 70°** for conventional fabrication; etch depth ~400 nm and RMS roughness 0.65 nm for adjacent unetched region after removing residual resist masks [28][29].
- Compact spiral microresonators achieved **intrinsic Q factors up to 5.1 × 10⁶, corresponding to a propagation loss of 0.08 dB/cm**; pulse-driven Kerr soliton microcombs with repetition rates near 24 GHz [28][29].

**Tien's formula for surface roughness scattering loss** (from Volk PhD thesis, 2018): shows 0.0016 dB/cm for conventional diffused waveguides vs. 0.62 dB/cm for LNOI at 2 nm roughness and 1.55 µm; bending radius calculations: Ti-diffused waveguides need ~7.9 mm radius vs. ~7.1 µm for LNOI at 0.1 dB/cm loss [4]. LNOI ridge waveguides via crystal ion slicing (2.1 µm wide, 9 mm long): propagation loss 1.2 dB/cm (TE) and 2.8 dB/cm (TM) at 1550 nm — lower than losses achieved by dry-etching at the time (10–17 dB/cm) [4].

#### D.3 Material Properties Relevant to Damage and Repair

- LiNbO₃: trigonal ferroelectric (3m point group, R3c space group, ilmenite-type ABO₃), spontaneous polarization 50 μC/cm², Curie temperature ~1210°C (also cited as ~1100–1140°C elsewhere), r33 ~30.8–31 pm/V, d33 = 25.2 pm/V, d31 = 4.6 pm/V at 1064 nm [5][8][9].
- Transparency window: ~350 nm to 5.5 μm; bandgap 4.9 eV; refractive index ordinary 2.21, extraordinary 2.13 at 1550 nm [39].
- TFLN platform: low-loss waveguides (<0.1 dB/cm), small bending radii (~30 μm), high bandwidth (>100 GHz), Vπ < 1 V [39].
- ELENA project targets: resonators Q-factor >10⁶, propagation losses <0.1 dB/cm [39].
- LNOI wafers of 6-inch diameter fabricated using Smart Cut technology (implantation of hydrogen ions in LiNbO3) — Optical Materials Express, Vol. 16, Issue 3, p. 744 [18].
- Ansys Optics thermal waveguide simulation: LNO is negative uniaxial; coherence lengths ~16 μm (ordinary) and ~19 μm (extraordinary) for SHG at 1550 nm; temperature variation of extraordinary index ~0.2% greater than ordinary index across 0–100°C [52].
- Thin-film LN modulation technology (Baidu encyclopedia): commercial bandwidth ≥110 GHz, laboratory >170 GHz; drive voltage 1–2V; wafer size up to 150 mm (6-inch), 200 mm under development [49].
- Liobate 2026 guide: TFLN modulators routinely exceed 100 GHz bandwidth, up to 220 GHz in leading-edge labs; r33 ≈ 31 pm/V; d33 ≈ -27 pm/V; energy consumption as low as 0.69 fJ/bit [50].
- Baidu TFLN overview: transmission loss <0.15 dB/cm, etching depth error within 10%, yield >85%; wet etching (hydrogen peroxide, ammonia water) can fabricate micro-ring resonators with Q factors approaching tens of millions [51].
