### PART D: Additional Damage Context, Roughness Data, and Loss Models

#### D.1 Plasma-Etch Damage Context

- Lithium niobate is hard (6.3 GPa), dense, and chemically inert, making etching difficult; issues include anisotropic etch behavior and material redeposition during reactive-ion plasma etching [4].
- Plasma etching of LN with fluorine gases is limited by redeposition of LiF (melting point >800°C), causing low etch rates and nonvertical walls [19][20].
- IEEE Spectrum (Jan 16, 2018) reported on Harvard's plasma etching breakthrough: argon ion bombardment created micro-ring and micro-racetrack resonators (~1 µm wide, 80 µm curvature radius); optical power losses of only 50% over 1 meter, compared to 99% loss in previous LN devices [17]. Marko Lončar: "Diamond is actually easier to etch than niobate, but it doesn't exist as thin films" [17].
- Kaufmann, Finco, Maeder, Grange (Nanophotonics, Vol. 12, pp. 1601–1611, Jan 16, 2023, "Redeposition-free inductively-coupled plasma etching of lithium niobate for integrated photonics"): **argon etching of lithium niobate waveguides in an ICP system has been shown to provide the best optical quality devices for integrated photonics**; 52 citations [40].
- Siew et al. (IEEE OMN 2016, "Loss characterization of waveguides in lithium niobate on insulator"): LN is difficult to pattern and etching typically induces rough sidewalls; LNOI was created to circumvent these issues; commercial devices use diffusion-type processes with small index increases, large footprints, and high cost [41].
- The Chinese Optics Letters photonic crystal review (Ge, Wu, Liu, Chen, Chen — Chin. Opt. Lett., Vol. 22, Issue 3, 033602, 2024) reviews fabrication methods: FIB (Ga+ at 30 kV with Cr or Au masks), EBL with Ar+ plasma etching (sidewall angles 60°, 70°, 85°), IBEE (90° sidewalls), RIE + proton exchange (85°), etchless LNPhC, and laser-writing-assisted nanolithography (100 nm holes) [7].
- Q-factor results (Table 1): highest simulated Q 1.23×10⁸ (mode-gap cavity, 2019, EBL+Ar+ etching) with experimental 1.41×10⁶ and modal volume 0.78 (λ/n)³; experimental Qs range from 75 (redeposition-free FIB, 2022) to 1.41×10⁶; 3.51×10⁵ (2019), 4.7×10⁵ (2020), 12,010 (BIC etchless, 2022); L4/3 inverse-designed cavity 9.7×10⁶ (simulation, 2020) [7].
- SHG efficiencies: 6.4×10⁻⁹ (L3 cavity), 0.078% W⁻¹ (mode-gap cavity Q~10⁶), 2×10⁻⁴ (pulsed); slow light SHG 8×10⁻⁵ W⁻¹ [7].

#### D.2 Surface Roughness and Loss Quantification

**Hammer, Farheen, Förstner (Optics Express, Vol. 32, No. 13, pp. 22878–22890, June 17, 2024, Paderborn University, "Estimation of losses caused by sidewall roughness in thin-film lithium niobate rib and strip waveguides")**: [46]
- Four waveguide samples fabricated via dry etching with SiO2 etching mask (Argon plasma) at λ=1.55 µm: two rib waveguides (LNOI600b13, LNOI600b29) and two fully etched strip waveguides (LNOI450b14(1), LNOI450b14(2)); X-cut, Y-propagation; no=2.1836, ne=2.1220 [46].
- Losses measured with Fabry-Pérot method: **measured losses ranged from ~3.8 to ~9.4 dB/cm** across the samples [46].
- Surface roughness modeled as thin lossy layers (thickness s=20 nm) at sidewalls; single fit parameter **ε'' = 0.0194 with Δε'' = 0.0027**; individual measurements showed 1.7–2.3 × 10⁻² [46].
- Loss decreases with growing waveguide top width w due to reduced relative field strength at sidewalls; near anti-crossings of effective indices, attenuation curves cross, leading to unexpected higher loss levels [46].

**Wu, Wang, Xu, Qi, Chu, Fang, Zhang, Zhou, Qiao, Chai, Lin, Cheng (Nanomaterials, Vol. 8, Issue 11, Article 910, 2018, "Long Low-Loss-Lithium Niobate on Insulator Waveguides with Sub-Nanometer Surface Roughness")**: [34]
- CMP-based fabrication (no ion beam etching, avoiding residual sidewall roughness): **record-low propagation loss of 0.027 dB/cm**; surface roughness Rq = 0.452 nm measured by AFM [34].
- Whispering-gallery microring (160 μm diameter, ~3 μm width): loaded Q 5.70 × 10⁶, intrinsic Q 1.14 × 10⁷ at critical coupling; loss calculated as α = 2π·n_eff/(Q·λ) with n_eff 1.79 at 1560.48 nm [34].
- 11-cm-long continuous waveguide fabricated (femtosecond laser ablation took 90 minutes); X-cut LNOI (400 nm LN on 2-μm SiO2 on LN substrate) [34].
- Loss still one order of magnitude higher than the theoretical absorption limit of crystalline LN (~10⁻³ dB/cm), attributed to radiative loss, surface contamination, absorptive defects, and remaining CMP roughness [34].

**Photoresist reflow for roughness reduction** (Prabhakar & Reano — IEEE Photonics Journal, Dec 1, 2022, DOI: 10.1109/JPHOT.2022.3222184): [33]
- Lithography and argon plasma etching of LNOI rib waveguides using reflowed photoresist etch masks and 405 nm photolithography; melting the photoresist at temperatures greatly exceeding its glass transition temperature reduces sidewall surface roughness and allows the photoresist to serve as both pattern mask and hard etch mask, resulting in waveguides with sub-nanometer sidewall surface quality [33].
- References prior work: LNOI waveguides with sub-nanometer surface roughness achieving 0.027 dB/cm propagation loss (2018); wet-etched LN ridge waveguides (2007); sidewall polishing techniques for scattering-loss reduction (2018) [33].

**Angle-optimized ion-beam etching** (Zhang, Zhan, Chi, Liu, Liu — Optics Express, Vol. 34, Issue 4, pp. 6870–6879, Feb 17, 2026): [28][29]
- Soft positive-tone resist mask; IBE incidence angles from 0° to 30°; **sidewall verticality approaching 80°, compared to typical values below 70°** for conventional fabrication; etch depth ~400 nm and RMS roughness 0.65 nm for adjacent unetched region after removing residual resist masks [28][29].
- Compact spiral microresonators achieved **intrinsic Q factors up to 5.1 × 10⁶, corresponding to a propagation loss of 0.08 dB/cm**; pulse-driven Kerr soliton microcombs with repetition rates near 24 GHz [28][29].

**Tien's formula for surface roughness scattering loss** (from Volk PhD thesis, 2018): shows 0.0016 dB/cm for conventional diffused waveguides vs. 0.62 dB/cm for LNOI at 2 nm roughness and 1.55 µm; bending radius calculations: Ti-diffused waveguides need ~7.9 mm radius vs. ~7.1 µm for LNOI at 0.1 dB/cm loss [4]. LNOI ridge waveguides via crystal ion slicing (2.1 µm wide, 9 mm long): propagation loss 1.2 dB/cm (TE) and 2.8 dB/cm (TM) at 1550 nm — lower than losses achieved by dry-etching at the time (10–17 dB/cm) [4].

#### D.3 Material Properties Relevant to Damage and Repair

- LiNbO₃: trigonal ferroelectric (3m point group, R3c space group, ilmenite-type ABO₃), spontaneous polarization 50 μC/cm², Curie temperature ~1210°C (also cited as ~1100–1140°C elsewhere), r33 ~30.8–31 pm/V, d33 = 25.2 pm/V, d31 = 4.6 pm/V at 1064 nm [5][8][9].
- Transparency window: ~350 nm to 5.5 μm; bandgap 4.9 eV; refractive index ordinary 2.21, extraordinary 2.13 at 1550 nm [39].
- TFLN platform: low-loss waveguides (<0.1 dB/cm), small bending radii (~30 μm), high bandwidth (>100 GHz), Vπ < 1 V [39].
- ELENA project targets: resonators Q-factor >10⁶, propagation losses <0.1 dB/cm [39].
- LNOI wafers of 6-inch diameter fabricated using Smart Cut technology (implantation of hydrogen ions in LiNbO3) — Optical Materials Express, Vol. 16, Issue 3, p. 744 [18].
- Ansys Optics thermal waveguide simulation: LNO is negative uniaxial; coherence lengths ~16 μm (ordinary) and ~19 μm (extraordinary) for SHG at 1550 nm; temperature variation of extraordinary index ~0.2% greater than ordinary index across 0–100°C [52].
- Thin-film LN modulation technology (Baidu encyclopedia): commercial bandwidth ≥110 GHz, laboratory >170 GHz; drive voltage 1–2V; wafer size up to 150 mm (6-inch), 200 mm under development [49].
- Liobate 2026 guide: TFLN modulators routinely exceed 100 GHz bandwidth, up to 220 GHz in leading-edge labs; r33 ≈ 31 pm/V; d33 ≈ -27 pm/V; energy consumption as low as 0.69 fJ/bit [50].
- Baidu TFLN overview: transmission loss <0.15 dB/cm, etching depth error within 10%, yield >85%; wet etching (hydrogen peroxide, ammonia water) can fabricate micro-ring resonators with Q factors approaching tens of millions [51].

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

## (a) Plasma Gas Chemistry and Gas Mixtures

### Fluorine-based chemistries (SF6, CHF3, CF4, C4F8) — LiF redeposition problem

**Core problem statement (stated by multiple sources):** Plasma etching of lithium niobate with fluorine gases is limited by the redeposition of LiF, which has a melting point above 800°C. This results in low etch rates and non-vertically etched walls. LiF redeposition also causes non-vertical sidewall profiles, increased roughness, and reduced etching rates (Ulliac et al., Optical Materials 2016; Hu, Milenin, Wehrspohn, Hermann & Sohler, J. Vac. Sci. Technol. A 24(4), 2006, DOI: 10.1116/1.2207150; Kozlov et al., Applied Sciences 2023). The melting point of LiF is given as >800°C (Hu et al. 2006; Aryal et al. 2022) and "evaporate only at ~800°C" (Aryal et al. 2022). The problem is compounded by the fact that NbF5 is volatile (boiling point ~234°C), so the temperature dependence of etching confirms the role of NbF5 volatility in the process (Hu et al. 2006). F-based processes produce LiF by-products that limit sidewall angles to 60°–75° (Huang, Liu & Wu, J. Micromech. Microeng. 36(3), 2026, DOI: 10.1088/1361-6439/ae36b6). Cl-based methods form easily-removed LiCl (Huang et al. 2026). Shen et al. (Nanomaterials 13(20):2789, 2023) state: "F-based gas creates LiF by-products that accumulate on sidewalls and reduce sidewall angles (e.g., Kozlov 2023 achieved only 60-75° angles). Cl-based gas creates easily-removed LiCl by-products but has lower etching rates."

**Detailed results from Hu, Milenin, Wehrspohn, Hermann & Sohler, "Plasma etching of proton-exchanged lithium niobate," J. Vac. Sci. Technol. A 24(4), 2006 (DOI: 10.1116/1.2207150):**

The study demonstrated that etching proton-exchanged lithium niobate (PE-LN) prevents LiF deposition to a large extent because proton exchange greatly reduces the lithium concentration in the material (up to 85% substitution of Li ions). Z-cut LN samples were proton-exchanged in pure benzoic acid at 240°C for 5 hours (PE depth 2.8 µm). A 120–400 nm Cr layer served as etch mask (Cr stripes of 9.5–19.5 µm width for ridge waveguides; pore diameter 340 nm, interpore distance ~500 nm for photonic crystal waveguides). Etching used either a Tepla parallel plate RIE reactor or an Oxford Plasmalab System 100 with ICP 380 source. Five experimental conditions were tested:

1. **CF4 at 500 mTorr** (parallel-plate RIE): PE-LN etch rate 480 nm/h (pure LN: 157 nm/h), selectivity PE-LN/Cr = 3.43; surface cracks observed on PE-LN (SEM analysis revealed cracks on CF4-etched PE-LN).
2. **SF6 at 500 mTorr** (parallel-plate RIE): PE-LN etch rate 1.53 µm/h, selectivity PE-LN/Cr = 46; pure LN not etched at all; highly isotropic etching with significant underetching (3.5 and 4.0 µm/h lateral rates on each side of stripes) and strongly non-vertical sidewalls. SEM revealed smooth surfaces on SF6-etched PE-LN.
3. **SF6 ICP-RIE at 6 mTorr, 1500 W, 153 V dc bias, He-cooled**: PE-LN rate 2.74 µm/h, selectivity ~30.
4. **CHF3/Ar ICP-RIE at 6 mTorr, 122 V dc bias, He-cooled**: PE-LN rate 2.88 µm/h, selectivity 48.
5. **CHF3/Ar ICP-RIE at 6 mTorr, 130 V dc bias, NO cooling**: PE-LN rate 5.76 µm/h (≈5.7 µm/h), selectivity 32; nearly vertical etched walls with angle of 82° and negligible underetching. This was the optimal recipe. The etching rate ratio between PE-LN and pure LN was approximately 3.

The etching rate nearly doubled (2.88 to 5.76 µm/h) without He-backside cooling due to the volatility of NbF5 (boiling point ~234°C), confirming substrate temperature dependence. First photonic crystal waveguide structures were successfully fabricated with etching depth of ~1.5 µm (interpore distance 500 nm) using CHF3/Ar at 1500 W ICP power, 130 V dc bias, 6 mTorr, no substrate cooling.

**ECIO 2008 conference paper (H. Hu, R. Ricken, W. Sohler, "Etching of Lithium Niobate: From Ridge Waveguides to Photonic Crystal Structures," ECIO'08, Eindhoven, pp. 75–78, 2008):**

- **ICP-etching of X-cut LN using C4F8/He (1:1) plasma with a Cr mask.** The key challenge is LiF formation and re-deposition (melting point >800°C), which lowers etch rate and prevents vertical sidewalls. The solution is an iterative process: ICP-etch for several minutes, then clean in SC-1 solution (70% H2O, 20% H2O2, 10% NH4OH) for 1 minute to remove deposition, repeating until desired depth. Demonstrated ridges of 5.8 µm height and 8 µm width with nearly vertical walls, plus more complex microstructures.
- **ICP-etching of H+-exchanged X-cut LN (photonic crystal structures):** Proton exchange (PE) to 1.4 µm depth reduces Li concentration and thus LiF re-deposition, increasing etch rate and improving profiles. Process: PE of congruent X-cut LN, 110 nm Cr film sputtered, 120 nm photoresist, optical contact lithography (smallest features 170 nm), wet etching to transfer pattern to Cr, then repeated ICP-etching and SC-1 cleaning. This produced photonic crystal structures in PE-LN. Reverse proton exchange (RPE) can form buried waveguide profiles.
- **Wet etching of Z-cut LN (HF/HNO3 mixture):** A modified three-step process to fabricate low-loss Ti-doped ridge waveguides: (1) ridge fabrication using Cr-mask wet etching in a mixture of 21 ml HF (40%), 14 ml HNO3 (100%), and 5 ml ethanol; (2) selective Ti-stripe definition; (3) Ti-indiffusion at 1060°C for 8.5 hrs in Ar/O2. Resulting ridge guides (6.5 µm height, 10 µm top width) achieved TE losses dropping from 0.22 dB/cm at 5 µm width to 0.05 dB/cm at 7 µm width; TM losses 1.3 dB/cm at 5 µm and 0.36 dB/cm at 9 µm. Etching temperature can control ridge wall slope, enabling interdigital lamellas (2.6 µm width, 2.8 µm separation, 7.7 µm etching depth at 8°C).

**Kozlov, Moskalev, Salgaeva, Bulatova, Krishtop, Volyntsev & Syuy, "Reactive Ion Etching of X-Cut LiNbO3 in an ICP/TCP System for the Fabrication of an Optical Ridge Waveguide," Applied Sciences 13(4):2097, 2023 (DOI: 10.3390/app13042097):**

- Study of RIE of unmodified (non-proton-exchanged) X-cut LiNbO3 using a chromium hard mask in an SF6/Ar gas mixture with an ICP/TCP plasma source (Ethna-100 system).
- 80 nm Cr hard mask deposited via DC magnetron sputtering (500 W, Ar flow 0.7 L/h, 200°C), annealed at 300°C for 1 hour in dry N2; Cr mask LER measured at 20–30 nm.
- RIE parameters tested: ICP power 300–600 W, TCP power 50–200 W, pressure 0.007–0.8 mbar, etching time 8 min. Etching depths ranged 0.23–0.60 µm; mask selectivity 1:4 to 1:8; best slope angle 70–75°.
- **Recipe #13** (0.03 mbar pressure): slope angle ~62°, smooth near-waveguide surface, microtrenches formed at waveguide base, mask selectivity 1:5.3, bias voltage 186 V.
- **Recipe #14** (0.007 mbar pressure): slope angle ~75°, dramatically increased surface roughness in near-waveguide region, no microtrenches, mask selectivity improved to 1:8, bias voltage 141 V. EDX analysis of the surface revealed O:F:Nb = 18.56:36.56:44.88 wt%, with a brown film-like layer suggesting LiFx compound (Li not detectable with the tool).
- The difference in bias voltage (186 V vs 141 V) caused a transition from RIE to radical chemical etching. Based on Hoekstra et al.'s ion energy distribution data, estimated Ar+ ion average energies were ~90 eV (recipe #13), ~40 eV (transition region), and ~30 eV (recipe #14). A transition point from plasma-chemical etching to RIE was estimated between 30–90 eV ion energy. At ~90 eV, ion energies were sufficient to create vacancies in the LiF layer, enhancing diffusion of reaction products and surface sputtering (producing smooth surfaces). At lower energies, LiF layer blocks product out-diffusion causing swellings and rough surfaces.
- Microtrench formation (recipe #13) attributed to ion trajectory deflection toward sidewalls from electron accumulation — characteristic of RIE with significant physical plasma component at low pressure (<0.1 mbar) and high bias.
- A non-monotonic bias voltage vs. pressure relationship was found, with an inflection point at 0.05–0.03 mbar.

**Aryal, Stricklin, Behzadirad, Branch, Siddiqui & Busani, "High-Quality Dry Etching of LiNbO3 Assisted by Proton Substitution through H2-Plasma Surface Treatment," Nanomaterials 12(16):2836, 2022 (Editor's Choice):**

- Fluorine-based plasma etching of LN causes redeposition of LiF byproducts, reducing etch rate and preventing vertical etching profiles. Adding Argon enhances physical sputtering for more uniform profiles.
- Etching used **CHF3/Ar plasma (CHF3: 30 sccm, Ar: 30 sccm, pressure: 5 mTorr, RF power: 100 W, ICP power: 150 W, DC bias: 40 V)**. Argon enhanced sputtering and etch rate.
- A novel **H2-plasma pre-treatment** (H2: 30 sccm, pressure: 15 mTorr, RF power: 150 W, ICP power: 300 W, DC bias: 53 V) applied in the ICP chamber before lithography/metallization was used as a cost-effective alternative to the PE process. This substitutes protons for Li ions at the surface and relieves surface tension, remarkably improving Ti/Al/Cr mask quality on X- and Y-cuts.
- Structures with etch depths as deep as 3.4 µm were achieved with smooth sidewalls and near-perfect verticality (~3° offset) across crystallographic orientations (128YX, 128Y, 64Y bulk LN and X/Y thin-film LN on Si).
- Surface roughness was quantified using ImageJ with SurfChaJ plugin; RMS roughness ~10 for one sample and ~1.5 for another — representing state-of-the-art smooth sidewalls vs. previously reported 60°–78° verticality with rough sidewalls in other groups' work. 64Y bulk LN exhibited minimum surface roughness compared to other bulk LN and thin films on Si.
- Etch rates were nearly the same across orientations (with 64Y and 128Y cuts slightly lower); the reported etch rate ~650 nm/h for PE bulk LN is close to this study's bulk LN rate.

**Mi-Net Technology Application Note ("High-Quality Etching of Lithium Niobate Ridge Waveguides"):**
- SF6/Ar plasma mixtures on a SENTECH Instruments SI500 ICP plasma etcher have proven effective for producing smooth ridges. A Cr mask is used for its resistance to high bias power, preserving the etch profile and ensuring high selectivity.
- "Due to the low volatility of reaction by-products such as LiF and NbFx, relatively high bias power is required to physically remove these residues. Without sufficient energy, micro-masking can occur, resulting in surface roughness."
- Benefits: smooth LiNbO3 ridge waveguides with minimal optical loss, no sidewall redeposition, high etch selectivity and pattern fidelity using Cr masks.

**Mitsugi, Shima, Ishizuka & Nagata (Sumitomo Osaka Cement), "Analyses of LiNbO3 wafer surface etched by ECR plasma of CHF3 and CF4," 1998 Dry Process Symposium (paper VI-3, pp. 129–133):**
- ECR (electron cyclotron resonance) plasma of CHF3 and CF4 for fabricating high-speed (>40 Gb/s) LN optical modulators with ridge waveguides. Conditions: pressure ~1–4×10⁻² Pa, gas flow 3 sccm, microwave power 400 W, ion acceleration voltage 500 V, water-cooled (21°C) rotating substrate holder (17 rpm).
- Typical etching rates: 800 nm/h (CF4) and 700 nm/h (CHF3). Ni film masks (3 µm thick, electroplated) with etching rate ratio of LN:Ni of ~3.7; remaining Ni removed with dilute HNO3. The deviation in etched depth for a 3 in. diam substrate was ±20 nm for 240 nm deep etching by CHF3.
- AES analysis revealed that ECR-etched LN surfaces had significant fluorine and carbon contamination (LiF precipitates and polymers from the etching gases), causing weak adhesion between the SiO2 buffer layer and the etched LN surface, leading to electrode and buffer layer peeling at the LN/SiO2 boundary.
- Notch lines grew along ridge waveguide feet during CF4 ECR etching, causing catastrophic waveguide breakage. F and C contaminants were successfully removed by either wet etching with dilute HNO3 or O2 annealing at 600°C for 1 hour (O2 plasma ashing also tested).
- The notch problem was solved by switching the etching gas from CF4 to CHF3, which produced clean ridge waveguides (4–5 µm height) without notches across the entire 3-inch wafer.

**Milenin (Academia.edu summary of same 2006 JVST A paper):** Etching selectivity of PE-LN to the chromium mask was 32:1 under optimal conditions (approximately 46:1 with SF6). SF6 achieved an etching rate of approximately 1.5 µm/h for PE-LN, significantly higher than for pure lithium niobate. SF6 produces underetching and asymmetric etching, while CHF3/Ar produces nearly vertical walls.

### Chlorine-based and mixed chemistries (Cl2, BCl3, Cl2/BCl3, Cl2/Ar/H2)

**Huang, Liu & Wu, "Characteristic of LiNbO3 thin film ICP etching for micro/nano fabrication," J. Micromech. Microeng. 36(3):035002, 2026 (DOI: 10.1088/1361-6439/ae36b6):**
- Systematically investigated and optimized ICP etching by varying RF bias power, chamber pressure, and Cl2/Ar/H2 gas flow ratios.
- **Optimized ICP etching recipe: ICP power of 600 W, RF bias power of 120 W, chamber pressure of 10 mTorr, and gas flow rates of Cl2/H2/Ar = 10/20/50 sccm.**
- This recipe achieved a steep sidewall angle of 79.1°, an etching rate of approximately 32 nm/min, and a selectivity of 1.43:1 relative to a SiO2 mask.
- A five-step ICP reaction model for the Cl2/H2/Ar recipe is proposed, elucidating the synergistic mechanisms of chemical chlorination, hydrogen-assisted oxygen removal, and argon-ion-induced anisotropic etching.
- Ion beam etching (IBE) was first investigated (DC bias 300–500 V) but showed limitations including low etching rates and surface roughness; ICP etching proved superior by enabling synergistic regulation of physical bombardment and chemical reactions.
- Using the optimized process, LiNbO3 lateral vibration resonators (LVRs) were successfully fabricated, with a representative resonator operating at ~400 MHz exhibiting a quality factor exceeding 1750.
- Prior work cited: Bahadori et al. (2019) achieving 1.45:1 selectivity and 83° sidewall angle using Ar/Cl2/BCl3; Shen et al. (2020) achieving ~80° sidewall angle.

**Shen, Hu, Dai, Yu, Tan, Sun, Jiang & Jiang, "Advanced Etching Techniques of LiNbO3 Nanodevices," Nanomaterials 13(20):2789, 2023 (DOI: 10.3390/nano13202789):**
- Ten X-cut, 5 mol.% Mg-doped LNO samples with different mask types (Cr, Ni, SiO2) etched in RIE and ICP tools.
- **Sample 9 (Ni mask, ICP):** 79 nm/min, ~83° sidewall angle (best ICP result).
- **Sample 10 (SiO2 mask, ICP with SF6/BCl3/Ar):** 108 nm/min etching rate, 0.86:1 selectivity, ~65° sidewall angle.
- **Sample 8 (Cr mask, ICP):** 37 nm/min, ~71° angle, but Cr mask severely consumed under high-density plasma.
- RIE results: Sample 1 (Cr mask, RIE): 10 nm/min, ~60° sidewall angle, 3:1 selectivity. Sample 2 (Ni mask, RIE): 11 nm/min, ~72° sidewall angle, 5.5:1 selectivity. Sample 5 (Cr mask, high-temp reduction + RIE): 11.5 nm/min, ~85° sidewall angle.
- Ni masks outperform Cr masks in both RIE and ICP due to higher hardness and better shape retention.

### Argon (Ar) sputtering/ion milling chemistries

**Ulliac, Calero, Ndao, Baida & Bernal, "Argon plasma inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etching study for smooth sidewall thin film lithium niobate waveguide application," Optical Materials 53:1–5, 2016:**
- Fabricated ridge waveguides on 700 nm thickness thin film lithium niobate (TFLN) using argon plasma etching on an ICP-RIE system rather than fluorine-containing gases.
- Using argon plasma eliminates the problem of LiF redeposition that occurs with fluorine-based gases (CF4, SF6, CHF3).
- Etching used argon-based chemistry at low pressure (2 mTorr) with an S1828 photoresist layer as the etching mask (with a soft post-bake to increase etching selectivity).
- Fabrication was optimized in three key steps: mask fabrication, plasma etching parameters, and a final wet chemical cleaning step to remove lithium niobate redeposition on side walls.
- Results: single mode propagation achieved with overall optical losses of only 5 dB/cm at 1550 nm — superior to previously demonstrated argon etching of photonic wires with propagation losses of 7.5 dB/cm and 9.9 dB/cm for both light polarizations.
- Parametric study was performed on 1.1×1.2 cm² chips of X-cut 500 µm thickness lithium niobate before fine-tuning on a 3-inch X-cut 700 nm thickness LN film bonded to an LN substrate via a 2 µm SiO2 layer (NanoLN).
- Background notes: ion-beam enhanced etching showed losses around 61 dB/cm; Ti in-diffusion and proton exchange waveguides offer low losses (0.01 dB/cm) but suffer from large mode sizes.

**Kaufmann, Finco, Maeder & Grange, "Redeposition-free inductively-coupled plasma etching of lithium niobate for integrated photonics," Nanophotonics 12(8):1601, 2023 (DOI: 10.1515/nanoph-2022-0676):**
- Addresses Ar sputtering of LNOI waveguides, which provides the best optical quality but suffers from micro-masking effects caused by material redeposition and close-to-one etch mask selectivity. Argon (Ar) based processes "have been shown to provide the smoothest sidewalls and allow the manufacturing of photonic integrated circuits of the best optical quality, with reported propagation losses as low as 2.7 dB/m in multimode structures operating in the telecom C-band."
- Etching performed in a Plasma Pro 100 (Oxford Instruments) ICP system. Only Cl2, SF6, O2, and Ar gases were used, as CHF3 was found to contaminate the chamber and harm reproducibility. Etch depth (200–250 nm) was controlled via interferometric endpointing (Horiba, 670.1 nm).
- **DC bias sweep (Ar flow 10 sccm, pressure 1 mTorr, 20 °C):** Sweeping DC bias from 100 V to 800 V showed total redeposition decreased almost fourfold from 100 V to 800 V, trending toward redeposition-free etching above 1 kV (though not readily achievable). Trench depth increased by a factor of five with higher bias. Selectivity remained near one; sidewall angle 60–63° for both +Z and −Z crystal faces. Sample bow changed from concave to flat to convex with increasing bias: 300 V gave 20 nm thickness variation over 8×8 mm², while 600 V gave below 5 nm. Surface roughness (Sq) was ~0.08 nm for biases above 200 V, four times better than the un-etched surface (0.31 nm).
- **Chamber pressure sweep:** Sweeping pressure from 1 to 15 mTorr (400 V) and 0.3 to 13 mTorr (600 V) showed redeposition vanishing completely after 7 mTorr, but with significant structural damage. Redeposition-free regime occurred at 5–7 mTorr for 600 V (preferred DC bias) and around 11 mTorr for 400 V. Etch rates dropped to minimum values of 27 nm/min (400 V) and 12 nm/min (600 V) before increasing again at higher pressures. Surface roughness degraded with pressure (Sq of 0.10, 0.12, 0.15 nm for 3, 5, 7 mTorr).
- **Aspect ratio dependent etching (ARDE):** Redeposition decreased with decreasing gap size (from 1 µm to 100 nm) due to ions bouncing between sidewalls. Trench merging occurred at gaps up to 400 nm, with loading effects below 400 nm. Dense structures were redeposition-free down to 1 µm gaps at 300 W ICP power, 600 V DC bias, and 11 mTorr.
- **Etch depth and IBE:** Redeposition decreased with increasing etch depth (110–260 nm). Ion beam etching (IBE) experiments at incidence angles 0°–35° simulating trapezoidal masks (85°, 70°, 60°, 50°) showed reduced redeposition with increasing angle, confirming trapezoidal masks help achieve redeposition-free etching.
- **Reproducibility and optical results:** Four samples etched with 300 W ICP power, 600 V DC bias, 1 mTorr showed excellent reproducibility with Q-factor variation below 2% and calculated propagation loss of 1.55 dB/cm. Etch rate scaled linearly: 0.09 nm/min per watt of ICP power and 0.10 nm/min per volt of DC bias. Optical measurements used ring/racetrack resonators with 600 nm top width, 80 µm bend radius, operating near 1550 nm; a resonance linewidth of 25 pm was observed.

**IEEE Spectrum article (A. Hellemans, Jan 16, 2018) and Design World (M. Crouse) on Harvard (Lončar group) work:**
- Applied plasma reactive ion etching — bombarding the chip surface with argon ions to remove material exposed by an electron-beam lithography mask — to create micro-ring and micro-racetrack resonators (~1 micrometer wide, 80 µm curvature radius).
- Results showed optical power losses of only 50% over 1 meter, versus 99% loss in previous lithium niobate devices — a dramatic improvement attributed to better optical confinement. Marko Lončar: "Diamond is actually easier to etch than niobate, but it doesn't exist as thin films."

**NIST paper (Kumar, Klimov & Kuo, "Optimization of waveguide fabrication processes in lithium-niobate-on-insulator platform," NIST Author Manuscripts):**
- 4-inch LNOI wafer (700 nm x-cut film, 2 µm SiO2 insulation, 525 µm Si substrate from NANOLN) diced into 10×10 mm² chips. LN etching performed in Oxford PlasmaLab 100 ICP RIE tool with Ar gas; ICP power 1500 W, pressure 5 mTorr, Ar flow 20 sccm, temperature 5°C. Etch performed in 1-minute segments with 5-minute cooldown periods to prevent thermal damage.
- **RF Power Optimization:** RF power varied from 50 W to 500 W; etch rate ranged from 50 nm/min (50 W) to 107 nm/min (500 W). At low RF power (~50 W), sidewalls fully enveloped by redeposit; at 300 W, redeposit completely eliminated from sidewalls. However, above 300 W, line-edge roughness transferred to the WG causing striations, and WG damage (trenches/pits) occurred. Optimal RF power range determined as 100–200 W.
- **Redeposit Cleaning:** RCA-1a solution (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O = 2:2:1) heated to 85°C was superior to Piranha and RCA-1b. Optimized cleaning: 15 minutes each at 0° and 90° boat orientations (30 min total). Prolonged cleaning (beyond 30 min) caused chipping and peeling of WGs. Cleaning for 24 hours changed WG geometry (sidewall angles became asymmetric, film thickness reduced from 700 nm to ~630 nm). Properly cleaned samples had equal sidewall angles of ~70°.
- **Soft vs. Hard Mask:** Soft (resist) mask produced striated sidewall defects that persisted regardless of RF power tuning; Cr hard mask produced markedly improved sidewall profiles. Cr hard mask produced granular features on sidewalls (due to Cr polycrystalline grain size of ~55 nm), while SiO2 mask produced striations and "trenching" at the base of sidewalls (attributed to charge buildup on insulating materials deflecting ions). Cr hard mask was selected for final fabrication.
- **Optical Characterization:** Rib LNOI WGs fabricated with Cr mask using optimized parameters (RF 150 W, ICP 1500 W, 5 mTorr, 20 sccm Ar, 5°C, 30 min cleaning). WG dimensions: top width 600 nm, sidewall angle 70°, rib height 350 nm over 350 nm slab, single-mode at 1550 nm. Eight identical 4.5 mm straight WGs measured with lensed fibers: average transmission 8.9 ± 1.3%, corresponding to -10.5 ± 0.6 dB total insertion loss. Upper-bound propagation loss estimated at ~2 dB/cm (assuming 4.8 dB/facet coupling loss).

**Ar ion milling + GCIB smoothing (Optics Express 26(4), 2018, via HAL, "Ultra-low loss ridge waveguides on lithium niobate via argon ion milling and gas clustered ion beam smoothening"):**
- Two-step process: argon ion milling followed by gas clustered ion beam (GCIB) smoothening. Z-cut LNOI wafer (700 nm thick LN). Fabrication: 100 nm Cr deposition as hard mask, 300 nm ma-N 2403 negative resist patterned via e-beam lithography, Cr removal and argon ion milling of 700 nm LN, then GCIB smoothening.
- Argon ion milling: initial high-power milling at 7° off normal (17 nm/min, ~40 min for 680 nm), followed by a low-power 3-min step at 60° off normal for intermediate smoothing. ICP with fluorine was avoided because it reacted with sidewalls and redeposited lithium fluoride.
- GCIB: argon ion clusters (many nm in diameter) accelerated to bombard sidewalls, with monomer ions filtered out via analyzing magnet; samples mounted at an angle.
- SEM images showed clear sidewall smoothening after GCIB; AFM measured RMS roughness of ~8.3 nm (Rq) and 6.9 nm (Ra) on 800×800 nm scan region.
- Propagation losses measured using Fabry-Perot resonance method: best results were 0.268 dB/cm (TE, 7 µm waveguide) and 0.33 dB/cm (TE, 5 µm waveguide). TM losses were higher, especially at smaller widths. Authors claim the lowest reported etched ridge waveguide losses at the time: 0.33 dB/cm for a 5 µm waveguide with 700 nm deep etching. Comparisons: etched rib waveguide 17.4 dB/cm; optical dicing 1.2 dB/cm TE; wet etched ridge 7 dB/cm TE; RIE + wet etching 55 dB/cm.

### Atomic Layer Etching (ALE) — sequential plasma exposure chemistries

**Caltech/Oxford Instruments/JPL, "Isotropic atomic layer etching of MgO-doped lithium niobate using sequential exposures of H2 and SF6/Ar plasmas" (arXiv:2310.10592, published version in Nanophotonics 2024):**
- First ALE process for lithium niobate. Isotropic ALE for x-cut MgO-doped LN using sequential exposures of H2 and SF6/Ar plasmas.
- Etch rate of 1.59 ± 0.02 nm/cycle with a synergy of 96.9%. Both half-steps exhibit saturation (self-limiting behavior); the SF6/Ar step shows soft saturation attributed to a hydrogen concentration gradient into the LN film. The H2 plasma half-step alone produced a thickness increase (attributed to amorphization volume expansion); the SF6/Ar step alone gave 0.06 nm/cycle.
- **Alternate recipes:** SF6/O2 plasma replacement: EPC of 2.24 ± 0.02 nm/cycle, synergy of 99.5%. Cl2/BCl3 plasma replacement: EPC of 1.65 ± 0.03 nm/cycle, synergy of 91.5%. SF6/Ar recipe at saturation produced the smoothest surface (Rq = 0.57 ± 0.18 nm after 20 cycles).
- **Surface smoothing:** The ALE process reduced sidewall surface roughness of TFLN waveguides etched by physical Ar+ milling by 30% (from Rq = 0.82 ± 0.25 nm to 0.55 ± 0.13 nm) after 50 cycles, without additional wet processing. The lateral etch rate was 1 nm/cycle per side, confirming the largely isotropic nature. PSD decreased over all measured spatial frequencies.
- **Exact recipe:** 40-second H2 plasma exposure (300 W ICP, 52.5 W RIE, 209 V DC bias, 50 sccm H2) followed by 40-second SF6/Ar exposure (300 W ICP, 3.5 W RIE, 50 V DC bias, 17 sccm SF6, 35 sccm Ar), with 5-second Ar purges between steps. Chamber pressure 10 mTorr, substrate cooled to 0°C. Performed in an Oxford Instruments PlasmaPro 100 Cobra system.
- XPS Analysis: After ALE, increased F, Li, and Mg fractions were observed, with evidence of LiF and MgF2 formation and redeposition (peak shifts of 0.3 eV for Nb4s and Li1s, 0.6 eV for Mg2p). Surface lithium content increased after H2 plasma exposure.

**Caltech/Oxford Instruments/JPL, "Directional atomic layer etching of lithium niobate using Br-based chemistry" (arXiv:2511.01825):**
- First directional ALE process for LN using sequential exposures of HBr/BCl3/Ar plasma (40s, 300 W ICP, 5 W RIE, 30 V DC bias) followed by Ar plasma (60s, 300 W ICP, 6 W RIE, 45 V DC bias) at 10 mTorr chamber pressure.
- At 0°C: etch per cycle (EPC) of 1.04±0.01 nm/cycle with 84.6% synergy; half-cycle EPCs were 0.02 nm/cycle (HBr/BCl3/Ar) and 0.14 nm/cycle (Ar). At 200°C: EPC increased to 1.25 nm/cycle but synergy dropped to 30% (due to increased spontaneous etching and ion energy distribution); surface remained atomically smooth (Rq=0.25±0.03 nm after 20 cycles, unchanged from control).
- HBr chemistry reduces redeposition compared to F- and Cl-based plasmas due to higher vapor pressures of Br-based etch products. A Cl2/BCl3 comparison process produced rougher surfaces at the same temperature.
- An isotropic HBr-based ALE process was also developed (H2 plasma + HBr/BCl3/Ar plasma) yielding 1.43 nm/cycle with 97.9% synergy at 0°C and smoother surfaces (Rq=0.77 nm) than previously reported Cl2/BCl3 chemistry.
- XPS analysis showed surface bromine concentration of 0.50±0.04% after 50 cycles at 0°C, decreasing to 0.35±0.06% at 200°C, confirming better removal of Br etch products at higher temperature.
- A TFLN grating structure (total etch depth 223 nm, 200 cycles) etched entirely by ALE at 200°C showed NO aspect ratio dependent etching (ARDE) down to the smallest tested gap of 150 nm, in contrast to ion milling where ARDE manifests at gaps below 300 nm for similar depths.
- 50 cycles of ALE on a TFLN waveguide chip reduced surface roughness from Rq=2.07 nm to Rq=0.34 nm (84% reduction), with minimal lateral etching (waveguide top width maintained). At 200°C, 120 cycles (149 nm etch) produced no surface roughening (Rq=0.28 nm).
- Bulk 3-inch 5% MgO-doped LN wafers (G & H Photonics), diced to 7×7 mm substrates; patterned with AZ5214E photoresist (0°C) or HSQ via e-beam lithography (200°C); etched in Oxford Instruments PlasmaPro 100 Cobra system.

## (b) ICP/RF Power Levels, Chuck Bias Voltage/Power, Process Pressure, and Substrate/Chuck Temperature Effects

### Temperature effects

**Osipov, Alexandrov & Iankevich, "The effect of a lithium niobate heating on the etching rate in SF6 ICP plasma," Materials Research Express 6:046306, 2019 (DOI: 10.1088/2053-1591/aafa9d):**
- Custom substrate holder with built-in heater; Z-cut single-crystal LiNbO3 substrates (76.2 mm diameter, 370 µm thickness) from MTI Corporation, with Cr-Cu-Ni and Cr-Cu-Cr masks. Fixed parameters: ICP power 700 W at 6.78 MHz, SF6 flow 10.15 sccm, O2 flow 3.0 sccm, bias voltage −50 V, pressure 0.75 Pa. Substrate temperatures ranged 373–598 K, 10-minute etching times.
- **Etching rate showed a complex, three-region dependence on substrate temperature:**
  - First region (373–423 K): Small increases in etching rate (only 31 nm/min growth).
  - Second region (423–523 K): Large, nearly linear growth in etching rate, reaching 711 nm/min at 523 K, attributed to thermally activated etching reactions.
  - Third region (523–598 K): Sharp decrease in rate increment due to formation of non-volatile LiF compounds that block chemically active particle delivery.
- Maximum etching rate achieved was 812 nm/min at 598 K (more than 800 nm/min), double prior rates that used higher source powers but no additional substrate heating, with ICP power below 1000 W.
- **Gas mixture comparison:** SF6/O2 mixtures were significantly more effective than SF6/Ar at 598 K: 812 nm/min versus 337 nm/min etching rate, and surface roughness Rms = 30.52 nm versus 119.37 nm respectively. The SF6/O2 mixture provided four times lower RMS roughness.
- **Deep etching experiment:** A 270-minute deep etch produced a 113.7 µm deep profile (etching rate of 421 nm/min) at T = 523 K and Ub = −80 V, with hydrofluoric acid treatments (30 s) applied after every 90 minutes to remove non-volatile LiF. Sidewall angle was 78° due to increased isotropic chemical etching; selectivity to Cr-Cu-Cr mask exceeded 77.

**Osipov, Osipov, Iankevich, Speshilova, Shakhmin, Berezenko & Alexandrov, "Deep Etching of LiNbO3 Using Inductively Coupled Plasma in SF6-Based Gas Mixture," J. Microelectromech. Syst. 30(1):90–95, 2021 (DOI: 10.1109/JMEMS.2020.3039350):**
- Plasma chemical etching (PCE) of single-crystalline LiNbO3 in SF6/O2-based ICP. Increasing substrate holder temperature from 100°C to 200°C gradually raises the etching rate from 127 to 282 nm/min. Further increase to 250°C results in a sharp jump to 711 nm/min. Maximum achieved rate was 812 nm/min at a substrate holder temperature of 325°C.
- XPS revealed that a nonvolatile LiF compound forms on the treated LiNbO3 surface during etching in fluorinated plasma.
- An optimal deep etching process (>80 µm) was developed with an etched wall inclination angle of ≈110°, a selectivity ratio to Cr mask of ≈20, and an etching rate of about 300 nm/min.
- Notes that typical ICP etching rates for LiNbO3 range from 50–150 nm/min at RF power up to 1000 W, with rates up to 350 nm/min achievable at 2000 W RF power. The main challenge in forming deep structures is the generation of non-volatile LiF compound on the etching surface, which slows or can completely stop the etching process.

**Hu et al. 2006 (JVST A):** Etching rate nearly doubled (2.88 to 5.76 µm/h) without He-backside cooling due to NbF5 volatility (boiling point ~234°C). This temperature dependence confirms the role of NbF5 volatility in the process. (See also section (a).)

**Aryal et al. 2022:** Periodic process implemented: 20 min etching followed by 4 min cooling (plasma off), with chemical cleaning (Acetone, IPA, DI water, N2 blow) after each 1 hour of etching to prevent heating effects (LN has low thermal conductivity) and byproduct redeposition.

**NIST paper (Kumar, Klimov & Kuo):** Etch performed at temperature 5°C, in 1-minute segments with 5-minute cooldown periods to prevent thermal damage.

**Kaufmann et al. 2023:** Etching performed at 20 °C (DC bias sweep); substrate temperature influence not the focus but noted for reproducibility.

### Pressure effects

**Kaufmann et al. 2023 (see section (a) for details):** Redeposition-free regime occurred at 5–7 mTorr for 600 V DC bias and around 11 mTorr for 400 V. Etch rates dropped to minimum values of 27 nm/min (400 V) and 12 nm/min (600 V) before increasing again at higher pressures. Surface roughness degraded with pressure (Sq of 0.10, 0.12, 0.15 nm for 3, 5, 7 mTorr). Lower pressures favored for surface quality.

**Kozlov et al. 2023:** Pressure tested 0.007–0.8 mbar; recipe #13 at 0.03 mbar gave slope angle ~62°, smooth near-waveguide surface, microtrenches, mask selectivity 1:5.3, bias 186 V; recipe #14 at 0.007 mbar gave slope ~75°, increased roughness, no microtrenches, selectivity 1:8, bias 141 V.

**Huang et al. 2026:** Chamber pressure 10 mTorr in optimized Cl2/H2/Ar recipe.

**Ulliac et al. 2016:** Argon-based chemistry at low pressure (2 mTorr).

**Hu et al. 2006:** CHF3/Ar at 6 mTorr chamber pressure and 130 V dc bias optimal; CF4 and SF6 at 500 mTorr (parallel plate RIE).

### Bias/RF power effects

**Kaufmann et al. 2023:** DC bias sweep 100 V to 800 V (Ar flow 10 sccm, pressure 1 mTorr, 20°C): total redeposition decreased almost fourfold; trench depth increased fivefold; selectivity remained near one; sidewall angle 60–63°; Sq ~0.08 nm for biases above 200 V (vs 0.31 nm un-etched). Etch rate scaled linearly: 0.09 nm/min per watt of ICP power and 0.10 nm/min per volt of DC bias.

**Kozlov et al. 2023:** Bias voltage difference between recipes (186 V vs 141 V) caused a transition from RIE to radical chemical etching; Ar+ ion average energies ~90 eV (recipe #13) vs ~30 eV (recipe #14); transition point between 30–90 eV ion energy. At ~100 eV, vacancies form in LiF layer, increasing diffusion of reaction products and enhancing surface sputtering, yielding smoother surfaces. At lower energies, LiF layer blocks product out-diffusion causing swellings and rough surfaces.

**NIST paper (Kumar, Klimov & Kuo):** RF power varied 50–500 W; etch rate 50–107 nm/min. At low RF power (~50 W), sidewalls fully enveloped by redeposit; at 300 W, redeposit eliminated. Above 300 W, LER transferred causing striations and WG damage. Optimal RF power range 100–200 W.

**Chang, Yu, Hsieh, Lin, Huang, Lin, Kao, Hsiao & Shiao, "A parametric study of ICP-RIE etching on a lithium niobate substrate," 10th IEEE NEMS, 2015 (DOI: 10.1109/NEMS.2015.7147473):**
- Under suitable ICP-RIE processing parameters on LiNbO3, achieved surface roughness less than 40 nm, structure depth greater than 3 µm, and sidewall angle estimated at 120°, all within 28 minutes, corresponding to an etching rate greater than 117 nm/min.

**Ren, Heard, Marshall, Thomas & Yu, "Etching characteristics of LiNbO3 in reactive ion etching and inductively coupled plasma," J. Appl. Phys. 103:034109, 2008 (DOI: 10.1063/1.2838180):**
- Studied congruent LiNbO3 single crystals, including doped LiNbO3 and proton-exchanged LiNbO3, in RIE and ICP tools with different gas mixture recipes. Examined effects of working pressure, RIE power, and ICP power, analyzed through etching depth, selectivity, uniformity, etched surface state, and sidewall profile. Also investigated the effects of a sample carrier wafer coating. Optimized processes with high etching rates, good mask selectivity, and near-vertical profiles were achieved. Ridge waveguides on proton-exchanged LiNbO3 were fabricated and optically measured.

**Parker et al., "High verticality InP/InGaAsP etching in Cl2/H2/Ar inductively coupled plasma," J. Vac. Sci. Technol. B, 2011 (related III-V process-relevant study):**
- Optimal etch conditions at 800 W ICP, 125 W RIE with gas flows of 9 SCCM Cl2, 19 SCCM H2, and 2 SCCM Ar at 1.5 mTorr. Achieved selectivity ~20:1 (InP:SiO2), etch rate 24 nm/s, sidewall slope angle 89.2°–89.5° for ~7 µm depths. Optimal H2 fraction 62%–66% of total flow. Verticality maintained for pressures ≤2 mTorr. Ar flow should be minimized to reduce surface etch damage while maintaining stable plasma conditions.

## (c) Etch Mask Selection and Its Impact on Etch-Induced Damage

### Chromium (Cr) masks

- **Mi-Net:** Cr mask used for its resistance to high bias power, preserving the etch profile and ensuring high selectivity. SF6/Ar + Cr gives smooth ridges, no sidewall redeposition, high selectivity and pattern fidelity.
- **Hu et al. 2006:** 120–400 nm Cr mask; PE-LN/Cr selectivity 32:1 (CHF3/Ar, no cooling), 46:1 (SF6), 3.43:1 (CF4), 48:1 (CHF3/Ar He-cooled), 30:1 (SF6 ICP-RIE).
- **Hu/Ricken/Sohler ECIO 2008:** Cr mask with C4F8/He ICP etching; 110 nm Cr film for PE-LN photonic crystals.
- **Kozlov et al. 2023:** 80 nm Cr hard mask via DC magnetron sputtering; Cr mask LER 20–30 nm; selectivity 1:4 to 1:8; best slope 70–75°.
- **Shen et al. 2023:** Cr mask RIE: 10 nm/min, ~60° sidewall, 3:1 selectivity. Cr mask ICP: 37 nm/min, ~71° angle, but Cr mask severely consumed under high-density plasma. Cr mask + high-temp reduction + RIE: 11.5 nm/min, ~85°. Cr mask RIE + Al layer + annealing + wet etch: ~115 nm depth, perfect 90° sidewall angle — the optimized hybrid process that preserves ferroelectric properties.
- **NIST (Kumar et al.):** Cr hard mask (50 nm, e-beam deposition) produced granular features on sidewalls (due to Cr polycrystalline grain size of ~55 nm), but was selected over SiO2 for final fabrication. Soft (resist) mask produced striated sidewall defects that persisted regardless of RF power tuning; Cr hard mask produced markedly improved sidewall profiles.
- **Latitude Design Systems:** EBL + ion milling with hard masks (e.g., chromium) resistant to milling, optimized ion energy/current, and multi-step etching achieved waveguide losses as low as 0.027 dB/cm and Q factors >10^7.

### Nickel (Ni) masks

- **Shen et al. 2023:** Ni mask RIE: 11 nm/min, ~72° sidewall, 5.5:1 selectivity. Ni mask ICP: 79 nm/min, ~83° sidewall angle (best ICP result). "Ni masks outperform Cr masks in both RIE and ICP due to higher hardness."
- **FEMTO-ST Institute (Microelectronic Engineering 105:95–98, 2013), "Electroplated Ni mask for plasma etching of submicron-sized lithium niobate" (via HAL):**
  - 50 nm seed layer (10 nm Cr + 40 nm Ni) DC sputtered onto X-cut LiNbO3 chip (1.5 cm × 1.5 cm); 450 nm-thick negative e-beam resist (maN 2405); Ni electroplated from nickel sulfamate bath at 50°C, current density 15 mA/cm², to 350 nm thickness; resist stripped in NMP (Remover 1165).
  - LiNbO3 etched via RIE using SF6 chemistry (10 sccm, 2 µb pressure, 220 W RF power).
  - Ni mask achieved 350 nm thickness with perfectly vertical profile (angle ≈ 90°). High air filling fraction holey arrays achieved: 1800 nm diameter openings with 300 nm inter-hole spacing, or 330 nm diameter holes spaced by 440 nm.
  - LiNbO3/Ni selectivity close to 6 with etch rate ~6 nm/min. Nanometric holes etched in LiNbO3 exhibit sidewall slope angles of ~60°.
  - Post-etch cleaning in NH4OH/H2O2/H2O (1:2:7) solution removes LiF residue; Ni mask removed in Cl3Fe, Cr seed layer removed in commercial Cr wet etchant.
  - "A metallic mask is essential, because organic resists are etched faster than LiNbO3. Electroplated metals are an interesting alternative to sputtered or evaporated metallic masks... electroplating allows obtaining high aspect-ratio, high filling fraction patterns."
- **Mitsugi et al. 1998:** Ni film masks (3 µm thick, electroplated) with LN:Ni etch rate ratio ~3.7; remaining Ni removed with dilute HNO3.

### Titanium (Ti), Aluminum (Al), and Gold masks

- **Aryal et al. 2022:** Hard mask deposition of Titanium (Ti), Aluminum (Al), and Chromium (Cr). Ti/Al stack (20 nm/1.3 µm) works on all LN cuts, but Ti/Al/Cr (20 nm/750 nm/750 nm) peeled off on X- and Y-cuts on Si substrate due to crystal orientation and stress from LN film transfer onto Si. Ti/Al mask caused redeposition of Al byproducts ("pyramids"/"cones"), prevented by protecting Al with a Cr layer since CrF4 byproducts are more volatile than AlF3. Metal masks removed using diluted HF.
- **Randles 2002 thesis (RIT):** Chrome gold mask used with HF/HNO3 wet etching at 90°C, achieving 50 µm/hour etch rate on the -z face and 250 nm/hour on the +z face.

### Dielectric masks (SiO2, SiNx, HSQ)

- **Shen et al. 2023:** SiO2 mask, ICP with SF6/BCl3/Ar: 108 nm/min etching rate, 0.86:1 selectivity, ~65° sidewall angle. SiO2 masks enable semiconductor-process compatibility. SiO2 mask + high-temp reduction + SC-1 wet etch: ~49 nm depth, asymmetric sidewalls (44° in +Z, 85° in −Z).
- **Huang et al. 2026:** SiO2 mask with optimized Cl2/H2/Ar recipe: selectivity 1.43:1 relative to SiO2 mask.
- **NIST (Kumar et al.):** SiO2 hard mask (500 nm PECVD + 10 nm Cr) produced striations and "trenching" at the base of sidewalls (attributed to charge buildup on insulating materials deflecting ions); Cr mask preferred.
- **Hou et al., "Improved selectivity in dry etching of lithium niobate with thermal annealed hydrogen silsesquioxane mask," Nanotechnology 2025:** The low dry etching selectivity between TFLN and HSQ resist can be improved by thermal annealing of HSQ masks before dry etching. The LN/HSQ etching selectivity increases from 0.55 to ~1 when the developed HSQ masks are annealed, while microring Q factor tests confirm optical losses remain unchanged.
- **Kaufmann et al. 2023:** Used HSQ-based flowable oxide (FOX16) as negative resist (~500 nm thick) patterned by 100 kV EBL. Proposed trapezoidal masks via SiO2 PECVD hard mask deposition, or SiNx/a-Si which can be removed without damaging the thermal oxide layer.
- **KTH thesis (Mohamedelhassan, 2012):** Proton exchange (PE) weakens the LiNbO3 surface structure, enhancing dry etching rate, allowing use of standard photoresist masks instead of more expensive Chromium masks. Ridge waveguides fabricated on both -Z and +Z faces of undoped and MgO-doped congruent LiNbO3; etching depths ~500 nm on undoped and ~300 nm on MgO-doped.

### Photoresist masks

- **Ulliac et al. 2016:** S1828 photoresist layer as etching mask with soft post-bake to increase etching selectivity; argon at 2 mTorr.
- **NIST (Kumar et al.):** Soft e-beam resist mask produced striated sidewall defects that persisted regardless of RF power tuning.
- **Awan, "Navigating plasma etching of photonic chips in shared cleanrooms," J. Phys. Photonics 7:046001, 2025 (tutorial):** Positive-tone resists (ZEP520A, PMMA) used when large areas need masking; negative-tone resists (HSQ, ma-N 2400 series) when small areas need masking. HSQ exhibits inherently lower LER than organic resists due to its inorganic short-chain structure. Low-temperature EBL development suppresses resist swelling and reduces mask LER. Etch selectivity defined as s = substrate etch rate / mask etch rate; selectivity can be improved by lowering RIE power or increasing pressure.

## (d) Process Sequencing Tricks

### Iterative/interrupted etching with wet clean steps

- **Hu/Ricken/Sohler ECIO 2008:** Iterative process for C4F8/He ICP etching of X-cut LN: ICP-etch for several minutes, then clean in SC-1 solution (70% H2O, 20% H2O2, 10% NH4OH) for 1 minute to remove LiF deposition, repeating until desired depth. Demonstrated ridges of 5.8 µm height and 8 µm width with nearly vertical walls.
- **Aryal et al. 2022:** Periodic process: 20 min etching followed by 4 min cooling (plasma off), with chemical cleaning (Acetone, IPA, DI water, N2 blow) after each 1 hour of etching to prevent heating effects (LN has low thermal conductivity) and byproduct redeposition. Etch depths as deep as 3.4 µm achieved with smooth sidewalls and near-perfect verticality (~3° offset).
- **NIST (Kumar et al.):** Etch performed in 1-minute segments with 5-minute cooldown periods to prevent thermal damage; post-etch cleaning in RCA-1a (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O = 2:2:1) heated to 85°C, 15 minutes each at 0° and 90° boat orientations (30 min total).
- **Ulliac et al. 2016:** Three-step optimization: mask fabrication, plasma etching parameters, and a final wet chemical cleaning step to remove lithium niobate redeposition on side walls. Achieved 5 dB/cm overall losses.

### Soft-landing / low-bias final steps and multi-step recipes

- **Ar ion milling + GCIB smoothing (Optics Express 2018):** Two-step process — initial high-power argon ion milling at 7° off normal (17 nm/min, ~40 min for 680 nm), followed by a low-power 3-min step at 60° off normal for intermediate smoothing, then gas clustered ion beam (GCIB) smoothening. Achieved 0.268 dB/cm (TE, 7 µm) and 0.33 dB/cm (TE, 5 µm).
- **Kaufmann et al. 2023 (three proposed methods for redeposition-free etching):** (1) careful balancing of ICP parameters (especially DC bias and chamber pressure); (2) increasing structure density so ion deflection between neighboring walls aids redeposition removal; (3) tailoring the etching mask toward a trapezoidal shape. Alternative approaches include using dense structures with positive masks, keeping a remaining slab near waveguides, or using trapezoidal masks (e.g., via SiO2 PECVD hard mask deposition, or SiNx/a-Si which can be removed without damaging the thermal oxide layer).
- **ALE post-processing (Caltech arXiv:2310.10592):** ALE can serve as a post-processing treatment after Ar+ milling to smooth sidewall roughness and corrugations in periodically-poled TFLN devices — 30% roughness reduction (Rq from 0.82±0.25 to 0.55±0.13 nm) after 50 cycles without wet processing. Directional ALE (arXiv:2511.01825): 50 cycles reduced roughness from Rq=2.07 nm to Rq=0.34 nm (84% reduction).
- **Osipov et al. 2019:** Deep etching with hydrofluoric acid treatments (30 s) applied after every 90 minutes to remove non-volatile LiF; achieved 113.7 µm depth at 421 nm/min.
- **Awan 2025 (shared cleanroom protocol):** Begin with high-power oxygen plasma clean (10–15 min at max ICP/RIE powers and highest O2 flow), then condition the chamber with the target etch chemistry on a dummy wafer (5–15 min). Operate near lowest base pressure (typically 10⁻⁶–10⁻⁸ Torr). Post-etch: oxygen plasma + solvent for polymer resists (ZEP520A, PMMA); dilute HF or BOE for HSQ (e.g., 20 s in 10% HF). Wet post-processing after dry etch can smooth rough sidewalls and reduce propagation losses.

### Plasma pre-clean steps

- **Aryal et al. 2022:** Novel H2-plasma treatment (H2: 30 sccm, pressure: 15 mTorr, RF power: 150 W, ICP power: 300 W, DC bias: 53 V) applied in the ICP chamber before lithography/metallization as a cost-effective alternative to the PE process, substituting protons for Li ions at the surface and relieving surface tension, remarkably improving Ti/Al/Cr mask quality on X- and Y-cuts.

### Proton exchange (PE) as process pre-treatment

- **Hu et al. 2006:** PE in pure benzoic acid at 240°C for 5 hours (PE depth 2.8 µm) reduces Li concentration up to 85%, preventing LiF deposition. Etching rate ratio of approximately 3 between PE-LN and pure LN. Reverse proton exchange can restore LN optical properties after etching.
- **Hu/Ricken/Sohler ECIO 2008:** PE to 1.4 µm depth for photonic crystal structures; RPE can form buried waveguide profiles.
- **KTH thesis 2012:** PE increases extraordinary refractive index by ~0.12 at 633 nm, creating the guiding layer, and weakens the surface structure to enhance etching rate, allowing standard photoresist masks.
- **Shen et al. 2023:** PE at 180°C in molten benzoic acid for 0.5 h: 13 nm/min, ~70° sidewall, exchange depth ~210 nm, β1 phase detected by XRD. PE damages ferroelectric properties, making it unsuitable for domain-wall memory devices.
- **Deng, Si & Danner, "Dry etching of LiNbO3 using inductively coupled plasma," Photonics Global Conference, 2010 (DOI: 10.1109/PGC.2010.5706006):** Ridge waveguides fabricated on X-cut proton exchange (PE)-LiNbO3 using ICP. Smooth etched surfaces achieved using Cr as a mask combined with SF6/Ar etching gases; high etch rate of 97.5 nm/min achieved using CHF3/Ar gases. Ridge waveguides with approximately 600 nm depth, smooth surfaces, and nearly vertical sidewalls successfully fabricated.

### Hybrid processes (dry + wet + annealing)

- **Shen et al. 2023 (Sample 7):** RIE dry etching + Al thin-film coverage + reduction annealing (400°C in 10% H2 + Ar) + wet etching produced a perfect 90° sidewall angle and ~115 nm depth, preserving ferroelectric properties — the optimized hybrid process suitable for large-scale LNO domain-wall memory array fabrication. Sample 6 (RIE + high-temp reduction + wet etch): ~112 nm depth, inward concavity sidewall due to Cr-LNO alloying.

### Mask material redeposition issues

- **Aryal et al. 2022:** Ti/Al mask caused redeposition of Al byproducts ("pyramids"/"cones"), prevented by protecting Al with a Cr layer since CrF4 byproducts are more volatile than AlF3.
- **Kozlov et al. 2023:** Cr mask LER (20–30 nm) inherited by etched structures.
- **NIST (Kumar et al.):** Above 300 W RF, line-edge roughness transferred to the WG causing striations; Cr hard mask granular features from Cr polycrystalline grain size ~55 nm.
- **Giuffredi et al. (AFR Milan, "Sidewall roughness AFM analysis of Lithium Niobate"):** Additional roughness parameters like skewness are important to account for sidewall "waviness" caused by hardness differences between mask and LiNbO3 during dry-etch pattern transfer. The developed AFM processing method achieved on-wafer sidewall roughness of RQ ≤ 1 nm with propagation losses of 0.5 dB cm⁻¹ for LiNbO3 waveguides etched by an optimized process. This compares to prior work achieving 0.21 dB cm⁻¹ losses with RQ down to 2 nm.

## (e) Parameter Windows Preserving Optical Quality (Smooth vs Rough Sidewalls, Loss vs Bias/Pressure)

### Propagation loss and Q-factor results

- **Kaufmann et al. 2023:** Four samples etched with 300 W ICP power, 600 V DC bias, 1 mTorr: Q-factor variation below 2%, calculated propagation loss of 1.55 dB/cm, resonance linewidth 25 pm (ring/racetrack resonators, 600 nm top width, 80 µm bend radius, near 1550 nm). Surface roughness (Sq) ~0.08 nm for biases above 200 V, four times better than un-etched surface (0.31 nm) — the Ar process has a "polishing character."
- **Ar ion milling + GCIB (Optics Express 2018):** 0.268 dB/cm (TE, 7 µm waveguide) and 0.33 dB/cm (TE, 5 µm waveguide); AFM RMS ~8.3 nm (Rq) before characterization; claims lowest reported etched ridge waveguide losses at the time.
- **Wu, Wang, Xu, Qi, Chu, Fang, Zhang, Zhou, Qiao, Chai, Lin & Cheng, "Long Low-Loss-Lithium Niobate on Insulator Waveguides with Sub-Nanometer Surface Roughness," Nanomaterials 8(11):910, 2018 (DOI: 10.3390/nano8110910):** Record-low propagation loss of 0.027 dB/cm in LNOI waveguides using Cr hard mask (600 nm) patterned via femtosecond laser ablation followed by chemo-mechanical polishing (CMP); surface roughness Rq = 0.452 nm (AFM). Whispering-gallery microring (160 µm diameter) with intrinsic Q of 1.14 × 10⁷, loaded Q of 5.70 × 10⁶, effective refractive index 1.79 at 1560.48 nm. Continuous 11-cm-long waveguide fabricated (laser ablation 90 min). Method avoids ion beam etching, which inherently leaves residual sidewall roughness. Measured loss still one order of magnitude above theoretical absorption limit (~10⁻³ dB/cm).
- **Chang et al., "Heterogeneous integration of lithium niobate and silicon nitride waveguides" (Optics Letters 42(4), 2017, via Bowers group):** Propagation loss of 0.2 ± 0.4 dB/cm (or 0.3 ± 0.6 dB/cm by Fabry-Perot) for the LN-Si3N4 heterogeneous waveguide; Si3N4 waveguide 0.11 dB/cm.
- **Roughness-Limited Performance in Ultra-Low-Loss Lithium Niobate Cavities (Optica, arXiv:2505.01913):** Quality factors up to 27×10⁶ demonstrated in wide waveguides (2.2λ ≈ 3.5 µm width) where interface roughness dominates, and up to 1.2×10⁷ in narrower waveguides (0.8λ ≈ 1.2 µm) where sidewall roughness is the primary limitation. Intrinsic absorption of TFLN ~0.2 dB/m, corresponding to absorption-limited Q of ~160×10⁶. Sidewall scattering scales as σ² and dominates losses in narrow waveguides. Z+ surface showed significantly higher roughness (σ = 1.4–2.45 nm) than Z− surface (σ = 0.4–0.5 nm), with correlation lengths 40–65 nm. Top interface roughness ~180–220 pm RMS with ~80–100 nm correlation length. PPLN poling experiments showed narrow devices (1.2 µm) experience >30% degradation, while wider devices (2.5 µm) showed <7% degradation due to crystal-axis-dependent etch roughness. Devices fabricated on X-cut (Ar-trimmed, removing 200 nm) and Y-cut (CMP-polished) LNOI wafers.
- **Giuffredi et al.:** On-wafer sidewall roughness RQ ≤ 1 nm with propagation losses of 0.5 dB cm⁻¹ for LiNbO3 waveguides etched by an optimized process; prior work achieved 0.21 dB cm⁻¹ losses with RQ down to 2 nm.
- **Ulliac et al. 2016:** 5 dB/cm overall losses (Ar plasma, 2 mTorr, S1828 resist); superior to previously demonstrated argon etching of photonic wires with 7.5 dB/cm and 9.9 dB/cm for both light polarizations.
- **Latitude Design Systems overview:** Early ion milling produced ~4 dB/cm waveguide losses due to sidewall roughness from redeposition, mask erosion, and low etch selectivity. Optimized EBL + ion milling achieved losses as low as 0.027 dB/cm and Q factors >10⁷. PLACE (CMP) produced ultra-smooth surfaces (<0.5 nm RMS) with record-low 0.027 dB/cm propagation losses and Q factors up to 4.7×10⁷. Mechanical dicing produced sidewall losses as low as 1.2 dB/cm.
- **NIST (Kumar et al.):** Upper-bound propagation loss estimated at ~2 dB/cm (RF 150 W, ICP 1500 W, 5 mTorr, 20 sccm Ar, 5°C).
- **Kozlov et al. 2023:** Numerical simulation (FDFD) determined optimal waveguide cross-section: 1.4 µm width, 0.3 µm etching depth, single-mode at 1.5–1.6 µm, critical bend radius 50 µm, optical losses <0.001 dB/90°.

### Parameter windows that preserve LN optical quality

- **Kaufmann et al. 2023:** Redeposition-free regime at 5–7 mTorr for 600 V DC bias (preferred), ~11 mTorr for 400 V; DC bias above ~1 kV trends toward redeposition-free (not readily achievable); Sq ~0.08 nm for biases above 200 V. Trade-off: redeposition vanishes after 7 mTorr but with significant structural damage.
- **NIST (Kumar et al.):** Optimal RF power range 100–200 W (Ar, 1500 W ICP, 5 mTorr); low RF (~50 W) → sidewalls enveloped by redeposit; 300 W → redeposit eliminated but striations and WG damage above 300 W.
- **Kozlov et al. 2023:** Ion energy ~90 eV (recipe #13, bias 186 V, 0.03 mbar) produces smooth surfaces; ~30 eV (recipe #14, 141 V, 0.007 mbar) leaves LiF and rough surfaces. Transition 30–90 eV.
- **Hu et al. 2006:** CHF3/Ar at 6 mTorr, 130 V dc bias, no cooling: 82° wall angle, negligible underetching, 5.76 µm/h — "dramatically improved over literature values of ~0.6 µm/h for PE-LN."
- **Huang et al. 2026:** Cl2/H2/Ar = 10/20/50 sccm, 600 W ICP, 120 W RF, 10 mTorr: 79.1° sidewall, ~32 nm/min, selectivity 1.43:1 vs SiO2. Finite element simulations showed sloped sidewalls scatter acoustic waves, causing mode conversion, reduced resonant displacement amplitude, and degraded Q factor with spurious modes.

### Surface morphology, stoichiometry, and crystal-orientation effects

- **Randles, Tanaka & Esashi, "Etch Rate Dependence on Crystal Orientation for Lithium Niobate," 2007 IEEE Ultrasonics Symposium:** 30 mm diameter LiNbO3 spheres etched in HF and 1:2 HF:HNO3. Maximum etch rate on the −Z face (0001) plane; etching showed three-fold symmetry about the Z axis. Crystal planes in the (2203) family showed the lowest etch rate in the −Z hemisphere; this plane is close to (1102), which is parallel to layers of Nb, Li, and O atoms. The etch rate on the +Z face is less than 0.1% of the etch rate on the −Z face.
- **Shen et al. 2023 (Sample 4):** SiO2 mask + high-temp reduction + SC-1 wet etch: asymmetric sidewalls (44° in +Z, 85° in −Z directions).
- **Kaufmann et al. 2023:** Sidewall angle 60–63° for both +Z and −Z crystal faces in Ar ICP etching.
- **Ren Congxin et al., "Reactive ion beam etching characteristics of LiNbO3," Nucl. Instr. Meth. B 19–20:1018–1021, 1987:** Examined etch rate dependence on ion beam energy, beam current density, and gas flow rate during RIBE with CF4 and CHF3; discussed causes of surface roughening; reported changes in relative dark conductivity of LiNbO3 surfaces etched by different ions. RIBE can be successfully applied to etching surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices.
- **KTH thesis (Mohamedelhassan 2012):** Ridge waveguides fabricated on both −Z and +Z faces of undoped and MgO-doped congruent LiNbO3; etching depths ~500 nm on undoped, ~300 nm on MgO-doped. PELN ridge waveguides achieve lateral index step ~1.2 (air-LN) vs only ~0.12 for embedded PELN channels.
- **Latitude Design Systems:** LNOI wafer fabrication via crystal ion slicing produces sub-micrometer films with surface roughness below 0.5 nm in both Z-cut and X-cut orientations.

### Chamber contamination / shared-cleanroom issues

- **Kaufmann et al. 2023:** Only Cl2, SF6, O2, and Ar gases were used, as CHF3 was found to contaminate the chamber and harm reproducibility. Redeposition-free etching requires a very sensitive, well-maintained system — challenging in research environments with mixed use.
- **Awan 2025:** Shared academic cleanrooms typically maintain two dedicated etch chambers — one for fluorine-based chemistries (silicon materials) and one for chlorine-based chemistries (III-V semiconductors, metals). Some materials (metals, lithium compounds) are difficult to remove and require prohibitions on metal masks in silicon chambers. In single-chamber facilities, time-sharing between chemistries (e.g., monthly rotations) with extensive oxygen cleans between is recommended. Severe contamination may require manual wet cleaning with acetone/IPA.

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### (a) Physical and Ion-Based Etching Methods (IBE, Ion Milling, FIB, RIBE) and Known Damage Profiles in Lithium Niobate

**Ion Beam Etching (IBE) / Ion Milling for Lithium Niobate**

- AARD Technology (a supplier of ion beam equipment) states that materials like lithium niobate (LN, LiNbO₃) are difficult to etch with common ICP-RIE technologies, so they offer ion beam etching (IBE) as a solution for both R&D and manufacturing. Their stated capabilities for LN waveguides include: physical etching of all materials, optional F- and Cl-based reactive gases for tuning etch selectivities, vertical or slanted smooth sidewalls, excellent uniformity (<1%), in-situ sidewall redeposition/fencing removal, SIMS or OES end point detection, tiltable and rotatable substrate, He backside contact cooling with water (plus chiller option for lower temperatures), and capability for reactive ion beam etching (RIBE) by adding F- and Cl-gases to the Ar mixture. Their SCIA Mill equipment is offered for this application. The page notes that waveguides for PIC applications require vertical, smooth sidewalls for proper optoelectronic properties. [1] (aardtechnology.com/photonics-ion-beam-solutions)

- A NineScrolls engineering comparison guide provides general characteristics of ion beam milling (IBE): it is purely physical sputtering (typically Ar⁺, 300–1000 eV), works on any material, but has low rates (10–100 nm/min), poor selectivity (~1:1 to 3:1), and redeposition risk. Ion beam milling is highly anisotropic (collimated beam, tunable 0°–70°+ via a tiltable stage), often delivering higher anisotropy than RIE since it has no isotropic chemical component. RIBE (Reactive Ion Beam Etching) bridges the gap, combining RIE's chemical selectivity with IBE's directional beam control for damage-sensitive materials; RIBE etch rates are 100–500 nm/min, aspect ratios ≤5:1, and selectivity is moderate-tunable. Surface damage from ion milling can be mitigated by reducing beam energy to 300–500 eV and post-etch annealing; an example given: reducing GaN HEMT beam energy from 800 to 400 eV recovered channel mobility to >95% of pristine value. Redeposition in ion milling can be reduced by rotating the sample stage and using 30°–60° oblique incidence; 45° Ar⁺ with rotation reduced MRAM MTJ short-circuit defects by ~80%. [2] (ninescrolls.com/insights/reactive-ion-etching-vs-ion-milling)

- The ETH Zurich group (Kaufmann et al., Nanophotonics 2023) reported on redeposition-free ICP etching of lithium niobate and explicitly discussed ion beam etching (IBE) experiments at incidence angles 0°–35° simulating trapezoidal masks (85°, 70°, 60°, 50°), showing reduced redeposition with increasing angle, confirming that trapezoidal masks help achieve redeposition-free etching. [3] (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321)

**Argon Ion Milling + Gas Cluster Ion Beam (GCIB) Smoothening**

- Siew et al. (Optics Express, 26(4):4421-4430, 19 February 2018, DOI: 10.1364/OE.26.004421, PMID: 29475292) titled "Ultra-low loss ridge waveguides on lithium niobate via argon ion milling and gas clustered ion beam smoothening" fabricated significantly smoother ridge waveguides using argon ion milling followed by gas clustered ion beam (GCIB) smoothening, achieving propagation losses as low as 0.3 dB/cm at 1.55 µm. The paper notes that "sidewalls of etched waveguides are typically rough in most etching procedures, exacerbating propagation losses." Authors: Shawn Yohanes Siew, Eric Jun Hao Cheung, Haidong Liang, Andrew Bettiol, Noriaki Toyoda, Bandar Alshehri, Elhadj Dogheche, Aaron J Danner. [4] (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29475292)

**Focused Ion Beam (FIB) Milling Damage Profiles**

- FIB milling is known to produce lattice damage. A paper on "Damage in III-V Compounds during Focused Ion Beam Milling" (PubMed PMID: 17481325) reports that "The damage on the side walls of the milled trenches is in the form of amorphous layers associated with direct amorphization from the gallium beam." [5] (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17481325; researchgate.net/publication/6349892)

- A paper "Raman characterization of focused ion beam fabricated lithium niobate film" (Journal of Applied Physics, 135(3), 033101) states: "It has been widely reported that the presence of lattice defects caused by FIB milling can significantly degrade the optical performance of" lithium niobate. [6] (pubs.aip.org/aip/jap/article/135/3/033101/3000637)

- Jin et al. (Chinese Optics Letters, Vol. 20, Issue 11, page 113602, 2022, DOI: 10.3788/COL202220.113602) "Fabrication of lithium niobate metasurfaces via a combination of FIB and ICP-RIE" describe that FIB-only milling of LN "produces round-topped nanostructures with crystal lattice damage requiring hydrofluoric acid treatment that causes lateral etching of the SiO2 bonding layer." Their combined process used Ga+ ion beam at 80 pA current and 30 kV acceleration voltage to mill both Cr (40 nm conducting layer) and LN layers, then ICP-RIE with SF6/Ar using the patterned Cr as hard mask, followed by SC-1 solution (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O = 1:1:5) for 5 min at 80°C to remove lithium fluoride (LiF) byproduct, and Cr removal with standard Cr etchant. Results: ridges with trapezoidal cross-sections, sidewall angles larger than 80° (specifically ~82° for a grating with period Pd = 400 nm, top width 211 nm, bottom width 275 nm, duty cycle 62.5%), metasurface array footprint 20 µm × 20 µm. Sharp quasi-bound states in the continuum (QBIC) were observed matching COMSOL simulations. [7] (researching.cn/articles/OJ8c8a1b62c7c6c8d2)

- General FIB damage layer thickness data from the "Practical Electron Microscopy and Database" (Globalsino): 30 kV FIB ≈ 23 nm damaged layer thickness, 5 kV FIB ≈ 6.5 nm, 1 kV Argon ≈ 1.6 nm. A 2 kV Si amorphous layer remains 3 nm thick even at very low beam energy. Amorphous thickness is independent of beam current over the 100–500 pA range. High-energy beams (e.g., 30 kV) create near-surface defect layers extending more than 100 nm deep. Two mechanisms cause amorphization: (i) sufficient atom displacement within the collision cascade leading to loss of long-range order when point defect density reaches a critical value at the surface, and (ii) local melting and quenching of solid in the sample. The amorphization layer on the top of specimens is thicker than on the side-walls. Argon milling can be used to remove FIB-induced damage. [8] (globalsino.com/EM/page4493.html)

- A Covalent educational video (YouTube, 25 April 2022) on FIB lamella defects notes: a 30 kV gallium ion beam creates an amorphous damaged layer approximately 20 nanometers thick; dropping FIB energy to 5 kV (polishing) reduces the damaged layer to about 6 nm thick; dropping to 2 kV reduces damage to roughly 3 nm thick. "The damaged layer correlates nearly 1:1 with the FIB energy used." Redeposition also occurs due to beam tails/sides milling surrounding material. [9] (youtube.com/watch?v=_pKw8SMnFiM)

- Tong and Luo (Strathclyde, "Investigation of focused ion beam induced damage in single crystal diamond tools," published in Applied Surface Science 2015) showed FIB-induced damage layer thicknesses increased from 11.5 nm (8 kV) to 19.4 nm (16 kV) to 27.6 nm (30 kV), increasing with beam energy; damage layers are amorphous carbon accommodating significant implanted gallium; maximum gallium implantation depths were 10.5 nm (8 keV) and 12.8 nm (16 keV). (This is for diamond, provided as general FIB damage scaling reference.) [10] (strathprints.strath.ac.uk/53356/1/Tong_Luo_ASS_2015)
